b: LemmaLoom is a macOS application for qualitative and grammar analysis of text. You can use it to code passages in documents and interrogate those codes against the document's grammar. You can, of course, use LemmaLoom just as a coding tool, or just as a grammar analysis tool as well. The mixing of qualitative and grammar analysis, however, will allow you to ask questions about your documents that might otherwise be more difficult to ask with qualitative data analysis tools that are not grammar-aware. LemmaLoom includes an example project called “Climate Debate” that you can import to explore the different tools and features available in the application. Much of the user guide, and the entirety of this Quick Start chapter, uses the “Climate Debate” project as a contextual theme for examples and explanations. The “Climate Debate” project is composed of fictional op-eds, columns, a speech, and other media, such as a report and a recorded radio debate. Any resemblance to real persons or publications is coincidental, and the content, being fictional, is not representative of any opinions or meant in any way as persuasive material. In this chapter you build the beginnings of “Climate Debate” from scratch. You begin from eleven invented texts of various kinds (op-eds, a speech, blog posts, and columns). Of these, six are written by climate activists, and five are written by climate skeptics. The figures throughout this guide show the finished project. Follow along with this guide by importing the example project via File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. When imported, the language of the example project will depend on which interface language you are using in LemmaLoom. This could be English, German, or Mainland Simplified Chinese. Refer to Supported languages in . In the example project, the attribute, sets, and codes from the first few steps are already created. Therefore, when working with the example project, skip to Read with a lens. Skip Create codes when you reach it. In this guide, you may opt to import your own set of texts instead. The details on what kind of files you can import are covered in . Substitute your own materials if desired whenever the instructions mention specific documents, stances, or passages in “Climate Debate”.

When you first launch LemmaLoom, there will be one window displayed with three columns. You may read all about the interface in A tour of the main window in . Currently, your navigation sidebar on the left is empty, while your inspector tab icons on the right are disabled. Your middle column displays the title LemmaLoom with the buttons New Project and Example Project. Here it is with a project loaded and a document open: “Running Out of Time” in the reader, its statistics in the Text tab of the inspector Projects appear in the navigation sidebar on the left.  describes project structure in more detail. Under Project in the navigation sidebar, you can find ten detail views of the overall project, such as Codebook, Code Matrix, and Queries. Further down in the navigation sidebar come sets, documents, and tags (see ). You may search the active project for documents via Edit ▸ Find Document (⇧⌘F); alternatively, you can type the name of a document you are looking for directly into Search Documents at the top of the navigation sidebar. Documents and detail views are opened in tabs inside the reader in the middle of the window. Across the top of the reader lies the title band containing the lens menu, as well as functions for searching and manipulating text, and for changing how the text and reader look.  details these various options and functions. The inspector on the right displays information on the document in the active tab. The inspector is divided into four tabs (Text, Grammar, Coding, and Multimode) accessible via buttons at the top right corner of the inspector. , , , and  provide descriptions of what these four tabs display. A button will be disabled either because it isn't relevant to the active document or tab, or because it is not available for use yet (lenses require the document's indexing process to finish first, for example). Hovering the mouse pointer over any disabled button provides the reason for it being disabled, such as Lenses become available when indexing completes.

Everything for one study goes into a project. A project is the topmost container in LemmaLoom. It holds the documents and the data you compile as you work on them. That data includes codes, memos, bookmarks, sets, and queries. Generally, you want to keep all relevant material for a study in a single project. LemmaLoom has limited capabilities for cross-project analysis, though queries can be performed across projects. Working across projects in  explains how such queries work. Attributes store factual information about your documents. An attribute could be, for example, the stance an author holds, the publishing date, where you found it, etc. You can define attributes when first creating a project or at any other time after. More details about how to work with attributes can be found in Attributes in . For following along in the “Climate Debate” project, all you need is the “Stance” attribute, for comparing activists with skeptics later in this chapter. Choose File ▸ New Project (⇧⌘N). In Name, type Climate Debate. Under Attributes, click Add Attribute. In the new row, type Stance in the name field. In the menu beside it, choose Picker. A picker accepts only the values you list. That keeps the spelling of each value the same from one document to the next. In the field that appears, type Activist, Skeptic, Neutral. “Neutral” is for documents that report on the debate without taking a side. Click Create. Setting up “Climate Debate” with the attribute “Stance” and its three choices Your new project will appear in Projects in the navigation sidebar with its title in bold face. Titles in bold indicate the active project; everything below the list of projects in the navigation sidebar is only relevant to the active project.

Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I). Select the eleven texts. To select several files, hold down ⌘ as you click. Click Open. The Import Document dialog opens for the first file, with 1 of 11 at its top right. Check the Name (LemmaLoom takes it from the file name), and leave the other fields as they are. Click Import. The dialog opens again for each of the remaining files. Click Import each time, or Skip to leave a file out. The Import Document dialog for “A Mayor's Promise”, the first of the eleven texts, with 1 of 11 at its top right LemmaLoom lists the texts under Documents and starts indexing them in the background. Indexing first splits each text into sentences and words. Then each word gets its dictionary form; this form is called its lemma. It also works which noun is the object of which verb and every other way the words of a sentence depend on one another.  describes indexing in more detail. All documents in “Climate Debate” have been pre-indexed for your convenience. Large documents or media files may take longer to fully index. The hardware capabilities of your computer also play a role in how quickly documents are indexed. LemmaLoom uses hardware acceleration where it is available. If a document is being indexed, the title will have a gray coloration, along with a small progress ring to the right of it. When the ring disappears, the document has been successfully indexed. If you wish to view all documents currently being indexed, choose Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0). The Import Document dialog allows you to designate dates, groups, tags, and languages for each document, as outlined in The Import Document dialog in . That chapter also explains how to import PDFs, web pages, and audio and video recordings.

“Stance” could also have been specified per-document on the Import Document dialog. With eleven documents, specifying the value using the Attributes window requires significantly less effort than doing it individually. The Attributes window allows setting values in bulk. Right-click “Climate Debate” under Projects and choose Attributes, or choose Project ▸ Attributes. The window lists every document in the project. Select the checkboxes beside the six activist texts (“Running Out of Time”, “Letter from the Climate Strike”, “Why We Block the Roads”, “Farmers Are Not the Enemy”, “A Mayor's Promise”, and “Hope Takes Work”). The row with Search now shows 6 documents selected. Beside it, choose Set Value ▸ Stance. In the Set Value dialog, choose “Activist” and click Apply. Deselect the activists' checkboxes, then select those of the five skeptic texts (“The Models Keep Missing”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, “Let's Not Panic”, “Who Pays for the Transition”, and “Science Is Never Settled”). Choose Set Value ▸ Stance again, choose “Skeptic”, and click Apply. Close the Attributes window. The Attributes window for “Climate Debate” with the six activist texts checked and Set Value open on “Stance” Alternatively, the active document's values may be updated using Details on the Text tab in the inspector. This will modify one document at a time. In the Attributes window, performing a search will restrict which rows get affected by the Set Value action. See Setting one value for many documents in  for further information.

The keyword list later in this chapter allows you to compare the contents of activist documents versus skeptic documents. This means each party has to have their own set, a collection of documents under a name. Under Documents, click “Running Out of Time”, then hold down ⌘ and click each of the other five activist texts. Right-click one of the selected documents and choose Add to Set ▸ New Set from Documents. The new set appears under Sets with its name ready for editing. Type Activists and press Return. Select the five skeptic texts the same way and make a set called Skeptics. The shortcut menu over six selected texts under Documents, with Add to Set open and New Set from Documents at its end “Wide Reach” in the example project contains all documents where “Readership” is greater than or equal to 100,000 people. This set is determined by a rule and is called a smart set. See Smart sets in .

Clicking “Running Out of Time” in Documents will open it for viewing. The example project has stored it inside the group “Print”. On the left margin of the reader, there are two columns numbering the paragraphs and sentences of your document. Along the right edge of the reader is the document overview, which is a colored scroll bar indicating the current location within your document and its composition in relation to the active lenses (codes, for example). Hovering the mouse pointer over the document overview will also give you a preview of the text at that specific location. The appearance of content inside the reader is controlled by lenses. Each lens styles text according to a characteristic property of it. More information on this topic is provided in , where all available lenses and their annotations are described in depth. When you initially view a document, Codes and Bookmarks lenses are already turned on; hence, the lens menu reads 2 Lenses. Those two lenses draw your existing annotations onto the text. To activate a lens based on grammar analysis, for instance, follow the instructions below: Click 2 Lenses in the title band. Choose Modality. The Modality lens on “Running Out of Time”, with its legend above the text Modality annotates words that talk about ability, necessity, obligation, possibility, and volition. For instance, in “Running Out of Time”, might in “nothing we might spend on prevention” is annotated with Possibility, while can in “No one can say exactly where each threshold lies” is annotated with Ability. Above the text sits a row of colored aspect lenslets that represent the legend of the lens. By clicking any one of the lenslets, you disable the selected aspect and remove its annotations from the document. Another click restores both the aspect and its annotations in the document. To the right of the lens menu is a button whose tooltip says Show only the sentences a lens annotates. By clicking this button, you shrink the document to show sentences that contain annotations made by active lenses only; click again to expand the document fully.

You give passages about some topic or aspect a code that you define yourself (“Urgency”, for example). All of a project's codes together make up its codebook. You can think of your codebook as a collection of adjectives or ideas you use to describe or highlight details in your project. Your codes can then be used to help you answer questions you might have about the documents in your project. Usually, you will start with some questions you want to ask about your documents, and from there create the codes that you think would help you answer those questions. The following procedure adds a code called “Urgency” and its subcode, “Deadlines”. Under Project in the navigation sidebar, click Codebook. It opens in a tab. Click Add Code at the bottom of the code list. In the New Code dialog, type Urgency in Name. Under Color, click a color. Click Save. Right-click “Urgency” in the list and choose Add Subcode. In the New Code dialog, type Deadlines in Name, choose a color, and click Save. The New Code dialog over the Codebook of “Climate Debate”, with “Urgency” typed in Name The shortcut menu on “Urgency” in the Codebook, with Add Subcode at its top Subcodes enable the creation of hierarchies between related codes. This may be helpful if your study has many similar codes that you want to be logically grouped together.

Click the tab of “Running Out of Time”. Select a passage, for example, “A deadline that falls after everyone in office has retired is not a deadline at all.” In the bar that appears at the bottom of the reader, click Code. In the list of codes, click “Deadlines”. Picking a code for a sentence of “Running Out of Time” from the bar at the bottom of the reader Your passage has been given the color of “Deadlines”. In addition, a bar of the same color appears to the left of the passage. You can still continue browsing the codes available from the list that is currently open, apply a second code to the passage, or hit the Escape key to close the code list. If the codebook contains many codes, you may simply enter the start of a code's name to locate the one you want. In the event you enter a name no existing code matches, the list provides an option labeled Add Code “…”, which allows you to create and apply the code simultaneously. Clicking the number adjacent to the paragraph selects everything contained within the paragraph itself without having to manually select the text. Document ▸ Code (⇧⌘C) invokes the very same list of codes. Edit ▸ Undo Apply Code (⌘Z) revokes the most recent application of a code made to any passage. To remove a code later, select the passage again, after which you'll notice there is a check mark in the list beside codes already assigned; unchecking one removes that code. You should code a few more passages per text, because the upcoming examples require codings to count and visualize. Coding provides additional context regarding how memos, links, and bookmarks work. That chapter also covers auto code for coding several passages at once.

The Code Matrix is in tabular form. It contains columns for every document, and rows for each code you've made and used. Each individual cell within the matrix gives the total number of passages carrying its row's code within its column's document. Grouping the Code Matrix by an attribute will turn that matrix into a comparison between groups of documents. Under Project, click Code Matrix. In the menu showing Documents, choose Attribute. In the menu that appears beside it, choose “Stance”. In the row of buttons below, click Documents. In the switch beside it, click %. Each code's share of the activist, skeptic, and neutral documents in “Climate Debate”, with the Code Matrix grouped by “Stance” With % chosen, each cell represents the percent of a particular group's documents where a code occurs at least once in those documents. Selecting a code within the table displays those same values for each group as a bar chart above the table. The “Climate Debate” project has the “Uncertainty” code occur in only one of the six activist texts; thus, the activists' cell has 16.7%. Of the five skeptic texts, four contain at least one passage with the “Uncertainty” code; hence, the skeptics' cell has 80.0%. Additionally, note that the table for the “Climate Debate” example project has a “Neutral” column since there are documents representing a neutral stance on climate change included in it. These documents consist of the heat wave report, the news article, and the radio debate. Codings represents the number of coded passages while Coverage represents the measure in characters of how much of the text is annotated with a code. Whichever metric you choose, the last columns of the table test the groups against each other, with each test assessing whether or not chance alone could explain the difference between the groups in the share of documents containing each code. The current project includes eleven documents divided into two groups, “Activist” and “Skeptic”. With two groups in the comparison, the table tests them against each other using Fisher's exact test with a reported p-value (p (Fisher)). The “Climate Debate” example project, however, has three groups. Hence, the table applies the chi-square test to test the differences and provides a statistic (χ² (df = 2)) and the associated probability (p). Consider the case where stance makes absolutely no difference. Then, the p-value for a code indicates the probability of finding the observed difference, or a larger one, purely by chance alone, i.e., without any real differences in stance. When the p-value is less than 0.05, then chance alone produces that difference fewer than once in twenty trials. Accordingly, the results with significance are printed with darker colors and an asterisk () next to their corresponding p-values. With the Significant Only option active, the table retains only the codes with significant differences. The strength of these differences is measured using the Cramér's V metric from 0 to 1 (no difference to maximum difference). Consider the darker test values as justification for reviewing the corresponding passages more carefully. Code Stats lives directly above Code Matrix within the sidebar. Each row in the table is a unique code you have used; it shows how many passages and documents, and what percentage of total characters, are covered by each code.  discusses both views further, with an example of the tests.

A word sketch demonstrates what other words a particular word combines with grammatically. Those words are classified based on relations. Relation refers to the grammatical connection between the two words. All relations are described in . The verbs that take a certain word as their object comprise one relation type, for instance. Adjectives describing that word constitute another relation type. Under Project, click Word Sketch. In the Word field, type climate and press Return. If another mode is chosen, click Grammar in the bar at the top of the tab. The partners of climate across “Climate Debate”, drawn as a map In the map, climate occupies the central position, while its partners are positioned according to their relations. Each color represents one type of relation. Change lies under Subject of because in “the climate is changing”, climate is its subject. Crisis is one of the words listed under In compounds with, as in “the climate crisis”. In a relation, the size of the font representing a partner increases with the strength of the partnership. The measure used in assessing the strength of the partnerships is known as the logDice score, whose calculations are covered in logDice. The logDice score signifies how much of the two words' use is accounted for by their occurrences as a pair. Consider the score to be a mathematical expression of collocations. The logDice score ranges up to 14, the maximum for words that co-occur exclusively. Each point below 14 halves that share. Hover the mouse pointer over any partner to view the logDice score beside f; here, f stands for frequency. This value signifies how many times the two words were seen together. You may activate a sketch for any partner, including crisis, by clicking the word. To return to climate, click on it in the line above the sketch or press ⌘[. To see the sentences behind a particular partner, click List above the sketch and subsequently select a row with your chosen partner. LemmaLoom navigates you directly to the first sentence linking both words in question. Click the Word Sketch tab to return, then click the same row again to continue looking at other sentences involving both.

Certain words tend to appear significantly more frequently within a set compared to another. Other words will appear significantly less frequently. A keyword list will highlight the difference between the frequencies of occurrence in both directions. Compare the keywords of “Activists” against “Skeptics”. Click “Activists” under Sets in the navigation sidebar. The set opens in a tab. In the row of buttons at the top of the tab, click Queries. In a narrow window the row is a menu. Choose Queries from it. In the column on the left, under Recipes, click Keywords. The query builder is to the right of the column. It is made of boxes called conditions.  describes both. In the Show condition, set the menu showing Rest of Project to Set. In the menu that appears below it, choose “Skeptics”. Keywords of “Activists” against “Skeptics” Leave the menu showing Lemma unchanged, so that cost and costs become cost. Leave the menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 unchanged. The abbreviation LL stands for the Log-Likelihood score. By chance alone, a score greater than or equal to 3.84 occurs only about once out of every twenty trials. Any word with a lower score is omitted from the result list. The result will display underneath the builder, and is updated as you alter the parameters. On a larger project, run the query manually by clicking on the triangle icon above the builder, or pressing ⌘R. Positive Keywords lists words used more frequently by the activists compared to the skeptics. Negative Keywords lists those used less frequently by them. In this comparison, “Activists” serves as the target, while “Skeptics” serves as the reference. The line above the tables tells you how many total words were considered in each set, respectively labeled Target Words and Reference Words. In the table, a word's count in the “Activists” set appears in Count, whereas the same in the “Skeptics” set appears in Reference. Both lists are ranked according to Log-Likelihood. Near the top of either list are words whose differences are least likely to be due purely to chance. Log Ratio indicates the degree of difference taking into consideration the overall sizes of the two sets. The value 1 indicates usage twice as often, 2 indicates four times, 3 eight times, and so forth, doubling with each further step. For negative keywords, the ratio falls below zero, indicating usage half as often at −1. Keywords in  calculates both scores step by step. Keyword lists reveal to you distinctive words; however, they tell you nothing about why they stand out. Analyze the contexts surrounding the listed words in passages. To save the keyword query: In the bar above the builder, click the button with a square and an arrow pointing into it. Its tooltip reads Save. Choose Save. In the Save Query dialog, replace the text in Name with Keywords: Activists. Leave Available In at Set. Click Save. The Save Query dialog for the keywords of “Activists”, with the name “Keywords: Activists” and Available In at Set The saved query will appear under Set at the top of the left column whenever you access the queries in the “Activists” set. Clicking on this item restores the keyword list that you saw earlier. In the example project, there is already a saved query here.

Keyword lists may be exported as comma-separated values (.csv) files for use with spreadsheet applications. In the bar above the results, click the export button, a square with an arrow pointing up. Its tooltip reads Export. Choose CSV. Choose a folder and click Save. The Export menu above the keyword results of “Activists” Each line contains a keyword paired alongside its counts, scores, and whether it was marked positive or negative. The format here is Comma-Separated Values (CSV), a simple text-based spreadsheet format which many applications including spreadsheets and statistical software packages support. The other items under Export in this same menu export results as images (PNG and PDF), Markdown files (Markdown format combines the results file with metadata regarding the query used), or copy the result to your clipboard (Copy). Most table and graph displays offer an export option, just as this one does. Exporting tables and charts in  provides greater detail on what each export menu does, along with where it appears. To review concordances for any particular keyword, click Concordance below Recipes in the left column. The concordance feature allows you to explore each instance of the word along with its immediate context within the surrounding text. This topic is discussed further in Concordance in ; Recipes in  explains how to choose the word.

Help ▸ Glossary opens a glossary window with short explanations for LemmaLoom terminology. You may leave it up while working with your documents for quick referencing of any abbreviations or technical terms you might not know. LemmaLoom is a qualitative data analysis application that is also grammar-aware. You can code passages just like you would in any other QDA-style application, but with LemmaLoom, you can interrogate those codings against the grammar used throughout the document. Say you coded passages for implying “Uncertainty”; you could then query the document for certain grammatical patterns that occur within those codings, like uses of hedging and modal verbs.

LemmaLoom can work with any kind of text. Whether you have essays, opinion pieces, news articles, surveys, interviews, or works of literature, LemmaLoom can consume them. There are only certain formats that are supported though. Plain text files, PDFs, web articles (via URL), audio, and video recordings are supported for import. Audio and video recordings are also transcribed into text using speech to text models; additionally, a diarization model will automatically code the unique speakers in the transcribed text for you.

There are three columns in the main window. A tour of the main window in  takes an in-depth look at each element of the window. The op-ed “Running Out of Time” open in the reader, with the navigation sidebar to its left and the inspector's Coding tab to its right. The navigation sidebar, which appears on the left side of LemmaLoom, displays all your projects. Within the navigation sidebar is the active project's project shelf under Project, where all ten sections are found, Codebook, Code Matrix, and Queries being among them. Each section opens as a detail view in a tab of the reader. Below the shelf are the project's sets, groups, documents, and tags of those documents. The reader takes up the center of the main window. Each document and detail view gets its own dedicated tab. In the title band across the top of the reader you will find the lens menu and the buttons for searching text and changing its font and text size. At the right side of the title band is Edit, which switches the reader to editing mode. Upon selecting text within the reader, the selection bar pops up at the bottom of the reader. This is where you can click Bookmark, Code, Memo, and Link; if your project uses a dictionary, this is where you find Add to Dictionary. On the right side of LemmaLoom is the inspector, containing everything concerning the document in the active tab. Its four tabs include Text, Grammar, Coding, and Multimode, which contains Sketch Space and a query builder for the document. Tabs may also be accessed via View ▸ Inspector (⌥⌘1 to ⌥⌘4). Each tab is divided into several parts, called facets, with the button row atop the tab changing what facet you're viewing.
Should there be any terms in this chapter you are unfamiliar with, jump to the Key terms section to learn them.

Coding consists of attaching labels called codes to any passages where text relating to your code appears. A code can be thematic, emotional, technical, a question, anything you want it to be. Usually, codes are designed to help you answer specific questions about your source material, so start with your questions and try to identify what aspects of the text might help you answer those questions in a qualitative or quantitative manner. In the bundled example project “Climate Debate”, there are codes called “Urgency”, “Science”, and “Emotions”; you can see how these codes are applied throughout the documents in the project, and how they help answer questions about how the documents present climate information differently. Usually, you set up your codes from the project's Codebook (click Codebook under Project in the navigation sidebar) and apply them as you read through your texts, though codes can also be created as you go about reading, or in vivo. To code a passage, select the passage in the reader and click Code in the selection bar at the bottom. You can pick a code from your codebook, or create a new code as aforementioned. Coding a selected passage in “Running Out of Time” with the list from the Code button in the selection bar. Memos, links, and bookmarks are similar to codes and are applied the same way, but each serves different purposes. Codes and coding later in this chapter describes each of them and when you would choose one over the other. LemmaLoom can also auto-code passages for you (Auto Code…) using some of the other tools described later in this guide; tools such as dictionaries, queries, and analyzers can all be used to help automate the process of coding certain patterns in your texts. Projects and sets contain three coding table reports. Code Stats gives you a breakdown on how many times each code occurred; Code Matrix provides an interactive cross-reference of codes against either documents or particular values of an attribute; Relations gives an interactive view of codes found together within the same text passages. If you go into the inspector's Coding tab for any document, you will find similar information but specifically for the active document, plus a Portrait, which displays where in the text each code falls. Any software supporting the REFI-QDA standard for exchanging qualitative data analysis projects can exchange them with LemmaLoom. To import such a project into LemmaLoom, select File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Project; to export a project from LemmaLoom to another application, select File ▸ Export ▸ REFI-QDA Project. A codebook alone can be exchanged similarly via REFI-QDA Codebook in the same two menus. Moving an entire project to another Mac entails exporting the project through File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project; everything will come along with it, including indexing and media files. To restore an exported project archive on another Mac, use File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive.  has the details of both kinds of exchange.

LemmaLoom indexes documents that are in English, German, or Chinese when you import them. Indexing is when LemmaLoom identifies the dictionary form and part of speech of every word in your text, identifies how words function within a sentence, and how a word relates to other words in the same sentence. This information is “indexed” within a database to power the rest of LemmaLoom's grammar tooling and features like Queries and Analyzers. By default, LemmaLoom provides some built-in analysis of indexed data that you can visualize via lenses or the grammar inspector (, ); some of these are findings of cohesion, metadiscourse, and rhetoric (Analysis tools later in this chapter explains these terms). Within the reader, lenses style your text to help you identify and visualize where an aspect of a lens exists in your document. An example would be the Word class lens, which color codes every word in your document by the class it belongs to (part of speech). There are a number of built-in lenses you can apply to help you find certain grammatical patterns, forms, or functions in your text. You can also develop your own lenses using queries and analyzers (, ). Another place that helps you extract grammatical information from your text is the inspector (the right-hand panel next to the reader). The various tabs in the inspector perform different kinds of analysis on your document to help you understand its contents and what that content is doing, grammatically. A word sketch takes one word and sorts all the words it occurs with according to grammatical relation. Examples of this are verbs whose subjects are climate and adjectives modifying summer. A query is a measurable question about your document. You can build a query to find specific words, phrases, patterns, how these things interact with your codings, or general statistics about your text. A query can cover a single document, a set of documents, or the entire project. Queries can even perform some analysis across projects, though this capability is more limited. The type of question you are asking will determine how the result of your question is formatted. For example, if your query was just to “find all phrases where a modal verb is used”, you would receive a list of all those phrases, but if your query was “count all phrases where a modal verb is used”, then you would just receive a numerical value as the output. The different types of outputs determine what you can do with the result in LemmaLoom (see  and ). One sentence from “Running Out of Time” in the Structure facet of the Grammar tab, its words linked by dependency and grouped into phrases.

Codes, attributes, and grammar analysis all live within a single project. One question or query can ask anything of those aspects in your project. Take the Code Matrix of “Climate Debate” with its columns grouped by the attribute “Stance” as an example; it shows how often each code was applied in the activists' texts, the skeptics' texts, and the neutral sources. Here you can combine the use of codings and attributes to visualize how different codes are applied in reference to another aspect, like the value of an attribute. A query can count the terms of a dictionary matched in your corpus and compare how often those matches occur in relation to some other filter, like an attribute. An example from the “Climate Debate” project would be a query that takes the “Hedges” dictionary to see how often matches occur per 10,000 words for documents attributed as “Activist” or “Skeptic”. This type of query would produce a rate. In this example, the rate is the count of hedges found divided by the total number of words multiplied by 10,000. Six hedges in a 600-word column (round numbers, invented for illustration) would then produce $6 / 600 times 10{,}000$, or 100 hedges per 10,000 words. There are a number of recipes in the project level query builder that act as starting places for different types of queries and results. Sketch Space is a visual tool to help you understand the distribution of grammatical partners across other aspects of your documents, like codes or attributes. For example, you can compare which verbs take climate as their subject in activist attributed documents as well as skeptic attributed documents. This will help you visualize whether certain groups of documents differ in how often something happens in them. You can see how large that difference is by showing a query as Compare. The Code Matrix grouped by the attribute “Stance”, with codings counted for the activist, skeptic, and neutral texts. A query result that outputs passages from documents allows you to see where those passages came from. You can navigate directly to those passages.  covers how to interpret query results in full.

The Glossary at Help ▸ Glossary contains definitions of most of the terms below. It also contains definitions for grammatical labels used in LemmaLoom, including part-of-speech tags and dependency relations. Type your search into the Glossary's Search field or choose from the list of categories to browse in the sidebar. You can keep it open beside your work. The Glossary from the Help menu, open on the Concepts category.

Each project holds one study in LemmaLoom, that is, its documents and everything that goes with analyzing them. All the codings, codes, memos, sets, attributes, saved queries, and dictionaries that you create belong to that project. Projects are separate from one another, and only three things are shared across them. Custom analyzers and tags are shared globally. So are queries you save for all projects. More detail can be found in Working across projects in . Documents refer to individual texts in the project. They may have been written in plain text files or PDFs. They could have been pulled straight from websites or from web articles. Recordings of audio and video also qualify as documents and are transcribed for you when you import them. Word files are imported by first saving them as plain text or PDF. Further detail is provided in Text files in . Every document contains metadata such as a name and language, authors, dates, publishers, and DOIs; they are edited in Document Properties. You access Document Properties via the shortcut menu for the document in the navigation sidebar; Control-click the document name and select Properties from its menu. Shortcut menus are described in Conventions later in this chapter. When importing a recording as a document, every passage of its transcript has a time stamp and, when more than one voice is detected, an associated speaker. “Radio Debate” is an example of a transcribed audio recording, having three distinct speakers, namely “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”. A translation is a version of a document in another language. To make a translation, choose Translate in the document's shortcut menu. The navigation sidebar will list translations under the document they originated from. The translated document is named after the original with the language it was translated to appended in parentheses, for example “Running Out of Time (German)”. The original and translated document are aligned (as closely as possible) so that a coding or memo you add to one appears in the other in the correct spot. Links and bookmarks carry over the same way. Counts and searches across a set or a project use only the original document unless explicitly decided otherwise. To include translations, set a query's Corpus to Translations or Both. For a word sketch, choose a translation language as its Corpus.  goes over more details of how translations can be used.

“Climate Debate” in the navigation sidebar, from the project shelf down through its sets and smart set, the groups “Print” and “Online”, and its document tags. Groups act like folders for you to organize your documents. A document can exist only in a single group or in no group at all. Unlike document sets, groups are not a semantic unit; they are mainly a way to organize your list. To analyze the documents of a group, make a smart set with a Group condition, or use a document set instead. In the “Climate Debate” project, you can see how some documents exist in groups and others do not. A set (or document set) refers to a named collection of documents within a project. Typically, you will use a set to tell LemmaLoom which documents should be included in an analysis. Multiple sets may overlap; one document may belong to multiple sets simultaneously. Clicking on a set within the navigation sidebar opens it; it contains the same ten sections as the project shelf, limited to its documents. “Climate Debate” has two sets of documents, “Activists” and “Skeptics”. A smart set determines its membership automatically through conditions. LemmaLoom will dynamically keep track of whether the documents meet the set criteria. A condition allows testing an attribute, tags, or groups. Furthermore, you can test conditions on a document's format, language, or metadata such as titles and dates. For example, the smart set “Wide Reach” contains one condition stating “Readership” is at least 100,000. Tags represent free-form labels that can be applied to both projects and documents. Also, you can apply tags to codes, links, and memos. Tags can be used to filter lists or to choose documents. All your projects share a unified list of tags. From Window ▸ Tags, you get access to the tag list with each tag having a count of the items that carry it. Tag naming does not differentiate between capitalization; thus, tags “Viral” and “viral” are the same tag. Furthermore, each tag on the project's documents acts as a set and appears in the Tags section of the navigation sidebar. Several documents within “Climate Debate” are tagged “op-ed” and “viral”. An attribute represents one piece of factual data about each document. Examples of attributes could be the stance taken in the text and its date of publication. Every attribute needs to have a name and a type. The types available include Text, Integer, Decimal, Boolean (yes or no), Date, and Picker (one value from a fixed list). To input data into attributes, you can go to Attributes via a project's shortcut menu. This opens the Attributes window, a table with documents as rows and attributes as columns. Click Add Attribute to introduce a new attribute and populate its values across all documents. Alternatively, you can enter one document's values from within its Document Properties. “Climate Debate” has four attributes: Attribute Type Values Stance Picker Activist, Skeptic, or Neutral Readership Integer a whole number Publication Date Date a date Outlet Text any text The Attributes window of “Climate Debate”, with six texts checked and the Set Value menu open. Attributes may be tested for in a smart set's conditions. An attribute can serve as a means for grouping columns in the Code Matrix. You could split the output of a query by attribute to form a comparison between different groups of results. Tags, sets, groups, and attributes are all covered in detail in . For attributes on codes, see Codes and coding below.

Coding in LemmaLoom refers to assigning passages in documents to thematic labels referred to as codes. A code may refer to any theme, idea, question, topic, etc., in your documents, while a code placed beneath another code becomes a subcode. For instance, the codes “Tipping Points” and “Deadlines” in “Climate Debate” are both subcodes of “Urgency”. Codes' appearances in the reader are determined by the color and formatting style chosen for each code (formatting styles being Highlight, Underline, or Boxed). A code's description, tags, and attributes may be set, as well as a scope for where it applies, which can be the entire Project, a single Document set, or a single Document. Typically, you would define your codes in the codebook (Codebook under Project in the navigation sidebar); this list shows the description and the total amount used for each code defined. For filtering or comparing a subset of codes, you can put them in code sets. “Climate Debate” has the code set “Arguments”. The Edit Code dialog for “Urgency”, showing Format, Scope, and About. Each time you assign a code to a passage, you make a coding, with the passage named the coding's segment, or interchangeably its coded segment. One coded segment consists solely of a single passage with one code; hence, a passage coded both “Costs” and “Responsibility” counts as two separate codings. Overlapping and nesting of codings can occur. In cases where the codes have attributes, the attribute's values are associated individually with each coding and not the codes. Imagine you have a code representing emotions with an attribute indicating how intense the emotion is; when applying the code to various passages, you would assign an intensity level to each coding. Memos, links, and bookmarks share many similarities with codings as all are applied similarly (select passages and click their respective button in the selection bar); however, they each serve separate functions. Applying a memo allows commenting on selected passages. Select your desired passage and click Memo. Memos could also be assigned to codes (coded memos) and carry the code's tags; they also have their own values for the code's attributes and can be counted by queries alongside that code's codings. Creating links enables connecting passages between each other, in the same document or across documents; this functionality helps keep track of passages that are related to one another (contradicting passages, passages responding to each other, etc.). First, select one passage and then click Link; then, select another passage and click Finish Link. Your link will extend from the former passage to the latter one. Links may be given a relation between the two ends, in your own words, as well as a comment and tags. Bookmarks are meant solely for bookmarking passages you want to come back to later; select a passage and click Bookmark, optionally giving the bookmark a comment and a color. You can view bookmarked passages in the Bookmarks lens in the reader and in the inspector's Text tab. The selection bar in “Running Out of Time” after Link, with a passage selected and Finish Link ready.

When you add a document to a project, LemmaLoom indexes it by analyzing its grammar. This means that the text is broken down into sentences and tokens, consisting of individual words and punctuation marks. Then, every word is given its lemma, its part of speech, and its grammatical features. A lemma refers to the dictionary form of each word; thus, both ran and running will yield run in a lemma form. In addition to indexing individual words, LemmaLoom captures word relationships in a sentence and records the phrases they form. Large texts and lengthy recordings may take considerable amounts of time to process or transcribe, depending on the computational capacity of your Mac. During indexing, a progress ring will appear next to the document in the navigation sidebar to indicate its current progress level. The Activity window, accessible via Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0), displays all ongoing activities. Importing a document does not necessarily require immediate indexing; documents can be added with Index for grammar analysis toggled off and indexed later via the Index Now option in Document Properties. A lens is responsible for styling the text or adding annotations to help highlight the places where categories appear in your document, whether word classes, codes, or something else you need. From the lens menu, the first of the controls at the right end of the title band, you select lenses. Multiple lenses can be selected simultaneously. Some lenses, like Word class, Modality, and Negation, render the grammar analysis, while the others, like Codes and Bookmarks, render your own work with the tools you have made. Codes and Bookmarks are already enabled the first time you open a document. Every dictionary, custom analyzer, and query saved as a lens is added to the lens menu as a lens of its own. If a document has not been indexed yet, the lens menu remains disabled. The lens menu for “Running Out of Time”, Modality on beside Bookmarks and Codes, with the dictionary “Hedges” and the saved query “Urgency Talk” near the bottom. An analyzer is a module that adds analysis results to the document being indexed. LemmaLoom comes equipped with three built-in analyzers. Cohesion traces connections between each sentence and the previous context, Metadiscourse annotates words that guide the audience (like hedges and boosters), and Rhetoric identifies stylistic features like the use of the passive voice and parallelism. You can create your own analyzer with scripts written in JavaScript from Window ▸ Analyzers; a custom analyzer can be accessed in every project. Results added by an analyzer can be rendered as a lens or searched with queries; you choose which analyzers run when you import a document, although Document Properties can trigger an analyzer on an existing document or remove it. A query searches your documents, returning a result containing the elements of interest according to specified conditions. To construct a query, you use conditions in the query builder; some conditions dictate the content of your search (e.g., words, sentences, codings, or documents), while others set out the criteria for the search and presentation format (e.g., List, Count, Compare if you want to compare groups). Depending on the extent of your search, a query may be constructed from Window ▸ Queries (across projects), the Queries section of a project or document set, or the Multimode tab of the inspector (for a single document). Saved queries can belong to documents, sets, projects, or all projects and serve as lenses, smart sets, and even custom analyzers; additionally, LemmaLoom can apply auto-codings based on queries. Not everything must be built from scratch though, as you have access to a collection of recipes consisting of prebuilt queries under Recipes wherever you build queries; examples include Concordance, Keywords, or Codings by Attribute queries. The “Climate Debate” project hosts two saved queries, “Urgency Talk”, which is stored as a lens, and “Keywords: Activists”, which belongs to the set “Activists”. The Queries section of “Climate Debate” with the recipes in the left column and the saved query “Urgency Talk” loaded. Dictionaries collect terms under named categories, allowing you to locate these words in documents and generate statistics according to their category. Any dictionary can also be rendered as a lens. Dictionaries for each project reside in its Dictionaries section, while adding terms from the selection into a dictionary is performed via Add to Dictionary located on the selection bar (where you can choose a dictionary and the category). As an example, the “Climate Debate” project possesses a dictionary titled “Hedges”. Within this dictionary there exist two categories: Category Terms Approximators about, around, roughly, approximately, more or less, almost, nearly, just about Shields I think, perhaps, maybe, probably, it seems, I suppose, I'd say, I'm not sure

Most examples, diagrams, and screenshots in this guide come from one project, “Climate Debate”. This fictional dataset includes op-eds, columns, and other kinds of texts regarding climate change published in the course of some public debate on the matter. LemmaLoom ships with this example project to give you the ability to reproduce each step mentioned in this guide yourself by importing “Climate Debate”. Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project to import “Climate Debate” into your LemmaLoom library as the active project, with its documents already indexed. Item In “Climate Debate” Documents 15 in all. Eleven plain-text documents, including op-eds, columns, blog posts, and a speech, with “Running Out of Time”, “Letter from the Climate Strike”, “Why We Block the Roads”, “Farmers Are Not the Enemy”, “A Mayor's Promise”, and “Hope Takes Work” by activists, and “The Models Keep Missing”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, “Let's Not Panic”, “Who Pays for the Transition”, and “Science Is Never Settled” by skeptics. “Heat Wave Report 2024”, a PDF; “Carbon Tax Debate”, a web page; “Radio Debate”, an audio recording with its transcript; and “Running Out of Time (German)”, a German translation of “Running Out of Time” Groups “Print”, “Online” Sets “Activists” (the six texts by activists), “Skeptics” (the five texts by skeptics) Smart set “Wide Reach”, whose condition is “Readership” is at least 100,000 Tags “op-ed”, “viral” Attributes “Stance”, “Readership”, “Publication Date”, “Outlet” Codes “Urgency” (with the subcodes “Tipping Points” and “Deadlines”), “Science” (with the subcode “Uncertainty”), “Costs”, “Responsibility”, and “Emotions” (with the subcodes “Fear” and “Hope”); “Radio Debate” also has “Speakers” (with the subcodes “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”) Code set “Arguments” Dictionary “Hedges”, with the categories “Approximators” and “Shields” Saved queries “Urgency Talk” (saved as a lens), “Keywords: Activists” (in the set “Activists”)

For example, if your work involves a lot of coding, you should check out  and . For grammar and word counts, go on to , , and the query chapters. Whenever you encounter a term in boldface type, whether it is a menu, label, etc., such as Code, Word Sketch, or Auto Code…, it is safe to assume that it will appear precisely as written within LemmaLoom. If this guide is the German or Chinese version, the term would refer to the German or Chinese version of the interface respectively. Menu commands follow the path notation where the menu name precedes an action separated by ▸. Choosing File ▸ Import ▸ Web Pages entails opening File, navigating to Import, and then selecting Web Pages. LemmaLoom's application menu will always be under LemmaLoom, while settings will be under LemmaLoom ▸ Settings…. Whenever you click on a menu item whose name ends in an ellipsis (…), expect a dialog or a window to open, allowing you to configure your preferences prior to any action taking place. Shortcut menus exist for many LemmaLoom items. Accessing one is achieved using either the secondary click or Control-click, depending on your device input method. A document's shortcut menu in the navigation sidebar will allow you to Translate, modify its Properties, or Delete Document, for example. Here are the symbols macOS uses for the modifier keys in keyboard shortcuts: Symbol Key ⌘ Command ⇧ Shift ⌥ Option ⌃ Control Pressing ⇧⌘C means holding down both the Shift and Command keys before pressing C. Each command with an associated shortcut is followed by its shortcut in parentheses, as in Document ▸ Code (⇧⌘C). See  for a list of keyboard shortcuts. Italics indicate where a term is defined, along with quotations made directly from any documents being analyzed, for instance, climate and perhaps. Text typed literally will appear in monospace font, while file names and extensions like .qdpx also appear similarly; example names in the “Climate Debate” project, such as the “Activists” set and the “Deadlines” code, will appear in quotation marks. If controls are grayed-out or disabled, either they are irrelevant to your current context or they are not available for it at the moment. To discover why a particular button or option in a window or dialog is disabled, hover the mouse pointer over it.

LemmaLoom requires a minimum macOS version of 26.6. The application includes all required components for grammar analyses and for transcription with the Whisper models. The default Apple Speech model uses speech components from macOS, which LemmaLoom downloads if they are not yet installed on your Mac. Translation depends on the installed translation languages within macOS. When you initially translate between two languages, macOS may prompt you to install them.

The interface language in LemmaLoom may be English, German, or Mainland Simplified Chinese. This applies to menus, windows, and messages throughout the app. LemmaLoom defaults to whatever among the three languages ranks highest based on your preference setting in System Settings ▸ General ▸ Language & Region. Otherwise, the app resorts to English should none of the three languages be listed in your Language & Region settings. LemmaLoom can also have an interface language of its own, regardless of your system selection: Choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,). Click General. Under Language, choose English, Deutsch, or 简体中文 in the Interface language menu. System Default goes back to following macOS. Click Quit LemmaLoom, then open LemmaLoom again. The General pane of Settings with the Interface language menu open.

There is a Language menu in the Import Document dialog where Automatic will let LemmaLoom figure out the language for you automatically. Alternatively, you may set English, German, or Chinese manually. You can change the language at any time in the document's properties; the document will be re-indexed for that language when you do so. For all three supported languages, the full grammar analysis, including the three built-in analyzers, will take place. Analysis tools earlier in this chapter describes the grammar analysis. However, several lenses depend on one language or another: Lens English German Chinese Word class, Grammatical function, Phrase yes yes yes Modality, Negation, Connectives yes yes yes Cohesion, Metadiscourse, Rhetoric yes yes yes Morphology yes yes no Sentence fields no yes no Constructions, Particles no no yes The Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric lenses all rely on their respective analyzers. Only once the analyzer has run on the document will its lens appear in the lens menu. If you disable an analyzer at import, or later remove it from Document Properties, the associated lens will disappear from the lens menu. The Morphology lens provides grammatical annotations such as tense, number, degree (big, bigger, biggest), and verb form. In German, it provides additional annotation for case, mood, and gender. Since Chinese does not inflect any words based on these grammatical features, the Morphology lens is available exclusively to documents written in English and German. Sentence fields annotates the two parts of the verb (Linke Klammer, Rechte Klammer) in German. It also annotates the fields before, between, and after them (Vorfeld, Mittelfeld, Nachfeld), which taken together are known as topological fields. Constructions annotates the common sentence constructions in Chinese (e.g., constructions containing 把 and 被), while Particles annotates aspect particles, structural particles, and classifiers in Chinese. You may import documents in other languages as text documents. They can be read, searched, coded, noted upon in memos, linked to, and bookmarked. The language code appears alongside each document in the navigation sidebar; examples include EN, DE, and ZH. Other languages receive a question mark beside the code. Hovering the mouse pointer over that will reveal Language not supported for indexing. These documents cannot access any functionality involving an indexed document, including the lens menu, Grammar tab, word sketch, or queries about words and sentences. They may be queried, nonetheless, about codings, memos, or documents generally. Recordings are an exception. LemmaLoom transcribes speech into text only as English, German, or Chinese, depending on which matches most closely with the initial 30 seconds of the recording. The transcribed Chinese speech uses simplified characters throughout. How transcription works in  gives the details. In order to analyze grammar in a document in another language, translate it. A translated document in English, German, or Chinese gets the status of any other indexable document. When making a query or word sketch for your document's set, simply choose the translations as the Corpus.

LemmaLoom includes an example project called “Climate Debate”. You can import it to try out the application's tools. Most of this guide draws its examples from it. Its op-eds, columns, and speech are fiction, as are its report and its recorded radio debate. Any resemblance to real persons or publications is coincidental, and the texts represent no one's opinions and aren't meant to persuade you of anything. To add this example project to your library as a new project, select File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. An Importing Example Project dialog displays the status. Once it closes, “Climate Debate” will become your active project. The language of the imported project depends on the current language of LemmaLoom’s interface, meaning it could either be English, German, or Mainland Simplified Chinese. Refer to Supported languages under  to know how to switch the interface language. All the documents, document sets, codes, attributes, and saved queries mentioned in this chapter exist in the imported project. Alternatively, you may proceed through the examples with a few texts of your own; instead of referring to the documents included in “Climate Debate”, refer to yours.

t: Starting LemmaLoom for the first time
b: Upon initial launch, the LemmaLoom application window displays three columns (the navigation sidebar, the reading area, and the inspector). While there are no existing projects, both the navigation sidebar and the inspector remain blank. Likewise, until a project has been created and a document opened, the four tab icons at the top of the inspector are disabled. You may access all settings of the application via LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,). Two settings to check before you start are configured through General. First among these is the Theme setting, which applies the chosen color scheme throughout LemmaLoom's user interface. Theme can either follow the light or dark appearance selected on the Mac system (System), or be overridden by Cream, High Contrast Dark, or another theme. Interface language determines both the display language used by LemmaLoom and the language of the example project when it is imported. With System Default, Interface language matches the language on your Mac; other languages available are English, Deutsch, and 简体中文 (Mainland Simplified Chinese). Any changes made in Interface language take effect once the application is closed via Quit LemmaLoom below the menu and relaunched. The Interface language menu in Settings ▸ General, with System Default, English, Deutsch, and 简体中文. Within the Settings window, General also holds the speech recognition Model for recordings and the Exclusion Presets for import dialogs. Other sections include Reader (settings that control text styles in the reader) and Lenses, where you can customize the lens styles.  goes through the Settings window option by option. Only documents written in English, German, or Chinese are analyzed for grammar. A document in any other language can be imported as plain text and still be read, coded, and searched. If a document written in another language needs grammar analysis performed on it, a translation to English, German, or Chinese would need to be analyzed instead. The analysis would then reflect grammatical structures present in the translation.  explains further how to manage translations within LemmaLoom. For brief explanations of various terms used in the application, visit Help ▸ Glossary. The Glossary window can remain open while you work in the main window.

Your library contains everything you do within LemmaLoom. The library is essentially just a folder stored on your Mac computer. More details are discussed further in Where work is stored below. Each study gets a project of its own inside the library. A project holds the texts you're studying. It also holds whatever you make as you analyze them. It keeps your codes and their codings, your memos and links, and your sets and groups. Dictionaries and saved queries are kept there too. Projects are kept apart. A query run over a project only sees that project's documents. Generally, you want to keep all relevant material for a study in a single project. Three things are shared by every project. Tags come from the same list, accessible via Window ▸ Tags. Queries saved for All Projects are accessible from all projects; moreover, you may also query multiple projects simultaneously. Working across projects in  covers how to accomplish such actions. Analyzers you develop for LemmaLoom consist of small scripts that annotate your passages. Such analyzers are accessible in every project via Window ▸ Analyzers.  covers how analyzers function in LemmaLoom. Every imported text constitutes a document within a project. Your document may be a newspaper piece, a speech, or the contents of a PDF file; alternatively, it could be an article from a website page or a transcription of an audio or video recording. When you import a document in LemmaLoom, LemmaLoom maintains its own copy of said document, regardless of changes made elsewhere. Corrections should be done directly within LemmaLoom, although its correction functionality is fairly restricted. As a rule of thumb, import only documents that either are finished or will undergo minimal edits. Large edits should be carried out outside of LemmaLoom. You would then paste the edited text into LemmaLoom's editor or re-import the document once the edits are complete. When you import documents into a project, LemmaLoom processes those documents in the background. This step is known as indexing, and consists of splitting text into sentences and words while working out the grammatical structure of each sentence. LemmaLoom finds each word's dictionary form (i.e. its lemma); the lemma of runs and ran is run. Additionally, LemmaLoom determines word classes (nouns, verbs, etc.).  provides further insights into indexing. Word sketches, lenses, most queries, and the Grammar tab of the inspector depend on indexing results. Neither coding nor reading requires them; therefore you can conduct both before indexing has completed. Document size and computer capabilities affect indexing time. LemmaLoom's main window contains one project at a time, referred to as your active project. Each project's open tabs and your position in each document, as well as its lens selections, persist from session to session.

Your project just requires a name, although a color and tags can be assigned alongside the attributes shared among all documents in the project. Attributes store one factual piece of information per document, such as publication dates and the stances they represent. These attributes pertain to your whole project and may hold a value within each document. Defining your attributes at the creation of a project allows you to specify those attribute values when importing documents. Eventually, the values stored in attributes enable grouping and comparison of documents according to various attributes, so consider the factual pieces of information worth comparing as attributes. Tags can be applied to projects and documents as an organizational tool without holding a value; a tag means whatever you decide it means. “Climate Debate” defines four attributes: Name Type Choices Purpose Stance Picker Activist, Skeptic, Neutral Comparing the two sides of the debate, and the sources that report on it without taking a side Readership Integer  Selecting widely read texts, as the smart set “Wide Reach” does Publication Date Date  Placing each text in time Outlet Text  Recording where each text appeared Every attribute has an associated data type. See  for details on the available types and modifying the type of an attribute. “Stance” is an example of a picker type, which is only capable of receiving the choices you list. If you cannot enumerate the values ahead of time, like in the case of the outlets in “Climate Debate”, Text should be used. Integer attributes store whole numbers, while Decimal and Boolean attributes store decimals and yes or no values, respectively. Creating “Climate Debate” with its four attributes. For creating a project: Choose File ▸ New Project (⇧⌘N). In Name, type the project's name. If you leave the field empty, the project is called “New Project”. Under Color, click a color if you want one. It tints the project's icon in the sidebar. Under Tags, type a tag and press Return or type a comma. Tags come from one list that all your projects share. Under Attributes, click Add Attribute once for each attribute. In the new row, type the name in the left field and choose a type from the menu. For a Picker (a fixed list of choices), type each choice in its own row below the name and type; Add Choice adds a row. Click Create. The new project appears in the sidebar under Projects, and becomes the active project immediately thereafter. To switch between projects, select one under Projects. At the top of the sidebar is Favorites, which lists projects you want to easily access. Add a project to Favorites by hovering the mouse pointer over it, then clicking on the star that appears. Right-clicking on a project gives options such as Rename, Properties, and Attributes, among others.  describes them all.

LemmaLoom supports importing four kinds of sources: plain-text files, PDF files, audio and video files, and web pages via File ▸ Import ▸ Web Pages (⌥⇧⌘I). For the sample project “Climate Debate”, all four types are represented. Op-eds, columns, blog posts, and a speech were imported as plain text sources, while “Heat Wave Report 2024” was imported from a PDF file. “Radio Debate” was imported from an audio file, while “Carbon Tax Debate” was imported as a web page. All imported documents include their publication dates and values for the attributes defined in the project. An example of such metadata for “Running Out of Time” is that it was published on August 21, 2024. It is assigned a “Stance” value of “Activist”. Its “Readership” is 412,000, and the document belongs to the group “Print”. Importing “Running Out of Time”, with “Stance” and “Readership” filled in. For importing a text file: Make sure the project you want is active (its name is bold under Projects). Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I). Select the file and click Open. You can select several files at once. The Import Document dialog opens. Check the details described below and click Import. Organization allows you to assign the document to a Group in the project or leave it Ungrouped, assign the document a Color, and add Tags. A group behaves much like a folder in the navigation sidebar; it groups documents of a similar kind, much like “Print” and “Online” do in “Climate Debate”. While a document may belong to many sets simultaneously, it belongs to one and only one group (unless it's ungrouped). Groups are meant primarily as organizational aids in the navigation sidebar, where sets and smart sets instead have functions in analysis. Under Attributes, you fill in the actual values of the document for the various attributes defined in the project. As you begin typing an attribute's name, a list of suggestions appears with the names of existing attributes followed by their type (“Stance · Picker”). Click Add Attribute, then choose or type the value in the row that appears. Alternatively, you can simply create a new attribute. You do that by simply entering its name as long as it's not taken, and a menu opens up beside the name to let you define the type of the attribute. For pickers, type each option in its own row. Another alternative is to leave the values for later and fill them in for many documents at once; you can alternatively complete that task document by document in the Details facet of the Text tab later. More on that topic can be found under Filling in attribute values below. Indexing determines whether and how this particular document is indexed. The default setting for Language is Automatic; the program tries to guess the language based on the document contents. If there might be issues with accuracy, you can manually set Language to English, German, or Chinese. A very small text containing another language is an example case where it might help. Index for grammar analysis starts checked; uncheck it if the document needs reading or coding alone and not indexing. You can also defer indexing a large document until later. The button Index Now in the status bar at the bottom of the reader starts indexing later when pressed. Further down, under Analyzers, are checkboxes to enable specific analyses; these include the built-in Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric analyzers plus any you've written yourself, and all of them are selected initially. Unselecting a box will disable that analyzer for that document. Exclude from indexing contains regular expression patterns to match text that mustn't count toward analysis. Speaker labels and time stamps are the most common examples. You'll typically require it when working with transcripts.  lists some common examples of patterns to exclude. Regular expressions are a special syntax describing types of texts. An example of it is [d+:d+:d+]; that pattern refers to sequences of three numbers separated by colons within square brackets, e.g., [00:12:31]. Enter the pattern yourself and click Add, or select one from Presets, which provides Timestamps [hh:mm:ss] (this same pattern) among others. The matched texts will remain visible in the reader, although they won't contribute toward analysis, and they can still be coded. The lower half of the Import Document dialog for “Radio Debate”, with the Presets menu open. When importing multiple files at once, the dialog pops up once for each file, and indicates the order in the upper-right corner (e.g., 2 of 10). Skip advances to the next file without importing the current file, while Cancel terminates importation of all remaining unconfirmed files. Any confirmed file continues to get imported regardless of cancellation.

Under the Documents heading of the sidebar, your document will be found; the name of your document will also be followed by the code of the detected or selected language, for instance, EN. While being indexed, the title becomes grayed out and is accompanied by an indicator which fills itself up during the process. Once indexing completes, the indicator disappears. Activity (Window ▸ Activity, ⌥⌘0) monitors activity in all your projects and categorizes documents according to their status into the lists for Importing, Translating, Indexing, Failed, and Waiting. Next to the projects menu in the Activity window, there is an Import menu which allows importing documents or web pages into your projects. The Activity window during an import, with “Radio Debate” under Importing, two documents under Indexing, and one under Waiting. By clicking on the document’s row in the sidebar, you’ll be able to get a separate tab opened for this particular document. Even without indexing, you can see its text in the reader, but until indexing has finished: the lens menu in the title band is disabled, showing a tooltip saying Lenses become available when indexing completes; the Grammar tab and the Sketch Space facet of the Multimode tab of the inspector display Grammar becomes available when indexing completes; Statistics become available when indexing completes replaces actual statistics on the Text tab; the status bar below the reader shows the current stage, for example Parsing structure, and a percentage. When LemmaLoom can't index the document’s language, a question mark icon is shown beside the document’s title in the sidebar. The status bar displays, for instance, No grammar analysis for French.

t: A tour of the main window
b: The main window has the navigation sidebar on its left side, followed by the reading area, followed by the inspector on its right. In the navigation sidebar, you will be able to choose which project to open and access its documents, sets, and detail views. On top of the reading area is a row of tabs, and above them, the title band, which holds the controls for the document in the active tab. Within the reading area, the reader shows the contents of the active tab, either the document itself or a detail view. At the bottom is the status bar, which shows the position of the selected text and the size of the document. And finally, the inspector describes the active document, offering further inspection tools on it. “Running Out of Time” in the main window, with the Codes lens enabled and the code system in the inspector's Coding tab. Some buttons may appear disabled here. These buttons do not apply to the currently selected document/tab, or are not available for it yet. Hovering the mouse pointer over one provides the reason it is disabled.

Search Documents is located above the rest of the navigation sidebar and below the window buttons. Typing text in the field will narrow the sidebar to the active project's documents whose titles contain the entered text. Hitting Return will open the very first match, while Esc will reset the field. Edit ▸ Find Document (⇧⌘F) focuses the Search Documents field. Should your sidebar be collapsed, the command will expand the sidebar first. Below Search Documents resides a list in sections. First in this list comes Favorites. As soon as you star your first project, it appears, populated with each starred project. Below Favorites, you have access to all the projects inside your library under Projects. Clicking a project makes it active, and Project lists ten sections of the active project. These sections range from Codebook and Codings down to Queries, each opening as a detail view in a tab of the reader, and together they make up the project shelf; refer to The project shelf below to get a closer look. Sets contains all sets created in the active project. Each set shows its name and document count. Clicking a set's name opens it in a tab. Hitting its disclosure triangle will reveal all members inside the set. New Set and New Smart Set at the end of this section provide ways to create sets. Documents contains the documents within the active project. Groups appear as folders first, and then the remaining documents follow. Each translation is shown under its original document. At the bottom, Tags contains all the tags you assigned to this project's documents, and the number of documents assigned each tag follows. Unless at least one document carries a tag, this section won't show itself at all. Click a tag to open its documents in a tab, much like a set. The sidebar of “Climate Debate”, with the “Activists” set and the group “Print” expanded. In each document row, there is an icon showing what sort of document it is. The document’s icon is tinted according to the document’s color, should it have one. Next is the document’s title, followed by the language code, and then an indexing badge whenever necessary. Should your lens or query miss out on including a particular document, check whether that document has a badge. A row with no badge has been indexed. The badges indicate the following: Badge Meaning Progress ring Being indexed; hover the mouse pointer over it for the stage and percentage Dotted circle Waiting to be indexed Pause symbol Indexing is off for this document Question mark Language not supported for indexing Red triangle Indexing failed; right-click the document and choose Retry Indexing Indexing badges in the sidebar: a progress ring, a dotted circle, a pause symbol, and the question mark of a French text. To open a document, simply click on it in the navigation sidebar. To navigate using your keyboard keys, use ↑ and ↓ to navigate rows, and Return to open the currently highlighted row. Select multiple rows by holding ⌘ or ⇧ while clicking. Right-clicking a document in the sidebar gives access to contextual commands related to that row, including Open in Split View, Rename, Move to Group, Sets, Properties, Translate, Export, and Delete Document. If multiple rows are selected, there will be contextual commands for adding them into a set (Add to Set) or deleting the selected documents (Delete Documents). In the Project menu in the menu bar, there will be several of the commands from above for actions performed on whatever row is currently selected in the sidebar.
