The Project menu adds commands for making new sets (New Set) and smart sets (New Smart Set), as well as adding codes (Add Code). Its delete command (⌘⌫) will delete whatever project, set, group, or documents are selected.

Everything accessed through Project has its own detail view opened in a tab. The detail view contains information for the entire project. Using the project shelf allows you to interact with all your documents simultaneously. Section What it shows Described in Codebook The project's codes as a tree, where you create, edit, and organize them  Codings Every coded passage in the project, with its document and code  Memos The project's memos  Links Links between passages  Code Stats How often each code is used and how much text it covers  Code Matrix A table of codes against documents or groups of documents  Relations A table of how often each pair of codes occurs together  Word Sketch The words a word combines with grammatically, for example the nouns climate modifies in climate crisis and climate policy, across the project  Dictionaries Word lists with categories, for example a list of hedges  Queries The query builder, run over the whole project  When working with a particular part of a project, open a set. Its tab will give you access to all the same ten sections within the set, and not the entire project. The row of buttons at the top gives you quick navigation to each section in this way. In narrower windows, this row converts into a menu that displays the currently selected section's name as its title. The “Activists” set in a tab, with the row of section buttons above the Codebook. A detail view's header is just a single row. The name of the section appears on the left side while tools related to that section are displayed on the right, such as a search field. You may keep a detail view alongside your document using the Open in a window button. This button appears on the far right of the header. Window ▸ Codebook and Window ▸ Queries provide you access to the respective sections in their own windows. Project ▸ Open gives you access to any section on the shelf in a separate tab.

Each document, detail view, or set opened has its own tab in the row above the reader. An × on the tab closes that particular tab. For a quick look, you can open a preview tab by clicking a hit in the results of your queries, or an example from a word sketch. The titles of preview tabs are italicized. The following quick look replaces this preview tab automatically. If you wish to preserve the preview tab, click the tab itself. Command Shortcut File ▸ Close Tab ⌘W Window ▸ Show Previous Tab ⇧⌘ **Window ▸ Show Next Tab** ⇧⌘] Right-clicking on a tab provides options to open a document either in a new window (**Open in New Window**) or in split view (**Open in Split View**). Split view displays the selected document alongside the currently active document. Use it if you wish to compare two documents side-by-side, or if you wish to read a translation alongside its source document. [ describes it further. The Window menu provides the same options.

The reader displays the active tab's document in text format. To the left of the text lies the gutter. It shows paragraph numbers, sentence numbers, and colored bars next to each coded passage. Clicking on a paragraph number selects the entire paragraph, clicking a sentence number does the same for the sentence, and clicking a passage bar selects the passage itself. The document overview is located alongside the right edge of the reader. Like a color-coded scroll bar, the document overview indicates the current location in the document, but unlike a scroll bar, it also indicates where the enabled lenses, bookmarks, and search hits fall. Clicking or dragging anywhere in the document overview scrolls you directly to that part of the document, while hovering the mouse pointer over it previews the text at that point. Selection can either be done by clicking and dragging over a passage of any length or by clicking a word. Within an indexed document, simply clicking on a word selects just the clicked word. The inspector's Grammar tab will display grammar details about that word. If you click the same word again, your selection is cleared. When working in the transcript of a recording, clicking a word moves playback to the point in the file where that word resides. The selection bar appears at the bottom of the reader as long as something remains selected in your document. The beginning of your selected text appears in quotes at the far left, followed by Bookmark, Code, Add to Dictionary, Memo, and Link. Only projects with a dictionary show Add to Dictionary. Application of codes will be discussed in detail in Applying codes later in this chapter. In the Document menu you can also find the Bookmark (⇧⌘B), Code (⇧⌘C), Memo (⇧⌘M), and Link (⇧⌘L) commands. Pressing Esc or clicking the × in the selection bar will clear the selection. The status bar is found along the bottom of the reader. On the left it shows the position of the selected text. If you select a word, it reads something like ¶ 4 · S 17 · T 3, indicating that it's paragraph 4, the document's sentence 17, and the third token therein (punctuation included in counting tokens). If you select a passage, the status bar displays the number of tokens within it, as well as its start and end. On the right side, it displays overall document size by paragraphs, sentences, and words; though, while indexing takes place, it displays indexing progress instead.

The title band spans the top of the reading area at the same level as the window's buttons. On the left-hand side, it displays the LemmaLoom name. Controls related to the document being viewed in the currently active tab sit on the right-hand side; from left to right, they include: Lens menu. This control displays Lens when no lenses are enabled; when one lens is enabled, it displays the name of that lens; when multiple lenses are enabled, it displays how many lenses there are, for example 2 Lenses. While reading your document, a lens helps highlight patterns found in it. A lens either highlights the text based on word class or another property, or based on your own annotations. Prior to indexing a document, the lens control is disabled.  covers more on lenses. Collapse button, which has a tooltip of Show only the sentences a lens annotates. When clicked, this button will hide everything apart from the sentences that the currently enabled lenses have annotated in your document. The button is visible only if your document is indexed and a lens is capable of annotating some portion of text, that is, an enabled lens besides Codes and Bookmarks. It also appears when some codings or bookmarks exist that can be shown via the Codes and Bookmarks lenses. Upon clicking the button once again, your full document returns, and the button's tooltip changes to Show the whole document again. Magnifier icon, with a tooltip of Find in document. When clicked, this icon opens a search bar directly above your document's text. Alternatively, Edit ▸ Find (⌘F) does the same action. Find Next (⌘G) and Find Previous (⇧⌘G) move through your results sequentially. Font, gutter, and text size, the control featuring large and small A symbols. Its drop-down menu consists of Font, Gutter (Off, Paragraphs, Sentences, or Both), Layout (Single Column or Two-Page Spread), Larger Text (⌘+), Smaller Text (⌘−), and Reset Text Size (⌘0). Edit, switching the reader interface mode to editing the current document's text content. Cancel and Save buttons replace it until editing ends.  describes editing. The Font, gutter, and text size menu in the title band of “Running Out of Time”. The open lens menu, with Word class, Bookmarks, and Codes checked. Every new document has two lenses enabled, Codes and Bookmarks, both of which display codings/bookmarks as annotations on your text. Hence the label shows 2 Lenses in documents whose lenses have not been modified from default settings. The lens menu groups its lenses. The first group holds the grammar analysis lenses, which are Word class, Grammatical function, and all other options available for the language of the document. Next comes Clear Lenses, which clears out those lenses listed above and any query lenses. Then come your own analyzers and Clear Analyzers before ending with Bookmarks, Codes, the project's dictionaries and query lenses, and Clear Annotations, which disables that last group. Clicking on each one of these enables/disables them accordingly. All lenses display their legend in a line on top of the document, where a series of aspect lenslets appear in the form of colors. Clicking a lenslet disables or enables its aspect. At the beginning of the legend appears the name of the lens itself, along with the options of enabling/disabling all aspects via clicking on All or None, respectively. There could be multiple colors in a single lens, and you may want to show just one of them. Right-click on the required lenslet and choose Enable only this for that purpose. The Modality legend of “Running Out of Time”, with the shortcut menu of the Obligation lenslet open. Clear All, which is found at the top of the lens menu, will disable the Codes and Bookmarks lenses as well. Clear Lenses, however, only disables the grammar colors and any query lenses, and leaves your codings in place. In case your codings ever seem to vanish, reselecting Codes in the lens menu will bring them back.

The inspector applies to the document currently displayed in the active tab. It allows you to look more closely at the document you are working with. Four icons at its top represent each tab individually. The book represents Text and the line of spaced words represents Grammar. The tag represents Coding and the four squares represent Multimode. Hover your mouse pointer over an icon to reveal its name, or use the View ▸ Inspector menu item and its various keyboard shortcuts. Each tab is subdivided into a number of facets. , , , and  will explain each facet individually. Navigate among facets via the row of buttons under the icons above. Tab Shortcut Facets What it is for Text ⌥⌘1 Overview, Details, Bookmarks The document's statistics, for example word counts and readability; its attributes and tags; its bookmarks Grammar ⌥⌘2 Grammar, Sentence, Structure, Form × Function, Collocates, Word Sketch, Discourse The grammar of the selected word or sentence and the grammatical patterns of the whole document Coding ⌥⌘3 Codes, Codings, Links, Code Stats, Portrait, Code Sketch The code system, this document's codings and links, and statistics about them Multimode ⌥⌘4 Sketch Space, Query Comparisons of a word's use across codes or attribute values, and queries run on this document The Grammar facet works on the currently selected word. The Sentence facet works on the currently selected sentence. Prior to selection, they display Select a Word and Select a Sentence, respectively. The Grammar tab describing the word climate in “Running Out of Time”. The inspector tab, facet, and pane width are saved separately for each document. If the active tab contains a detail view or a set, the inspector closes. Their tools appear in the reading area instead. If you open a document in another window, that window will have its own inspector.

For reading documents alone, hiding the side panels lets you use the full window space. Both the navigation sidebar button and the inspector button are found on the top window toolbar. The navigation sidebar button is located immediately beside the window buttons in the upper left corner. The inspector button is in the upper right. The View menu contains the equivalent commands: Command Shortcut View ▸ Toggle Sidebar ⌃⌘S View ▸ Toggle Inspector ⌃⌘I Dragging the line between the reader and the sidebar or the inspector allows adjusting the width of either element. The inspector can fill as much as two-thirds of the window. This provides space for displaying a broad table or a long sentence diagram. Whether the inspector was hidden is remembered separately for each document. Tabs of detail views and sets display their tools in the reading area and therefore disable the inspector button and View ▸ Toggle Inspector.

The coding process entails two phases, creating your codes and applying them to passages. Codes may be defined using the inspector's Codes facet, or via the Codebook. Applying codes to passages happens using the code palette.

There are five top-level theme codes within the codebook of the “Climate Debate” project. They each relate to one of the themes investigated by this research study, which are “Costs”, “Emotions”, “Responsibility”, “Science”, and “Urgency”. Some of these codes contain subcodes that describe the various ways the related theme appears in the texts. Examples include “Tipping Points” and “Deadlines” for the code “Urgency”, and “Fear” and “Hope” for the code “Emotions”. There is also a sixth top-level code, “Speakers”, which contains the three speakers in “Radio Debate”, namely “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”. Here's how you can create a new code: Open a document. In the inspector, click the Coding tab (⌥⌘3) and then Codes. Click + at the right of Code System. In the New Code dialog, type the name in Name. Click a color under Color. Codes without a color are rendered in the theme's accent color. Pick one if you plan to use several codes. Leave Format at Highlight and Scope at Project, and click Save. Beyond these fields, the dialog also includes others;  covers every available option in this regard. The Format field may contain an Underline or Boxed style. Scope may limit the code to apply only within one Document set or one Document. Tags applies labels to your codes. Via Attributes, individual codings of each code can be assigned individualized values. The About description defines the meaning of each code and provides guidelines on when it should be applied. The New Code dialog with “Urgency” typed in Name, Format at Highlight, and Scope at Project. Creating subcodes breaks down general themes into subthemes that take various forms within your dataset. Right-click on any code in the Codes list, then click Add Subcode to generate your subcodes. Codes will show up again in the Codebook section of the project shelf. The Add Code button found at the bottom of the list there adds more codes. Codes can also be created via Project ▸ Add Code within the menu bar; it opens the same New Code dialog.

The fourth paragraph of “Running Out of Time” names three targets, “Net zero by 2050. Coal gone by the end of the decade. Emissions halved by 2030.” All of these deadlines refer to particular dates by which certain actions must be undertaken, hence their code “Deadlines”. The figure below shows a later sentence found within the same paragraph, selected with the code palette open. This particular sentence says, “A deadline that falls after everyone in office has retired is not a deadline at all.” The code palette, opened from the selection bar for a passage in “Running Out of Time”. To code a passage: In the reader, select the passage you want to code. To code a whole paragraph or sentence, click its number in the gutter instead. In the selection bar at the bottom of the reader, click Code, or choose Document ▸ Code (⇧⌘C). In the palette, click the code. Once a code is applied to a passage, the passage adopts the color of the chosen code. A matching bar is displayed next to it within the document gutter. Within the Codes facet, the number next to the code increases by one. The palette remains open until you hit Esc; multiple codes may be assigned to a single passage. Upon the palette's opening, the Search codes field receives focus automatically. Inputting parts of names searches among existing codes for matching results. Hitting Return assigns the first match found; if the code is already applied to the passage, hitting Return removes the coding from it. Use the arrow keys (↑ and ↓) to navigate through the matches prior to Return if you wish to assign something else. When no code has the typed name, Add Code “…” pops into existence; upon choosing it, a new code of the name specified will be created and applied. The last item on this list is In Vivo “…”. Instead of adding a predefined code, this option creates an ad hoc code, which is applied immediately afterward. Such a code is named after the actual contents of the selection. Without opening the palette, Document ▸ In Vivo Code (⇧⌘V) offers the same function. If you are coding a single word within an indexed document, simply click that word to select it. From there, click Code in the selection bar and select the desired code from the palette. Removing a code from a passage works much like applying one. Clicking the passage's bar in the gutter is one way to select it once again; from there, open the palette. Codes already on the passage possess an icon of a checkmark; clicking one removes all codings of that code overlapping the current selection. Should you regret your coding choice, Edit ▸ Undo Apply Code (⌘Z) retracts the last performed action. For removing a code from a passage, this action is titled Undo Delete Coding instead. ⇧⌘Z acts as redo in both cases. More information about available undo and redo actions may be found in . Codes may themselves contain attributes. Prior to assigning an attribute-based code to a passage, a small dialog asks for the values of those attributes.  explains how to code passages based on codes containing attributes. Additionally, that chapter talks about memos, links, and bookmarks.

In most cases, LemmaLoom will save your changes automatically. There are two cases where you must manually save a change made in LemmaLoom though (saving queries and editing text in documents). When editing a document's text, you must explicitly hit the Save button to make sure that LemmaLoom saves the change. In addition to this, unsaved queries will be lost once you quit the LemmaLoom application. The library holding everything is a folder named LemmaLoom.lemmadb, in the application's container inside your user Library: ~/Library/Containers/app.LemmaLoom/Data/Documents/LemmaLoom.lemmadb The Finder hides the Library folder in your home folder. To get there, choose Go ▸ Go to Folder… (⇧⌘G) in the Finder and paste the path. All your work in LemmaLoom resides inside a single library. This includes everything such as documents, projects, indexing results, codes, codings, memos, links, bookmarks, sets, groups, attributes, dictionaries, saved queries, and your own analyzers. For each imported PDF document, the library stores text content only and retains its filename. For each imported web page document, LemmaLoom retains its text content only and retains its URL address. For imported audio and video recordings, LemmaLoom retains both the transcript and a copy of the file itself. Finally, your favorite projects, tabs open in each project, and locations in each document will be stored in the library. Your settings in LemmaLoom's Settings window are kept on the Mac, as detailed in Where settings are stored in . If you want to move a project to another machine or simply back up your project somewhere else, LemmaLoom offers options to exchange and export projects (see ). LemmaLoom's File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project will export your project as a .llz compressed archive containing documents, their codings, and indexing, along with any attached audio/video recordings; the archive keeps everything. File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive will import such archives back to your LemmaLoom. File ▸ Export ▸ REFI-QDA Project exports your project to the REFI-QDA interchange format; software which adheres to this specification can open this type of file. This format is best suited for projects intended to leave LemmaLoom and be opened in compatible software instead. Project deletion is irrecoverable. You can manually copy your LemmaLoom library folder for backup or relocation purposes. First, quit LemmaLoom. Next, copy the entire LemmaLoom.lemmadb folder.

Help ▸ Send Feedback opens a window where you write your message. Once you finish, clicking Compose Email passes the message to your email client as a new email. You can edit the message before sending once it arrives in your email client. Include system information is initially selected; the option includes your versions of LemmaLoom and macOS, the name of the processor type, RAM size, and the interface language used by LemmaLoom. What is written beneath the option specifies what gets included. The Send Feedback window with a message typed and Include system information selected. LemmaLoom exports the full content of every document in a .llz archive file or REFI-QDA project.

t: From import to a first analysis
b: Analysis begins by bringing your texts into LemmaLoom and describing certain properties of these texts. Afterward, your texts are divided into sets and coded; differences between these sets will be analyzed. The final product of this particular analysis of “Climate Debate” is an identification of words which distinguish the activists' texts from the skeptics'.

There are eleven commentary texts in the “Climate Debate” project. Six were written by the activists and include “Letter from the Climate Strike”, while the other five were written by the skeptics, including “Net Zero Will Cost You”. In order to keep these separate, two different sets are employed along with the attribute “Stance”. When importing multiple texts: Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I). Select all the files and click Open. The Import Document dialog appears once for each file. Its position shows at the top right, for example 1 of 10. Check each dialog and click Import. Attribute values can be filled out on each dialog. Alternatively, you may use the attributes table to assign a shared attribute value across multiple documents. See Filling in attribute values below for instructions. You can follow the indexing progress by going to Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0) or by watching the progress rings in the sidebar. Aside from creating a list of keywords, the steps below do not require indexing. See Comparing two sets with keywords below.

In the project “Climate Debate”, all four attributes hold a value in each document. For instance, in all six documents by the activists, “Stance” has the value “Activist”. Choosing just one Set Value ▸ Stance in the attributes table suffices to assign that value to all six. Other values vary among the documents, like their readerships; you would enter them individually in the table. The Attributes window with the six activist texts checked and the Set Value menu open at Stance. For bulk assignment of values: Choose Project ▸ Attributes, or right-click the project under Projects and choose Attributes. The attributes table opens in a window of its own. In the table, check the boxes beside the documents that share a value. Choose Set Value and then the attribute, pick or type the value in the dialog that opens, and click Apply. Uncheck those documents, check the ones that share the next value, and set it the same way. For values that differ from one document to the next, type each value in the attribute's column.

A set refers to a collection of documents assigned a name. Sets are the normal approach for letting LemmaLoom know which documents your analysis should consider. The “Climate Debate” project contains the sets “Activists” and “Skeptics”. Each set contains the writings of one faction. Your query could compare the sets, or you can conduct queries within them individually. Smart sets have conditions. If a document meets certain conditions, LemmaLoom will automatically add the document to the smart set. Documents with a “Readership” attribute value greater than or equal to 100,000 belong to the smart set “Wide Reach”, for instance. More information about sets in general (including smart sets), groups, tags, and attributes can be found in . The shortcut menu of the selected activist texts, with Add to Set open. To create a set containing documents: In the Documents section of the sidebar, click the first document, then ⌘-click the others. Right-click one of the selected documents and choose Add to Set ▸ New Set from Documents. A set called “New Set” appears under Sets with its name ready for editing. Type a name and press Return.
You will code multiple texts in the exact same way that you code one text; refer back to Coding a passage from earlier in the chapter for guidance on doing that.

t: Looking at the coding of one text
b: In the “Climate Debate” project, “Running Out of Time” is coded 13 times. Two each are for “Costs”, “Responsibility”, and “Tipping Points”. The Code Stats facet for “Running Out of Time”, with 13 codings. To view a document's codes: Make the document active. Click the Coding tab of the inspector. Click Code Stats. Code Frequencies & Coverage in the Code Stats facet lists all codes used in the current document, along with their frequencies and percentages. Each row tells how many passages contain the code and the percentage of the document's text they take up, known as the code's coverage. Clicking a row shows one of its passages in the reader. Above the list, Count sorts the codes and scales their bars by the number of passages; Length sorts and scales them by the amount of text covered. Co-occurrences below it displays co-occurrences of those codes;  describes it and the project-wide tables in the project shelf. Two codes used five times each can cover very different amounts of text. Coverage shows what portion of the document the passages containing the code represent, and it is calculated using the following equation: Here, $c$ represents the number of characters in the passages containing the code, while $n$ represents the total number of characters in the document; note that spaces and line breaks also count toward the totals. Should two passages with the same code partially overlap each other, the shared characters are accounted for once in the calculation of $c$. For instance, “Running Out of Time” consists of about 5,000 characters. So $n = 5{,}000$. Suppose three separate passages are coded as “Urgency”. The passages are 150, 100, and 200 characters in length respectively. Note that this coding of the text is hypothetical; the actual example project codes the text differently. With no overlapping passages, $c = 150 + 100 + 200 = 450$, and: The “Urgency” entry reads 3 and 9.0%. If the last two passages overlap by 33 characters, then $c = 450 - 33 = 417$. Therefore, the coverage percent is $417 / 5{,}000 times 100% = 8.34%$. The row displays 8.3%. There are still three codings of “Urgency”. Codings with “Tipping Points” or “Deadlines” have rows of their own. The number of passages is summed up separately for each row and code.

A keyword list retrieves those words that are used much more or less frequently by one set of documents compared to another. The “Activists” set in “Climate Debate”, for instance, includes a saved keyword query titled “Keywords: Activists”. This keyword list compares the set with “Skeptics” and retrieves those words that differentiate the language used by the activists. Keyword lists retrieve the frequency of occurrence of words found by indexing. Documents in both sets must first be indexed. Keywords of “Activists” against “Skeptics”. Making a list of keywords: Click the first set under Sets in the sidebar. The set opens in a tab. Click Queries in the row of buttons at the top of the tab. In a narrow window, the row is a menu; choose Queries from it. In the column on the left, under Recipes, click Keywords in the Words group. In the Show condition, open the menu showing Rest of Project and choose Set. In the menu that appears, choose the other set. Leave the menu showing Lemma as it is. Then cost and costs count as one word. Leave the menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 as it is. The results of the comparison will be presented beneath the builder in two separate lists, Positive Keywords and Negative Keywords. Positive Keywords contains those words which occur more frequently in the first (target) set compared to the second (reference) set. Negative Keywords, conversely, shows the words which occur less frequently in the target set compared to the reference set. On the top of these two lists, the target set will have its total word count indicated as Target Words, while the reference set will likewise show its total word count as Reference Words. As illustrated in the figure, “Activists” is the target set, whereas “Skeptics” is the reference set. The following information is presented per row of the table: Count, number of occurrences in the target set; Reference, number of occurrences in the reference set. The scores normalize both counts; Log-Likelihood, strength of the evidence that the difference is not chance; Log Ratio, amount of difference between the two sets, measured in doublings of the word's rate. Rate is a word's proportion of the total number of words of its respective set. At 1, the word's share of the target's words is twice its share of the reference's; at 2, it is four times as large; at −1, half as large. Suppose money takes up 2 in every 1,000 words in the activists' texts and 1 in every 1,000 in the skeptics' texts. Thus, if it appears twice as frequently in the target set compared to the reference set, the word rate ratio between the target and reference set is 2. Therefore, the Log Ratio would become about 1 because the rate doubles. Base-2 logarithms count doublings by calculating the power of 2 needed to produce a number. Thus, since the ratio between the rates in the above example equals $2 = 2^1$, the logarithm is 1. Conversely, a ratio of $tfrac{1}{2} = 2^{-1}$ gives −1.  explains both of the scoring methods using examples and describes in detail how thresholds should be chosen. The rows are sorted according to the Log-Likelihood score. A high score shows that a difference likely arises due to reasons other than mere chance. Should any documents remain under indexing, an additional label showing how many documents were included is displayed alongside hit counts, e.g., 4 of 6. The Save Query dialog for the keywords of “Activists”. In order to preserve your query: Click the Save button (a square with an arrow pointing into it) and choose Save. Type a name and leave Available In at Set. Click Save. That saved query is stored within the set.

t: Reading the passages behind a keyword
b: Farmer is listed in the activists' keyword list within the “Climate Debate” project. Almost all mentions by the activists of the term appear within one text called “Farmers Are Not the Enemy”. The search bar takes you to each instance individually within one text: Open one of the texts in the set. Press ⌘F and type the word. The text marks the current hit, and the document overview shows all of them. The search bar shows where you are among them. It matches the letters anywhere in the text and ignores capitals. A search for our therefore also finds your and fourteen. Pass over those. Press ⌘G or Return to move to the next hit (⇧⌘G goes back), and read the passages around them. Code the passages that matter for your question. The search bar in “Farmers Are Not the Enemy” on farmer, with the current hit marked in the text and every hit shown in the document overview. In order to find such a pattern in an entire set of documents, use the Concordance recipe in the set's Queries section. Input the word as the lemma to get started. See Concordance in . More on codes and coding is covered in  and . Grammar-based analyses can be conducted via , , and .  explains how to construct a query.

LemmaLoom keeps all of your work in projects. A project holds your documents and the codes, codings, memos, and links you add to them. The sets, groups, attributes, dictionaries, and saved queries you organize and analyze them with are kept there too. Generally, you want to keep all relevant material for a study in a single project. Most of LemmaLoom's views only look at one project at a time. This chapter exclusively uses examples drawn from the sample project called “Climate Debate”. “Climate Debate” contains eleven invented texts that discuss climate change. The texts consist of op-eds, columns, blog posts, and a speech; six were written by activists (e.g., “Running Out of Time”), while five were penned by skeptics (e.g., “The Models Keep Missing”). Additionally, there are three extra documents included in “Climate Debate”. “Heat Wave Report 2024” is a PDF file; “Carbon Tax Debate” is an imported online news article; and “Radio Debate” is a recorded and transcribed radio debate. Lastly, “Running Out of Time (German)” is a translation of “Running Out of Time”. Thus, altogether, there are 15 documents included. You can explore the project directly from inside LemmaLoom as well. Add it as a new project in the language of the interface by going to File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. This will automatically import the “Climate Debate” project, making it the active project.

All the codes, sets, groups, attributes, and dictionaries you define belong exclusively to their respective projects. Tags and custom analyzers belong to all your projects, as do queries saved for All Projects. Within a project, a document represents a piece of material. Document material can be plain text files, PDF documents, web pages, as well as transcripts of audio and video recordings. Translating a document will generate another document known as a translation (); this document is listed under its original and carries all tags assigned to its original. Groups work similarly to folders in the navigation sidebar; each document sits in one group at most (or none). Groups are used mostly to keep the list of documents in order. The Code Matrix even allows combining its columns according to groups. Smart sets and queries can also pick documents by group. Sets are collections of documents used in analyses of certain documents or comparisons between multiple sets of documents. Any number of sets may contain the same document. A smart set contains documents based on specified criteria (for instance, having “Readership” greater than or equal to 100,000). A smart set automatically maintains its contents according to said criteria. Tags (such as “op-ed” or “viral”) represent labels you create yourself. Tags can represent virtually anything meaningful to your research. One common list of tags applies across projects, documents, codes, memos, and links. Attributes refer to properties of each individual document (e.g., its “Stance” or its “Publication Date”). Once defined, attributes apply universally across an entire project. Your project shelf, near the top of the sidebar, displays ten views, with Codebook first and Queries last. These very same views open for any set and any tag as well, covering only its documents. A scope refers to the documents a view operates upon. A scope can be a whole project, a set, or documents bearing a specific tag. A few of these overlap with one another, and it pays off to know which one serves better in what situation before proceeding to your actual analysis. If you intend on comparing documents by a fact (stance or date, for example), define it as an attribute. Sets are useful for analyzing certain documents (i.e., limiting your scope). Smart sets prove convenient when an attribute or a tag can pick those documents for you. Groups only sort the list. Labels that should mean the same thing in every project go in tags. Within “Climate Debate”, “Stance” is defined as an attribute. Hence Code Stats and the Code Matrix can break their results down by side. For the keyword list, which compares sets, two additional sets, “Activists” and “Skeptics”, were included. “Print” and “Online” represent groups that only sort the list. The tag “op-ed” marks one kind of text.

The sidebar exists on the left side of the main window. Your list of projects is followed by everything inside your active project. Clicking the sidebar button located at the left edge of the toolbar will show or hide the sidebar. View ▸ Toggle Sidebar (⌃⌘S) performs the same action. “Climate Debate” in the sidebar, from the project shelf down to its tags. The sections of the sidebar from top to bottom are these: Section What it lists Favorites Projects you have starred. The section appears once at least one project is a favorite. Projects All your projects in alphabetical order. The active project's name is in bold. Project The project shelf of the active project (see The project shelf later in this chapter). Sets The sets and smart sets of the active project, each with its number of documents, followed by New Set and New Smart Set. Documents The groups of the active project, then the documents that are in no group. Translations are listed under their originals. Tags Every tag used on a document in the active project, with the number of documents that carry it. The section appears once at least one document has a tag. The Search Documents field is located at the very top, above everything else. What you write narrows down the sidebar to only those documents in the active project whose names contain what you are typing. Return opens the first result. Down Arrow lets you move into the list. Escape clears what you've typed and shows the full sidebar again. You can bring back a hidden sidebar and put the insertion point right into the search field by choosing Edit ▸ Find Document (⇧⌘F). Rows begin with icons indicating the kind of each document. Audio is denoted by a waveform, video by a strip of film. Text, PDF, and web documents get a page icon. When documents don’t come with source files (e.g., a text imported from a REFI-QDA project), you will see a square with a pencil. Any color you gave a document tints its icon too. The row ends in a two-letter language code such as EN, DE, or ZH (FR for a French text); hover the mouse pointer over the code to see the language's full name. Next to the code, a badge shows the degree of completion of the indexing process.  talks about indexing. Badge Meaning None The document is indexed and ready for every analysis. Progress ring The document is being indexed, or an analyzer is running on it. Hover the mouse pointer over the ring to see the stage and the percentage done. Dotted circle Waiting to be indexed. The document is in the queue, and indexing starts by itself. Circle with a pause sign Indexing is off. The document was imported without indexing. Index Now in Document Properties starts it (see Indexing later in this chapter). Circle with a question mark Language not supported for indexing. You can read and code the document, but lenses, the Grammar tab, and word sketches need English, German, or Chinese. Red warning triangle Indexing failed. Hover the mouse pointer over the triangle to read why. To try again, right-click the document and choose Retry Indexing. Indexing badges in the sidebar: a progress ring, a dotted circle, a pause sign, and the question mark of a French text. The sidebar displays the document's name and icon in gray during indexing. It is possible to access, open, view, and code the document at this stage. The lens menu becomes active alongside the Grammar tab in the inspector once indexing completes. When an audio, video, or PDF file is imported, a row for it first appears at the end of the Documents section. A progress indicator appears in the row until the file is ready as a document. When translating, a similar row appears below the original and shows both the target language and a progress ring.

“Climate Debate” is a project for one study. It features four attributes defined across its documents. The “Stance” attribute uses the picker data type. Values for “Stance” come from the pre-defined list “Activist”, “Skeptic”, and “Neutral”, which keeps them consistent. The report, the news article, and the radio debate are the neutral ones. The attribute “Readership” stores integers, while “Publication Date” stores dates. “Outlet” contains text, since its values can't be listed in advance. As depicted below, the dialog has only the first two of these attributes defined. The New Project dialog, with “Stance” and “Readership” filled in. Creating a project entails these steps: Choose File ▸ New Project (⇧⌘N). Type a name for the project in Name. If you leave the field empty, the project is called New Project. To give the project a color, click one of the swatches next to Color. The first swatch, No color, is chosen at the start. To tag the project, type a tag in Tags and press Return. A comma also ends a tag. To set up attributes now, click Add Attribute under Attributes once for each attribute. Type its name and choose its Type. For a Picker, also type its choices in the rows below, one per row. Click Create, or press Return. Once you create the project, LemmaLoom will set it as the active project.  explains how to populate your project with documents. Attributes come in six types. Text stores text, Date stores dates, Integer stores whole numbers, Decimal stores numbers with a decimal part, Boolean has yes/no options and uses checkboxes, and Picker stores one choice from a fixed list. Attribute types in  shows how to match the appropriate type of attribute according to its intended use. Auto-complete features will suggest an existing attribute from your projects as you type an attribute's name. If the name matches one of them, its type and choices are automatically carried over. Adding new attributes can happen later via Project Properties or a document's properties, or directly from the Attributes window (Project ▸ Attributes).  covers how documents get their values. An exported LemmaLoom project can either serve as a backup or be shared among colleagues. To load the project, choose File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive. Another option is importing via File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Project; this loads a project created in another application that supports the REFI-QDA standard. You could alternatively open a .llz or .qdpx file with LemmaLoom from the Finder to import it the same way. Details on both formats can be found in .

Clicking on the name of any project under Projects or Favorites makes it the active project. Once selected, the project's shelf, sets, documents, and tags fill the rest of the sidebar. You are taken right back to where you were, starting with the project that was most recently used before quitting LemmaLoom. Every project has its own tabs, which are all restored along with the tab that was active when you revisit that project again. Furthermore, every open document in that project restores its enabled lenses as well as its scroll position. Any other document opened alongside it in split view returns as well. So does the state of the inspector.

Projects can be listed at the top of the navigation sidebar as well. To do so, hover your mouse pointer over the project entry under Projects, and then click on the star icon that appears at the right of its row. Starred projects will then also appear in another section called Favorites. Clicking the star a second time, or using the project's shortcut menu, will take a project off Favorites again.

The following commands appear on your shortcut menu should you right-click or Control-click a project: Command What it does Add to Favorites, Remove from Favorites Stars or unstars the project. Rename Turns the name into a text field. Type the new name and press Return; press Escape to keep the old one. Edit ▸ Undo Rename (⌘Z) restores it. Properties Opens Project Properties (see Project properties below). Attributes Opens the Attributes window, a table of every document's attribute values. See The Attributes window in . Codebook Opens the project's codebook in the Codebook window. Word Sketch Opens the Word Sketch window for the whole project. See . Delete Project Deletes the project after asking (see Deleting a project below). The shortcut menu of “Climate Debate” under Projects. In the menu bar’s Project menu, most items have one of two targets. They either affect the active project or depend upon what you have selected within the sidebar. For instance, New Set, New Smart Set, and Attributes affect the active project, while the document commands (namely, Rename, Properties, Move to Group, Add to Set, Remove from Set, and Translate) work as in the document’s shortcut menu on the currently selected documents from the sidebar. Open lists the ten views of the project shelf. Edit Smart Set is for the smart set in the active tab. The delete command (⌘⌫) targets whichever item you clicked most recently in the sidebar. The command will read Delete Project, Delete Set, Delete Group, or Delete Document accordingly. If you attempt to delete a project or document, LemmaLoom will prompt for confirmation beforehand. Sets and groups will be removed without asking, though. Use Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z) afterwards to bring the set or group back.

The Project Properties dialog can be opened by choosing Properties from the shortcut menu of a project. With the same fields as New Project, it lets you change a project’s name, color, tags, and/or attributes. The Save button stays disabled until Name has some entry. Color changes the tint of the project’s box icon in the sidebar. It also tints the highlight behind the icon when the project is the active one. The star of any favorite project in the Projects list assumes the tint too. The Tags window counts the Tags labeling the project. A query over all projects in Window ▸ Queries can find projects by them. In Attributes, there will be a list displaying the names and types of each attribute found within a project. Each item has a remove button (Remove attribute) at the end. Creating an attribute involves clicking Add Attribute. Project Properties for “Climate Debate”, with its four attributes and their remove buttons. All modifications will be applied at once using Save, as a single step that Edit ▸ Undo Project Properties (⌘Z) takes back. Removing an attribute here takes it out of the project immediately once you hit Save; along with that, the attribute value from all the documents within the project will be deleted. In order to change only an attribute's name, type, or choices, use the Attributes window. See Changing an attribute in .

Right-click the project and choose Delete Project. Or click the project and choose Project ▸ Delete Project (⌘⌫). An alert names the project and warns that everything in it will be deleted. Click Delete. All documents of the project are erased along with the project itself. Their media files, translations, codings, memos, links, and bookmarks are erased too, as is everything made for the project as a whole. The same applies to its codes and code sets, sets and groups, and attributes and their values. The dictionaries and the queries saved in the project are erased too. When deleting the active project, the first project left in the list will become active. Once a project has been deleted, there's nothing left to restore from the undo history for it. To back up the active project, go to File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project.

Usually, everything within a project (codes, sets, groups, attributes, dictionaries, and saved queries) is isolated. Views generally consider only one project at a time. Some examples of this are the Codebook, Code Stats, the Code Matrix, word sketches, and Sketch Space. Some features reach across all of your projects. With these features, comparisons can be made between studies, or previously developed tools can be reapplied to other studies. Choosing All Projects in the scope menu at the top of Window ▸ Queries allows querying of the original documents of all your projects together at once. Details regarding this scope can be found in The Queries window and Scopes in . When using rules, testing of the Project field can only occur here. Only at this scope level can a Count or Compare group its results by project. The result list will consequently have a Project column. Some recipes even operate under this scope level, including Codings by Attribute, Rhetoric by Group, and Document Table. The Queries window with the scope at All Projects and a Count grouped by project. When saving a query, choosing All Projects in Available In makes the query available in every project. If saved as a lens in this manner, then this query can be enabled in any document. Refer to Saving queries in . Tags function this way already; they operate across every project at once. Every instance of a tag (“op-ed” in multiple projects, for example) is the same tag. Tags can also apply to projects as well as individual documents. In turn, a query across all projects can match either documents or projects with specified tags. Further details about tags across all projects can be found in One list for all projects in . Also shared across all projects are custom analyzers (); whatever is written in Window ▸ Analyzers belongs to the whole library and can run on documents in any project, and a query across all projects can count what such an analyzer finds. If the codebook, the code views, or word sketches need to span several studies, then the material should remain within a single project. Sets, groups, or an attribute can distinguish the studies.
Documents enter a project via import operations.  covers each form of material.

Clicking a document in the sidebar will open it in a tab directly above the reader and make that tab active. This applies to documents listed in a set as well. If the document is currently opened somewhere in the tab strip, selecting it again in the sidebar will merely make its existing tab active. From the keyboard, navigate the sidebar with the Up Arrow and Down Arrow keys; hitting Return will open the selected document. Detail views for the project shelf, sets, and tags all open in tabs in the tab strip as well. More information about this is available later in this chapter under The project shelf. When you have at least one tab open, the tab strip itself becomes visible, and you scroll it sideways once there are more tabs than can be displayed in a row. Two op-eds, the Codebook, and the “Activists” set in tabs, with “Hope Takes Work” in a preview tab. Navigating tabs from the keyboard can be done by choosing Window ▸ Show Next Tab (⇧⌘]) or Window ▸ Show Previous Tab (⇧⌘). Following the last tab leads you back to the first tab. When right-clicking on a tab, **Open in New Window**, **Open in Split View**, and **Close Tab** appear on the shortcut menu. When you choose **Open in New Window**, the document goes to the separate Document window. The Document window always contains a single document; opening a second document replaces the previous one. For a set or tag, **Open in New Window** will be restricted to those tabs showing **Word Sketch** or **Queries** content; for a shelf view, it opens the Codebook, Word Sketch, or Queries window. **Open in Split View** opens a side-by-side split view containing both your document and whichever other document is active. Split view is described in [. Open in New Window and Open in Split View can be accessed from the Window menu as well. Their usage changes when invoked from this menu; these commands apply their effect on the active tab. In addition, Open in Split View there lists the open documents that can go beside it.

Preview tabs have italicized titles, and occur whenever you open a result from a query, or display an occurrence from the word sketch of a set or the project itself. Subsequent results open in the same place in the strip, replacing any previous results there. To keep a preview tab, click on the tab, or select it via the commands Show Next Tab or Show Previous Tab. The title of the tab returns to its normal, upright state, and the tab stays open like any other tab. Clicking on the document within the sidebar will have the same effect. When a document containing a result is already opened in an ordinary tab, LemmaLoom displays the result in that tab. When the document is open in split view, the right-hand pane comes into focus.

If you click × in a tab, the tab is closed. Alternatively, pressing ⌘W (or choosing File ▸ Close Tab) will close the active tab. When this happens, whichever tab ends up being rightmost after the closure will become active. With a split view open, ⌘W in the right-hand pane will close the split view; elsewhere, ⌘W acts normally by closing the active tab. In split views, closing the final tab on the left causes the document in the right-hand pane to move to its location. While a tab is open, selecting File ▸ Close Window (⇧⌘W) will close the main window. In case there isn’t any open tab in the window, instead of Close Window you get to see File ▸ Close (⌘W). This command closes the window and, if it's the last LemmaLoom window, also quits LemmaLoom.

Documents can be selected in bulk. Once selected, the execution of a command occurs on each document simultaneously. In the Documents section, you can ⌘-click a document to add it to the selection. A second ⌘-click removes it from your selection. A ⇧-click selects a whole range of documents, from the document you clicked last to the one you click now. The range follows the list and includes documents in any closed group and translations underneath the originals. As you make selections, note the number of selected documents at the top of the shortcut menu before attempting to delete. A plain click on any document selects just that one document and opens it. The same clicks select documents under a set in the Sets section. When right-clicking on any document in your selection, you'll open the shortcut menu. At its head, there is the count of selected documents, for instance, 3 documents selected. If exactly two documents are selected, then the Open Side by Side command puts the one higher in the list in the main pane, while placing the lower one in split view. You can select Move to Group, choosing from Ungrouped, each possible group, and New Group. Choose Add to Set to see a list of each set you fill by hand and New Set from Documents. If a set already holds all selected documents, it appears disabled there. When a translation is among your selection, its original gets added. Export saves the selected documents in a LemmaLoom archive (see ). The menu ends with Delete Documents (see Deleting documents later in this chapter). The shortcut menu of six selected documents, headed “6 documents selected”, with Add to Set open.

Right-clicking on a single document in the Documents section will produce this shortcut menu for it: Command What it does Open in Split View Opens the document beside the active one. Disabled when no other document is active, or when this one is already in split view. Open Beside Original Shown for a translation. Opens the original on the left and the translation on the right. Rename Turns the name into a text field. Move to Group Moves the document and its translations into a group, or out of every group with Ungrouped. Sets Adds the document to a set, or makes a new set from it with New Set from Document. Properties Opens Document Properties (see Document properties below). Translate Translates the document. See . Export Saves the document in a LemmaLoom archive. Retry Indexing Appears when indexing failed, below a line that says why. Delete Document Deletes the document after asking (see Deleting documents later in this chapter). Translations travel together with their originals wherever you move them. Use Move to Group and Sets actions on the original document. When you require an additional translation for the document, translate the original document once again. Under any set, a document’s shortcut menu begins with Open; within a manually populated set, it ends with Remove from Set. Right-clicking “Running Out of Time” in the sidebar.

Right-click the document and choose Rename. Type the new name and press Return. Press Escape to restore the old name. Clicking elsewhere keeps the new name. Edit ▸ Undo Rename (⌘Z) restores the old name. Alternatively, you may rename your document in Document Properties.

Beyond the text itself, all the metadata LemmaLoom stores on a document can be found in Document Properties. For example, “Running Out of Time” from “Climate Debate” has the date August 21, 2024. It bears the tag “op-ed”. Its values for the project's four attributes will let you categorize it and compare it with the rest of the documents within the project. The properties of “Running Out of Time”, from Details down to Attributes. To modify a document’s properties: Right-click the document in the sidebar and choose Properties. Make your changes in Details, Organization, Attributes, Citation, and Indexing. Click Save. Save applies your changes as a single action. Edit ▸ Undo Document Properties (⌘Z) will revert all of them simultaneously. Cancel discards all of your changes and closes the dialog.

Name appears in the navigation sidebar, on the document's tab, as well as in the results of every analysis. Name must be filled for Save to be enabled. Authors contains one author per line. Add Author adds another line for an author. If multiple lines exist, each has a remove button (Remove author). Lines that are left empty are automatically deleted upon saving. Date refers to the date the document was recorded, written, or published. Date always contains a date for a document. For a document without a date, it initially has today’s date; this is the date which Save stores. Documents can be selected in smart sets and queries based on dates; therefore, select the appropriate date prior to saving.

Color sets the color for your document from the eleven colors available, or No color. Filtering documents based on color can be accomplished with smart sets and queries. Color affects both the icon for the document in the navigation sidebar and its tab highlight. Tags takes tags one-by-one. As soon as you finish entering your tag, hit the Return key or put a comma next to it to complete it. Entering just three characters brings up autocomplete suggestions for previous tags that match what you are entering; these matches ignore case differences. If you type in Viral, LemmaLoom automatically assigns the existing tag “viral”. There is also an × button beside every tag which removes the tag. Should the document happen to possess translations, then the document shares the same tags as its translations. Editing the tags for one affects all others.

In this part, the values of the attributes of this document are provided, with controls depending on their types. The checkbox control represents the value of a Boolean attribute; the date picker controls represent Date attributes; number controls represent Integer and Decimal attributes; and text controls represent Text attributes. Finally, Picker attributes are represented by menus of their choices that allow None as well. The addition of a value for another attribute requires these actions: Type the attribute's name in the empty field at the bottom. Suggestions appear as you type. If the name is new to the project, choose its Type. For a Picker, also type its choices, one per row. Click Add Attribute, or press Return. The attribute joins the list. Enter the value. When an attribute is made using this dialog, the attribute belongs to the whole project and no other documents currently hold a value for that attribute. The remove button (Remove attribute) next to a value deletes that attribute's value from this document without deleting the attribute altogether. The Add Attribute button is disabled if there isn't a name in the name field, if the attribute is already listed (Already added), or if a new picker has no choices (No options). Hover the mouse pointer over the Add Attribute button to discover which reason matches your situation. For setting an attribute value across multiple documents, visit the Attributes window. This lists the attribute values for all the documents side-by-side. See The Attributes window in .

Citation details include the Publisher, Publication, URL, and DOI fields, which tell you where the published document came from. The Publication field refers to where the document was published, such as in a journal or on a website. In the bundled “Climate Debate” project, the URL field for “Carbon Tax Debate” is the web address from which the document was imported. Both Import Document and Import from Web dialogs have these same fields. These can all be filled out at import time (refer to  for more details). Smart sets and queries may filter based upon citation details as well as the authors and the date. Exported projects in REFI-QDA file format save all citation details in each document's description. Programs supporting REFI-QDA are capable of recognizing these details within the exported documents' descriptions.

At the top of this section, a document imported without indexing shows Indexing is off. You will see an Index Now button there to begin the indexing process. Please refer to Importing without indexing in  for whether to leave indexing off at all. The grammar analysis a document gets depends on what you select in Language. Your choices here include English, German, and Chinese. Or, you could choose Automatic, which makes LemmaLoom detect the language based on the content of the text. If the language is detected to be French, for instance, it will be displayed along with the other options in the menu. Saving a change to your choice of language results in reindexing the document. Automatic will then make the language detected by LemmaLoom appear in the menu. Nonetheless, you can still read and code a document in any other language; its badge in the navigation sidebar shows Language not supported for indexing. Analyzers lists out the analyzers available to you in this language for your document. These consist of the built-in Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric analyzers, as well as any custom analyzers for this language you have defined (see ). Next to each analyzer is its status, which could be Done, Out of Date, Not Run, Running, or Failed. Results become Out of Date when a previous version of an analyzer was responsible for creating them, or due to editing a document that caused existing results to cover less than the entirety of the document's text. Hover the mouse pointer over rows with a status of Failed to find out the cause. The Run button enables you to update results of an analyzer whose results have become Out of Date or haven't been generated yet. This button remains disabled until indexing is complete for the document. The trash button (Remove Output) removes all results produced by this analyzer for this document; the analyzer won't run during subsequent indexing sessions until you click Run. Run, Remove Output, and Index Now actions take place immediately upon clicking. None of them require confirmation with Save. Patterns under Exclude from indexing prevent grammar analysis from analyzing specific text. Examples of such text are timestamps and labels identifying speakers in transcripts. Matching text stays visible in the reader, and you can still create codings within it. Patterns need to be defined using a regular expression notation, which describes a particular kind of text concisely. The example \d+:\d+\]` refers to timestamps such as `[12:04]`, whereby `\d+` matches one or several digits, whereas both `\[` and `\]` match the square brackets themselves. This is equivalent to the preset pattern **Timestamps [mm:ss]**. Type a pattern directly in the field provided and click **Add** or press Return. **Presets** provides access to five predefined patterns, including **Timestamps [hh:mm:ss]**, **Timestamps [mm:ss]**, **Speaker labels**, **Web addresses**, and **Email addresses**. After these comes the list of your saved patterns in Settings (see [). If a preset is already included in the list, Presets shows it disabled. The pattern Speaker labels catches numbered speaker labels such as Speaker 1:, while you should write your own custom pattern for named speakers. One example could be something like (Host|Activist|Skeptic):. The alternatives are separated with the vertical bar character. The Indexing section of the properties of “Carbon Tax Debate”, with a pattern typed and the Presets menu open. Under every pattern you define is an example matching it, in a line starting with Matches text like. Valid pattern appears under a valid pattern if it can't provide any examples. As you type, the field shows the same line under it. Invalid patterns will make LemmaLoom display the message Not a valid pattern below, and Add then stays disabled. Each pattern's row ends in a remove button (Remove pattern). Clicking Save also adds a valid pattern that's still in the field. Saved changes to patterns trigger indexing the document again. Citation and indexing details for “Carbon Tax Debate”.

LemmaLoom keeps track of where your document originates. It may be the name of the file or web page address your document came from. Smart sets and queries are equipped with two fields that rely on this metadata. For example, you could use Source File to locate all the documents you had imported from a file whose name contains report. Your document’s Format can be Text, PDF, Web Pages, Audio, or Video. If your document comes from an audio or video recording, its format depends on which media it came from. For documents from a REFI-QDA project, Source File is empty. Their Format is Text if they aren't recordings.

Right-click the document and choose Delete Document. For several documents, select them first (see Selecting several documents earlier in this chapter) and choose Delete Documents. With the documents selected under Documents in the sidebar, Project ▸ Delete Document or Delete Documents (⌘⌫) does the same. An alert names the document, or gives the number of documents, and warns that everything in them will be deleted. Click Delete. Deleting a document removes its text, media file, and grammar analysis. Its codings, memos, links, bookmarks, and attribute values will be removed too. Codes scoped to the document will be removed along with it. See Where a code can be used in . All sets that included the document will have it removed as well. If queries were saved for this document alone, they become project-level queries. Deleting an original deletes its translations too. Deleting a translation by itself moves codes scoped to it over to the original. If you delete a document accidentally, it can be restored via Edit ▸ Undo Delete Document (⌘Z), or Edit ▸ Undo Delete Documents should you delete multiple documents simultaneously. All the previously mentioned items will return alongside the document, with indexing being done in the background. The undo history exists until you quit LemmaLoom. See  for undo history and other undoable actions.

Groups serve as containers for organizing documents. Only one group may contain each document, while translations are always contained within the same group as their original. “Climate Debate” has two groups called “Print” and “Online”; they categorize documents according to whether they appeared in print or online. These groups are for reading the list. Comparisons in “Climate Debate” rely on the attribute “Stance” and document sets. Documents lists the groups chronologically based on creation time. Ungrouped documents follow below all of the existing groups. Whenever you open LemmaLoom, all groups begin collapsed; expand them by clicking their disclosure triangles. Creating a group involves these steps: Choose File ▸ New Group (⌥⌘N). A group called New Group appears, with its name selected. Type a name and press Return. When you have two or more documents selected, right-click on one of them and select Move to Group ▸ New Group. All of those documents move to the new group, and it is already open. You can immediately give the group its name. Project ▸ Move to Group ▸ New Group performs the function on a single selected document similarly. Move a single document via right-clicking on it and selecting the appropriate group under Move to Group. Notice that if the document already belongs to a group, that particular option will be disabled. Selecting the Ungrouped option moves the document alongside other ungrouped documents. Within its new group, a moved document appears as the last member. When importing a document using the Import Document dialog, you may specify the Group you wish to place the document in. Right-click the group for Rename and Delete Group. Alternatively, click on it and choose Project ▸ Delete Group (⌘⌫). Deleting the group results in moving its documents outside of it to join other documents that do not belong to any groups. Smart-set conditions that named the deleted group lose it, so a condition such as Group is any of “Print” is left with nothing chosen; such a condition evaluates to false against every document. Editing that smart set is necessary thereafter. Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z) allows undoing group changes made previously, deletions included. For analyzing the documents within a group, create a smart set whose Group condition names it. Please refer to Groups in . The resulting smart set will open in its own tab with access to the project shelf's views.

t: Sets and tags in the navigation sidebar
b: Each set under Sets displays its number of documents next to it. A set you fill manually has a stack icon next to it. There will be a filter icon next to a smart set instead. Clicking the triangle beside a set will display its list of documents, while clicking a document from that list will open it. Opening a set in its own tab requires a click on its name (refer to The project shelf below). New Set will create an empty set, with its name in an active text field. New Smart Set, meanwhile, will launch the editor for a new smart set's conditions. Each set has a shortcut menu with Open Set, Word Sketch, Rename, Edit (only applies to smart sets), Export, and Delete Set. More on sets can be found in . Right-clicking a document within a manually filled set will display Remove from Set. If multiple documents are selected under that set, they will all be removed. The shortcut menu of the “Activists” set. Translations belong to the same sets as their originals. Only the original document is listed in sets. Adding a translation to a set adds its original. Tags are listed under Tags. Clicking a tag opens a tab with the same ten views as a set, covering the tag's documents. Each tag has Word Sketch available via its shortcut menu, for a word sketch of its documents. Also available are Rename and Delete Tag, which work as in the Tags window below; either one changes the tag globally, across all projects.

In Window ▸ Tags, you will see the list of tags all your projects share, together with the number of times each tag is used. For example, there are three documents tagged “op-ed” in the project “Climate Debate”; namely, “Running Out of Time”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, and “Who Pays for the Transition”. There are two documents tagged “viral”, which are “Letter from the Climate Strike” and “Let's Not Panic”. You also rename, merge, and delete tags in this window. Each tag and its counts in the Tags window. The Tags window displays five counts adjacent to each tag, in the columns Projects, Documents, Codes, Memos, and Links. While the first count includes every project that uses the tag, whether on the project itself (in New Project or Project Properties) or on any of its documents, codes, memos, or links, the latter four counts are specific to the active project, allowing each of the numbers to correspond to the result obtained upon clicking. Even a tag that is found exclusively in other projects gets listed in the table; its counts under Documents, Codes, Memos, and Links equal 0. The Documents count reflects how many documents contain the tag, counting an original and its translations once, since they carry the same tags. Tags can be filtered by typing part of a name in Search. No distinction is made between capitalization in tags; “viral” is considered to be identical to “Viral”, and whichever spelling is seen more often is displayed. Tags can be selected via clicking, and opened in a tab within the main window by double-clicking or pressing Return. Clicking a tag under Tags in the navigation sidebar does precisely the same thing. Every count greater than zero can be clicked. Documents counts bring forth the tag's documents in a new tab, the same as double-clicking the row, whereas Codes counts filter the Codebook of the active project to what carries the tag; similarly Memos and Links counts filter the Memos and Links views. The × on the tag at the top of the view (Remove filter) returns to displaying all entries. A count under Projects displays a list of projects that use the tag; selecting one makes it the active project. The Codebook filtered by the tag “op-ed”, after adding that tag to the code “Costs” and clicking the tag's Codes count. Renaming tags can be performed as follows: Right-click the tag and choose Rename. Type the new name and press Return. Escape cancels. When renaming a tag, the new name applies to every project, document, code, memo, and link that has that tag attached to it. All smart set conditions and query rules which name the tag are updated accordingly. If the tag is open in a tab, the tab uses the new name. Renaming a tag with the name of another tag merges both tags under the latter's name. Choosing Delete from a tag's shortcut menu deletes the tag. Every occurrence of the tag gets deleted from everything that carries it across all projects. Any tab displaying the tag within the main window is closed automatically. Edit ▸ Undo Rename Tag (or Edit ▸ Undo Delete Tag, ⌘Z) reverts your last rename or deletion. The command is available while the Tags window is active.

The project shelf is used for interacting with the entire project itself. Within the Project section of the navigation sidebar are ten detail views available, each applying to all documents within the currently active project. Once clicked upon, these views open in tabs adjacent to your documents, titled according to which view they are (such as Code Stats). If you are interested in seeing one specific subset of your project, then you need to open either a set or tag of your choosing. Doing so results in the opening of these same ten detail views, now restricted only to the documents within this subset. Within the “Climate Debate” project, opening the “Activists” set will load these ten views exclusively on its six activist texts. Tabs for these subsets of documents feature both the name of the subset and its number of documents. The tab also has a row of buttons representing each view. By default, the Codebook view will be displayed, but clicking any of the others switches to that particular view. Should your window width become insufficient, a menu will replace these buttons. Code Stats for the “Activists” set, open in a tab. View What it shows Described in Codebook The code tree with each code's number of segments. For the selected code, its description, its segments, documents, and coverage in the scope, the documents that use it, and the codes it occurs with.  Codings Every coded segment in the scope with its code and document. You can search and filter the list, and open a segment in its document.  Memos The memos in the scope, with the document and code each one belongs to.  Links The links between passages in the scope, with both of their ends.  Code Stats How often each code is applied and how much text it covers, with breakdowns by attribute.  Code Matrix A table of how often each code is applied in each document, with a row for each code. Group columns by combines the documents by an attribute, group, language, or format.  Relations A table of how often codes overlap in the same passages.  Word Sketch For a word you choose, the words it combines with, grouped by grammatical relation, across the scope.  Dictionaries The project's dictionaries, and counts of each category's terms across the scope.  Queries The query builder, searching the documents in the scope.  When opening a view in its own window beside the reader, use Open in a window. This button looks like two diagonal arrows and sits at the right end of the bar above the view. The Word Sketch window will contain Word Sketch, whereas the Queries window contains Queries. All eight other views will open within the Codebook window; this window contains buttons for each of the ten views aligned horizontally at its top. From a set or tag tab, only Word Sketch and Queries will open in their respective windows. This action can either be performed from the button or by right-clicking on the tab itself and choosing Open in New Window. You can also open the Codebook window using the menu item Window ▸ Codebook or by right-clicking on the project and choosing Codebook. The Codebook window with “Urgency” selected, and the ten view buttons along its top.

In LemmaLoom, work begins by ingesting the content of your material into the project itself. Files, web pages, and recordings are all imported as documents. Then reading, coding, and analysis take place the same way for each type. Depending on your source, LemmaLoom automates varying degrees of processing before ingestion. A plain text file, for instance, comes in untouched. Importing a PDF document or a web page means that the text is automatically extracted for you by LemmaLoom. An audio or video document results in automatic transcription.

Material Command What the project keeps Plain text files File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I) The text PDF files File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I) The text of the pages Web pages File ▸ Import ▸ Web Pages (⌥⇧⌘I) The text of the article Audio and video files File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I) A transcript, and a copy of the recording for playback REFI-QDA projects and codebooks File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Project or REFI-QDA Codebook See  LemmaLoom archives File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive See  The example project File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project A new project, “Climate Debate”, already indexed Attribute values in a spreadsheet Import in the project's Attributes window Values for documents already in the project Use plain text in UTF-8 encoding whenever you can. With a plain text import, LemmaLoom keeps exactly what was typed. However, some of your material may come from a PDF-only source such as a published report. After importing your PDF, check whether your paragraphs got imported correctly. LemmaLoom can import web articles if it can access them without a login. When a web article is behind a sign-in, save a PDF using your browser and then import it. If you plan on playing a recording back while reading and coding it, import it directly into LemmaLoom. When playback isn't important, a typed transcript may be imported as a plain text file. REFI-QDA is the standard format used for exchange between LemmaLoom and other qualitative data analysis software packages. Use REFI-QDA for exchanging projects and codebooks. You can also import files directly from the Finder. Double-click any .llz LemmaLoom archive file, .qdpx REFI-QDA project file, or .qdc REFI-QDA codebook file. Where they will end up depends on their content. A REFI-QDA project will always be added as a new project, and so will an archived project file. Codebooks and archive files of a set or of documents are added to whatever project is currently selected in the navigation sidebar at the time.
