Ensure your current selection is correct before importing. Most examples provided in this guide are from “Climate Debate”. You can import the project using File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. This project will arrive ready for use with full indexing already done, in the interface language. Most documents are plain text imports; specifically, the op-eds, columns, blog posts, and one speech are. The remainder is a PDF report, a news article taken from the internet, and a radio debate recording. Each document must belong to only one project. The Documents and Web Pages menu options remain disabled until you select a project in the sidebar first. The Activity window provides the same two commands and also includes the menu showing the project's name. See The Activity window in the latter half of this chapter. LemmaLoom can generate translations based off existing documents within your project. Each generated translation will appear below its source document. As seen in “Climate Debate”, “Running Out of Time (German)” is listed beneath “Running Out of Time”. See . A translation you import from outside acts as a regular document. The File menu with Import open.

In an import dialog for a PDF or web page, there will always be a source preview at the top. This preview provides information about your source before it has been imported into LemmaLoom. The source preview can reveal issues, such as a wrong file or unreadable text, prior to importing. The text layer of a PDF contains actual readable text and not an image representation of the document's pages. Many scans will lack this layer. Transcript is a term used in LemmaLoom to refer to the output text generated by LemmaLoom based on recordings or media items. Every transcription has many transcript segments, usually one sentence long, that correspond to specific points in time in media. Every passage in the transcript is tied to its respective place in media, and includes information such as the speaker, starting time point, and ending time point. Grammar analysis of your documents in LemmaLoom, called indexing, involves breaking down your text into sentences and tokens (words and punctuation marks), determining how those tokens depend on each other and group into phrases, and tagging tokens with their respective part-of-speech tags. New documents are indexed in the background upon import, unless you uncheck the Index for grammar analysis option when importing them. See After import later in this chapter. Analyzers look for specific linguistic features once indexing has finished, and annotate the passages they find. Two examples are Metadiscourse and Rhetoric.

Text files, PDFs, and recordings share the same command to bring them into LemmaLoom. Mixing all three file types is possible in one selection of your files. “Radio Debate” in the “Climate Debate” example comes from an audio file, whereas “Heat Wave Report 2024” comes from a PDF file. Meanwhile, the eleven commentaries in the example come from plain-text files. To import documents: In the sidebar, select the project. Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I). Select the files and click Open. The Import Document dialog opens for the first file. Check the name and fill in whatever you know about the document (see The Import Document dialog below). Click Import. If you chose more than one file, the dialog opens again for the next one. A counter displays in the top-right of your current dialog when importing multiple documents, displaying the position of the current file versus the total number to import. The counter displays 2 of 6, for instance. Skip skips the current document and loads the next in the queue, while Cancel cancels the current document and everything after it, then closes the dialog. Previously imported documents from the batch continue to live inside the project normally. Work freely while imports occur since they run in the background. Imports of text documents populate the sidebar almost immediately, unlike others which show a progress row at the end of the Documents section until finished. A progress ring appears during an import process; if there is no percent completed display, as in some stages of processing a recording, the progress icon takes the form of a spinner. Hover the mouse pointer over a progress row to see the current stage of importation, e.g., Reading PDF or Transcribing speech. A percentage appears too if one is available. The sidebar while “Radio Debate” is imported, with a progress row at the end of the Documents section. Imports execute in one-by-one order according to the sequence of your clicks on Import; thus a typed document confirmed after a lengthy recording is imported only after the recording's transcription completes. Before attempting to import a recording, first import the typed documents you plan to work on immediately in LemmaLoom. Quitting LemmaLoom terminates the currently executing import process along with those waiting behind it. Any document imported prior stays in the project normally, but those awaiting import must be reimported later. Closing the final window in LemmaLoom counts as quitting. Once imports commence, allow them to complete entirely without interruption. Import operations terminate prematurely upon encountering errors. When this happens, a pop-up dialog titled Something went wrong informs you of the issue preventing the operation. LemmaLoom queues these error messages until the completion of all remaining dialogs within the current batch, then shows them together. The Something went wrong dialog after importing an empty file, “Radio Debate.m4a”. When importing a file, most earlier steps in the project's undo history are deleted. You must therefore undo any changes you still want undone prior to importing, since undo may no longer be available for them afterward. Should you discover any documents which ought not to be part of the project, delete them. See .

All documents except web pages are imported using the dialog Import Document. Web pages are imported using the dialog Import from Web. PDF and web documents both receive a source preview at the top as well. While most properties can be changed afterwards via Document Properties, moving the document to another group can be done by right-clicking the document in the sidebar and selecting Move to Group. If you're unsure of any property, skip it. For instance, each of the eleven commentary texts within the example project “Climate Debate” contains data regarding each of the four attributes defined within the project. Each document has a publication date and belongs to either the “Print” or the “Online” group. Here “A Mayor's Promise” is the first of six documents imported together. Its “Stance” and “Readership” fields are already filled in. Importing the first of six activist texts. Name is based on the file name without its extension. Running Out of Time.txt becomes “Running Out of Time”. The Name is displayed in the navigation sidebar, in tabs, and in every results table. When the Name field is left blank, the Import button stays disabled. Authors contains one entry per author. Click Add Author to add any additional authors. Every document possesses a Date, which may also be queried and selected by smart sets. LemmaLoom determines Date automatically for PDFs and web pages when it can. For text files and media, the initial Date is the current date. A date attribute, e.g., “Publication Date”, is separate from Date. You provide “Publication Date” manually, for example when the document requires a second date. Group places the document inside of one of the groups in the project, such as “Print”. Ungrouped leaves the document at the root level of the Documents section. Color changes the tint of the document's icon in the navigation sidebar. Tags can take as many tags as needed. Type in the tag and hit Return (or a comma). As you start typing, LemmaLoom provides suggestions for any previously used tags based on the one tag vocabulary that all your projects share. See . This is where the document receives its values for its attributes. Attributes are the variables describing properties of the whole document. Examples include an op-ed's “Stance” and “Readership”. Type the name of an attribute in the field at the bottom of the section. As you type, LemmaLoom suggests attribute names from this project and your other projects. Each suggestion shows its type. If the project already has an attribute of that name, click Add Attribute. A row appears for it. Enter or choose the value there. If the name is new, choose a Type from Text, Integer (a whole number), Decimal, Boolean (yes or no), Date, or Picker (one of a fixed list of choices). For a Picker, also type the choices, one per row. Click Add Attribute and enter the value in the new row. The attribute itself is created for the whole project when you import. Selecting a suggested name from another project means importing its type and choices as well. Deleting a row can be accomplished by clicking on its remove button found at the end of each row. The Attributes section of the Import Document dialog while “Read” is typed, with the suggestion “Readership · Integer” below the field. The Attributes section of the Import Document dialog with the new name “Region” typed, Type set to Picker, and the field for the choices below. The dialog starts clean for each document file included in the batch process. Your grouping settings, colors, tags, attribute values, languages, analyzers, and exclusion patterns will be reset. To assign attribute values to multiple documents simultaneously, consider importing a spreadsheet afterward, as discussed in Importing attribute values from a spreadsheet later in this chapter. If the source is published, bibliographic information should be entered in the fields labeled Publisher, Publication, URL, and DOI. Publication stores the name of the container in which the source has been published, such as the journal or website. Some fields may be automatically completed by LemmaLoom for PDFs and web pages. The last section contains Language, Index for grammar analysis, Analyzers, and Exclude from indexing. See Choosing the language, Analyzers and indexing, and Excluding text from indexing.

Language determines which grammatical analysis will be performed on your documents. You can either choose English, German, or Chinese, or you can leave Language set to Automatic. With Automatic selected, LemmaLoom will identify the language based on the first 4,096 characters of the document (or several hundred words); with a recording, it bases the decision on the transcription. See How transcription works below in this chapter. When you choose English, German, or Chinese instead of Automatic, LemmaLoom skips the recognition step altogether. With the Automatic setting, a German document starting with an extensive English summary may be indexed as English throughout, for instance. Manually specify the language for any document whose opening differs from the rest. Documents in languages other than English, German, or Chinese are imported but stay unindexed. You can observe their index status on the reader's status bar, where text like No grammar analysis for French shows this. You can still view and code them. To fix a wrong guess, set the correct Language parameter in Document Properties for LemmaLoom to re-index the document. The language displays in the navigation sidebar next to each document as a two-letter language code (e.g., EN for English, DE for German). Hover your mouse pointer over these codes to get the actual name of the language used in the document.

Index for grammar analysis begins pre-checked. If you wish to read and code documents without grammar analysis, however, you may uncheck this checkbox, delaying the process until such time when grammar analysis becomes necessary. Once a document has been added in this manner, you will notice that the reader's status bar shows Indexing is off for the document. To index it, click Index Now there or in its Document Properties dialog. The status bar of “Science Is Never Settled” imported without grammar analysis, reading Indexing is off with the Index Now link. Analyzers lists what will run after a document's indexing completes. Cohesion tracks each sentence back to previous sentences through ties such as pronouns and repetition of words. Metadiscourse tags words in speech and writing used to comment on statements made in the discourse itself. Such examples could be hedges, boosters, and connectives. Finally, Rhetoric analyzes the presence of the passive voice and other devices.  and  visualize findings from these analyzers. Custom analyzers, written in Window ▸ Analyzers, follow directly afterward in the list. See . By default, with Language set to Automatic, LemmaLoom offers you the full list of available analyzers. Choosing a particular language will filter this list to the analyzers capable of handling it. Each of the analyzers is checked at first and will operate upon the document. Deselecting one skips it for this document; Document Properties can still run it later. Unchecking the Index for grammar analysis checkbox will disable everything in the list.

The problem with typed transcripts lies in the fact that they often contain extra text beyond whatever was said in the recording. These may take on many forms, such as time stamps enclosed in brackets, like 00:12:31]`. They may be speaker labels such as `Host:` and `Skeptic:` which precede every turn in a transcript. Keeping such labels will increase the number of words. Imagine that a typed transcript of the “Radio Debate” were to prefix every turn with `Host:`, `Activist:`, or `Skeptic:`. Then the top three nouns in that transcript would be *activist*, *skeptic*, and *host*. This distorts keyword lists and [word sketches. When generating its own transcripts from recordings, LemmaLoom preserves its speakers in the form of codes and transcript segments. See Speakers later in this chapter. In order to avoid timestamps and labels in grammar analysis, use Exclude from indexing. This means that excluded texts will persist inside documents for reading and coding but be kept out of indexing and therefore grammar analysis. You need to define what to exclude via a regular expression. Regular expressions are patterns that match entire families of text strings. If you've never made one yourself, start with the basic pieces below. Piece Matches d any digit + after something one or more of it in a row [ and ] an opening and a closing square bracket (the backslash makes them literal) . a period (a bare . matches any character) S any character that is not a space ? after something that thing or nothing When looking at the pattern piece by piece, [d+:d+:d+] starts off with an opening bracket. Then follow three sequences of one or more digits that are colon-separated. Finally, there is a closing bracket. This would match something like [00:12:31] or [1:05:09]. But the pattern does not account for anything with only a single colon, like [12:31]. In parentheses, the pipe symbol separates alternative possibilities. (Host|Activist|Skeptic): represents Host:, Activist:, and Skeptic:. Note that a pattern is case-sensitive; hence host: will not match the above pattern. If you wish to ignore capitalization, precede the pattern with (?i). On its own, the caret ^ character signifies the beginning of the entire string. The (?m)^(Host|Activist|Skeptic): pattern represents Host:, Activist:, and Skeptic: only if they occur at the beginning of lines. To add a pattern: Type it in the field under Exclude from indexing. The line below the field shows an example of text it matches, Valid pattern if it has no example to show, or Not a valid pattern. Click Add, or press Return. There is a Presets menu next to Add. The Presets menu provides pre-existing patterns: Preset Pattern Timestamps [hh:mm:ss] [d+:d+:d+] Timestamps [mm:ss] [d+:d+] Speaker labels Speaker d+: Web addresses https?://[^sp{Han}u3000-u303FuFF00-uFFEF]+ Email addresses [^sp{Han}u3000-u303FuFF00-uFFEF]+@[^sp{Han}u3000-u303FuFF00-uFFEF]+.[^sp{Han}u3000-u303FuFF00-uFFEF]+ The Presets menu in the Import Document dialog for “Radio Debate”, listing the preset patterns for exclusion. You can create your own presets based on patterns you frequently encounter. Open the General pane of Settings. In the Exclusion Presets area, click Add Preset, give your new preset a name, and enter its pattern. Your presets come after LemmaLoom's default presets in the Presets menu. The Exclusion Presets section of the General pane in Settings, with the “Transcriber notes” preset. A timestamp pattern added under Indexing. The patterns will be saved with the document itself. They may be edited later in the Document Properties dialog. Upon editing, LemmaLoom reindexes the document.

All text files with extensions such as .txt enter as-is. Other text-only files such as Markdown (.md), for example, enter in the same way, including any special characters like # and . LemmaLoom reads text files as UTF-8. A text file with an older encoding scheme than UTF-8, such as Windows Latin 1, may show up with accents replaced by � symbols. To fix this, re-save the file with a text editor using UTF-8 encoding and import it again. Documents saved as either .docx or .doc must be exported from Word before importing. Export as plain text UTF-8 or PDF and opt for the former where possible since it retains your paragraphs intact. A PDF only retains information about each line of text in a page; thus, LemmaLoom will need to recreate the original paragraphs from the imported data. See How text is extracted later in this chapter. RTF and HTML files can likewise be selected in the file dialog, being text files themselves. They retain all their formatting codes upon entering. Be sure to export an RTF document as plain text before importing into LemmaLoom. Web pages may be imported using File ▸ Import ▸ Web Pages. It is up to LemmaLoom to discern between paragraphs within text files. Knowing the location of paragraphs matters for the paragraph numbers in the reader, as well as for queries that use the Paragraphs unit. First off, LemmaLoom considers whether blank lines are present. If there is any blank line, then only blank lines separate paragraphs. Single line breaks in documents with blank lines belong inside a paragraph. Without any blank line, every line is its own paragraph, so a transcript typed with one line per turn gets one paragraph per turn.

PDFs may contain actual text, scanned page images, or a mixture of both. Any text layer in the file is parsed directly, while any page without a text layer undergoes text recognition. The project then only keeps the text.

When importing a PDF, LemmaLoom first reviews the document before actually allowing you to do so. At this stage, the source preview displays Reading PDF while Import remains disabled. After review, the completed preview tells you the file name along with the total number of pages and word count in the text layer. For “Heat Wave Report 2024”, it would say 6 pages · 504 words. Pages without a usable text layer are counted separately (e.g., 2 pages need text recognition). The opening lines from the text appear below that. Review the opening lines to ensure you have the correct file, and to make sure that readable text exists within the first few lines. Word counts are based on pages having a text layer; hence, the word count for “Heat Wave Report 2024” excludes two pages needing text recognition. Note, however, that the importation itself recognizes words on these pages and includes them in the document. The heat wave report's source preview, with two scanned pages. LemmaLoom extracts information from your PDF to populate the dialog. Name pulls the PDF's title field unless it is a placeholder title or you have already changed the name. Titles that qualify as placeholders include “Untitled”, any filename with the extension .docx, and any title beginning with “Microsoft Word -”. Authors retrieves the authors' names in the PDF's author field. It splits multiple names at semicolons. Date captures the creation date in the PDF. DOI captures the first Digital Object Identifier found in the PDF's subject field or on the first two pages with text in your PDF.

When you click Import, LemmaLoom will process the PDF page by page, while the navigation sidebar row and the Activity window indicate Reading PDF with a percentage. The text layer of each PDF page is tested before the page begins getting processed. A successful test requires at least 20 letters per page and a ratio lower than 1 unreadable character per 3 letters on average per page. An unreadable character refers to the kind that copies out as a box or �. If a page tests successfully, its text will be extracted line by line. Anything else is treated as a scan. A scan is rendered into images for text recognition, which often commits errors in cases where scans are not very high-quality or contain many tables. Compare results with the original. A PDF only knows about lines. LemmaLoom recreates paragraphs based on the line structure. Lines that separate from each other vertically by a greater margin mark the start of a new paragraph. An indented opening line and a short line that ends a sentence will also mark the beginning of a new paragraph. Whenever the next line begins with a lowercase character, any hyphenation that ended the previous line gets eliminated. “Infra-” and “structure” will become “infrastructure”. Similarly, compounds split at their own hyphen have those hyphens stripped away; “long-” and “term” turn into “longterm”. Pay attention to instances like this. A paragraph may also continue onto the following page should the next page start with a lowercase character and the previous page end without terminal punctuation. In Chinese text, no spaces separate lines that get joined together. Page numbers and running heads are detected and stripped from documents. Running heads refer to titles that recur repeatedly throughout the document at the top or bottom of each page. Instances in the form of short paragraphs at the heads or feet of pages can be running heads. Such cases will qualify as a running head if the same text repeats itself on at least 40 percent of the pages. Numerical digits and capitalization do not affect this comparison. Therefore, “Heat Wave Report 2024, page 3” and “Heat Wave Report 2024, page 4” will count as identical text. On six pages total, “Heat Wave Report 2024” qualifies as having a running head if the same text occurs on at least 3 pages out of 6. LemmaLoom finds that 40 percent of 6 equals 2.4, rounding up to 3 pages. Page numbers appearing alone (“12”, “iv”, “Page 12”, “Seite 12”) get stripped from the heads and feet of every page. Text flow follows the order established in the PDF, meaning lines may be ordered incorrectly relative to each other due to multiple-column pages and tables. Footnotes and captions might also disrupt text order in this way. Review the results for inconsistencies in reading order and fix them where needed. For instructions, see .
The imported document is just the article on the web page and not the navigational elements, advertisements, or comments surrounding it.

“Carbon Tax Debate” is a news piece in “Climate Debate”, imported from the web. Its web address is preserved in URL. The first Import from Web dialog with two web addresses, one per line, and the addresses LemmaLoom recognized below the field. A news article on the carbon tax, ready to import. To import a web page: Select the project in the sidebar. Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Web Pages (⌥⇧⌘I). Paste one or more web addresses into the Import from Web dialog, one per line. Below the field, LemmaLoom lists the addresses it recognized. It adds https:// where it's missing and lists a repeated address only once. Click Continue. A second Import from Web dialog opens for the first address. As LemmaLoom loads the page and extracts the article, the source preview shows Fetching page and then Reading article. Once the preview shows the article, check the title and the site. Check the word count and the opening lines too. Then fill in the rest of the dialog. Click Import. If you entered several addresses, the dialog opens again for the next one. It has Skip and a counter, as for files.

When LemmaLoom imports a web page, it loads the page in a private browsing session. LemmaLoom will scroll to the end of the page once and wait briefly, to extract the text that loads on scrolling. LemmaLoom then extracts the article. In the article document, the text appears in reading order. Any images, videos, forms, and embedded content get stripped away. Every heading, paragraph, list item, and table cell becomes a paragraph in the document. A first paragraph that merely repeats the title is removed. The source preview provides metadata regarding the word count and name of the site. The article title is included, followed by any description of the article that exists in the page itself. If no summary exists in the page itself, then the initial text is provided instead. The import dialog will only fill up missing fields with the available data from the page. Name gets filled with the article title. Authors become whoever is listed as author on the page. Publication becomes the name of the website, while URL becomes the page link (or the page's own preferred address). Date is the exception here; if the publication date is stated explicitly in the page, that becomes the date regardless of what you had put earlier.

LemmaLoom accepts recording files of any format your macOS computer understands how to decode. For audio recording formats, these include MP3, M4A, WAV, and AIFF; for video recordings, MP4 and MOV formats are accepted. LemmaLoom transcribes the speech in the recording and automatically assigns speaker codes accordingly. Additionally, a copy of the file is kept for playback at any point while reading the transcript. Should you wish to attach a pre-existing transcription to its recording, both can be imported at once as part of a REFI-QDA project. More information can be found in Importing a REFI-QDA project in . Imported alone, a transcript is a text file without playback.

In LemmaLoom, “Radio Debate” from “Climate Debate” is an imported audio file featuring three speakers, namely, a host, an activist, and a skeptic. Its transcript is linked to the recording, so any passage can be played back as you read it. The speakers are kept as codes. To import an audio or video file: In the sidebar, select the project. Choose File ▸ Import ▸ Documents (⇧⌘I). Select the recording and click Open. In the Import Document dialog, check the name and fill in the details. Leave Language at Automatic. Click Import. There is a row at the end of the Documents section representing the recording; a waveform symbol represents an audio file whereas a film strip icon represents a video. If you hover your mouse pointer over the row, you’ll notice a tooltip with information about the currently active step. Alternatively, check the Activity window. Step What happens Preparing LemmaLoom copies the file into its library and reads its length. Extracting audio The sound track is read and prepared for transcription. Downloading speech model The first time Apple Speech transcribes a language, its speech model is downloaded. A percentage shows the progress. Transcribing speech The speech is written down. A percentage shows the progress. Identifying speakers The voices are told apart and each sentence is given to a speaker. Once all steps are completed, the newly generated document replaces the row entry, and the indexing phase commences. Transcription time varies according to your particular machine; import just one file to get a rough estimate prior to importing many files. Recording files require audio tracks; files lacking these cannot be imported, displaying instead a message stating The file has no audio track to transcribe. Empty files return messages naming the file, e.g., “Radio Debate.m4a” is empty.

LemmaLoom can transcribe speech in English, German, and Chinese. The transcription model listens to the initial 30 seconds to determine which language your recording is in, then transcribes everything in that one language. Chinese transcriptions are rendered using simplified characters. There are three models you may use. To change your current transcription model to any of these three, select your choice of Model under Transcription on the General pane of Settings. The default model is Apple Speech and the quickest. Compared to Whisper Large v3, Whisper Large v3 Turbo is somewhat quicker yet perhaps slightly less accurate on hard files. Chinese-language recordings are transcribed solely via Whisper regardless of which model you've selected, Apple Speech included. Any alteration of the model impacts future transcriptions alone. The Model menu under Transcription in the General pane of Settings, listing Apple Speech, Whisper Large v3 Turbo, and Whisper Large v3. Names, terminology, dialect, multiple voices speaking simultaneously, and background noises tend to produce errors in speech recognition software most often. Prior to proceeding with coding, review the transcript while listening to the recording, editing errors accordingly. See . When editing, your codings, transcript segments, and additional annotations migrate with your edits.

After the transcripts of your audio and/or video files are created, LemmaLoom identifies voices and codes them based on who is speaking in each sentence. Once a second or third (or more) voice is detected, the sentences are assigned to their respective voices, and those speakers are labeled “Speaker 1”, “Speaker 2”, etc., according to how early each speaker starts talking in the conversation. LemmaLoom will automatically generate a code named “Speakers”, with subcodes for each voice applied to their turns. Each turn represents a series of sentences spoken by a single person consecutively. Each subcode receives its own color and is assigned to every turn by its speaker. Codes here belong solely to one document. See . The Codebook of “Climate Debate” with the code “Speakers” and its subcodes “Activist”, “Host”, and “Skeptic”. The “Radio Debate” is used again in the example below. In it, the host talks first, followed by the activist, followed by the skeptic. If you imported a file where the host came first, followed by the activist, and then the skeptic afterward, your “Speaker 1” code will refer to the host, your “Speaker 2” code will refer to the activist, and finally, your “Speaker 3” code will refer to the skeptic. Afterward, you would rename the three codes to “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic” respectively in the codebook. In the example project, the “Radio Debate” already has named speakers in its codes and transcript segments. When you rename a speaker code, only the name of the code changes, not the speaker label in your transcripts' segments. The player bar and the Speaker field of queries will still display “Speaker 1”, “Speaker 2”, and “Speaker 3”. Speaker detection only has the voice itself to detect from. Similar-sounding voices and short interjections can confuse this process. The overlapping of multiple voices and background sounds can also disrupt this process. On occasion, the detection process may split one voice into two different speakers. Compare your speaker codes with the actual recording. Recode any section attributed to the incorrect speaker. When a voice becomes split between two speakers, merge the speaker codes back together. Where there is only one voice detected in total, no speakers or speaker codes get added at all.

Transcripts consist of segments, typically one per sentence. Every segment contains the start time and end time for the segment, and its speaker when more than one voice is detected. Your transcript text is organized according to these segments. When two consecutive sentences belong to the same speaker, they are kept together within the same paragraph. However, if the speaker switches or pauses beyond 1.5 seconds, a new paragraph starts. Segments link text with recording. Segments give information to the player telling which part of the transcription is currently playing. Additionally, you can move directly to any part in a transcript. Queries can operate on segments via the Speaker Turns unit. See . The Speaker Turns unit holds an item for each segment. A turn of five sentences translates to five items. Items contain the fields Speaker, Start, End, and Duration.

Open a recording document, and the player bar appears directly above your text, as seen in . This player bar contains controls for playing a recording, time positions, and information on who spoke the current passage being listened to. When dealing with indexed documents, clicking a word will take the player to the beginning of that particular word's segment. While indexing a document, which happens again after you edit it, moving around in the player is done solely through the slider. To the right of play, the Scroll with audio button enables scrolling with playback. As you play a recording in the document, the reader shows the passage being played and keeps it in view. This button is initially off. Once enabled, it remains enabled for every recording until you disable it manually. Passages scrolled with audio can appear as Spotlight (default), Solid block, or Highlight. Under Audio Playback on the Reader pane of Settings, choose the appearance of passages scrolled with audio. The Audio Playback menu in the Reader pane of Settings, with Spotlight checked and Solid block and Highlight below it. With videos, the viewer appears above the text. Resize the viewing area of a video using the divider located below it. The chevron button collapses the player down to its controls. Next to it, the video placement button switches a video between playing above text and playing to the left of text. “Radio Debate” playing with Scroll with audio on.

All imported recordings are copied into the library and played from there. For more on the library, refer to . After importing has been completed, you may freely move or delete the original file. When you export your project into a LemmaLoom archive, the exported project retains all recordings within it. See .

t: Importing attribute values from a spreadsheet
b: An attribute represents factual information about your document. Stance and readership are two examples. The outlet and publication date also fit. Refer to  for their types and choices. Should you have these facts stored in a spreadsheet elsewhere, LemmaLoom will import them all at once, associating each row with a document based on its title.

Export your spreadsheet as either tab separated or comma separated (CSV). Regardless of whether it’s tab or comma separated, there must be a first row of column names. One column should have the titles of each document, precisely as seen in the sidebar, though capitalization may differ. Additionally, each attribute gets a column as well. A file for the “Climate Debate” texts could include lines like these: The separator will automatically be calculated for you by LemmaLoom. Comma, semicolon, and tab separators will work fine. Whichever occurs most frequently on the first line gets used. If your spreadsheet program writes sep=; on the first line, LemmaLoom will follow that instruction as well. Values which include the separator go in double quotes. Files are capable of using UTF-8, UTF-16, and the old Windows/Mac character sets. Dates should always be written 2024-08-21 (year-month-day). Dates frequently become localized to something like 8/21/2024 during spreadsheet processing. Make sure to format the date column as text prior to saving the file. Numbers need to use a point for decimals (7.5), rather than a comma. Do not write numbers with leading zeroes or thousand separators. 7 and 412000 are valid; 07 and 412,000 are not. With Export in the Attributes window, you obtain a file that has correct document titles. This export saves the current table as a CSV file, in which a “Document” column holds your document names, and another column exists for each attribute in your project. Complete the values using spreadsheet software of your choice, then import it back into LemmaLoom. Export won't appear until your project contains at least one attribute, so click Add Attribute before exporting. The Attributes window of “Climate Debate”, with Import and Export above the table of attribute values.

Select the project in the sidebar and choose Project ▸ Attributes, or right-click the project and choose Attributes. Click Import in the Attributes window. Choose the CSV file and click Open. The Import Attributes dialog opens. In Document, check the column that holds the titles. LemmaLoom picks the column that matches the most documents. Below the column, it says how many rows found their document (10 of 11 rows matched, for example). Under Attributes, go through the columns. For each one, choose the attribute it fills, New Attribute, or Skip. For a new attribute, check the Type too. Click Import. LemmaLoom writes the values and closes the dialog. In the undo history, the import takes place as a single transaction. Edit ▸ Undo Import Attributes (⌘Z) reverts every attribute created and every value written during the import process simultaneously. Importing attribute values, ten of eleven rows matched.

When trying to match a document for each row, LemmaLoom checks the Document column of each row against the list of titles in your project, ignoring case sensitivity and leading/trailing whitespace on both ends. Any values written to an original document will be carried forward to its translations. A row won't match a document if its title isn't listed anywhere within the project, or if multiple documents share that title. Also, multiple rows cannot refer to the same document; otherwise, none will be kept. In the example file provided, there are eleven rows under the headings. Ten out of eleven rows match the documents correctly. However, the “Lets Not Panic” row does not have a match. The document has the title “Let's Not Panic” instead (the difference being an apostrophe mark before “s”). This is indicated by the dialog reporting 10 of 11 rows matched. Rename the document or correct the file, then import again.

Each column starts with a default assignment. If the column’s heading matches the name of an existing attribute (disregarding case sensitivity), then the column is assigned to fill this attribute. Columns without headings, or values, are assigned the value Skip; all others will be assigned New Attribute, which will attempt guessing its data type based on its values. If every value is The type is a date written as 2024-08-21 Date true, false, yes, or no Boolean a whole number Integer a number, at least one of them with a decimal point Decimal one of at most 12 different values, at least one of which occurs more than once Picker anything else Text The guess skips all empty cells. Be sure to examine your guessed types carefully prior to importing. If you were working in a project with no attributes, the example file would provide “Stance” with a Picker type, since its two values, “Activist” and “Skeptic”, each repeat. “Readership” becomes an Integer type while “Publication Date” becomes Date. “Outlet” becomes another Picker. The eleven rows list six outlets, which repeat sometimes. Should you anticipate that additional outlets will be freely added later on, you should choose Text for “Outlet”; the project “Climate Debate” uses this strategy. Each value in a cell is assigned individually to documents while ignoring empty cells. An empty cell leaves the existing value untouched. Non-empty cell values overwrite whatever value the document currently has. Value assignment is skipped whenever the value doesn’t match the type of the attribute in question, and the dialog counts this in the column's row (1 skipped, etc.). With “Readership” as the Integer type, cells containing “about 400,000” are skipped. Boolean attributes accept 1, 0, yes, no, true, and false as values. In a Picker, every value not among the existing choices results in adding another choice. If a new value matches an existing choice aside from capitalization, it’s considered equal to the choice. Whenever an attribute used to construct a smart set gains new values, the set updates. “Wide Reach” (“Readership” at least 100,000), for instance, is one such smart set.

The Activity window will tell you everything going on behind the scenes in LemmaLoom with regard to your projects. Activities include imports, translations, and indexing activities. To view this, choose Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0). A recording being transcribed while three skeptic texts are indexed. Sections contain different parts of your work. Each section displays its number of items in parentheses: Section What it lists Importing Recordings being transcribed and PDFs being read, with their current step; REFI-QDA and archive imports, such as Importing LemmaLoom Archive; files and web addresses whose import dialog has not been confirmed yet, shown as Waiting Exporting A REFI-QDA or archive export under way, such as Exporting LemmaLoom Archive Translating Translations being made or waiting to start Indexing Documents being indexed, with the step and a percentage, such as Parsing structure 35%, or an analyzer at work, such as Running Cohesion Failed Documents whose indexing failed and translations that failed, with the reason Waiting Documents in the queue for indexing, shown as Waiting to be indexed Status, names, and project names appear in each row. Ongoing work will display a progress ring (or spinner icon) at the end of the row. Pending work will instead show a dotted circle at the end of the row. If indexing was unsuccessful for a document, a Retry Indexing link will be displayed instead. Unsuccessful translations will show a Retry link. At the top of the window, the toolbar includes its own Import menu, which breaks out Documents and Web Pages. There is also the menu showing the project's name, such as “Climate Debate”. Both allow importing into any selected project, regardless of which project the main window shows. Dialogs for imports will open up in the Activity window.

Once a document joins your project, LemmaLoom begins indexing. Deselecting Index for grammar analysis upon import prevents the indexing from occurring. The indexing splits texts into sentences and words before determining their dictionary forms and parts of speech. Then comes grammatical parsing of the sentences, followed by the analyzers, and finally computation of statistics of the whole document. Please refer to  for details. These processes happen in the background. You may continue your workflow without interruption while the indexing happens. The performance depends on the hardware specifications of your Mac computer and the size of your documents. Indexing interrupted by quitting LemmaLoom continues the next time you open the application. You can open, read, and code a newly imported document right away. However, functions that depend on indexing must wait until it is done before being functional. The lens menu's text styling relies on the results of grammatical parsing; therefore, the lens menu is disabled until indexing finishes, with the tooltip Lenses become available when indexing completes. See . The Grammar tab of the inspector displays the message Grammar becomes available when indexing completes until indexing finishes. Likewise, the Text tab shows Statistics become available when indexing completes until completion. Queries concerning words take account of indexed texts. Clicking a word to move the recording requires completed indexing. The reader's status bar tracks the indexing progress with messages such as Parsing structure 35%. A document opened during indexing, with the lens menu disabled, the Grammar tab showing its message, and the status bar showing the indexing progress. Similarly, the sidebar monitors indexing progress as well. Badges beside each document show how far along its indexing process is, as detailed in The navigation sidebar in . Hover your mouse pointer over the badge to get an explanatory message regarding the current indexing process stage and percentage. Should the process fail for some reason, both the sidebar's document shortcut menu and the reader's status bar show why and display the Retry Indexing command. In particular, editing a document's text and changing its language trigger automatic re-indexing. Changing exclusion settings for indexing also triggers re-indexing.

The reader in LemmaLoom is the center pane in the main window that contains the text of your document. It is where you read your documents, conduct searches within the texts, select words and passages for coding or annotation, and edit the text itself. If the document was imported as an audio or video file, the reader displays the transcript along with the player bar above it so that you may hear the recording alongside reading the transcript. The examples mentioned in this chapter relate to the sample “Climate Debate” project (see The example project in ); most examples use its op-eds and columns, such as “Running Out of Time” or “Net Zero Will Cost You”, whereas examples related to recordings employ the document “Radio Debate”. You may load the sample project for yourself using File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project; LemmaLoom imports it as a new project in the interface's language.

Clicking a document in the navigation sidebar opens it in a tab in the reader, which contains the same components for every document. These components consist of: The title band lies above the text column at the height where the window buttons reside. Title bands contain the LemmaLoom title to the far left and the reader's tools at the far right. The text column makes up the bulk of the reader, where all the text resides. Lines stop at a comfortable reading width. Located to the left of the text column, the gutter numbers paragraphs and sentences and displays all your annotations. These include any codings (passages you have coded), memos, bookmarks, and links. Each annotated element has its corresponding symbol displayed in the gutter. Located at the extreme right side of the reader, the document overview provides you with an overall picture of where everything lies in the document relative to the current view. Located beneath the text column, the status bar gives you your position within the document, as well as the total length of the document. The search bar, a legend for most enabled lenses, and the player for audio and video can also appear between the title band and the text. As seen in the figure below, a skeptical opinion piece from “Climate Debate” titled “Net Zero Will Cost You” includes mostly codings associated with the code “Costs”. A few passages carry other codes, such as “Uncertainty”, “Responsibility”, “Urgency”, or “Deadlines”. One sentence, about a bill that “runs into the hundreds of billions”, carries both “Costs” and “Responsibility”, so a combined annotation with two dots stands beside it in the gutter. “Net Zero Will Cost You” in the reader, with paragraph and sentence numbers and coded passages in the gutter, the document overview on the right, and the status bar below.

The buttons on the right-hand end of the title band apply to the document currently being viewed. When two documents are opened side by side, these buttons apply to the currently active pane, the last one clicked (see Reading two documents side by side further ahead in this chapter). From left to right, here is what these buttons mean: The lens menu displays either the currently enabled lens's name or how many lenses are enabled at once when several are, or Lens when none is. A newly opened document comes equipped with Bookmarks and Codes lenses enabled, resulting in 2 Lenses in the menu. This menu is disabled until the document has been indexed. Collapse, which displays the tooltip Show only the sentences a lens annotates, collapses the entire document down to the sentences annotated by the currently enabled lenses. Clicking this button again will undo the collapse effect. This button appears only when a lens has something to annotate (see ). Find in document, represented by the magnifying glass icon, displays the search bar. Font, gutter, and text size, represented by a big A next to a small one, brings up a menu of options related to the appearance of the document. Edit switches the reader to editing mode. During editing mode, the title band buttons are limited to Cancel and Save.

The gutter has two main sections. On the extreme left side are the numbers, where paragraphs are numbered in the left column and sentences in the right column. Sentences are numbered continuously through the whole document. Where multiple sentences start in the same line, their numbers share that line, separated by commas, as many as fit in the column. To select a whole paragraph or sentence, click on its corresponding number in the gutter. If both columns are visible at once, clicks in the left column select paragraphs, whereas clicks in the right column select sentences. Once a passage is selected, you may treat it like other selections, including coding it. In fact, clicking a number is the fastest way of coding a whole paragraph or sentence (see Selecting text later in this chapter). Between the numbers and the text is the margin, in which all additions to the document show. Codings display here when the Codes lens is enabled; bookmarks likewise show when Bookmarks is enabled. All memos and links display regardless of the current lens. Coded passages show with a small bar next to them, colored with their respective code colors. Where overlapping codings occur, they line up side by side. Any bars beyond the third share the third slot. Hovering the mouse pointer over a bar highlights the corresponding passage in the text. Each coding, memo, bookmark, and link has a small annotation where it begins. Coding annotations contain code names; memo annotations show the beginnings of each memo. Bookmark annotations show comments associated with the bookmark, whereas link annotations indicate link types. Where annotations might overlap one another, all overlapping annotations compress into one gray annotation, accompanied by colored circles and a count. By clicking the annotation or bar itself, you select the passage the element corresponds to. Instead, clicking a link annotation navigates to the passage linked to on the opposite end of the link, opening the other document if needed. In the “Climate Debate” project, for example, the link on a passage in the op-ed piece “Net Zero Will Cost You” takes one directly to the speech it addresses, “A Mayor's Promise”. Hovering the mouse pointer over an annotation shows a memo, a link, or a long bookmark comment in full; a link's popover shows the link information along with Go to the other end. Pointing at or clicking a combined annotation shows all its entries in a list, and clicking an entry selects its passage or, for a link, goes to the other end. A link annotation in “Net Zero Will Cost You” with the mouse pointer over it, showing its popover with the link to “A Mayor's Promise” and Go to the other end.

The document overview, found along the right side of the reader, is a scroll bar that is color-coded according to the enabled lenses. It tells you where in the document you currently are and what portions of your document the enabled lenses annotate, such as codes. Everything contained within your document fits within the confines of the document overview panel. The actual text appears as faint lines running from top to bottom, with breaks where the paragraph divisions lie. Short paragraphs containing entirely capital letters denote heading-like text and appear as darker strokes. Coded sections and the words your lenses color show in their respective colors. Here are a few additional features of the document overview: your current viewing location in the document is marked by an outlined rectangle; your bookmarks appear as little square symbols on the far left side; search matches appear as small tick marks on the far right side; the selected word appears as a line across the document overview panel. When hovering the mouse pointer over sections in the document overview, you get previews of the text in that area, namely the paragraph under the mouse pointer, with its number, and the four paragraphs before and after it. You can either click to jump to that paragraph in the text (which highlights momentarily), or you can drag up and down the document overview to move through your text document. The document overview of “Net Zero Will Cost You” with the mouse pointer over it, showing the preview of the paragraph under the mouse pointer.

The left end of the status bar tells you the location of the currently selected item. When selecting a word, the status bar displays the paragraph and sentence it belongs to, along with its token order in the sentence (e.g., ¶ 4 · S 22 · T 6 refers to the fourth paragraph, twenty-second sentence, and sixth token). A token is one word or punctuation mark. Selecting passages results in their starting and ending paragraph and sentence locations being displayed, along with their total number of tokens. When indexing has completed, the right end gives you statistical information about your document in a concise format, for example, 10 ¶ · 65 S · 1,029 words for “Running Out of Time”. Word counts are based on tokens (that is, punctuation included); which counts appear depends on your gutter numbering. Setting your gutter to Paragraphs will give you counts of paragraphs and words; Sentences, sentences and words; and Off only words. Until indexing has finished, or when it cannot run, the document's current indexing status will appear in place of the stats (see In the reader in ). These statuses include: Name of the stage and a percentage indicator during the initial indexing pass; Running and a name of the active analyzer during the running of an analyzer pass (extra processing of a specific feature, such as ties between sentences); No grammar analysis for, followed by the language name of a language that does not undergo grammar analysis; Indexing is off with an Index Now link for indexing turned off during importation by unchecking Index for grammar analysis; The reason and a Retry Indexing link when indexing encounters an issue.

The document becomes readable immediately upon opening. However, several functions in the reader remain inactive until the indexing of the document is completed: Gutters contain paragraph numbers alone, since sentences are found during indexing; You select a passage in the document manually by clicking and dragging; The lens menu is disabled; The status bar displays indexing progress rather than any statistics. Indexing duration will depend both on the size of the document and the specifications of your computer. Grammar analysis in LemmaLoom supports English, German, and Chinese languages. Documents in other languages stay as described above but retain the ability to be read, searched, coded, and edited.

Each document retains memory of where you left off reading, what lenses were on, and the inspector state. Projects retain knowledge of tabs opened, the currently active tab, and which document has been opened side by side with split view. LemmaLoom keeps all this when you quit, so the reader opens where you left it.

The settings you can configure include your choice of font family, text size, the content of gutters, and text layout. Your chosen settings will be saved globally across all documents in all projects until you change them. There are three places from which you may customize these options: The Font, gutter, and text size menu in the title band, which includes submenus Font, Gutter, and Layout, along with Larger Text, Smaller Text, and Reset Text Size options; The View menu, which affects the text size setting only; LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,), in its Reader pane, which also configures the display of selections and shows a preview. If you need to revert your choices, and the display of selections, back to their default state as when you first launched LemmaLoom, select Reset All to Defaults from atop the Reader pane.

The reader includes eleven font options including System Serif, System Sans, System Rounded, System Mono, Georgia, Palatino, Baskerville, Times New Roman, Helvetica Neue, Avenir Next, and Menlo. Everything displays using System Serif until changed. All Chinese text uses whatever Chinese font Macs use by default, regardless of the font you choose. To switch between fonts, click Font, gutter, and text size in the title band, then select one under Font. From Settings, it's available in the Typography section's Font row.

Text sizes are available in increments of 10% from 70% to 200%. The default size at 100% is 17 points. You can incrementally adjust your text sizes one step at a time using View ▸ Larger Text (⌘+) and View ▸ Smaller Text (⌘-). If you need to restore your text to its default size, you can use View ▸ Reset Text Size (⌘0). Alternatively, in Settings, you can use the Text Size slider under Typography. The percentage appears beside it, and the reset button next to that returns you to 100%. The text column's width adjusts accordingly to keep the average number of words per line consistent, and the text editor (referenced later in this chapter under Editing a document's text) maintains the same settings.

The Gutter submenu, named Gutter Numbering under Settings, selects the numbering scheme used in the gutters: Setting The gutter shows Both paragraph and sentence numbers (the setting you start with) Paragraphs paragraph numbers only Sentences sentence numbers only Off no numbers If you use paragraphs alone as the passage reference, you'll notice that Paragraphs helps keep the gutter less busy. Even with Off, however, the margin shows annotations such as codings, memos, bookmarks, and links.

The Layout submenu, under Page in Settings, contains two different layouts, Single Column and Two-Page Spread. By default, documents are displayed using Single Column. Text is presented in a single column with the gutter adjacent to it. Documents in Two-Page Spread have their text laid out across pages, appearing two pages at once like an open book. Each page is as tall as the reader, and you scroll down from one pair of pages to the next. Each page displays paragraph and sentence numbering, similar to the Single Column layout, while the document overview functions similarly as well. Resizing the window dynamically flows the text onto new pages. A Two-Page Spread layout suits larger screens and initial readings of lengthy documents prior to coding. Whenever you switch between layouts, your current location within the document remains saved. “Carbon Tax Debate”, the news article imported from the web, in the Two-Page Spread layout.

The appearance of the reader, including text color and background, comes from the theme chosen for the whole application. You may choose a theme with the Theme setting under Appearance in the General pane of Settings. If you need help understanding themes, visit . The effect of choosing a theme for the reader includes the following: Theme Reader System, Protanopia, Deuteranopia, Tritanopia follows the light or dark appearance of macOS Light, High Contrast dark text on white Dark, High Contrast Dark light text on a dark background Cream dark brown text on warm off-white paper Solarized Light gray-blue text on pale cream Solarized Dark pale gray text on deep blue-green

The selected word or passage, and a word's grammatical relations, appear in the text when you select them. Their look is determined by your Settings within the Selection section of the Reader pane. There is a preview at the bottom of the pane where you can check what the end result looks like based on changes to the rows. Row Choices What it controls Selected Text Solid block, Highlight A rounded block in the text color with the selected words in the background color, or a light tint behind them. Head and Dependents Arcs, Lines, Labels, Highlight, Off How the reader shows which word the selected word depends on (its head) and which words depend on it (its dependents). Surrounding Text Fade, Light fade, Highlight sentence, Off Whether the rest of the text dims around the selection, or the selected word's sentence is tinted. Audio Playback Spotlight, Solid block, Highlight How the passage being played is rendered when the reader follows the recording (see Following the transcript later in this chapter). The Reader pane of Settings in its default state, with the Typography, Page, and Selection sections and the preview below. For each row, the option selected as default will be the first option. In linguistics, the head of a word is what it modifies or depends on. For instance, in the example a national program to insulate homes, national modifies or describes program, making program the head, and national is one of its dependents. Fade lets you maintain focus on your sentence. When you'd rather be able to keep your context clearly visible during the coding process, you can pick Light fade or Highlight sentence.

The search bar lets you search your currently opened document for the characters you are typing, bringing you directly to the matched passages. If you need to match all word forms, e.g., pay and paid, or search multiple documents simultaneously, you should use a query rather than the search bar. Queries incorporate consideration of word forms and grammatical context (see ). The figure shows the column “The Models Keep Missing”, written by a skeptic author who once “built models for a living”. When searching for model with the search bar, LemmaLoom returns twelve matching results, including models and modelers, and the document overview shows how they spread. The search bar in the column “The Models Keep Missing”, searching for “model”, with the current match picked out in the text and every match shown in the document overview. To search for text in a document: Choose Edit ▸ Find (⌘F), or click Find in document (the magnifying glass) in the title band. The search bar opens above the text, with the cursor in its search field. Type what you are looking for. LemmaLoom searches as you type and scrolls to the first match. Press Return or ⌘G, or click the down arrow, to go to the next match. Press ⇧⌘G, or click the up arrow, to go back to the previous one. After the last match the search starts again at the first, and from the first match ⇧⌘G goes to the last. To close the search bar, press Esc, click the × at its right end, or choose Edit ▸ Find (⌘F) again. In the search field above, the counter shows you which match number you are currently on along with the total number of matches, so 3/12 indicates that this is the third of twelve total matches. Should there be no matching results, Not found is displayed. The reader will highlight the current matching passage in your text automatically, and depending on the settings of Surrounding Text (Fade or Light fade), everything surrounding the match becomes dimmer, whereas Highlight sentence or Off means your matches get tinted. All matches show up as ticks on the right edge of the document overview of the reader. Matching works as follows: Capitals and accents are ignored, so model will match Model and cafe will match café; Spaces before and after your input are ignored; Matches can lie inside longer words, so model will match models or modelers as well. To find a phrase as a whole, type it with its spaces, for example, error bars; Chinese text is searched the same way, as a run of characters. Every document gets a separate search bar in LemmaLoom; closing it resets your search. If your reader is collapsed into the annotated sentences of a document, then opening the search bar expands the reader and gives you access to the whole document body. Collapsing the reader will automatically close the search bar again. When editing documents, Find is disabled.

In the LemmaLoom reader, you can code passages in your text, bookmark passages, attach memos to passages, link passages, and/or add passages to a dictionary, once you select them. Passages can consist of a word or a longer stretch of text.

Choose a word by clicking on it. Clicking the same word again, or pressing Esc, removes the current selection. Selection works on individual words when the document has already been indexed. Selecting a word also shows how the word connects to the rest of its sentence. By default, connections in the form of arcs show how the selected word is connected to its head and its dependents. Additionally, everything around the selected word's sentence is faded out. If the inspector is currently visible, then the Grammar tab within it provides details about the selected word (see ). How the selection looks and how its connections are shown can be configured from Settings (refer to How selections are displayed above). The word “deadline” selected in “Running Out of Time”, with arcs to its head and its dependents and the rest of the text faded.

Select your passage by clicking the beginning of the passage and dragging to its end. Spaces at either end are left out. Alternatively, you can click the numbering in the gutter next to paragraphs or sentences to select them directly, as well as annotations or bars in the margin to select passages. How much to select depends on your needs. However, it is recommended to select enough passage text for the selection to be self-contained, as passages are read separately outside of context once coded. In “Climate Debate”, the majority of selections coded were made from one or two complete sentences. Copying the passage text is done using Edit ▸ Copy (⌘C).

The instant any word or passage has been selected in the document, a bar appears near the bottom of the reader. The bar starts by displaying the first words of your selection and the actions that can be performed on it. The figure shows a sentence selected from “Running Out of Time”, which is ready for coding under “Deadlines” as in the Quick Start. The previous passage was already coded with “Deadlines”. Next to the following sentence, there is an annotation attached to a memo beginning with “Distant targets are read as evasion”. A passage selected in the op-ed “Running Out of Time”, with the selection bar at the bottom of the reader. The selection bar includes the following features: Bookmark creates a bookmark in the current passage, optionally accompanied by a comment such as “Rhetorical question at the turn to the closing appeal” on a bookmark in “Running Out of Time”. When a selection lies atop a bookmark, however, the button switches to Remove Bookmark. Code opens the code palette. Select one to code the passage, type into the box to look up the code from the list (the highlighted code, the first match until you move with ↑ and ↓, is applied when pressing Return), and pick a code with a checkmark (one already on the passage) to remove it. After all the codes in the list, the option Add Code “…” creates a new code whose name matches what was typed, assuming there's no code with such a name already. Finally, there's the In Vivo “…” option for coding the selection with a new code named after the selected text. Add to Dictionary will insert the selected text into a category of a project dictionary (see ). This button will only appear if the project contains at least one dictionary. Memo creates a memo related to the selected passage. Link initiates creation of a link between two passages. The second passage, in this document or another, must be selected before clicking Finish Link. In the meanwhile, you get a crossed-out link button, Cancel the pending link, which deletes the unfinished link. Clicking × at the end of the selection bar clears the current selection, like Esc. The code palette opened from the selection bar in “Running Out of Time”, with “Dead” typed and “Deadlines” highlighted above Add Code and In Vivo. A passage in “Running Out of Time” with a link pending, showing Finish Link and the button that cancels the pending link in the selection bar. For information regarding appropriate use of coding, memos, bookmarks, or linking, see . The Document menu contains commands for performing these actions with their respective keyboard shortcuts: Command Shortcut Document ▸ Code ⇧⌘C Document ▸ In Vivo Code ⇧⌘V Document ▸ Memo ⇧⌘M Document ▸ Bookmark (or Remove Bookmark) ⇧⌘B Document ▸ Link (or Finish Link) ⇧⌘L Document ▸ Cancel Link ⌥⇧⌘L

All document texts may be edited. Editing in LemmaLoom allows you to correct minor errors, including typos in an article, errors introduced during PDF text extraction, incorrectly transcribed words in a transcription, poorly translated phrases in a machine translation, etc. When you edit, LemmaLoom keeps any codings, memos, links, and bookmarks associated with their respective text fragments. Once saved, the whole document gets indexed anew. The editor presents the text of your document as plain text in a monospaced font. To edit significant portions of the text, first edit it somewhere else and paste it back into the editor. Alternatively, import the modified document file and begin coding anew. After pasting, be sure to review any annotations, which could now refer to incorrect text (see the note at the end of How annotations follow edits below).

The kinds of texts you would want to edit the most are probably those generated by LemmaLoom, either a transcription, a translated text, or a PDF's text extracted by LemmaLoom. In “Climate Debate”, these are “Heat Wave Report 2024”, the transcript of “Radio Debate”, and “Running Out of Time (German)”. Below is an image showing one of the skeptic opinion pieces, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, in the editor, with blank lines separating its paragraphs and no options except for the Cancel and Save buttons in the title band. The op-ed “Net Zero Will Cost You” in the text editor, with Cancel and Save in the title band. To modify a document's text: Open the document. Click Edit at the right end of the title band, or choose Document ▸ Edit (⇧⌘E). The reader becomes a plain text editor with a monospaced font. Lenses, the gutter, the document overview, and the status bar are hidden while you edit, and the line Editing replaces the document text; the index rebuilds on save. appears below the text. Make your changes. While you type, ⌘Z undoes your last changes in the editor. Click Save in the title band, or choose Document ▸ Save (⌘Return). Separate paragraphs with a blank line. In the absence of blank lines, a document has one paragraph per line. Once you introduce even a single blank line, only blank lines separate paragraphs; hence, the number of paragraphs decreases drastically. Clicking Cancel, or choosing Document ▸ Cancel (⌘.), will take you out of the editor while losing your current changes; any input you entered since clicking Edit will vanish immediately. Should the reader have been collapsed to only the annotated sentences, clicking Edit opens up the complete document first. Other actions within a project (coding passages and writing memos, for instance) are automatically saved as you perform them; changes in text are saved only via Save. So long as the editor is open, switching tabs keeps your edits. However, switching to a different project or quitting LemmaLoom without having saved your edits results in losing them permanently.

After you save an edited text, LemmaLoom: replaces the document's text with yours; moves the codings, memos, bookmarks, and links in the document so that they stay with their text (see How annotations follow edits below); indexes the document again from the beginning. During indexing, the reader displays the newly modified text underneath the label Saving. Your title band will display Saving in place of Edit as well. Once indexing completes, your lenses, word counts, and inspector will update according to the new text. For documents in a language where LemmaLoom does not conduct grammar analyses, the reader is ready again immediately. The long text “Who Pays for the Transition” just after a save, with Saving in the title band and over the text, and the indexing progress in the status bar. The time required to index modified documents is about equal to the time needed to initially index them. You can track the progress using the status bar, or the Window ▸ Activity menu item (⌥⌘0). Should indexing be disabled for a particular document, LemmaLoom will re-index it only once you click Index Now in the status bar, and until then the reader keeps showing Saving.

When you save changes made to a document, LemmaLoom analyzes differences between versions by comparing letters in the previous and updated text in order to figure out what additions and deletions were made. Then, it shifts all associated items, including codings, memos attached to a passage, bookmarks, links, transcripts-to-audio/video associations (see Correcting a transcript later in this chapter), and alignments of originals and translations, to correspond with updated locations. Scroll Together and the placing of new copies of annotations rely on that alignment (see Annotations in both languages in ). When you make an edit, it applies only to the language version, original or translation, that you perform edits in; annotations in the other language version remain unchanged. If you know ahead of time that you intend to translate a document, consider fixing any errors in it beforehand to avoid translating errors from it into another language. Additions or deletions made earlier in the document will shift the passage along with its text. Additions made within a passage will become included in it. Additions made immediately after a passage will fall outside it (unless they end with the same character as the last character of the passage, in which case they become part of it). Deletions within a passage will shorten it. Additions made immediately before a passage will stay outside it. Text that replaces a passage will become the new passage. Deleting all of a passage's text will leave the annotation intact, with an empty passage. The speech titled “A Mayor's Promise” has the following passage: We will plant twelve thousand trees, starting in the neighborhoods that need them most. Suppose that twelve thousand trees is coded with “Hope”. The table shows what changes happen to the coded passage after making each one of these edits, one at a time, to the original sentence: Edit Coded passage afterwards We will plant changed to The city will plant twelve thousand trees, moved with its text twelve thousand changed to 12,000 12,000 trees street added between thousand and trees twelve thousand street trees around added before twelve twelve thousand trees; around stays outside by 2035 added after trees twelve thousand trees; the addition stays outside along our streets added after trees twelve thousand trees along our streets twelve thousand trees replaced by a grove a grove twelve thousand trees deleted an empty passage Since the addition by 2035 ends in 5 whereas trees ends in s, LemmaLoom places the addition after the passage. Since the addition along our streets also ends in s (like trees), however, LemmaLoom considers it as occurring inside the passage; the new text could equally be the letters s along our street inserted inside the passage, before its last letter. If you delete the text of a coding, as in the last row, that coding can be found only in the Codings view of the project shelf, where you may right-click the coding and select Delete Coding. Memos and bookmarks whose text you delete are kept in the same way. To avoid empty annotations, remove them before deleting their text. Once editing close to a coding occurs, check in the reader whether the coding still covers the right part of the modified passage. If it needs modification, remove the coding from the passage, and then re-code it (see Removing a code from a passage in ). LemmaLoom will compare letters between the two versions one to one only if there were about a thousand or fewer letters inserted and deleted in total. Should you insert or delete more than that number at once, such as pasting in a newer version of a long passage, LemmaLoom compares lines, sentences, and words first, and letters only within the parts that changed. A changed part that is still too large will be considered a replacement block. Annotations within this block preserve their original positions relative to this new span of text as much as possible, meaning they might end up on different words. Save your work after each larger change and review annotations in the changed part afterward.

Saving an edit results in one entry in the undo history (see ). To restore the previous state of the edited text, along with all of its codings, memos, bookmarks, and links to their previous positions, choose Edit ▸ Undo Edit Text (⌘Z). This will reindex your document accordingly.

When working with an audio or video document like “Radio Debate”, you work with the transcript in exactly the same way as you would with any text document. Once you import the recording, LemmaLoom generates the transcript for you (see ). Each stretch of the transcript is tied to the stretch of the recording it came from. Paragraphs begin at points where the speaker shifts or there is a pause in speaking longer than roughly a second and a half. You will code the recording using its transcript. Whenever there are passages whose meanings cannot be determined based purely on the transcript, e.g., if it was the speaker’s intonation or sarcasm that made something meaningful, you can listen to them directly. The speakers and text remain separate in LemmaLoom. If a recording contains multiple speakers, they will be indicated in the player bar as you listen along. The names of the speakers will follow a naming convention of “Speaker 1”, “Speaker 2”, etc. for LemmaLoom-transcribed recordings; in “Radio Debate”, they will be labeled “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”. Each speaker’s utterances are automatically coded with a subcode of the code “Speakers”. The names on the player bar retain their original values when you rename your speaker codes (see Speakers in ).

Above the text lies the player bar. The contents of this bar, from left to right, are shown below: For video only, buttons to collapse the video player down to the controls (Collapse to the controls) or show it again (Show the video), and to move the video beside the text or back above it; Play or Pause control button; Scroll with audio control button, which makes the reader follow the recording; Elapsed playtime, a playback slider control, and total recording length; Speaker of the current passage for any recording with multiple speakers, e.g. “Skeptic”. The timings on both the elapsed playtime counter and total length counter are displayed in minutes and seconds form, such as 2:14. Any recordings of an hour or more have hours displayed along with minutes and seconds, such as 3:56:32. In the illustration below is the recording “Radio Debate”. This particular recording is roughly five minutes long, currently paused at 1:09, during a speech made by the Skeptic. As Scroll with audio is on, the current passage is highlighted while the remainder of the text is grayed out. The speaker codes appear in the gutter beside each turn.
