The audio document “Radio Debate”, with Scroll with audio on and the current passage in the spotlight. To play a recording: Open the document. Click Play (the triangle), or choose Document ▸ Play (⇧⌘P). To stop, click Pause or choose Document ▸ Pause (⇧⌘P). To move to another point, drag the slider. When pressing Play at the end of a recording, playback will begin anew from the starting point. If you switch tabs or close the document during playback, playback pauses immediately.

t: Playing from a point in the transcript
b: Clicking a word in the transcript moves the player to the start of the passage it belongs to. It does nothing more than move the playhead; hit Play to hear from this point onward. Only if the document is indexed can you navigate by clicking on words (see Before indexing has finished earlier in this chapter). If a document uses a language lacking grammar analysis, use the slider instead. When checking an uncertain passage, click on a word inside it, then hit ⇧⌘P. This lets you listen, and then pressing ⇧⌘P pauses the playback.

With Scroll with audio turned on (the button is highlighted), the reader will highlight the passage playing and will keep it centered within the pane as the recording progresses. Dragging the slider will drag the highlighted passage along with it. When turned on, Scroll with audio immediately jumps to wherever the recording currently plays. Initially, Scroll with audio is set to off; like the size and position of videos, it applies to every audio and video document. If you scroll, click, or navigate with the keyboard during playback, the reader stops following for a few seconds and scrolls back once the next passage in the recording begins. With a passage selected, the reader holds its position. Clicking Play jumps instantly back to the passage being played. Scroll with audio is especially helpful when coding a recording while listening, or checking the transcripts against the recording. Pause playback with ⇧⌘P when you come across an interesting passage to code, and the reader stays on that passage while you select and code it. Within the Reader pane of Settings, Audio Playback determines how the currently playing passage should be displayed. Spotlight dims everything else except the currently played passage. Solid block places the currently played passage on a block of color. Lastly, Highlight highlights the currently played passage slightly.

t: Video above or beside the text
b: A video is played within a frame above the text area. You may drag the divider beneath the video frame up to increase the space available to the text area. Alternatively, clicking Collapse to the controls will collapse the video and leave behind only the player bar. The video “sample-video” playing in a frame above its transcript, with the player bar between them. The video “sample-video” collapsed to the controls of the player bar, above its transcript. Clicking the Show the video beside the text button will place the video to the left of the text area, with the player bar beneath the video. Adjusting the divider between them will resize both areas accordingly, while the text keeps a readable width. Click the Show the video above the text button to restore the original configuration. With wider screen sizes, having the video displayed beside the text increases visible lines in the transcript. The video “sample-video” beside its transcript, with the player bar beneath the video.

Transcripts will inevitably contain some errors, especially in names and domain-specific vocabulary. Correcting transcripts works the same as any other text editing (refer to Editing and saving earlier in this chapter). Your player bar stays put throughout editing, and playback can still be toggled with ⇧⌘P while editing your transcript. It makes most sense to find errors in your transcription first, and then address them. Use the reader's playback functionality while having Scroll with audio enabled to locate the passages requiring corrections (you can use bookmarks for this purpose). Proceeding to the editor, you then fix the errors accordingly. Ideally, you should correct the transcript prior to coding. The ties established between the transcript and the corresponding recordings follow your edits similarly to how codings do (refer to How annotations follow edits earlier in this chapter). This means that a corrected word within a passage continues playing as a part of the passage, and clicking it takes you to the same place in the recording as before your changes.

When LemmaLoom is running in full screen mode, the whole window takes the entire screen. The title band hides, and the tools go to the toolbar at the very top of the screen. Full screen mode proves particularly helpful for initial readings of large documents. It’s possible to keep the inspector open while you work on coding documents, for example, to keep the document’s codes in view in its Coding tab. The figure below demonstrates how “Running Out of Time” looks when displayed in full screen, where both the sidebar and inspector remain open alongside the open Reader Settings menu in the toolbar. The toolbar of the full-screen reader, with the Reader Settings menu open. How to read in full-screen mode: Open the document. Choose View ▸ Enter Full Screen (⌃⌘F), or click the green button at the top left of the window. To give the text the whole width of the screen, hide the sidebar with View ▸ Toggle Sidebar (⌃⌘S) and the inspector with View ▸ Toggle Inspector (⌃⌘I). To leave full screen, choose View ▸ Exit Full Screen (⌃⌘F). All menu commands and shortcuts in this chapter function identically within full-screen mode.

t: Reading two documents side by side
b: Split view splits your reader into two panes with each displaying one document. Split view lets you juxtapose two documents, say an op-ed written by activists on a topic and another one written by skeptics on the same issue, or an article next to its own translation. It is also helpful when you are in the middle of coding. Having already coded a document in one pane, you can see the exact nature of how you coded something, and now you can continue applying the code consistently on the document you are currently coding. More information on how to use translations along with split views can be found in . The figure illustrates the op-ed titled “Running Out of Time” on the left, followed by its German translation titled “Running Out of Time (German)” on the right. The translated document contains copies of the codings made to the original document, and Scroll together keeps the two aligned as you scroll. The op-ed “Running Out of Time” on the left and its German translation, “Running Out of Time (German)”, on the right, with Scroll together turned on. There are several ways to open a second document beside the current one. In the sidebar, right-click the document and choose Open in Split View from the shortcut menu. Alternatively, right-click the tab of another open document and choose Open in Split View from its menu. For opening two documents side by side simultaneously, hold down ⌘ while clicking the second document in the sidebar, right-click one, and choose Open Side by Side from the shortcut menu. Whichever document is positioned higher in the sidebar opens on the left. In the case of a translation, right-click it in the sidebar and choose Open Beside Original. The original will open on the left and the translation on the right. The shortcut menu on “Running Out of Time (German)” in the sidebar, with Open Beside Original. All mentioned options can also be found under Window in the main menu. From there, Open in Split View lists the open documents available to go beside the active document. The newly opened document opens in the right pane. Its tab gets moved out of the tab strip onto the header of the right pane. Split view functions in the following manner. By clicking either pane, you activate it, which highlights its tab. Tools, menus, and the inspector now pertain only to the activated pane; thus, ⌘F will look through the document inside that pane only. By dragging the divider between the two panes, you control their respective sizes. There are minimum size limits for the panes, and LemmaLoom remembers the division and restores it accordingly upon reopening split view. Every pane contains its own set of lenses and search bar as well as independent selections and scrolling positions. This allows you, for instance, to enable a grammar lens in one pane, leaving only your codes in the other. Fonts, text size, gutter, and layouts are synchronized between both panes. If the two documents correspond to each other as an original and translation or even two translations from an identical original, a lock button, Scroll together, appears on the far right of the header of the right pane. Click that to synchronize scrolling, or alternatively choose View ▸ Scroll Together (⌥⌘L). To close split view, click the × on the right pane header, choose Close Split View from that header’s shortcut menu, or select Window ▸ Close Split View from the main menu. The document in the right pane closes with it.

t: Opening a document in its own window
b: Alternatively, you could read your document within its own window. This might be useful if you had another monitor to work with or if you wish to have a text visible while the main window shows something else, perhaps the codebook or a query. To open your document in a separate window, right-click on the tab for that document and select Open in New Window. You could also choose Window ▸ Open in New Window for your current active document. The Document window displays the reader alongside an inspector of its own. LemmaLoom has only one such window, so opening another document in a new window replaces the one it shows. The Document window showing “Running Out of Time”, with the reader on the left and its own inspector on the right. From here, you may use the available menu commands and their respective shortcuts, for example, searching for text with ⌘F, resizing text with ⌘+ and ⌘-, editing the document with ⇧⌘E, revealing/hiding the inspector with ⌃⌘I, completing editing with ⌘Return, or using ⌘. to cancel it.

A lens annotates words in the reader according to their category. Examples of categories would be parts of speech and codes. The Word class lens, for instance, underlines all nouns in blue and all verbs in red, whereas the Codes lens renders your codings in the respective code's color. Lenses assist you in spotting patterns in texts as you read them. When you enable Negation in the op-ed “Running Out of Time”, for instance, all instances of not, never, and nobody, along with whatever they negate in the sentence, become visually obvious to you. Similarly, enabling a dictionary of hedges as a lens can reveal where the author softens a claim. Typically, you will use lenses to identify passages relevant to your question and then conduct a close reading of them prior to coding and counting. All examples used in this chapter were taken from “Climate Debate”, the example project of this guide, which File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project adds to your library (see The example project in ).

Every category annotated by a lens is an aspect of the lens. Some examples include Noun in Word class or Obligation in Modality. There are only certain aspects that have colors in common; all other aspects have a unique color associated with them. Above the text, most lenses show a legend, which is made up of colored lenslets that represent aspects. You use the legend to determine what each color means and to enable or disable individual aspects of the lens. Reading a lens later in this chapter provides further detail. There are five different types of lenses offered by LemmaLoom: Built-in lenses ranging from Word class to Rhetoric render the grammar analysis performed on the document during indexing (see ). The Codes and Bookmarks lenses render your annotations made on the document. Dictionaries have their own lenses, dictionary lenses, which annotate their terms. Each category has its own color (see ). Query lenses render the hits of a saved query (see ). Analyzer lenses represent findings made via one of your own analyzers (see ). Built-in lenses are helpful to understand the wording and grammatical structure of texts and apply to any indexed document in LemmaLoom. To view a document without any lens, select Clear All in the lens menu. Each currently open document stores its own lenses. If two documents are viewed side by side (see Reading two documents side by side in ), for instance, you can view “Running Out of Time” with Modality and the column “The Models Keep Missing” with Cohesion at the same time. Documents opened for the first time have the Codes and Bookmarks lenses enabled. For any document left open, LemmaLoom keeps track of enabled lenses and disabled aspects, and restores them upon opening the project again. Enabling or disabling a lens or aspect, or collapsing a document, takes effect immediately, while reversing these actions requires doing the opposite (see Changes outside the project in ). The lens menu is disabled until indexing completes. Additionally, the menu remains disabled for documents in languages other than English, German, and Chinese, although codings and bookmarks will still be displayed in them. Importing without indexing will also result in the menu staying disabled until indexing finishes (see Importing without indexing in ).

The lens menu is the first of the tools at the right end of the title band, appearing before the magnifying glass and the Font, gutter, and text size menu (see The title band in ). The label of the menu tells you whether lenses are enabled, how many lenses are enabled, and which: Lens when none is enabled; the lens's name, e.g., Modality or Hedges, when one is enabled; the number of lenses, e.g., 2 Lenses, when multiple lenses are enabled. When you hover the mouse pointer over the menu, you can see the names of the lenses that are currently enabled. Prior to indexing finishing, you'll get a tooltip that reads Lenses become available when indexing completes. When editing a document's text, both the lens menu and the legends will disappear from view. “Running Out of Time” currently has three lenses enabled simultaneously in the figure below (Modality, Bookmarks, and Codes), hence 3 Lenses in the menu. Coding of both “Tipping Points” and “Deadlines” appears along the margin and within the text itself. After Bookmarks and Codes come two additional lenses in the menu that belong to “Climate Debate” (“Hedges”, the project dictionary, and “Urgency Talk”, a query lens). The lens menu for “Running Out of Time”, with Modality, Bookmarks, and Codes enabled, and the dictionary “Hedges” and the query lens “Urgency Talk” listed below them. The menu contains a maximum of three groups, separated by lines: Group What it contains Built-in lenses The built-in lenses available for the document's language, in the order of the table under Built-in lenses later in this chapter, followed by Clear Lenses Analyzers Your own analyzers for the document's language, followed by Clear Analyzers. The group appears only when there is at least one such analyzer. Annotations Bookmarks and Codes, then the project's dictionaries in alphabetical order, then any query lenses, then the Auto Code… items, and last Clear Annotations The Clear All item is located above the groups. To toggle a lens on or off: Open the document in the reader. Click the lens menu in the title band. Choose a lens. A checkmark appears beside it in the menu, and for most lenses a legend appears above the text. To add another lens, open the menu again and choose it. The menu closes after each choice. To disable a lens, choose it again. The four Clear items will disable multiple lenses simultaneously: Item What it disables Clear All Every lens, Codes and Bookmarks included Clear Lenses The built-in lenses in the first group, and any query lenses Clear Analyzers Every analyzer lens Clear Annotations Codes, Bookmarks, dictionary lenses, and query lenses If an item is disabled, then none of the lenses it would disable have been turned on. You may turn off the built-in lenses to stop their coloring from being displayed, while still reading with your codings, by clicking Clear Lenses. The Clear All and Clear Annotations commands remove your codings and bookmarks from view. To view them again, select Codes or Bookmarks. The Auto Code… item codes the passages annotated by a dictionary, query, or analyzer lens (see Auto-coding from a lens in ). You'll find this item visible only when at least one such lens is enabled. If you've got multiple such lenses enabled, you get this item repeated for every lens you have enabled; for example, Auto Code with Hedges…. The lens menu for “Radio Debate” with “Hedges” and “Urgency Talk” enabled, with an Auto Code item for each of them. If you have the application opened up in full screen mode, the title band is hidden and the lens menu is relocated to your toolbar at the very top of your screen. There you have the same items, and the collapse button talked about later in this chapter becomes Collapse to Matches, whereas Expand Document is shown during the time the current document remains collapsed. During the time the indexing hasn't completed yet, you see the disabled menu's tooltip Not indexed yet (see The full-screen reader in ). When viewing two documents simultaneously side-by-side, your title band tools affect the currently active document pane. To switch active panes, click inside the other document pane.

For most lenses, a legend appears above your text as soon as you enable the lens. This legend includes the lens's title written out in capitals followed by its aspects, displayed as colored lenslets in the aspects' respective colors. Clicking a lenslet will disable the aspect of the lens while clicking it again enables the aspect, causing its annotations within your document to disappear and reappear respectively. A disabled lenslet appears faded. Your legends will display themselves according to the sequence of activation of your lenses. Most lenslets include a small square in the aspect's color. However, the lenslets representing aspects that a lens underlines by default, such as New ending (stress) in Cohesion, show a short colored bar instead.

Enabling a lens enables all of its aspects. Usually, you will narrow a lens so that only certain colors are displayed when you know you wish to ask questions about one or two of them specifically. It could be that you wish to study only the verbs, or perhaps only where the author states obligation. None disables all aspects, while All enables all aspects. All stays disabled while all aspects are enabled, and None stays disabled while none are. Right-clicking a lenslet brings up a shortcut menu. Enable only this enables only this aspect. Disable or Enable toggles the aspect, while Enable all enables all aspects again. Disabling aspects causes their words to appear faint. Any annotations made by other lenses override the fading effects caused by disabling aspects. The following figure shows the Modality legend of “Running Out of Time” with the shortcut menu of the Obligation lenslet displayed. Selecting Enable only this will show only the words expressing obligation, like should in “That should not reassure anybody.” The Modality legend of “Running Out of Time” with the menu of the Obligation lenslet open. For keeping only a particular aspect of the lens: Enable the lens. In the legend, right-click the aspect's lenslet and choose Enable only this. To enable every aspect again, click All. Collapsing a document to annotated sentences means that the only thing left will be sentences containing annotations from an enabled aspect (for further explanation see Showing only annotated sentences in a later section of this chapter). Since the rows of the Auto Code dialog contain only the aspects which are enabled, any disabled aspects will be skipped in the auto code procedure. You can also enable three lenses from the Grammar tab of the inspector. Open a category within its Discourse facet, under Cohesion, Metadiscourse, or Rhetoric, and click Highlight in text. LemmaLoom enables the lens if needed and filters it to display the contents of the selected category. Clicking the link again reverts all aspects to normal visibility (see Highlighting a category in ).

Annotations of the same word from two different lenses with identical annotation styles show both annotation colors together. Highlights become gradient blends with the top of the highlight rendered in the first lens color, and the bottom rendered in the second. Similarly, underline annotations become gradient blends where the left side of the underline is in the first annotation color, and the right side in the second. Finally, text color annotations are also gradient blends where each letter transitions from the first annotation color at the top to the second annotation color on the bottom side. It's advisable to pair lenses in ways that maximize readability, with one lens highlighting and the other underlining. By default, Word class and Grammatical function lenses use the underline annotation style while most others highlight words. Therefore, Modality should pair with Word class and not with Phrase, because Phrase highlights most words in your document, hiding the highlights of other lenses. Additionally, four of the lenses can have their annotation styles changed in Settings to make room for a third lens (see Lens colors and styles later in this chapter). “Running Out of Time” with Modality and Word class enabled together, each with its own legend above the text. The document overview, the narrow vertical strip located at the right edge of the reader, displays the colors of the enabled lenses. This proves useful in cases where you're dealing with very large documents because the document overview allows you to quickly locate clusters of annotations and move around the document using clicks (see The document overview in ).

Lenses can also be used to collapse the document to the sentences that they annotate. You could thus read all of the sentences referring to requirements, or all coded passages, consecutively. Collapse proves especially useful in cases where you have a large document to deal with, or when comparing multiple instances of similar sentences before coding them. You initiate document collapse via the collapse button. It is located immediately to the right of the lens menu and displays just an icon (a rectangle flanked by two arrows) that turns tinted while the document is collapsed. This button displays itself whenever any of the built-in, dictionary, query, or analyzer lenses are enabled, or whenever Codes or Bookmarks is turned on and the document has codings or bookmarks. While the document is collapsed, sentences remain visible if annotated with any lens currently enabled. That means that a built-in, dictionary, query, or analyzer lens will retain sentences containing one or several words carrying one of the aspects marked as enabled; while for Codes and Bookmarks, a sentence remains when a coding or bookmark, respectively, overlaps it. Should there be any omitted sentences between two retained ones, a line of three spaced dots will indicate such omission. Sentences before the first retained one and beyond the last are excluded from the view without dots. Take the example below wherein “Running Out of Time” features only the Modality lens enabled, with every aspect except Necessity disabled. Only three sentences were left after collapsing, two with must and one with need. Yet the latter, We do not need another report, denies a necessity rather than proposing one. “Running Out of Time” collapsed to the sentences that the Modality lens annotates as Necessity. For a lens to show you only annotated sentences: Enable the lens, and disable the aspects you do not need in its legend. If you do not want coded and bookmarked sentences kept as well, disable Codes and Bookmarks. Clear Annotations disables both and keeps the built-in lenses enabled, though it also disables dictionary and query lenses. Click the collapse button. To read the whole document again, click the collapse button once more. Its tooltip now reads Show the whole document again. When a document is collapsed, changes in lenses and aspects are immediately reflected in the document. When there are no sentences left, the entire document is revealed. Initiating an edit or opening Find (⌘F) does the same. Codings, bookmarks, and memos added in the collapsed document will persist at their place in the full text.

The built-in lenses provide the analysis of the document's grammar. This includes its words, the word class and morphology of those words, the relationships between them, and the phrases which are made from those words. Incorrectly performed grammar analyses will show up in the lenses as well. Most of the analyses are performed accurately in edited writing; however, they are less accurate on spoken language, which contains repetitions, interruptions, and incomplete sentences. It is advisable to first find potential passages via the lens, and review a sample of those passages before making claims about their frequency. Certain lenses, including Modality, Connectives, and Metadiscourse lenses, use short word lists rather than grammar. These annotate an occurrence of a listed word whenever it fits within its proper grammatical word class, whatever it means in context. Which built-in lenses are available within LemmaLoom depends on the language of the analyzed document: Lens English German Chinese Word class Yes Yes Yes Grammatical function Yes Yes Yes Phrase Yes Yes Yes Morphology Yes Yes No Modality Yes Yes Yes Negation Yes Yes Yes Connectives Yes Yes Yes Sentence fields No Yes No Constructions No No Yes Particles No No Yes Cohesion Yes Yes Yes Metadiscourse Yes Yes Yes Rhetoric Yes Yes Yes Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric all come from analyses carried out via analyzers during indexing. You can find which analyzers were used on your document in Document Properties under Indexing (right-click your document in the navigation sidebar, then choose Properties). Should you remove any of their output there, then their corresponding lens will vanish from the lens menu for your document; clicking Run will bring it back (see Removing an analyzer's output in ).

Word class underlines every word in the document according to its part of speech. The legend consists of ten aspect lenslets, and includes Noun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, Pronoun, Determiner, Preposition, Conjunction, Number, and Interjection. This lens offers you a quick glimpse into the structure of your texts by looking at how much weight a text puts on certain word classes; for example, official reports often rely heavily on nouns. By keeping just the Adjective aspect on, you will get a visualization of what kinds of adjectives writers use to evaluate. When taking apart The fuel tax rarely spares a rural family in the Word class lens, fuel, tax, and family are underlined as nouns, spares as a verb, rarely as an adverb, rural as an adjective, and The and a as determiners. The figure below shows the opening of “Running Out of Time”, the story of one hot night, with Word class enabled. Word class in “Running Out of Time”, with the legend above the text. The classes are wide categories, and a few of them contain words beyond what they seem to categorize at first glance: Verb contains auxiliary verbs and modals like have, be, can, and should. Pronoun, in English, includes possessive pronouns such as my and their, as well as there in there is. Possessive pronouns in German, such as mein and ihr, fall under Determiner. Particles, including English to in to work, up in pick up, and the possessive 's; German zu and nicht; and Chinese 的 and 了 all belong to the class Preposition. In English, Preposition covers subordinating conjunctions such as because, if, and that (I think that). These are labeled like prepositions in English analyses and categorized as Conjunction in German and Chinese. Any word that does not fit into the ten classes, such as foreign words, receives a gray underline.

Grammatical function underlines each word according to its role within the sentence structure. The lens will indicate who or what performs actions within texts, e.g., whether the climate is the subject of a verb, as in the climate changes, or its object, as in protect the climate. All words besides the main verb are linked to one other word, their head, within a sentence structure. For example, in a rural family, the term rural is linked to family. Each word is colored according to its own relation to its head. Within a phrase structure, therefore, the main word shows the phrase's job, and the terms that function as modifiers to it will be colored as either Adjectival or Adverbial. In The fuel tax rarely spares a rural family: tax is marked Subject, while The and fuel are colored as Adjectival; rarely is colored Adverbial; family is marked Object, and both a and rural are colored Adjectival; finally, the main verb spares is left uncolored. “Running Out of Time” with the Grammatical function lens enabled and its legend above the text. There are ten aspect lenslets within the legend: Aspect What it annotates Example Subject The subject of a verb, including it and there used as empty subjects students in two students fainted Object The object of a verb or of a preposition petitions in signed more petitions; road in on a road Predicative A word that completes a linking verb such as be or seem expensive in floods are expensive Complement The verb of a clause that completes another verb share in the country has to share the bill Adjectival A word that modifies a noun, such as an article, adjective, possessive, number, noun used as a modifier, or preposition attached to a noun rural in a rural family; of in the end of the decade Adverbial A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb, including prepositions attached to a verb, adverbial clauses, and not rarely; after in voted after midnight Appositive A noun phrase that renames the one beside it carrier in one of my regulars, a retired mail carrier Agent The by that introduces the doer of a passive verb by in filtered by fear Conjunct The second and later members of a coordination skeptics in activists and skeptics Connector Small linking words, such as conjunctions, subordinators, auxiliary verbs, and particles and; because; have in have warned There are separate analyses for German and Chinese, with their own sets of relations. LemmaLoom sorts both into the same ten functions, and thus the colors represent nearly the same roles within each language. With the German analysis, though, the von phrase of a passive construction receives the label passive subject; thus, in von der Regierung beschlossen, von becomes colored as Subject. If a word does not correspond to any of the ten functions, for instance the sentence's main verb, then no color will be applied.

Phrase highlights words according to the smallest phrase that contains them. Noun phrases in official prose such as “Heat Wave Report 2024” stand out easily due to how long they usually are, allowing you to contrast these noun phrases with those of a speech. “Heat Wave Report 2024” with the Phrase lens enabled, showing noun phrases and noun chunks. In the legend, each type of phrase receives an aspect lenslet, namely Noun phrase, Verb phrase, Prepositional phrase, Adjective phrase, Adverb phrase, Conjunction phrase (as well as, rather than), and Interjection. Words whose smallest phrase is of another type (e.g., up in pick up) receive gray highlighting. Another aspect, Noun chunk, marks the nucleus of a noun phrase as a block. This means a noun or pronoun functioning as a subject or object in addition to the preceding words that form part of the same noun phrase. For instance, in We wrote to the city council after the flood, the three noun chunks are We, the city council, and the flood. Consequently, words that lie within a noun chunk receive two highlights, which blend into each other (see Combining lenses earlier in this chapter). You can toggle off the Noun chunk aspect in the legend to observe phrases alone, or keep only Noun chunk to observe the chunks.

Morphology color-codes every word according to one of its grammatical features, which include tense, number, degree, verb form, and, in German, case, mood, and gender. Aspect lenslets name a feature, followed by one value of that feature, such as Tense: Past or Number: Plural. With the lens enabled, you would be able to trace a change of tenses, such as how “Running Out of Time” transitions from telling a story about one hot night into the present tense. This change often marks a transition in a text from anecdote into argument. “Running Out of Time” with the Morphology lens enabled, where the text moves from past tense into present tense. Every word may express several features simultaneously. For example, the German noun Aktivistinnen expresses case, number, and gender. With the lens enabled, each word only receives the first available feature from this list: Language Order English Tense, Number, Degree, Verb form German Case, Mood, Tense, Verb form, Degree, Number, Gender Verbs in English usually indicate their tense; nouns and pronouns indicate their number; and adjectives indicate their degree (positive hot, comparative hotter, superlative hottest). Past participles such as warmed in has warmed are marked with Tense: Past since tense takes precedence. Base forms such as act in to act are marked with Verb form: Infinitive. Pairs of aspects sometimes share a color in LemmaLoom. Aspects such as Tense: Present and Verb form: Infinitive in English share the same teal color, making acts and to act look alike; in German, Case: Genitive shares the purple of Tense: Past. If you need to tell them apart, change the color of either aspect under Settings. The Lens colors and styles section later in this chapter covers lens color and style customization further. Nouns, articles, adjectives, and pronouns in German indicate their cases. When a verb is in Mood: Subjunctive or Mood: Imperative, it indicates its mood. All other finite verbs indicate their tense; infinitives and participles indicate their verb form (Verb form: Infinitive, Verb form: Participle). Thus, with all aspects enabled, Number and Gender are limited exclusively to words lacking any case in German.

The Modality lens highlights words that express possibility, necessity, and volition within the texts. Through it, you are able to observe how much certainty there is within a document. For instance, you may compare how often activist and skeptical writings say that something must happen, and how often that it might. Modality works from lists of words which are matched according to dictionary forms. Each word in a list is annotated only as a verb, auxiliary, or adverb (in English also as an adjective, for able). Aspect English German Chinese Ability can, could, able können 能, 会, 可以, 能够 Possibility may, might, perhaps, maybe, possibly mögen, dürfen, vielleicht, möglicherweise, eventuell 可能, 也许, 或许, 大概, 恐怕, 兴许 Necessity must, need müssen 必须, 需要, 务必, 必得 Obligation should, ought, shall sollen 应该, 应当, 该, 理应 Volition will, would, want, wish, intend wollen, möchten 要, 想, 愿意, 打算, 希望 Subjunctive  any other verb in the subjunctive, such as hätte or wäre  The Subjunctive aspect is unique to German alone. When a German modal verb is in the subjunctive mood, like könnte for example, it retains the aspect of its modal verb, which would be Ability. The lists match words irrespective of meaning. In the quote In 2050 she will be thirty-five from “Running Out of Time”, the word will, a plain future, carries the aspect of Volition.

Negation highlights the negating word(s) as Negator and underlines the scope they operate on within the sentence as Negation scope. The lens detects denials, and the places where writers refute a particular stance, as in “not a slow decline we can manage at our leisure” in “Running Out of Time”. Negators are words such as not, n't, never, no, nobody, nothing, none, neither, nor, and nowhere in English, along with any other word tagged as negation via the English analysis. In German, the negators include nicht, kein, nie, niemals, niemand, nichts, weder, and noch. However, the word noch is annotated regardless of its meaning; therefore, wir haben noch Zeit (we still have time) would receive annotation too. Chinese negators include 不, 没, 没有, 别, 无, and 未 among others. The negation scope consists of the word the negator is attached to plus everything grammatically dependent on it. If the negator modifies the main verb, which is the case with most uses of not, then nearly the whole clause would become the scope. An example of such a case would be We do not need another report, in “Running Out of Time”. Not would be highlighted as the negator while all other words, including We and do, would be underlined as scope. In No minister wanted the carbon tax, No is attached to minister, so only minister is underlined. The sentence “We do not need another report” in “Running Out of Time” with the Negation lens enabled.

Connectives classifies connecting words according to their meaning, which may include causation (e.g., because) or opposition (e.g., but). The lens allows you to map the logic of your documents, such as determining where reasons were provided and where points were conceded. Working from word lists, Connectives specifically focuses on finding where connecting words function as conjunctions/adverbs. “Net Zero Will Cost You” with the Connectives lens enabled and its legend above the text. Aspect English German Chinese Additive and, also, moreover, furthermore, besides, likewise, similarly und, auch, außerdem, zudem, ferner 而且, 并且, 此外, 另外, 以及 Adversative but, however, yet, nevertheless, instead, whereas, rather aber, jedoch, allerdings, hingegen, sondern 但是, 但, 然而, 不过, 可是, 却 Causal because, therefore, thus, hence, consequently, since, so weil, denn, daher, deshalb, folglich, da, also 因为, 由于, 所以, 因此, 于是 Temporal then, meanwhile, afterwards, before, after, finally, next, when, while dann, danach, bevor, nachdem, schließlich, während, als 然后, 接着, 随后, 之后, 最后, 首先 Conditional if, unless, otherwise, provided wenn, falls, sofern, sonst 如果, 要是, 假如, 只要, 除非, 否则 Concessive although, though, albeit obwohl, obgleich, dennoch, trotzdem 虽然, 尽管, 即使, 哪怕 The table provides just a sample; the list for most aspects is slightly longer. In speeches and debates, Additive annotates almost every usage of and, so disabling it is recommended if it crowds out the other aspects. The Temporal aspect applies to before in before the money runs out because it connects two clauses but not in before an election since it is used there as a preposition. Among conjunctions and adverbs, all of the words listed retain their particular aspect no matter how they are used. So in so hot becomes Causal even when there is no cause being discussed, and the word since remains Causal even in since the flood reached her street; while is Temporal even when it means whereas. Additionally, the German word da (meaning there, frequent in speech) becomes Causal regardless of meaning. The Metadiscourse lens contains its own specific Connective aspect, which annotates, whatever the relation, only the linking adverbs a speaker uses to steer the listener, such as however and therefore (see Metadiscourse later in this chapter).

Sentence fields displays the word order of a German sentence in accordance with the field model employed by German grammar. Finite verbs, those conjugated to agree with the sentence subject, constitute the left bracket (Linke Klammer). Participles, infinitives, and separable prefixes of verbs typically occur at the end of the clause in the right bracket (Rechte Klammer). Any elements preceding the left bracket constitute the Vorfeld, while elements appearing between both brackets make up the Mittelfeld; anything following the right bracket belongs to the Nachfeld. This lens becomes handy during studies analyzing which elements German authors lead off their sentences with because the Vorfeld usually contains topics or information stressed by writers. Below is an example sentence containing all five fields: Meine Nachbarin hat gestern bis drei Uhr draußen gesessen, weil ihre Wohnung unerträglich heiß war. Field Words Vorfeld Meine Nachbarin Linke Klammer hat Mittelfeld gestern bis drei Uhr draußen Rechte Klammer gesessen Nachfeld weil ihre Wohnung unerträglich heiß war If the sentence has no right bracket, like Wir streiken heute vor dem Rathaus, Mittelfeld encompasses anything following the finite verb. Separable prefixes, like an in Der Streik fängt um acht an, act as right brackets. The lens sees sentences as single clauses and regards the first occurrence of a finite verb as the left bracket. If the sentence starts with a subordinate clause, such as Weil es so heiß war, bin ich nach Hause gegangen, then the fields come out wrong; the first finite verb is actually war, which means war is the left bracket. Consequently, the main verb, bin, becomes part of the Mittelfeld. Determining the right bracket follows the same method where the last participle, infinitive, or separable prefix forms the right bracket; in the case of Wir haben versucht, die Abgeordneten zu überzeugen, the right bracket is überzeugen and versucht belongs to the Mittelfeld, while the sentence has no Nachfeld. If a sentence lacks a finite verb, then LemmaLoom leaves it uncolored. Punctuation marks stay uncolored too. The following figure shows part of “Running Out of Time (German)”, the translated text from the op-ed article “Running Out of Time” in the project “Climate Debate”. Here, the opening line of the German translation begins with Um Mitternacht an diesem heißen Sommertag zeigte, making Um Mitternacht an diesem heißen Sommertag the Vorfeld, zeigte the left bracket, and the separable prefix an at its end the right bracket. Sentence fields in “Running Out of Time (German)”.

Two lenses are available for analyzing Chinese documents only. They allow you to understand your text better if your study concerns how events are framed, including actors acting upon objects in 把 sentences and actions performed upon somebody in 被 sentences. Constructions highlights the typical keywords found within four sentence constructions: Aspect What it annotates Example 把 disposal 把, which brings the object before the verb 他们把太阳能板装在屋顶上。 被 passive 被 and the other passive markers the analysis recognizes 铁轨被高温晒弯了。 是…的 focus 是 and the sentence-final 的 when they frame a sentence 我是去年开始参加罢课的。 Existential 有 有 (and 没有) used as a verb 广场上有两百个学生。 The analysis tags both possessive 有, as seen in 我有时间, and existential 有 with the same tag; thus, Constructions will annotate it. The Chinese text “时间不多了” with the Constructions lens enabled, marking 被 passives and 没有. Particles highlights grammatical particles and classifiers: Aspect What it annotates Example 了 perfective 了 as a perfective particle after a verb 我们签了请愿书 着 durative 着 after a verb 她举着牌子 过 experiential 过 after a verb 我去过那个农场 的 attributive 的 linking a modifier to a noun 我的女儿; 种大麦的农民 地 adverbial 地 linking a modifier to a verb 慢慢地走 得 complement 得 introducing a complement of degree or result 涨得很快 Classifier measure words 个 in 两百个学生 Sentence-final 了, which the analysis treats as a modal particle, has been excluded here. The Metadiscourse lens labels it as a Final particle.

Cohesion shows how each sentence relates back to what had been said previously in the document. This is based on the premise that each sentence usually begins with what has been established beforehand (theme), while ending with new information. According to text linguistics, texts become easier to understand when each theme connects back to a previous sentence. The lens discovers each sentence's theme and highlights it according to its relation with preceding sentences. In the English language, the theme consists of the complete subject phrase of the main verb in the sentence. For German, the theme is the Vorfeld, or else the complete subject phrase when there is no Vorfeld. In Chinese, the theme is the topic, or the complete subject phrase when the analysis finds no topic. Aspect When it is used Opening The first sentence of the document, which has nothing to tie back to Pronoun tie The theme contains a third-person pronoun such as she, it, or they Possessive tie The theme contains a third-person possessive such as his, its, or their. Her counts as a Pronoun tie, because the pronoun test comes first. Demonstrative tie The theme contains this, that, these, those, or such Repeated word A noun, pronoun, number, or adjective in the theme has the same dictionary form as a noun, pronoun, number, verb, or adjective in one of the two sentences before Zero anaphora Chinese only. The main verb has no subject, so the sentence continues the topic of the one before (anaphora is a reference back to something already mentioned). Its lenslet appears in the legend of every document. New topic None of the above. The theme brings in something new, or the sentence has no theme at all. The tests are performed in the order they are listed in the table above, with the first passing test resulting in the assignment of its aspect. While both Pronoun tie and Repeated word aspects appear in green coloration, they are differentiated in the Cohesion section under the Discourse facet. All sentences that lack a subject (commands, fragmentary sentences such as Net zero by 2050.) lack themes and therefore belong to New topic (typically Zero anaphora in Chinese), with only their ending underlined. Finally, New ending (stress) is underlined in every sentence. It refers to the smallest phrase containing the last word of a sentence, unless the phrase exceeds six words; then, it refers to the last word alone. See the sample below: Our village had four buses a day. (Opening) They ran to the market town and back. (Pronoun tie) Their timetable was cut twice in two years. (Possessive tie) The town now pays for an electric minibus. (Repeated word, since town repeats sentence 2) Fuel prices keep climbing. (New topic) A run of New topic sentences may indicate jumps made by the audience without aid; however, the lens measures ties crudely. The lens identifies pronouns based on their morphological form. Ties involve solely repetitions of the same words; therefore, related terms like village and town would be considered new words by this measure. Pronouns qualify as repetitions too. When consecutive sentences start with the pronoun we repeatedly, for example in “Letter from the Climate Strike”, multiple themes appear under the category of Repeated word. In the figure below, the news article “Carbon Tax Debate” presents various perspectives one group at a time. Sentences introducing a new group like “Rural members on both sides”, “Some”, and “Others” begin with a New topic according to this criterion. Since a quote attributed to a backbencher includes a pronoun in the quote itself (They), the measure detects this instance as a Pronoun tie. Cohesion in the news article “Carbon Tax Debate”, with the theme of each sentence highlighted and its end underlined. In the Cohesion section of the Discourse facet in the Grammar tab of the inspector, there is a list of all ties in every sentence of your document (even those with no theme; see Cohesion in ).

There are many words which allow speakers to comment on what they say and speak directly to their listeners. Some examples would be words like perhaps, obviously, and you. All these can be highlighted via the Metadiscourse lens, which allows for an examination of the author's stance based on hedging, bolstering, and addressing. The lens uses lexical lists and determines the word class of every word analyzed. Aspect What it annotates English examples Hedge Softens a claim perhaps, probably, roughly, may, might, could, seem, suggest, often, usually Booster Closes down doubt clearly, obviously, certainly, indeed, always, never, demonstrate Attitude marker States the speaker's feeling about what is said fortunately, unfortunately, surprisingly, sadly, hopefully Connective Steers between ideas however, therefore, thus, nevertheless, meanwhile, instead; also, so, then, and finally at the start of a sentence Engagement Addresses or includes the listener you, your, we, us, our, let; imperatives such as consider, imagine, and note Modal particle German only. Particles that tone a sentence toward the listener. ja, doch, eben, halt, mal, schon Final particle Chinese only. Particles at the end of a sentence. 吗, 呢, 吧, 啊 German and Chinese have separate lists. In German, Sie used as the polite you outside of the start of a sentence counts as Engagement. In public speeches and open letters where the author frequently uses the pronouns we and you, there are numerous instances of Engagement which overwhelm the visualization. If necessary, you may disable Engagement in the legend so as to view the other aspects clearly. “A Mayor's Promise” with the Metadiscourse lens enabled, showing Engagement and a Hedge.

Rhetoric calls attention to stylistic devices such as the passive voice and parallelism, which authors use consciously. The use of Rhetoric will be the most effective on pre-written texts such as op-ed pieces and the speech titled “A Mayor's Promise”, allowing you to analyze how the persuasive pieces for each side were constructed. Most devices will be highlighted, whereas Nominalization, Power word, and Anaphora will be underlined. Passive voice and Correlative pair will both get a purple highlight. “A Mayor's Promise” with the Rhetoric lens enabled and its legend above the text. The table organizes the devices in testing order: Aspect What it annotates Passive voice A passive verb group, as in the schools were closed Nominalization A noun made from a verb or adjective. In English, a noun of seven letters or more ending in -tion, -sion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance, -ence, or -ism (decision, payment); in German, endings such as -ung, -heit, and -keit Fronted opener Words placed before the subject at the start of a sentence, such as an adverbial or a participle phrase (After the flood, the council…) Parallelism Three or more coordinated items, or two coordinated clauses that each have a subject (we marched and they watched) Periodic sentence A sentence of at least twelve words with at least 55 percent of them before its main verb (in a sentence of 20 words, at least 11). In German, a sentence whose Mittelfeld holds eight words or more before the right bracket closes it Question / command A whole question or imperative sentence Focus construction Sentences reshaped to put one element in the spotlight, such as there is…, what we need is…, and it was the farmers who… Absolute phrase A noun with a participle, standing apart from the clause (the vote taken, we went home) Appositive A noun phrase that renames the one beside it Power word A superlative, an intensified adjective or adverb (extremely hot), or a stressing adverb such as only, never, or even Correlative pair Paired conjunctions such as both … and, either … or, and neither … nor Cohesion check The theme of a sentence of six words or more that the Cohesion lens counts as a New topic Anaphora The first two words of consecutive sentences that open with the same word, other than the, a, an, and, but, so, and then. This is the rhetorical figure, unrelated to Zero anaphora in Cohesion. Every word annotation displays one rhetoric device from the table, the first in the table's order whose test applies to it. Since Question / command affects the entire sentence while Periodic sentence affects everything preceding the sentence's main verb, these two have precedence over other devices lower in the table. First-person pronouns like I and we count as openers, hence Anaphora will tag plenty of beginnings of sentences in “Why We Block the Roads”. German and Chinese have their own versions of most tests. For instance, Fronted opener marks a Vorfeld that does not hold the subject in German, while in Chinese it will highlight a fronted topic. Absolute phrase is detected only in English documents, while Periodic sentence is detected in both English and German. Lenslets pertaining to all devices, including these two, will display in the legend of each document. The Rhetoric section under the Discourse facet in the Grammar tab of the inspector contains a list of all identified rhetoric devices with brief explanations of why they were tagged. The list includes any findings concealed within the body of the text; namely, those which were tagged with a disabled aspect or whose words show earlier devices (see Rhetoric in ).

Codes visualizes all coded passages in the document in the format and color of the particular code itself (choose Highlight, Underline, or Boxed from Format during creation and editing of codes; see The fields of a code in ). It draws colored bars next to each coding in the gutter to the left side of your text as well. Disabling Codes hides these visualizations. When coding, keep Codes enabled. Once you're done coding, however, disable Codes when you want to read your text without seeing all your coding. Bookmarks will highlight every passage marked with a bookmark in the bookmark's color, and draw that bookmark both in the gutter and document overview. Both memos and links will be visible regardless of which lenses you may have enabled, as codings are while Codes is enabled.

Dictionaries appear in the lens menu, under their own names, in the annotations group. A dictionary lens highlights the terms of each of its categories using the specified category colors, and its legend contains a single aspect lenslet per category. The “Climate Debate” project includes one dictionary, “Hedges”, containing two categories, Approximators and Shields. When “Hedges” is enabled, its legend will include these two lenslets. Consider It seems to me the burden falls on just about everyone from “Radio Debate”; It seems is highlighted as a shield and just about as an approximator. A dictionary lens is useful if your study uses its own categorizations of particular words. Some examples include hedges, blaming language, or terms within a specific policy field. “Radio Debate” with the dictionary “Hedges” enabled, with Approximators and Shields in the legend. Dictionary matching matches a term as a whole word and does not take capitalization or accent marks into account, but matches Chinese terms anywhere they appear (see How terms are matched in ). Each form must be entered separately as separate terms. For example, if you wish for both model and models to match, then they should each be added as terms. Dictionary matching does not consider grammar. About in Here's the thing about panic, from “Let's Not Panic”, is highlighted as an approximator despite being a preposition. Enabling the lens causes the legend to appear immediately, whereas highlighting will happen only after the terms are matched. Editing your dictionary when the lens is enabled causes annotations to be updated accordingly. Unlike the predetermined set of hedges available in the pre-built Hedge list of Metadiscourse, dictionaries contain user-defined terms and categorizations. Rules, however, such as a part of speech, may be added using a query lens.

You can save a query lens from any query which finds passages within the text. Open the Save menu (the box with the arrow pointing down, in the query header) and click on Save as Lens… (see Saving a query as a lens in ). The “Climate Debate” project has a saved query lens called “Urgency Talk” which highlights sentences containing the words urgent, urgency, crisis, emergency, or deadline if they overlap passages with the code “Urgency”. A query lens is suitable for answering any questions involving the combination of rules, for instance the presence of words combined with the word's grammatical features, or codings combined with words. The availability of a query lens in documents relies upon the Available In choice made when the query was saved: a query saved for All Projects or for the Project appears in every document of the project; a query saved for a Set appears in the documents of that set and in their translations; a query saved for a Document appears in that document only. “Urgency Talk” has been saved for the Project, and is thus available for annotation in each document in the “Climate Debate” project. “Running Out of Time” with the query lens “Urgency Talk” enabled, with its legend above the text. A query lens marks up the hits from its parent query. When there are no categories involved in a query lens, its legend displays one lenslet whose name corresponds to the query; all hits are highlighted. If the query lens contains categories, each category is an aspect, and has its own distinct color and style (Highlight or Underline, as set in the query's Categories condition). With Color By, each unique value in the hits gets its own aspect, up to sixteen total. The first eight of these values are highlighted; the next eight get underlined in the same eight colors (see Categories and Color By in ). Each query lens displays its legend with lenslets showing squares. When codings or bookmarks in the document change, the query lenses run again, so a query that looks for coded passages stays current as you code. To remove a query lens from its place in the lens menu, access the Save menu of the query and click on Remove Lens. See the conditions required to transform a query into a lens in Which queries can be lenses in .

Analyzers you define through Window ▸ Analyzers find spans of text and assign them keys. The keys in the analyzer's legend define aspects of its lens. All your analyzers are found as the second group in the lens menu under their individual names, and only available in documents where the languages match those the analyzer can process. Only spans assigned a key within the analyzer's legend will show up in your lens, colored and styled (Highlight, Underline, Text color, or Bold) according to that particular key's definition in the legend. Essentially, an analyzer is needed whenever you seek out a pattern repeatedly across your documents and none of the existing lenses, dictionaries, or queries capture it. “Running Out of Time” with the analyzer lens “Climate Roles” enabled, with the Analyzers group open in the lens menu. Skipping an analyzer for a document or removing its output within Document Properties will cause its lens to disappear from the lens menu of that document (see Analyzers for each document in ). For additional detail on writing analyzers and execution timing, please refer to .

Four of the lenses (Word class, Grammatical function, Phrase, and Morphology) are customizable with regard to their color and style. Your customizations will affect the appearance of the lens regardless of which document within which project you're looking at. All other built-in lenses have preset colors. Lenses generated by dictionaries, queries, and analyzers derive their colors based on the categories and keys of those objects. Adjust colors whenever two aspects become visually indistinct to you, or whenever you need to overlay extra lenses beyond their default styles' capabilities. Each aspect may appear as one of four styles: Style How the word looks Highlight A pale band of color behind the word Underline A colored line under the word Text color The letters in the color Bold The letters in bold and in the color Word class and Grammatical function lenses underline by default. The Phrase and Morphology lenses highlight instead. The figure below demonstrates the Settings window's Lenses pane with rows for each aspect of Word class and Grammatical function lenses, each set to Underline. The Lenses pane of Settings, showing the Word class and Grammatical function sections. To modify the appearance of an aspect: Choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,) and click Lenses. Find the lens's section and the aspect's row, such as Noun under Word class. Choose a style from the menu in that row, which shows the current style, such as Underline. Click the color well beside it and choose a color. Open documents update immediately when you make a change. In Help ▸ Glossary, tags and terms representing an aspect, like NN for Noun, are colored and styled in accordance with that aspect's color and style settings. Lenslets in the legend display the default colors and shapes of aspects, and therefore after a modification the lenslet and its words in the text differ. Each modified aspect receives a reset button, shown at the end of its row as a curved arrow with a tooltip like Reset Noun. Clicking on it resets the aspect to its defaults. At the very top of the pane, the Reset All to Defaults button resets all aspects of all four lenses simultaneously (see The Lenses pane in ). When you want to view three lenses simultaneously, style each one differently. Style all ten aspects of Word class as Text color, then combine this lens with Grammatical function, which underlines, and Modality, which highlights.

Coding labels what passages mean; this is done by assigning codes. Most studies start out with questions regarding documents, and codes are used to help answer those questions. Your codes comprise the codebook of your project, and codes can contain subcodes in hierarchies when appropriate for a study. LemmaLoom retains every coded passage; later you may collect all passages for each code and compare them between documents (see ). Memos, links, and bookmarks start from a selection in the reader, just as codings do. Whereas coding applies labels to passages, memos, links, and bookmarks offer means to comment on passages, relate them to each other, or find them again. Should passages already be found by dictionaries, queries, or custom analyzers, they can all be coded in one run via auto code. Examples used in this chapter are based on “Climate Debate”, which is the bundled example project of this guide. You can add it through File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project (see The example project in ). Its codebook includes five top-level codes that represent its themes, “Costs”, “Emotions”, “Responsibility”, “Science”, and “Urgency”. Within “Emotions” lie the subcodes “Fear” and “Hope”; “Uncertainty” belongs to “Science”. “Urgency” has two subcodes as well, “Deadlines” and “Tipping Points”.

A code refers to a label for topics or concepts that can be applied to passages of text. Codes have a structure that looks like trees, where one code may contain subcodes, and subcodes can themselves contain more subcodes. The entire tree of all codes within a project is referred to as the code system. You can see the code system and descriptions along with frequency of application in the Codebook view of the project shelf. Coding means the application of a code onto a segment of text. That particular segment of text receiving a code application is referred to as a coded segment, or simply segment. You could apply multiple codes onto the same passage of text; these applications could overlap with each other, or some could lie nested within others. Every code will have a format setting (highlighting, underlining, or boxing), determining how the reader displays passages with this code applied, and a scope parameter, which can limit the code to one document set or individual document. A code set is a named collection of codes taken from anywhere in the tree, meant for use in Sketch Space and queries. Codes can also have attributes of their own, such as an intensity for “Fear”. These are the same kind of attribute as a document's “Stance” or “Readership”, but each coding holds its own value. Memos represent your notes made upon a passage of text; when associated with a particular code, memos become coded memos. Coded memos count as codings of that code, take on its tags, and have their own values for its attributes. Linking refers to connecting two passages of text together with a link; these could be from the same document, or from two separate documents. A link allows adding a comment and a relation (for example, “contradicts”) between linked text passages. Bookmarks are another form of annotation for marking passages of text you want to find again. They have their own comment field, as well as a coloring option. All annotations described above are attached to passages of text. This implies that whenever changes are made to documents while editing, these annotations will follow their text (see How annotations follow edits in ). If documents have translations, annotations will also be copied to the matching passages (see Codings in translations later in this chapter).
You assign codes via the reader. You create and maintain them both via the Coding tab of the inspector and via the Codebook and Codings project shelf views.

t: The selection bar and the Document menu
b: Whenever you select text in the reader, the selection bar will appear near the bottom. Each button acts upon the selection, and each button corresponds to a command in the Document menu: Button Command Shortcut What it does Bookmark (or Remove Bookmark) Document ▸ Bookmark ⇧⌘B Bookmarks the passage, or removes the bookmark it overlaps Code Document ▸ Code ⇧⌘C Opens the code palette Memo Document ▸ Memo ⇧⌘M Opens a new memo for the passage Link (or Finish Link) Document ▸ Link ⇧⌘L Starts a link here, or ends the link you started The bar also has the command Add to Dictionary, which inserts the selected text into a category of a project dictionary (see Adding terms from a document in ). This bar ends with ×, which clears the selection, as Esc does. See Selecting text in  for more on selecting words, sentences, and passages. A passage of “Running Out of Time” selected, with the selection bar showing Bookmark, Code, Add to Dictionary, Memo, Link, and the button that clears the selection. The selection bar in “Running Out of Time” after Link, showing Finish Link and the button that cancels the pending link. When editing text in the document, this bar becomes invisible, and the commands are disabled. There are three additional commands related to coding in the Document menu. In Vivo Code (⇧⌘V) codes the selected passage with a code named after its constituent words (see Coding a passage in this chapter). Auto Code… (⇧⌘A) automatically codes any passages annotated by a particular lens (see Coding passages automatically in this chapter). Cancel Link (⌥⇧⌘L) gives up a link you are in the middle of making.

The Coding tab of the inspector (tag icon, ⌥⌘3) applies to the currently active document. This tab contains six facets: Facet What it shows See Codes The code system, with the number of codings of each code in this document. Here you create, edit, and merge codes, and see the code sets. The Codes facet Codings This document's codings and memos in reading order, with the attribute values of each coding The Codings facet Links The links with at least one end in this document Following a link Code Stats How often each code is used in the document, how much of the text it covers, and which codes overlap Code frequencies and coverage in  Portrait Two pictures of the document's coding, Mosaic and Codeline Portrait in  Code Sketch A word sketch that splits a word's uses by the codes around them Code Sketch in  Instead, bookmarks are found on the Text tab (see Bookmarks later in this chapter).

Out of ten views on your project shelf, four contain your codes and annotations, which include Codebook, Codings, Memos, and Links. All four views span the entirety of the project if opened from Project in the navigation sidebar; conversely, should they be opened from a set's or tag's tab, they cover only documents included in the respective sets or tags. More details regarding the views themselves and their tabs can be found at The project shelf in . This chapter introduces Codebook, Memos, and Links. The Codings view enumerates all coded passages in scope and enables filtering of these passages by attribute values. Alongside Code Stats, Code Matrix, and Relations, the Codings view is covered in The Codings view in .

Creating a code happens from either the Codes facet in the inspector or the Codebook view. The coding process itself involves selecting passages in the reader and applying codes to those selections via the code palette. Creating a code on the fly from the palette while performing analysis is covered below in Coding a passage. It generally helps to create initial codes for your questions ahead of time, but adding additional codes based upon the data during analysis is also acceptable. Codebooks typically evolve in the first several documents, and editing and merging of codes can happen anytime (see Organizing codes later in this chapter). To create a code in the inspector: Open a document. In the inspector, click the Coding tab and then Codes. Click + at the right of Code System. In the New Code dialog, type a name in Name. Set the other fields as described in The fields of a code below, or leave them as they are. Click Save. For creating a subcode, right-click the parent within the Codes facet and choose Add Subcode. The same dialog opens, with the new code appearing below its parent. When in Codebook view, clicking Add Code below the list creates a top-level code. Right-clicking a parent code while still in Codebook view will bring up Add Subcode. From the menu Project ▸ Add Code, you can get the dialog for a top-level code; while from Project ▸ Add Subcode, the dialog opens for a subcode of the currently selected code either in the Codes facet or the Codebook view. The Save button remains disabled until the code is assigned a name (it has Name is empty as its tooltip). Always remember to assign a unique name to each code because distinguishing two codes with identical names can become rather confusing in menus and tables.

Both New Code and Edit Code dialogs share identical fields. Each theme code, including “Deadlines”, in “Climate Debate” has its own color, the format Highlight, the scope Project, and a description under About that tells you what the code refers to. The description of “Deadlines”, for instance, reads “Target years, countdowns and cut-off dates, whether demanded, promised or criticized.” The Edit Code dialog for “Deadlines”, opened from the Codes facet of “Running Out of Time”. There is a Color setting with which you configure what the code looks like in the reader. This setting allows for the use of No color, or alternatively eight colors spanning the spectrum between Red and Pink. There is a Pick any color well at the far-right end should none of those options suffice. A code with No color shows in the theme's accent color in the text and in yellow in the gutter. When coding your documents, consider using distinct colors for multiple codes to avoid having overlapping codings clash in the text and the gutter. Format sets how the reader renders coded text. Highlight fills the background in the color corresponding to the code; Underline places a horizontal bar below the text in said color, while Boxed draws a border frame around the text. Using combinations of formats may help differentiate codings better where they overlap; for instance, a highlighted phrase embedded within a box will still show clearly. The selected format will affect all applications of the code, including coded memos. More details on Scope, as well as the Tags and Attributes you can attach to a code, appear in separate sections of this chapter, namely Where a code can be used, Tags on codes, and Codes with attributes. You can describe a code within its About property to explain what it entails and provide guidelines for applying the code consistently throughout the research process. The description appears under the code's name in the Codebook view and goes into the codebook export.

t: Where a code can be used
b: There are three possible scopes for any code in the Scope menu: Project makes the code available for all documents of the project. Newly created codes default to having a Project scope. Document set restricts usage of the code to only documents of one set. Choose the document set from the drop-down Document set menu below. It is also possible to define the scope as a smart set whose documents are selected based on conditions (see Smart sets in ). With the code defined as a Document set scope, LemmaLoom makes the code available whenever new documents enter the set and stops offering it in documents no longer belonging to the set. Document defines the scope of the code as a particular document, and the code applies to both that document and its translations. Pick your target document from the Document drop-down menu below. The Document set menu in the Edit Code dialog for “Fear”, listing the sets and smart sets of “Climate Debate”. The code palette, the Codes facet, and the Auto Code dialog show codes relevant to particular documents according to their scope. For codes defined as Document set and Document scopes, it will be necessary to first select a set/document from the respective drop-down menus. The Codebook view shows codes of any scope. In most cases, setting the Project scope is sufficient. However, when dealing with codes that are only meaningful in a certain subset of documents, such as a code for protest tactics in the “Activists” set, you could use a Document set or Document scope. Speaker codes generated during the transcription process by LemmaLoom are document codes because they relate to individual documents (recording transcripts). For instance, “Speakers”, whose subcodes are “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”, is a document code of “Radio Debate” in the “Climate Debate” project; as such, the palette will not provide access to it while you code “Running Out of Time” (see Speakers in ). When narrowing a code's scope later, previous codings will remain unchanged in the text and in every count. They can be deleted in documents outside the narrowed scope only via the Codings facet or the Codings view of the shelf (see Removing a code from a passage later in this chapter). Deleting a code's set means giving the code a new scope before applying it again. Deleting a document deletes its document codes. Translation deletion results in passing its document codes to the original. For details about the treatment of document codes in word sketches for a set/project scope, see Document codes in .

Within the Codes facet and the Codebook view, the codes on each level of the tree are sorted alphabetically, while subcodes are indented beneath their parent. You use subcodes whenever your research benefits from hierarchy. This allows you to divide a broad theme according to the different ways that it manifests itself. For instance, within the “Climate Debate” example project, “Urgency” has been broken down into “Deadlines”, in reference to target years and cut-off dates, and “Tipping Points”, in relation to thresholds after which damage is said to become irreversible. In the absence of such natural hierarchy, however, a simple flat list suffices. A parent code is simply another code. You use a parent code when the passage belongs to the broader theme but falls outside of its various manifestations captured by subcodes. In “A Mayor's Promise”, “We do not have the luxury of a slow start” has been coded “Urgency”, since it belongs to neither “Tipping Points” nor “Deadlines”. Only the passages coded with a parent itself contribute to the count beside it. Moving a code entails dragging the code onto its new parent code within the Codes facet or Codebook view, or right-clicking the code to invoke Move To. The Move To submenu displays a drop-down tree excluding the moved code itself as well as its subcodes. At the top of this list, Top Level unparents the selected code. Project ▸ Move To does the same thing for the currently selected code. The code keeps its codings, and its subcodes move with it.

The code “Deadlines” applies to three targets in the fourth paragraph of “Running Out of Time”, “Net zero by 2050. Coal gone by the end of the decade. Emissions halved by 2030.” On the other hand, the passage selected in the figure, from “Farmers Are Not the Enemy”, is coded both as “Costs” and “Responsibility”, since it talks about who pays for the shift as well as who should act. Thus, the palette displays a checkmark next to both. A passage in “Farmers Are Not the Enemy” selected from its gutter bar, with the code palette showing that “Costs” and “Responsibility” are already applied. For coding a passage: Select a passage, click a paragraph or sentence number in the gutter, or click a single word. Click Code in the selection bar, or press ⇧⌘C. In the palette, click the code. If it has attributes, a dialog first asks for their values (see Codes with attributes later in this chapter). What is selectable depends upon the document. Word and sentence number selections are available only after a document is indexed. Passage selections are usable with all documents, even those written in languages aside from English, German, or Chinese. The palette displays every code applicable in the current document in alphabetical order. Each entry lists the code name with its associated color. Since this list is linear and not hierarchical, “Deadlines” occurs somewhere after “Costs” yet before “Emotions”. The Search codes field has focus when displaying the palette, allowing typing of partial names into it to narrow down the list and highlighting the top entry in the results. The highlighted entry gets applied to the passage when pressing Return, while ↑ and ↓ navigate highlights, even prior to searching, so with a few letters and Return you can code a passage from the keyboard alone. Once a code is applied to a passage, the palette remains open to allow application of additional codes to the same passage immediately. Close the palette by pressing Esc, or clicking elsewhere on the screen outside the palette area. A checkmark icon appears beside the names of any applicable code already covering parts of the selected passage; click a checked code, or press Return with that code highlighted, to remove that code from coverage in the passage (see Removing a code from a passage below). Changing what parts of the passage a coding covers requires removal of the existing coding and coding anew. Giving an existing coding another code can be done using Change Code in the Codings facet (see The Codings facet below). You may add codes thought up mid-analysis directly into your codebook from your document context using the palette. Should none of the codes in the displayed list have your intended code's name, Add Code “…” shows at the bottom of the list, adding a code bearing that name and applying it. In Vivo “…” is always last in the list; it adds an in vivo code based on the currently selected text in your document, naming the code with that selected text and applying it. Selecting “a wish with a calendar attached” in “Running Out of Time”, for example, offers In Vivo “a wish with a calendar attached”. Document ▸ In Vivo Code (⇧⌘V) does the same without the palette. Names over 60 characters long get truncated with ellipses. If a code you can use in this document already has that name, ignoring capitalization, that code is used instead of a newly created one.
