Codes added through either the Add Code or In Vivo function appear at the top level of the codebook's hierarchy, with No color, in Highlight format, with the scope Project. When you next look over your codebook, consider giving these codes a color and a place in the tree (see Organizing codes later in this chapter). In vivo codes may prove useful during initial coding sessions as they keep codes closer to original phrasing in materials, and you can rename or merge them once your codes settle. Edit ▸ Undo Apply Code (⌘Z) removes both the coding and the new code.

With the Codes lens enabled, as it is when a document opens, each coding is visually marked with its respective code's coloring and formatting scheme. Beside each coded passage in the gutter is a thin bar colored the code's color, along with the code name appearing in a small annotation next to the start of the coded passage. Overlapping codings stand side by side, up to three bars across; any further codings share the third bar. Hover the mouse pointer over the bars to highlight the respective passages; clicking either a bar or the code annotation selects the passage. Should multiple annotations overlap in nearly the same vertical position within the gutter, LemmaLoom displays only one annotation for those multiple annotations, much like the one shown next to the selected passage in the figure above. Codings, memos, bookmarks, and link ends are combined alike; each combined annotation has colored dots for the first three items and counts the items in it. Hovering or clicking a combined annotation lists the individual items, allowing a click to select each item's passage; if it concerns a link end, then clicking it navigates you to the other end of the link. A combined annotation in “Running Out of Time”, with its list open, showing the code “Uncertainty” and the link “contradicts”. Disabling the Codes lens removes all the visual markers of codings at once (see Codes and Bookmarks in ).

t: Removing a code from a passage
b: Select the passage. Clicking its bar or annotation in the gutter selects exactly the coded text. Open the palette (⇧⌘C). Click the code with the checkmark. When clicking the code, you will delete all codings associated with that code that overlap with your selection, regardless of whether those codings extend outside your selection range. Exercise caution while making the selection when there may be multiple codings of the same code near each other. Should you wish to remove a specific coding rather than all overlapping codings, use the Codings facet. You can click the coding and then Delete beneath the coding's text, or you can right-click the coding and select Delete Coding from the menu. Alternatively, if you are viewing the Codings view of the shelf, right-click the segment and select Delete Coding. Deleting a coding means deleting that coding's attribute values, and its copies in the document's translations.

The Codings facet displays all codings in the current document according to their reading order. The toggle on top alternates between Codings and Memos. Each has its own counter next to its label in parentheses; for instance, Codings (13) for “Running Out of Time”. Reading, editing, and deleting memos discusses the latter in greater detail later in this chapter. Every coding has its own row consisting of the code's color and name, location, and first line of its text. Paragraph 4, sentence 2 translates to a location of ¶4·2. For a document without sentences, such as one that has not been indexed, it shows just the paragraph alone, as in ¶4. When you click a coding, LemmaLoom scrolls the reader to the passage coded. The click also opens the row to reveal up to four lines of the text along with any attribute values set for it and a Delete button. Another click closes a coding. Alternatively, right-clicking brings forth options to either Go to Source, Change Code, or Delete Coding. The Codings facet of “Running Out of Time”, showing Codings (13) with the “Deadlines” coding expanded. In Change Code, the possible codes to assign are displayed hierarchically as a tree. After choosing one, both the coding and its copies in translated versions adopt the selected code. The coding retains its attribute value for each attribute that the new code possesses under the same name and type, while losing any other attributes' values. You undo changing a code, values included, with Edit ▸ Undo Change Code (⌘Z). The Codings view of the shelf features an analogous shortcut menu item in every segment. The shortcut menu of a “Costs” coding in the Codings facet of “Farmers Are Not the Enemy”, with the Change Code submenu open. There are three additional controls above the codings list: With Search, you narrow the list by searching the code names or text. Filter by code, the funnel button, lets you limit the display of codings only to one chosen code at once. Choosing All Codes reverts to displaying all codings. With Export, you can export all codings currently shown on screen to a CSV file with Code, Location, Start, End, and Text as columns. Of these, Start and End indicate where in characters the passage lies relative to the document's start position.

Sometimes codes will require more nuance than yes/no responses. In a study on the presence of fear within climate-related writings, for instance, you might record the intensity level of each coding for fear. The attribute here would be “Intensity”, while the options could be either “Low”, “Medium”, or “High”, and each coding of “Fear” would hold one of them. Typically, use attributes when there is a qualitative aspect of your codes which always exists within each passage coded (in this case, how intensely the emotion is felt). Use subcodes when there is another layer to a code which deserves to become its own distinct entity within the palette and code tables. To assign an attribute to a code: Open the code's dialog, for example, by double-clicking the code in the Codes facet. Under Attributes, click Add Attribute. Type the attribute's name. Names of attributes already in the project are suggested as you type, and choosing one also takes over its type and choices. Choose a type in the menu showing Text beside the name, namely Text, Integer (a whole number), Decimal, Boolean (true or false), Date, or Picker (one of a list of choices). For Picker, type the choices in the rows that appear, one per row. Click Save. Above Add Attribute are listed the code's existing attributes, including each one's type. The pencil button (Edit) will open the Edit Attribute dialog where you will be able to edit the attribute's name, choices, Description, and type if possible depending on existing values recorded in the attribute. Its Save button immediately applies the changes without requiring confirmation in the code dialog itself; they stay even if you then cancel the code's dialog. The minus button (Remove attribute) deletes the attribute along with all of its values upon saving the code. More information regarding the types mentioned above can be found in Attribute types in . The Edit Code dialog for “Fear”, with the attribute “Intensity” of the type Picker and the choices Low, Medium, and High. Whenever an attribute-containing code is applied to some piece of text, LemmaLoom first prompts you to fill out the associated attributes in a small dialog. Fill in the values you need and click Apply Code. The dialog that asks for the value of “Intensity” when “Fear” is applied to a passage of “Running Out of Time”. After applying an attribute-containing code to text, revising values becomes possible by clicking the coding itself within the Codings facet. Changes are saved instantly upon modification of a value control. Within the Codings view of the shelf, the selected segment's attribute values are displayed alongside controls to modify them directly. Additionally, segments within that view can be filtered based on their values. The Attribute Breakdowns section of Code Stats, both within the facet and the shelf view, breaks each code's codings down by attribute value. See Attribute breakdowns in . The query builder allows querying codings based on their attribute values (see ). A coded memo assigned to a code with attributes has its own set of values (see Coded memos later in this chapter).

Translating documents allows you to create versions of your documents in different languages. “Running Out of Time (German)” is an example of a translated document in German, listed under its original in the navigation sidebar. Coding any passage in “Running Out of Time” applies to its corresponding passage in the translated version, and vice versa. Any memos, links, and bookmarks made in either document are copied too. All copies remain linked together. How exactly a copy fits its passage depends on how the sentences of the two texts align (for more information, see Where copies are stored in ). If one copy gets deleted or edited, then all copies of that particular instance of coding follow suit. A coding and its copies share identical attribute values as well. Any analysis performed on sets or projects defaults to original documents. Thus, a coding and its copies count once in the analysis output (see Translations in analyses in ).

To open the Edit Code dialog: Double-clicking the code in the Codes facet opens it directly, while right-clicking it and choosing Edit opens it too. Similarly, in the Codebook view, double-clicking the code, clicking Edit beside the code name in the details, or right-clicking and selecting Edit does the job. In both places, selecting a code only takes a single click, and pressing Return with the code selected brings up the Edit Code dialog. After making changes as necessary, pressing Save will reflect any changes instantly in your currently open documents.

The Codes facet lists, under the Code System heading, the codes whose scope includes the active document. In this case, those codes applicable to the active document (“Running Out of Time”) are everything in “Climate Debate” except “Speakers” and its subcodes, which belong to “Radio Debate”. “Costs” and “Uncertainty” both have a memo of their own, and hence have note icons displaying that information, and the code set “Arguments” appears below the code system. The Codes facet of “Running Out of Time”, with the code set “Arguments” below the code system. In each row starting from the left side, you will see: a color and name of the code; a note icon if there is a memo attached specifically to the code, possible only if the project has been imported (see Memos on documents, codes, and the project later in this chapter); and on the far right side, how many times the code was used in this particular document (including coded memos related to that code). Click on the value (Show Codings) to view the list of codings in the Codings facet. In the heading, two buttons are provided. The first option, Export, will export the whole list as a CSV file while + allows adding a new code. When you right-click a code, options such as Edit, Add Subcode, Show Codings, Move To, Merge Into, Add to Code Set, and Delete appear; the Project menu offers Add Subcode, Move To, Merge Into, Add to Code Set, and Delete Code for the selected code. The shortcut menu of the code “Deadlines” in the Codes facet, with the Add to Code Set submenu open. Beneath the code system, if your project contains any code sets, these will appear under a separate section labeled Code Sets (see Code sets below).

Tags are short labels for projects, documents, codes, memos, and links. All tags exist as one list throughout LemmaLoom, which means that a tag such as “follow-up” means the same wherever it is used (see Tags in ). Similar to the use of tags elsewhere, tags on codes serve the purpose of organization, not meaning-making. Perhaps you could use tags to identify the codes you need to review further. Tagging a code happens in the code's dialog. Type a tag into the Tags field (its placeholder reads Add a tag) and press Return. A comma denotes the end of a tag input. Suggestions of existing tags anywhere within LemmaLoom appear during typing. The removal of a tag happens by clicking the button next to the tag (×). If viewing the codes within the Codebook view, you get an option to filter the codes via tag when at least one code gets tagged. Filter by tag appears as a button below the list. Selecting a tag filters the list so that only the codes carrying the tag appear. The parents of such codes remain visible, maintaining the structure of your tree. The selected tag displays above the list; click its × to view all codes. The Codebook view of “Climate Debate” filtered by the tag “follow-up”. Memos assigned to a code take on the tags of that code automatically. With queries, a Tags rule allows searching for specific codes based on tags attached to the code (see ).

A code set allows you to bundle multiple codes from any place in your code tree for use in comparisons or queries. For example, you could make one for the codes of a particular research question. In the “Climate Debate” example project, the code set “Arguments” includes the codes “Costs”, “Responsibility”, “Science”, and “Uncertainty” from different parts of the tree. To create a code set: Right-click a code, in the Codes facet or in the Codebook view. Choose Add to Code Set ▸ New Set from Code. LemmaLoom then makes a code set containing this code, and its default name, New Code Set, is selected so that you can type your own and press Return. Name each code set based on the common feature of the codes inside, something like the research question they are addressing. Later on, should you decide to rename the set, right-click the set in the Code Sets section and select Rename. If you want to add another code to a particular set, first right-click the code, then choose Add to Code Set and select the destination code set from the menu. The Code Sets section, below the code tree in the Codes facet and the Codebook view, contains each existing set along with a statistic showing the number of codes they hold. Expand/collapse each set by clicking it. To discover the set(s) a specific code belongs to, right-click the code, open Add to Code Set, and the sets it already belongs to will be disabled. Should you wish to delete any code set, either right-click it and select Delete, or click the nearby trash can in the Codes facet. To take a code out of a set, expand the codes of the required code set, then right-click the targeted code and select Remove from Code Set. In Sketch Space, code sets may provide columns for comparisons between codes (see Grouping the codes in ). Code sets can also become items for a query, listed as Code Sets, and a rule on a code's Code Set finds the codes a set holds (see ).

When you merge two codes, you are essentially folding one code into another. All codings applied using the first code are now folded into the second, while the first code is deleted. Merges happen when you realize that the two codes mean the same thing, or when you want to fold a subcode back into its parent code. If you wish to move a code around within the hierarchy without folding it, you should use Move To (see Subcodes and the code tree earlier in this chapter). You can start fine-grained and merge later as necessary. Right-click the code you want to merge away, in the Codes facet or in the Codebook view, or select it and open Project ▸ Merge Into. Choose Merge Into, then the code that is to remain. The menu leaves out the code itself and its own subcodes. In the Codes facet, it lists only the codes you can use in the open document; in the Codebook view, it lists every code of the project. An alert names both codes and says how many coded segments and subcodes will move. Click Merge. “Deadlines” is made up of 12 segments while “Urgency” is made up of 10 segments in the Codebook of the “Climate Debate” project. When you choose to merge “Deadlines” into “Urgency”, an alert appears reading Merge “Deadlines” into “Urgency”? and informs you that 13 coded segments will move to “Urgency”, while “Deadlines” will be deleted entirely. Once you confirm, the Codebook will display 10 + 12 = 22 segments in the code “Urgency”. The alert that asks whether to merge “Deadlines” into “Urgency”. All counts in this alert, and in the alert for deleting a code, refer to all instances of coding within the project, and that includes copies found in translations such as “Running Out of Time (German)”. Since the Codebook view does not consider copies in a translation, you will find that, for a code used in “Running Out of Time”, the number in the alert is higher than Segments. In “Deadlines”, there is only one coding in “Running Out of Time”, making the total in the alert, with its copy, 12 + 1 = 13. The items moved include: All the codings and coded memos of the merged code. Its subcodes become subcodes of the remaining code. Memos about the merged code itself. Its place in code sets; wherever the two codes occurred together in a set, the remaining code now occurs once. Attributes along with their respective value(s); where there is an existing duplicate name/type pair with the remaining code, both are merged into one. All saved queries that refer to the merged code automatically refer to the remaining code henceforth. The merged code's name, color, format, scope, tags, and description are deleted, leaving behind only the remaining code. If a passage carried both codes over exactly the same text before the merge, it is afterward coded twice with the remaining code. Each of them shows up individually in the Codings facet, and both are counted toward your counts of total codings of that code in your project. If that causes trouble with your counts, remove one of the codings (refer to Removing a code from a passage earlier in this chapter).

Right-click the code and choose Delete (in the Codes facet) or Delete Code (in the Codebook view), or select it and choose Project ▸ Delete Code. The alert says how much will go with it, for example, This removes 2 subcodes and 31 coded segments. Click Delete. When you delete a code, the deletion cascades through all subordinate codes underneath it, removing any coding of the parent and subordinate codes as well as attribute values associated with those codings. Deleting the code “Urgency” would, for example, erase 31 codings in total, which includes 11 for “Urgency”, 13 for “Deadlines”, and 7 for “Tipping Points”, and each count also includes the copies in “Running Out of Time (German)”. When deleting a code, any memos assigned to it convert to regular memos. The alert that appears when the code “Urgency” is deleted. Edit ▸ Undo Delete Code (⌘Z) restores everything lost by deleting the code.

The Codebook view displays the complete system of codes in the current project, along with descriptions, figures, and tags for each code. Access it via the navigation sidebar under Project, or click Codebook on any set's or tag's tab. A set's or tag's tab opens on Codebook. In this figure, “Costs” is selected in the Codebook of “Climate Debate”. It has 19 segments in 10 documents, with the most (five) appearing in “Net Zero Will Cost You”. The code accounts for 3.6 percent of the total project text. Segments of the code overlap with the “Responsibility” code five times. The Codebook view of “Climate Debate”, with “Costs” selected. On the left side is the code tree, and beneath this is the list of the code sets contained in this project (see Code sets earlier in this chapter). Each code in this tree has a number indicating the quantity of coded segments it has in the current scope. Underneath the code tree are Add Code, the tag filter (see Tags on codes earlier in this chapter), and Export. Move the divider between the tree and the details to give more space to either of them. Select a code to see its details on the right side, where the following appear: its color, name, and Edit button; a description taken from About; Scope and Format settings; USE IN THIS SCOPE, with three numbers (Segments, Documents, and Coverage percentage) and bars for all documents that contain this code, ordered by most segments used first; CO-OCCURS WITH, a list of all other codes whose segments intersect with the segments of this code, along with how many intersections occur; TAGS, all tags applied to the code. By clicking on any bar under USE IN THIS SCOPE, you can open the corresponding document at this code's first segment in the reader. At the right of the heading USE IN THIS SCOPE is an export button, which allows saving these bars as an image (PNG or PDF) or the numbers as a CSV file. Double-clicking Segments or right-clicking it and selecting Show Codings opens the segments of this code in the Codings view. A code listed in CO-OCCURS WITH acts similarly, and lists the segments of this code that intersect it. If necessary, you can also add the subcode segments via the Include Subcodes option beside the filter in the Codings view (see The Codings view in ). Numbers only account for codings in the original documents (i.e., a coding in “Running Out of Time” and its copy in “Running Out of Time (German)” count once). A parent's numbers count the parent's own codings, and coded memos are left out. Segments is the number of codings of the code in the scope's documents. Documents is the total number of documents containing at least one of the code's segments. Coverage is the proportion of the total number of characters in documents in the scope covered by the code's segments. This statistic answers the question whether a particular code covers only a few lines here and there, or large sections of documents. $c$ is the total number of characters in the segments of the code. Where segments from the same code overlap in the same document, the overlapping characters are counted only once. $n$ is the total number of characters in all the documents within the scope, irrespective of being coded or not. Spaces and line breaks are also counted. Within the Codebook of the “Skeptics” set, the “Costs” code has 9 segments in 3 out of 5 documents. Imagine that the documents in this scope hold 18,000 characters altogether, while the 9 segments in total take 1,080 of these characters. These numbers approximate actual figures quite accurately. The view displays Segments 9, Documents 3, and: The “Let's Not Panic” and “Science Is Never Settled” documents have no segments of “Costs”, yet they contribute to $n$. Within the project's Codebook, $n$ includes all the activist texts, “Heat Wave Report 2024”, and all the rest, whereas $c$ encompasses the “Costs” segments from all these documents. Assume that the project contains 50,000 characters, whereas the segments of the “Costs” code account for 1,800 of these, i.e., the 1,080 mentioned above plus another 720 characters from elsewhere in the project. Thus, the project's Codebook yields $1{,}800 / 50{,}000 = 0.036$, or 3.6%, though no coding has changed. Use this statistic in conjunction with Segments to compare several codes' coverages within one and the same scope, where $n$ is the same for all codes in question. The Code Stats facet offers this same measurement for individual documents, as described in Code frequencies and coverage in . CO-OCCURS WITH counts the number of overlapping pairs of segments. Every instance where one “Costs” segment overlaps one segment of another code adds +1 to that other code's CO-OCCURS WITH count, whereas if the same “Costs” passage overlaps 2 distinct “Responsibility” segments, this contributes +2 to “Responsibility”. A high number here may merely suggest that both codes were frequently used, since a code with many long segments overlaps other codes by chance. Within the “Climate Debate” project, “Costs” and “Responsibility” were used more than any other two codes, having 19 segments each, with “Costs” listing “Responsibility” with 5. For a quantitative assessment of the degree to which two codes tend to co-occur within the same document, refer to the Co-occurrences section of the Code Stats facet, explained in Co-occurrences in a document in . Export below the tree produces an export of codes displayed in the tree as a CSV file, which contains six fields (Code, Path, Level, Count, Description, and Color). The Path field displays where the code lies in relation to other codes within the tree hierarchy. So, if you were looking at the code called “Deadlines” under the code “Urgency”, its path will display Urgency / Deadlines. Level displays the level at which the code falls within the hierarchy (i.e., Level 1 for the top-level codes, Level 2 for subcodes, etc.). The Count displays the total number of coded segments in the scope. When a tag filter has been defined, only those codes displayed within the view will be exported. Alternatively, if you wish to export the codebook in the REFI-QDA format, see Exporting a codebook in . For keeping your codebook side by side with your reader, first access the Codebook view from Project in the navigation sidebar, then click Open in a window (the two diagonal arrows) located at the rightmost edge of the bar above the view. Alternatively, open your codebook window by choosing Window ▸ Codebook, or right-clicking on your project in the navigation sidebar, then selecting Codebook. Your codebook window spans across your entire project. Your codebook window includes a button for every view of the project shelf along its top edge. Your project's Codings, Memos, and Links views share the same Open in a window button, which opens the window on that view. The Codebook window of “Climate Debate” with “Urgency” selected.

A memo contains your thoughts regarding the significance of a particular passage. This could include comparisons between passages, your reflections, and any questions that might arise during the coding process. Typically, you would draft your memos concurrently while coding your documents, and you return to them later while drawing conclusions. In the example project called “Climate Debate”, there are memos associated with several passages in four separate documents. Within the document “Running Out of Time”, for instance, the memo on the passage “It is a wish with a calendar attached” notes that distant targets are read as evasion rather than ambition.

Select the passage the memo is about. Click Memo in the selection bar, or press ⇧⌘M. The New Memo dialog shows the selected text at the top. Type your note in Memo. To tag the memo, type tags in Tags. To make it a coded memo, choose a code in Code (see Coded memos below). Click Save. The Save button remains disabled until you put something inside your memo (its tooltip reads Memo is empty).

When a memo has had a code selected in the Code menu, that memo becomes a coded memo. Coded memos are used when your note pertains to the code you've selected rather than the selected passage itself, such as why a particular passage qualifies for the code you're applying. Within “Running Out of Time”, the example sentence involving approaching the edge of a cliff amid heavy fog has been coded “Fear”. Selecting “Fear” as the Code in your memo on this passage, as in the figure, results in double-counting “Fear” within both the Codes and Code Stats facets, once for the coding and once for the memo. If you wish to discuss something related to your coding but don't wish to add any further counts to your coding statistics, select None in the Code menu. The New Memo dialog for a passage of “Running Out of Time”, with “Fear” chosen as its code. A coded memo is rendered in the code's color and format, and its annotation in the gutter takes the code's color. Furthermore, a coded memo counts as a coding of its code, both in the Codes and Code Stats facets, as well as in query results, unless you uncheck Coded Memos Count as Codings (see Options in ). The Codebook and Codings views count codings only. Memos coded using a code adopt that code's tags. Upon selecting a code for coding a memo, the Tags entry field converts itself to Inherited Tags, which shows them, while deleting anything that you may have entered previously in that field. If your code does not have any tags assigned to it, the dialog shows the explanation A coded memo inherits its code's attributes and tags. The New Memo dialog for a passage of “Running Out of Time”, with “Fear” chosen as its code, showing Inherited Tags and an Intensity attribute. If the code has attributes, an Attributes field appears, with a control for each. From the Code drop-down menu, you'll see the available codes to use in this document. Selecting None reverts your coded memo to an ordinary memo.

The passage of a memo is colored yellow, while the passage of a coded memo uses the color and format of its associated code. The annotation at the start of the passage in the gutter displays the first words of the memo, and hovering the mouse pointer over it reveals the entire content of the memo. Clicking on the annotation selects the passage. The memo annotation “Distant targets are read as evasion” in “Running Out of Time” with the mouse pointer over it, showing the full memo. Memos always display regardless of lenses being active or inactive, and coded memos stay visible even when the Codes lens is switched off.

Your active document's memos appear in the Codings facet of the inspector. Toggle to Memos on the switch at the top. Memos appear as rows containing the memo's icon (which looks like a speech bubble), the name of its code for a coded memo, the location of its passage, its first line of text, and its tags. Coded memos have colored icons that match their codes, and those icons are filled. Clicking a row scrolls the reader to the passage while opening the row to show up to six lines of text, the values of its attributes, an Edit button, and a Delete button. Right-clicking a row opens a shortcut menu with Edit, Go to Source, and Delete. The Codings facet of “Running Out of Time” switched to Memos, with its memo expanded. Search looks across the text of the memos themselves as well as any tags assigned to them. The filter button (Filter by code) gives you options to filter memos by code. The Export button exports the rows shown into a CSV file. That file includes the columns Code, Location, Text (the actual passage itself), Memo, and Tags. The Edit button brings you to the Edit Memo dialog, which provides all of the same fields as New Memo and adds a Delete button on the bottom left.

The Memos view of the project shelf displays your memos in a table. You can display them from the entire project or the documents belonging to a particular set. The table has the three columns Document, Code, and Memo. At the top left, you will notice the number of rows currently being displayed, e.g., 2 memos for the “Activists” set. The Memos view of the “Activists” set, showing 2 memos with the detail pane open. Search lets you search for memos by text, document title, code name, or tag. Selecting a row opens a pane below the table displaying the full memo, its tags, and its attribute values, with Edit and Go to Source buttons for editing the memo and going to the source document where the memo was added. You can drag the divider between table and pane to give either more room. Alternatively, double-clicking on a row, or selecting the option Go to Source, opens the document at the location of the selected memo. On right-click, you get the options Edit, Go to Source, and Delete. The Export button exports the rows currently shown into a CSV file.

t: Memos on documents, codes, and the project
b: You attach memos directly onto passages in LemmaLoom. When importing projects from applications that support the REFI-QDA standard, however, memos attached to entire documents, codes, and the project itself can also get imported (see Importing a REFI-QDA project in ). Document memos are located in the document’s Codings facet under Memos. Alternatively, memos are listed within the project’s Memos view, or in the Memos view of any set which includes the document within it. Code memos and project memos only occur in the Memos view of the project. Their Document column shows Untitled. Any notes related to the same code end up combined together as a memo in the Memos view. The project itself includes a memo describing its contents. Notes added onto links in the imported project turn into comments on the links.

Links denote relationships between pairs of passages. Those relationships could be responses, explanations, contradictions, repetitions, or anything you decide. Links prove helpful in cases where texts are reacting to each other, or where keeping an argument close to its evidence matters. There are five links in “Climate Debate”. “Let's Not Panic” contains a “contradicts” link to “Running Out of Time”, because both documents agree that no one knows where thresholds of the climate system reside, but come to different conclusions from it. Also contained in the project is a “supports” link going from “Radio Debate” to “Heat Wave Report 2024”, as the host cites a statistic from the latter text.

An additional link is being drawn between two excerpts shown in the figure. In “Climate Debate”, “Running Out of Time” and “Net Zero Will Cost You” mistrust target dates, yet both authors reason in vastly distinct ways. In “Running Out of Time”, target deadlines beyond the near future are referred to as “a wish with a calendar attached”. By comparison, in “Net Zero Will Cost You”, any date referred to as a goal year is labeled as “a political decision, not an engineering one”. The link runs from the first excerpt to the second with the relation “contrasts with” and takes you from one excerpt to the other. The New Link dialog linking a passage of “Running Out of Time” to a passage of “Net Zero Will Cost You”. Here's how you can link two passages: Select the first passage. Click Link in the selection bar, or press ⇧⌘L. LemmaLoom remembers the passage as the start of a link. Select the second passage, in the same document or in another one. The start of the link is kept while you move between documents. Click Finish Link in the selection bar, or press ⇧⌘L again. The New Link dialog shows the document and passage where you started and, below an arrow, the passage where you finished. Type the relation in Relation. Add a Comment and Tags, or leave them empty, and click Save. Links are directed connections, so a link runs from the passage where you started to the one where you finished, and its relation is read in that direction. By default, a link has a relation of relates to if nothing else was indicated upon creation. Choose relations which you foresee yourself reusing a lot (e.g., “contradicts”, “explains”, “example of”); this makes finding links by those relations easy later on. Links need both the starting and ending passage within the same project, while both passages may exist in the same document. When you click Cancel in the New Link dialog, the starting point of a link remains intact, allowing you to create a link from there to elsewhere in the project. To cancel a link prematurely, choose Document ▸ Cancel Link (⌥⇧⌘L), or alternatively select a passage anywhere, then click Cancel the pending link (a crossed-out link icon), located directly beside the Finish Link button.

There is an annotation in the gutter at both ends of each link. The annotations appear in the accent color and show the relation between both passages. Hovering the mouse pointer over the annotation reveals information about the link, including the relation between the two passages, the other document (or in this document), the other end passage itself, and any comment associated with the link. By clicking the annotation or Go to the other end in its popover, you can navigate to the other end of the link. If the other end is in another document, navigating to the other end of the link will take you to that document, which opens in a separate tab. A link annotation in “Net Zero Will Cost You” with the mouse pointer over it, showing the relation “responds to”, the other document “A Mayor's Promise”, the other end passage, the comment, and Go to the other end. The Links facet appears in the Coding inspector. It includes all links with an end in the active document, under a heading that says something like Links (3). Export on the right of the heading exports the complete list of links as a CSV file. The list consists of entries, each containing the start point, the arrow representing the link with the relation specified, and the end, along with the associated comment and tags below them. An end appearing in the current document displays its location within the text, while an end appearing in another document displays the title of that document. You can navigate to either of the end points by clicking the arrow button next to the corresponding end point (Go to this end or Open in the other document); clicking an endpoint in the current document takes you there, whereas double-clicking an endpoint in another document opens it. The Links facet of “Running Out of Time”, listing its link to “Let's Not Panic”.

In the Links facet, right-click on the link and select either Edit or Delete. Similarly, in the Links view of the shelf, right-click on the link and select Edit or Delete Link. The Edit Link dialog allows you to change the relation, comment, and tags associated with the link. If you wish to attach the link to a different passage, you'll need to delete the existing link and create a new one.

In the Links view of the project shelf, you can look at either all links in a project, or links with at least one end in a set's documents. The total number of links displayed will appear in the upper-left corner. Search in the Links view (at the right of the bar at the top) allows you to filter based on the passages, relation, comment, tags, or document titles involved in the link. The figure shows the five links of the project “Climate Debate” with relations being “supports”, “contradicts”, and “responds to”. The Links view of “Climate Debate”. Links appear in rows showing the start document and the end document with an arrow connecting them. Following that are the relation and the two passages (the end passage appearing fainter). The tags associated with the link appear last, below the passages. You can click on a document title and navigate to that end directly. Alternatively, double-click on a row to navigate to the start of the link; alternatively, select a row and hit Return to do the same thing. Finally, you can right-click on any row and access the Edit, Open Source (start), Open Target (end), and Delete Link options. If a link is copied to a translation, you will only get a single instance of that link in your list. Export allows you to save your list as a CSV document. That file contains the columns Source document, Source text, Relation, Target document, Target text, Comment, and Tags. During times when there are no links to export, the Export button becomes disabled and displays Nothing to export when hovered upon.

A bookmark marks a passage you may need access to later on, such as a quote for a paper or where you left off coding. Four documents in the “Climate Debate” project have bookmarks, each with a comment attached. For instance, “Let's Not Panic” has a bookmark on “Some things, at least, are settled.”; the comment reads “Ironic closing line”. The New Bookmark dialog for a passage of “Let's Not Panic”. Here's how you bookmark passages in LemmaLoom: Select the passage. Click Bookmark in the selection bar, or press ⇧⌘B. In the New Bookmark dialog, type a note in Comment (optional) and click a color under Color. Bookmarks offer No color and the eight swatches of codes. Click Save. If you enable the Bookmarks lens (enabled by default whenever you open a document), you will find passages highlighted in the bookmark's color, or in yellow for a bookmark without one. There will be an annotation showing the comment in the gutter next to the passage, while the document overview will show a little square box at its left edge showing you where the bookmark resides. Whenever your selection overlaps a bookmark, Remove Bookmark replaces Bookmark on the selection bar. If you press ⇧⌘B, the bookmark will disappear immediately, and you can restore it again using the menu item Edit ▸ Undo Remove Bookmark (⌘Z). The list of bookmarks of a particular document can be found in the inspector under Bookmarks within the Text tab (see The Bookmarks facet in ). The rows will include a bookmark icon colored in accordance with your bookmark's color, the comment itself or the passage in case no comments were added, and its location. Click on any row to navigate to the passage in the reader, while right-clicking it provides the options Edit (opening the Edit Bookmark dialog, which has a Delete button) and Delete. Search looks up bookmarks either by their comment or text. To export bookmarks to CSV format with columns Location, Text, and Comment, click on the Export button. Should you wish to bookmark all the hits made by a query, there is an option in the query's Actions menu called Bookmark Hits… (see Bookmark Hits in ). You can construct a query that lists Bookmarks to view the bookmarks of multiple documents at the same time. The units Memos, Links, and Codings share similar functionalities (see Choosing what to find in ).

Auto code uses a lens to locate annotations and then codes whatever passages are marked by those annotations all in one run. Auto code works well for anything that can be searched based on wording or grammatical patterns, including hedge expressions in dictionaries and results of saved queries. Think of one run as your first pass (see An example later in this chapter). Among lenses, auto coding is available solely with those that you build yourself: the lens generated by a dictionary, a collection of words and phrases that you compile (see ); the lens derived from a query saved as a lens (see Saving a query as a lens in ); and the lens provided by a custom analyzer (see ). Alternatively, you could auto code the passages returned by a query directly in the inspector.

In “Climate Debate”, the dictionary “Hedges” is provided as a lens on each document. Each category in the dictionary has its own aspect lenslet, namely “Approximators” and “Shields”. To auto code from a lens: Open the document and enable the lens in the lens menu at the top of the reader. The menu is disabled until the document is indexed. Choose Document ▸ Auto Code… (⇧⌘A). The lens menu has the same item, just above Clear Annotations. If more than one such lens is enabled, you get one item per lens, named after it, such as Auto Code with Hedges…, and ⇧⌘A chooses the first. In the Auto Code dialog, set up the run as described in The Auto Code dialog below, and click Auto Code.

There is a saved query called “Urgency Talk” in the “Climate Debate” project, with zero categories defined. In this query's Auto Code dialog is a single row entry titled “Urgency Talk”. For this row entry, either select “Urgency” if you'd like LemmaLoom to auto-code passages with “Urgency”, or leave it as New Code: Urgency Talk. To perform an auto code operation based on a query: Open a document. In the inspector, click Multimode, then Query. Build the query, or load a saved one. Open the Actions menu (the circled ⋯) and choose Auto Code…. Set up the run in the Auto Code dialog and click Auto Code. Regardless of whether a query is saved or not, the dialog uses the query precisely as defined using the query builder. The Auto Code… item will become disabled when a query does not permit passage annotation, for example because it finds documents or codes rather than passages, or because Show is not set to List. Hover the mouse pointer over the item for the exact reason behind it being disabled. For an exhaustive explanation on what queries qualify as lenses, refer to Which queries can be lenses in . The Actions menu of the query “Urgency Talk”, with Auto Code… at its top. The Auto Code dialog opened from the query “Urgency Talk”.

As you can see in the figure below, the dialog for the lens “Hedges” in “The Models Keep Missing” has two rows, one corresponding to each category in the dictionary. The Auto Code dialog for the “Hedges” lens in “The Models Keep Missing”. The first line, Lens or Query, gives you the name of the lens or query whose output provides your passages. Every aspect lenslet in the lens will get its own row under Codes, starting off as checked. For dictionaries, every category in the dictionary gets its own row, while queries will give either one row per category or a single row named after the query, depending on whether or not there is any category, and finally analyzers provide one row for each item in their legends. Only aspect lenslets in the legend that are enabled will have rows here. Disabling a particular lenslet prevents it from having its own row, so it is skipped in the run (refer to Choosing which aspects are enabled in ). Choosing an existing code from the menu showing New Code: … at the right of each row assigns that code to the row, and when no preexisting code is chosen, New Code: … is used for that row, creating a code with the row's name and color. The menu preselects the code with a matching name, regardless of case and accents. It will show all the codes applicable to your current document. If you uncheck a particular row, it will get ignored during the run. In the Documents menu, you may select This Document, any set of documents belonging to the project, or Whole Project. Choosing This Document allows you to know how many passages this lens finds in the document for the checked rows (Passages). Any passage that already has the selected code is included in that number but will be ignored. Auto Code is disabled during loading of passages (Loading) and when there is no checked row (Nothing selected). Clicking Auto Code begins the run. It keeps the dialog open and locks all settings in place; thus, you need to choose Auto Code… once again to perform another run with new settings. While running, the Auto Code button changes to Stop. Progress tracks how many of the documents are done. You see values such as 3 of 5. Pressing Stop terminates the run after coding the current document. All previous codings remain. Once completed, Progress shows Codings added: and the number. Auto Code reads Done, and pressing that closes the dialog. The Auto Code dialog for “Hedges” after a run on the “Skeptics” set, showing Codings added: 47 and Done.

A passage already coded with the chosen code over exactly the same stretch of text is skipped (i.e., a second run skips the passages the first run coded). However, passages that existing codings of the chosen code only overlap, such as one inside a whole paragraph coded with that code, will be coded. When running on a document set or the whole project, each original document is treated in turn as if you opened it in the app; if you started your run from the translation of a document, e.g., “Running Out of Time (German)”, then your auto code would proceed through the translation in place of “Running Out of Time”. A dictionary-based lens also codes unindexed documents because it works directly with text. However, an analyzer-based lens can code only indexed documents and only if they're in a language supported by the analyzer; furthermore, a document for which you have unchecked that analyzer will be skipped. The rows come from the open document. In the case where a query lens has colored its results according to Color By (see Categories and Color By in ), only the values that appear in the current document get rows, and only those values are coded in all others. For a row with a new code, its first passage found creates the new code at the top level of the code tree. Such a code will have the scope Project, the format Highlight, the row's name, and the row's color. An existing code that belongs to a single document or set is applied only within that document or set. Codings made during an auto code operation will not have attribute values specified, even for codes with attributes. Like any manual coding, newly created codings are added to the document's translations. The whole run is one step in the undo history, so Edit ▸ Undo Auto Code (⌘Z) will erase every coding the run added and every code it created, including those made before you clicked Stop.

The dictionary “Hedges” has two categories, “Approximators”, which includes such entries as about, around, and roughly, and “Shields”, which includes I think, maybe, and perhaps. The skeptic documents hedge much more frequently than the activist documents; thus, coding the hedges of the “Skeptics” set puts these hedges in the code tables alongside your existing codes. With “Hedges” active in “The Models Keep Missing”, Document ▸ Auto Code… produces the dialog as seen in the figure above. The two rows, Approximators and Shields, provide the options New Code: Approximators and New Code: Shields as the names do not appear among any codes in this project yet. With This Document selected, Passages displays 10 passages total, namely 6 approximators and 4 shields found in “The Models Keep Missing”. Unchecking “Shields” reduces the figure to 6. Checking both rows and changing Documents to Skeptics makes Progress count through the five documents in this set and stop at Codings added: 47. Among these, there are 10 in “The Models Keep Missing” and 37 elsewhere. Following this, the codebook features two new top-level codes, “Approximators” and “Shields”, colored according to the categories in the dictionary. During a run over a set that holds “Running Out of Time”, “Running Out of Time (German)” receives copies of these codings, while the Codings added: counter only shows the originals. When you open the dialog again, “Approximators” and “Shields” are selected by default as the names coincide. After running again, Progress shows Codings added: 0, meaning there were no additional passages to be coded. Edit ▸ Undo Auto Code immediately after the initial run deletes the entire batch of 47 codings and the respective two codes. Each match gets coded regardless of accuracy. Within “The Models Keep Missing”, the “Approximators” entry about is coded both in “About twelve years ago”, where it is a hedge, and in “a tool for reasoning about the future”, where it does not qualify as such. Read through the coded passages carefully and delete incorrect instances in the Codings facet or the Codings view.

Reversing any change made to codes, codings, memos, links, or bookmarks can be done via Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z), while redoing previously reversed actions can be done via Edit ▸ Redo (⇧⌘Z). The action being undone or redone is named in the menu: Action Menu item Creating, editing, or moving a code Undo New Code, Undo Edit Code, Undo Move Code Merging or deleting a code Undo Merge, Undo Delete Code Making, renaming, filling, or deleting a code set Undo New Code Set, Undo Rename, Undo Add to Code Set, Undo Remove from Code Set, Undo Delete Code Set Applying, changing, or removing a code Undo Apply Code, Undo Change Code, Undo Delete Coding Changing an attribute value of a coding Undo Set Value Auto-coding Undo Auto Code Memos Undo New Memo, Undo Edit Memo, Undo Delete Memo Links Undo New Link, Undo Edit Link, Undo Delete Link Bookmarks Undo Bookmark, Undo Edit Bookmark, Undo Remove Bookmark Refer to  to find out more about how the undo history works between windows and when it gets cleared.

A typical study compares two parts of a project, such as activists' texts against skeptic texts, or one outlet against all others. LemmaLoom offers multiple ways to characterize the two parts. An attribute stores factual information pertaining to each document. Sets and smart sets represent named collections of documents that an analysis could cover, groups organize your list of documents in the navigation sidebar, and finally tags provide a completely freeform way of labeling documents in all your projects. Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z) allows you to undo changes made to sets, smart sets, tags, and attributes. The menu item specifies precisely what is being undone, such as Undo New Set or Undo Set Value. More detail can be found in .

Sets are named collections of documents manually added to the set by you. Any number of sets may contain a document, and sets can act as scopes of analyses, which are the documents analyzed in an analysis task. Smart sets are sets whose documents depend on conditions. Whenever something their members depend on changes, LemmaLoom recalculates members of the smart set accordingly. Conditions test the value of one particular property in a document and consist of a field, comparison, and usually a value. As an example, the condition might test whether “Readership” is at least 100,000. Groups are folders in the Documents section of the sidebar. Unlike with sets, documents belong to at most one group each. Tags are brief, free-form labels used to describe aspects of documents, such as “op-ed” or “viral”. Tags exist globally across all of your projects. Attributes are facts about each document within a project, defined once for the project, such as “Stance” or “Publication Date”. Every document belonging to a project can have its own value of an attribute. Original documents refer to those that are not translations. Sets always consist of original documents. Any analysis task involving sets, tags, or full projects reads original documents unless you ask for translations.

Set Smart set Group Tag Attribute A document gets in when you add it it meets the conditions you move it there you type the tag you enter a value Per document any number of sets any number of smart sets at most one group any number of tags one value per attribute Belongs to the project the project the project the project (names shared by all projects) the project Opens in a tab with the project's views yes yes no yes no Which of the options listed above works for you depends on what you wish to achieve with your documents afterward. An attribute holds any factual value of interest, which could help you compare and filter your documents later. The position taken by the text in question, the publication outlet, date, etc., are common examples. Where there are no specific criteria for collecting documents, you can opt for a set. The set option is appropriate where analyses must focus exclusively on your selected subset of documents. A set would come in handy during analyses of documents picked by hand, for instance, for close readings or discussions with colleagues. A smart set fits when attribute values, tags, or other properties already say which documents belong together. It keeps up by itself as you add texts or correct a value. Unlike document sets, groups merely organize the documents in the navigation sidebar, for example, by the kind of material or where it came from. A tag is a free-form label without a value. Tags fit labels you use the same way in several projects, and each tag opens its documents in a tab, much like a set. The “Climate Debate” project has documents organized in various ways; the activists' texts and the skeptics' texts make up sets named “Activists” and “Skeptics”. A few articles have been assigned the tags “op-ed” and “viral”. The documents also appear sorted based on the publication medium, in the groups “Print” and “Online”. Attributes in “Climate Debate”, for instance, the “Stance” attribute, make it possible to analyze the difference in codings applied to activist versus skeptic texts. The smart set “Wide Reach” automatically updates itself according to a predetermined criterion of high “Readership”.

The examples use “Climate Debate”, which is the example project for this guide (see The example project in ). This example project comes pre-indexed and contains 14 original documents with these values, groups, and tags: Document Stance Readership Publication Date Outlet Group Tags Running Out of Time Activist 412,000 2024-08-21 The Northern Herald Print op-ed Letter from the Climate Strike Activist 186,000 2024-09-02 Greenline Blog Online viral Why We Block the Roads Activist 41,000 2023-11-14 Greenline Blog Online  Farmers Are Not the Enemy Activist 23,000 2024-08-09 Farm & Field Print  A Mayor's Promise Activist 8,500 2024-10-08 City Hall Bulletin Online  Hope Takes Work Activist 72,000 2023-12-02 The Weekly Ledger Print  The Models Keep Missing Skeptic 96,000 2024-03-12 The Weekly Ledger Print  Net Zero Will Cost You Skeptic 398,000 2024-10-22 The Northern Herald Print op-ed Let's Not Panic Skeptic 254,000 2024-09-26 Plain Talk Online Online viral Who Pays for the Transition Skeptic 57,000 2024-11-05 Plain Talk Online Online op-ed Science Is Never Settled Skeptic 68,000 2024-06-18 The Weekly Ledger Print  Heat Wave Report 2024 Neutral 3,100 2024-09-16 Weather and Climate Agency   Carbon Tax Debate Neutral 875,000 2024-09-19 The Northern Herald   Radio Debate Neutral 310,000 2024-09-17 Radio Northline Online  Neither “Heat Wave Report 2024” nor “Carbon Tax Debate” belongs to any group or has any tags associated with it. “Running Out of Time (German)” is the project’s fifteenth document; because it is a translation, it shares its values, group, and tags with the original “Running Out of Time”. The set “Activists” contains the six documents whose “Stance” is “Activist”, while “Skeptics” contains the five documents whose “Stance” is “Skeptic”. Lastly, the smart set “Wide Reach” contains the documents with a “Readership” of at least 100,000. The recording of “Radio Debate” lasts 4 minutes and 49 seconds.

Sets specify which documents are analyzed. In “Climate Debate”, both “Activists” and “Skeptics” consist of texts from one side. There is a keyword query in the “Activists” set which contrasts the words in its documents against those in the “Skeptics” set. A keyword list contrasts a set against another set or against everything else in the project. If your study involves comparing categories of text, each category should get its own set. In the Sets section of the navigation sidebar, the sets and smart sets in your project are organized according to when they were added, along with the number of documents each contains. Handmade sets feature a stack icon, while smart sets have a filter icon. Expanding the disclosure triangle next to a set reveals its documents. Clicking on one of the documents will open it. The Sets section of the navigation sidebar with “Activists” expanded, and “Wide Reach”, a smart set, with its filter icon.

Making a set is quickest from preselected documents. The figure below shows six texts from the activist side of “Climate Debate” already selected in the navigation sidebar, with Add to Set open in their shortcut menu. “Activists” is disabled in the submenu because it already contains all six documents. The six activist texts selected in the navigation sidebar, with Add to Set open in their shortcut menu. To turn your selection into a set: Select the documents in the Documents section (⌘-click or ⇧-click to select several). Right-click one of the selected documents and choose Add to Set ▸ New Set from Documents. Type the set's name and press Return. In a large project, you can input part of the name into the Search Documents bar at the top of the navigation sidebar and select your desired documents from the results list. Project ▸ Add to Set gives you access to the same commands as the shortcut menu. Should you wish to make a set from a single document, then right-click the document and then go to Sets ▸ New Set from Document. Until renamed, the resulting set retains the placeholder name “New Set from Document”. An empty set may also be made first, to be filled at your convenience, by selecting New Set at the bottom of the Sets section or selecting Project ▸ New Set. Enter the desired name, then confirm by pressing Return; pressing Escape maintains the placeholder name “New Set”. Alternatively, you could construct a set out of the documents with hits from a particular query. Choose Create Set from Hits under the query's Actions menu; the set is named after the query (see Create Set from Hits in ).

Adding one document to a set involves selecting the document in the Documents section, opening the shortcut menu via right-clicking, going to Sets, and picking the set to add it to. Adding multiple documents would involve selecting the documents first, then right-clicking one document and choosing Add to Set followed by selecting the set to place them into. Any sets which contain every selected document will be disabled. Only ordinary sets are listed, since the conditions of a smart set dictate its content. The shortcut menu of “Running Out of Time” under the set “Activists”, with Remove from Set. To remove a document from a set: Click the disclosure triangle beside the set. Right-click the document and choose Remove from Set. There's also the Project ▸ Remove from Set menu entry, which you access after clicking the document below the set. Once you delete the document from the project, the document leaves all existing sets. To remove several documents, ⌘-click on them all underneath the set. Either right-click one of them or open the Project menu to access Remove from Set. Remove from Set becomes disabled when the selection also holds documents under another set or in the Documents section. Document sets contain only originals. When a translation is added with Add to Set, its original is added instead. Translations later in this chapter goes deeper into the implications of having translations involved in analyses.

Sets are opened in tabs, containing all ten views seen under Project on the navigation sidebar (Codebook to Queries). However, the ten views contained within sets pertain only to the documents that belong to the set. Open a set by clicking on its title, or right-clicking the set and choosing Open Set. The header of the tab shows the name of the set and how many documents it contains. For more detail about each of the ten views, refer to The project shelf in . Word sketches drawn from the set are opened in their own window via the shortcut menu option Word Sketch.

t: Renaming, exporting, and deleting a set
b: These options appear in the shortcut menu for a set: Rename transforms the set's name into an editable field. Enter your desired name, then hit Return. Export exports all the documents contained within a set along with the set itself in a LemmaLoom archive file. This option lets you pass one part of a project on to a colleague (see ). Delete Set immediately deletes the selected set. Edit ▸ Undo Delete Set (⌘Z) recovers the deleted set. After you click a set, Project ▸ Delete Set (⌘⌫) deletes it too. The shortcut menu of the set “Activists”. After deleting a set, codes with a Scope equal to the deleted set show None in the Document set menu. Choose another document set or scope to use them again (see Where a code can be used in ). Any queries saved in the set move to the project's Queries view.

Smart sets contain the documents which match their conditions. Within the example project “Climate Debate”, the smart set “Wide Reach” contains six documents whose “Readership” is at least 100,000. Were the “Readership” of “The Models Keep Missing” corrected from 96,000 to 104,000, the document would instantly become part of the “Wide Reach” set, reflected by an increment of one, to 7, in the count next to the set title. In most respects, a smart set behaves as a regular set would. A smart set opens in a tab with the same views, and a smart set can serve as a scope anywhere a set might. Since a smart set's membership comes solely from its conditions, you would modify its content by editing its conditions. Anytime an analysis is run on a smart set, its current documents get read by that analysis. This means running an analysis on the “Wide Reach” smart set today could potentially return different results compared to doing the same thing on the “Wide Reach” set next week, if values have changed in between.

“Wide Reach” requires just one condition, but a smart set can combine several. Shown below is the dialog while creating the narrower smart set “Widely Read Activists”, which requires both conditions, “Stance” is any of “Activist” and “Readership” is at least 100,000. As shown by its count (2 documents), the smart set includes just “Running Out of Time” and “Letter from the Climate Strike”. The New Smart Set dialog for “Widely Read Activists”, with two conditions and a count of 2 documents. To make a smart set: Click New Smart Set at the end of the Sets section, or choose Project ▸ New Smart Set. The New Smart Set dialog opens with one condition. In Name, type a name for the smart set. Set up the condition. Choose the field in the first menu (for Attribute, also the attribute in the second), then the comparison, and give the value (see Values in a condition later in this chapter). To test something else as well, click Add Condition and set up the new condition in the same way. In Match, choose All or Any (see All or Any below). Check the count below the conditions, and click Save. Each condition occupies one row. The first menu allows choosing a field, such as Attribute, Tags, or Title. When choosing Attribute, a second menu selects the attribute. Then the next menu lets you pick from all comparisons applicable to the field. Finally, you input the value. The remove button at the end of a row (Remove condition) removes a condition, though this button becomes disabled when there is just one condition remaining (Only one left). By default, a new condition always uses the project’s first attribute, along with that attribute’s first comparison. Thus, a fresh condition for “Climate Debate” will automatically use Attribute, “Stance”, is any of. If there were no attributes defined within a project, then the initial condition would automatically default to Tags with has any of. The counter updates dynamically, allowing you to preview your smart set as you build the conditions, seeing how many of the original documents in the project satisfy the conditions you have finished. Until you complete a condition, the counter includes all original documents. So, while building the initial condition for “Climate Debate”, the counter reads 14, because there are fourteen original documents. Save will stay disabled until you fill the smart set’s Name (Name is empty) and finish every condition (Incomplete). You can hover the mouse pointer over Save to learn the exact reason why. Incomplete means that a condition requires a value and lacks one, for example, is at least when nothing has been entered into the field or is any of without selecting items. Changing a condition’s field resets its value but retains the comparison whenever possible, or selects the field’s first comparison otherwise. If you change a condition’s comparison, the value is retained, so you can switch from is at least to is greater than without typing the number again. Queries for finding documents may also be stored as smart sets (see Saving a document query as a smart set in ).

Match controls the logic between your conditions. When setting Match to All, all of your conditions must hold true for a document; adding another condition narrows your smart set. Matching by Any requires that one of your conditions holds true for a document. In the case of “Widely Read Activists” shown in the figure above, two conditions are specified. First, six documents have a “Stance” of “Activist”, which include “Running Out of Time”, “Letter from the Climate Strike”, “Why We Block the Roads”, “Farmers Are Not the Enemy”, “A Mayor's Promise”, and “Hope Takes Work”. Second, six documents have a “Readership” of at least 100,000, which include “Running Out of Time”, “Letter from the Climate Strike”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, “Let's Not Panic”, “Carbon Tax Debate”, and “Radio Debate”. Match Documents in the smart set Count All those on both lists, “Running Out of Time” and “Letter from the Climate Strike” 2 Any those on either list, namely the six activist texts, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, “Let's Not Panic”, “Carbon Tax Debate”, and “Radio Debate” 10 There are two documents common to both lists. Summing the sizes of the two individual lists, 6 and 6, would result in counting the two documents twice; hence, Any returns 6 + 6 − 2 = 10 documents. All conditions of a smart set combine in the same way, considering only properties pertaining directly to the document itself. The rule “activists with a readership of at least 100,000, or any skeptic,” or a rule querying membership in another set requires a query rather than a smart set. Queries allow nesting of rules (Add Group), which has nothing to do with document groups, and have a Set field (see Groups in ).

A condition's first menu contains the fields listed below. Attribute shows up here only if there are attributes defined within your project. Field What it tests Comparisons Attribute the value of the attribute chosen in the second menu depend on the attribute's type (see Comparisons for attributes) Tags the document's tags has any of, has all of, has none of, is empty, is not empty Group the group the document is in is any of, is none of, is empty, is not empty Language the document's language is any of, is none of Format Text, PDF, Characters the number of characters in the text, spaces included as for Tokens Media Duration the length of an audio or video recording as for Tokens Has Media whether the document is an audio or video recording is true, is false, is empty Has Translations whether the document has at least one translation as for Has Media Indexing Skipped whether the document was imported without indexing and
