original documents are written in. “Climate Debate” is a project consisting of just English originals since its sole German document is a translation. Modified refers to the last time your document was edited, renamed, moved between groups, or had its tags or properties altered. Changing its attribute values in the Attributes window, or renaming or deleting a tag in the Tags window, does not affect its Modified date. LemmaLoom automatically computes Tokens and Sentences during indexing. Both remain equal to 0 until the process has occurred. You may want to include documents based on conditions like Tokens is less than 700. Such a condition also catches documents still waiting to be indexed, and adding a condition like Index Status is any of Indexed helps filter them out. The Characters count uses your document text directly as a source and is there from the moment of import. Has Media, Has Translations, and Indexing Skipped all evaluate to either true or false. Likewise, Index Status always evaluates to one of the seven values below: Value The document Indexed has been indexed Indexing is being indexed now Running Analyzer is indexed, and an analyzer, built in or your own, is running on it (see Choosing analyzers for a document in ) Failed could not be indexed Not Indexed is waiting to be indexed Unsupported is in a language other than English, German, and Chinese Skipped was imported without indexing and has not been indexed since A smart set with Index Status is any of Failed, Not Indexed, and Skipped contains all of the documents that are waiting for some sort of action to be taken. Documents leave the smart set once they are indexed. To find every document imported without indexing, use Indexing Skipped is true. For more information on the states, see Finding documents by their index status in .

Comparisons on attributes depend on the attribute's type: Type Comparisons Text is, is not, contains, does not contain, matches, is empty, is not empty Integer, Decimal is, is not, is less than, is at most, is greater than, is at least, is between, is empty, is not empty Date is, is before, is after, is on or after, is on or before, is between, is empty, is not empty Boolean is true, is false, is empty Picker is any of, is none of, is empty, is not empty

The method you use to enter a condition value differs according to both the comparison and the field: For text and numbers, enter the condition value in the Value field. When entering values for is between, note that it shows two fields, that the two values can go in either order, and that both are inclusive. Thus, when searching for “Readership” is between 50000 and 100000, results would include documents whose “Readership” value equaled exactly 50,000 or 100,000. Dates are selected via a date picker, starting from the current day. is empty, is not empty, is true, and is false count as complete as soon as they are selected. For conditions involving is any of, is none of, and the various comparisons that begin with has, first click the value. Doing so causes a checklist to appear. Select one or more items, then click outside the checklist to close it; the value then shows your choice. Example values include “op-ed” or “viral”, or None when nothing is selected. Available list entries include: for a Picker attribute, its choices, followed by any other values that documents still have; for Tags and Authors, the tags and authors used on documents in the project; for Group, groups belonging to the project; for Language, languages the original documents are written in; for Color, the eleven available document colors, from Red to Gray; for Format, the five available formats, and for Index Status, the seven states above. Durations in Media Duration are typed as minutes and seconds (e.g., 30:00) or hours, minutes, and seconds (e.g., 1:05:30). The time is converted to seconds before comparing values; thus, 1:05:30 is equal to 1 × 3,600 + 5 × 60 + 30 = 3,930 seconds. Single values correspond to seconds. For example, “Radio Debate” lasts 4 minutes 49 seconds (4 × 60 + 49 = 289 seconds), so both Media Duration is greater than 4:00 (240 seconds) and is greater than 5 (5 seconds) match it. Since recordings are timed to the thousandth of a second, is rarely matches a duration exactly. Instead, is at least, is at most, or is between should be employed.

Text comparisons disregard capitals, accents, and whitespace either at the beginning or end of a string. Comparisons ignore whether a character is full-width or half-width (wide vs narrow representations of letters and numerals in Chinese and Japanese text). A comparison with is compares the entire value, whereas contains locates your text anywhere within it. “Outlet” contains herald will locate three documents in “The Northern Herald”. “Outlet” contains the will locate seven documents, the six in “The Northern Herald” and “The Weekly Ledger” and one other document, “Heat Wave Report 2024”, since its outlet, “Weather and Climate Agency”, has the inside Weather. Be sure to check the count before saving when performing a comparison with short text strings. A matches comparison matches the whole value with a simple text pattern. The matches comparison uses  as a wildcard meaning any sequence of characters and ? as a wildcard meaning exactly one. Title matches Debate will locate “Carbon Tax Debate” and “Radio Debate”; Title matches Debate will locate nothing, since the pattern must match the whole title. Number comparisons compare numbers numerically; therefore, 9 comes before 10. Dates are compared by their calendar days. is before disregards the day itself, whereas is on or before includes it. Both Created and Modified dates and times are recorded by LemmaLoom and turned into a day in your Mac's local time zone for comparison. “Publication Date” is between September 1, 2024 and September 30, 2024 will locate five documents published within this range in “Climate Debate”. Comparisons of lists require at least one of the selected entries for is any of or has any of; all selected entries for has all of. Neither is none of nor has none of allows documents containing any of the selected entries. Comparison of list entries, such as tags, authors, and Picker choices, disregards only capitalization and whitespace either at the beginning or end of an entry's name. In “Climate Debate”, three documents have been tagged “op-ed” and two others “viral”: Condition Documents Count Tags has any of “op-ed”, “viral” Running Out of Time, Letter from the Climate Strike, Net Zero Will Cost You, Let's Not Panic, Who Pays for the Transition 5 Tags has all of “op-ed”, “viral” none 0 Tags has none of “op-ed” the 14 originals except “Running Out of Time”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, and “Who Pays for the Transition” 11 The figure below illustrates the first of these conditions, and its tag list is expanded. The list of tags open in a Tags condition, with “op-ed” and “viral” selected. A document without a value fails most comparisons. “Readership” is less than 10000 returns “A Mayor's Promise” and “Heat Wave Report 2024”, while anything with no “Readership” at all won’t match. Examples of such documents may include newly imported documents. The five comparisons is not, does not contain, is none of, has none of, and is empty accommodate those documents. The difference matters most with is none of. Every original in “Climate Debate” has all four attribute values, yet two originals belong to no group. Group is none of “Print” matches 8 documents, the six in “Online” along with “Heat Wave Report 2024” and “Carbon Tax Debate”, which have no groups assigned. For narrowing it down to just the six “Online” documents, add a second condition, Group is not empty, with Match left on All; this reduces the number to 6. Boolean attributes treat unassigned documents as empty. is false returns solely those documents whose values are set to false, whether the checkbox was selected and then deselected, imported as false, or specified via the Set Value option with the checkbox deselected. Use is empty for the rest.

If you need to modify conditions in your smart set, right-click the smart set in the list in the navigation sidebar, and click Edit from the shortcut menu, or click the smart set and click Project ▸ Edit Smart Set. Editing in the Edit Smart Set dialog works in the same way as creating does in New Smart Set. Only clicking Save applies your modification. To rename a smart set, right-click the smart set, and click Rename in the shortcut menu. This changes only the name. Renaming attributes or groups causes smart sets to adapt accordingly. Here is what deletion and other changes do: If you delete a group, it is removed from any condition referencing it. A Group is any of condition with nothing left selected causes a smart set that tested only that group to be emptied, and when you edit the smart set next time, you see None displayed, while Save remains disabled until you specify another group or remove the condition. Deleting an attribute means a failure for every document in conditions testing the attribute. With All, the smart set becomes empty; with Any, the other conditions keep working. When you open the smart set with Edit, the broken condition's attribute menu is blank, and Save stays disabled until you change or remove the condition. Changing an attribute's type can make conditions fail as well. When an attribute changes its type (e.g., “Stance” going from Picker to Text), comparisons no longer applicable to this new type mean failures for every document. Among attribute types, comparisons such as is any of are exclusive to the Picker type, so “Stance” is any of “Activist” fails. When you open the smart set with Edit, such conditions show the first comparison of the new type with an empty value; you must input the value manually, here as “Stance” is Activist, and save. Finally, renaming or deleting tags in Window ▸ Tags affects smart sets containing Tags conditions accordingly. Renaming a tag changes the reference name into the new name in any Tags condition. Deleting a tag removes it from has any of and has none of conditions, whereas it remains in has all of conditions and thus causes failures for every document until you edit them.

The REFI-QDA exchange format understands only ordinary sets. Anytime you choose to export your project in this format, all of your smart sets are exported as ordinary sets consisting of their members at the point of export. A LemmaLoom archive retains all conditions used to define a smart set, which allows for future use within another instance of LemmaLoom. For additional details about these two formats, refer to .

Groups serve as organizational folders for sorting documents within the Documents section in the navigation sidebar. For instance, the “Climate Debate” project contains “Print” and “Online”, which keep the print pieces apart from the online ones, and “Online” also includes “Radio Debate”. Documents may reside in a maximum of one group, while the translations of any document automatically reside within its respective group too. For more information on making, filling, renaming, and deleting groups, see Groups in . To analyze the documents of a group, make a smart set with a Group condition (see Creating a smart set earlier in this chapter). Choose Group in the condition's first menu, keep is any of, and select the group. Such a smart set changes as documents move into or out of the group. In “Climate Debate”, Group is any of “Print” collects the six documents in “Print”, and Group is empty collects the two in no group, “Heat Wave Report 2024” and “Carbon Tax Debate”. LemmaLoom queries can also read groups through a Group field, and recipes allow the creation of query results containing counts by group (see Recipes in ). The Code Matrix allows you to aggregate its columns by group via Group columns by (see ).

Tags can be applied to projects, documents, codes, memos, and links. Every tag that you type belongs to one global list available to the entire library. Queries can even search your entire library based on tags for documents or projects that contain particular tags (see Working across projects in ). When you tag a document “viral” inside of “Climate Debate” and then type vir when adding tags to a code within another project, LemmaLoom will recommend “viral”. The name of a tag ignores capitalization, so “Viral” and “viral” refer to the same tag. Choose Window ▸ Tags to view the global list. Double-clicking a tag will open its documents in a tab. Alternatively, clicking one of its counts will reveal which items in your active project carry the tag, or which projects employ it. To change the name of a tag globally or remove it from everything carrying it, right-click the tag. See The Tags window in  for further discussion.

“Climate Debate” has three documents tagged “op-ed”, entitled “Running Out of Time”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, and “Who Pays for the Transition”. Meanwhile, there are two documents tagged “viral”, entitled “Letter from the Climate Strike” and “Let's Not Panic”. Tags can be assigned while importing a document, in Document Properties, or in the inspector. The latter is faster: Open the document. In the inspector, click Text, then Details. Under Tags, click the field that reads Add a tag, type the tag, and press Return. Typing a comma also ends a tag. As soon as you have typed three characters, LemmaLoom suggests matches based on the list of shared tags. Any tag already present in another case keeps its existing spelling, regardless of the capitalization you type. To remove a tag, click the × button on the tag (Remove tag). Whatever changes you make in the inspector are immediately saved, both for the document and all translations thereof. Tags can only be added one document at a time. For anything you wish to repeat among many documents, consider making an attribute rather than using tags. With Set Value you can even quickly assign a value to several documents at once, and a Boolean or Picker attribute can serve much as a tag would (see Setting one value for many documents later in this chapter).

The Tags section found at the bottom of the sidebar lists the tags that appear in the active project's documents alphabetically. Next to each tag is the number of original documents bearing the tag; “Climate Debate” shows 3 documents tagged as “op-ed” and 2 documents tagged as “viral”. This section only counts tags in documents. The Tags window also counts tags in projects, codes, memos, and links. Tags are shortcuts to sets of documents bearing them, making tags a quick way to review a few documents at once. Click a tag to load it into a tab. The tab features the same ten views as a set but restricted solely to the documents bearing the tag. Right-click a tag and choose Word Sketch to generate word sketches based on the tagged documents. Right-click a tag and choose Rename or Delete Tag to rename or delete the tag in the same way as you do in the Tags window, with the effect being applied in every project in which the tag exists. The Tags section at the bottom of the navigation sidebar, with “op-ed” and “viral” and the shortcut menu of “viral”. As soon as you tag any other document with “viral”, the count next to “viral” increases to 3, and the document becomes visible in the views associated with the tag. Once the last document in the project loses a tag, the tag disappears from the Tags section. For tags in smart sets, refer to the Tags field presented earlier in this chapter, namely in the section titled How values are compared. Tags attached to codes can serve to filter the codebook entries; learn about tagging in codes, memos, and links in .

The majority of comparisons made within LemmaLoom rely on attributes. Smart sets use attributes to collect documents based on their attribute values, while several analyses partition their outputs by those attributes (refer to the Where attributes can be used section below). Within “Climate Debate”, there are four attributes defined. “Stance” separates the texts by sides, “Readership” allows the “Wide Reach” set to extract broadly read texts, “Publication Date” timestamps each text, and “Outlet” keeps track of each text's origin.

Every attribute has a type among six options. The type dictates what a value may be, how it should be entered, and what comparisons a condition may make about it. Type A value is Entered with In “Climate Debate” Text any text a text field Outlet Integer a whole number, which may be negative a number field Readership Decimal a number that may have a decimal part a number field  Boolean true or false a checkbox  Date a calendar day a date picker Publication Date Picker one of a list of choices you set a menu “Stance”, with the choices “Activist”, “Skeptic”, and “Neutral” The Picker ensures consistent spelling, while the Attributes window sorts its values according to their choice order. Either an Integer or Decimal attribute type permits comparative operators like is at least, as well as range-based grouping via the Code Matrix or Sketch Space. A Date attribute enables both is before and is after operators, while the Code Matrix can group dates by year or month. Free text should be entered as values into a Text attribute. The “Outlet” attribute of “Climate Debate”, for example, uses a Text attribute type. Changing an attribute's type (possible within limits) is discussed later in this chapter.

The Attributes window displays each original document of a project alongside its attribute values in tabular form. The window can be accessed via the main menu option Project ▸ Attributes, or via the shortcut menu of the project under Projects in the sidebar (right-click on it and then choose Attributes). The window can remain open during work. The illustration depicts the window for “Climate Debate” ordered by “Readership” descending with the six activist documents selected. The Attributes window for “Climate Debate”, sorted by “Readership”, with the six activist texts selected. The row across the top contains Search, followed at the end by Import, Export, Manage, and Add Attribute. The body displays the table, which includes a checkbox column, a Document column, and a column for every attribute within the project. Without attributes in a project, the window will display only Import and Add Attribute. The window displays original documents exclusively. Translation documents take on the attribute values of their original document counterparts, meaning that whatever value you enter for “Running Out of Time” will also apply to “Running Out of Time (German)”.

The New Attribute dialog in the Attributes window, with the name “Region”, the type Picker, and four choices. How to define attributes in the Attributes window: Click Add Attribute. In the New Attribute dialog, type a Name. Choose its Type. For a Picker, type its choices in Choices, one per row; Add Choice adds a row. If you like, describe in Description what the attribute records. Click Add. The Add button is disabled if the Name field is left blank (Name is empty), if another attribute exists in your project with the same name, ignoring capitalization (Name already used), and when you add a Picker attribute without any choice options (No choices). Upon creation, the attribute shows itself as the right-most column of the table and contains no values per document. You can also add attributes to your projects via the New Project and Project Properties dialogs, Document Properties, the Import Document dialog, the inspector, and by importing attribute values from spreadsheets. Aside from adding attribute values from spreadsheets and the New Attribute dialog, LemmaLoom provides suggestions of attributes available in all of your projects if at least three characters of a name were inputted. Suggestions show the attribute's type. Picking one from the suggestions or directly entering its name copies its type and choices, keeping consistency among attributes in multiple studies. The newly added attribute belongs exclusively to this project.

Click on a cell in the Attributes window and enter the value in a way that depends upon the attribute type: For Text, type out the text value. For Integer and Decimal, enter the number and press Return, or click somewhere else outside the cell. Only numeric inputs are valid here, and deleting the input will delete the attribute value. For Boolean, select or deselect the checkbox. For Date, choose a particular date from the date picker. For Picker, select an option from the menu, or choose None to remove the value. All changes made while editing attributes are automatically saved. Cells for dates that contain no values display today's date. Cells for Booleans that contain no values appear deselected. Both store their respective values upon any edits you've made. If you deselect a checkbox, it will store a false value, rather than storing nothing (refer back to Documents without a value discussed above). To distinguish between the two cases, sort by the column, whereupon documents without a value appear last. Removing a date or Boolean value requires the remove button in the inspector, detailed next. The inspector is typically faster when dealing with individual documents. It displays the attributes and tags of the active document (see image below showing “Running Out of Time”, which has four values and the tag “op-ed”). The Details facet of the Text inspector for “Running Out of Time”, with its attribute values and tags. To investigate what the value of an attribute is for a specific document, you should open the document and click Text and then Details in the inspector. You will find each attribute with a value for this document listed below Attributes, each in a separate row. You can edit the value in its row. To delete the value while keeping the attribute intact in the project, click the remove button at the end of its row (Remove attribute). Changes are immediate. The Details facet for “Running Out of Time” with a new attribute named “Region” typed into the field below the list and the Type menu open. To assign a value to an attribute not currently shown: Type the attribute's name in the field below the list. Suggestions appear once you have typed three characters. If the name is new to the project, choose a Type in the menu that appears. For a Picker, also type its choices. Click Add Attribute, or press Return. Enter the value in the new row. The Add Attribute button is disabled in three instances, when the name is empty (Name is empty), when the attribute is already assigned to the document (Already added), and when creating a new Picker with no choices (No options). Every time you enter a new name in the field below the list, you add that attribute to the entire project. A row left with an empty value is deleted only after you leave the document, and the attribute stays in the project. Any changes made to a translation's value inside the inspector affect its corresponding original value. Document Properties features identical fields in its Attributes part, which get saved once Save is pressed (refer to Attributes in ). See Importing attribute values from a spreadsheet in  for importing attribute values from spreadsheets.

t: Setting one value for many documents
b: If several documents have the same value for an attribute, you can assign the value to them simultaneously. In the “Climate Debate” project, six documents share the value “Activist” of “Stance”, five share “Skeptic”, and three share “Neutral”; hence, each value can be assigned to its documents in one step. See the figure showing the six activist documents selected in The Attributes window earlier in this chapter for the purpose of assigning their common value. The Set Value dialog for “Stance” with “Activist” chosen, opened with six documents selected in the Attributes window. How to assign one value to several documents: In the Attributes window, select the checkboxes beside the documents. The checkbox at the top of the column selects or deselects every row shown. Beside Search, the window now shows the number of selected documents, such as 6 documents selected, and a Set Value menu. Choose Set Value and then the attribute. In the Set Value dialog, choose or enter the value. Click Apply. The value replaces anything previously stored for that attribute in the selected documents. Edit ▸ Undo Set Value (⌘Z) reverses it. Depending on whether your attribute is of type Picker, Boolean, Date, or any other type of value, the Set Value dialog offers you a menu, checkbox, date picker, or text field. When you are entering a Decimal, you can type the decimal separator that your Mac uses. Apply becomes disabled either when there isn't anything in the input field (No value) or the entered value doesn't meet the restrictions imposed by the attribute's type (Invalid value), like entering about 40000 into “Readership”. Set Value is a feature for inputting values only; deleting existing values requires clearing the value in each document individually. Set Value operates on selected visible rows. If you select multiple rows prior to entering something into Search, the search can hide some of them, even though the hidden rows stay selected. The number shown next to Set Value is thus equal to the actual number of currently selected and visible rows. To set the same value across multiple documents retrieved by searching, execute a search and click the checkbox at the top of the column.

Search lets you show only the rows containing the term you type in their titles or cells. Search ignores case. In the example project “Climate Debate”, a search term of ledger produces the texts titled “Hope Takes Work”, “The Models Keep Missing”, and “Science Is Never Settled”, which are the three texts from “The Weekly Ledger”. When you click a column heading, the rows are sorted in increasing order based on the values in that column. A subsequent click reverses the sorting order. Arrows show which sorting direction is selected. Values of numeric type are sorted according to their magnitudes. Hence, 8,500 comes before 23,000. Picker values are sorted in the order of the Choices. With the choices “Activist”, “Skeptic”, and “Neutral”, activists come before the others. Textual items are sorted alphabetically, and numbers included within a text value are sorted numerically, e.g., “Draft 2” precedes “Draft 10”. Dates are sorted chronologically, whereas Boolean values are sorted false before true. Documents missing a value are positioned last, irrespective of sorting direction. In cases of ties involving identical ranking, documents are sorted alphabetically by title, ascending or descending depending on whether sorting is lowest-to-highest or highest-to-lowest. Clicking the “Readership” heading twice sorts the rows from the highest “Readership” value. According to the figure in The Attributes window earlier in this chapter, this produces a sorted list from high to low, starting with “Carbon Tax Debate” (875,000), “Running Out of Time” (412,000), and “Net Zero Will Cost You” (398,000). Documents with fewer readers follow, ending with “A Mayor's Promise” (8,500) and “Heat Wave Report 2024” (3,100). All documents lacking a value for this attribute come last. Sorting remains active until you close the window.

To edit an attribute, choose Manage, then the attribute, then Edit, or right-click on the attribute's column heading and select Edit. The Edit Attribute dialog has the fields Name, Type, Choices (only for a Picker), and Description (which REFI-QDA format export includes); these correspond directly to the fields for New Attribute. Pressing the Save button updates the attribute definition; the Save button becomes disabled when the Name field is blank (Name is empty), or when there are no choices in a Picker (No choices). The Manage menu of the Attributes window for “Climate Debate”, with “Readership” chosen and Edit highlighted. Choices in a Picker attribute may be edited to include additional options, to reorder existing options, or delete choices. The order of choices reflects how options appear in the menu and how they are sorted. Documents retain their choice value regardless of whether the list of choices changes. When deleting a choice that some documents have, those documents continue to hold that choice. The choice appears after all the listed choices in their menu and continues to be used in smart sets. Renaming a choice (e.g., changing “Skeptic” to “Critic”) leaves documents with the old choice, so moving them requires adding a new choice with the renamed label. Once added, documents having the old choice may then be reassigned to the renamed choice with Set Value before removing the old choice.

It may occur that a certain attribute ends up needing a different type altogether; perhaps the values of your Text attribute should be limited to a predetermined number of options in order to maintain consistency, thus necessitating a Picker attribute type. The drop-down list under Type in the Edit Attribute dialog lists the current type along with each other type that is compatible with all the values currently set in the attribute. When you save, LemmaLoom rewrites the values in the new type. Compatibility of values is defined by: Type Values that fit Text any value Picker any value Integer whole numbers written with digits, with a minus sign if needed and no leading zeros; 12.0 fits and becomes 12 Decimal numbers written with digits, a minus sign if needed, at most one decimal point, and no leading zeros, up to 15 significant digits (0.5 fits, .5 does not); 14 becomes 14.0 Boolean true, false, yes, no, 1, and 0, in any capitals; they become true or false Date dates in exactly the form 2024-08-21 (four-digit year, two-digit month and day, hyphens); 21.08.2024 does not fit The “Climate Debate” project has the following types available for its attributes in the menu: Attribute Current type Types offered Stance Picker Text, Picker Readership Integer Text, Integer, Decimal, Picker Publication Date Date Text, Date, Picker Outlet Text Text, Picker Imagine if somebody had entered about 40000 into a Text attribute used to track the number of readers. Integer would be made available to you only once you discovered that particular entry via Search or by sorting the column, then changed it to an integer. Upon switching to Picker, if Choices is empty at first, LemmaLoom automatically enters whatever values the documents already have, sorted alphabetically. The figure below demonstrates this; “Outlet” was switched to Picker, and Choices included all eight outlets from “City Hall Bulletin” to “Weather and Climate Agency”. Reorder or extend the choices before you click Save. The Edit Attribute dialog for “Outlet”, switched to Picker, with its choices filled in from the existing values. The new type also determines what types of comparison a condition can use. Changing between Integer and Decimal maintains all your comparisons without issue. Should you change an attribute's type in any other way, however, you must verify your smart sets after the fact, as discussed in Changing a smart set earlier in this chapter.

Attributes display in the order that you created them. If you want to move an attribute, choose Manage, followed by selecting the attribute, and Move Left or Move Right; alternatively, right-click on the attribute column heading itself. The order is consistent anywhere that attributes appear. This includes the columns of the Attributes window, the inspector, Document Properties, Project Properties, and the attribute menu of smart set conditions. New conditions begin with the first attribute, so the one tested most frequently should come before others.

Deleting an attribute means selecting Manage, then the attribute, then Delete, or right-clicking its column heading and choosing Delete. The attribute will be instantly deleted along with its value from each of your documents in the project. Smart set conditions set on the attribute now become false for every document (see Changing a smart set earlier in this chapter). Edit ▸ Undo Delete Attribute (⌘Z) will restore the deleted attribute and its values. Deleting an attribute from Project Properties results in identical consequences when you click Save; Edit ▸ Undo Project Properties restores everything.

Export creates a CSV file which spreadsheets can open, containing one row per item shown, in the order shown. It contains the document titles in the Document column, followed by all attributes as columns. The file name will be based on your project name, e.g., Climate Debate-attributes.csv. Import reads attribute values from either a CSV or tab-delimited file, and even creates attributes during import if needed. See Importing attribute values from a spreadsheet in  for details on how this works. Often, the simplest way to add or change many attribute values will be to export the table, modify it within a spreadsheet program, and reimport it.

Smart sets examine attribute values as discussed previously in Smart sets in this chapter. The Code Matrix can group its columns by attributes (refer to ). Sketch Space will compare the grammatical properties of words among different attribute values (refer to Comparing attribute values in ). Queries will test attribute values in rules (refer to Fields in ). Compare will show counts for each value of an attribute side by side, along with a statistical test (refer to ). Codes can hold attributes too, which hold values for each individual coding instance. These are added directly to codes, and the Attributes window only displays the attributes pertaining to documents. Refer to Codes with attributes within  for more information.

The documents analyzed can be constrained by a set, a smart set, or a tag. The table below lists the locations where you choose each one: Where Sets and smart sets Tags A tab opened from the sidebar, with its ten views yes yes The menu after the word field in the Word Sketch window yes yes The scope menu of Window ▸ Queries the sets of the active project no Documents in the Auto Code dialog yes no Export in the shortcut menu yes no Scope ▸ Document set in the New Code and Edit Code dialogs (see Where a code can be used in ) yes no Compare With ▸ Set in a Keywords query (see Keywords in ) yes no The drop-down menu after the word field in the Word Sketch window reflects the scope you are using currently. It begins by listing the whole project, followed by its sets (in alphabetical order), tags, and lastly the document in the active tab. Where only sets are offered, switch to the Queries view within the tab of a particular tag, or make a smart set with a Tags condition.

Regular sets, smart sets, and tags in the navigation sidebar consider only the original versions of documents. The translation will follow the original wherever it goes. For example, only the original document is listed under a set (refer to Adding and removing documents above), while the smart set considers the values of the original document. Tags, attribute values, and the group are shared by an original and its translations, so they are always the same for both. Analyzing a set, tag, or project will by default take place among original documents. Thus, analyzing “Running Out of Time” and “Running Out of Time (German)” would amount to analyzing one piece of text. The coding views of a set count codings in original documents too. When coding a passage in a translation document, LemmaLoom creates a coding instance in the same place in the corresponding original document; thus, the coding instance in “Running Out of Time (German)” will be counted once, in the original “Running Out of Time”. There are two kinds of analysis methods that can read translations rather than original documents. Queries have a Corpus parameter in their Options condition; its settings allow for the corpus to consist of Originals, Translations, or Both (see Options in ). Word sketches for a set, a tag, or the project provide options in a dropdown menu after the word field if translation documents are included. This menu has a Corpus section containing options Originals and an option for each available translation language, such as Translations (German) (see ). For additional information about working with translations, visit .

LemmaLoom can translate documents into other languages. When you translate a document, the translation will be kept as its own separate document, appearing under the original in your navigation sidebar. This new document can be read, coded, and queried normally. Furthermore, all of the codings, memos, bookmarks, and links added to one language version will be copied to the others. Translations can be used in lieu of language support in LemmaLoom's grammar analysis; for example, since LemmaLoom indexes only English, German, and Chinese, a Spanish opinion piece can be read and coded, yet an automatic English translation will allow lenses and word sketches. Alternatively, you can use a translation to compare your text with itself in another language or to read a translation of material in a language you know less well alongside its original text. By translating your texts, you let colleagues follow your coding in languages they understand better; grammar results from translations, however, will always describe the wording of the machine-translated text (see Translations in analyses later in this chapter). All examples shown in this chapter will come from “Climate Debate”, LemmaLoom's example project available from File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project (see The example project in ). In the “Climate Debate” example project, the English-language activist op-ed titled “Running Out of Time” is translated once into German, titled “Running Out of Time (German)”. The codings, memo, bookmark, and link added to the original are carried forward into the translation.

In LemmaLoom, an original is a document that you imported. A translation, meanwhile, refers to any document generated from an original by LemmaLoom. Only originals can be translated, and an original can have translations in several languages. When you manually import a translation document, it is considered an ordinary document because only LemmaLoom-generated translations belong to an original. Language versions are a document's original and all of its translations. Both “Running Out of Time” and “Running Out of Time (German)” are language versions of the same op-ed. The alignment represents a mapping of each sentence in the original to its translation counterpart. LemmaLoom creates the alignment during translation for proper placement of annotations as well as synchronized scrolling of the two language versions. A copy is LemmaLoom's term for the annotation it adds to the other language versions of a document whenever you annotate one of them with a coding, memo, bookmark, or link. Split view is the splitting of the reader into two panes side by side. Specifically, the reader splits into the left pane, or main pane, and the right pane; the former retains the tab strip while the latter displays one document under a header of its own. Your active pane is whichever pane had the most recent click. Your active pane also determines which document the inspector and the commands in the menu bar work on.

LemmaLoom uses macOS' integrated translation functionality. The first use of a pair of languages requires that you download those languages via macOS. Available languages depend upon your version of macOS. Translating from the source language to any language other than English, German, or Chinese results in documents you can read, search via the search bar, code, and annotate as usual. Lenses, grammar views, and word sketches require English, German, or Chinese (see Other languages in ).

“Running Out of Time (German)” is a translation of the English op-ed piece in the “Climate Debate” project. This figure depicts the Translate dialog set to translate “Net Zero Will Cost You”, the skeptical op-ed piece, into German. The Translate dialog for “Net Zero Will Cost You”, set to translate from English into German. To make a translation: In the sidebar, right-click the document and choose Translate, or select it and choose Project ▸ Translate. The command is available for originals only. The Translate dialog shows the document's title under Document and its language under From. Under To, choose the language to translate into. Click Translate. If macOS has not yet downloaded the two languages, it asks whether to download them. Confirm the download. Translate stays disabled while macOS prepares the languages, and once they are ready, the dialog closes and the translation starts. Should your Mac have both languages already, the dialog closes immediately upon clicking Translate. The translation happens in the background. In the navigation sidebar underneath the original, a new row is added with the language name. This row has either a spinner while the translation waits to start processing, or a progress ring showing translation progress. Once the translation completes successfully, LemmaLoom swaps out the row with the new document. An example name might be “Net Zero Will Cost You (German)”. The indexing process begins next, keeping the translation's lens menu disabled during this phase (refer to What is available without the analysis in ). The sidebar while “Net Zero Will Cost You” is being translated, with the pending “German” row and its spinner below the original. Once the translation has been generated, LemmaLoom will clear out the undo steps associated with modifying the original document, including any codings or changes made to the text (see Translating a document in ).

From displays the document's language. This language may either be selected during importing or detected by LemmaLoom upon importing. Should the language be wrong, fix it via Document Properties prior to translating (see Document properties in ). To contains a listing of all languages macOS supports translation into. The languages are sorted alphabetically. The language of your document is omitted, along with any language that your document is already translated into or being translated into, since an original can have one translation per language. Initially, LemmaLoom selects the first supported language on macOS according to your preferences specified in System Settings under General ▸ Language & Region; if there aren't any, it defaults to English, or failing that to the first option in the To menu. In case macOS does not provide any suitable languages for translation, then this menu displays Not supported, whereas in case there remain no languages available for selection, the To menu states Already translated. When translation between two specific languages isn't supported by macOS, then Translation isn't available for these languages appears right underneath From and To. In case Translate is disabled, hover the mouse pointer over it to see what prevents it from becoming active: Reason What to do Loading Wait while LemmaLoom asks macOS which languages it offers, or whether it can translate between the two chosen. No language chosen Choose a language under To. Not supported macOS offers no language to translate into, or cannot translate from the document's language. If From is wrong, correct it in Document Properties. Already translated Every language on offer has a translation. To translate into one of them again, delete its translation first (see Translating again later in this chapter). Preparing Wait while macOS downloads the languages. Should the download fail or should you choose to decline it, an explanation will appear in red beneath the input fields. You can click on Translate once more thereafter.

Languages that macOS uses to translate text are shared with every other app that translates on your Mac. You can check what languages have been installed for translation, and remove the ones you no longer need, via System Settings under General ▸ Language & Region ▸ Translation Languages. If a translation is currently pending when you delete one of its languages, the translation fails. Translate the document again, and macOS will offer to install the language once more.

Many language pairs have a larger, higher-quality translation model beyond the default translation model provided by macOS. Whenever the larger model is available for both languages being considered, LemmaLoom uses the improved model; otherwise, LemmaLoom uses the default model. The larger model requires several gigabytes of working memory during its operation. On a computer with 8 GB of total memory, performing a lengthy translation might noticeably hinder the indexing of other documents or running any apps in addition to LemmaLoom. Generally, start long translations after finishing transcriptions and imports of large amounts of text.

Translation happens one document at a time within LemmaLoom. When multiple translations are initiated, they enter a queue and await their turn to proceed. Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0) lists them under Translating, and each row shows the title the translation will have, such as “Net Zero Will Cost You (German)”, and the project the document belongs to. Until a translation begins, the row will say Waiting, while during the process itself, it will provide a translation percentage, such as Translating 40%. The Activity window with the translation of “Net Zero Will Cost You” in progress and the translation of “Hope Takes Work” waiting. In the case of failure, the translation moves to the Failed section of the Activity window, showing the reason. Its row will disappear from the sidebar. In the Translate dialog interface, the language option becomes available again. Click Retry to begin translating the document anew. Retry works only if you haven’t deleted the languages. In the event that you did so, the translation must restart from the sidebar, prompting macOS to redownload. Once the translation fails, it remains in the Activity window until you retry it, delete the original, or quit LemmaLoom. Should a translation be waiting or in progress when you quit LemmaLoom, it is canceled, and restarting the translation will be required.

The translation feature in LemmaLoom uses the macOS translator, which will translate your text sentence-by-sentence. LemmaLoom divides up your texts according to where line breaks occur in the text, then divides those into individual sentences. If your text is the transcript of an audio/video file, LemmaLoom will divide your transcript according to its segments first, then into sentences. Your sentences will get individually translated and assembled back together in the order they appeared: Paragraphs and line breaks will be preserved in the output. Every sentence of your text gets translated to one contiguous stretch of the translation. The alignment retains a record of this correspondence. Sentences are separated in translations by one space, except for languages that don’t require spacing between words, such as Chinese; they are directly concatenated. Any sentences for which macOS couldn’t produce a translation are retained in the original language. Since the translation software sees only the current sentence during the process, any word that depends on the previous sentence, such as a pronoun, may be translated incorrectly. Sentences broken across two lines, as in a text file with a line break at the end of every line, will be translated as two pieces; therefore, join such lines, and correct any other errors, in the original before proceeding with the translation (refer to Editing a document's text in ). Translations of audio or video documents play back the original document’s media file and retain the segmentation by speaker with the timing intact. An example translation from English to German of “Radio Debate” would thus list the turns of “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”, and play the recording from any passage of the German text.

Translations appear in the Documents section of the sidebar under the original. For instance, in “Climate Debate”, “Running Out of Time (German)” can be found in the “Print” group beneath “Running Out of Time”. The name of the translation document is the name of the original, followed by its language within parentheses. This can be edited just like any other document’s name. Searches in the Search Documents field will yield results for both the translations and the originals. Because translation titles end with their languages, a search for German would return all German translations within a project, except if you have renamed them. “Running Out of Time” in the navigation sidebar, with its German translation listed below it. Disclosure triangles for originals let you collapse or expand their translations. The sidebar listing of a set contains only the originals, while the counts beside a set or tag include only the originals (see Translations in analyses later in this chapter).

t: What a translation shares with its original
b: When you translate a document in LemmaLoom, the translation receives the author names, date, publisher name, publication title, URL, DOI, color, group location, tags, and attribute values from its original. All language versions share certain characteristics: Tags. Tagging a document version “Running Out of Time (German)” tags “Running Out of Time” as well, and vice versa. Attribute values. Specifying “Readership” in the properties of any version sets it equally for all language versions. Group membership. Moving “Running Out of Time” into the “Online” group automatically moves its German counterpart there too. Set membership. The original documents are members of document sets, and their translations follow them. Codes with scopes of one document or one set. A code whose Scope is Document and names “Running Out of Time” can also be applied in “Running Out of Time (German)”, and a code limited to the “Activists” set can be applied in the translations of the activist texts (see Where a code can be used in ). Codings, memos, bookmarks, and links, through copies. Annotations in both languages later in this chapter discusses copies between language versions in more detail. Every language version retains other elements exclusively for itself: the title, author names, date, publisher name, publication title, URL, DOI, and color; the language; the text, and any edits you make to it; its index, with its lenses, statistics, and grammar views.

The indexing of a machine translation in English, German, or Chinese is the same as that of any other imported document. Machine translations get their own lenses and separate Text, Grammar, Coding, and Multimode tabs in the inspector, and, as usual, Query under Multimode reads only the translation itself. Machine translations often require a bit of editing because of terms translated in two different ways or sentences translated nonsensically. Make an edit to a translation much the same as you would to a regular document. Select Document ▸ Edit (⇧⌘E), edit the document, and hit the Save button. Edits move the alignment along with annotations so that both languages continue to align correctly despite edits (see How annotations follow edits in ). Edits always affect only one language version of the same text. When you make an edit to an original, you must delete the translation to generate another translation from the newly edited text (see Translating again later in this chapter).

When exporting an original document to a LemmaLoom archive, translations are included in the export. Therefore, if exporting “Running Out of Time”, the resulting archive includes “Running Out of Time (German)” as well. In contrast, a REFI-QDA project treats the translation document separately. If the relationship between the two must remain in place during the transfer, opt for LemmaLoom archives. Additional guidance can be found in Exporting documents in .

t: Reading a translation beside its original
b: Comparing both versions next to each other allows you to examine how macOS has rendered a passage prior to using it. This allows you to keep the translation open as a reference while conducting a close reading of the original version. You can also compare the codings of the two versions this way. This figure shows “Running Out of Time” on the left and “Running Out of Time (German)” on the right, with both scrolled together. Because the translation is in the active pane, the inspector displays its 13 codings, which mirror those of the original. “Running Out of Time” and its German translation side by side and scrolled together, with the inspector showing the codings of the translation. To read a translation next to its original: In the sidebar, right-click the translation and choose Open Beside Original, or choose Window ▸ Open Beside Original while the translation is selected in the sidebar or active in the reader. The original opens in a tab in the main pane, and the translation in the right pane, which becomes active. To scroll the two together, click the lock button, Scroll together, at the right end of the right pane's header, or choose View ▸ Scroll Together (⌥⌘L). If the right pane had displayed another document previously, the translation replaces that document.
Split view allows you to look at two documents simultaneously, like “Running Out of Time” next to “Net Zero Will Cost You”, representing two opposing viewpoints in the discussion.

t: Opening two documents side by side
b: There are a few ways in which you can open a document in the right pane: Right-click a document in the sidebar, then click the Open in Split View option in the shortcut menu that appears. The document opens in the right pane next to the document in the main pane. The option is disabled if the document itself is already shown in the main or right pane, or if a set, detail view, or tag is active. Right-click a tab above the reader, then select the Open in Split View option from the resulting shortcut menu. If a document is active, the other tabs containing documents become available to be opened in split view. The document leaves the tab strip and moves to the right pane. Select the Open in Split View option from the Window menu, followed by choosing the document you wish to view. The submenu under Window ▸ Open in Split View displays the document selected in the sidebar, as well as other tabs of documents. Select two documents in the sidebar (by clicking on one and ⌘-clicking on the other), then right-click either of them and choose the Open Side by Side option from the shortcut menu, or select Window ▸ Open Side by Side from the menu bar. The document higher in the list will be displayed on the left, and the other on the right. For a translation, select the Open Beside Original option in the shortcut menu, as described above. The shortcut menu with Open Side by Side after “Running Out of Time” and “Net Zero Will Cost You” are selected in the sidebar. The shortcut menu of the tab “Running Out of Time” while “Net Zero Will Cost You” is open, with Open in Split View and Open in New Window. There is only ever one document opened in the right pane at once, so opening another there closes the one it replaces. A document is shown in only one pane at a time.

The active pane's tab, or its header in the right pane, is highlighted in full, whereas the non-active pane's tab or header is lighter. Opening a document in split view activates the right pane. Clicking on a tab, or selecting Window ▸ Show Next Tab (⇧⌘]) or Window ▸ Show Previous Tab (⇧⌘), activates the left pane. All of the following affect the document currently opened in the active pane: The inspector; All tools available in the title band (lens menu, collapse button, find, display settings, and **Edit**); Menu commands, including **Edit ▸ Find** (⌘F), **Document ▸ Edit** (⇧⌘E), and **Document ▸ Auto Code…** (⇧⌘A); The key Esc to clear the current selection or close any opened search bar in the active pane; The **Diagram** window (refer to [The Diagram window in ); and finally, The document scope for the Word Sketch window. In the sidebar, the active pane's document is highlighted. Clicking a document in the sidebar will load it in the left pane and activate that pane, unless it is already in the right pane, in which case the right pane becomes active. Clicking into the other pane will change the inspector to show that pane's document but retain the inspector's tab, facet, and width while maintaining whether the inspector is currently visible or not. If, for instance, the Codings facet of the Coding tab is displayed for “Running Out of Time”, then clicking into “Running Out of Time (German)” will display the codings for the translation document right in that spot.

The lenses, search bar, selection, and scrolling position are separate for each pane. With split view activated, you could read “Running Out of Time” with the Modality lens enabled and “Net Zero Will Cost You” with the Cohesion lens enabled. Font, text size, gutter, and layout are shared by both panes. Initially, both panes have equal widths. Change this proportion by dragging the divider between them. Each pane has a minimum width. The splitting ratio will apply to all your projects. For windows whose size doesn’t accommodate both minimum-width panes, each pane still has an equal share of the width. When viewing the project shelf, a set, or a tag in the left pane, the right pane becomes hidden until a document tab becomes active once again. LemmaLoom remembers the right pane’s document for each project. Returning to a project or opening LemmaLoom again shows the right pane document as-is but without the Scroll Together toggle enabled.

Here is how you could close split view: Click the × in the header of the right pane. Right-click the header and select Close Split View from the shortcut menu. Go to Window ▸ Close Split View. Click in the right pane and then select File ▸ Close Tab (⌘W). The document on the right side gets closed along with the split view. In split view with the left pane active, ⌘W closes its active tab as usual. In case you have only one tab open on the left and close it, the right-pane document moves into the main pane. Right-clicking the header gives the option Open in New Window, opening the document in its very own Document window complete with its own inspector (see Opening a document in its own window in ). From the menu bar you also get Window ▸ Open in New Window doing the exact same thing, but for the document in whichever pane is currently active. The shortcut menu on the header of the right pane, which shows “Net Zero Will Cost You”, with Open in New Window and Close Split View.

Scrolling together maintains the vertical positions of your original and translation such that corresponding paragraphs appear next to each other as you progress through both. When the two panes display the language versions of the same document, the lock icon becomes available in the header area at the right edge of the right pane. This applies to both an original and translation pair, as well as two translations of one original. You can click the lock button or select View ▸ Scroll Together (⌥⌘L) to enable scrolling the two panes together. The lock icon will close, and the menu item will feature a checkmark symbol. Immediately following activation, the right pane jumps to the passage at the top of the left pane, and scrolling one pane results in the automatic scrolling of the other. Any other combination causes Scroll Together to be disabled. LemmaLoom synchronizes scrolling based on the alignment between the two versions. LemmaLoom takes the point at the top of the pane you scroll and finds the sentence it lies in. It then scrolls the other version until the corresponding part of the sentence arrives at the top of its own pane. Inside of a sentence, LemmaLoom maintains the proportional distance, meaning one fourth into an English sentence corresponds to one fourth into its German translation. The synchronization continues despite any difference in the number of lines per sentence. Activating any other document in the left pane removes the lock and terminates scrolling synchronization. Making the original, or another of its language versions, active again resumes scrolling synchronization. Closing the split view terminates Scroll Together.

Translations maintain separate codings, memos, links, and bookmarks per language version. If you code a passage in “Running Out of Time”, then LemmaLoom will automatically apply the same code to the corresponding passage in “Running Out of Time (German)”, and vice versa. Once you code a text, the codings remain linked, and you could analyze either version on its own or compare how a coded passage reads in each language.

When making a new translation of a document, LemmaLoom will copy its codings, memos, links, and bookmarks into the new translation. As such, when adding any new items to a language version, LemmaLoom will automatically duplicate them to all the other language versions: a coding, complete with the code; a document memo or passage memo, complete with the text, code, and tags; a bookmark, complete with the comment and color; a link, complete with the relation, comment, color, and tags, unless it joins two language versions of one document. When copying a link, only the end of the link that occurs inside the translated document is moved in the copy. For instance, in the “Climate Debate” project, there exists a link connecting a passage in the document “Let's Not Panic” to another in “Running Out of Time”. The resulting copy of this link in the German translation of “Running Out of Time” connects to the translated passage of “Running Out of Time (German)” from the very same passage of “Let's Not Panic”. Were “Let's Not Panic” translated as well, then two more copies of the link would connect from the corresponding passage of that translation to “Running Out of Time” and to “Running Out of Time (German)”. A link between two passages of “Running Out of Time” is duplicated into a link between the respective passages of the German translation. Annotation copies, together with the annotation, can be undone in one step via Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z). Additionally, any automatically generated codings by means of Auto Code… are also copied across your translations. See Coding passages automatically in .

Changes made to an annotation are automatically made to all of its copies: editing a memo's body text, its code, or tags affects all of its versions equally; changing a bookmark's comment or its color, a link's relation, comment, color, or tags affects all of them equally; attribute values assigned to a coding apply equally to all of them. If the annotation itself is deleted from one document, all of its copies will be deleted at once; deleting the “Urgency” coding on the sentence in “Running Out of Time (German)” removes it from “Running Out of Time” as well. Positions of annotations, however, belong to individual documents. As you edit one version of the text, your annotations will shift accordingly (see How annotations follow edits in ); the copies of these annotations in other versions retain their positions. If a copy that mistakenly coded a passage gets deleted, the coding is deleted across all language versions, including the passage you coded yourself. Leave such a copy in place, and read it as a pointer to the sentence (see Where copies are stored below).

Placing copies uses sentence alignments, which pair sentences between the two versions of a text. Hence, your copy will be placed correctly into the corresponding translated sentence. Annotations made on complete sentences are copied perfectly as-is. When working on parts of sentences, however, LemmaLoom calculates at what proportion of a sentence a passage begins and ends, relative to its total character count. This proportion is then used to place the copy at an equivalent place within the translated sentence: $q$ denotes the total number of characters, spaces, and punctuation marks prior to the beginning (or the end) of the selected passage within the original sentence. Dividing it by $L$, the length of this sentence measured in characters, gives the proportion $q/L$. Multiplying it by $L'$ (read “L prime”), the length of the translated sentence, yields $q'$ (“q prime”), the place within the translated sentence. This figure is rounded to the nearest integer, always toward the larger integer when halves occur. In languages where spaces separate words, the copy will then extend to full words. Additionally, spaces at the beginning and end of any copy will be trimmed. Consider this sentence taken from “Running Out of Time”: On a podium these dates certainly sound impressive, but look closely at who will still be in office when they arrive. Its translation into German says: Auf einem Podium klingen diese Daten sicherlich beeindruckend, aber schauen Sie genau hin, wer noch im Amt sein wird, wenn sie ankommen. These sentences have lengths of 117 and 136 characters, respectively, counting spaces and the period. Suppose the passage these dates in the first sentence is coded with “Deadlines”. Counting On a podium and the space after it, there is a distance of 12 characters. The entire phrase On a podium these dates amounts to 23 characters. Therefore, the passage begins after 12 characters and ends after 23: Rounding to 14 and 27, the copy stretches from after position 14 up to and including position 27 within the second sentence, namely, um klingen di. Expanding this copy to encompass whole words produces Podium klingen diese. Another annotated passage reads who will still be in office when they arrive, coded with “Responsibility”. Starting after 72 characters, this passage extends to 116 characters. Hence, positions of $72/117 times 136 approx 83.69$ and $116/117 times 136 approx 134.84$ yield 84 and 135 as rounded numbers. The copy runs from after position 84, inside genau, extending through exactly position 135. Thus, expanding the copy to whole words results in genau hin, wer noch im Amt sein wird, wenn sie ankommen. As German places the verb klingen (sound) before diese Daten (these dates), the expanded copy Podium klingen diese captures klingen but not Daten. At the same time, the copy stays in the right sentence. Words before wer (who) take up a larger share than before who, therefore making the latter copy start early and take in genau hin. Counts of codings per document and queries looking for sentences coded with a certain code remain accurate. The sentence in “Running Out of Time” with its “Deadlines” and “Responsibility” codings, and their copies in the German translation. Where your method allows, try to code complete sentences, because their copies are exact. With smaller selections, use the copy to locate the appropriate sentence, since the words it covers can differ from the ones you coded.

In order to delete either the original or a translation, right-click on it, choose Delete Document, and hit Delete in the alert. (Refer to Deleting documents in .) Deleting a translation removes that translation only: Any codings, memos, bookmarks, and links associated with it will be deleted; the corresponding codings, memos, bookmarks, and links in the original and other translations will remain. Any links made between the translation and the original will be deleted. The codes whose Scope is set to the translation will now name the original, and can be applied in the original and its remaining translations. For a recording, its media file stays, since the original itself uses the media file. If you delete the original document, all translations of it are deleted together, despite the alert only mentioning the original document. Should the original have an unfinished translation pending in the Activity window, that translation is canceled right away. However, any ongoing translation finishes, and the Activity window lists it under Failed with Document not found. The undo operation Edit ▸ Undo Delete Document (⌘Z) retrieves the deleted document including its translations and annotations.

When updating the translation based on changes made to the original or starting anew with a translation, delete the existing translation and create a new translation based on the original. This will erase all edits made to the old translation, its title, should you have changed it, and any links connecting it back to the original. Right-click the translation and choose Delete Document, then click Delete. Right-click the original, choose Translate, and choose the same language under To. Click Translate. Each of your annotations from the previous translation will have been duplicated in the original document; therefore, your new translation will inherit every annotation with the new alignment applied.

When analyzing a set of documents, or even an entire project, the analysis takes into account only the original documents unless you specify differently. Single-document analyses consider the actual document regardless of whether it’s the original document or a translation, so to analyze “Running Out of Time (German)” on its own, open it and use the inspector. Analysis What it reads The inspector, and queries in a document's Multimode tab That document Codebook, Codings, Memos, Code Stats, Code Matrix, and Relations for a set or the project Originals Links for a set or the project Each link once Queries for a set, the project, or all projects Originals, unless you change the corpus Word sketches and Sketch Space for a set or the project Originals, unless you change the corpus The counts in the Dictionaries section Originals Auto Code… for a set or the whole project Originals. If a translation is active when you open Auto Code…, that translation is read in place of its original. Smart sets Originals Codings applied to a translation are tracked in the relevant views via their copies in the original document. For instance, when you code a passage in “Running Out of Time (German)”, the Code Stats view of the “Activists” set records this as one occurrence, in “Running Out of Time”. The alerts for delete or merge operations on codes are exceptions, where both the copy and original are accounted for. An “Urgency” coding in “Running Out of Time” and its copy in “Running Out of Time (German)” appear as two coded segments in these alerts. Adding a translation to a set adds its original instead, as discussed in Translations in . Results obtained from translations reflect how macOS has phrased the text. Translation may introduce or drop hedges and modal verbs and modify the word order. It is advised to use results to identify passages and follow with close readings of those passages in their originals.

In the Queries sections of a set and the project, and in Window ▸ Queries, the menu showing Originals at the top of the Options condition sets the corpus (see Options in ). You could choose Translations to query the grammar of originals in a language other than English, German, or Chinese through their translations, or Both for hits from every language version. Originals, the default corpus, reads the documents within the defined scope. Translations reads the translations of those documents instead, in every language they have been translated into. Both reads both the original and translated documents. The scope is derived by LemmaLoom from the originals. In “Climate Debate”, with the corpus changed to Translations, a query on the “Activists” set reads the translations of the activist texts, specifically “Running Out of Time (German)” here. A query in a document's Multimode tab reads only its own document. The Options condition of a query in the “Activists” set, with the corpus menu open. Both means both originals and their translations, so an annotation and its copy are two hits. When querying Codings on the “Urgency” code for instance, a coding in the original “Running Out of Time” is found alongside its counterpart coding in the “Running Out of Time (German)” translation. When originals have translations into more than one language, Translations and Both mix the languages. Adding a rule Language is any of German in the Where condition keeps only German translations. In a keyword list comparison, either side depends on the corpus too, making both sides composed of translations when choosing Translations (see Keywords in ). Your query retains the choice you picked. When exporting query results as Markdown, the provenance lists it under Corpus (see Markdown with provenance in ). The document field Is Translation helps distinguish originals from translations. By navigating to the project's Queries section and setting the corpus to Both, then finding Library · Documents with the rule Is Translation is true, every translation document will be listed. Smart sets operate solely on originals and thus have Has Translations instead which, with the rule set to is true, returns the original documents having translations.

When generating a word sketch or Sketch Space for a set, tag, or project in LemmaLoom, it will read the originals. If any documents in your scope have translations in English, German, or Chinese, then a menu will become available in the bar at the top, after the word field. Your initial selection will read Originals. In the menu, under Corpus, you can choose between Originals and each translation language. As word sketches focus on analyzing text in one language at a time, there is one option per translation language. In “Climate Debate”, for example, the translation option would be Translations (German), for “Running Out of Time (German)”. In the Word Sketch window, the same menu also sets the scope and then shows both, such as “Climate Debate” · Originals. The Word Sketch view of “Climate Debate” with the menu of originals and translations open. Language choice dictates which translations are included. Once a language is chosen, type the word in that language, in this case Klima instead of climate. Further reading on word sketches is in , and on Sketch Space in .

You may wish to query your alignments themselves, for instance when you know how a passage reads in the translation and want to find it in the original. For example, in “Running Out of Time”, you may wish to know what English sentences have a translation that includes the word Klima. The unit Translation · Alignments in the Find menu returns a hit for each pair of a sentence and its translation. The fields returned are Source Text, Translation Text, and Translation Language. Source Text is always the sentence in the document of your query, while the other two describe the sentence paired with it. In original documents, this refers to the translation, and a separate hit is made for each language of translation. In translated documents, this refers to the sentence of the original. The Translated As relation in a context row preserves the hits in any sentence whose translation matches your rules (see Context in ). To get hits for the sentences of your document whose translation matches a criterion, say, containing a particular word: The Find and Where conditions of a query in “Climate Debate”, with a Translated As context row over Alignments and a Translation Text rule that contains Klima. Open the document. In the inspector, click Multimode, then Query. In the Find condition, choose Text · Sentences. In the Where condition, click Add and choose Add Context. Change the row to Some, Translated As, and Alignments. Click the Add button inside the context row, choose Add Rule, and choose Translation Text as the field. Set the comparison to contains and type the word as the value. The results list all matching sentences immediately once the rule has its value.

The Text tab in the inspector describes the active document as a whole. This tab has three facets. Overview shows stats for your document, including counts of sentences and words, readability figures, vocabulary, sentence structures, and charts of word class frequencies, grammatical functions, and phrase counts. Details contains the attribute values and tags associated with the document, while Bookmarks shows the passages that you bookmarked in your document. Statistics describe only the surface of a text. They can help you characterize the document, allow you to choose documents for closer reading, and help you detect anomalies within a dataset (such as transcripts where there never was a break between sentences). However, statistics cannot inform you of what someone intended with the writing, nor can they give insight into why two op-eds differ.

When indexing documents, LemmaLoom parses them into their constituent sentences and tokens; tokens refer to individual words and punctuation (see ). Statistics are derived from this division. Word refers to any token that is not punctuation or a symbol. Number tokens will also qualify as words. LemmaLoom recognizes unique words according to each word's dictionary form, or lemma; model and models count as one unique word, and so do was and were. These terms are known in linguistics literature as types, giving rise to the term type-token ratio. A syllable count represents a rough guess made solely based on the orthography of each word. Long words are defined by LemmaLoom as having more than six letters. Stopwords are words found in a predetermined list for each language; these refer to commonly used words such as the, of, and is. Words not found in this list are termed content words. Shares refer to the proportions expressed as percentages. Given 17 stopwords out of 30 total words, the resulting share will be $17 div 30 approx 0.57$, shown as 57%.

The examples throughout this chapter come from “Climate Debate”, the bundled example project of this guide; you can add the example project to your library with File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project (see The example project in ). See below for the Text tab of “Running Out of Time”, an activist op-ed with 910 words spread out over 65 sentences. There is only one column in the Overview facet. It starts from the top and includes five sections of measures (namely Overview, Readability, Lexical, Syntax, and Structure), followed by three bar charts (Parts of speech, Functions, and Phrases). The first section, titled Overview, contains simple counts related to the text, sharing its title with the facet. The Overview facet of the Text tab for “Running Out of Time”, showing its counts and readability scores. To open the Text tab: Open a document in the reader. If the inspector is hidden, choose View ▸ Toggle Inspector (⌃⌘I). Click the book icon at the top of the inspector, or choose View ▸ Inspector ▸ Text (⌥⌘1). Click Overview, Details, or Bookmarks in the row of facets below the icons. By default, your document shows its Text tab and Overview facet until you manually change it. Changes to your tabs and facets are remembered independently by each document whenever you switch document tabs. When viewing documents side-by-side in split view mode, the inspector will show the document in the currently active pane. Click the other pane to inspect the statistics of the other document, although whichever tab and facet had been selected previously will remain intact. Inspectors will remain closed during detail views and when viewing a set; separate inspectors will appear per individual document window. Statistics need an indexed document in order to display. If indexing isn’t complete yet for the first section of text, then you’ll see the placeholder Statistics become available when indexing completes.
