The Details facet does what it’s supposed to do regardless of whether or not there are statistics available yet. While indexing occurs, statistics relate strictly to the already processed portion. Document statistics work only with English, German, and Chinese documents; for other languages, the placeholder remains.

Every document in the “Climate Debate” example project comes with values for four attributes. Values for the “Stance” attribute denote whether the text came from activists, skeptics, or neutral sources. “Readership”, “Publication Date”, and “Outlet” denote the size of the audience, when the article was published, and where, respectively. In the Details facet on the “Running Out of Time” document, Attributes shows “Stance” as “Activist”, “Readership” as 412,000 readers, “Publication Date” as August 21, 2024, and “Outlet” as “The Northern Herald”. Below the Attributes section, under Tags, is the only tag for this document, “op-ed”. Attributes lists every existing attribute-value pair for the currently active document, providing editing fields for the attributes. It is a place for assigning and modifying attribute values for a single document as you browse through it. For setting attribute values for several documents simultaneously, please see Setting one value for many documents in . The Details facet for “Running Out of Time” after the “Outlet” attribute was removed, with Out typed in the new attribute field and “Outlet” suggested. When you need to set a value for an attribute not listed in the current list of attributes for a document: Type the attribute's name in the field below the list. LemmaLoom suggests names already in use in your projects, with their type, as in “Outlet” · Text. If the project has no attribute of that name, choose a Type. For a Picker, also type its choices, one per row. Click Add Attribute, or press Return. Enter the value in the new row. An attribute is listed only once in each document. If you attempt to add an attribute the document already lists, Add Attribute remains disabled, and its tooltip reads Already added. When clearing a value, click the remove button at the end of the value's row (Remove attribute). Tags are inputted via the field that reads Add a tag. Begin typing the desired tag and then press Return, or type a comma after a tag to move to the next one. Suggestions for existing tags appear while typing, and to delete a tag, click the × on it. All edits happen immediately and affect the document's translations too. Editing values or tags can both be undone using Edit ▸ Undo Set Value and Edit ▸ Undo Edit Tags (⌘Z); undoing an addition of an entirely new attribute happens via Edit ▸ Undo Add Attribute. For further reading about Entering values and Tagging a document, please refer to .

The list of measurements shown is determined based on the language of your document. The majority of them are common across English, German, and Chinese documents, though the readability formulas are different since most of the formulas were developed with only one language in mind. Section Measure English German Chinese Overview Sentences, Words, Unique words, Paragraphs, Characters yes yes yes Readability Avg. sentence length yes yes yes  Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Coleman-Liau, ARI yes    Flesch-Amstad, Wiener Sachtextformel  yes   LIX yes yes   Characters per sentence, Avg. word length (in characters), Particle density   yes Lexical Type-token ratio, MATTR, Lexical density, Hapax ratio, Stopword share yes yes yes  Avg. word length (in letters) yes yes  Syntax Mean dependency distance, Avg. tree depth, Clauses per sentence, Embedded clause share, Passive sentences yes yes yes Structure Dialogue share, Questions and exclamations, Sentences per paragraph yes yes yes In the Syntax section, only measures that were provided by the grammar analysis are listed. Where the grammatical structure of a document's sentences is unknown, this section does not appear. All values are rounded for presentation purposes. Counts and LIX are whole integers. The Type-token ratio, MATTR, and Mean dependency distance all have two decimal places. The Hapax ratio and shares are expressed as whole percentages. The rest have one decimal place. Many measures are accompanied by an ⓘ button next to their name. Click on it for a brief explanation of what the measure represents and the scale in which it operates; clicking elsewhere dismisses it. The description of Flesch Reading Ease, opened from its ⓘ button in the Readability section.

To export all statistics in a document to a single file: In the Overview facet, find the heading of the Overview section, at the top of the facet. Click the export button at the right of the heading (Export as CSV). Choose a name and a folder, and click Save. The name suggested is the document's title followed by -statistics, as in Running Out of Time-statistics.csv. The file has three columns called Section, Measure, and Value, and one row per measure displayed, plus one row per bar of each of the three charts. The value displays the same way as it does in the inspector (rounding and units included), as in 57% or 10.0 words. There is an export button on the right side of each chart's heading. This opens a menu containing options for export in PNG and PDF formats (with the chart's title), and CSV for category counts alone (in Category and Count columns). The default naming suggestion combines the document and chart titles together, for instance Running Out of Time-Parts of speech.png. Only one document can be viewed in the inspector at once. In order to consolidate statistical figures of several documents into spreadsheet form for comparative purposes, export each document into a separate file first, and then combine the files, removing the unit symbols and % signs before your calculations.

Each measure shown in the table above can function as a rule in a query. A query of this nature allows you to select particular documents that fit the rule, e.g., those that are more difficult to comprehend than plain English, or those containing an exceptionally large proportion of passive sentences. The following image shows a query of this sort within the “Climate Debate” project, seeking documents having a Flesch Reading Ease below 60 (the lower boundary of Flesch’s plain English range), yielding a single document called “Heat Wave Report 2024”. A query in “Climate Debate” that finds the documents whose Flesch Reading Ease is below 60. To query documents based on statistics: In the navigation sidebar, click Queries under Project. In Find, choose Library · Documents. In Where, click Add and choose Add Rule. Click the field, choose Statistic, and choose the measure, such as Flesch Reading Ease. Choose a comparison, such as is less than, and enter the number in Value. The following are some rules concerning statistic fields in queries: The Statistic field is only available in queries made on document sets, projects, and All Projects. While all statistics fields are provided in queries, the only statistic fields in a smart set are Tokens, Sentences, and Characters, which LemmaLoom tracks once a document has been indexed. Tokens counts punctuation marks too; hence, Tokens will be greater than Words. Please refer to Fields in  to know where each statistic field is provided. The comparison made in a query is against the unrounded number. For example, a score displayed as 86.7 may actually be 86.705; therefore, use comparisons such as is less than, is at least, or is between in place of is. Measures shown as percentages, Hapax ratio included, are represented as fractions between 0 and 1 in queries. When searching for documents where the Lexical density is at least 45 percent, the number to input should be 0.45. A rule skips documents that have no value for its measure. Measures such as Flesch Reading Ease are calculated for English documents only; thus, a rule like is less than 60 skips any non-English documents during evaluation. Documents currently being indexed are excluded from the evaluation until their statistics become available.

LemmaLoom calculates statistics on documents and stores them alongside the documents. Statistics on documents are used in the Text tab and the Statistic field in queries, which means that both will always show consistent statistics. Document statistics pertain to the entire document although only annotated sentences may be shown in the reader (see Showing only annotated sentences in ). LemmaLoom recalculates the statistics only when changes are made to the document's text or indexing configuration. Changes include editing and saving the document's text, altering the document's language settings, and changing the patterns that exclude text from indexing. Should the statistics not yet be calculated when you visit the Text tab, a spinner icon will appear momentarily until LemmaLoom finishes processing. Statistics for a translation document, e.g., “Running Out of Time (German)”, will be unique to the translation document and be based on calculations using the measures of its own language.

The Overview section lists five: Measure What it counts Sentences Sentences, as indexing divides the text Words Words, without punctuation and symbols Unique words Different lemmas among the words Paragraphs Paragraphs, divided at blank lines or line breaks Characters Every character of the text, including spaces, line breaks, and punctuation

Words refer to indexing tokens without punctuation marks and special characters, according to whatever indexing sees as constituting a token in the language of interest. In English, for instance, indexing splits contractions (don’t = do + n’t), and hyphenated words get split at the hyphen punctuation mark (eighty-four = eighty + four). Since Chinese text contains no word separations in the written form, indexing decides where a word stops and the next starts for counting purposes. Unique words ignores the capitalization of words, thus making The (capitalized at the beginning of sentences) and the (in the middle of a sentence) equal to each other as a unique word. Text excluded from indexing, such as timestamps in a transcript, counts only under Characters and, when it forms a paragraph of its own, under Paragraphs (see Text excluded from analysis in ). The word count on the far-right side of the reader's status bar includes punctuation marks, making it higher than the count for Words in the inspector, which does not count punctuation marks. Queries which count per 10,000 words base their count on the inspector instead.

Sentence boundaries are usually indicated by periods, question marks, and exclamation marks in written texts. In transcripts, sentence boundaries occur anywhere such punctuation is inserted during transcription. Paragraph breaks are based on the line breaks in your text. If there is a blank line found anywhere in your text, then blank lines function as paragraph breaks, whereas adjacent lines with a line break separating them form a single paragraph. Otherwise, a line break always results in a new paragraph beginning. Blank lines refer to lines containing nothing but whitespace. Transcripts produced by LemmaLoom automatically insert paragraph breaks if there is any change in speaker identity or any pause lasting more than one and a half seconds.

A letter count counts each alphabetic letter in the text, including any Chinese characters. Digits, punctuation marks, and apostrophes do not count toward the letter count measurement. Among all readability formulas, ARI is the only formula that takes into account letters and digits together. The estimation of syllable count relies on counting consecutive vowel clusters within a word, where vowels include the five letters a, e, i, o, and u, plus the letter y in English and German, and the umlauts ä, ö, and ü in German. Consider heat (ea), again (a and ai), and families (a, i, and ie). When estimating English syllable count, a final e after other vowel clusters is considered silent, except for words ending in le. As a result, words such as wave and were are estimated with one syllable while people has two syllables. Each word must contain at least one syllable; therefore even 2050, which has no vowels, has one syllable. Words like warned, which is estimated with two syllables due to its -ed suffix, or science, which is estimated as one syllable, not two, are examples of error cases. Words with consecutive a, y, and o vowels such as mayor, estimated at one syllable, are another error case. In German, the word Familien is incorrectly counted with three syllables due to the presence of the cluster ie. Such errors may partly cancel out in practice when calculating overall scores for whole documents.

The following sections provide examples. These use a made-up passage similar to what you might encounter in activist literature. The passage below is treated as a complete document. We were hit by the heat again this summer. So the schools shut for a week and nobody could sleep. The families felt that our mayor had already given up. Below are its counts: Sentence Words Syllables Letters Long words Words of 3+ syllables Words of 1 syllable We were hit by the heat again this summer. 9 11 33 0 0 7 So the schools shut for a week and nobody could sleep. 11 13 43 1 1 10 The families felt that our mayor had already given up. 10 15 44 2 2 7 Whole passage 30 39 120 3 3 24 The long words are schools, families, and already. The trisyllabic words are nobody, families, and already. Syllable counts use the estimate of 1 syllable for mayor (which actually has 2 syllables). No digits are used, so the letter count plus digit count comes out to 120. Because the repeats three times, the number of unique words is 28.

Readability formulas calculate the ease of readability of a text based on just two metrics (sentences' lengths and words' lengths), which are relatively straightforward measures to extract objectively from text. Sentence length correlates directly with higher demand on working memory capacity, so longer sentences are harder. The longer words are, the rarer and more abstract they will likely be too. The relationship between the two lengths and the comprehension levels of test subjects (e.g., children at school) was found during studies where test texts were presented to individuals and their comprehension ability assessed. The seemingly bizarre and precise constant factors such as 206.835 come from fitting a mathematical function to these observations. In a study, you could use readability scores to compare the texts of any media organization to others', or even assess which side of an argument uses simpler or more complicated linguistic structures than the other. Grade levels provided by certain formulas describe the necessary schooling years to be able to comprehend the given text adequately without significant effort or confusion. When grades are given without specifying another school system, assume them to belong to the American educational system, where grade 8 equates roughly to age 13 or 14. Even a sentence composed fully of shorter words can still be hard to understand, and familiar and understandable technical vocabulary still counts by its length in these formulas regardless of the actual understanding of a term. Notation for readability formula symbols: Symbol Meaning In the example passage $W$ Words 30 $S$ Sentences 3 $Y$ Syllables 39 $L$ Letters 120 $C$ Letters and digits 120 $P$ Words of three or more syllables 3 $G$ Long words, of more than six letters 3 $M$ Words of one syllable 24 There are two measures that recur. $W/S$ refers to the mean number of words per sentence; here, $W/S$ = 30 ÷ 3 = 10. $Y/W$ represents the mean number of syllables per word; here, $Y/W$ = 39 ÷ 30 = 1.3.

Avg. sentence length is the average number of words per sentence and is calculated by $W/S$. This measure is provided for all three languages, for instance an average of 10.0 words per sentence for the sample. Most of the scoring metrics introduced below rely on this statistic; hence, it explains a great deal of their behavior. Breaking a long sentence into two makes every score show easier reading.

The Flesch Reading Ease, developed by Rudolf Flesch, is a rating system for English texts based on average sentence length and average number of syllables per word in your text. Its values usually fall between 0 and 100, where higher numbers signify easier-to-read texts. The equation looks like this: $W$, $S$, and $Y$ are your text's metrics from the table above. In effect, your starting score is quite high; however, the formula deducts points for having long sentences and words that contain lots of syllables. The syllables weigh far more than sentence length; every additional 0.1 syllables per word in your average costs you around 8.5 points, roughly equal to 8 more words in your average sentence length. In this example case: The inspector shows 86.7. Rudolf Flesch described his scores as ranges: Score Description 90–100 Very easy 80–90 Easy 70–80 Fairly easy 60–70 Standard; plain English 50–60 Fairly difficult 30–50 Difficult 0–30 Very difficult The score here is 86.7, meaning that the passage is easy. That is what you'd expect, since the sentences tend to be brief, comprising mostly one-syllable words. The score for “Running Out of Time” (shown earlier in this chapter) is 73.3, meaning it is fairly easy to comprehend. Very long sentences could cause scores less than 0, while very short words could give scores higher than 100.

The Flesch-Kincaid Grade index, developed for instructional manuals used by the U.S. Navy, uses the same two metrics as Flesch Reading Ease but converts them into grade levels within the U.S. educational system. Plugging the numbers in gives: Rounded up to the nearest tenth, 3.7 corresponds to the grade level where third and fourth graders understand a passage. As both the Flesch-Kincaid Grade formula and Flesch Reading Ease score depend on the same metrics, a high score in one measure typically means a low score in the other.

Robert Gunning’s Fog Index tries to measure what educational grade level will be necessary to understand your document based on its sentence length and word difficulty. According to Gunning, hard words include any word which has three or more syllables, excluding compound words whose components were common, names, and any word which reaches three syllables only through suffixes such as -ed. $H$ is the number of hard words; LemmaLoom excludes only names, meaning words that indexing tags as proper nouns, such as Larkhaven. The multiplication factor of 100 turns the ratio of hard words into a percentage. In the sample passage, there are three hard words (nobody, families, and already), along with no names whatsoever. Calculating this results in: A Fog Index of 8 suggests around 8 years' worth of schooling needed, while 12 corresponds to the last year of high school in the United States. Since the second portion of the equation considers exclusively words having three or more syllables, a few such words have considerable influence on the outcome.

The SMOG grade (Simple Measure of Gobbledygook) was created by G. Harry McLaughlin. This readability measure involves counting words with three or more syllables, which McLaughlin did within a sample size of 30 sentences. In LemmaLoom, this calculation takes place over the entire document, normalizing the results to 30 sentences. Here, $P$ denotes the number of words of three or more syllables. The square root causes the grade to increase ever more slowly with an increasing number of such words. For example, the sample passage above has $P = 3$ words with three or more syllables in 3 sentences. If scaled up to 30 sentences, that makes for $3 times 30 div 3 = 30$: The SMOG grade index measures the grade level at which people understand a piece of writing completely. As a result, the number should generally be larger than the Flesch-Kincaid Grade (8.8 vs. 3.7) of the same passage. Words with three or more syllables carry much weight in shorter pieces of writing, leading to the large outcome for this passage.

The Coleman-Liau index differs from the readability indices above because it predicts grades based on letter counts rather than syllable counts. Being computer-friendly was essential to its creation, so instead of estimating the number of syllables, which may produce errors, it counts the exact number of letters. In the formula, $100,L/W$ refers to letters per hundred words while $100,S/W$ refers to sentences per hundred words. More letters per word increase the grade prediction, while more sentences per hundred words (shorter sentences) decrease it. Consider the example passage, whose 120 letters and 3 sentences make 400 letters and 10 sentences per 100 words: The predicted grade level falls somewhere between school years four and five.

Similar to Coleman-Liau, the Automated Readability Index calculates the equivalent American school grade level without syllables, based on characters per word. Characters here consist of letters and digits (variable $C$ in the table above). If $C/W = 120 div 30 = 4$ and $W/S = 10$, then: Since ARI includes digit counts in its calculations whereas Coleman-Liau ignores these, a document containing a lot of digits like “Heat Wave Report 2024” receives a relatively higher grade on ARI compared to Coleman-Liau.

The Readability Index (Läsbarhetsindex) of Carl-Hugo Björnsson, or LIX for short, is the sum of the average sentence length and the percentage of long words within a passage. This measure is offered for English and German passages. Its mathematical expression is as follows: In the above formula, $G$ is equal to the total number of long words within the passage. With 3 long words out of the 30 words in the example passage: Its range lies roughly from 20 (very easy) to 60 (very difficult), and 40 (medium difficulty) for the average case. For the example passage, since it is scored as 20, it is considered very easy. Because LIX measures long words based on letter counts rather than syllable counts, the exact same algorithm applies for calculating LIX regardless of the language. Comparing LIX values across languages, however, is impossible. Partly because German writes compound nouns as one word (like Hitzewelle for heat wave), a German translation of any given text tends to score higher than its English equivalent. As an example, the “Climate Debate” project contains a document called “Running Out of Time”, scoring 32, while its German counterpart is scored as 43. The German version of the example passage (below) has nine long words and scores $10 + 100 times 9 div 30 = 10 + 30 = 40$.

Toni Amstad extended the Flesch Reading Ease scale to German texts, in which words tend to have a greater number of syllables. Similar to the Flesch Reading Ease formula, results generally range between 0 and 100, wherein larger numbers indicate greater readability. The German examples use this German adaptation of the excerpt: Auch in diesem Sommer hat uns die Hitze wieder getroffen. Die Schulen blieben eine Woche zu, und niemand konnte schlafen. Die Familien glaubten, dass unser Bürgermeister schon längst aufgegeben hatte. Count Value Words $W$ 30 Sentences $S$ 3 Syllables $Y$ 54 Letters $L$ 166 Words of three or more syllables $P$ 4 (getroffen, Familien, Bürgermeister, aufgegeben) Long words $G$ 9 (getroffen, Schulen, blieben, niemand, schlafen, Familien, glaubten, Bürgermeister, aufgegeben) Words of one syllable $M$ 12 The syllable estimate counts Familien as three syllables even though it has four. Now, with $Y/W = 54 div 30 = 1.8$: As per Flesch's table, whose bands apply here as well, the German version in question is of standard difficulty. Comparing this number with that of the English version from before, 86.7, says nothing about which is easier to read, since the two equations were fitted to different languages. The figure below illustrates the German translation of “Running Out of Time” within the “Climate Debate” project. It has a score of 61.1 in Flesch-Amstad and 7.3 in the Wiener Sachtextformel. The Overview and Readability sections for “Running Out of Time (German)”, with the German readability measures.

The Wiener Sachtextformel (Vienna formula for non-fiction) was invented by Richard Bamberger and Erich Vanecek for German-language texts. The formula approximates the grade level of a text in the German-speaking education systems, on a scale ranging roughly from 4 (easy) to 15 (very difficult). The version implemented in LemmaLoom is the first of several iterations of the formula, taking into account four measures (the percentage of words of three or more syllables, average sentence length, percentage of long words, and percentage of monosyllabic words) as follows: For the German-language passage provided above, the percentages calculated according to the order specified by the formula are $100 times 4 div 30 approx 13.333$, $100 times 9 div 30 = 30$, and $100 times 12 div 30 = 40$, respectively. The fourth component is subtracted because many one-syllable words make a text easier. Substituting gives: This results in: Thus, rounded to one decimal place, the final score is around 6.0, placing it near the lower end of the scale, so the passage counts as easy.

The formulas above measure readability in relation to syllables or letters in the case of alphabetic languages. Since the metrics don't work for Chinese texts, the Readability section of a Chinese document provides three alternatives below Avg. sentence length: Characters per sentence measures the ratio between the count of Chinese characters and sentences in your text. Non-Chinese alphabet letters also count here. Furthermore, numbers written in characters will contribute toward character count; for example, 十二 equals two characters. However, numbers written using Arabic numerals such as 12 aren't considered Chinese characters. As usual, punctuation doesn't increase character count either. Avg. word length is measured in characters. This metric calculates character count divided by word count. Documents containing many two-character words such as 气候 or 邻居 receive higher scores compared to ones where single-character words are common. Particle density measures how many particles occur in every hundred words. Particles include words that are annotated with the Particles lens, which are verbal 了, 着, and 过 particles; 的, 地, and 得; and classifiers such as 个 (see Constructions and Particles (Chinese) in ). Sentence-ending particles such as 吗, 呢, and 吧 aren't counted. For these two sentences, indexing splits the words as follows: 我们 / 等 / 了 / 十二 / 个 / 小时 。 邻居 / 也 / 非常 / 担心 。 This results in ten words having sixteen characters distributed within two sentences. Two particles occur, namely 了 and the classifier 个. Thus, Characters per sentence comes to $16 div 2 = 8.0$, Avg. word length equals $16 div 10 = 1.6$ characters, and Particle density reaches $100 times 2 div 10 = 20.0$ particles per hundred words. The metrics for Chinese don't map onto any grade levels. Instead, the three serve only to compare one Chinese document with another; on its own, a higher Particle density says nothing about how hard the text is.

Using these formulas on the 30-word example passage in English yields the following results: Measure Score Kind of scale Flesch Reading Ease 86.7 Ease, 0 to 100 Flesch-Kincaid Grade 3.7 US school grade Gunning Fog 8.0 Years of schooling SMOG 8.8 US school grade Coleman-Liau 4.8 US school grade ARI 2.4 US school grade LIX 20 Difficulty, about 20 to 60 Estimates of schooling for the same excerpt via the five formulas range from 2.4 to 8.8. The difference in numbers comes from the weighting assigned to each feature within a particular formula. This excerpt has several words with three or more syllables in relatively short sentences, leading to high Gunning Fog and SMOG scores but little impact on ARI. The variance among formulas decreases in lengthier documents, but it never disappears entirely. Estimates for the document “Running Out of Time” with the five formulas range from 6.1 to 9.5.

The Lexical section deals with the words in your document. Through these measures, you get insights regarding whether your document tends to rely heavily on recurring vocabulary or has a varied vocabulary. The type-token ratio, for instance, will inform you about how many unique lemmas were used relative to the total number of words in your text. In it, as in MATTR and the hapax ratio, different forms of a lemma will still be counted as one.

The type-token ratio calculates vocabulary diversity as the number of unique words over the total number of words: Here $V$ represents the number of unique words and $W$ represents the number of words. If the ratio equals 1, then each word appears exactly once; thus, the fewer times a word repeats itself in the document, the closer to 1 the ratio gets. The example passage repeats only the, which occurs 3 times altogether, making $V = 28$ and the type-token ratio $28 div 30 approx 0.93$. If a report of 4,000 words had 800 unique words, its ratio would be $800 div 4{,}000 = 0.20$. A lower ratio doesn't necessarily imply a worse vocabulary. The ratio will always fall with longer documents since common words keep repeating and new words occur increasingly less frequently.

MATTR, or moving-average type-token ratio, quantifies lexical diversity irrespective of the size of the document. In LemmaLoom, MATTR begins with finding the type-token ratio in a sliding window of the first hundred words of a text, shifting one word along, finding the type-token ratio for words 2 to 101, and so on up until the very end. MATTR is therefore the mean of those ratios. Here, $u_1$, $u_2$, etc. represent the number of unique words found within each window of 100 words sequentially across the document; $n$ equals the total number of windows, or, equivalently, the number of words less 99. Dividing each $u$ by 100 yields the respective ratio per window; summing and dividing by $n$ gives you the mean. For a smaller-scale illustration, imagine a window of 4 words instead of 100, and consider these eight words, we warn and we wait and we warn. The five windows are thus: Window Unique words Ratio we warn and we 3 0.75 warn and we wait 4 1.00 and we wait and 3 0.75 we wait and we 3 0.75 wait and we warn 4 1.00 Here, the mean is $(3 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4) div (4 times 5) = 17 div 20 = 0.85$. The type-token ratio of the eight words, with 4 unique words, is only $4 div 8 = 0.50$. In a document with 100 words or fewer, the MATTR formula simplifies to being equal to the type-token ratio.

The word hapax, Greek for “once”, denotes any word appearing exactly once in your document. The hapax ratio is the proportion of unique words that are hapaxes: Here $V_1$ is the number of unique words occurring exactly once, while $V$ is the number of unique words in total. Sometimes $V_1$ is divided by the number of words instead, which yields a smaller figure. With the example passage, out of the 28 unique words, 27 appear exactly once for a ratio of $27 div 28 approx 0.96$, shown as 96%. In the hypothetical 4,000-word document containing 800 unique words with 400 hapaxes, the ratio would equal 50%. A high hapax ratio tends to show that many words appear in passing, including proper nouns. As is the case with the type-token ratio, the hapax ratio depends upon length; with a short document most words occur exactly once.

Stopword share is the proportion of words in a document that are in the list of stopwords for that document's language. Conversely, Lexical density is the proportion of words in a document that are not stopwords; thus, both proportions add up to 100 percent. Consider the example passage, for instance, which consists of thirty words. There are seventeen stopwords here, namely we, were, by, the, again, and this in the first sentence; so, the, for, a, and, and could in the second; and the, that, our, had, and up in the third. The stopword share of this passage would then be $17 div 30 approx 57%$, whereas the lexical density is $13 div 30 approx 43%$. Natural speech tends to have less lexical density than edited writing does, due to pronouns and auxiliaries. Finding that the stopword proportion in a transcription is low compared to natural speech can be a sign that the transcript was summarized rather than transcribed word for word. Lists of stopwords come built in, and they are fixed per language: The list of English stopwords contains around 160 words including articles, pronouns, prepositions, and conjunctions; conjugations of be, have, and do; modal verbs like can, should, must, and the rest; negative not and no; and common adverbs like very, also, and again. The list of German stopwords contains roughly 210 words, including, besides articles, pronouns, prepositions, and auxiliaries, the modal particles ja, doch, mal, eben, and halt. The list of Chinese stopwords contains about 150 words, among them 的, 了, and 是; pronouns; 不 and 没有; and common prepositions and adverbs. A word qualifies as a stopword if it matches the list in terms of its lemma or token form. Content words that can appear to be function words include nobody in the example passage. The query field Stopword uses the same lists. The measure of lexical density that linguists usually take depends on parts of speech, considering only nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs to be content words. LemmaLoom's measure of lexical density uses its stopword list. It is therefore not directly comparable to figures based on parts of speech.

Avg. word length in the Lexical section is the ratio of letters to words, $L/W$, represented in letters. The example passage has $120 div 30 = 4.0$ letters per word, while the German translation has $166 div 30 approx 5.5$. Since numbers contain no letters, texts with lots of numbers will have a slightly lower Avg. word length than those that don't. In the case of Chinese texts, the metric appears under Readability, expressed in characters.

The Syntax section analyzes your sentences for how they are constructed beyond measuring sentence lengths. Measures include looking into the distance between words related to each other, nesting of clauses inside other clauses, and other similar measures that reveal the complexity of the sentence structure. They rely upon two parts of the grammar analysis. The dependency analysis refers to analyzing the relationship between words within a sentence in terms of the head word on which each word depends. In a fair share, for instance, fair and a depend upon share. Each sentence has one root word, which does not depend upon any word (generally the main verb in a sentence). The links between words and their heads are displayed graphically via the inspector under the Grammar tab (see ). The phrase analysis groups the words of a sentence into phrases and clauses nested inside one another.

Dependency distance measures the distance between a word and its head measured in terms of positions in the sentence. Mean dependency distance is calculated by taking the average of dependency distances for every word within a document having a head: Here, $d_1$ to $d_k$ refer to individual dependency distances, while $k$ denotes the number of words having heads, that is, every word except the root of each sentence. Punctuation occupies positions, yet does not contribute toward the total dependency distances. The word pay functions as the root verb in the sentence The richest countries rarely pay a fair share. Word numbers indicate positional order, beginning with 1. Words along with their heads appear below: Word Position Head Head's position Distance The 1 countries 3 2 richest 2 countries 3 1 countries 3 pay 5 2 rarely 4 pay 5 1 a 6 share 8 2 fair 7 share 8 1 share 8 pay 5 3 The sum total of these 7 dependency distances is 12. Thus, the mean dependency distance of this sentence is $12 div 7 approx 1.71$. Dependency distances are high when there is significant separation between the related words. In research on sentence processing, higher dependency distances correlate with increased processing done by the reader. Lengthier sentences, embedded clauses, and verb-final construction of German clauses contribute to higher scores here. Mean dependency distance has no universal scale; it only holds significance when compared with other documents in the same language.

For every word, the path upwards through its heads to the hierarchy’s root defines its depth. The number of hops needed is equivalent to the depth of the word. Depth for a sentence is calculated by finding the highest depth value among all of its words. Avg. tree depth is merely the average depth of sentences in a document. In the sentence above, the words countries, rarely, and share link directly to the root, meaning they only take 1 hop (depth = 1). The words the, richest, a, and fair all need 2 hops before reaching the root; therefore, the depth of this sentence is 2. For instance, consider another document containing sentences with depths of 2, 4, and 6. Then the average tree depth is $(2 + 4 + 6) div 3 = 4.0$.

t: Clauses per sentence and embedded clauses
b: Clauses per sentence calculates how many clauses, according to the phrase analysis, occur per sentence on average. This measure calculates $K/S$, where $K$ is the total number of clauses in your document, while $S$ is the total number of sentences in your document. Embedded clause share calculates what share of your document’s clauses are not main clauses. Every sentence with at least one clause is considered to have exactly one main clause. As such, this measure divides $K - S_K$ by $K$, where $S_K$ is the number of sentences having at least one clause. The combination of these measures allows you to gauge the degree to which a writer embeds one idea within another rather than setting them side by side. Formally, Clauses per sentence is $K/S$, while Embedded clause share is The count follows the phrase analysis closely. For instance, an English subordinate clause because the heat was dangerous counts as two layers. It includes its inner clause the heat was dangerous. As a consequence, the sentence We stayed inside because the heat was dangerous. has three clauses in total (the whole sentence, the because clause, and the clause inside it). On the other hand, the sentence Nobody complained. has just one. Consider the calculation for a document consisting of those two sentences: Clauses per sentence equals $4 div 2 = 2.0$. Embedded clause share equals $(4 - 2) div 4 = 0.5$, or 50%. Because of the layering, the values come out higher than a school grammar's count of clauses.

Passive sentences refers to the proportion of sentences within your document that have one or more occurrences of passive constructions. Multiple occurrences of passives in a single sentence will not change the count. For instance, in a document with 40 sentences in total, and six of those having passives, the proportion becomes $6 div 40 = 15%$. What counts as a passive depends on the language: In English, the grammar analysis detects the subject and auxiliary verb in a passive sentence; one example is this from “Heat Wave Report 2024”, This report was prepared by the agency's climate monitoring service. For Chinese, any occurrence of a sentence with 被 and other recognized passive constructions will be included, as with the 被 passive aspect of the Constructions lens. In German, a passive with werden and a past participle counts whether or not the agent is named, as in Dieser Bericht wurde erstellt and Dieser Bericht wurde von der Klimaüberwachung des Amtes erstellt. A passive with sein counts only when a von or durch phrase names the agent, as with the Passive voice device of the Rhetoric lens. Occasionally, passives omit information on who performed an action. In “Heat Wave Report 2024”, for instance, responsibility for checking on older people living alone was not clearly assigned.

The Structure section contains three metrics. Dialogue share calculates what percentage of words occur between double quotation marks. Consider, for instance, the artificial sentence My neighbor always said, “Our summers are mild.” Four out of eight words occur in quotations here, making a dialogue share of 50%. In news reports, such as “Carbon Tax Debate”, quotation marks are used to highlight direct quotations from speakers, and the share shows how much of the text overall is other people's words. LemmaLoom pairs the quotation marks to estimate the share: Straight quotation marks (") open and close sequentially. Curly quotation marks open with “ and close with ”. In German documents, „ opens and “ closes. « and the Chinese corner brackets 「 and 『 open, and », 」, and 』 close. In German documents, » opens and « closes. Single quotation marks are ignored. An unpaired quotation mark causes all subsequent words to count as quoted. A surprisingly high value often suggests there may be a rogue quotation mark somewhere in the document. Questions and exclamations calculates the percentage of sentences ending with a question mark or an exclamation mark. It includes the full-width characters in Chinese texts. Note that only sentences whose final token is either an exclamation or question mark qualify; sentences ending with a closing quotation mark after the question mark are excluded. In a document containing 80 sentences, among which there are 18 questions and 2 exclamations, Questions and exclamations amounts to $20 div 80 = 25%$. A high value in opinion pieces and speeches may suggest the presence of rhetorical questions, such as the one bookmarked in “Running Out of Time”. As usual, the statistics pertain to the document's entirety, including the host's questions in a transcript such as “Radio Debate”. Finally, Sentences per paragraph is obtained by dividing the total number of sentences by the number of paragraphs. For example, 120 sentences spread over 40 paragraphs produce a ratio of 3.0 sentences per paragraph. Transcription with LemmaLoom produces transcripts with paragraphs ending at every change of speaker and at substantial pauses; hence, the metric provides a rough idea of how many sentences speakers utter continuously.

t: Parts of speech, functions, and phrases
b: Below the measures, three bar charts show word and phrase distribution across categories in your selected document. Each row includes the category name, a bar, and a number that represents how many times the category was used in the selected document. Note that these statistics do not contain unused categories; the bars use the standard colors of the matching lens, even when other colors were chosen in the Lenses pane of Settings. Parts of speech shows word count statistics in the ten classes of the Word class lens from Noun to Interjection (see Word class in ). Note that all other types of words, including foreign words, are excluded from this statistic. Functions represents word count statistics in each of the ten functions in the Grammatical function lens, ranging from Subject to Connector (see Grammatical function in ). Note that the root words without a function (typically the main verb) in each sentence are ignored, as well as words where the relationship does not fit into the ten types of grammatical functions, so these statistics' totals will be lower than the total number of words in the document. Phrases shows the phrase count for each kind of phrase in the Phrase lens from Noun phrase to Interjection (see Phrase in ). Note that nested phrases each count, e.g., in our valley would count as a prepositional phrase and our valley would be counted once more in the noun phrase category, while clauses are tracked separately under Syntax. In the “Climate Debate” sample project, “Heat Wave Report 2024” is heavily focused on nouns and prepositions but uses very few pronouns compared to the op-eds or “Radio Debate”. The figure below illustrates the Parts of speech and Functions charts of the “Running Out of Time” document. The Parts of speech and Functions charts for “Running Out of Time”, with the export menu of Parts of speech open. To see what words comprise each bar, turn on the matching lens in the reader.

The Bookmarks facet displays the document's bookmarks ordered by position in the document. In “Climate Debate”, for instance, “Running Out of Time” has 1 bookmark located in its final paragraph, specifically at the question What exactly are we waiting for? with the comment “Rhetorical question at the turn to the closing appeal”. The heading displays how many bookmarks are associated with the document, which is why the heading is Bookmarks (1) in this case. For instructions on bookmarking, refer to Bookmarks in . The Bookmarks facet for “Running Out of Time”, with its one bookmark at the question in the last paragraph. Each row lists: a bookmark icon in the color of the bookmark, or gray if it has No color; the comment of the bookmark, or, if there isn't a comment, the bookmarked text itself up to three lines long; and the location of the bookmark, like ¶10·5 for the fifth sentence of the tenth paragraph. Hovering the mouse pointer over this location will reveal it in full, as in Paragraph 10, sentence 5. Clicking on a row navigates to the bookmark. Should only annotated sentences appear in the reader and not the selected bookmark, everything else in the document gets displayed before navigating to the bookmark. Above the list is the Search field. Typing anything in this field filters the list to the bookmarks whose comments or text contain what you typed; case sensitivity doesn't play a role here. Nonetheless, the number in the heading counts all the bookmarks regardless of this action. The Edit Bookmark dialog for the bookmark at the question What exactly are we waiting for? in “Running Out of Time”. To change a bookmark's comment or color: Right-click its row and choose Edit. In the Edit Bookmark dialog, which shows the bookmarked passage, change Comment (optional) or Color. Click Save. To remove a bookmark, right-click the row associated with it and select Delete. Alternatively, click Delete at the bottom of the Edit Bookmark dialog. Your changes are immediate; use Edit ▸ Undo Remove Bookmark (⌘Z) to restore a deleted bookmark. Edit ▸ Undo Edit Bookmark (⌘Z) will undo an edit action performed on a bookmark. If there were translations available for the document where you marked a bookmark, then that bookmark exists in every translation. It is linked to the matching passage in each translation; edits and deletions of bookmarks happen across all of them. When creating bookmarks based on hits in a query (Bookmark Hits…), the resulting bookmarks will show up here just as regular bookmarks do (see Bookmark Hits in ). Bookmarks can be exported by clicking the export button at the right of the heading (Export as CSV). The exported file includes three columns (Location, Text, and Comment) containing all of the bookmarks currently listed, which means that only matched bookmarks would be included following a search operation. The filename suggestion is the document's title followed by -bookmarks.

Grammar analysis is shown in the Grammar tab of the inspector, which contains all grammar analysis results from your active document. The tab is broken up into seven facets. Most of these facets are concerned with grammatical features of the word or sentence you selected; two are concerned with the entire document. Use this tab to inspect your passage's structure before proceeding with counting, querying, or coding. Everything shown in this tab derives from LemmaLoom's automatic grammar analysis during indexing of your document (see ). The grammar analysis does occasionally contain errors, especially when analyzing transcripts of speech. When in doubt, it's best to consult the actual passage itself.

Facets use the following terminology from the grammar analysis: Token refers to the unit of grammar analysis; hence couldn't becomes two tokens, namely could and n't, and the period at the end of a sentence is a token of its own. Tokens can refer to both words and punctuation. Each word has a dictionary form known as a lemma. For example, leaders has the lemma leader, and was the lemma be. The part of speech of a word denotes its broad classification into categories like noun and verb. Tags are finer categories; the English tag NNS is short for plural noun, for instance. Tags derive from tag sets particular to languages. Each word in a sentence is dependent on one other word; that word is called its head. Thus, the and hottest are both dependent on day in the phrase the hottest day, making the latter their head. Only one word depends on nothing; usually, this would be the main verb. Such a word is the sentence's root. Dependencies specify how a word relates to its head using relations labeled with codes, including nsubj (nominal subject) and amod (adjectival modifier). LemmaLoom categorizes numerous relations into ten distinct functions, such as Subject, Object, and Adverbial. These are the aspects of the Grammatical function lens. Please see the description under Grammatical function in  for additional detail. An adverbial indicates when, where, how, or why something happens, like the phrases this summer and in our valley. A phrase denotes a series of words belonging to each other. Examples are noun phrases such as a warmer world and prepositional phrases like on a podium. Phrases are nested within other phrases up until the whole sentence itself. Common labels include NP (noun phrase), PP (prepositional phrase), VP (verb phrase), and others. A clause is a group of words whose core is its own verb; an example would be because her apartment had turned into an oven. One can find multiple clauses within sentences. Should you ever need clarification of the code meanings, Help ▸ Glossary lists all tags, relations, and phrase labels per language. See sections labeled Part-of-speech tags, Dependency relations, and Phrase labels respectively.

The facets display themselves as a series of buttons underneath the inspector's tab icons. Facet Works on What it shows Grammar The selected word Its lemma, word class, tag, function, head, and grammatical features, and its other uses in the document Sentence The selected sentence Its number, its pattern (English only), its length, its root, and its phrases Structure The selected sentence Three diagrams, showing the parts of the main clause, the links between words, and the phrases Form × Function The whole document How often each kind of phrase does each grammatical job Collocates The selected word, across the document The words that occur near it unusually often Word Sketch The selected word, across the document Its grammatical partners, grouped by relation Discourse The whole document How sentences tie back to earlier ones, the words writers use to comment on their own text, and rhetorical devices The selected sentence is the one containing the clicked word or the starting sentence of the selected passage. Until you select something, Grammar and Collocates display Select a Word. Similarly, Sentence and Structure display Select a Sentence. Word Sketch displays Sketch a Word. The Word Sketch facet sketches the word you select in the reader. To generate another word sketch, type the desired word into the Word field and press Return. The back and forward buttons will navigate you to previous word sketches generated. Map, List, and Web decide the format in which the word sketch is represented. The export button saves the generated word sketch. Finally, Open in a window opens the generated sketch in the Word Sketch window. See  for more details. The Word Sketch facet for climate in “Running Out of Time”, shown as a map.

Each document in “Climate Debate” has already been indexed (refer to The example project in ). As such, you can analyze its grammar immediately. Most of the examples provided here come from the opinion piece titled “Running Out of Time”. Your own document receives its grammar upon completion of indexing. Until that time comes, the tab shows Grammar becomes available when indexing completes. Here's how you examine a document's grammar: Open the document in the reader. Choose View ▸ Inspector ▸ Grammar (⌥⌘2), or click the second icon along the top of the inspector, a line of spaced words. The menu command also shows the inspector if it is hidden. Click a facet. Click a word in the reader, or select a passage. Facets follow selections made in the reader. Selecting a word, phrase, or sentence within a facet will also select that word, phrase, or sentence in the reader and scroll it into view. Each document remembers the facet you last chose. In split view, the inspector describes the document in the active pane, and when you click into the other pane, it shows that document's grammar in the same facet (see ).

Documents can be indexed in English, German, and Chinese. If you add a document in another language, the Grammar tab always shows Grammar becomes available when indexing completes. A translation document gets indexed in its own language, which explains why “Running Out of Time (German)” gets German grammar. The facets work in each language, with minor variations. Sentence shows the sentence pattern only in English documents. In Discourse, German documents feature an additional category under Metadiscourse called Modal particle, while Chinese documents have Final particle under Metadiscourse and Zero anaphora under Cohesion. Two Rhetoric devices are searched for only in certain languages (see Rhetoric later in this chapter). There are separate tag sets for each language, with the facets using the respective tags of the language's tag set. English documents use Penn Treebank tags (such as NNS and VBD), German uses Stuttgart-Tübingen tags (NN and VVFIN), and Chinese uses Penn Chinese Treebank tags (NN and VV). Word classes, functions, and phrase types remain constant across languages, so their colors mean the same everywhere.

The Grammar facet covers a single word. It describes what the word is, its function in a sentence, the word it depends on, and where else it occurs in the document. This facet comes in handy to verify how LemmaLoom parses the words before creating a query about them, for example. The figure displays the Grammar facet of leaders in the sentence Our leaders have answered the warnings with dates. from the document “Running Out of Time”. The Grammar facet describing the word leaders in “Running Out of Time”. From the top, the following items are shown: The word as it appears in the text, along with the word class, in this case Noun, colored according to the Word class lens. Lemma, which, in this case, is leader. This row appears only when the lemma does not match the word. Part of speech, which, in this case, displays Noun · NOUN, showing both the name and its corresponding code from the universal scheme used by all three languages. Tag, in this case, displays Noun, plural · NNS. Tag represents the word's fine-grained tag from the tag set of the language. FUNCTION displays the relationship between the current word and its head, as Nominal subject · nsubj, including its grammatical function, Subject, which is displayed in that function's color. The line beneath it rephrases the relationship as Subject of “answered” (a verb). More details about functions, including all ten of them, are discussed in Grammatical function in . For warnings in the current sentence, the line will say Object of “answered” (a verb). For Our, it says Modifies “leaders” (a noun); doing an adjective's job. A relation that fits none of the ten functions, such as the period's punct, has no colored function; the line beneath it reads Punctuation of “answered” (a verb). HEAD provides access to the word's head, displaying the head word, answered, as a link, followed by its part of speech. It lets you climb up a sentence toward its root. Clicking on answered makes the facet describe the word answered, whose FUNCTION row reads Root of the sentence · ROOT, indicating that this is a root word. The HEAD row reads Root of the sentence, and the line under FUNCTION reads The root of this sentence. MORPHOLOGY describes the grammatical features of the word, here Grammatical number Plural. For instance, the word answered in this sentence displays Aspect Perfect, Tense Past, and Verb form Participle, whereas in German, a noun could show its case, number, and gender. Only words possessing morphological properties display a MORPHOLOGY section. In Chinese, words never inflect in regard to tenses and numbers, so the MORPHOLOGY section does not appear for Chinese words. OTHER USES IN THIS DOCUMENT lists the other places where a word with the same lemma occurs.

The OTHER USES IN THIS DOCUMENT section displays up to 12 other instances in which the lemma occurred. In each instance, you have information showing how the word appeared (spelling), its word class, and role in the sentence (such as Noun · Object). The sentences containing those instances will be displayed as well; selecting an entry selects its corresponding occurrence in the reader. Entries in which the word has a different word class or function appear before others; entries within a form/role group appear according to order of appearance within the document. The first entry group displays two arrows pointing across each other; hovering the mouse pointer over these arrows reveals A different form or function. This means that either the form or function (or both) of the word differs between the two occurrences. For instance, in “Running Out of Time”, fear appears as a noun in Although that fear is understandable, but as a verb in Some readers might fear that climate policy will land hardest on families who already struggle. Selecting the noun instance puts the other sentence at the top of the list, with the arrow icons, since fear takes a different word class within that sentence. A noun that occurs as the subject in one sentence, but object in another also receives these arrows. So the arrows represent differences in grammar that could be associated with meaning changes. Use the list to confirm whether a word you intend to count or code is used consistently throughout a document. The Grammar facet for the verb fear in “Running Out of Time”, with the noun use listed under Other uses in this document and marked with crossed arrows.

If, however, your selection is a passage instead of a word, then the facet describes the head word of that passage, which means the first word whose head falls outside of the selected passage itself. For the warnings, that would mean just warnings. However, for answered the warnings with dates, it would mean answered.

Sentence is a facet containing a brief description of the currently selected sentence. The facet tells you something about the structure of the sentence (pattern), how long it is, and any phrases contained within it. The facet begins by stating the number of the selected sentence relative to the beginning of the document, e.g., Sentence 18. If the selection happens to span multiple sentences, then there will be an additional note indicating this, such as Selection spans 3 sentences, followed by a description of the first sentence alone. The Sentence facet for a sentence in “Running Out of Time”, with its pattern, root, and phrases. Below the sentence number come the following: In English documents, the sentence pattern, represented with a concise formula such as S · V · DO, the name of the pattern (in this case, Transitive), and a description thereof (see Sentence patterns below). Words, the token count in the sentence. Note that punctuation is counted here, too; thus, Our leaders have answered the warnings with dates. has 9 tokens. ROOT, the root word, as a hyperlink. Clicking the ROOT word selects the word in the reader. PHRASES, each and every phrase detected by the grammar analysis of the sentence, from the sentence itself all the way down to individual-word phrases. The rows of phrases below the PHRASES header indicate, respectively, the label of the phrase (such as NP, colored according to the phrase type), the phrase type itself (such as Noun phrase), and the constituent words. They appear in the order they appear in the sentence; phrases starting at the same word are sorted by decreasing length. Clicking a row selects the corresponding phrase in the reader. Word selections will shade the rows of all phrases containing the selected word.

English clause structure falls into a few basic patterns according to what the main verb requires (nothing, an object, two objects, a description of the subject, and so on). The Sentence facet assigns each English sentence to one out of ten possible patterns. Pattern Formula Example Intransitive S · V Two students fainted. Transitive S · V · DO We do not need another report. Ditransitive S · V · IO · DO The mayor gave every school a heat plan. Complex transitive S · V · DO · OC The drought left the fields bare. Linking S · LV · SC We feel frightened. Be + complement S · be · SC None of this is radical. Be + adverbial S · be · ADV The cooling center is in the library. Imperative (You) · V Come to the farm gate. Question ? What exactly are we waiting for? Fragment a dash Net zero by 2050. In the formulas above, S denotes Subject, V Verb, DO Direct Object, and IO Indirect Object. SC represents the Subject Complement, which can be either a noun or an adjective describing the subject. OC is the Object Complement, a descriptor of the object. LV refers to Linking Verb, while ADV refers to Adverbial. See Help ▸ Glossary under Abbreviations and symbols for definitions. LemmaLoom tests the patterns in the following order, displaying the first match: A sentence that ends with a question mark, or that the grammar analysis parses as a question, is a Question. A sentence whose root is not a verb is a Fragment, unless the phrase analysis finds a clause in it (a label such as S or SBAR), in which case it is Intransitive. A sentence for which the analysis finds no root is a Fragment as well. A sentence whose main verb is in its base form and has no subject is an Imperative. Be is left out of this test, so Be careful counts as Be + complement (rule 4). When the main verb is be, the sentence is Be + complement if a noun or adjective follows that describes the subject. Otherwise, it is Be + adverbial, as in She was on her front step until three. A linking verb followed by a complement makes the sentence Linking. The verbs that count as linking are seem, become, appear, feel, look, taste, smell, sound, remain, prove, stay, grow, turn, get, and go. A direct object with an object complement makes it Complex transitive. An indirect object and a direct object make it Ditransitive. A direct object alone makes it Transitive. Anything else is Intransitive. A pattern suggests a frame that a writer uses regarding an event. For instance, the sentence We block the roads is Transitive, and the writer acts on something. On the other hand, the sentence We feel frightened is Linking and describes a state. Patterns refer to main clauses only. For example, in I think we need a plan, the main verb think is followed by a clause and not an object, so the sentence is classified as Intransitive despite need having an object in its clause. In columns and debates, sentences that start with I think are therefore mostly Intransitive. When the analysis misreads a sentence, the pattern assigned to it reflects that misreading, and the Structure facet shows how the analysis read it.

The Structure facet allows viewing the selected sentence in three diagrams stacked below each other, under the headings Anatomy, Dependency graph, and Constituency Tree. Selecting any element within these views selects it in the reader. The Structure facet for a sentence in “Running Out of Time”, with the word leaders selected.

The Anatomy bar segments a sentence into the various parts of its main clause. One slot, known as the Verb slot, contains the main verb along with any auxiliary verbs and not that belong to it. Every other slot, meanwhile, contains one particular element which depends directly on the main verb, with all the words that belong to it; the element can be the subject, an object, or an adverbial. Slots are labeled according to their function and colored depending on the function's color scheme. Parts that cannot be fit into any particular function will be shown in gray with a label showing their relation, and the Verb slot is shaded more strongly than the others. Each slot's size is proportional to how many tokens are contained in the slot; hence, a sentence such as Our leaders have answered the warnings with dates. will have four equally sized slots, Subject (Our leaders, 2 tokens), Verb (have answered, 2), Object (the warnings, 2), and Adverbial (with dates, 2). Slots which contain too few tokens may have their sizes exaggerated somewhat to retain visibility. Below the bar is a control button for each slot. The button displays the slot's name and corresponding color. Pressing any slot button selects its words in the reader. Alternatively, clicking on a slot in the bar itself does the same thing. In the grammar analysis of German sentences, the finite verb (the verb form that changes with the subject) becomes the root of the sentence rather than the main verb. So for the sentence Die Wissenschaft hat ihre Arbeit eindeutig erledigt, the Verb slot will hold the finite verb hat, while the participle erledigt (‘done’) and the words that depend on it form another slot called Complement, ihre Arbeit eindeutig erledigt.

In the Dependency graph you'll see a graphical representation of the head of each word in a sentence. Each word is shown arranged on a horizontal line in sentence order, while tags are displayed beneath each word, colored according to word class. Arcs connect each word with its head. The arc points toward the dependent word, while relation codes are shown above the arc, colored according to function. Finally, a dashed line connects the root to ROOT above. In Our leaders have answered the warnings with dates., there are five arcs emanating from answered, namely nsubj (leaders), aux (have), dobj (warnings), prep (with), and punct (the period). Our modifies leaders as poss, while the modifies warnings as det; dates depends on with as pobj. Shorter arcs are drawn lower. Anytime an arc passes over another arc, it is drawn higher, giving insight into how nested the sentence structure is. Hover the mouse pointer over relation codes and tags to display their full names, e.g., Nominal subject for nsubj, or Noun, plural for NNS. German has unique relation code names as well, e.g., sb for subject and oa for accusative object. Chinese uses most relation code names used in English, but does have additions like nmod:topic for a topic. Select any word by clicking it. Selected words will be shaded, while their head is outlined. Additionally, all arcs originating from or leading to selected words will be made thicker, while the remaining arcs are faded out. The dependency graph is the right place to look if you are confused about the interpretation of some sentence structures. Consider “Why We Block the Roads”. One of its sentences begins I have marched through the city center with forty thousand people. The prepositional phrase with forty thousand people could modify either marched (the writer marched alongside them) or center (a center containing forty thousand people). Find the arc whose arrowhead touches with; whichever word touches the opposite end, marched or center, shows the reading the analysis chose. A wrong decision here propagates into the Grammatical function lens, sentence patterns, Form × Function, and word sketches.

The Constituency Tree is a view of how words organize into phrases. At the top level lies the entire sentence, usually designated by the label S. Every phrase breaks down into smaller constituent phrases and individual words contained inside. A word will hang below the smallest phrase it belongs to, along with its part-of-speech tag. Therefore, a word in a deeply-nested phrase is displayed at a lower depth level than those in less nested phrases. Each type of phrase receives a distinct color based on the Phrase lens coloring scheme (see Phrase in ). Clauses have their own distinct color. For the example sentence, the Constituency Tree breaks down the sentence S into the noun phrase Our leaders and the verb phrase have answered the warnings with dates. Within that latter verb phrase lies another verb phrase answered the warnings with dates. This final verb phrase contains both a noun phrase the warnings and a prepositional phrase with dates. The exact breakdown you see may differ from the one shown here. To see the full name of a phrase, hover the mouse pointer above its label, such as Prepositional phrase for PP or Subordinate clause for SBAR. You can click either a label or a word node to select the corresponding phrase or word in the reader. When the grammar analysis finds multiple parts to one sentence, the Constituency Tree organizes all of those beneath another higher-level label S. Labels differ depending on the language. English uses Penn Treebank labels like NP, VP, PP, and SBAR. German makes use of AP and AVP labels for adjective phrases and adverb phrases respectively. Chinese labels follow Penn Chinese Treebank conventions, with IP for a clause and DNP for a phrase with 的.

Dependency graphs and constituency trees are initially shown scaled to the width of the inspector, up to their true size. A long sentence will therefore start out quite small. The anatomy bar will consistently be shown at the width of the inspector. Beneath both the dependency graph and the constituency tree lies a zoom bar: Zoom out and Zoom in, the magnifying glasses with either a minus or plus sign, will respectively shrink or grow your diagram by 1.25 times per click until reaching their minimum/maximum limit, where they become disabled, showing the tooltip Fully zoomed out or Fully zoomed in. The Fit button rescales your diagram to the width of the inspector. Percentages indicate the relative size of the diagram, which is always between 25% and 600%. In addition to clicking buttons, you may pinch-zoom using a trackpad or scroll through the diagram if its contents don't fit the inspector. Before you've begun to manually zoom in/out, changing the width of the inspector will rescale your diagram accordingly. Selecting another sentence keeps your zoom; click Fit to fit the new sentence. The Diagram window provides additional viewing space when necessary.

The Diagram window displays either a dependency graph or constituency tree at any size, up to fullscreen. To open it, click Open in a window (icon showing two diagonal arrows) next to either Dependency graph or Constituency Tree in the Structure facet. The Diagram window comes up showing the chosen diagram. Dependency and Constituency in the upper-left corner toggle between both diagrams. The two arrows in the upper-right corner (Previous sentence and Next sentence) navigate through the document, and the text beside them displays what sentence you are currently viewing (e.g., Sentence 18 of 65). The Diagram window showing the constituency tree of a sentence from “Running Out of Time”. The Diagram window always shows the selected sentence of the active document. When you click on any word in another sentence of the reader, the Diagram window follows. Clicking on an arrow selects the root word of the next/previous sentence and scrolls the reader to show it; at the first and last sentence, the arrow that would go further is disabled, with the tooltip Already first or Already last. Clicking on a word or phrase in the diagram will select it within the reader. When the window opens, the diagram is fitted to the window at no larger than its actual size. There is a zoom bar located on the bottom right corner of the Diagram window that acts similarly to the inspector zoom bar, going from 10% to 800%. The Fit option fits the whole diagram into the window. Other view actions you can do include: Zoom in/out with pinch gestures on trackpads, or via the menu options View ▸ Zoom In (⌘+) and View ▸ Zoom Out (⌘-) respectively. Choose View ▸ Actual Size (⌘0) for actual-size views. Double-click the diagram or choose View ▸ Zoom to Fit for fitting it inside the window. Drag the diagram, or scroll with two fingers, for navigation around diagrams. When stepping between sentences, the Diagram window retains the current zoom level and pan position. Double-click or click Fit to fit a newly loaded diagram. When no sentence is selected in the reader, the Diagram window shows Select a Sentence.

Each of the three headings within the Structure facet has an export button, which looks like a square with an arrow. Within the Diagram window itself, the Export menu is located alongside Dependency and Constituency. The export button of the Dependency graph heading in the Structure facet, with its menu open to PNG and PDF. Exporting a diagram: Click the export button and choose PNG or PDF. In the save dialog, choose a name and a place. The suggested name gives the diagram and the sentence number, such as arcs-sentence-18 for a dependency graph, tree-sentence-18 for a constituency tree, and anatomy-sentence-18 for an anatomy bar. Click Save. The contents of your diagram are saved at its true scale regardless of zoom. Your anatomy bar is exported 640 points wide. PNGs are images at double resolution, sufficient for slideshow presentations and documents in a word processor. For printing purposes, opt for PDF since this format ensures clarity at any size. PNGs and PDFs both render using your selected color theme accordingly, meaning that a diagram with a dark theme would have a dark-colored background. If you require a diagram with a white background, set Theme to Light under Appearance in the General pane of Settings before you export (see ).

Grammar separates the structure of a phrase (known formally as form) from its purpose or role in the sentence (known formally as function). Form and function operate independently from one another. The following examples illustrate that the same form (noun phrase) can fulfill various functions. In our leaders have answered the warnings, the noun phrase our leaders acts as a subject; in we do not need another report, the noun phrase another report acts as an object; in this summer the heat closed schools, the noun phrase this summer acts as an adverbial. Similarly, a specific function may be performed by different forms. As seen in “Running Out of Time”, a neighbor sat on her front step until three in the morning because her apartment had turned into an oven. The adverbial on her front step is a prepositional phrase, while the adverbial because her apartment had turned into an oven is a clause. The Form × Function facet computes how often each form fulfills each function across the entire document. These calculations are organized in a matrix. The matrix essentially provides a profile of a document's stylistic preferences, for instance whether or not the writer tends to compress ideas in noun phrases, or elaborate reasons and conditions through clauses (see Using the matrix later in this chapter). The Form × Function facet for “Running Out of Time”, with the cell for noun phrases as subjects selected.

The rows represent the six forms (Noun phrase, Prep. phrase, Adj. phrase, Adv. phrase, Verb phrase, and Clause). Each row is displayed only if there are phrases of that form in your document that have been counted. To the right of each row name is the total of all numbers in that row. The columns are functions in short form, Subj (subject), Obj (object), Pred (predicative), Comp (complement), Adj'l (adjectival), Adv'l (adverbial), Appos (appositive), Agent (agent), and Conj (conjunct), nine of the ten grammatical functions from the Grammatical function lens. Grammatical function in  will introduce each of these functions along with an example. Each cell contains the number of phrases of its particular form performing its particular role. The deeper the shade of the cell, the nearer its number gets to the maximum number in the whole matrix. An empty cell does not contain a number and states No matches when hovered over. The matrix in a narrower inspector reduces its size and becomes horizontally scrollable. How to view the actual phrases behind a cell: Click the cell. Click an entry in the list below the matrix to select the phrase in the reader. Click the cell again to close the list. The list is headed with the type of phrase, its purpose (i.e., the function it performs), and the total number of occurrences, such as NOUN PHRASE AS SUBJECT; 143. Each entry is a phrase in quotation marks, followed by its sentence. The actual list contains the first 40 examples and includes a line like and 103 more below them. If your document contains no phrases to count, the facet will say No Phrases Yet rather than show the matrix.

Phrases are labeled according to their form from the grammar analysis. In other words, the form is the exact same label you would get for the phrase's subtree on the constituency tree diagram. Phrases' functions are determined by the function of their head word, the first word in a phrase that has its own head lying outside of the phrase itself. Thus, in the phrase on the farm, the words the and farm depend on words inside the phrase, whereas on depends on a word outside of it. Therefore, on is the phrase's head word, and its relation determines the function. Depending on whether the phrase is attached to a verb (we work on the farm) or a noun (the fields on the farm), the function becomes either adverbial or adjectival. All phrases, including nested phrases, count toward the matrix. For instance, the sentence Our leaders have answered the warnings with dates adds four separate phrases to the matrix: Phrase Head word Row Column Our leaders leaders Noun phrase Subj the warnings warnings Noun phrase Obj with dates with Prep. phrase Adv'l dates dates Noun phrase Obj The verb phrases have answered the warnings with dates and answered the warnings with dates get dropped; indeed, the whole sentence gets dropped too, because all three are headed by the root answered, which has no function in the matrix. Additionally, a phrase whose head word is a connector or has a relation that fits no function is left out. A preposition object, such as dates in with dates, belongs to Obj because Obj comprises both preposition objects and verb objects. Thus, every prepositional phrase contributes a noun phrase into Noun phrase × Obj, making this cell one of the biggest cells in the matrix in most documents. If one phrase has two labels as determined by the automatic analysis, such as to protect the climate our children will inherit in “Running Out of Time”, which is both a clause and a verb phrase, the phrase receives an entry in each row, meaning the sum total of rows may exceed the actual number of phrases in some cases.

When Adj'l features a large share of prepositional phrases (a preliminary analysis by the agency's climate science unit), that indicates complex noun phrases, as is common in written reports such as “Heat Wave Report 2024”. A high share of clauses in Adv'l (such as because…, when…, if…) signifies the presence of elaborations on reasons, time, and conditional contexts. The presence of mostly single pronouns (per the list behind the cell) as noun phrases in Subj indicates spoken language, as in “Radio Debate”.
