Note that the cell numbers indicate raw counts, so larger documents automatically have greater numbers across the board. In “Running Out of Time”, 143 out of the total 333 noun phrases act as the subjects, giving the proportion a value of 143 ÷ 333 = ~43%.

At the top left of the matrix, beside Form × Function, is a button to export the entire matrix in PNG, PDF, or CSV format. If exporting in CSV format, you receive a file containing rows for each unique form and columns for Form, Total, and each function, under its complete name. The suggested filename is form-function. In the list below the matrix, you'll find another export button that exports all the phrases found in the selected cell to a CSV file. In this case, the suggested filename is the form and function combined with a hyphen, e.g., Noun phrase-Subject. This CSV file contains the columns Sentence (sentence number), Phrase, and Text (complete sentence).

Collocates of a word are words that appear around it more frequently than would be predicted by random distribution alone. As seen in “Running Out of Time”, the word climate appears in phrases such as climate science, the climate crisis, today's climate policy, and protect the climate. Collocates of a word tell you what topics and fixed phrases the word typically occurs with, which can inform you about how the topic was conceived by the writer. The word being analyzed here is referred to as the node. The Collocates facet looks for collocates within the active document. When looking for collocates of a word in multiple documents, use the Collocates recipe in the Queries of your set (see Collocates in ). The Word Sketch facet also serves as an alternative to finding collocates; however, unlike the Collocates facet, word sketches find partners based on grammatical relations rather than distance (see ).

The figure below displays the collocates of climate in “Running Out of Time”, sorted by log-likelihood score. The Collocates facet listing the collocates of climate in “Running Out of Time”, ranked by log-likelihood. The process for listing the collocates of a word: Select the node in the reader. Click Collocates. The heading names the lemma, such as Collocates of climate, because every form of the word counts (climate and climates alike, and for a word such as cost, the verb as well as the noun). Choose a measure from the menu at the top left. It shows Log-likelihood at first; the other measures are MI, t-score, and logDice (see The association measures later in this chapter). A line below the controls says what kind of collocate the chosen measure favors. Set the size of the window with the stepper at the right. It shows ± 4 at first and goes from ± 1 to ± 10 (see What counts as near below). This list displays each collocate found sorted according to your selected measure, highest first. Every row contains: the rank; the collocate (followed by its part of speech); a line like f=8 · LL 36.8 · MI 4.32, where f stands for the frequency of the collocate near the node, LL denotes log-likelihood, and MI represents mutual information; at the right, the actual value of your selected measure. The collocates are counted according to lemmas, just like your node is. They appear according to their exact spelling in their first occurrence in the document, with the part of speech they have there. When you click any row, it will select the first occurrence of the collocate in your document. The facet follows the selection, displaying the collocates of whatever you clicked on instead. Selecting climate again will reverse the action. Your facet retains the measure and window parameters during any selections. After switching facets or documents, however, both revert to Log-likelihood and ± 4 respectively. When no word is suitable as a collocate, the facet shows No content collocates within ± 4. The export button to the right of the stepper exports your current collocates into a CSV file named after the node, such as collocates-climate. The order of the rows reflects the sort order of the list. The columns are Rank, Collocate, Part of speech (coded like NOUN), Frequency (f), Expected, Log-likelihood, MI, MI3, t-score, z-score, Dice, and logDice.

With regard to each instance of your node, LemmaLoom considers the positions up to the window size before it and after it within the same sentence. With ± 4, that means looking four tokens prior to your node and four subsequent tokens thereafter. Each token occupies one position regardless of whether it is a punctuation mark or a stopword. Stopwords refer to very common words such as the, and, of, and we, and each language has its own list. Punctuation marks, stopwords, and further instances of the node will not be included in your collocates. Consider Some readers might fear that climate policy will land hardest on families who already struggle. with climate as the node, and a ± 4 window. Positions preceding the node are comprised of the words readers, might, fear, and that; positions succeeding it are made up of the words policy, will, land, and hardest. Words like might, that, and will are all stopwords, so the window counts five words (readers, fear, policy, land, and hardest). When there are two occurrences of the node close to each other, any word occurring between them is within the range of two windows simultaneously and is counted twice. The Collocates recipe in queries counts differently. There, only words occupy positions, and stopwords and other occurrences of the node become collocates; the window size starts off with 5 instead of 4 as well. Thus, the lists generated in either place may differ greatly from each other for the same word.

The measures used in the facet quantify how often a collocate has occurred near the node compared to how often it would have occurred by chance alone. What makes each measure unique is the relationship between the magnitude of the difference and the total number of observations used in calculating that difference, and each measure favors a particular type of partner accordingly. Suppose there is a fictional 5,000-word magazine feature article on the topic of a summer heat wave in which climate is observed 20 times. The numbers in the following calculations are purely made up to simplify them; the documents in the example project are substantially shorter. With ± 4, the windows would contain 100 counted words in all. Suppose that crisis is observed 20 times within the document, but 8 of these occurrences fall within the windows around the node climate. This gives four numbers as follows: $o = 8$, the number of times crisis occurred within the windows (the f of its row); $R = 100$, the total number of counted words in all the windows; $C = 20$, the total number of occurrences of the word crisis in the document; $N = 5{,}000$, the total number of counted words in the document, not including punctuation or stopwords. If crisis occurred randomly throughout the feature, it follows that the windows should get their fair share of the occurrences of crisis. Holding 100 out of the total 5,000 words, the windows should have 0.4 instances out of 20 instances of crisis, as shown by the following equation for the expected count: The expected number of occurrences does not necessarily take integer values because this is just an average figure. On average, then, less than one occurrence of crisis is expected within the windows, whereas there are 8 occurrences of crisis in reality. All statistical measures below quantify how far 8 occurrences deviate from an expectation of 0.4 occurrences. The export lists $E$ in its Expected column. Mutual information, shown in the menu as MI, expresses how much more often the collocate occurs near the node compared to expectation, as a number of doublings: The logarithm with base 2, denoted as $log_2$, measures the number of doublings, so $log_2 8 = 3$ since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Similarly, $log_2 1 = 0$, values greater than 1 give positive logarithms, whereas values between 0 and 1 provide negative results. If your calculator lacks $log_2$, calculate the logarithm of the value over the logarithm of two, as in $ln x div ln 2$. In the case of crisis, $o / E = 8 / 0.4 = 20$, meaning it occurs twenty times as often near climate as chance predicts. Since 20 is between 16 (which equals four doublings) and 32 (five), $log_2 20 approx 4.32$. An MI value of 0 indicates occurrence as often as expected, whereas an increase by one represents double that frequency. The scoring system used for MI penalizes non-exclusive relationships and thereby favors rare words. Consider the hypothetical scenario wherein neutral occurs two times in the feature and occurs exclusively alongside climate. Then its expected occurrence will be $100 times 2 / 5{,}000 = 0.04$, giving it a mutual information score of $log_2 (2 / 0.04) = log_2 50 approx 5.64$, exceeding the score of crisis. Apart from words counted twice in overlapping windows, no other word could score higher than that. A word that appears exclusively with climate obtains $o = C$, resulting in $o / E = N / R = 50$ regardless of its number of occurrences being 1 or 20. The t-score is calculated by dividing the difference between the observed frequency and expectation by the square root of the observed frequency. The equation looks like this: For crisis, $t = (8 - 0.4) / sqrt{8} = 7.6 / 2.83 approx 2.7$. As the square root in the denominator increases slower than the count above it, the higher the number of observations of a pair is, the greater its t-score can become. Therefore, t-scores tend to favor common pairs that occur consistently. In corpus linguistics, a t-score exceeding 2 is usually taken as a sign that the pair is more than chance. For neutral, $t = (2 - 0.04) / sqrt{2} approx 1.4$, which does not exceed 2 although both of its occurrences fall near climate. The Dice coefficient compares the number of times the two words meet ($o$) with the words in the windows plus the occurrences of the collocate ($R + C$): Dice lies between 0 and 1. A score of 1 for Dice indicates that all of the words within the windows are instances of the collocate and that every occurrence of the collocate falls in the windows. logDice uses a range up to 14, where each decrement by 1 is equivalent to dividing the Dice ratio by 2. If, for example, the collocate was crisis, then $text{Dice} = 2 times 8 / (100 + 20) = 16 / 120 approx 0.133$; its base-2 logarithm will be around −2.91; thus, the logDice score becomes $14 - 2.91 = 11.09$. Because logDice ignores the overall length of the document ($N$), changes to logDice scores tend to be minimal regardless of variations in text length. However, logDice does rely on the number of words in the windows ($R$). Log-likelihood is the statistic the list starts with. Essentially, it tells you the strength of the evidence that the collocate's count around the node occurs not by mere coincidence. It considers all combinations of “is or is not crisis” and “lies in a window or elsewhere.” Each word falls into exactly one of the four cells below:  crisis Other words Total In the windows 8 92 100 Elsewhere 12 4,888 4,900 Total 20 4,980 5,000 The 92 is $R - o$, meaning the number of occurrences of the other words in the windows. The 12 is $C - o$, the number of occurrences of crisis elsewhere. The 4,888 is $N - R - C + o$, meaning everything else. The cells have an expected count, calculated just as before by taking the product of the row total and column total, then dividing by the grand total. This results in expected counts of 0.4 (for crisis in the windows, $100 times 20 / 5{,}000 = 0.4$, the $E$ from above), 99.6, 19.6, and 4,880.4 respectively. The score calculates how far away the actual counts of each cell lie from their expectations: Here $O$ refers to the observed count of each cell, $E$ to its expected count, and $sum$ (the capital letter sigma of the Greek alphabet) stands for “add up over the four cells.” Finally, $ln$ represents the natural logarithm function, found on calculators with the ln button. Similar to $log_2$, the function returns 0 if its argument is 1, a positive value if greater than 1, and a negative one otherwise. Thus, if the observed count of a cell matches its expectation perfectly, nothing is added to the total; otherwise, if greater, a positive contribution is added, while if lesser, a negative contribution is added. Since positive contributions will always outweigh negatives, the score cannot take a negative value. The score is written $G^2$, where the 2 does not mean that anything is squared. In the case of crisis, the four parts are: When multiplied by 2, the approximate outcome becomes 36.8, the value found in the row for crisis. By including the factor of 2 and applying the natural logarithm function, this score now aligns itself with the entries of the chi-square table with 1 degree of freedom, a table normally used when doing chi-square tests on 2 × 2 crosstabs. According to that table, scores equal to or higher than 3.84 would occur purely by coincidence 5% of the time for unrelated words, while 6.63 is equivalent to 1%, and 10.83 to 0.1%, or 1 in 1,000. Such a percentage is called the p-value; it reflects how surprising a given score would be if the two words were unrelated. Note, however, that the p-value does not indicate whether or not the relationship between the two words actually exists; rather, it provides information as to how surprising a particular observation was assuming independence. In this example, crisis received a score of 36.8, considerably greater than all three figures mentioned. Since the list tests each potential word candidate, among 100 completely unrelated words, about 5 would, on average, achieve 3.84 purely by coincidence. Also note that values in the chi-square table assume that expected counts are not tiny. The score does not show which way the counts differ. If heat occurs 200 times in the feature but only once near climate, its expected count is $100 times 200 / 5{,}000 = 4$, its log-likelihood 3.4, and its MI $log_2 (1 / 4) = -2.00$. A negative MI in the row shows that the word occurs near the node less often than chance would predict. Log-likelihood favors large differences and high frequencies of the counts. This explains why log-likelihood is the default measure. For instance, neutral occurs 50 times as often as expected but only twice; its log-likelihood is 15.7. Consider another word. If people occurs 100 times in the 5,000-word feature, but only 6 times in proximity to climate, its expectation would be 2, so it occurs 3 times as often as expected. Three times over six occurrences is weaker evidence than fifty times over two, so log-likelihood comes to only 5.5. Ranking the three words yields varied results based on the measure: Collocate $o$ $C$ $E$ Log-likelihood MI t-score logDice crisis 8 20 0.4 36.8 4.32 2.7 11.09 neutral 2 2 0.04 15.7 5.64 1.4 9.33 people 6 100 2 5.5 1.58 1.6 9.94 Log-likelihood ranks crisis first and neutral second because even two occurrences in the context of a 0.04 expected count are unlikely. As both instances of neutral appear close to climate, MI ranks it first. The t-score, however, has reservations regarding so few occurrences and favors people over neutral because six occurrences carry more certainty than two occurrences. logDice sides with the t-score on this one. In general, begin with Log-likelihood. Apply logDice if you require a measure that you can compare between documents, and use t-score if you want the partners of a particular word with the highest frequency. MI, meanwhile, is meant for exclusive partnerships; check their f values. The CSV export provides an additional three measures. MI3 equals $log_2 (o^3 / E)$; the third power means that common occurrences receive heavier weighting than in MI (10.32 for crisis). z-score is calculated as $(o - E) / sqrt{E}$. This results in extreme numbers for rare occurrences due to the denominator becoming vanishingly small (12.02 for crisis). Finally, Dice equals the coefficient without taking its logarithm (0.133 for crisis). Help ▸ Glossary defines every measure under Association measures, and Word association scores in  sets them side by side.

Discourse is a whole-document facet for questions about the structure and style of the text itself. There are three sections of this facet, chosen with the buttons at the top: Cohesion indicates the relationships between a sentence and the sentences prior. Metadiscourse lists the words with which speakers comment on what they say and address their listeners. Rhetoric includes stylistic choices, including the use of passives, nominalizations, and fronted openers (a phrase placed before the subject). Nominalizations involve turning actions into nouns; decision, derived from decide, is an example of nominalization. The categories within each section are annotated in the text according to the lenses of the corresponding names. Cohesion and the two sections after it in  describe each annotation procedure in detail. The findings come from built-in analyzers of the same names that run at indexing. As these analyses load, the facet shows a spinner. If the analyzer does not run for the document, for example because its output was removed in Document Properties, there is either a No Cohesion Data, No Metadiscourse, or No Rhetorical Devices message displayed depending on the analyzer (see ). Such messages will also show up when the document simply does not contain anything of the kind. If there is no space for the section buttons, they are replaced with a menu where each button is represented. Your choice will persist separately for every document you inspect.

There is consistency in the layout between each of the three sections. Right underneath the section buttons is the Search field, followed by rows corresponding to each category with findings, displaying the category color, its name, and the number of findings in it. The category rows are collapsed initially. For viewing findings within a category: Click its row to open it. In Metadiscourse and Rhetoric, a line describing the category appears first. Click a finding to select its sentence in the reader. To see the category annotated in the text, click Highlight in text (see Highlighting a category below). Categories display their first 200 findings, followed by a line such as and 38 more. Navigating away from this section will cause the opened categories to collapse again.

Cohesion categorizes each sentence based on its theme, what the sentence begins with. A theme is defined as the subject of the main verb along with all its words in English; everything preceding the verb (or the subject if nothing precedes the verb) in German; and the topic in Chinese, or the subject when the analysis finds no topic (see Cohesion in ). If a theme includes a third-person personal pronoun or possessive (they, their) or demonstrative (this), or repeats a word from either of the previous two sentences, then the sentence is tied. Otherwise, the sentence opens a new topic. Two counts above the categories give totals for tied sentences and new topics. For “Carbon Tax Debate”, these two totals are 20 tied and 13 new topic. The opening sentence of a document, under Opening, counts as tied. The Cohesion section of the Discourse facet for “Carbon Tax Debate”, with New topic open. Categories show up in the following order, each followed by the sentences which belong to it. Following each sentence is a line which provides an explanation for why it is so classified: Category Line below the sentence Opening Opens the passage Pronoun tie Known: pronoun “They”, naming the pronoun Possessive tie Known: possessive “Their” Demonstrative tie Known: “This” points back Repeated word Known: repeats “climate”, naming the repeated word Zero anaphora Known: omitted subject continues the topic (Chinese only) New topic New topic in the subject; possible cohesion gap All the sentences listed under New topic should be read successively. In “Carbon Tax Debate”, clusters of new topics can indicate where jumps occur in the text, gaps the reader has to cross without any guidance. Note, however, that in this context, a sentence lacking any testable theme (no subject in English, no subject or anything preceding a finite verb in German), e.g., Around five times., qualifies as a New topic as well; such sentences are frequent in transcripts. When working with Chinese texts, a sentence may qualify as Zero anaphora rather than a New topic provided that its omitted subject continues the previous topic. The Cohesion check category of Rhetoric does not account for them and lists only those new topics that contain a subject and at least six words.

Metadiscourse organizes its findings into Hedge (perhaps), Booster (clearly), Attitude marker (unfortunately), Connective (however), and Engagement (you, we). Metadiscourse also has Modal particle (ja, doch) for German texts and Final particle (吗, 吧) for Chinese texts. Every finding comes with the word in quotation marks and its sentence. The Metadiscourse section of the Discourse facet for “Running Out of Time”, with Hedge open. Comparing the metadiscourse categories of one particular document will give you an idea about the writer's stance on their topic. If a columnist uses lots of hedges (perhaps, probably, might) and few boosters (clearly, certainly), they may sound tentative. Engagement often makes up the biggest metadiscourse category in political speeches and opinion columns since engagement includes both we and you. LemmaLoom comes equipped with the lists for counting metadiscourse. However, if you wanted to count hedges with your own list of words, for example, the “Hedges” dictionary from the example project, then read . Unlike the default list, the “Hedges” dictionary also includes I think (under “Shields”). The counts returned by this facet pertain exclusively to the selected document. Comparing counts from documents of different sizes can be misleading without normalization. As an example, 6 hedges in a 600-word column equal 6 ÷ 600 × 1,000 = 10 occurrences per 1,000 words (see Measures in ).

Rhetoric has categories for each of the thirteen devices found in the Rhetoric lens that the document contains, including Passive voice, Nominalization, Power word, and Correlative pair (see Rhetoric in ). The Absolute phrase device is looked for solely in English, while the Periodic sentence device (sentences in which the main verb is delayed) is looked for in English and German. Findings include all of the words found along with notes explaining the reasoning for identifying those words as instances of the device. An agentless passive, for example, will receive the note Agentless passive; the doer goes unmentioned entirely. If the doer is retained but in a by phrase, then the note will reflect that. For periodic sentences found in English, the notes include the main verb of the sentence as well as its location within the sentence. Notes appear in the interface language. Queries and custom analyzers receive the notes in English. The Rhetoric section of the Discourse facet for “Heat Wave Report 2024”, with Passive voice open. Annotation in the lens will only tag one device per word, while the facet will list each finding regardless of duplicates. It follows that the same words can come under two different devices in the facet. Passive voice is the category to read for questions of agency. In “Heat Wave Report 2024”, irrigation was restricted in 63 municipalities, and responsibility for monitoring elderly persons living by themselves was not clearly assigned. In both examples above, neither specifies who exactly restricted the irrigation or who failed to assign such a task. Likewise, Nominalization is similar but applies to nouns rather than verbs. At the conclusion of “Heat Wave Report 2024”, the suggestion for further investment doesn't indicate whose duty it is. Similar patterns in your documents will highlight instances where writers leave the actors out.

Use the Search field to filter the list based on your input. A category whose name contains your input is shown whole. Any other category will show you only the findings whose text or note contains it, and update the number next to it accordingly. The matching process ignores capitalization. All matching categories will open and stay open during searching. If none match, then the list shows No matches. In Cohesion, the counts of tied sentences and new topics disappear temporarily during searching. For example, searching hedge returns everything in the Hedge category in Metadiscourse. Searching perhaps returns, in each category, only the findings containing perhaps in either their word or sentence.

Highlight in text, in an open category, shows that category within the reader: When the matching lens is currently disabled, it is enabled exclusively for this category. If the lens is currently enabled, its scope is restricted exclusively to this category. If the lens is currently exclusively enabled for this category, it is enabled again for every category. “Heat Wave Report 2024” after Highlight in text on Passive voice in the Rhetoric section of the Discourse facet. You can use the lens’ legend to see which of its lenslets are disabled (see Choosing which aspects are enabled in ). To see the annotated sentences consecutively, collapse the document too, with the button whose tooltip reads Show only the sentences a lens annotates (see Showing only annotated sentences in ).

There is an export button at the far right end of the section buttons that allows you to save the current section as a CSV file. This file stores all findings of all categories in that section regardless of what you search for or the 200 limit. The suggested filename of this CSV file is the name of the document with the section appended onto the end, e.g., Heat Wave Report 2024-Rhetoric. This CSV file has four columns, which are Category, Sentence (the number of the sentence in the document), Text, and Detail. The contents of the latter two depend upon the section itself: Section Text Detail Cohesion The sentence The line below it, such as Known: repeats “climate” Metadiscourse The word found The sentence Rhetoric The words found The note

A word sketch provides a summary of the grammatical context surrounding a word. In doing so, it gives you the words that occur around yours in a grammatical sense, such as the adjectives used to describe your word, or perhaps the verbs your word acts as the object of. In each relation, the words are ranked by the strength of their association with your word. If you were to create a sketch for climate in the op-ed “Running Out of Time” in the example project, you would find information about how the author refers to climate science, climate policy, and the climate crisis, how the author says the climate changes, and how they seek to protect it. Furthermore, from any partner you can go straight to the sentences containing your original word paired with it. Word sketches come in handy when trying to understand how something is presented in your documents, such as what an author writes that the climate does, or which adjectives are used in relation to the word policy in an author's writings. Generally speaking, sketches can be conducted on individual documents as you browse them, or on sets or entire projects to see how a group of texts uses a word. Instead of sorting partners according to their relations, the Code Sketch option sorts partners according to the codes that cover each occurrence. Sketch Space, which compares a word's sketches between codes or between the values of an attribute such as “Stance”, is explained separately in .

The sketched word refers to the word in focus in the current sketch. Word sketches operate on dictionary forms of words, or lemmas; therefore, costs and cost refer to the same word in word sketches. Pooled together are the word classes of the sketched word, while those of its partners remain separate (see Grammatical relations below). Relation refers to the particular grammatical relationship linking the sketched word with another word, such as subject, object, or adjective modifier. LemmaLoom recognizes twelve relations, and each of these collects one or more dependency relations recognized in the grammar analysis, including nsubj and nsubjpass for Subjects. The relations differ from the ten functions outlined under Key terms in . Links represent occurrences within a text where the grammar analysis connects the sketched word to another word. Partners are words that are connected with the sketched word in links, as illustrated in “the climate crisis,” where crisis acts as a partner of climate in the relation In compounds with. Frequency, f, is the quantity of links existing between the sketched word and one of its partners in one particular relation. logDice determines the ranking order of the partners. As such, logDice considers the proportion of occurrence of the two words together out of their individual occurrence frequency. The score peaks at 14 when the two words occur only with each other, and every point below that lowers this proportion by half (see Scores for details). The scope defines which documents serve to generate the sketch, namely one document, a set, a tag, or the entire project.

Place What it sketches How to get there Word Sketch in the inspector's Grammar tab the document in the reader View ▸ Inspector ▸ Grammar (⌥⌘2), then Word Sketch Code Sketch in the inspector's Coding tab the document in the reader, grouped by code View ▸ Inspector ▸ Coding (⌥⌘3), then Code Sketch The Word Sketch view every document in a set, a tag, or the project Word Sketch under Project in the navigation sidebar, or in the tab of a set or tag The Word Sketch window the project, a set, a tag, or the active document right-click the project, a set, or a tag in the sidebar and choose Word Sketch The view and the window both come with three modes. Those are Grammar, which provides the word sketch, Coding, which gives the Code Sketch, and Multimode, which offers Sketch Space. Any scope opened for the first time starts in the mode you last chose. In the inspector, the three modes are listed among the facets in the Grammar, Coding, and Multimode tabs as Word Sketch, Code Sketch, and Sketch Space, respectively. Word sketches are generated based on the grammatical structures found when LemmaLoom indexes a document in English, German, or Chinese (see ). Until the index has been computed for a particular document, the inspector shows Grammar becomes available when indexing completes for that document, and sketches of sets and projects leave it out.

t: Sketching a word in a document
b: The word sketch of climate in “Running Out of Time” in the “Climate Debate” example project lists most of the partners introduced earlier in this chapter in map format in the inspector. The word sketch of climate in “Running Out of Time”, shown as a map in the Grammar tab of the inspector. To sketch a word in a document: Open the document and choose View ▸ Inspector ▸ Grammar (⌥⌘2). Click Word Sketch in the row of facets at the top of the tab. Click a word in the reader. The Word Sketch follows the reader, and whichever word gets clicked becomes the word that gets sketched. Selecting multiple words results in sketching the word that heads the rest grammatically. Selecting the climate crisis yields crisis. To sketch a word before you find it within a document, enter it in the Word field and hit Return. Only the dictionary form is accepted in the field in the case of a document; bill will represent bills, for instance. The comparison does not consider capitalization. The bar in the upper portion of the facet lists, from left to right: Back and Forward buttons (two arrow icons that move back to words that were previously sketched); you may refer to Going back and forward for more detail, Word field, Display options Map, List, and Web (they switch between displays), Export button (for more detail, refer to Exporting), Open in a window icon (two diagonal arrows icon), opening the same document and word in the Word Sketch window (details are discussed in The Word Sketch window). After the bar comes Word sketch of, with the sketched word. The facet displays Sketch a Word prior to choosing a word in the document. Should the chosen word not engage in any of the twelve relations, the facet shows No grammatical partners found for this word. The Code Sketch facet and Sketch Space facet also contain the bar mentioned earlier, with options for Map and List displays. The Code Sketch and Sketch Space facets update with the chosen word like the Word Sketch does too. The selected display applies to all word sketches, Code Sketches, and Sketch Spaces until changed again; while Web display is active, both Code Sketch and Sketch Space display maps.

The grammar analysis analyzes each word in every sentence by linking it to the word it depends on. For example, adjectives depend on nouns, subjects on verbs, and nouns following a preposition depend on the preposition itself. A word sketch summarizes all links of one particular word, grouping them into twelve relations. While some relation types point downwards toward the dependencies, other relation types point upwards toward what the sketched word depends on. Hence, a single link appears twice in two different word sketches, once each according to the direction it points toward. Take the phrase “the climate changes,” for example. Climate appears in the sketch of change as one of the Subjects, whereas change appears under Subject of in the sketch of climate. Relation What it lists Example Subjects the subjects of a verb heat in “the heat closed schools” (sketch of close) Objects the objects of a verb, indirect objects included school in “the heat closed schools” (sketch of close) Complements words and clauses that complete a verb, such as the adjective after feel or the verb after want to hopeful in “to feel hopeful” (sketch of feel) Subject of the verbs the word is the subject of warn in “Scientists warn” (sketch of scientist) Object of the verbs the word is the object of close in “the heat closed schools” (sketch of school) Adjective modifiers adjectives that describe the word terrible in “a terrible summer” (sketch of summer) Adverb modifiers adverbs that modify the word together in “decide to act together” (sketch of act) Modifies the words this word modifies, as adjective or adverb step in “the most urgent steps” (sketch of urgent) In compounds with nouns that form a compound with the word, before or after it carbon in “carbon tax” and break in “tax breaks” (sketch of tax) Prepositional phrases phrases attached to the word, shown as preposition and noun on fuel in “a carbon tax on fuel” (sketch of tax) Coordinated with words joined to it by and, or, and similar words flood in “fires and floods” (sketch of fire) Complement of the words this word completes feel in “to feel hopeful” (sketch of hopeful) The sketch provides a description of the relations the word participates in, following the order provided by the table above. One-line definitions are available in Help ▸ Glossary under Word sketches. Four factors influence what will be included in the sketch: If a word is the subject of a passive verb construction, it counts as a subject. E.g., in “Those bills were paid too,” pay will appear under Subject of in the sketch of bill. In Prepositional phrases, the partner is always presented along with the preposition. On fuel and for fuel are two distinct partners. Partners are distinguished based on their word classes. When the grammar analysis assigns the same partner both as a noun and a verb in various constructions, the partner can appear twice in one relation. The CSV export specifies the word class of each partner (Exporting). The grammar analysis fails occasionally, most often with false starts, enumeration, and incomplete sentences in transcriptions of spoken language; thus, occasionally, incorrect partners can be attached to the analyzed word. Reviewing the sentences containing a suspicious partner usually reveals whether the attachment is indeed erroneous. Sketches of German and Chinese words use twelve relations similarly, though there are several exceptions: Since compound words in German are almost always written as one unit (e.g., Klimapolitik), In compounds with remains empty for German-language documents. The German grammar analysis considers the preposition the head of the preposition phrase. Even so, a German sketch displays this phrase under Prepositional phrases, and the order of its elements is identical to English; the preposition precedes its noun. Additionally, the bare preposition can function as a partner in several roles, under Adverb modifiers of the verb the phrase belongs to (mit in the sketch of leben), under Adjective modifiers of a noun it follows, and under Modifies in the sketch of the noun in the phrase (mit in the sketch of Ergebnis). The German grammar analysis links subjects to the finite verb. In “Die Wissenschaft hat ihre Arbeit eindeutig erledigt,” Wissenschaft is considered the subject of the auxiliary verb haben, not of the main verb erledigen. Therefore, auxiliaries and modal verbs such as haben, werden, and müssen can be seen frequently in Subject of. In German, Adjective modifiers contains not only adjectives but also nouns, proper names, numbers, genitive attributes (Klimapolitik in “den Ergebnissen der heutigen Klimapolitik”), and appositions. Similarly, in Chinese, Adjective modifiers contains nouns and pronouns functioning as modifiers, often followed by the particle 的 (学校 in 学校的屋顶). The Chinese grammar analysis links a preposition to the noun that follows it. Chinese prepositional phrases show the preposition before its noun.

Word sketches can be visualized in LemmaLoom with the Map display. The sketched word appears at the center of the display in the accent color, with its partners surrounding it. In your word sketch, partners appear grouped together according to their relation. Relations are sorted clockwise starting at the top of the map following the order in the table above, and each relation occupies an amount of space proportional to how many partners it shows. Each relation has its own unique color shared by its partners and the lines connecting them to the sketched word. Small labels with colored dots are used to name relations near their respective partners whenever possible. Within a single relation, the partner possessing the highest logDice score has the largest font size and boldest line weight compared to others. Hovering the mouse pointer over a partner shows its frequency and score, for example f=4 · logDice 11.83. All other partners temporarily fade during this time. The mouse pointer over crisis in the word sketch of climate for the “Activists” set, with its frequency and logDice shown in a tooltip. The exact number of partners shown per word sketch is dependent upon available space. At least two but not exceeding eight partners can be shown per relation, and partners likely to cause overlapping will be omitted from the display. When your inspector width is restricted, you may only see the two or three strongest partners per relation at once, but widening your inspector, switching to List, or opening the word sketch in the Word Sketch window provides you with access to additional detail. The map allows clicking a partner to sketch it. Alternatively, right-clicking a partner offers the option to either Sketch this word (equivalent of a click) or Show in context, which shows the partner in the text (see Showing partners in the text). The shortcut menu of the partner crisis in the word sketch of climate for the “Activists” set, offering Sketch this word and Show in context. A zoom bar is provided at the lower-right side of the map that allows you to Zoom out, Zoom in, and Fit, and shows the current zoom in percent. On trackpads, pinching performs the zoom action, while double-tapping with two fingers switches between the fitted view and twice the size. Holding down ⌘ enables zooming by scrolling as well. Once zoomed in, use drag or scrolling actions to pan around the zoomed image. Zoom-in is maxed out at fourfold.

The List display displays the exact same sketch as lists, with separate sections for each relation according to how they are arranged in the table. The sections display the color, name, and total number of partners included in each section. Within each row are displayed the partner itself, frequency, and logDice measure up to two decimal places. Rows are ranked by logDice score with descending ranking order; rows having equal logDice scores are then ranked by frequencies. A section lists up to 12 partners. The word sketch of climate in “Running Out of Time” in the List display, with one section per relation. On the list, click functions operate opposite to how they function on the map. By clicking on the row in question, you bring up the partner in the text (see Showing partners in the text). Right-click it and select Sketch this word to sketch the partner.

Web, being the third display, adds the partners' partners. This reveals the relationship of the words around the sketched word with one another. Web display is exclusive to Grammar. It has two stages: The sketched word gets its six strongest partners by logDice, taken across all relations. Each of those gets its own six strongest partners. The prepositional phrase's noun gets turned into the web node, so on fuel and fuel are one node, labeled the way the web first reached it. Any word that was already placed will appear once, with one line to every word that counts it among its six. The web diagram displays concentric rings containing the sketched word in the middle, surrounded by its partners on the first ring, followed by their own partners on the outer ring. Colors represent relations like those in the map, and lines' thickness represents logDice. To keep track of nodes within the web structure, hover the mouse pointer over a node. That node and its partners stay bright while all other nodes fade, and its tooltip indicates the logDice of the line that brought this node into the web. Where nodes crowd each other, those near the mouse pointer move apart so that you can read them. The web of climate in the “Climate Debate” project, with the partners of its six strongest partners on the outer ring. When science is among the strongest partners of climate, the outer ring of the web may show what the authors say science does through verbs whose subjects are science. Examples include describe and project. In order to create a word sketch, click any word on the web, and the web of that word takes its place. When clicking Show in context on a word within the web, LemmaLoom searches for occurrences next to the selected sketched word; in the Word Sketch view and window, this works for the words linked to the sketched word itself. Within the inspector, however, it selects the word's first occurrence. The web can be zoomed from a quarter of its size up to six times its size. Given the time it takes to generate a web in a large set, a spinning icon displays in its place until generation has completed. Stopping the process occurs when Map or List has been chosen instead.

The navigation history feature allows LemmaLoom to keep track of the path you took while navigating through your word sketches. Navigation history in Word sketch of above the sketch would look something like climate › science › describe, where the current word is shown last. Clicking on any previous words takes you back to them. The Word Sketch view of the “Activists” set after sketching climate, science, and describe in turn, with the path above the sketch and Back and Forward in the bar. All sketched words, regardless of whether they are input via typing, clicking on partners, choosing candidate words according to dictionary category, or, in the inspector, selecting within the reader, will be added onto the navigation path. Navigation with Back or Forward follows that exact same path (as if moving around within a browsing history of a web browser). When navigating backwards and sketching a new word, the word(s) you went back past will automatically be replaced by the newly sketched word. There are several commands listed under View ▸ Word Sketch, each command having its own dedicated keyboard shortcut. Back (⌘[) and Forward (⌘]) Focus Word Field (⌘L) Grammar, Coding, and Multimode (⌘1, ⌘2, and ⌘3) Within the inspector, the commands Grammar, Coding, and Multimode will switch to Word Sketch, Code Sketch, and Sketch Space, respectively, in the Grammar, Coding, and Multimode tabs. In terms of navigation, within the inspector, the three facets of the document will maintain one path, meaning if you navigate to a particular word in Word Sketch, Code Sketch, or Sketch Space, that exact word will appear within each of the other two facets.
Each pair has a frequency and logDice value. Frequency indicates the number of times both words are linked, while logDice indicates their relationship strength.

The frequency of a partner refers to the number of occurrences where your grammar analysis identified the occurrence of the partner word in connection with the sketched word in the given relation. Consider the example project “Climate Debate”. Suppose the texts contain the phrase climate crisis four times. In this case, the frequency f=4 of the word crisis within In compounds with in the sketch of the word climate will show up. However, frequency alone isn’t sufficient to tell what’s typical of a word. Ranking partners purely by frequency will give a list headed by common words like new. This is because high-frequency partners are connected with pretty much any other word imaginable (new roads, new licenses, new deadlines, new bridges, and so forth). Word sketches rank partners by their logDice score, taking account of the frequency of each word individually.

logDice is based on the frequency of appearance of the pair divided by the sum of frequencies of both words taken separately (a quantified measure of collocation). This computation makes use of three values: $a$, the number of times the pair is linked, denoted by f $r$, the frequency of appearance of the sketched word within the relation, with any partner $c$, the frequency that the other word in the relation appears in the scope without considering pairing Each inflectional form of a word contributes toward its lemma, and word classes are tracked independently. Therefore, when the partner is the noun plan, only its uses as a noun count toward $c$. The Dice coefficient was named after ecologist Lee R. Dice and measures the frequency of the pair relative to the sum of the above two values: If the three counts were to be identical, the Dice coefficient would equal 1, meaning that the word takes part exclusively in that pairing and the partner occurs nowhere else. Low values suggest few occurrences of the pair compared to the two counts combined. Due to there being two values added together in the denominator of Dice, the multiplication factor 2 compensates for this fact. Comparing Dice coefficient scores visually presents a difficulty due to their being ratios; thus, values 0.02 and 0.04 differ by a factor of two but look nearly similar numerically. This is where the logDice transformation helps convert ratios onto a logarithmic scale where each increment corresponds to a doubling of the preceding value: The base 2 logarithm ($log_2$) measures how many times the doubling should occur before reaching a certain number. Thus, $log_2 8 = 3$ because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. In the range 0 < x < 1, logarithms are negative, representing halving operations; $log_2 0.5 = -1$ while $log_2 0.25 = -2$. Should the $log_2$ button be missing on your calculator, compute the quotient of natural logarithms $ln x div ln 2$. Therefore, a partner receiving one fewer logDice point than another will have a Dice coefficient half that partner’s. The constant 14 offsets logDice points so that 14 is the highest possible score in scenarios with Dice equal to 1. In order to fall under 0 logDice points, the Dice coefficient needs to be smaller than 1 divided by 16,384 ($2^{14}$), an event uncommon in a project of opinion pieces and columns. For example, assume “Climate Debate” uses climate in compounds with a second noun 28 times total, which means each partner's $r = 28$ under the relation In compounds with. While invented for the purpose of demonstration, the numbers represent realistic values relative to the example project. Policy compounds with climate 4 times out of 8 occurrences total in the project. Since 0.222 lies between 0.125 and 0.25, the binary logarithm of the number lies between −3 and −2. Specifically, $ln 0.222 div ln 2 approx -1.5041 div 0.6931 approx -2.17$. Thus, With this logDice score, the tooltip on the map reads f=4 · logDice 11.83. Below, there are three additional examples of partners: Partner f ($a$) Occurrences of the partner ($c$) Dice logDice crisis 4 4 8/32 = 0.250 12.00 policy 4 8 8/36 ≈ 0.222 11.83 science 4 12 8/40 = 0.200 11.68 denier 1 1 2/29 ≈ 0.069 10.14 The words crisis, policy, and science all form compounds with climate four times apiece. Yet their rankings will differ from one another. Every crisis in the project is a climate crisis; hence, crisis ranks first. Of the eight uses of policy, half are climate policies. Twelve instances of science appear, predominantly unmodified (science and the science). Thus, science finishes behind crisis and policy, while denier, seen only once and only in climate denier, ranks lowest of the four. In cases where two partner words tie for equal frequency with the sketched word, whichever word is less frequent elsewhere scores higher.

While the Collocates facet of the Grammar tab and collocate lists generated via queries offer other measures, among them mutual information (MI) and log-likelihood (see  and ), the partners in word sketches are ranked using logDice exclusively, as MI gives preference to rare partners while depending on the text length. MI measures the ratio between the actual frequency $a$ and the expectation based on chance occurrences. If $N$ is the length of the text measured in number of tokens (both words and punctuation), then out of these $N$ tokens, $c$ tokens are the partner. Therefore, a random link to any token will end up pointing to the partner with probability $c/N$. Given the sketched word's $r$ links, $r times c / N$ will be the expected amount of occurrences, which equals the expected frequency $E$ in The association measures of . This gives the following equations: Here MI is calculated in doublings and therefore equals 3 for instances eight times more frequent than expected by chance. Take a project containing 10,000 tokens (roughly 9,000 words plus punctuation), and the result is $E = 28 times 8 / 10{,}000 = 0.0224$ for policy and $4 / 0.0224 approx 179$, giving MI $approx log_2 179 approx 7.48$. Similarly, $E = 28 times 1 / 10{,}000 = 0.0028$ and $1 / E approx 357$, resulting in MI $= log_2 357 approx 8.48$ for denier, which occurs only once in the sketch. MI thus ranks denier above policy. The effect comes from the small expected frequency, which turns the single instance of denier into a huge surprise. In comparison, logDice places policy ahead of denier as a single instance does not constitute a substantial share of 28 links. It should also be noted that MI relies heavily on $N$; with the same counts, all MI values in a project twice as long would be increased by one due to halved expected frequencies. Since $N$ is nowhere to be found in the logDice calculation formula, a project of greater length will neither increase nor decrease logDice without other modifications. Scores still change with the scope, because $r$ and $c$ do (see Word sketches for sets, tags, and the project).

Code Sketches partition partners according to codes rather than relations; that is, they partition partners according to the codes that cover your word where it occurs. If you hypothesize that your word associates with different groups of partners based on what topic a passage covers, then you could use Code Sketches to explore that hypothesis in your documents. In “Running Out of Time”, for example, a Code Sketch shows the partners of climate in passages coded “Science” and in those coded “Tipping Points”. The Code Sketch of climate in “Running Out of Time”, with partners grouped by code and the uncoded occurrences in gray. To make a Code Sketch of a document: Open the document and choose View ▸ Inspector ▸ Coding (⌥⌘3). Click Code Sketch in the row of facets at the top of the tab. Click a word in the reader, or type its dictionary form in the Word field and press Return. Like in the word sketch, the map and the list show codes in place of relations, where each code has its own group and color, and the Uncoded group gathers, in gray, the partners of all occurrences not captured in any code passage. Codes are ranked according to how many links of the word lie in their passages, with the highest numbers being first. The Uncoded group comes at the end. Include uncoded, which follows Code sketch of and the word below the bar, starts selected, meaning occurrences with no coding are included. Deselect it if you do not want any occurrences without coding in the sketch. Occurrences of the word belong to a code when the code covers any part of them. Occurrences that fall inside passages with more than one code are counted under each code involved. For instance, if in “Running Out of Time” there is a phrase “a cliff edge in thick fog” lying in passages coded “Fear” and “Tipping Points”, then your Code Sketch of fog will have thick in the groups “Fear” and “Tipping Points”. Each code counts only its own codings. If you separately coded certain passages for “Urgency” and others for its subcode “Tipping Points”, then these two become separate groups. Coded memos count as codings. Occurrences falling in passages coded via a memo are considered occurrences coded directly with the memo's code. Should your document contain no codings at all, all occurrences will be put under the Uncoded group and produce the equivalent of the word sketch with all relations pooled. Should Include uncoded be deselected, however, this will produce No Partners. For each code group individually, a partner's frequency reflects the number of links between the partner and the word in all the relations in which they participate. Thus, should the word climate occur as the object of protect in some sentences and be linked to it in another fashion in others, the word protect is listed only once. Prepositions in Prepositional phrases stay with their nouns; for example, the partner occurs as on fuel. The scoring algorithm for each partner within each code individually remains logDice, but it gets calculated independently per code group. The total number $r$ of the sketched word becomes its total number of links, of any kind, inside passages of the particular code. The partner's count $c$ still refers to the whole document or the whole scope in a set or project. Thus, a common partner appearing in many locations scores lower under every code than one occurring mostly in the code's passages. As an example, if climate has 5 links within passages coded “Science” in some document, 2 of them to model, which itself occurs 8 times in the document altogether, Dice $= (2 times 2)/(5 + 8) = 4/13 approx 0.308$, hence logDice $= 14 + log_2 0.308 approx 14 - 1.70 = 12.30$. Clicking and right-clicking behave similarly to the word sketch, and partners sketched join the path above. Within the inspector, the action Open in a window opens the Word Sketch window on the document in Coding mode. Comparing relations across codes requires you to use Sketch Space instead (see ).

t: Word sketches for sets, tags, and the project
b: Word sketches are generated for a set, tag, or project as a whole. The totals $a$, $r$, and $c$ will be aggregated across all of the documents prior to calculating the score. Word sketches of the same word in two distinct scopes illustrate differences between authors, as seen with the sets “Activists” and “Skeptics”.

The set “Activists” of “Climate Debate” holds the activist texts; thus, its word sketch of climate tells you how they use the word. The Word Sketch view of the “Activists” set, sketching climate in Grammar mode. To open the Word Sketch view: For the whole project, click Word Sketch under Project in the sidebar. For a set or a tag, click it in the sidebar, then click Word Sketch among the buttons in its tab. Type a word in the Word field and press Return. Choose Grammar, Coding, or Multimode in the bar. Your very first opening of a sketch for a scope will involve preparing the grammar of each document in the scope. This is signified by Preparing, a progress ring, and the number of documents prepared out of all total documents, e.g., 4 of 6. Subsequent openings of sketches within the same scope commence immediately. Editing a particular document requires only that particular document to undergo preparation, thus making Preparing appear as smaller text in the bar. The bar remains consistent throughout modes. In the project's Word Sketch section, it begins with the title, followed by the various modes and Map, List, and Web. On the right are Back, Forward, the Word field, a menu of translations when the scope has any (see Sketching translations below), the export button, and Open in a window. The arrows and the Word field come first in a set or a tag and in the Word Sketch window. Following those items are the remaining ones, in the same order. In Coding and Multimode, Web is disabled, with a tooltip stating Web is not available in this mode. Beneath the bar is either Word sketch of or Code sketch of, depending on whether a word sketch or Code Sketch is being generated, showing the path of what you've sketched so far (see Going back and forward). Include uncoded, which includes occurrences with no coding, shows beneath it in Coding mode, and Include document codes shows beside it when the scope contains document codes.  explains the additional controls for Multimode.

In the view, the Word field accepts any word form. If you input scientists, you will get back scientist; likewise, warned returns warn. A phrase is sketched under the word which most often heads it in the text in your scope, so climate crisis returns crisis. If you enter text written in Chinese without spaces, the system splits it into words occurring in your scope before processing it the same way. For a non-occurring word, the view states No grammatical partners found for this word. Upon hitting Return on your keyboard, the Word field changes to the sketched word, meaning that scientists becomes scientist and climate crisis becomes crisis. This word applies to all three modes and stays when you switch between them. After you sketch a partner, the inputted word remains in your Word field while the partner becomes part of the path above the sketch.

Documents must be original. If a set has translated documents, the sketch uses the original documents instead. If you want a translation sketch, pick your desired translation language from Corpus (see Sketching translations below). Documents must be indexed. When some documents lack indexing, a note at the bottom, such as 13 of 14 documents indexed, says how many indexed documents are included. When none of the documents have been indexed, you get a note saying Grammar becomes available when indexing completes. Any frequency of partners. In contrast with Sketch Space, Grammar and Coding will include even partners seen only once. In a large scope, however, a particularly rare partner may go unscored. This view automatically refreshes whenever a document text is edited, coding applied, or a new code created.

A code can belong to a single document (see ). When it does, the document title follows the code name, in parentheses, in Code Sketches and Multimode analyses of sets or projects. In the project “Climate Debate”, the speaker codes belong to the document “Radio Debate”. As such, the code “Skeptic” becomes “Skeptic (Radio Debate)”. Long titles are shortened to the distinguishing portion of the title, with an ellipsis (…) for what is left out. If there happen to be document codes within the scope being analyzed, an Include document codes checkbox appears next to Include uncoded. It is selected initially. Deselect it if only codes that apply across documents need be considered in analyzing occurrence counts; the occurrences that document codes cover then count under any other code on the passage, or under Uncoded. The Code Sketch of climate in the project “Climate Debate”, with Include document codes selected and the groups “Activist (Radio Debate)” and “Host (Radio Debate)”.

When your scope contains documents translated into English, German, or Chinese, a menu appears in the bar, with a tooltip labeling it Source and at first showing a selection labeled Originals. Under Corpus, this menu has entries labeled Originals, as well as one for each translation language, such as Translations (German), because the word sketch operates on one language at a time. The Word Sketch window for “Climate Debate” with its menu open, offering the German translations under Corpus. Choose a language to generate a word sketch of translations exclusively into that language. Normally, this option would be used when your documents' languages are different from English, German, or Chinese. In the “Climate Debate” project, for example, Translations (German) contains only one translation, “Running Out of Time (German)”. When choosing a language for translation purposes, type the word in that language, e.g., Klima rather than climate. Changing your corpus will prepare your documents again. Codings done on an original appear in its translations (see ). Thus, Coding and Multimode are capable of working on a translation corpus.

The Word Sketch window displays the exact same thing as the Word Sketch view does, except in a separate window that you can keep beside the reader. The tab and window will contain one shared sketch per scope selected. Thus, the same word, path, mode, corpus, checkboxes, and candidate words used in either the view or the window remain consistent between views. Type a word in the window, and it will appear in the corresponding Word Sketch view of the set. Opening the window can be done in several ways: In the sidebar, right-click the project, a set, or a tag name, then choose Word Sketch. Within the Word Sketch view of the project, a set, or a tag, click the Open in a window button at the far right side of the bar. The same button is found in the Codebook window's Word Sketch section. In the inspector's Word Sketch, Code Sketch, or Sketch Space facet, click the Open in a window button to bring up the window on the current document, with the facet's mode and word intact. On the Word Sketch tab of the project, or the tab of a set or tag showing Word Sketch, right-click the tab name and select Open in New Window (see ). The Word Sketch window maintains only one instance at any point in time. Thus clicking to show a Word Sketch window again will replace the old scope with a new one according to whichever scope is selected currently, and the window always reflects the active project in LemmaLoom. The window's menu with its tooltip label as Source contains controls to change the scope. Thus whatever scope is displayed in this window will show in the menu label alongside an indicator for the corpus whenever the scope has translations, e.g., “Climate Debate · Originals”. The Scope section lists the project (with a folder icon), sets alphabetically ordered, tags, and the active document in the reader, if there is one. In “Climate Debate”, these are the sets “Activists”, “Skeptics”, and “Wide Reach” and the tags “op-ed” and “viral”. For sketching the documents of the group “Print”, for instance, a smart set must be created based on a Group condition (see Groups in ). When you choose another scope, the window preserves the word, path, mode, corpus, and checkboxes used, allowing direct comparison between different scopes. Thus you can compare climate between “Activists” and “Skeptics” by changing the scope. The Word Sketch window for “Climate Debate”, with the scopes listed in its menu. The document scope presents a sketch very similarly to the inspector except that there are three distinctions between them: The window keeps its word when you click in the reader; It allows entries in its Word field to take any form of words (refer to The Word field); And, finally, the option Show in context iterates over the locations at which both words are linked (refer to Showing partners in the text).

A word sketch can start off from terms within a dictionary category so that you may go through each individually. Within the “Climate Debate” project, there is a “Hedges” dictionary which contains a category “Shields”, and its word sketch results will tell you what the writers hedge about. To initiate a word sketch based on a category: Click Dictionaries under Project in the sidebar, or in the tab of a set. Select a dictionary. Right-click one of its categories and choose Word Sketch, which is disabled if the category contains no terms. To begin your word sketch directly from a particular term, double-click the desired term among the category's terms. Alternatively, you may select Sketch this word via right-clicking on the selected term. Choosing Open in Window from the same shortcut menu results in opening the sketch in the separate Word Sketch window. The view then switches to Word Sketch for the same project or set and retains your previous mode. The word sketched will either be your chosen term or, after Word Sketch, the one which occurs in the scope most frequently. Beneath the bar, you will find the name of your category along with its color, and finally its candidate words. For “Shields”, for instance, candidates include think, perhaps, and maybe among others. Clicking the desired candidate will generate the sketch. The currently selected candidate word has highlighting. Your terms get mapped onto the lemmas they contain when they appear in your scope, and phrases onto the word that heads them, meaning that both I think and I'd say map onto think and say respectively. All terms which reduce to the exact same word share a common candidate word. Hovering the mouse pointer over a candidate word reveals which terms map to this word. Your list of candidate words gets sorted by occurrence frequency in your scope. Candidate words of a term never appearing in any form inside your scope appear at the end of the row, disabled, along with the tooltip Not found. Entering a word outside the candidate words into the Word field removes the whole row. For more information, see Word sketches from a category in .

Sketch Space is presented in Multimode for the scope. Word sketches are compared among the columns, which refer to the set of codes covering the word's occurrences or the set/project-level values of an attribute, such as “Stance”. In a grid, each row represents a relation, while each column represents a code or value, and each cell counts the word's links of that relation in that column. Maps highlight the strongest partners for each column. Under the inspector's Multimode tab, the same comparison occurs on the level of one document. More information regarding the concept of Sketch Space can be found in . In the grid, an asterisk next to a counted number, explained by a line under the grid, signifies a characteristic relation. This means that a particular relation occurs clearly more often in a given column than in the rest of the scope. An asterisk appears in a cell only when all three criteria are fulfilled simultaneously, namely: the count must be greater than or equal to three, so one or two sentences will not qualify as characteristic; the count must exceed its expected count; and a one-sided Fisher's exact test results in a p-value below 0.05.

Say target had 12 grammatical links within the project, but all occurred within activist and skeptic texts, and you compare its counts across the values of “Stance”. The numbers here are invented for illustration: Relation Activist Skeptic Whole project Object of 6 · 6 Adjective modifiers 1 3 4 In compounds with · 1 1 Prepositional phrases 1 · 1 All links 8 4 12 A dot means zero occurrences. Totals are provided for both rows and columns as an illustration for this example. Target appears mostly as an object of set within the activists' texts while the skeptics refer to national targets. “Activist” receives a  next to Object of whereas “Skeptic” does not receive any next to Adjective modifiers despite having three of its four links there.

Out of the total 12 links across the project, there are 6 links that are classified as Object of. That is exactly half of them. Given the number of links for activist documents (8), half of them, or 4, would fall into Object of classification if the activists used target the way the whole project does. Hence, the expected count $E$ is 4, which is what you'd expect if no difference existed between the column and the whole scope. There are actually 6 Object of links in “Activist”. $E$ is the expected count for a given cell. $n_1$ is the total number of links in the column under test (8 for “Activist”). $k$ is the total number of links of this kind within the entire scope (6 for Object of). $N$ is the total number of links for the particular word within the entire scope (12). Here it counts links, not tokens as in the formula for MI. In the case of “Activist”, $E = 8 times 6/12 = 4$. For “Skeptic” with Adjective modifiers, $E = 4 times 4/12 approx 1.33$. Both counts exceed their respective expected counts, and therefore proceed onto the test. Testing against the project-wide scope or against the rest of it results in the same statistical test, anyway.

Fisher's exact test is a measure of significance for whether chance variation could explain the results you see in the table. Six occurrences where four were expected might mean something, but with 12 links total, there are plenty of possibilities that arise simply due to randomness. The test calculates what proportion of possible tables would give “Activist” six or more Object of links. Suppose you had twelve playing cards representing links. Six of them were marked with the label Object of, and you shuffled all of them prior to picking eight at random for “Activist”. Given no connection between “Stance” and how the word is employed, “Activist” will just draw a hand at random. You want to determine the likelihood that six or more of the eight cards bear the label Object of. To do so, you first need to know how many distinct combinations of $j$ objects you can choose out of $m$ options regardless of order, which follows the formula: This is pronounced “m choose j.” An exclamation point ($!$) after a number denotes its factorial, the multiplication of all integers starting with one up to this number; thus, $4! = 4 times 3 times 2 times 1 = 24$. Of four cards, two can be picked in $binom{4}{2} = 4!/(2!,2!) = 24/(2 times 2) = 6$ combinations. There are combinations of eight that you can extract from the twelve cards. The factors $8 times 7 times dots times 1$ appear in both $12!$ and $8!$, so they cancel out. For a hand with all six Object of cards, you choose all six, which gives one combination; to complete your hand, you choose two additional cards from the rest, which can be done in $binom{6}{2} = (6 times 5)/(2 times 1) = 15$ combinations. No hand can hold more than six Object of cards; thus, there will be 15 favorable outcomes out of the total 495: The probability above constitutes a p-value. That is the chance that six or more links of this type occurred simply due to coincidence under the null hypothesis, which says that the column under consideration consists of randomly sampled word links. This is not the probability of the difference being real. An asterisk added by LemmaLoom implies that there is a less than 5 in 100 chance ($p$ below 0.05) that such a count would arise in random hands. The 0.030 of “Activist” is within that limit; accordingly, LemmaLoom adds a  to its Object of count. Of the twelve cards, “Skeptic” gets four; four of the twelve carry the label Adjective modifiers. In a fashion similar to before, there are $binom{12}{4} = 495$ total hands possible here. To find a hand holding exactly three Adjective modifiers, you take three of the four ($binom{4}{3} = 4$ combinations) alongside a card from among the other eight (eight combinations). That makes 32 hands in total; additionally, there exists a hand including all four Adjective modifiers. Thus, With the p-value exceeding 0.05, an asterisk is not added by LemmaLoom. While three out of four sounds impressive, this count appears nearly seven percent of the time with a random hand. More generally, the p-value is the sum of the probabilities of every count equal to or greater than the observed count: In detail: $a$ is the observed count of links within a cell ($6$ for “Activist”, $3$ for “Skeptic”); $sum$ adds up the fraction for each whole number $x$ from the value below the sign to the value above it; $binom{k}{x}$ counts the combinations to pick $x$ items out of $k$ (number of links of this type); $binom{N-k}{n_1-x}$ counts the ways to fill the remaining positions in the column ($n_1-x$) with other links; $binom{N}{n_1}$ is the total number of combinations for a column of this size; $min(k, n_1)$ refers to the smaller value between $k$ and $n_1$. No column can hold more links than its own size or than there are links of this kind. So with “Skeptic”, you sum the probability values when $x=3$ and $x=4$ ($32/495$ and $1/495$). This test is one-sided since it tests only for abnormally high numbers. If relations occur fewer times than anticipated, no asterisk is assigned to the relation. The activists’ single occurrence of Adjective modifiers receives no asterisk. It is an exact test because it counts every combination possible; thus, it is well suited for small numbers of observations. See Reading the asterisk in  for limitations regarding drawing inferences. Every individual cell is tested separately. It means that having many cells can generate an accidental  on occasion. Columns with small numbers of occurrences seldom receive an asterisk.

Going from a partner to its underlying sentences depends on where the sketch is displayed.  Click a partner on the map Show in context on the map Click a row in the list Inspector, Word Sketch or Code Sketch sketches the partner first occurrence of the partner first occurrence of the partner Word Sketch view and window sketches the partner next place where the two are linked next place where the two are linked Clicking Show in context or picking a row within the inspector will bring you to the first occurrence within the document of your partner word, regardless of whether it is near the word being sketched. Repeating this procedure will send you back to this location, every time. Given that facets follow whatever selections you've made within the reader, your facet will display the sketch of the partner word. You may navigate backward to your previous sketch via Back or by selecting the preceding word in the path above the current sketch. Alternatively, opening the sketch in the Word Sketch window with Open in a window will allow you to investigate the places where the two words are linked, one after another. The preview tab of “Farmers Are Not the Enemy” after Show in context on crisis, with climate selected and the text up to crisis highlighted. In the Word Sketch view or window, clicking Show in context will locate instances where the two words are linked regardless of their relation: The first click opens the document that holds the first such place in the preview tab (see The preview tab in ), or makes its tab active if the document is already open. The reader scrolls to the sentence, selects the sketched word, and highlights the text from it to its partner. Each further click on the same partner moves on to the next place, in the order of the documents' titles and then of the text. After the last place, the next click starts again at the first. If you step to a place in a document that isn't currently open, that document will automatically take over your preview tab. In the case of a prepositional phrase like on fuel, the places considered include all instances of fuel linked to the word sketched, regardless of relation or preposition. Entering a new word in the Word field restarts the process at the first place. When stepping from the Word Sketch tab of either a set or the project, the tab belonging to the document will become active; click on the Word Sketch tab again prior to making the next step. If you would rather keep looking at the sketch during the process, use the Word Sketch window instead.

There is a button in the bar to export the content displayed in your sketch. It looks like a box icon with an arrow. In both Map and Web displays, this button pulls out a menu which lets you choose whether to export your image or a CSV table of the partners. PNG and PDF save a picture of your sketch. In the List display, the button will save your CSV table directly. The export menu in the Word Sketch view of the “Activists” set, offering PNG, PDF, and CSV. Your saved image gets laid out again at a fixed size. This allows eight partners per relation max, which can be more than a narrow inspector shows. Your saved CSV file contains rows for every partner in the sketch, up to 12 per relation. Each row contains Relation, Collocate, Lemma, Part of speech, Frequency, and logDice. Collocate is your partner as shown (on fuel). Lemma is your partner in its lemma form (fuel). Part of speech denotes its word class. If you were viewing a Code Sketch, your Relation column stores the name of your code. A save dialog asks for the directory to which you want to save your exported content. The suggested filename will look something like word-sketch-climate, made from word-sketch- or code-sketch- and the sketched word. Multimode uses this button to export its Sketch Space, as covered in Exporting in .

Once you have coded enough passages in your documents, you can take a look at the distribution of codes, and the ways in which groups of documents may use your codes differently. LemmaLoom’s views count occurrences of each code and how much text it covers. One view displays the location of each code occurrence in each document. Another view shows how different codes co-occur. Views are available for single documents in the Coding tab of the inspector, and for projects, sets, and tags in the project shelf (see The project shelf in ). Additional explanations on setting up codes and coding passages are in . The following demonstrations use LemmaLoom’s example project entitled “Climate Debate” (File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project). LemmaLoom adds “Climate Debate” in the language of the interface, complete with its documents indexed and all codings pre-applied. The “Climate Debate” example project uses the codes “Urgency” (subcodes “Tipping Points” and “Deadlines”), “Science” (“Uncertainty”), “Costs”, “Responsibility”, and “Emotions” (“Fear” and “Hope”). Additionally, “Radio Debate” includes “Speakers” (with the speaker codes “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic” as subcodes), which groups the speaker codes, so that the project's Code Stats lists 13 codes.
