For more information on each relation, see Grammatical relations in . Disabling any sector by clicking its lenslet means that its partners will vanish from the map and the lists. Additionally, the sector's rows fade in the grid, and a partner's evidence list leaves out those relations. Exports leave out disabled sectors too. All and None enable and disable all sectors, respectively. Right-clicking a lenslet offers Enable only this. For example, to see only what the center word does as an object or complement in each column, right-click Objects and choose Enable only this.

Grid brushing establishes a connection between your grid and map so that you can tell which partners belong to a particular row or cell in your grid without opening a list. When you hover your mouse pointer over sections of your grid, the corresponding partners remain highlighted on your map while the rest dim out: Over a relation name like In compounds with, all partners belonging to the relation in all shown columns. Over a grid cell, all partners associated with the cell. Over a column heading, all partners belonging to the column within all visible sectors of your map. In collapsed grids, rows of the profile do the same. When your mouse pointer is hovering over In compounds with in “Running Out of Time”, science, scientist, crisis, policy, and law remain highlighted, but change and protect get dimmed. Once you have clicked a cell, the partners associated with the selected cell will stay highlighted while your mouse pointer is outside your grid. After a click on Object of in the Uncoded column, protect stays bright on the map and the other partners fade.

Changing the center word without leaving the comparison works as follows: Enter a word into the Word field and press Return. In the inspector, the field takes the word in whatever form you give it, so enter the dictionary form, e.g., scientist instead of scientists; the matching process ignores case, and another form yields the message No grammatical partners found for this word. In a set or project, it does not matter what form you enter. Right-click a partner on the map or in the list and click Sketch this word. In the inspector, pick another word from the reader. Every word sketched is stored in a history, which displays in the line Word sketch of with the previous words separated by an arrow, e.g., climate › protect. You may click any previous word in order to revisit it or use the Back and Forward buttons in the bar; View ▸ Word Sketch ▸ Back (⌘[) and Forward (⌘]) do precisely that.

The List display replaces the Map display and uses lists to show your data. Clicking List in the bar will switch displays. The grid precedes the lists, which scroll along with the grid. Every visible column gets its own list, titled with its color, name, and number of occurrences. The List display for money in “Running Out of Time”, with one section per column and colored dots for partners that other columns list too. For each row, the list shows: The partner, followed by sector symbols. Colored circles for up to three other columns containing the same partner. A tooltip reveals their names. Occurrences of the partner appearing alongside the center word in this column, across all its relations. The logDice score achieved by the partner, the maximum among all its relations with the center word. Rows are sorted based on score. Each section displays eight rows initially. Selecting Show all displays all available rows, while selecting Collapse hides all but the top eight rows. Hovering the mouse pointer over a row highlights the corresponding partner in all sections. Clicking on a row brings up its evidence list, and right-clicking it brings up the Sketch this word and Show in context commands. When Sketch Space is very narrow, it always uses the List display. Map and List buttons are disabled, with tooltips saying Pane too narrow. Whether Map or List is selected will be passed on to the word sketch and the Code Sketch (see ). If Web is selected for the word sketch, Sketch Space uses Map.

There is a  marker next to a count if the occurrence frequency of the relation for that column exceeds the rest of the document significantly. In a set or project context, the comparison is done with the rest of the set or project instead. More information on statistical testing can be found in . The criteria for Sketch Space including a , all of which must hold, are the following: There are at least three relations in a cell so that no  would appear on a cell with fewer. The relation in the column occurs more frequently than expected. The probability value returned from the one-sided Fisher's exact test is lower than 0.05. “Running Out of Time” does not have enough content for a . Out of its cells for climate, only one has more than two relations, namely In compounds with under Uncoded. However, the column does not have higher frequencies of compound relations than the document as a whole, with 4 out of 6 versus 6 out of 8. Consider instead another hypothetical longer op-ed piece in which climate takes part in 20 relations. Among all codes, there are only two covering this word (“Science” and “Costs”), and assuming no passage carries both, here are the numbers: Relation Science Costs Uncoded Whole document Subject of 3 · 2 5 Object of 2 1 1 4 Adjective modifiers 3 · · 3 Prepositional phrases · · 2 2 In compounds with 1 4  1 6 All relations 9 5 6 20 The final row and column contain totals, which were added here for illustrative purposes. Only the number 4 under In compounds with in the “Costs” column gets the  marker.

Across the entire document, climate takes part in 20 relations. Out of these, six (or 30%) of the relations are In compounds with. Assuming that the passages in “Costs” would use the term climate similarly to how it is used across the document, 30% of their five relations should be compounds. That equates to 1.5 relations; this figure is called the expected count. In “Costs”, there are actually 4 relations of In compounds with. The formula to calculate the expected count is as follows: Where: $E$ = expected count of the current cell $n_1$ = total number of relations of this column (five in “Costs”) $k$ = total number of relations of this row in the whole document (six for In compounds with) $N$ = number of relations of the center word in the whole document (twenty) $k/N$ gives the share of the particular relation in all relations in the document. For “Costs”, $E = 5 times 6/20 = 1.5$.

That there are four relations but an expectation of 1.5 sounds like quite a difference. “Costs”, however, only contains five relations, and with so few numbers, random variations affect the counts a good deal. Fisher's exact test determines how likely it is for randomness alone to obtain this high a count. The test considers each cell as a table of four counts:  In compounds with Other relations Total Costs 4 1 5 Rest of the document 2 13 15 Total 6 14 20 Consider the 20 relations as 20 playing cards where 6 cards are labeled In compounds with (compound cards). Shuffle the deck of 20 cards and draw 5 random cards into a hand designated “Costs”. In the absence of connection between coding and grammar, the relations in “Costs” would be such a random hand. The hypothesis test seeks the probability $p$ of getting 4 or more compound cards in “Costs”. When calculating the number of ways in which $r$ cards can be chosen from $n$ without taking the order into consideration, the combinations formula gives read “n choose r”, where $n!$ is the factorial function, denoted by the sign $!$ following the number. The factorial refers to the multiplication of integers beginning from one up to the number itself. Thus, $5! = 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1 = 120$. For instance, two out of four cards can be picked in $binom{4}{2} = 4!/(2!,2!) = 24/(2 times 2) = 6$ different ways, namely AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, and CD. Choosing five cards out of twenty, $binom{20}{5} = 20!/(5!,15!)$, will involve many terms above and below the fraction line that will cancel. Only the first five terms above the line and the five below it remain, Thus, there are 15,504 different possible combinations of five-card hands from 20 distinct cards. A hand with exactly four compound cards involves picking 4 cards out of six in $binom{6}{4}$ ways, multiplied by choosing the fifth, non-compound card from the remaining fourteen cards. $binom{6}{4} = 720/(24 times 2) = 15$, and thus $15 times 14 = 210$. A hand of exactly five compound cards involves picking five cards out of six, $binom{6}{5} = 6$, and zero cards from the fourteen others ($binom{14}{0} = 1$); hence 6 total. Consequently, 216 hands satisfy the criteria, and the p-value is Counting for all the possible numbers of compound cards shows how unusual the value 4 is: Compound cards in the hand Hands Share of all hands 0 2,002 0.129 1 6,006 0.387 2 5,460 0.352 3 1,820 0.117 4 210 0.014 5 6 0.0004 Most random hands hold one or two compound cards, as the expected count of 1.5 suggests. Random hands containing four or more compound cards occur in only around 14 hands per 1,000. The ratio here is referred to as the p-value, the probability of observing a value greater than or equal to the value in question if the column were drawn randomly from the word's relations. The p-value is not the likelihood of an effect existing, however. When $p$ is below 0.05 (that is, a count would arise fewer than five times in 100 draws), Sketch Space adds a , indicating significant deviation. The threshold value of 0.05 is merely a tradition practiced commonly in the social sciences. With a p-value of 0.014, “Costs” has obtained a  on its In compounds with count. The formula for calculating the p-value involves summing the fraction for every count starting from the observed value. Where: $a$ is the count of the observed cell. The value for “Costs” is 4. $x$ is each integer from $a$ (inclusive) up to the limit $min(k,,n_1)$, indicated underneath and above $sum$, respectively. The sign $sum$ means “add up the fraction for each of these values of $x$”. $binom{k}{x}$ is the number of ways of choosing $x$ items among $k$ possibilities. This corresponds to choosing which compounds will be used. $binom{N-k}{n_1-x}$ counts the ways of choosing the remaining entries in the column among $N-k$. These would be non-compounds. $binom{N}{n_1}$ counts all possibilities of drawing $n_1$ items out of $N$. This corresponds to all the possible combinations. $min(k, n_1)$ is the minimum between $k$ and $n_1$, meaning no hand has more than $n_1$ items or more compounds than the $k$ that exist. As such, the $x$ of “Costs” ranges from 4 to 5 (5 being the smaller of 6 and 5). Their corresponding fractions are $210/15{,}504$ and $6/15{,}504$, respectively. The test is one-sided in nature since it searches for values only above what is expected. A relation that occurs in a column less frequently than anticipated will never get a . Additionally, the test is exact as it considers every possible hand.

“Science” has three relations under Subject of, out of nine overall. Given five Subject of relations in total, the expectation is $9 times 5/20 = 2.25$. While three is greater than this expectation, it is close. If nine cards were dealt from twenty, five being Subject of, then for $x$ taking on values between three and five inclusive, the probability of $x$ being greater than or equal to three would be: In random circumstances, “Science” should get three or more Subject of relations approximately 40 times in 100. No  marks appear here, since the probability of a random hand having three or more is high. All three Adjective modifiers relations in the document belong to “Science”. The expected count is $9 times 3/20 = 1.35$. Now $x$ takes only the value three, as there are only three such relations, and the probability would be: There is no , since the probability of getting all three Adjective modifiers is 0.074, above 0.05, or about 7 times in 100. Yet no other column has Adjective modifiers relations.

A  indicates that the count would be unusually high if the column represented a random sample of the word's relations. The reason behind it is not explained, however. Tests are conducted individually for each cell. In a grid containing six columns and twelve relations, the maximum number of cells is 72. Even in those cases where no real difference exists, up to 1 out of every 20 cells can receive a . A large grid may therefore display a stray  or two. For testing, the relations are treated like individual cards shuffled randomly in a deck. Documents are different from that, however; writers tend to repeat themselves, and a single paragraph coded “Costs” could provide multiple relations involving the exact same partner. Repeating oneself increases the chances of receiving a  beyond what the p-value indicates. An absence of  does not necessarily indicate similarity among the columns either. With smaller columns, the test usually fails to reach 0.05; refer to the Adjective modifiers example above for illustration. When the test is done with larger sets or projects, which can involve thousands of relations, even small differences receive  markers. Note, however, that the  symbol does not describe how big the difference is. Instead, you should compare the cells' percentages yourself. Your own codes create the columns, which means that any occurrences coded “Costs” partly because they referred to a climate levy or a climate tax include an intrinsic connection to In compounds with. When an occurrence relates to two different codes, the occurrence gets counted twice, once in each corresponding column. Hence, the two columns are not independent groups. Refer to  and  for guidance on comparing document groups via statistics.

t: Sketch Space for sets and projects
b: For your set, tag, or even whole project, Sketch Space analyzes every document simultaneously. With several documents, the number of occurrences in your columns becomes large enough for differences to stand out.

t: Opening Sketch Space for a set or project
b: Open the Word Sketch view for the material you want to compare, in one of these ways: For the project, click Word Sketch under Project in the navigation sidebar. In the sidebar, click the set or tag, then click Word Sketch among the buttons in its tab. Right-click on either the project, a set, or a tag in the sidebar, and click Word Sketch. This opens the Word Sketch window. Type a word in the Word field and press Return. Any form will do, so scientists finds scientist. Click Multimode in the mode control, next to Grammar and Coding, or choose View ▸ Word Sketch ▸ Multimode (⌘3). For more information on the other two modes, see . While preparing documents, LemmaLoom displays Preparing, along with a count of prepared documents. All three modes share the bar at the top, which contains the Back and Forward buttons, the Word field, the mode control, the Map, List, and Web options, and the export button. The Web option is disabled in Multimode, and upon hovering, its tooltip reads Web is not available in this mode. Opening the Word Sketch view in the Word Sketch window requires clicking the Open in a window button, located at the rightmost edge of the bar, with two arrows going diagonally across it. When documents in your scope contain translations, you will find a menu next to the export button, showing Originals initially, with the tooltip Source. Under Corpus, this menu allows you to toggle the corpus used for analysis among Originals, as well as each translation language; for instance, you may find Translations (German). See  for additional information on translation corpora. Within the Word Sketch window, the menu appears regardless of whether there are translations or not. Within this menu, the Scope section switches between the project level, set or tag level, and the document open in the reader. The menu then shows the scope's name, such as “Climate Debate”, followed by the corpus when translations are included. Once the document is selected, Sketch Space behaves similarly to its counterpart in the inspector, except that you change the center word with the Word field or Sketch this word. Everything explained above for a single document applies here as well, but with slight modifications: Unindexed documents are omitted during analysis. At the bottom, LemmaLoom notes how many documents are included, for example 13 of 14 documents indexed. Changing the center word involves typing in the Word field or using Sketch this word. The center word applies to all three modes and persists after switching between modes. To qualify for appearing on the map or lists, the partner needs to occur at least twice in the same relation and column. Single occurrences still count in the grid, though. In evidence lists, titles precede each document's sentences. Clicking a row opens the document in the reader and shows the particular sentence. A  compares the column with the rest of the set or project. If there are no codings in any document in the scope, the note reads No Codings.

A code can be confined to a particular document, too, as seen in . If there are such codes in any documents contained within a set or a project, the latter shows their names with the document's title in parentheses afterward, shortened when the title is long, to indicate this restriction. As seen in the “Climate Debate” project, for instance, there are codes specifically for each speaker of “Radio Debate”. Hence, the project's columns can include “Host (Radio Debate)”. If documents within the scope of your analysis have codes of their own, the Include document codes checkbox appears right beside the codes menu. It comes pre-selected with a tooltip saying Also group partners by codes that belong to a single document. You should keep this checkbox selected whenever these codes contribute toward answering your question, like those of the speakers in “Radio Debate”, and deselect it otherwise. When deselected, occurrences coded this way would still contribute toward any code other than these on the passage, or toward Uncoded. This checkbox and the one in the Coding mode are the same setting. Sketch Space for climate in the project “Climate Debate”, with Include document codes selected and a column for “Host (Radio Debate)”.

Attribute columns in a set or project consist of document attribute values as opposed to codes, and each column stores occurrences of the center word in documents that fall under that particular attribute value, coded or not. They should be used whenever your question concerns attributes of the document itself, such as who wrote it or where it appeared. The “Climate Debate” project contains several attributes including “Stance” (“Activist”, “Skeptic”, or “Neutral”), “Readership”, and “Outlet”, among others. The following figure compares climate mentions among all three “Stance” values. In the Word Sketch window, Multimode compares climate across the values of the “Stance” attribute. The second menu of Sketch Space in the Word Sketch view of “Climate Debate”, listing the attributes of the project. For comparing a word based on the values of an attribute: Open Sketch Space for a set or the project, and sketch the word. Below the line Word sketch of, click the menu that shows Codes, to the left of All Codes, and choose Attribute. This menu appears when the project has attributes. A second menu appears beside it, showing the name of the first attribute. In the second menu, choose the attribute whose values you want as columns. The legend, now renamed Attribute, contains one lenslet for every value. Documents without a value will form the final column named No value. How the values turn into columns depends on the attribute's type: Type Columns Text one per value Picker one per value, in the order of the picker's options Boolean Yes and No Integer and Decimal up to four ranges, each holding about a quarter of the documents Date one per year When working with numbers, LemmaLoom ranks the value of each document within the scope, and it places three range boundaries. It multiplies the number of values by ¼, ½, and ¾, discards the fractional part, and chooses the value after that many. Within the “Climate Debate” project, the fourteen original documents have “Readership” values of 3.1k, 8.5k, 23k, 41k, 57k, 68k, 72k, 96k, 186k, 254k, 310k, 398k, 412k, and 875k. For the highest boundary, 14 × ¾ = 10.5; hence, it becomes the 11th value. The boundaries become the 4th, 8th, and 11th values, namely 41,000, 96,000, and 310,000. The columns are, therefore, < 41000, 41000 to under 96000, 96000 to under 310000, and ≥ 310000, containing 3, 4, 3, and 4 documents, respectively. Repetition of values might cause two boundaries to converge into one, leaving fewer ranges. Where most of the documents possess the lowest value, so no boundary exceeds this value, Sketch Space creates columns for individual values instead. A translation contributes with the value of its original document. Column colors are taken in order from the code color palette, and evidence list dots display these colors accordingly. Like code columns, attribute columns possess similar characteristics. At most six columns appear on screen at a time, and the first six values that occur are displayed initially. A  indicates that documents under the column use the relation more often than other documents in the scope. Note, however, that it may rest upon the occurrences within only one document because it is counted by relation rather than document; thus, it is necessary to look into the document headings within the evidence list. Selecting Codes or Attribute in the first menu, or changing the attribute, closes the evidence list immediately. Select any attribute whose values differ within the scope. Each document under the “Activists” set possesses “Stance” value “Activist”; hence, comparison should be done based on “Readership” or “Outlet”.

In the bar at the top of Sketch Space, there is a button of a square icon with an upward arrow; it saves what Sketch Space shows. While there is nothing to export, the button becomes disabled, and its tooltip becomes Nothing to export. In the Map display mode, clicking this button shows a menu. PNG and PDF save a picture of the map itself; CSV saves the data table. In the List display mode, clicking the button will prompt a save dialog for the CSV table directly. The export menu of Sketch Space in the Word Sketch view of “Climate Debate”, offering PNG, PDF, and CSV. Whatever visualizations you have in the Map display, including the current columns and sector settings, will be included in the exported picture. For a CSV export, the exported table will consist of rows corresponding to each partner in each relation and column, and the headers will be Code (or Attribute), Relation, Collocate, Lemma, Part of speech, Frequency, and logDice. Collocate is the partner as shown in the visualization, such as without warming; Lemma is its dictionary form. Only each cell's top 12 partners available for maps will be exported, and disabled columns and sectors are left out. As usual, a save dialog asks you to provide a location to store the exported file. Its default filename suggestion will be based on sketch-space- and the center word, sketch-space-climate for instance.

A query searches through your documents to find elements that satisfy certain criteria you provide, and shows them as a list or as numbers. These elements may be words, phrases, sentences, coded passages, memos, speaker turns, documents, and codes themselves. Typically, queries originate from questions about the nature of your documents. For example, in the project “Climate Debate”, you may wish to know which sentences contain crisis or deadline within passages coded as “Urgency” in the activists’ documents. You might also wonder which documents currently lack “Costs” codings, or which words occur within five words of an “Emotions” coding. When building a query, you use conditions, one for each part of the question, with the outcome displayed beneath the conditions. Queries aim to help answer questions involving multiple criteria, like words, codes, and attributes together. If you simply want to explore the use of individual words, consider doing a word sketch instead (see ). For further details on interpreting the output of queries and statistics used in them, refer to . More information on grammatical queries and Query from Selection is available in . Creating a query-based lens, analyzer, or document set is covered in .

The following glossary applies to all four query chapters. Scope refers to which part of your library is queried. Scope options include one document, a set, a project, and all projects. Unit refers to the entity that the query is searching for. This option can be selected in the Find condition; everything found in a query is referred to as a hit. Rule refers to a test applied upon one property of the hit, such as Lemma is climate or Stance is any of “Activist”. Field refers to the property that a rule operates on. Examples of fields include a word's lemma, a sentence's number, a coding's code, and a document's attributes. Lemma refers to the dictionary form of a word (e.g., warned and warns → warn), thus joining its forms together (see ). Group refers to a collection of rules with an operator of All, Any, or None between them. A context row is similar to the regular rules except that it operates outside the hit and tests surrounding units, such as whether the hit overlaps with a passage coded “Urgency”. A Has row is a row that counts something belonging to the hit. For instance, it can count how many codings there are on a particular document. Category refers to labels and colors that get assigned to certain hits. Category becomes important mostly in lenses. Recipe refers to pre-made queries that one loads before modifying them according to need. Saved query refers to a query that is kept with a specific name for access within a document, set, project, or globally throughout LemmaLoom.

Queries may be constructed in one of three locations, all with the same builder, and which one to use depends mostly upon which documents you wish to query. When viewing a document, the inspector maintains a query next to your text. For queries across multiple documents in a set or entire project, use its Queries view; for many projects simultaneously, there is the Queries window. Place How to open it Scope Query facet in the inspector The Multimode tab of a document's inspector, then Query The document Queries view Queries under Project in the navigation sidebar, or Queries at the top of a set's tab The project or the set Window ▸ Queries The Window menu All projects, one project, or one of its sets Queries will be kept wherever they were created until LemmaLoom quits. If you start building a query in the “Activists” set and switch to reading “Running Out of Time”, the unfinished query stays in that set. b: To access the Queries view of a set: Click the set under Sets in the sidebar. The set opens in a tab of its own. In the row of buttons at the top of the tab, click Queries. In a narrow window the row is a menu; choose Queries from it. Click Queries under Project in the sidebar to open the Queries view for your whole project. Like a set, a tag in the sidebar opens in a tab that has a Queries view. This view gives the builder plenty of room. At the very top is a single header row with access to the menu of your saved queries, a query search field, and the Run Query and Save buttons (see The builder below). Below this header row is a narrow column on the left listing your saved queries, followed by the recipes, while the builder takes up all the room that remains. Results will span the entire width directly below everything, and you can adjust the room each part gets using a divider in between. The Find, Where, and Show conditions begin expanded upon loading; if you have the Pattern condition visible, this condition starts expanded too. Each of these conditions expands and collapses individually. When you double-click a result hit, the document opens in a preview tab and scrolls directly to that passage. The Queries view of the “Activists” set with the “Urgency Talk” query loaded and Open in a window at the right end of the header row. Should you need more space for your query, or want to leave it open next to the reader, click Open in a window, the button with two diagonal arrows at the right end of the header row. Alternatively, you could right-click on the tab itself and click Open in New Window. The Queries window will appear containing a duplicate copy of the current query, including any changes you haven't yet saved. The set or project keeps its own copy. Open in a window will always direct your query to the first Queries window. Your query will overwrite whatever previous query the Queries window had open, including unsaved changes to that query.

The Queries window is the place for queries across all of your projects. It is also meant for having your queries of projects or sets opened alongside your reader at once. Open the Queries window via Window ▸ Queries, or bring it to the front if it is already open. Queries windows share the very same interface as Queries views, with a scope menu located on the left edge of their headers. This menu provides options for All Projects, your projects by name, and the sets from your active project, displayed as “Climate Debate › Activists”. Upon first opening the window, the selected scope is All Projects and your query builder contains an empty query. Selecting another scope leaves the current query inside your query builder; however, it will switch its focus toward analyzing the selected scope's documents. The scope menu of a Queries window, listing All Projects, “Climate Debate”, and the sets of “Climate Debate”. Only when the selected scope is All Projects can you refer to a document's Project field and/or group results by projects. For more details on cross-project features, check out Working across projects in . The Queries window with the scope set to the “Activists” set and the “Urgency Talk” query loaded. Working simultaneously with two queries, such as a query and its variant, can be accomplished by choosing New Window from the Actions menu of a Queries window. Actions appears as a circled ellipsis button in the header row of any Queries window. The new window starts with a new query in the same scope. Any query currently displayed in such a window will be lost upon closing the window unless saved beforehand.

Scope also determines what offerings are made by the builder. Rules related to attributes of a document, for instance, come up when queries look at multiple documents. In this example, you recreate “Urgency Talk”, which is provided in the example project. The query looks for any sentence containing either urgent, urgency, crisis, emergency, or deadline and overlapping with a passage coded “Urgency” within any document in the set of activists' texts. Once you recreate your version of the query, you'll save it separately, allowing comparison later on. Click “Activists” under Sets in the navigation sidebar, then click Queries at the top of the set's tab. In the Find condition, choose Text · Sentences. In the Where condition, click Add and choose Add Text. A text row appears, set to Word and Terms. Change Word to Lemma, so that plural forms such as deadlines count as well. Click in Add term, type urgent, urgency, crisis, emergency, deadline, and press Return. Each term is listed on its own. Click Add again and choose Add Context. Leave the row at Some, Overlapping, and Codings. Click the Add button inside the context row and choose Add Rule. Click the rule's field and choose Code from the Coding section of the menu. The comparison becomes is any of. Click the value, which shows None, and check “Urgency”. Include Subcodes is already checked, so codings with “Deadlines” and “Tipping Points” count as well. Your results list will automatically get populated with sentences as you work on a small set like “Activists”, since such a small set will automatically run its query whenever the query is changed (see Running a query below). By clicking Query Text, you may view the actual query text: To retain your query: Open the Save menu (the square with an arrow pointing into it) and choose Save as Lens…. Type Urgency Talk 2 in Name. LemmaLoom accepts a name that is already taken, but two queries both called “Urgency Talk” would be hard to tell apart. Choose Project in Available In and click Save. Your query is available in each Queries view of your project and in Query facets on all of your documents right alongside “Urgency Talk”. You may select it as a lens in your reader's lens menu as well (see ); when comparing to the original, you would select “Urgency Talk” from the query's name at the left of the header, or click it in the left-hand column. Begin by selecting your desired unit from the Find condition, then add rules in your Where condition step by step while noting the effect of each added rule. If any particular rule causes you to lose hits unexpectedly, modify your query accordingly.

The header row includes, from left to right: the query's name, which acts as a menu to access the saved queries available here, and New Query sits at the bottom. The presence of a dot next to the name (e.g., “Urgency Talk” •) indicates that you made unsaved edits to that particular query; a search field, which restricts the list of saved queries and recipes on the left-hand side to those including your typed string in their names; Run Query (a triangle icon), which changes to Stop while the query runs; Save (an icon of a square with an arrow going inside); Actions (a circled three dots icon), which provides commands on the results, such as Create Set from Hits; Open in a window (diagonal double arrows), within the Queries view of a set or the project. The query name menu in the header of the Queries view of “Activists”, listing the saved queries and New Query. For Queries windows specifically, there will be a scope menu at the left of the header row. When the window is narrow enough, the Run Query, Save, and Actions icons go onto a second row below the header. Lastly, Export (square with an arrow pointing upwards) resides in the bar above the results when there are actually results (see Exporting results in ). In the inspector's Query facet, the header includes the query's name, Recipes icon (wand), Run Query, Save, Actions, and Export. The header will potentially wrap onto two lines depending on the inspector's width. After the header come the conditions, which are: Condition What it holds Find The unit, and for Text Matches the text to look for Pattern A sequence, dependency, or phrase pattern, shown only for Pattern Matches Where Rules, groups, text, context, and Has rows Show How the results are presented, such as a list, counts, or a comparison Categories Labels and colors for hits Options Translations, coded memos, and how many hits a list keeps Query Text The whole query written out as text On a closed condition, the right side shows a summary, such as the unit, type of result, or number of rules or categories (e.g., 3 rules). When starting a query using the command Edit ▸ Query from Selection, a row of options based on the selected terms will appear above the conditions. More information regarding this option can be found in Query from Selection in .

Each row of the results represents the unit of analysis, meaning whatever you want to read or count. Sentences tend to work best if you need to find something regarding your topic, whereas codings should be used for any questions related to your own codings. From the dropdown list under Find, the units will appear according to kind, with each entry reading as kind and unit, e.g., Text · Sentences or Annotations · Codings. By default, a new query retrieves Text · Words and shows a List. The Find menu in the Queries view of the “Activists” set, listing the units by kind. Kind Unit One hit is Text Words A word or a punctuation mark Text Pattern Matches A stretch of text that matches the Pattern condition Text Sentences A sentence Text Paragraphs A paragraph Text Text Matches One occurrence of the text set in the Find condition Grammar Phrases A phrase from the sentence's phrase structure, such as a noun phrase or a prepositional phrase Grammar Noun Chunks A noun with the words that belong to it, such as the climate crisis Analysis Findings A passage annotated by the Cohesion, Metadiscourse, or Rhetoric analyzer, or by one of your own analyzers Annotations Codings A coded passage Annotations Memos A memo. A memo on the whole document covers the whole text Annotations Bookmarks A bookmark Annotations Links One end of a link Media Speaker Turns A turn in a transcript Translation Alignments A segment of a document paired with its counterpart in a translation Library Documents, Codes, Code Sets, Sets, Groups, Attributes, Tags, Dictionary Terms, Analyzers, Projects One item of that kind Words, Pattern Matches, Sentences, Phrases, Noun Chunks, and Findings will require the document to be indexed prior to analysis. An unindexed document will be ignored in the process, with the number beside the hit count, such as 5 of 6, indicating how many documents were read. Other units do not need indexing. See  for specifics on the benefits of indexing in each language. Library units locate items rather than passages. As a consequence, their result tables contain one row per found item, rather than one per found passage. Document results display the document title, authors, date, language, group membership, tags, and token count. Code columns such as Codings and Coded Documents restrict their counts to the query's scope and to the codes themselves. With regard to the “Activists” set, these code columns restrict their scope to the codings within activist texts. When switching units, all incompatible rules are dropped. This includes incompatible Group By keys, too. The sorting reverts to Document Order; likewise, the Show condition reverts to List if it was previously set to something that is now unavailable due to the switch. Context and text rows, as well as Has rows, remain in place and need checking to ensure compatibility with the current unit. A Has row will only be compatible with the units listed under Has. Similarly, a context row will only work for passage units and Documents. A row left over from the old unit empties the results, so remove it.

The Pattern Matches unit brings the Pattern condition into the interface below the Find condition. Patterns describe stretches of text according to their grammar, thus making them useful for queries regarding constructions such as the pairing of verbs and objects regardless of what actual lexical content they may take on. The Pattern condition supports three different modes, including Sequence (a sequence of words separated by optional gaps), Dependency (words connected by grammatical dependency relationships), and Phrase (of a particular phrasal type). For more information on patterns, see .

Hit criteria are defined by the rows in the Where condition. An initially empty Where condition considers everything in the scope as hits; therefore, an empty query over Sentences considers all sentences as hits. At the bottom of the condition lies the Add menu for five possible types of rows to be added: Add Rule adds a rule on one field. Add Group adds a sub-group of rows (see Groups below). Add Text adds a search criterion over text content (see Matching text). Add Context adds a criterion based on context, specifically on other units surrounding the hit (see Context); it is available only to units that represent text passages. Add Has adds a criterion based on items associated with the hit (see Has); it is available only to documents, codes, code sets, sets, groups, tags, and projects. The Add menu of a Where condition in a query for Words. Clicking the minus button next to a row deletes it from the condition.

Both “Stance” and “Readership” are attributes of each document in the “Climate Debate” project. By setting rules on both attributes within a Library · Documents query in the project, you can extract only the widely read activist documents. The query identifies two documents, “Running Out of Time” and “Letter from the Climate Strike”. The query text would look like this: To add a rule: In Where, click Add and choose Add Rule. A rule appears with a field already chosen, outlined in red because it has no value yet. Click the field and choose the property to test, such as Attribute ▸ Stance. Choose a comparison, such as is any of or is at least. Enter the value in Value, or click the value and check the ones that should count. When there is more than one row, a control with options for All, Any, and None appears at the top of the condition. Under All, as in the previous example's query, the document needs to satisfy both rules. Rules with blank values (e.g., Readership is at least with an empty Value field) are not considered until values are entered.

The field menu gives you access to fields relevant to your unit in sections. Fields in your current unit appear first, followed by fields in higher-level units containing the former. If your unit is Words, the five sections would be Word, Sentence, Paragraph, Passage, and Document. When you use a field from outside of the current unit's section, the name of its section will precede it; an example would be Sentence · Passive when searching among words. Three items in particular give you access to another menu. Attribute provides the list of document attributes in your current project. Some examples include “Stance” and “Publication Date”. Statistic offers the list of statistical properties of documents covered in . These properties include Avg. sentence length and Lexical density. Code Attribute, under Coding, provides the attributes of codes, whose values you may define per coding.
