Comparisons allowed by rules depend on the type of values contained within the field. Kind of field Examples Comparisons Text Title, Lemma, Comment, Outlet is, is not, contains, does not contain, matches, is empty, is not empty Number Tokens, Length, Readership is, is not, is less than, is at most, is greater than, is at least, is between, is empty, is not empty Duration Media Duration, Start, Duration The same as for numbers Date Date, Created, Publication Date is, is before, is after, is on or after, is on or before, is between, is empty, is not empty Yes or no Passive, Stopword, Has Media is true, is false, is empty One value from a list Code, Word Class, Group, Speaker, Color, Stance is any of, is none of, is empty, is not empty Several values Tags has any of, has all of, has none of, is empty, is not empty Language and format Language, Format is any of, is none of Values are entered in relation to their respective types: Text and numeric values are provided directly to the Value field. is between displays two fields. Date values can be selected from a date picker. It begins by default on the current day, although the rule will not take effect until you modify it. Duration values should be entered as minutes and seconds (12:30) or as hours, minutes, and seconds (1:05:00). Single numbers represent seconds. List item values appear as checkboxes in a small panel that opens when you click the value; once checked, the value will show “Activist” or “Skeptic” etc.; None indicates that none are currently selected. Text values are case insensitive when compared in LemmaLoom. Differences such as diacritics or wide/narrow variations of characters (Ａ vs. A) do not matter either. As such, if you search with Title contains climate, you get results such as “Letter from the Climate Strike”. matches looks for a match on the whole value and allows wildcards ( replaces sequences, while ? replaces any single character). Title matches Wh?  gives you “Who Pays for the Transition” and “Why We Block the Roads”. Meanwhile, Title matches Time yields “Running Out of Time”, yet does not match “Running Out of Time (German)” because it requires the pattern to match the whole title value. Codes are listed with their paths in the Code field, e.g., “Urgency › Deadlines”. Within sets or projects, a code unique to a particular document comes with the document's title attached to it. Right underneath Code rules sits an Include Subcodes option, which is enabled by default, meaning that “Emotions” includes its subcodes “Fear” and “Hope”. The value panel of a Code rule in a Codings query, with “Urgency” checked and Include Subcodes checked beneath the value. Tag (a word's grammatical tag, not your own tags) lists the tag sets used for languages within the scope. Likewise, Dependency lists dependency relation sets and Phrase Label lists phrase label sets. When the scope contains more than one language, the entries in these three fields carry language badges, since English, German, and Chinese use different tag sets.

The control at the top of conditions and groups (All, Any, or None) determines what happens to those hits that comply with their rules. In other words, this control defines whether the condition/group keeps all hits complying with all the rules it holds (All), with any of the rules it holds (Any), or with none of the rules (None). The feature that makes groups special compared to regular conditions is their ability to combine an or within an and. Say, for example, that one wishes to locate “Emotions” codings in widely read texts of the “Climate Debate” project and in skeptic texts regardless of their readership. One may use a query targeting Annotations · Codings in “Climate Debate”. Within that query, there exists a rule for when Code is any of “Emotions”, with Include Subcodes checked. Underneath this rule lies a group set to Any. This group contains two criteria, namely that Readership is at least 100,000, and that Stance is any of “Skeptic”. The condition stays at All. The query text shows the group in parentheses: A Where condition with a Code rule and a nested Any group. To add a group: In Where, click Add and choose Add Group. The new group starts with Any and one rule. Set up that rule as you would any other. To add more rules to the group, click the group's own Add button and choose Add Rule. A rule cannot exceed nesting of three layers, although the Add menu permits nesting beyond the limit. While having a sub-group inside of a group is fine, nesting a group inside of that sub-group is considered nesting too deeply. Context and Has rows each account for two layers. On the Where condition itself, these rows may hold only rules. Inside groups, on the other hand, rules within these rows would be nesting too deeply already. Nesting too deeply results in the rule having a red outline (Too deeply nested), and the query waits until it is removed.

A frozen list is a list of words stored inside the query itself. You can create a frozen list from the results of Collocates or Keywords queries, via the Actions menu option Freeze Values (see ). Passages Like a Code also creates a frozen list (see Passages Like a Code in ). Freeze Values replaces the existing query with a new, unsaved Words query. It has only one rule, comparing the field the query counted by (Lemma, Word, or Word Class) to the words in the list. This new query and frozen list retain the name of the query you froze. Up to 200 words may be saved, each paired with its score from the results. Your query text shows the frozen list by name, such as Lemma is any of "Keywords: Activists". The words inside these lists won’t change, even as your documents evolve. To see where the activists’ keywords appear in the skeptics' texts, save the frozen query for the project and open it in the “Skeptics” set. When looking at the Where condition for a query with a frozen list, Lemma and Word rules will appear with the setting None selected. If you have Word Class rules, your frozen list will actually be evaluated against the available word classes and each class will either be checked or unchecked accordingly. Checking/unchecking individual classes removes the frozen list and uses your selection instead. Removing your frozen list from a query requires removing its rule. The Where condition of the “Keywords” query in the “Activists” set after Freeze Values, with a Lemma rule whose value reads None. Queries with frozen lists offer an additional sort order option for their resulting lists, Score, which ranks passages by the frozen words they contain. For more information on the score, see .

Two methods are possible for searching either words or characters. When you use Add Text in the Where condition, you add a text row to your query's rules as a hit requirement. As a consequence, your hit sentences contain one of your terms. If you use Text · Text Matches in Find, however, each match becomes a separate hit. The same text row appears in the Find condition. Text rows contain two menus. Through the first menu, you define which element your terms should match, and through the second menu, starting with Terms, where those terms come from. After entering your terms under the menus, use the two checkboxes Match Case and Whole Words.

First menu Compares each term with Capitals Accents Word Each word as it is written Ignored, unless Match Case is checked Ignored, unless Match Case is checked Word Form Each word's dictionary form Ignored Significant Lemma Each word's dictionary form Ignored Ignored Text The characters of the text, wherever they occur Ignored, unless Match Case is checked Ignored Lemma is normally going to give the best results for words. This is because all inflections of a given word will be matched in a search. Word is better suited if knowing precisely what form occurred is important for your analysis. This includes, for instance, singling out a word such as emergency as opposed to emergencies. Word Form does exactly the same as Lemma, except that accents are differentiated; thus, German schon and schön are considered different in Word Form but not in Lemma. All three of these options (Word Form, Word, and Lemma) match full-word occurrences according to indexing. Multiword terms must perfectly overlap adjacent words in order, uninterrupted and within a single sentence. The hyphen symbol is removed before matching, meaning that searching for carbon-neutral will return results containing both carbon-neutral and carbon neutral. If there is no indexing on a document, all three behave the same as choosing Text. Text matches literal instances of symbols instead of full-word matches based off of indexing, as Word Form, Word, and Lemma do. Choosing Whole Words restricts matches so that they occur only when no preceding or following character position contains letters or numerals. Unselecting it allows searching for words nested within longer sequences of characters. Whole Words influences Text exclusively. Every word of a term must be typed in its dictionary form for both Word Form and Lemma; this implies typing the term it seem rather than it seems, since its dictionary form is seem. Or use Word instead. New text rows in the Where condition default to Word when units require indexing such as Sentences, while for other units, such as Codings, they default to Text. Similarly, Text Matches defaults to Text. In searching Codes or Sets, text rows locate matches regardless of case or accent. They search for occurrences of any plain terms within the names, so point matches “Tipping Points”. Searching Documents uses a text row to scan document texts. Of the library units, text rows are applicable solely to these three.

In Terms mode, you manually input terms. Click in Add term. Type a term and press Return. To add several at once, separate them with commas, as in crisis, emergency, deadline. To remove a term, click the cross beside it. Here terms are alternate criteria such that a hit satisfies at least one of them. If a text row contains no terms, then LemmaLoom disregards the row.

In Dictionary mode, the terms come straight out of one of your dictionaries in the project. For example, “Climate Debate” has a dictionary labeled “Hedges” containing two categories, “Approximators” and “Shields”. The figure below depicts querying “Shields” in a text row. A text row that looks for the “Shields” category of the “Hedges” dictionary. To search with a dictionary: In the second menu, choose Dictionary. Choose the dictionary from the menu that appears. To limit the search to some categories, click the control below the dictionary and check them in the panel that opens. With nothing checked, the control shows None and every category is used. The dictionary is accessed with each run of your query; therefore, whenever you add a term to “Hedges”, it becomes searchable on the next execution. The first menu and both checkboxes pertain to all of your terms within your dictionary. The dictionary “Hedges” consists of phrasings as they are spoken, like it seems or more or less. Thus, Word is a better choice than Lemma for this particular dictionary. Further details regarding dictionary matches in the dictionary lens can be found in . Upon finding Text Matches via dictionaries, each matched instance also includes the dictionary category of the matched term. When a key row of the Show condition is set to Category, the matches will be counted based on their categories; this is how the Dictionary Categories by Document recipe works.

A regular expression is a string pattern of characters. This is handy if you are looking for items that vary beyond what can be defined as a list of terms, such as spelling variations. The pattern models?, for example, would locate both the words model and models, since the ? sign indicates that the preceding character is optional; it will also match model in the word modelers. Similarly, bheat- ]?waves?\b` will return results for *heat wave*, *heat-wave*, *heatwave*, and *heat waves*. In this instance, the `[- ]` pattern matches either a hyphen or space, and `\b` matches a word boundary. More building blocks are listed in [Excluding text from indexing in . In the second menu, choose Regular Expression. Type the pattern in Pattern. A regular expression will search all of the characters in your text regardless of the first menu option. Unless Match Case is checked, capitals are ignored; however, accents always count. Word boundaries must be specified by placing b around your pattern. Patterns cannot exceed 1,000 characters in length. If LemmaLoom cannot read the pattern, it is highlighted with a red border and the query waits for correction. The results area says Invalid pattern, and so does the row when you hover the mouse pointer over it.

Since Chinese does not separate words with spaces, the beginning and end of a Chinese search term with Word, Word Form, or Lemma have to match word boundaries found during indexing. Terms can consist of multiple words. The term 科学 (science) will match if the index identifies either 科学 as one word or 科 and 学 as two separate words. A longer word like 科学家 (scientist) is a different word for LemmaLoom. Any spaces in your term are disregarded. If you choose Text, then LemmaLoom matches the occurrences of a Chinese term regardless of where in other words those characters occur. Whole Words does not apply here. If you are unsure how indexing splits a word, use Text.

Context rows control whether hits stay or get discarded based on surrounding units. Context rows are typical means of relating your codes to text passages; they find, for example, the words inside passages you have coded with “Urgency”, or the sentences which remain uncoded. Context rows read as a phrase from left to right. So in the case of Some Overlapping Codings, LemmaLoom keeps any hits overlapping any coding. Below the row, you add rules for the other units. For example, the first query uses a context row with the rule Code is any of “Urgency”. Each new context row begins with Some, Overlapping, and Codings. In the first menu, you choose how many other units you require: Some denotes a minimum of one. No requires zero other units. At Least requires a minimum of the stepper number, ranging from 1 to 99. At Most allows no more than the stepper number, including zero as well. The second menu sets the relationship between the units, while the third menu allows for specifying what the other units are, which can be any passage unit. Pattern Matches and Text Matches appear in the third menu only when Find uses that same unit. Changing the unit removes the rules under the row. Relation The hit counts when it Overlapping Shares at least one character with the other unit Inside Lies wholly within the other unit Containing Wholly contains the other unit Same Span As Starts and ends exactly where the other unit does In the Same Sentence As Starts in the sentence where the other unit starts In the Same Paragraph As Starts in the paragraph where the other unit starts In the Same Turn As Lies, together with the other unit, inside one speaker turn Near Is no more than the set number of words away from the other unit, on either side Before Ends before the other unit starts, with no more than the set number of words between them After Starts after the other unit ends, with no more than the set number of words between them Linked To Overlaps one end of a link; the rules under the row test the link Translated As Overlaps a segment that is paired with a translation; the rules test that pairing The three relations, Near, Before, and After, all feature a distance stepper setting the number of words allowed between the two units, starting at 3, and ranging from 0 to 50 words. Only words count toward the distance. Any distance of 0 refers to the two units touching with no words separating them. Units that overlap will therefore always have a distance of 0. Near scans over sentence boundaries. Context is always sourced from units other than the hit itself. The document must first be indexed for the relations In the Same Sentence As, Near, Before, and After. The document must also have a transcript for the In the Same Turn As relation. A query making use of any of these relations will therefore locate hits only in such documents. A query for Sentences featuring the No Overlapping Codings context row, and with no rules underneath it, returns sentences that have not been coded yet. A query for Words in the project looking for child and children near emotion-related codings features the rule Lemma is child. The context row used in this case is Some Near Codings. The distance is set to 5 words. The row holds the rule Code is any of “Emotions”. The query text reads Lemma is "child" and Some Near 5 Codings (Code is any of "Emotions"). A context row that keeps words within five words of an “Emotions” coding. Linked To considers the links rather than the row unit. By choosing Links as the row unit, the rules listed below the row refer to the fields of the link, including Relation and Comment. Some Linked To Links with no row rules keeps each hit overlapping one endpoint of a link. Translated As considers the relationship between a document and its translations. This exists only after translating the document (see ). Alignments should be used as the row unit in order to consider Translation Language or Translation Text. In the Query facet of “Running Out of Time”, for instance, a query for Sentences may have a context row Some Translated As Alignments with the rule Translation Text contains Klima. It finds those English sentences with a German translation containing Klima.

A Has row counts all items belonging to the hit, which include the codings of a document and the documents of a set. The Has row reads like a context row and helps you manage your coding progress, including keeping track of any documents you have not yet coded. For example, the Has No Codings row will find documents that have not been coded at all. Add Has appears for the units listed in this table: When you find Has can count Documents Codings, Memos, Bookmarks, Links, Speaker Turns, Findings, Alignments Codes Codings, Memos Code Sets Codes Sets, Groups, Tags, Projects Documents The quantity menu includes Some, No, At Least, and At Most, much like in a context row. The value for At Least and At Most ranges from 1 to 999. Below the row, rules narrow down which items are counted. Has No Codings with the rule Code is any of “Costs”, for instance, returns documents that do not contain a “Costs” coding, regardless of whether they have any other codings. A Has row set to No Codings, with the rule Code is any of “Costs”, in a Documents query for the project. When finding codes, on the other hand, only codings within the scope and with the code itself are counted. In the “Skeptics” set, a query looking for Codes with Has At Least 5 Codings will return codes applied in skeptic documents five times or more. Assuming every “Urgency” passage has been coded with either “Deadlines” or “Tipping Points”, Has No Codings returns “Urgency”. Has Memos tallies up the number of memos linked to the code anywhere within the project's documents, including those not in the scope.

Categories sort the hits into labeled, colored groups. If the query is used as a lens, then the categories annotate their hits using different colors and styles, and the categories are listed in the legend of that lens. Lists get a Category column, and Group By ▸ Category in the Show condition allows you to examine how many hits belong to which category. In the “Climate Debate” project's query “Urgency Talk”, for instance, you could add a category named “Crisis” containing a text row set to Lemma for crisis and emergency, and another category named “Deadline” containing a text row set to Lemma for deadline. With the query acting as a lens, it would annotate both types of urgency in separate colors. The Categories condition with two categories for the “Urgency Talk” query. Categories consist of rules. To add one: Open the Categories condition and click Add Category. A row appears, named “Category 1”. Click the colored dot and choose a color. Replace “Category 1” with a name of your own. In the menu beside the name, choose Highlight or Underline. Add rules under the row, as in the Where condition. With regard to the ordering of categories, each hit takes the first available category from the top whose rules the hit satisfies. Checking Allow Several Categories results in each hit receiving all the categories that apply to it. Thus, if a sentence mentions both crisis and deadline, then it would belong to both the “Crisis” and “Deadline” categories. If you create a category with no rules, it ends up with no hits. A hit that meets no category's rules keeps an empty Category column. And finally, LemmaLoom ignores an incomplete rule; hence, a category whose only rule has no value yet takes every hit until the rule is filled. The feature called Color By, at the top of the Categories condition, creates categories based on fields rather than based on rules. All the unique values of the field chosen in the menu beside it become distinct categories with unique colors. With Codings, Color By Code behaves analogously; it assigns a distinct color to each of the unique codes. Thus, if you wanted to see Speaker Turns categorized in “Radio Debate”, you could select Color By Speaker and distinguish “Host”, “Activist”, and “Skeptic”. To remove the Color By field, click the minus button next to it. The Color By menu in the Categories condition of a Speaker Turns query in the Query facet of “Radio Debate”. Should a query contain categories based on both rules and Color By, a hit will take the first applicable category from the rules, and from Color By only if no rule category fits it. When checking Allow Several Categories, the hit will receive all applicable categories including Color By. Categories are automatically assigned the colors blue, red, green, orange, purple, pink, indigo, and yellow in succession, with Highlight styling; from the ninth on follows Underline styling. The maximum number of categories per query equals 16; once achieved, the Add Category button disappears. A lens displays a maximum of 16 entries, so a maximum of 16 values can have Color By colors. When the query has categories, the lens only applies itself to hits which fall under a category. Un-categorized hits remain visible within the results list nonetheless.

What result type the Show condition returns depends upon your unit and scope, and each result type has its own set of options. Typically, what you do is start with lists so that you verify whether or not your query retrieved what you intended, then move on to counts or comparisons after doing that. Show What you get Offered for Controls List One row per hit Every unit and scope the menu showing Document Order, Limit Count The number of hits, in total or by one or two Group By keys Every unit and scope Group By, the menu showing Hits, Limit Compare Counts by group, with a statistical test Sets, projects, and All Projects Group By, the menu showing Hits, the menu showing Automatic, Limit Over Time Hits across a document, across media time, or across a date field Passage units and Documents Group By, the menu showing Hits Collocates Words that occur near the hits Words, Pattern Matches, Text Matches the menu showing Lemma, Window, the menu showing logDice, Minimum Keywords Words the scope uses more or less often than a reference Words, in a set or project the menu showing Rest of Project (with a menu of sets after Set), the menu showing Lemma, the menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 Network Which values occur together Passage units Group By, the menu showing Overlapping Document Order is used by default when sorting lists. Other options include Match, Left Context, Right Context, Document, and Frequency, and Score if the query has a frozen list; library units may be sorted by Name or Document Order. The Limit checkbox restricts your results to just the first 50 hits, or whatever number you choose using the stepper next to it. Note that there is also a separate limit on the Options condition; whichever is smaller wins. For details regarding each kind of result, its measures and tests, refer to .

The menu showing Originals is found at the top of the condition; it specifies how a set/project-level query will handle any translations available for the documents within it. Originals is selected by default. Originals will read only the original documents, Translations will read the translations only of the documents in the scope, and Both will consider originals and translations together. Coded Memos Count as Codings is checked by default. If checked, a memo attached to a passage and linked to a code will be counted as a coding of that code whenever looking for Codings or in context rows about codings. The coding's Coded Memo field identifies these distinctively. Otherwise, only actual codings are counted. Regardless of this checkbox, Has rows count only codings. Limit 5,000 sets how many hits will ever appear in any list resulting from queries. It increases/decreases using the stepper shown, by multiples of 1,000, up to 200,000. Limit in the Show condition can only lower it. The hit counter above the results displays the number of all hits obtained. All computations, counts, and comparisons use all hits regardless. The Options condition of the “Urgency Talk” query in the “Activists” set, with Corpus set to Originals, Coded Memos Count as Codings checked, and Limit at 5,000.

Queries in a document, or in a set or project of moderate size, will rerun shortly after any change. LemmaLoom monitors when you pause while editing, then checks and reruns the query. As the query processes documents in a set or project, a progress ring next to Stop fills accordingly. The results appear incrementally, ahead of processing the last document. Queries on sets, projects, and All Projects will run by themselves if their documents contain fewer than roughly 300,000 tokens (words and punctuation). Queries that require none of the text will run by themselves as well, as with Library · Codes. Keywords queries count the documents they compare with toward the 300,000 threshold. If a query goes beyond this threshold, then you will see a button in the results area labeled Run Query whenever changes occur. Click it, click the triangle icon in the query header, or choose Edit ▸ Run Query (⌘R). Large queries take varying amounts of time, depending on document sizes and your computer's hardware. Long queries can be stopped by clicking Stop, which ends their computation. Edit ▸ New Query clears the builder and keeps the unit, so you can rebuild the query from an empty Where condition. When the conditions for running a query are not met, the triangle is disabled, and the results area displays one of the following messages. The violated rule appears with a red border around it, and hovering the mouse pointer over it reveals the reason. Incomplete appears only on the rule, because the query still runs. Message Meaning Runs Incomplete A rule has no value yet, or a text row has no terms. It is ignored until you complete it Yes Missing A code, attribute, dictionary, every checked category, group, set, code set, project, or document the rule refers to has been deleted No Not available here The field cannot be used in this scope, such as a document field in a document's Query facet No Invalid pattern A regular expression cannot be read No Pattern too long A regular expression is longer than 1,000 characters No Too deeply nested A rule lies more than three levels deep, such as under a context row inside a group (see Groups) No Too many nodes A dependency pattern has too many words No Needs a set or project A saved query that shows Compare or Keywords was opened in a document's Query facet No Nothing to compare with Keywords compares the scope with itself No No set chosen Keywords is set to compare with a set, but none is chosen No The Not available here message generally occurs when you load a saved query in a place it was not made for. A query based on the attribute “Stance” can be performed within the project level but produces this message in the Query facet of a document. The Query facet of “Running Out of Time” with a saved query on the “Stance” attribute loaded. The rule is outlined in red and the results area reads Not available here.

The Query Text condition shows the entire query written out in prose form, line-by-line, as illustrated for “Urgency Talk” in A first query above. The Query Text condition for the “Urgency Talk” query, with the Copy button below the text. Read the query text to ensure that your question has been posed correctly, particularly in the case of queries with groups. All, Any, and None appear as and, or, and not respectively, with not followed by parentheses. If your query uses Count or Compare, its Group By keys and measure are added to the last line, such as Show Count By Lemma · Hits. Use the query text for readability purposes, and for copying and pasting into research documentation like papers and research diaries; to change the query, change the conditions. Click Copy to place the query text onto the clipboard for insertion into other applications. Result exports retain the query text (see Exporting results in ).

A saved query will keep its name, its conditions, and its owner or location, which determines where it will appear in the interface. Available In Where the query is offered Document That document's Query facet Set The set's Queries view, the Queries window while it shows the set, and the Query facet of each document in the set and of its translations Project The project's Queries view, the Queries views of its sets, the Query facet of each of its documents, and the Queries window while it shows the project or one of its sets All Projects Everywhere Queries should be saved wherever you plan on reusing them. Queries pertaining to the activists' texts belong to the “Activists” set, while queries meant to be used across all sets and documents in a particular study belong to the project itself. All Projects is useful if you plan to reuse queries across studies (see Working across projects in ). In the “Climate Debate” project, the “Activists” set has a query saved in it called “Keywords: Activists”, which comes from the Quick Start. The Save Query dialog, saving a keyword list for the “Activists” set. To save a query for the first time: Open the Save menu and choose Save As…. Save does the same for a query that has never been saved. In the Save Query dialog, type a name in Name. Choose where the query belongs in Available In. The menu offers the place you are in, then Project and All Projects, and the first is chosen for you. Click Save. Once this happens, Save saves the changes on top of the saved version and the dot after its name disappears. Save As… makes a duplicate under another name. It is the same command to assign ownership of a query to another place. For a saved query, the menu also features Rename…. The Save menu of the saved query “Urgency Talk”, with Rename…, Remove Lens, and Delete Query. The Save menu includes three more options: Save as Lens… promotes the query to become a lens within the reader’s lens menu. When a new query needs saving before turning into a lens, it asks for its name and Available In through the Save as Lens dialog; a query already saved is saved with your changes and becomes a lens at once. Upon being made into a lens, the option now reads Remove Lens. Should a query fail to qualify for promotion to a lens, this option becomes disabled, and hovering the mouse pointer over this option explains the reason behind it. Save as Analyzer… transforms the query into a custom analyzer. Delete Query deletes the saved query while leaving an empty builder. For more on how lenses and analyzers derived from queries behave, see . Saved queries may be opened by choosing them from the query's name on the left end of the header bar, or by clicking them in the left column of a Queries view or the Queries window. Within the column, the queries are grouped under All Projects, Project, Set, and Document. Lenses show up with a pair of glasses next to their names. Typing a query’s partial name into the header bar’s search field will locate it amidst long lists of queries. Opening the query runs it immediately. Deleting queries within this column involves right-clicking the query followed by selecting Delete Query. Opening a saved query or recipe, or selecting New Query, replaces the current query in the builder immediately. Should the previous query have unsaved changes, Edit ▸ Undo can restore the previous query state. Steps including saving, renaming, deleting, making a query into a lens, or vice versa, are recorded as parts of the undo history. You undo them with Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z); the menu item specifies the action, e.g., Undo Save Query. More details on undo can be found in .

Recipes offer preconfigured queries that help answer basic research questions, including creating a concordance, generating a list of words, and querying codings based on an attribute. If you ever find yourself struggling with building a query from scratch, starting off with a recipe allows you to take a look at how conditions are filled out, allowing you to tweak things accordingly. Upon loading into the builder, a recipe has its own name followed by a dot to indicate it is unsaved, and it is immediately executed in its default state. From there, you may modify and save a recipe as any other query. Within a Queries view or the Queries window, the recipes appear below the saved queries under Recipes in the left column. In the Query facet of the inspector, open the Recipes drop-down (the wand) in the header. The list is divided into the categories Words, Grammar, Coding, Speakers and Time, and Documents and Library. Only recipes relevant to your current scope show in the list. Sets and projects display Passages Like a Code last under Recipes, giving a choice among the codes used in the scope. The Recipes menu, opened from the wand in the header of the Query facet of “Running Out of Time”. Recipes in  provides the full list of available recipes, which includes descriptions of each recipe along with the query generated and scope of application. Passages Like a Code in the same chapter details this particular recipe.

The Find, Pattern, and Where conditions determine what hits a query will collect, whereas the Show condition decides what you see of them. It could list out the hits, count them, run statistical tests comparing groups of documents, track hits through each document or across time periods, find their collocates and keywords, and/or determine co-occurrences among them. Each and every one of these results may be exported in tabular form, as a text file (including the query used to produce the result), or as an image. If you would like to know more specifics on these individual conditions, check out . These examples use “Climate Debate”, which is the example project of this guide. In order to replicate the examples, choose File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project, and LemmaLoom will load the project in your preferred interface language. Most numeric figures in the examples are invented for simplicity's sake; hence, they differ from those displayed in the screenshots. Where a particular example makes use of the example project's own counts, such a fact will be noted explicitly.

A hit is one of the things returned from executing a query, whether it is a word, sentence, coding, speaker turn, document, or code. The bar above the results displays the total number of hits in a query's output, for instance, 312 Hits. A Group By key groups hits by one of their features, such as codes, speakers, and attributes like “Stance” of their document. Each distinct value of the key becomes a separate row in the output. A measure refers to a quantitative value displayed in a row of results; measures may refer to the number of hits or documents, rates, coverage, or shares. A rate refers to dividing the number of hits by the number of words in which the hits occurred. With rates, comparison of texts of varying lengths is possible since normalization takes place. A document-level key refers to a type of Group By key which has only one value for each document. Examples of document-level keys are attributes such as “Stance”, the document's group, its language, and the document itself. Tests under Compare rely on document-level keys to run since comparisons take place on documents. A test estimates how easily chance alone could produce the differences you observe between groups. It returns a p-value and an effect size, both explained in p-values and effect sizes later in this chapter.

Clicking on the Show condition will show you up to seven kinds of results depending on what your query is. However, not all seven will appear depending on what the query analyzes (i.e., the unit of analysis, what Find looks for) and what range it is searching through (scope, at document, set, or project level). Show What you get Offered for List The hits themselves, as a concordance or a table of records Every query Count One number, or numbers for the values of one or two Group By keys Every query Compare Numbers for each group, with a statistical test Sets, projects, and All Projects Over Time A line chart, or a strip per document showing where the hits fall Passages and Documents Collocates Words that occur near the hits more often than chance would suggest Words, Pattern Matches, and Text Matches Keywords Words a set uses more or less often than a reference Words, in a set or project Network A table of how often values occur together Passages Passages are all the units of analysis that have a place in your document. This includes everything in the Find menu aside from items found in Library, such as Documents, Codes, and Sets. It is common to begin with List. Going over the hits returned by List can tell you if you’re getting what you need from your queries. Once satisfied with the quality of your hits, using Count gives you the total number of hits as well as how many there are in relation to your codes, speakers, or attributes. Compare statistically assesses whether the difference observed between document groups is greater than what could happen by coincidence. If you are dealing with location and time questions, Over Time would be useful. Collocates and Keywords both solve problems related to vocabulary, while Network allows visualization of co-occurrences between your codes or other values. Depending on the kind of result chosen, there are various options available in the Show condition. A Limit selected in List, Count, or Compare stays applied when switching to Collocates, Keywords, or Network. Although the Limit checkbox itself disappears from view, the limit still applies until you switch back, deselect it, and return to the chosen kind.

Your results show directly underneath the query builder wherever you create your queries. In sets and projects, your results occupy all the horizontal space of the Queries section beneath the left column and the conditions. In the Queries window (Window ▸ Queries), your results take the full horizontal width too. The divider bar between builder and results allows you to resize the two areas according to preference. If you are viewing a document, you will find the Query facet of the inspector has your results in its lower part. If a query does not involve analyzing the texts of a large set, project, or All Projects, it is run automatically whenever you edit it. But queries analyzing such texts wait for you. You can recognize these kinds of queries by noticing that the Run Query button now appears in their results areas. See Running a query in  for specifics regarding the set, project, or All Projects sizes where this happens. Running your queries is achieved via the Run Query button in the results area, the ⌘R keyboard shortcut (Edit ▸ Run Query), or the triangle icon in the bar above the builder. Background-running queries occur asynchronously in order to enable you to keep reading or coding during their execution. Background-running queries have their own progress ring in the bar above the builder, which becomes active when the execution starts, indicating the completion rate in percentages of how many documents they have analyzed. As long as the execution is ongoing, you can find the Stop button replacing the triangle. Your results get updated in real-time as your query analyzes your documents, remaining faded till execution is done. The lists in the results only show at maximum the first 5,000 hits until the execution ends. Also included at the bottom of those lists is the number of total hits found, like Showing 5,000 of 12,431. Lists sorted in any order other than Document Order stay in document order until then and are sorted afterward. Clicking Stop ends the execution at any time and keeps the partial results. Keyword lists appear solely once queries are complete. The bar at the top of the results area, or results bar, summarizes the results. It gives the hit count of most queries, e.g., 312 Hits. Library item queries show item counts, e.g., 14 Results, whereas networks report the number of values they link, e.g., 10 Nodes. Aside from these counts, the bar indicates how many documents were read when the query had to leave some out (see Documents left out below), and the value you have drilled into (see Drilling down later in this chapter). The right side of the bar includes the Filter field (for applying filters in query results), Export (the box with upwards pointing arrow), and Open results in a window (two outward-pointing arrows). Within a document's Query facet, the bar holds only the summary, the number of documents read, and the drill-down value. Instead, Export lies in the bar located at the top of the facet above results. If a query cannot run, the results area explains the reason, like Needs a set or project, No set chosen, or Invalid pattern. The triangle button is disabled in those cases. Its tooltip gives the same reason. If there were no matches returned after running the query, the results area displays No matches.

Queries finding Words, Pattern Matches, Sentences, Phrases, Noun Chunks, or Findings will only work on documents that have been indexed. Those documents that haven't been indexed will be excluded, as will documents in languages other than English, German, and Chinese. Results using word counts, e.g., Per 10,000 Words, the rank test, or DP, leave out such documents as well. The results bar will inform you of how many documents have been read, e.g., 12 of 14. This figure also appears if you stop your query prematurely. A rate, count, or statistical test performed on 12 out of 14 documents reveals nothing about those other two documents. For additional guidance on seeing and finishing the indexing of each document, please refer to .

The Filter field narrows what the results show. Imagine you received hundreds of hits from one query, which include a few hits from just one document or from a particular code. You now wish to focus solely on these hits; the solution lies in typing a few characters in the Filter field. Only rows containing that text will remain visible to you, while capitals will be ignored. How filters behave varies depending on which type of result you are working with. List filters assess the text of each hit and its surrounding context, the title of documents, and any extra columns such as code or speakers. Filters for counts, comparisons, collocates, keywords, and networks filter based on the name of the row. For Position in Document strips, filters evaluate document titles only. All result types besides a single number and a line chart can use filters. Keep in mind that filters simply conceal rows. The overall count of hits reported above in the results bar, the figures in all rows, and any test still consider all hits made in total. Limit defines how many hits will actually appear in the list; thus, applying a filter affects only the hits left after the limit. Exports keep only the rows that pass the filter.

Pressing the Open results in a window button on the right side of the results bar opens the currently displayed result in a new window with its very own results bar, Filter field, and Export button. This window has a title with the name of the query, scope, and value that you've drilled into (if any), and this name is repeated with the number of hits found next to it. The results for “Fear” by “Stance” in a results window, beside the Queries view of the “Climate Debate” project. Since this window retains the state of the result from when you opened it, you may adjust the query or scope, run it again, and compare its results against the previous results side by side. This could mean setting “Fear” codings by stance against “Hope” codings by stance, among other possibilities. Drilling down and opening hits function within the window too. Until the query finishes running, the button remains disabled. Clicking the window button in the bar above the builder opens the entire query in the Queries window (see The Queries window in ).

List presents the hits actually retrieved by the query. Hits which occur in some part of the text appear in concordance format, whereas library objects such as documents or codes appear in table format. If you ever come across an unexpected count, consult List for clarification.

Concordances are lists of hits on word(s) or passage(s) that show each occurrence of that word or passage in the middle column, with its context on either side. When scrolling down the middle column, you will notice multiple uses of a particular word or passage at once. A concordance of the lemma climate in the “Activists” set. The concordance columns are as follows: Document represents the document that holds the hit inside of a set, project, or All Projects. Left Context and Right Context show up to 70 characters prior to and after the hit, replacing all line breaks with spaces. Match refers to the actual match found during the search process. If any match exceeds 400 characters, it gets cut down with “…”. There are also several other columns related to the query's unit type. These are Code in regard to codings, Content and Linked Code in relation to memos, Comment related to bookmarks, Other Document and Relation pertaining to links, Speaker and Start regarding speaker turns, Finding associated with analyzer findings, Phrase Label and Phrase Function in regard to phrases, and Translation Text concerning alignments. Location provides exact information as to where within a document a particular hit occurs. Such locations resemble, say, ¶4·2, meaning the second sentence of the fourth paragraph of said document. If a hit takes place within a document that has not been indexed yet, the sentence numbers will be omitted, so that locations would instead resemble ¶4. Category displays in case you have categories involved or used Color By while creating the query. Likewise, Project displays should you choose the All Projects option. Finally, Score appears in case sorting happens by the hit score. Each hit in the list can take you right to its place in the document. This may be accomplished by double-clicking the hit itself, selecting the hit and pressing the Return key, or selecting the hit and picking the Go to Source item from its shortcut menu. LemmaLoom switches over to displaying the document containing the hit in the preview tab (unless it is open already) and highlights the match. In case your hit belongs to another project, LemmaLoom switches to that project. Within a document's Query facet, hits get presented as a narrower kind of concordance view. Every hit occupies its own row and displays both preceding and following words as well as a match in bold between them, with the location beneath. Whenever hits appear one after another in the same location, the location is displayed once, for the first hit only. A click on the hit makes it show up in the reader. The Query facet of “Running Out of Time” with a concordance of the lemma climate. Sorting hits within lists occurs based on the menu showing Document Order in the Show condition. The choices are: Document Order keeps the order of the set or project, and of the text. This is the default. Match sorting occurs alphabetically according to matches themselves. Left Context sorts hits by the preceding words, reading left contexts backwards starting from a match position. Right Context sorts hits by subsequent words occurring within the right context. Document sorts hits alphabetically by document titles. Frequency sorts by hit frequencies, counting appearances of hits' matches. Ignored in frequency counts are all differences caused by capital letters and accents. The hits that repeat most often come first. Score orders hits according to their scores, placing hits that scored better on top. Only if queries feature a weighted word list created with Passages Like a Code or Freeze Values would this option be available. Also, in this sort mode, hits that contain fewer than two words from the list get ignored. Thus, the total number of hits drops in comparison with the initial number. See How sentences are scored in  and Freeze Values in  for more. There are restrictions regarding the maximum number of hits a list shows. They come in the form of two settings. Select Limit from the Show condition and set the desired hit number; it starts at 50 and goes up to 10,000. Another restriction caps every list and appears in the Options condition as Limit, starting at 5,000 and allowing values between 1,000 and 200,000 in increments of 1,000. Every time you have queries returning more hits than those numbers allow, a line appears under the list, for example Showing 5,000 of 12,431. Note that the hit count in the results bar always includes every hit. When sorted by Document Order, the list keeps the first hits found. Otherwise, LemmaLoom analyzes all of the hits returned by queries to sort them in your specified manner, retaining only the top of the sorted list. It is advisable to keep your lists short. Set high hit limits only when you need every hit, such as for a complete export.

When Find is set to one of the Library units, List produces a tabular view with each row representing an item in your project. Use List when wanting to survey the documents, codes, and/or other items in a project with respect to their properties next to each other. For example, List can be used for finding documents lacking dates or rarely-used codes. The first column is titled Title for documents, and Name for everything else. The other columns depend on the unit.
