LemmaLoom analyzes each sentence on its own, word by word, from its first word. Commas, periods, and other punctuation marks count as words as well. A step without rules, gaps included, will consume any word or punctuation mark. In order to skip over words but not punctuation, use Add Word instead of Add Gap. Make sure your step has the rule Is Word is true. Set it to 0 to 3. As LemmaLoom scans positions along a sentence, it tries to find the longest stretch of words/punctuation marks that match the whole pattern. Should it succeed, then LemmaLoom has found a match and moves on to analyzing the remainder of the sentence beginning after the last matched word/punctuation mark. For each step within the matched stretch, it consumes as many words/punctuation marks as possible while the steps after it still fit. Here's an example taken from the document “Why We Block the Roads”, The people who won the rights we now take for granted were called extremists and troublemakers, often by commuters who were also late for work. At the first were in this sentence, Step A matches with a form of be. While Step B matches zero-length sequences, Step C requires an adjective, and called is a verb, meaning that no matches are made starting at this were. However, at the subsequent were, Step A matches. Step B matches with the adverb also, while Step C matches with the adjective late. Therefore the matching stretch becomes were also late. Similarly, are mostly too young in the document “Running Out of Time” is a match in which Step B contains two adverbs.

A word step retains its letter during its existence. Whenever a word step is added, it gets the first letter not in use. If B is deleted and a word step is added, it becomes B once again. In addition to recording pattern matches, LemmaLoom keeps a record of the actual words covered by each letter involved. In the sentence mentioned before, A covered the word were, B covered also, and C covered late. However, when is radical is considered, B does not cover any words. The letters used in the pattern will be visible on the Query Text condition, writing down the example as Find Pattern Matches A:Lemma is "be"] B:[Word Class is any of ADV]{0,2} C:[Word Class is any of ADJ]`. Note the curly braces that give information on the number range for a step if different from **1 to 1**. The Query Text condition for the three-step sequence in the “Activists” set, with the letters A, B, and C written out. Your count may also be grouped by the words of a particular letter. Consider the **Relation** recipe as an illustration; this recipe gives you the ability to count according to **Word · B · Lemma**, or the lemma of the word covered by letter B (see [Recipes later in this chapter). If B covers multiple words in one occurrence (such as if a pattern step had range 1 to 3), only the first word would be taken into account. Since field menus contain only fields of the entire match, you need to use the Relation recipe template to customize the count of your pattern using a single letter; for a sequence, choose Sequence from the Pattern condition, without changing the count criteria (still Word · B · Lemma).

During the indexing of sentences by LemmaLoom, all words are linked to the word they depend on, known as the head word. Adjective words depend on their nouns, while subjects or objects depend on their verbs. Within each sentence, one word (typically the main verb) depends on no other word. This word acts as the root word. When all dependencies between words are accounted for, a tree structure emerges, with the root word being the apex. The Structure facet within the Grammar inspector displays this tree graphically (see ). A dependency pattern defines a subset of the tree structure, consisting of up to six words, each having its own rules, and the dependency relationships between them. Words connected via a dependency link need not occur consecutively within the sentence. For instance, a dependency pattern for a verb with bill as its object yields share the bill, cut energy bills, and read their energy bills. On the other hand, a sequence pattern that allows gaps yields these too, but also added to the bills, where bills is not the object of added. Each word appears as an outlined box inside the Pattern condition, labeled with a letter. Each of the words except for one comes with the following three controls: Head menu containing the letter of the word it depends on; Relation menu whose initial content is Any Relation; and the Any Depth checkbox. The word without these controls is referred to as the anchor word. Anchor words are initially assigned letter A in new patterns. The anchor is the starting point of your dependency search and always remains in the pattern. Moreover, all words included within a dependency pattern must connect back to the anchor either directly or indirectly via intermediary words.

The figure below displays the pattern for the verbs the activists use with bill as their object. Word A, which acts as the anchor, has the rule Word Class is any of VERB · Verb. Word B is dependent on word A by the Object relationship, and has the rule Lemma is bill. The Hit menu at the foot of the condition is left at Matched Words. A dependency pattern for a verb (A) with the word bill (B) as its object. Among the matches, you find share the bill from “Farmers Are Not the Enemy” and read their energy bills from “Hope Takes Work”. The same shape works for any verbs and objects within your documents. Fix the noun in B, as done in this example, to investigate what happens with the noun, or fix the verb in A to investigate the object(s) associated with it. To build a dependency pattern: In the Find condition, choose Text · Pattern Matches, and choose Dependency in the Pattern condition. The condition starts with two words, the anchor A and the word B, which depends on A. Under each word, add the rules it must pass, as in a sequence. For each word other than the anchor, choose its head in the head menu and a relation in the relation menu (see Relations below). Click Add Word for each further word, up to six in all. In the Hit menu at the foot of the condition, choose how much of the sentence a match covers (see The anchor and the extent of a match below). Add Word adds a new word whose head word is the last word on the list, linked via an Any Relation relationship. You may specify another head word in its head menu. Add Word disappears when the pattern contains six words. Once you delete a word, the links to it are also deleted. Any word that depended on the deleted word loses its head menu, relation menu, and Any Depth checkbox. After you delete that word as well, the pattern will search for its matches again.

The relation menu is where you describe how a word relates to its head. The Any Relation option at the top of the menu accepts any link between words. The relation menu of word B in a dependency pattern in the “Activists” set, with Object ticked. After that come the grammatical functions, namely Subject, Object, Predicative, Complement, Adjectival, Adverbial, Appositive, Agent, Conjunct, Connector, and Main clause. Except for Main clause, these are the same functions that the Grammatical function lens uses to color code your documents (see ). Each function names the job that a particular word does for its head. Given B depends on A by Object, then B is an object of A. Object includes in English not only the objects of verbs but the object of a preposition too; therefore, in on a podium, podium is an object of on. Finally comes the set of word sketch relations (see ). In a pattern, these relations (Subjects, Objects, Complements, Adjective modifiers, Adverb modifiers, In compounds with, and Coordinated with) are the same as those in word sketches. They are read starting with the head word like the grammatical functions above, yet organize the links according to a word sketch's convention. Objects in a pattern includes only the direct and indirect objects and excludes the object of a preposition; Complements covers complements and predicatives, so it includes busy in He was busy as well as protect in we want to protect the climate. Coordinated with is equivalent to Conjunct. Subject of, Object of, Modifies, and Complement of express links in reverse, from the lower word up. Prepositional phrases links two words through a preposition. Links in the three languages differ in name from each other; thus, LemmaLoom translates them to the relations described above, allowing you to use one pattern on documents in English, German, or Chinese. Differences exist in analyses between languages nonetheless. For instance, consider the object of a preposition. In German, Podium in auf einem Podium is included in the prepositional phrase and treated by LemmaLoom as Adjectival, while in Chinese the preposition hangs below its noun as a Connector. Ensure you review a few matches in each language before comparing counts across languages.

Without Any Depth, a word needs to depend directly on its head. When you tick Any Depth, it allows the word to depend on its head indirectly via other words, as a child, as a grandchild, and beyond. If you tick Any Depth, the relation menu becomes irrelevant. Tick Any Depth if you care that two words belong together, regardless of how exactly they are connected grammatically. In “Running Out of Time”, the passage states, If you are walking toward a cliff edge in thick fog, the fact that you cannot see the drop is a reason to stop walking, not to walk faster. Here, edge is dependent on toward and not directly on walking. A query searching for a pattern where A has Lemma is walk and B has Lemma is edge picks up this passage only when Any Depth is ticked for B.

t: The anchor and the extent of a match
b: All words that pass the anchor's rules are considered anchors. LemmaLoom then tries to find words that fit each position in the rest of the pattern. The pattern requires that every position be filled by a different word in the sentence. As such, each anchor word can only provide one matching instance, even when more than one word would fit. Counting matches, therefore, is counting instances of anchors. The Hit menu at the foot of the condition controls the extent of each matched instance: Matched Words includes everything from the first word of the match to the last, including anything in between. For example, in the pattern A → B where A is walk and B is edge, the match would be walking toward a cliff edge. Whole Subtree matches include everything in the subtree rooted at the anchor. This means the matching instance will include the matching anchor and everything that depends on it. In “Running Out of Time”, this means If you are walking toward a cliff edge in thick fog, the clause headed by walking. Use Whole Subtree when you need context, such as before coding an instance of your query.

In addition to analyzing connections between words, the grammar analysis breaks down each sentence into phrases nested within other phrases. In the document “Heat Wave Report 2024”, the phrase water storage for the River Valley and the Central Plain is a noun phrase. Within it are the smaller noun phrase water storage, as well as the prepositional phrase for the River Valley and the Central Plain, containing the noun phrase the River Valley and the Central Plain. A phrase pattern locates phrases based on their form and span length. Use it to ask style-related questions about phrasing rather than questions about the meanings or contents of individual phrases; if you wanted to know how much detail a writer fits into a noun phrase, for instance, you could use a phrase pattern to investigate that. The Pattern condition for a phrase pattern includes: The Form button displays a list of general forms to tick off, namely Noun phrase, Prep. phrase, Adj. phrase, Adv. phrase, Verb phrase, and Clause. These have the same meaning regardless of the languages included in your analysis. The Phrase Label button shows the detailed labels assigned to phrases according to the language(s) being searched. The available labels are NP · Noun phrase and SBAR · Subordinate clause, among others, depending on your documents. If the documents are in multiple languages, then the name of the language follows the label. The At least … words stepper specifies the minimum number of words required for a phrase from 1 up to 50. Punctuation marks in a phrase count toward the span length. Outermost Only filters out phrases that occur within any other phrases located by the current pattern. As an example, the longer noun phrase water storage for the River Valley and the Central Plain includes the shorter noun phrase the River Valley and the Central Plain, so ticking Outermost Only leaves only the former in the results list. Include Noun Chunks identifies noun chunks, short noun phrases ending with their heads such as heat warnings or the national heat helpline. A noun chunk matches NP · Noun phrase. The Phrase Label list of a phrase pattern in “Heat Wave Report 2024”, with no label ticked. Entries currently ticked appear on each button. Ticking nothing shows None and means all phrases qualify. Ticking several entries in one list accepts any of them. When both lists have ticked items, a phrase meets the criteria only if it matches options from both. A phrase found twice over the same words, such as a noun chunk that matches a noun phrase exactly, is listed once. The figure below represents the phrase pattern built for “Heat Wave Report 2024” in the inspector. It uses the form Noun phrase, with At least … words set to 6 and Outermost Only ticked. The list holds each long noun phrase of the report once, at its widest. A phrase pattern for noun phrases of at least six words, outermost only, in “Heat Wave Report 2024”. To find phrases by kind and length: In the Find condition, choose Text · Pattern Matches, and choose Phrase in the Pattern condition. Click the Form button and tick one or more forms in the list that opens, or do the same with detailed labels under Phrase Label. Click outside the list to close it. Set the shortest length with the At least … words stepper. Tick Outermost Only to list only the widest of nested phrases, and Include Noun Chunks to count short noun phrases as well. The Grammar · Phrases unit in Find allows you to locate the individual occurrences of the very same phrases and provide rules according to Phrase Label, Form, Width, Phrase Function, and Phrase Head (see Choosing what to find in ). Choose this category of search when you are interested in your phrase's role within a sentence or its head word; only the phrase pattern has Outermost Only and can add noun chunks.

Edit ▸ Query from Selection builds a sequence pattern based on words selected in the reader. This feature takes you from a sentence you found interesting while reading to other sentences that are similarly constructed. It displays a ladder above the conditions where there is a column per word going downwards from the exact word form at the top to any word at the bottom. Clicking a lower rung expands the description of that particular word, and your query gets updated every time with fresh results accordingly.

t: Making a query from a selection
b: In the reader, select up to twelve words within one sentence. Punctuation marks count toward the twelve. Choose Edit ▸ Query from Selection. The item is disabled when nothing is selected and while you are editing the document's text. The inspector opens at Multimode ▸ Query. Your previous query will be replaced by a new unsaved query called New Query, while the results of the latter show immediately. Be sure to save your work prior to choosing the command if you were working on modifying your previous query. Your ladder will have as many columns as words selected, each titled by its letter. From top to bottom, each column offers: Word “activists” for this particular word form; Lemma “activist” for all variations of this word; Tag NNS for all occurrences of any words with identical detailed part-of-speech tags, if available in grammar analyses (NNS denotes a plural noun); Word Class NOUN for all instances of words sharing this word class; the word's grammatical function, such as Subject (if it's known); Any Word for all words in general (offered only for words, not punctuation marks). Capital letters and accents aren't taken into account on the first two rungs. Rungs currently selected will be highlighted in color. Columns will begin with lemmas on nouns, proper nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and numbers, and with word forms elsewhere.

“Running Out of Time” states If a factory town loses its old jobs, then the new ones must be built there, not in a business park three hundred kilometers away. Below is the ladder for the new ones, selected in that sentence. This ladder contains three columns, where column A begins on Word “the”, column B on Lemma “new”, and column C on Lemma “one”. Initially, the query returns the single instance of the new ones in the op-ed piece. Once you click Word Class ADJ in column B, as illustrated below, any adjective could precede one, and hence the next one becomes another instance included in the list. Likewise, clicking Any Word in column A as well allows any word to come first, and thus a better one gets added to the list. However, doing so also produces far harder one, where the adverb far comes first. The ladder for the selection the new ones, with column B widened to Word Class ADJ. Usually, you should widen a single column at a time and check what each change brings in. Once the widening introduces unwanted matches, as far harder one does here, you should step back up a rung or open the pattern in the builder and add a rule. Once opened, the ladder remains visible as you alter the Show condition. To display the frequency distribution of the variants, choose Count in the Show condition and click Group By. The new row groups by Text, the words of each match. Each subsequent click on a rung will update the counts. The Open in Builder button opens the Pattern condition while simultaneously closing the ladder. You can modify the pattern in the Pattern condition in exactly the same way as one you built yourself. Modifying any condition except Show causes the ladder to close as well. Your query operates solely upon the currently opened document. To apply a query upon an entire set or project, save your query with Project selected from the Available In menu of the Save Query dialog; by default this is Document, which keeps it in this document only. Your query will then appear in the left column of the set's or project's Queries section. For additional information regarding saving queries, refer to Saving queries in .

Below the ladder are up to four checkboxes that can add rules based on your selection in the text. Each one shows only if applicable. Codings appears if your selection overlaps codings. Ticking Codings adds a context to the Where condition that keeps only matches overlapping a coding with one of those codes (Some Overlapping Codings whose Code is any of them). Speaker Turn appears if you begin the selection within a speaker turn in your transcript. By ticking Speaker Turn, you constrain matches so that only the matches Inside this speaker's turns remain valid. For instance, if the selection comes from one of the skeptic's answers in “Radio Debate”, then the matches are limited to the turns of the speaker Skeptic. Findings appears when an analyzer's findings overlap the selection, for example a hedge found by the Metadiscourse analyzer. By ticking Findings, your matches are constrained to those that fall In the Same Sentence As a finding of one of the kinds generated there. Dependency appears if your selection has six or fewer words, punctuation included, that depend on each other grammatically, i.e., where each word except one depends on another word in the selection. When you tick Dependency, you convert your sequence into a dependency pattern which comprises dependency relations between your selected words, where each relation has the value Any Relation. Your anchor is whatever word's head lies outside the scope of your selected range, meaning that the anchor is not necessarily going to be A (here ones, column C, is the new anchor), and the Hit menu on the bottom of your Pattern condition is automatically set to Matched Words. While your rungs limit what the words could be, your words themselves can now stand apart from each other. For instance, taking your initial set of rungs, the dependency pattern would also match the genuinely new ones, where another word stands between the and new. The ladder for the selection the new ones in “Running Out of Time”, with Dependency ticked beneath it.

Query from Selection does plain text searching if the selected text contains several sentences, surpasses 12 words, or comes from a non-indexed document. In the query setup, Find is configured to be Text · Text Matches, while the text to search for is the selected text itself. Matches are whole words as long as the endpoints of the selection fall on word boundaries.

Passages Like a Code returns a list of sentences that contain the usual words found within passages coded with the selected code, while lacking the code themselves. Passages Like a Code analyzes the words within the passages of text that have already received a particular code, comparing those words to the words found within the remainder of your documents. Words typical of these passages become part of the profile associated with the code. Sentences lacking the selected code receive scores based upon the occurrence of these words and their weight in the code's profile. In addition, Passages Like a Code will analyze sentences that have received other codes. Passages Like a Code returns a list of sentences that you must manually evaluate before deciding whether to code them. Passages Like a Code will not understand irony, recognize a passage that makes its point without the usual words, or differentiate between sentences that mean different things despite using nearly identical words (e.g., we can always afford it vs. we can never afford it).

Passages Like a Code can run across a set or a project. It can be accessed at the end of the recipes in the left column of the Queries section, or in the Queries window. Its menu lists every code that has at least one coding in the documents you are querying over. The recipes in the left column of the Queries section of “Climate Debate”, with the Passages Like a Code menu open. To locate passages resembling a code: Click Queries in the row of buttons at the top of a set tab, or choose Window ▸ Queries and choose a project or set as the scope. In the left column, under Recipes, click Passages Like a Code and choose the code. When LemmaLoom is profiling your code, a spinner icon will appear beside the run button. Editing your query during profiling means the current profile will be discarded. A query named after your code is automatically generated and run once your code is chosen. Inside the “Climate Debate” project, selecting Costs results in a Passages Like Costs query configured as below: Find is Text · Sentences. Where uses a context of No Overlapping Codings whose Code is any of Costs, with the option Include Subcodes enabled. As a result, sentences with prior application of this code or any of its subcodes are excluded. Show is List, with the menu showing Score and Limit set to 200. Profiles are generated based on the word criteria specified in the subsequent paragraphs. Too few words pass in instances where only a few short codings exist, and the spinner stops; code some more passages with the code first.

LemmaLoom scans all the indexed documents in your set or project without taking into account translations. Every word is counted except for the punctuation and stopwords, which are very frequent words like the, and, and we. Word count happens per lemma regardless of capitalization and diacritical marks, or per form should the word lack a lemma. For a word to qualify as being inside, it must overlap a coding of the selected code; otherwise it is outside. Only the passages coded with the particular code itself are regarded as inside; passages coded with subcodes of the code are considered as outside. If most coding had been done with Deadlines and Tipping Points, then one would need to learn the profile of each of these codes instead of Urgency. For every word found inside, LemmaLoom measures how much more common it is inside than outside. This measurement yields two results for every word, how strong the evidence is and how much more common the word is inside, and those results are known as the log-likelihood and the log ratio, respectively. These are the same two scores a keyword list uses (see How the two scores are calculated in ). It would be incorrect to compare absolute frequencies since the total numbers of words contained within and outside the codings of Costs differ greatly. Therefore, log-likelihood begins with expected counts, that is, calculating how frequently the word would occur inside and outside if it made up the same share of the words on both sides. Consider an invented example with round counts (the example project is much smaller). There are 2,000 counted words inside the codings of Costs, and 48,000 counted words in the remaining part of the project. The word bill appears 12 times inside and 18 times outside, making a total of 30 appearances. Inside the codings of Costs are 2,000 out of 50,000 words, meaning that the inside makes up 1 in 25. Hence, if the word bill were spread evenly, 1.2 of its 30 occurrences would appear inside (that is, 1 in 25), while outside the codings of Costs the other 28.8 occurrences would appear. In general: In the above equations, $a$ and $b$ represent the number of occurrences of the word inside and outside the codings, respectively; $N_1$ and $N_2$ refer to the total number of counted words inside and outside the codings, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ stand for the expected counts of the word on both sides. The fraction is the word's share of all the words. For bill, $E_1 = 2{,}000 times 30/50{,}000 = 1.2$ and $E_2 = 48{,}000 times 30/50{,}000 = 28.8$. The log-likelihood statistic ($G^2$) assesses how different the actual observations are from the expected ones. The 2 is part of the name. $ln$ represents the natural logarithm function, explained in The association scores in . Three properties about logarithms are relevant to understanding this formula; first, $ln 1 = 0$; second, the logarithm of a number greater than 1 is positive; third, the logarithm of a fraction between 0 and 1 is negative. Every term involves dividing an observed frequency count by the respective expected count. When they're equal, the division results in a 1, and thus the term doesn't affect $G^2$ whatsoever. When a word appears more frequently than anticipated on one side, it must appear less frequently than anticipated on the other; thus one term will be positive and the other negative. Because the positive term will always outweigh the negative one, $G^2$ is guaranteed to remain non-negative; moreover, discrepancies between observations and expectations increase $G^2$. Terms with a count equaling 0 aren't included because the logarithm of 0 is undefined. In the case of bill, $12/1.2 = 10$, whose logarithm is about 2.3026, and $18/28.8 = 0.625$, whose logarithm is about −0.4700 (≈ means “about”): Since each logarithm is weighted by its count, a difference observed many times has more weight in $G^2$ compared to the same difference observed fewer times. The log ratio is a measure of difference size calculated via this formula: The numerator of the fraction stands for the inside rate of the word, i.e., how often it occurred divided by the sum total of all the words on the inside, after adding 0.5 to its frequency. Likewise, the denominator refers to the outside rate (how often it occurred divided by the sum total of all the words on the outside, again adding 0.5). Logarithms base 2 ($log_2$) count powers of two, thus a log ratio of 1 denotes twice the rate inside, of 2 four times the rate, and of 3 eight times. By adding the 0.5 figure, the values can be calculated regardless of whether or not a word was found on both sides. For instance, the word bill has an inside rate of $12.5 / 2{,}000 = 0.00625$ and an outside rate of $18.5 / 48{,}000 approx 0.000385$. Thus, the inside rate is some 16.2 times greater than the outside rate. As $2^4 = 16$, the log ratio comes out to about 4.02. Words qualify for entry into the profile based on meeting all three of the following conditions: they are more common inside than outside; their log ratios need to be greater than or equal to 1, which means their rate inside is roughly twice the rate outside, or more; they occur a minimum of 3 times inside. After LemmaLoom determines which words meet the criteria, it ranks the words according to their log-likelihood scores. The top 50 words will compose your profile, keeping their log-likelihood scores as their weights. The words meeting the three criteria and ranking among the top 50 will qualify for your profile regardless of how low their log-likelihood score is, although low-scoring words will have negligible weighting. Word Inside Outside Log-likelihood Log ratio In the profile bill 12 18 38.34 4.02 yes pay 9 30 18.25 2.90 yes cover 7 20 15.79 3.13 yes climate 6 140 0.00 0.15 no (log ratio below 1) wager 2 0 12.88 6.91 no (fewer than 3 inside) Cost passages contain climate at almost the same rate as anywhere else in the project, so it says nothing about costs in particular. Wager receives high scores for both metrics, although it occurs only twice, which is too few to depend upon.

For each sentence without the code, LemmaLoom gathers the different profile words contained therein. Sentences containing fewer than two such words are removed from the list (in cases where the profile has only a single word, a sentence containing at least one suffices). The scoring formula used by LemmaLoom for ranking is shown below: Here $w_1$ to $w_k$ are the weights assigned to the $k$ profile words occurring in the sentence (each counted once, regardless of how many times it occurs), and $n$ refers to the total number of words in the sentence, not including punctuation marks, while including stopwords. The square root of a number is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives it. For instance, $sqrt{9} = 3$ because $3 times 3 = 9$. To calculate a sentence's score using this approach, assume that the hypothetical profile is made up solely of the words bill, pay, and cover. In the piece entitled “Running Out of Time” there is the statement Those bills were paid too. The sentence contains five words, out of which two (bills and paid) correspond to the profile words bill and pay. In “Who Pays for the Transition” there is the sentence The heat pump program pays out to homeowners with the savings to cover the rest, while the renters next door pay toward it through their bills. There are twenty-six words in this sentence and three profile words. The word bills matches bill; pay (appearing twice as pays and pay) contributes only one weight. While having more profile words, this longer sentence scores lower since its weight is divided by a greater number of words. In “Running Out of Time” there is the sentence Third, a national program to insulate homes and cut energy bills, starting with the households that struggle most to heat them. It includes only one profile word, bill, making it ineligible for the list. If the score was not divided at all, the effect would have been to reward long sentences merely for their capacity to house many profile words. If the score was divided by the length itself, the result would favor very short sentences. With the square root, a sentence four times as long needs twice the weight to reach the same score.

Results of “Passages Like Costs”, sorted by Score. In the Score column, the score of each sentence is shown. Sentences are sorted in descending order of their scores. Since the score depends upon the size of both the inside and the outside, comparison between lists is not possible. By default, the list contains up to 200 sentences. For larger amounts of sentences, increase the number beside Limit in the Show condition; over 5,000, also increase Limit in the Options condition. Normally, one processes sentences starting at the top of the list, batch by batch, like so: Double-click a row, or choose Go to Source from its shortcut menu, to open the sentence in its document. Read it in context, and if it belongs with the code, code it (see ). When you have worked through a batch, go back to the query and press ⌘R. The sentences you have coded drop out of the list. The Filter field in the bar above the results allows you to filter the rows shown based on whether their text, context, or document contains the inputted text. By typing part of a document's title into the Filter field, you may narrow down the results to a single document at a time. The Open results in a window button, with two diagonal arrows at the right of the same bar, will allow you to keep the list in view alongside your documents. The results window keeps the list as it was when you opened it; if you wanted the updated list after pressing ⌘R, you'd need to open the window again. ⌘R reuses your query's original profile. If you wanted to incorporate your latest coding decisions into your profile, you could choose Passages Like a Code and the code again. Profile preservation requires you to save your query (refer to Saving queries in ). When you want to score paragraphs instead of sentences, pick Text · Paragraphs from Find, and then switch the menu showing Document Order back to Score, since changing Find resets the sort. Score shows up in the menu showing Document Order only when dealing with queries whose list is frozen (see Frozen lists in ). A frozen list can come from queries created via Passages Like a Code or the Freeze Values command. The scoring process remains the same either way. When using Freeze Values, each word's weight is the score it was frozen with. With a keyword list, the weights represent log-likelihoods; with a collocate list, they represent association scores. To apply sorting by Score, there must be at least two different words from the list per passage; and since a word holds only one, sorting by Score requires setting Find to a unit of several words, such as Text · Sentences or Text · Paragraphs, prior to sorting. For example, sort by Score the “Keywords: Activists” query from Freeze Values in , with Find set to Text · Sentences within the “Skeptics” set. The skeptics' sentences containing the activists' keywords most densely appear at the very top. The lens or analyzer creation process and Auto Code… require setting the menu showing Score to another option (see Which queries can be lenses in ).

A recipe is a pre-fabricated query for a common question you may wish to ask. Examples of queries served up as recipes might be a concordance, a word list, or the co-occurrences of codes. They can also give you a place to begin while learning to craft queries, or quickly provide an overview of your material prior to developing your own queries. Do not hesitate to alter conditions from a recipe into something more suited to your needs, saving the altered query under a new name. The Recipes list gives access to the available query recipes for sets or projects, displayed below saved queries in the left column of the Queries section and the Queries window. The Search field in the bar at the top finds a recipe or a saved query by its name. You can also find the recipes for a document's query in the inspector via the Recipes menu (the wand icon) in the bar at the top. Both locations display the recipe options categorized as Words, Grammar, Coding, Speakers and Time, and Documents and Library and show only the relevant recipes based on context. In sets and projects, there exists an additional recipe option titled Passages Like a Code at the end of the left column (see Passages Like a Code earlier in this chapter). Selecting a recipe replaces your active query with a new, unsaved query named after the recipe and runs it. If your old query had unsaved changes, use ⌘Z to restore it. In the table's center column, what comes before the semicolon is set in Find and Where, and what comes after it in Show. Recipe The query it sets up Offered in Concordance Words whose Lemma is a value you type; List everywhere Word List Words where Is Word is true; Count by Lemma, limited to 200 rows everywhere Collocates Words whose Lemma is a value you type; Collocates everywhere Keywords Words; Keywords a set; a project that has at least one set Relation Pattern Matches with a Dependency pattern, A a verb and B its Object; Count by Word · B · Lemma everywhere Passive Sentences by Group Sentences where Passive is true; Compare by Group, measured Per 10,000 Words sets, projects, and All Projects Rhetoric by Group Findings of the Rhetoric analyzer; Count by Group and Finding sets, projects, and All Projects Hedges in Coded Passages Findings whose Finding is any of Hedge, Some Inside Codings; List everywhere Coded Words Words where Is Word is true and Stopword is false, Some Inside Codings; Count by Lemma, limited to 100 rows everywhere Code Co-occurrence Codings; Network by Code, linked when they are Overlapping everywhere Codings by Attribute Codings; Count by Code and Group sets, projects, and All Projects Speaker Turns over Time Speaker Turns; Over Time by Media Time and Speaker wherever the documents include audio or video Dictionary Categories by Document Text Matches of a dictionary; Count by Document and Category sets, projects, and All Projects, when there is a dictionary Documents Without Codings Documents, with Has No Codings in Where; List sets, projects, and All Projects Codes Without Codings Codes, with Has No Codings in Where, counting only codings in the documents searched; List everywhere Document Table Documents; List with the columns Authors, Date, Language, Group, Tags, and Tokens sets, projects, and All Projects “Everywhere” means a document's query, a set's or project's Queries section, and Window ▸ Queries regardless of scope. The groups the recipes count by are document groups, such as “Print” and “Online” in “Climate Debate”. Certain recipes require an input value or a choice before their results mean much: Concordance and Collocates both come with a blank Lemma rule. Type the lemma of interest into this rule slot; until you do, the rule is ignored and the query covers every word. Keywords needs something to compare with. In a set, the recipe compares the set with the rest of the project. In a project's Queries section it compares the project with the first of its sets; choose another in the menu showing its name in the Show condition. The scores are explained in Keywords in . Relation counts the objects of all verbs; adding a rule to A, e.g., Lemma is pay, will yield the count of objects of this specific verb. Similarly, choosing another relation for B will change what Relation counts. Codings by Attribute starts grouping by document Group by default; in order to group by attribute values, you should select Attribute ▸ Stance or any other attribute via the field menu of the second Group By row. Dictionary Categories by Document uses one of the dictionaries included in the current project. Should there be several dictionaries included, you may wish to verify which one the Find condition names, and change it if needed. Hedges in Coded Passages uses the list of hedges detected by the Metadiscourse analyzer. If instead you are looking to count the categories of a dictionary of your own, e.g., “Hedges”, inside codings, then begin with Dictionary Categories by Document, followed by adding the context Some Inside Codings in Where (see ).

Once a query has found something useful in your documents, you may wish to turn it into a lens, which annotates its hits whenever you are viewing a document. Queries may also be saved as a custom analyzer that operates during indexing. Should a query be able to locate documents within your project, it can become a smart set. The Actions menu allows you to perform actions directly on your results (coding passages, gathering the documents into a set, bookmarking hits, freezing a word list, and adding words to a dictionary, among others). The current chapter requires familiarity with building and running queries;  and  cover these topics. Examples will refer to “Climate Debate”, the example project, which is added to your library via File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. Included in “Climate Debate” are two saved queries, titled “Urgency Talk” and “Keywords: Activists”. All other queries mentioned within this chapter can be constructed from the descriptions provided below.

In this chapter, a passage refers to any span of text found by a query. Passages include words, sentences, codings, and speaker turns. A query lens refers to a saved query that also shows up in the lens menu in the reader (see ). Once you enable it, LemmaLoom executes the query on your current document and annotates the hits according to your configuration. This happens similarly to how the built-in lenses highlight word classes and negations. If you edit a saved query and save it, its lens updates automatically too. A generated analyzer is a custom analyzer that is created based on a query. This analyzer uses JavaScript that LemmaLoom generates for it, similar to the scripts you develop in Window ▸ Analyzers. This analyzer runs automatically in all projects during indexing (see ). Findings of analyzers are the spans of text they annotate, stored with each document they are run on. A generated analyzer is essentially a snapshot of a query in time. The parity check runs both a query and a generated analyzer side-by-side and compares their results on a few documents. A generated analyzer can be saved only if both find exactly the same passages. A linked analyzer is a generated analyzer that retains knowledge of the saved query it comes from. Whenever you change and save the query afterwards, the analyzer shows Out of Date. A frozen list refers to a static list of words extracted from a Collocates or Keywords query. Collocates come with scores (i.e., association values), while keywords get their log-likelihood. These scores become weights assigned to each element of the frozen list. A query can search for the words of a frozen list in any scope.

Typically, one would test out a query on several documents until getting a result satisfactory enough to warrant keeping. The purpose behind the particular query affects how one stores it. Usually, the best place to begin is with lenses because they show hits in real-time while reading, picking up saved changes along the way. Lenses are appropriate for patterns one wishes to continue refining, as well as for viewing patterns within close reading sessions. Analyzers are more suited toward finalized patterns, since they apply in every project and store results within each document. Such stored results become accessible through other queries, which may involve counting results, comparing between document groups, or correlating hits with codes. Analyzers can only use words, sentences, and grammatical structures, but once they've been created based off of one version of a query, they keep that version until you update them. Smart sets represent a third option for storing a query pattern. In this case, queries select documents based off of certain attributes and characteristics rather than content patterns. As such, a smart set could contain the activist texts with large audiences, for example. A smart set appears in the navigation sidebar and can be used like any other set. The three options differ in scope of application and adherence to query changes:  Query lens Generated analyzer Smart set Made from a query that lists passages a query that lists passages and looks only at words, sentences, and their grammar a query that lists documents by their properties What you get colors and a legend in the reader colors in the reader, plus stored findings that other queries can search a set in the sidebar whose members are worked out from its conditions Where it applies wherever the saved query is available (one document, a set, a project, or all projects) every document in its languages, in all projects its project When the work is done each time you enable the lens in a document once per document, during indexing whenever the set is used After you change the query follows the saved query shows Out of Date until you update it keeps its own copy of the conditions Unlike these three, the Actions menu operates on your results once, creating sets, bookmarks, and codings based on the results. From there, they become independent of your query.

t: Where the Save and Actions menus are located
b: Each query has a header row above the query builder. This header appears no matter where you work with the query (the Query facet of a document, Queries views within sets and the project itself, or the standalone Queries window). The commands discussed here appear in two of its menus. Save (the icon showing a square with an arrow pointing into it) is used to save queries and turn them into lenses or analyzers. Actions (the ellipsis circle icon ⋯) acts upon the results the query has just produced. Both commands move to a second line when the first line cannot fit all of its buttons, placing themselves at the right end of that second line. Otherwise they sit to the right of Run Query (the triangle button). The remaining parts of the header are explained in The builder in . The Save menu contains options such as Save, Save As…, and, for queries already saved, Rename…. Further down the menu, a dividing line precedes Save as Lens… (or Remove Lens for queries that are already lenses) and Save as Analyzer…. Additionally, the Delete Query option appears below it when the query is already saved. Finally, the Delete Query action appears directly in the shortcut menu of saved queries in the left column of Queries views and the Queries window. When invoked, Delete Query deletes the query at once. If the query is loaded, the builder begins again with an empty New Query. Edit ▸ Undo Delete Query brings the query back. The Save menu of an unsaved query in the inspector's Query facet, with “Running Out of Time” open.

t: Saving a query as a lens
b: A lens is essentially what you should be looking for if you want to run your query alongside your reading experience. “Climate Debate” has a query named “Urgency Talk” saved as a lens, and this lens shows annotations on sentences containing any of five specific words (urgent, urgency, crisis, emergency, deadline) if they overlap a passage coded “Urgency” or any of its subcodes. This lens’s query is explained in detail in A first query in , and it locates Sentences through Lemma matching with a context row for Codings. The Show condition is set to List mode. If you wish to save your query as a lens: Run the query and look at a few of its hits. In a document's Query facet, click a hit to scroll the reader to it. In a Queries view or the Queries window, double-click a hit, or right-click it and choose Go to Source. Make sure Show is set to List. Open the Save menu and choose Save as Lens…. In the Save as Lens dialog, enter a Name. The lens menu will show this name. In Available In, choose where the lens should be offered (see the table below). Click Save. Once the query is saved, it immediately turns into a lens. In the query name menu or the left column of a Queries view or the Queries window, you will notice that each lens has a pair of glasses next to the query’s name. For a query that is already saved, Save as Lens… skips the dialog: it saves the query in its current state, including any unsaved changes, and turns it into a lens at once. The Save as Lens dialog for a new query being saved as “Urgency Talk 2”, available in the whole project. In Available In, the documents that will provide the lens are defined. For Available In, you want to define the smallest scope in which your documents fall; doing so will keep the lens menus of other documents brief. Your dialog will display options according to where you are working; the default option is always the first choice listed. Available In Offered when you save from The lens appears in Document a document's Query facet that document only Set a set's Queries view, or the Queries window with a set as the scope every document in the set, and their translations Project a document, a set, or the project every document in the project All Projects anywhere every document in every project When working in the Queries window with All Projects as the scope, only one option appears, All Projects.

t: Using a query lens in the reader
b: Query lenses are enabled similarly to regular lenses: Open a document in which the lens is available. Click the lens menu in the title band at the top of the reader. Query lenses are listed by name in the lower part of the menu, after Bookmarks, Codes, and your dictionaries. Choose the lens. A checkmark shows that it is enabled, and its lenslets appear in the legend. “Running Out of Time” with the “Urgency Talk” lens enabled; the legend has a single lenslet, “Urgency Talk”. Here are the rules for how a lenslet gets generated from your query: A query that has no categories generates a single lenslet. It's called whatever you named your query. A query that has categories generates a lenslet for each category, and colors it and styles it according to your choices in the Categories condition. Annotations are only applied to those hits that fall within a category. A query that uses Color By creates a separate category for each unique value of a field (see Categories and Color By in ). As many lenslets get created as distinct values occur within the open document; however, they don't exceed 16 in all. The lenslets get sorted alphabetically, while colors get assigned in that order. Consequently, the same value may receive two different colors in two different documents. When you enable the lens for the current document, LemmaLoom runs the underlying query. It runs again whenever you modify your query and save it or rename it. Also, whenever codings or bookmarks change within the document, LemmaLoom reruns the query. So, “Urgency Talk” reacts immediately to your coding activity, meaning that the annotation will appear the minute you apply the code “Deadlines” to the sentence beginning A deadline that falls after everyone in office has retired in “Running Out of Time”. Disabling a lens happens when you toggle it again from the lens menu or choose Clear All, Clear Lenses, or Clear Annotations; Clear Annotations also disables Bookmarks and Codes along with other query and dictionary lenses. If you decide to cease providing the lens altogether, then load the query you need to remove from the lens menus and go to its Save menu to choose Remove Lens. The query itself remains intact. Deleting the query removes the lens too, though. Edit ▸ Undo Remove Lens and Edit ▸ Undo Delete Query return it. Once the lens is enabled, you can invoke Document ▸ Auto Code… (⇧⌘A) or the corresponding item near the bottom of the lens menu, which opens the Auto Code dialog, which codes every passage the lens annotates. When multiple query, dictionary, or analyzer lenses are enabled, each menu contains multiple options, each related to its own particular lens, such as Auto Code with Urgency Talk…, and ⇧⌘A goes with the first. For instance, since “Urgency Talk” has no categories, its dialog has one row alone, called “Urgency Talk”. Auto-coding from a lens in  goes into more detail. The lens menu in “Running Out of Time” with the “Hedges” and “Urgency Talk” lenses checked, and Auto Code with Urgency Talk… and Auto Code with Hedges… near the bottom.

A lens will annotate stretches of text in the current document only. Your query should thus return a simple list of the passages. The Save as Lens… item is disabled if the query fails to meet that requirement. Hover the mouse pointer over it to find out precisely why. For the purpose of generating lenses, a query must satisfy certain criteria: Show should be set to List; Find must specify one of these kinds of passages, namely Words, Pattern Matches, Sentences, Paragraphs, Text Matches, Phrases, Noun Chunks, Findings, Codings, Memos, Bookmarks, or Speaker Turns; Sorting is performed on any criterion except Score. Score is offered for queries with a frozen list (see Freeze Values later in this chapter); No more than 16 categories are defined in the query’s Categories condition; And the query itself needs to be ready to execute. All the conditions for unavailability are detailed in Why an item is unavailable later in the chapter.

t: Turning a query into an analyzer
b: Custom analyzers are small JavaScript programs that run for each document when it is being indexed (see ). When saving a query as a custom analyzer via Save as Analyzer…, the code needed for this purpose is generated for you, and the resulting custom analyzer functions as follows: Runs for every document in the languages you choose, in all projects, except documents where you remove its output in Document Properties (see ); Results stored and computed once per document, so not repeated every time you enable a lens; Visible among other analyzers in the lens menu, and able to be run with Auto Code…; Results searchable through Find set to Findings, and thus available for use in further queries; Source visible in Window ▸ Analyzers for viewing, testing, and editing. “Urgency Talk” cannot be saved as a custom analyzer since it uses Codings in its context, which are unavailable during indexing, so Save as Analyzer… is disabled with the reason Uses codings or memos. However, the examples below show how to generate a custom analyzer from a query. The example query used is “Urgency Words”, saved in the project's Queries view with Available In set to Project. It finds Words with only a text row set to Lemma for threshold, collapse, unravel, deadline, target, and countdown. Unravel originates from the document titled “Running Out of Time”, wherein ice sheets, forests, and ocean currents begin to unravel on their own. Its Categories condition contains two categories. “Tipping Points” is a category containing a text row set to Lemma for threshold, collapse, and unravel, whereas “Deadlines” is another category that includes a text row for Lemma of deadline, target, and countdown. The names of the categories are identical to those of the two subcodes of “Urgency”, so the Auto Code dialog can match them (see Auto Code… later in this chapter). Here is how to create an analyzer from a query: Save the query first, with Save or Save As… (see the note below). Open the Save menu and choose Save as Analyzer…. Wait while the Parity line shows a spinner, then check the dialog (described below). Change Name or Languages if needed. Click Save. An analyzer mirrors what the builder displays. A query that was never saved leads to an unlinked analyzer. For a saved query with unsaved modifications, Save in the dialog saves the modifications to the query first and then links the analyzer to it. The Save as Analyzer dialog contains these fields: Name begins as the name of the query. Languages includes options for English, German, and Chinese. Initially, the languages of the documents covered by the query will be selected, or English if none are among those three. You should only check the languages intended for the query, as a query for English lemmas, for instance, should be run on English documents. Legend displays each category of the query colored appropriately. If there are no categories in the query, then Legend will display a single item labeled Match. Source contains the script generated for the query. Select and copy the contents of this field to use elsewhere; however, to edit the script, first save and then use Window ▸ Analyzers. Parity shows the outcome of the parity check (see The parity check below). Documents displays the number of documents across all your projects in the selected languages. The analyzer will process each document. Save is disabled when any of the following conditions applies; hover the mouse pointer over Save to learn more: Checking parity signifies the parity check is currently running. Source has errors denotes the generated script does not satisfy the criteria all analyzers must meet. The content of Parity changes to show the error message. Findings don't match indicates a discrepancy in the findings during the parity check. Name is empty or No language chosen specifies a field needs filling in. If the query cannot be represented as a script, the reason will be displayed, and the Save button shows it too. The Save as Analyzer dialog for “Urgency Words”, opened from the project's Queries view. Clicking Save makes the analyzer available in Window ▸ Analyzers, and LemmaLoom then runs it on the documents in its languages behind the scenes in all projects. See Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0) to watch the progress. This may take varying amounts of time depending upon the number of documents and capabilities of your Mac. Edit ▸ Undo Add Analyzer undoes this operation. If your query finds matches with words defined in a dictionary, the script stores a snapshot of the dictionary terms at the time you saved it. Your analyzer keeps this snapshot even as the dictionary evolves over time. In order to bring the changes in the dictionary into your analyzer, reload your query and choose Save as Analyzer… again (see Keeping an analyzer in step with its query below).

The generated script discovers passages automatically and independently of your query. But before it can be saved, LemmaLoom ensures that it actually identifies the exact same stretches as your query does. The validation procedure takes no more than three indexed documents within your query's scope and executes both the query and the script on those documents. The stretches discovered by each are compared. Stretches match if they coincide precisely in their beginning and ending word within the same sentence, as well as in their category. For “Urgency Words”, the line under Parity reads 8 of 8 findings match in 3 documents. The figure 8 of 8 indicates that the script and the query match perfectly; that is, all findings identified by either coincide. The left-hand side number represents the findings discovered in common, while the right-hand side number represents the total number of findings discovered by the query and/or script. Should these two numbers differ, then they indicate mismatches; that is, there are discrepancies in the identification of stretches. Suppose, to take invented numbers, that the query finds 9 stretches and the script finds 10 stretches in the three documents. Then, since the script includes 8 out of these 9 stretches, it fails to discover one, while finding 2 additional stretches that the query did not. Altogether, the query and the script discover 8 stretches in common. Adding the two totals counts these shared stretches twice, so the stretches found by either are: Here $Q$, $S$, and $M$ stand for, respectively, the number of findings discovered by the query, script, and both, and $T$ stands for the total number of findings discovered by either. In the example, substituting the numbers into this equation gives $T = 9 + 10 - 8 = 11$, and the line reads 8 of 11 findings match in 3 documents. The script misses one stretch, while discovering 2 new ones; thus, there are 3 mismatches overall. A mismatch prevents you from saving your script. Save is disabled, and LemmaLoom informs you that Findings don't match; therefore, retain your query as a lens. This verification procedure uses the scope defined by your query. For instance, in the Query facet of an open document, it is the current open document only. Otherwise, in the Queries view for a set or a project, it is the first three indexed documents in a set/project scope. To validate your script in relation to more than one document, use a Queries view or the Queries window for creating the analyzer. In the absence of indexed documents in your query's scope, LemmaLoom displays a No indexed documents message instead of numbers, and Save is available. As soon as documents become indexed in the scope, enable the analyzer in the respective document's lens menu, and verify whether the analyzer highlights exactly the same passages as your query does.

Like every custom analyzer, a generated one reads through one sentence at a time, considering the sentence’s words, phrases, and noun chunks along with each word’s lemma, word class, grammatical tag, morphology, and dependencies (see ). A query can only turn into an analyzer if these capabilities alone suffice to run it. Otherwise, Save as Analyzer… becomes disabled with an explanation tooltip on hover. To be suitable as an analyzer, the query should satisfy: being qualified as a lens (see Which queries can be lenses earlier in this chapter); finding Words, Pattern Matches, Sentences, Phrases, or Noun Chunks; using only fields of words, sentences, and phrases in the rules; matching text based on Word, Word Form, or Lemma, and Terms or Dictionary; making connections only inside a single sentence via Overlapping, Inside, Containing, Same Span As, or In the Same Sentence As relations only to words, sentences, phrases, or noun chunks; without any Has rows or any Color By option enabled; excluding references to the fields Negator, In Negation Scope, Connective, Modality, Topological Field, and Particle. They are reserved for the reader's built-in lenses. The query “Urgency Words” fits these requirements. This query searches for words and checks only their lemmas both within rules and category definitions.

t: Keeping an analyzer in step with its query
b: Once the query is modified and saved after creating the analyzer, the analyzer continues analyzing according to its original query until updated. Should the analyzer be linked (made from a saved query, with a source not altered manually since), LemmaLoom recognizes the discrepancy. Any modifications made to the saved query of a linked analyzer will mark the analyzer’s entry in Window ▸ Analyzers with Out of Date. Modifying the saved query to alter how results are sorted without modifying results counts too. Updating the analyzer via the Analyzers window involves: Choose Window ▸ Analyzers. In the list on the left, select the analyzer that shows Out of Date. Click Update Analyzer, to the left of Save in the row with the name and the languages. Window ▸ Analyzers with the “Urgency Words” analyzer showing Out of Date. Updating an analyzer via Update Analyzer takes the saved query and converts it directly to an analyzer script. While keeping the name and languages of the analyzer, this will replace its source and legend; therefore, you lose any changes made to label names or colors. If there are errors in the new script, LemmaLoom informs you right below the editor, leaving the analyzer with its old script. The button is disabled, with an explanation as to why, when the saved query can no longer become an analyzer. When an update changes the analyzer script, LemmaLoom runs the analyzer again for all the documents in its languages. To undo the latest update, select Edit ▸ Undo Update Analyzer. If you wish to update from the query, which runs the parity check first, open the saved query and then select Save as Analyzer… again. If the analyzer is linked, the dialog is titled Update Analyzer and shows the existing name and language(s), both of which can be edited. You can update the changes via Update, which takes the place of Save, and Edit ▸ Undo Edit Analyzer returns you to the state prior to editing. The Update Analyzer dialog for the linked analyzer “Urgency Words”, showing its name, languages, legend, source, and parity result. Two conditions will break the connection between the saved query and the analyzer: Changing the source via Window ▸ Analyzers, and then clicking Save. This results in an independent analyzer script separate from the saved query, and Save as Analyzer… on the query creates a new, separate analyzer. Edit ▸ Undo Edit Analyzer will restore both the old source and the link. Editing just the name or languages or legend retains the connection. Deleting the query. The analyzer keeps working as an unlinked analyzer.

t: Saving a document query as a smart set
b: A smart set gathers documents based on property and attribute conditions, determining its membership based on those conditions whenever it needs to (see ). If you already have a query which selects documents via property and attribute rules, then that query can be turned into a smart set. In the “Climate Debate” project, a saved query named “Widely Read Activists” in the project’s Queries view returns Documents. Its Where condition matches All of the two rules, “Stance” is any of “Activist” and “Readership” is at least 100,000 (see Adding a rule in ). This results in “Letter from the Climate Strike” and “Running Out of Time”. Saving a query as a smart set requires: Build the query in the Queries view of a set or the project, or in the Queries window with a project or set as the scope. Run the query and check the documents it lists. Give the query the name you want for the set, with Save As… or Rename…. Open the Actions menu and choose Save as Smart Set. A smart set draws on all of the documents in the project regardless of which set the query ran on. Consider a query in the “Activists” set with the single rule “Readership” is at least 100,000. It returns “Letter from the Climate Strike” and “Running Out of Time”; however, a smart set based off of it also includes “Net Zero Will Cost You”, “Let's Not Panic”, “Carbon Tax Debate”, and “Radio Debate”. The “Stance” rule can be added to limit results to activists. A smart set can be seen in the sidebar under the name of the query, and its conditions along with the All/Any choice are duplicated too. If the query was never named, the set is titled New Query, or after the recipe used to generate it. You can rename a smart set directly from the sidebar. If changes are needed, select Edit from its shortcut menu, or Project ▸ Edit Smart Set. Choose Edit ▸ Undo New Smart Set to delete the set. The option Save as Smart Set is only shown in the query’s Actions menu when the following requirements apply to its query definition: The Show mode is List, and the Find parameter is Documents. Scope is either a project, or a set. Rules in the Where condition are not nested in any manner; furthermore, no relations, Has rows, or text rows appear in it. All rules refer to document properties, attributes, Tags, Group, Language, or Format. No frozen list appears in a rule. The item becomes disabled when the Where condition is set to match None of its rules, whereas smart sets require matching All/Any of the conditions instead.

The Actions menu operates upon the result of the query that was just performed. Items are shown depending on the nature of the result; an applicable item that doesn’t have anything to operate on, such as Bookmark Hits… on an empty result list, is disabled. In a Queries view, if none of the items apply, then the entire Actions menu button itself is disabled, indicating No results before the query has run and No actions after. For the Query facet of a document, the menu always contains Auto Code…, while in the Queries window, it’s New Window. Each item operates upon the entire result, regardless of whether or not it was filtered by the Filter field located above the results (see Filtering the results in ). Item Offered when What it does Auto Code… the query is in a document's Query facet codes the passages the query finds Create Set from Hits Show is List and Find is a kind of passage or Documents; the scope is not All Projects makes a set of the documents with hits Save as Smart Set see Saving a document query as a smart set makes a smart set from the query's rules Bookmark Hits… Show is List and Find is a kind of passage; the scope is not All Projects bookmarks every listed hit Freeze Values Show is Collocates or Keywords replaces the query with one that searches for the listed words Add to Dictionary Show is Count or Compare with one Group By key, Collocates, or Keywords; Find is Words or Text Matches; the scope belongs to a project that has a dictionary adds the listed words to a dictionary category New Window the query is in the Queries window opens another Queries window with a new query in the same scope (see The Queries window in ) The Actions menu for the “Widely Read Activists” query in the project's Queries view.

Auto Code… auto-codes any passage found by the query, directly from the query. This feature may be useful for coding patterns once, within documents or across a set, without having to see them while reading. It is only available from the Actions menu of a document's Query facet since it relies on the open document's Auto Code dialog. With “Urgency Words” selected in the Query facet of the “Running Out of Time” document, with the “Activists” set selected under Documents, running this dialog codes any occurrences of the specified words in the five documents within that set that use them; however, “Hope Takes Work” does not contain any such occurrences. Because the two rows in the Auto Code dialog, namely “Tipping Points” and “Deadlines”, specify existing codes' names, those codes are selected for coding. The Auto Code dialog opened from the query “Urgency Talk” in “Running Out of Time”. Here is how you run Auto Code… from a query: In the document's inspector, open the Query facet (View ▸ Inspector ▸ Multimode, then Query). Build the query, or load a saved one from the query name menu. Open the Actions menu and choose Auto Code…. In the Auto Code dialog, the Query line shows the query's name. Under Codes, each category of the query has a row; a query without categories has a single row named after the query. Uncheck the rows you do not want. For each checked row, choose a code, or keep New Code: … to create a top-level code with the row's name and color. That code is created only if the run finds a passage for the row. A code whose name matches the row's name, ignoring capitalization and accents, is chosen for you. In Documents, choose This Document, one of the project's sets, or Whole Project. With This Document, Passages shows how many passages the query finds for the checked rows. Click Auto Code. While it runs, Progress shows how many documents are done; Stop ends the run after the current document. When Progress shows the number of codings added, click Done. The Auto Code button becomes disabled when the dialog is loading passages (i.e., Loading) and when no rows are selected (Nothing selected). If you launch Auto Code based on a query: LemmaLoom considers the query as it currently is built whether it has been saved beforehand or not. On a set or project-wide basis, the query is executed on every original document in isolation as though you opened each one up and ran the query within each. No translations participate except the active document itself, if applicable; starting on “Running Out of Time (German)” means using it in place of “Running Out of Time”. Similar to manual codings, each coding generated is inserted into each document’s translations too. Auto Code… is disabled for the reasons that apply to Save as Lens… (see Which queries can be lenses above for more details). The operation is undone as a single transaction using Edit ▸ Undo Auto Code (⌘Z), which eliminates every coding generated and code created during the process; any coding generated prior to clicking the Stop button is eliminated too. The rest of the behavior with regard to auto-coding is explained in What auto-coding does in .

Create Set from Hits creates a standard set consisting of all documents with hits in response to the current query. It assigns the query name to the set and creates it immediately in the sidebar. Consider a query in the Queries view of “Climate Debate” that searches for Sentences where the Lemma is equal to settle, saved as “Settle Mentions”. The resulting hits occur in the three documents, namely “Running Out of Time”, “Hope Takes Work”, and “Let's Not Panic”. Thus, using Actions ▸ Create Set from Hits results in the creation of the “Settle Mentions” set, which consists of precisely these three documents. Although the lemma settle occurs in “Science Is Never Settled”, it does so in its title only, not the body. All hits contribute to the set regardless of whether they are excluded from the list by either Limit (see Bookmark Hits below). As the set contains the originals, when the hit falls in a translation, the original document will join the set rather than the translation itself; a hit in “Running Out of Time (German)” adds “Running Out of Time”. For a query that finds Documents, the set would contain the listed documents alone. The set is a static list of documents. Edit ▸ Undo New Set deletes the set.

Bookmark Hits… puts bookmarks on all hits in the list so that you may locate the passages another time, for example with the Bookmarks lens. The Bookmark Hits dialog for the query “Urgency Talk” in the project's Queries view, with the color red chosen and the line 6 in 5 documents. To bookmark hits of a query: Run the query with Show set to List. Open the Actions menu and choose Bookmark Hits…. In the Bookmark Hits dialog, choose a Color. Check the Bookmarks line, for example 42 in 9 documents. It counts the new bookmarks, leaving out hits that are already bookmarked. Click Bookmark. A bookmark receives the query’s name as its comment. Only those hits that appear in the list are bookmarked. This is capped at the Limit parameter on the Options condition (5,000 hits unless specified otherwise) or sooner when Limit is selected on the Show condition. If the line below the list says something like Showing 5,000 of 6,212, increase the limit or deselect Limit on the Show condition before bookmarking. Should a hit match the starting and ending point of another bookmark (regardless of color), it is skipped. When all hits are matched, Bookmark becomes disabled with the reason Already bookmarked. Like manually created bookmarks, bookmarks created via this query automatically appear in other language versions of the same document. One Edit ▸ Undo Bookmark Hits clears all newly added bookmarks.

A Collocates or Keywords query yields results specific to the documents it was performed on. With Freeze Values, however, a fixed list of words may be generated based off of your result, allowing you to search for those words wherever needed. An example of a common application might involve finding the words that distinguish two separate sets of documents from each other, followed by searching the second set with those words. For example, the set “Activists” in “Climate Debate” contains a saved query called “Keywords: Activists”. This query provides the keywords found more frequently in activist texts compared to the skeptics'. After freezing this list and saving a new query with it in the project, you could load this new query onto the “Skeptics” set to discover with a Count grouped by Lemma which of the activists' keywords the skeptics use, and how often. Upon selecting Actions ▸ Freeze Values: The first 200 rows of your result will be converted into a frozen list. The frozen list is named for the initial query. When dealing with Keywords queries, only the Positive Keywords are used, namely, the words the set uses more often than its reference. The scores of each row in the result become weights for each of your words. Your builder is changed into a new, unsaved query which searches for Words whose Lemma is any of the frozen list, or whose Word or Word Class is, depending on what your previous query was counting. This new query inherits the name of the frozen query. While it has the same name as before, it actually is an entirely separate entity. Save requires a name. Edit ▸ Undo Freeze Values restores the old query, with any unsaved changes. Editing any words in the new rule converts it to an ordinary list without weights. The Queries section of the “Activists” set right after Freeze Values on the “Keywords” query, with the Lemma rule set to None. In a Queries view or the Queries window, you can display both lists side by side while working on the frozen list. Do so by clicking Open results in a window at the right of the results bar, prior to freezing. (See Results in a window in .) To find the words of the frozen list somewhere else: Run the Collocates or Keywords query, and check its list. Open the Actions menu and choose Freeze Values. The builder now holds a query that finds the listed words. Open the Save menu, choose Save As…, and give the query a name. Set Available In to a place that includes the documents you want to search; to load the query in another set, choose Project. Open the Queries view where you want to search, and load the query from the query name menu or the left column. Set Show to what you want to see, such as Count with a Group By key on Lemma, which lists how often each frozen word occurs. A Count within the “Skeptics” set produces raw counts. As the skeptics' texts diverge from the activists' texts in quantity and length, a rate should account for this divergence. Thus, for a rate that can be compared with results from the same query conducted on the “Activists” set, select Per 10,000 Words within the menu showing Hits (see Measures in ). The query with the frozen list can sort its results according to Score, ranking passages in accordance with the weight of the words within the frozen list (see Passages Like a Code in ). However, lenses need a sort order other than Score.

Add to Dictionary will append the words of a result to a category of one of your project dictionaries. Use it after having generated either a frequency list, collocates list, or keywords list, containing the desired words that should be appended to that particular category. Within “Climate Debate”, the “Approximators” category of the “Hedges” dictionary contains words that approximate amounts or numbers, namely about, around, roughly, approximately, almost, nearly, more or less, and just about. There are additional words, like often, usually, and mostly, which similarly hedge a statement without necessarily modifying amounts or numbers. In certain studies, often, usually, and mostly may even fall into the category of approximators. A query in the project's Queries view reveals which of those words were found in the documents. It searches Words whose Lemma equals about, around, roughly, often, usually, mostly, and occasionally, with Show set to Count and one Group By key, which is Lemma again. Six results appeared, namely about 26 times, roughly 7 times, around 5 times, usually 5 times, mostly 3 times, and often 3 times. Using Actions ▸ Add to Dictionary ▸ “Hedges” ▸ “Approximators”, the three words, mostly, often, and usually, got appended, whereas the other three were already inside the category. The occurrence count of about also counted the phrase the thing about panic in the document “Let's Not Panic”, as well as a market town of about nine thousand people in the document “Who Pays for the Transition”.
