Remember, occurrences don’t tell much about usage, so browse some results before adding words to categories. The Add to Dictionary submenu, showing the “Hedges” dictionary and its two categories. To add the words of a result to a dictionary: Run the query. Open the Actions menu and choose Add to Dictionary. In the submenu, choose the dictionary, then the category. Terms are included instantly upon selecting the category. Terms from the label of each row are included, up to the first 200 rows. For Keywords, only Positive Keywords are included. If you wish to include less than all rows from a Count, check Limit in the Show condition and select a value first. If a term already exists in the category, then it won't be included; term comparison is case insensitive. The category itself maintains alphabetical order. Only the dictionaries of the query's project are listed. The item is hidden if there aren't any dictionaries in the project (see Creating a dictionary in ). Edit ▸ Undo Add to Dictionary removes all the added terms in one step. If you only want to include a couple terms, or even terms that weren't included in your results, copy-paste those terms into the Add term field of the category in the project's Dictionaries view. Each term should be placed on its own line (see Adding and removing terms in ).

A disabled Save as Lens…, Save as Analyzer…, or Auto Code… reveals the cause upon hover. Only one cause will be revealed at once regardless of multiple causes being true; after you have resolved it, the next may reveal itself. The first six causes listed in the table prevent all three actions while the remaining prevent only Save as Analyzer…. Reason What it means What to change Not a list Show is not set to List. Set Show to List. Not passages Find is set to documents, codes, sets, or another library item, which have no place in the text. Find a kind of passage instead. Paired results Find is Links or Alignments; each hit joins two places. Find a kind of passage that lies in one place. Scored list The list is sorted by Score. Choose another sort order. More than 16 categories The Categories condition has more than 16 categories. Merge or remove categories. Incomplete A rule is unfinished, or something else stops the query from running. Complete the query; the results area names what stops it. Uses analyzer findings Find is Findings, or a rule refers to findings. Keep the query as a lens. Uses raw text Find is Text Matches or Paragraphs; a text row matches Text or uses a Regular Expression; or a rule tests the paragraph or the passage's Text or Length. Match by Word, Word Form, or Lemma with Terms or a Dictionary. Uses media Find is Speaker Turns, or a rule uses In the Same Turn As. Keep the query as a lens. Uses translations A rule uses Translated As. Keep the query as a lens. Uses codings or memos Find is Codings, Memos, or Bookmarks; a rule tests a coding, memo, bookmark, or link, or uses Linked To; a relation points to anything other than words, sentences, phrases, noun chunks, or findings; or the query has a Has row. Keep the query as a lens. Uses document fields A rule tests a property or attribute of the document, such as Title, Language, or the attribute “Stance”. Remove the rule, or limit the query with its scope instead. Uses Color By The Categories condition uses Color By. Define the categories with rules instead. Uses reader-only fields A rule uses Negator, In Negation Scope, Connective, Modality, Topological Field, or Particle. Keep the query as a lens. Crosses sentences A rule uses Near, Before, After, or In the Same Paragraph As. Use In the Same Sentence As, or keep the query as a lens. One more reason, Not word-level, applies solely within the context of the Save as Analyzer dialog. This reason implies that while the query passes the checks above, parts of the query cannot be translated into a script. Keep the query as a lens.

The archive file format of LemmaLoom (.llz) stores your saved queries along with the indexed documents and their associated codes (see ). The queries included depend on your exports: Export Queries included File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project every query saved for the project, for any of its sets, or for any of its documents File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Set, or Export in a set's shortcut menu queries saved for the project, for that set, and for the documents in it File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Document (LemmaLoom Documents for several), or Export in the shortcut menu of selected documents queries saved for the project and for those documents Queries that were saved for All Projects are excluded from an archive. The fact that a query acts as a lens remains intact upon import. An archive contains any analyzer whose findings are stored with your exported documents. Additionally, it will include any analyzer that an included query searches with Findings, and any analyzer derived from the queries themselves. Findings are always imported alongside their related document. Upon importing an archive via File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive, the following transformations happen: Any codes, sets, or other items referenced in queries are paired up with their imported counterparts. A query of a set or document not found in your archive becomes a project-level query. Analyzers sit outside of any particular project. When importing an analyzer that you already have, e.g., if you exported the archive yourself, LemmaLoom uses your copy of it with any changes you made since, and skips the archive's copy. Otherwise the analyzer is imported, and one derived from an imported query will stay linked to it. Should the query reference words from a dictionary, the analyzer appears Out of Date because the query references a different copy of the dictionary now or no dictionary at all. References pointing to items that don't belong to the archive are discarded. Since dictionaries, other sets, and code sets only travel in a project archive and never in a set or a document archive, queries from those archives may require selecting a dictionary or a set separately again.

A dictionary is a collection of words and phrases sorted by category. LemmaLoom identifies every place in your documents these terms appear, calculates counts of each category, and can also annotate them in the reader. Dictionaries should be used whenever you seek something recognizable by its wording, such as hedging language or the vocabulary of a policy field. In the case of the examples in this chapter, the focus will be “Hedges”, the dictionary of the “Climate Debate” project. The project can be imported into LemmaLoom via the menu action File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project (see The example project in ). “Hedges” includes two categories each with eight terms. “Approximators” includes words such as about, around, and roughly, alongside the phrase more or less. “Shields” includes phrases such as I think and it seems, as well as individual words including perhaps and probably. Both of these kinds are used by writers to weaken statements and claims in some capacity, which makes them hedges. Specifically, approximators weaken numeric information or descriptive phrases by qualifying their accuracy, for instance about twelve years. Meanwhile, shields weaken statements by keeping the writer from committing fully to a claim.

A dictionary lives inside one project. You can apply your dictionary to every document, set, and query within your project. Your dictionary is comprised of categories of terms. A category has a name, color, and list of terms associated with it. Your category's color is displayed for any of the terms in your category within the reader, as well as for its bars within any chart. A term refers to a word or phrase, such as perhaps or more or less. Terms may be in any language. LemmaLoom will match a term based on text alone; regardless of meaning, LemmaLoom only considers the literal content of terms (see How terms are matched and Checking what a term matches later in this chapter). Some functionalities in this chapter require indexing, the grammatical processing of each document performed after import. During indexing, LemmaLoom identifies each word and sentence within each document, lemmatizes each word, providing its dictionary base form, or lemma (e.g., seems/seemed → seem), as well as its word class (see ). When you change your dictionaries, LemmaLoom refreshes the search of all terms within those dictionaries. As a consequence, changes to your dictionary reflect immediately within the Dictionaries section count results, as well as within any enabled dictionary lens, and in any query that employs those terms the next time it runs. If you save an analyzer off your query containing your dictionary terms, that analyzer continues to operate on those original terms (see Saving a dictionary query as a lens or an analyzer later in this chapter). In order to retain the current matches as codings, use auto coding (see Coding the matches later in this chapter). The built-in Metadiscourse lens highlights hedges in your text via its own word lists and lemma/word-class tagging (see Metadiscourse in ). A dictionary stores only the terms added by you. Every term can be viewed, moved, and removed. Where What you can do with a dictionary Dictionaries section of a project or set Create and edit dictionaries; see how often each category and term occurs Lens menu of the reader Annotate the terms in the open document Add to Dictionary in the selection bar of the reader Add the selected text as a term Word Sketch section Sketch the terms of a category one after another Queries Find the matches, use them in rules, and list the terms with their hits

Dictionary categories share much of the visual appearance of codes, as they too have a name and a color and highlight selected passages within your documents. However, they differ significantly in their creation and usage in practice, and that decides which one suits a question. Codings represent interpretations made while performing qualitative analysis of the document passages. When you interpret a passage as expressing doubt and mark it as such, applying a code called “Uncertainty”, you are assigning it the interpretation, which persists until removed. A dictionary identifies passages based on word forms only, regardless of context and interpretation. LemmaLoom locates each occurrence of the defined terms throughout all documents contained in your project, even the newly added ones, whatever the words mean in their passages. As a rule, a dictionary is preferable for identifying elements which have distinct word forms associated with them, for instance hedge structures or political policies' names, particularly when counting them across many documents. Dictionaries also offer a rapid approach to locating occurrences prior to any close reading. Codes suit whatever depends on context, such as a passage that expresses doubt without any telltale word, or an argument that runs over several sentences. Many studies employ a mixture of dictionaries and coding operations. An example case would involve automatically coding passages based on their matches with dictionary terms and further examining each match individually, ultimately discarding misidentifications (see Coding the matches later in this chapter). Additionally, queries could combine dictionary and code rules, e.g., finding passages marked with the “Uncertainty” code containing shields (see Dictionary rules later in this chapter).

Dictionaries are constructed and edited from within the Dictionaries section. This section exists at the project level and in all sets. It displays the full list of all dictionaries within your project, regardless of whether they were created inside a set's section. Working in a set's section only affects what documents are counted toward your counts in that section and which documents a word sketch is generated for. Opening the Dictionaries section: For the project, from within the navigation sidebar, select Dictionaries under Project to load the section in a separate tab. For a set, click on the desired set from within the navigation sidebar, then select Dictionaries from the row of buttons at the top of the set's tab. In a narrow window, the row transforms into a menu. You must then choose Dictionaries from that menu. Note that both smart sets and tags in the sidebar operate the exact same as normal sets. The image below shows “Hedges” being displayed in the project's Dictionaries section. The Dictionaries section of the “Climate Debate” project, with the “Hedges” dictionary selected. The section comes in three panes. On the left, the dictionaries of your project are listed alphabetically alongside their number of categories. In the middle, the categories of the selected dictionary appear with their color, name, number of terms under Terms, and number of matches under Hits. Finally, on the right, the selected category is displayed with its name and color on top, the Add term field, and the list of its terms. Move the dividers between panes to give any pane more room; projects without dictionaries show No Dictionaries here. For the project's section, the header row contains the title, Search field, and Open in a window button, with an icon of two diagonal arrows. This option will open the section in the Codebook window so you may place it next to the reader. The header row of the set's section includes the Search field alone. During LemmaLoom calculations, the header row contains a spinner. Use the Search field above to filter the terms from all dictionaries within your project. Dictionaries and categories containing no matching term will disappear. As long as the search runs, numbers will show next to each dictionary indicating how many terms match. Numbers under Terms indicate the same amount for each category. If the selected dictionary has no matching term, LemmaLoom will automatically switch to the first dictionary whose terms match the search criteria. The Dictionaries section of the “Climate Debate” project with about typed in the Search field. Changes to your dictionaries, categories, and terms are always undoable via Edit ▸ Undo (⌘Z). The menu item describes the change performed, such as Undo Delete Dictionary (see ).

Generally, the dictionary houses a single concept (e.g., hedging), and the categories contain those types of that concept which you wish to distinguish (e.g., approximators, shields). The lens generates one legend for the concept, and the counts compare its categories. Open the Dictionaries section of the project or of a set. Click New Dictionary below the list of dictionaries. A dictionary called “New Dictionary” is added and selected, with its name ready to edit. Type a name and press Return.

To rename a dictionary, right-click on the dictionary in the list, click Rename, and input the new name for the dictionary before pressing Return. To cancel renaming and leave the dictionary's name unchanged, press Esc. Deleting a dictionary requires right-clicking on the dictionary and selecting Delete Dictionary. Deleting the dictionary happens immediately. When a dictionary has been deleted, the dictionary becomes absent from the lens menu of all documents. The lens will also become inactive wherever it may have been turned on previously. All queries that use the dictionary report Missing in the results area and re-run whenever another dictionary becomes selected in them.
Terms can come from your own reading, from query results, or from published word lists, which you can paste into a category in one step.

Click Add Category below your list of categories, and LemmaLoom adds a new category named “New category” in the first available named color, with its name ready to be changed. Give your new category a name and press Return. You may want to use color to visually differentiate between various categories in the reader. Selecting a category in the middle pane shows its swatches in the right pane, allowing you to change its color by clicking another swatch below its name, or selecting a color from Color after right-clicking on your selected category. The swatches range from No color, through eight named colors, to Pick any color (which brings up the system color picker). Each category should ideally be assigned its unique color. Without one, your categories left at No color will be displayed in the lens in the default color, namely the blue of the Blue swatch.

In “Climate Debate”, “Shields” has eight terms. They appear in the right pane, accompanied by the number of times they appear in the entire project. The “Shields” category of “Hedges”, with its terms and their hits. For adding terms to a category: Select the category. Type a term in Add term, or paste a list of terms, one per line. Press Return or click Add. Here are the rules that LemmaLoom applies as it adds terms: Spaces that precede and follow a term are stripped from it. A term that is already in the category (case insensitive), as well as repeat occurrences of a term in the list, are ignored. Adding a term sorts the whole list alphabetically. In this field, only a new line separates one term from the next. A comma becomes part of the term, so put the terms of a list separated by commas on lines of their own before you paste them. Columns for Hits and Documents will accompany every term in the term list. Here, you'll see how many times (Hits) and in how many documents (Documents) your term has occurred within your project or set. Zero Hits mean either that you spelled something incorrectly, or that the term never appeared within your documents; extremely high Hits compared to everything else deserve investigating further (see Checking what a term matches later in this chapter). Removing terms can be accomplished by selecting the terms and pressing the Delete key (⌫), or right-clicking terms and choosing Remove from the shortcut menu. The shortcut menu of the term “perhaps” in the “Shields” category of “Hedges”. Moving terms between categories of the same dictionary involves dragging terms onto another category within the middle pane; alternatively, you may accomplish moving terms either via Move to Category within the shortcut menu, or Edit ▸ Move to Category via the top menu bar. If the other category already holds a term, it keeps a single copy.

Renaming a category involves editing the name at the top of the right pane and pressing Return, or right-clicking on the category and selecting Rename from the shortcut menu. Word Sketch in the same menu, which sketches the terms of the category one after another, is discussed further below under Word sketches from a category. The shortcut menu of the “Shields” category of “Hedges”. Choosing Delete Category deletes the entire category along with all its terms.

You can add words and phrases while reading in LemmaLoom, directly from your texts. Select the word or phrase in the reader. In the selection bar near the bottom of the reader, click Add to Dictionary. Choose the dictionary, then the category. Adding a selected phrase from “Let's Not Panic” to the “Shields” category of “Hedges”. The new term is the selected text without any spaces at its beginning and end. Only words should be selected. If the selection begins or ends with a comma or period, the punctuation will become part of the term, requiring the same punctuation in the same place in the text for a match. Add to Dictionary will appear in the selection bar only if the current project contains dictionaries. If the chosen dictionary doesn't have any categories, an empty submenu will appear.

Word lists, collocate lists, or keyword lists can directly contribute content to a category in one action. Collocates are the words commonly found around a particular word, whereas keywords are the words used more frequently by one set of documents compared to another (see Collocates and Keywords in ). Your query needs to return Words or Text Matches, and its Show should be either Collocates or Keywords, or else Count or Compare with one Group By key. Additionally, the query needs to cover one project because a dictionary belongs to one project. For instance, in the “Climate Debate” project, there is a keyword query saved for the “Activists” set named “Keywords: Activists”. These keywords, which include words like we and farmer, are not hedging words and therefore belong in their own dictionary outside of “Hedges”. Here is how to add result rows to a category: Run the query. Open the Actions menu (the circled ⋯) and choose Add to Dictionary. Choose the dictionary, then the category. LemmaLoom adds the label of each row, limited to the first 200 rows, according to the order shown in the result. In the case of lists grouped by Document, the label is the title of the document; in a word list, it is the word. With keyword lists, only Positive Keywords, which are the keywords occurring more frequently within the set, are added. If the list is counted by Lemma, dictionary forms such as seem will be added, which the lens then finds only in that form, while counting by Word will add the actual word forms as they appear in the text. Rows matching existing terms within the category, regardless of capitalization, will be skipped. All new terms will comprise a single entry in the undo history, which means one use of Undo will delete them all. Lists generally contain unwanted items, such as proper names, so you should check your category afterwards.

The dictionary lens, the counts in the Dictionaries section, the Hits of dictionary terms in queries, and auto coding with a dictionary lens all look for dictionary terms in the same way. When you run a query, and the first menu of the text row is set to Text, that query searches for dictionary terms the exact same way. Two of the rules can be changed there, as explained in Finding dictionary matches later in this chapter. Terms match regardless of capitalization, accent marks, and character width differences. The term perhaps will match Perhaps and PERHAPS. Likewise, naive matches naïve. In German, schon also matches schön since the umlaut is regarded as an accent mark. If you'd like to differentiate between them, then use queries whose first menu is set to Word Form, which preserves accents. The full-width letter forms produced by some input methods (commonly Chinese input methods), as well as their numeric counterparts, will match ordinary ones; thus, CO2 matches ＣＯ２. All terms match entire words exclusively, meaning that spaces and punctuation marks, including apostrophes, hyphens, quotation marks, periods, commas, semicolons, colons, exclamation points, and question marks, delimit matching areas. Therefore, carbon matches carbon in carbon-neutral while about matches about in just about. All the individual elements comprising a phrase term should match the exact sequence with the proper spacing between consecutive words. As such, more or less has to have precisely three words separated by one space each. Only the form you typed is found, so enter each form as its own term; e.g., enter seem, seems, and seemed separately into the category. Instead, if a query has its first menu set to Lemma, entering just the lemma (e.g., seem) will return all its inflectional forms (seems, seem, seemed). Since Chinese doesn't use spaces to separate words, a term containing any Chinese characters matches any occurrence of those characters. Terms in Japanese kana or in Thai, Lao, Khmer, Myanmar, or Tibetan script match the same way. 可能 (perhaps) is therefore matched in 可能性 (possibility) and 不可能 (impossible) too. Verify potential matches in the lens for short Chinese terms, and use longer terms where a short one finds too much. In all other cases, terms follow the whole-word rule inside Chinese text, and Chinese characters are considered letters. Matching a term like CO2 or 2050 with Chinese characters adjacent on both sides, as in 到2050年 (by 2050), requires including those adjacent Chinese characters in the term itself, or alternatively deselecting Whole Words in queries. All terms are treated individually. “Approximators” contains the terms about and just about, so whenever the latter occurs in documents, it will increase the count for each of them. A term that appears in two categories counts in both. Terms that differ only in accents, such as cafe and café, produce duplicate matches. Keep one copy and remove the other.

In “Hedges”, about has the role of an approximator in “About twelve years ago” (“The Models Keep Missing”), but does not have it in “Here's the thing about panic” (“Let's Not Panic”). Furthermore, around does not have that role in “every climate plan I have read manages to step around” (“Who Pays for the Transition”). For “Approximators”, however, the counts include all three. When counting something from your dictionary, first turn on its lens for several of your documents, and read through your matches (see The dictionary lens below). You can find which terms constitute the bulk of your category counts by looking at the Hits column on your term list; check these terms first. If you find out that your term is primarily being used in some other sense, delete the term or use longer phrases that appear exclusively in the desired context. A query could be even more precise, for instance by searching only for about preceding numbers (see ).

Each of the dictionaries in the project also acts as a lens, allowing annotations to be made on the text of a document (see ). The lens highlights each of the matching instances in the sentences containing them. Below is the image of “Let's Not Panic”, the document of the “Skeptics” set with the most matches for “Hedges”, with the lens enabled. “Let's Not Panic” with the “Hedges” lens enabled, and the legend of its two categories above the text. For enabling the dictionary lens: Open a document. Click the lens menu in the title band of the reader. Choose the dictionary. Dictionaries are listed after Bookmarks and Codes, in alphabetical order. Upon completion of LemmaLoom searching your document for matches with the dictionary's terms, each match is highlighted in the color of the category it falls into. The legend above your text shows the name of the dictionary and an aspect lenslet for each category as follows: When you click on one lenslet, it switches off or on the annotations of that category. When you click None, it switches off the annotations of all categories, while All switches them on again. When you right-click on a lenslet, you get the options Enable only this, Disable (or Enable), and Enable all. To show only sentences containing matches, click the button next to the lens menu with the tooltip Show only the sentences a lens annotates; click it again to display the entire document. To turn the lens off, select the dictionary in the lens menu again; Clear Annotations turns the lens along with Bookmarks, Codes, and query lenses off while Clear All turns off all lenses. The full-screen reader offers the same options in its lens menu. Lens menus will be disabled before a document's indexing is completed, with the tooltip Lenses become available when indexing completes. LemmaLoom indexes documents in English, German, and Chinese; hence in documents in any other language, such as French, the lens menus remain disabled. The counts of terms shown in the Dictionaries section, Add to Dictionary, and the queries with the first menu set to Text continue functioning since they process the text directly (for additional information see Other languages in ). The lens searches for matches based on the visible text, so translations, e.g., “Running Out of Time (German)”, require matching terms in their respective languages. To perform hedging detection in this translation, add German terms such as etwa, ungefähr, and vielleicht to the relevant categories or create separate dictionaries for each language in your multilingual project, which keeps their counts apart.

To convert dictionary hits into codings, perform auto coding on them from the lens. The options available in the dialog can be found in The Auto Code dialog in . With the dictionary's lens enabled, choose Document ▸ Auto Code… (⇧⌘A), or Auto Code… in the lens menu. When several lenses that can auto code are enabled, both menus have one item for each, such as Auto Code with Hedges…. In the Auto Code dialog, each category has a row under Codes, with its checkbox selected. Deselect a category you do not want coded. Choose the code for each row. A code with the same name as the category, ignoring capitals and accents, is chosen for you. Otherwise the row offers New Code: …, which creates a code with the category's name and color once the category finds a passage. In Documents, choose This Document, a set, or Whole Project, and click Auto Code. When the dialog shows Codings added: with the number, click Done. A match is coded as a new coding, unless that exact segment of text already carries the code. Only enabled categories from the legend get their own row. If a category is left at No color, that category gives a blue code. If you code a set or an entire project, LemmaLoom searches for matches throughout the texts of all documents in that set or project, thus documents still being indexed and documents in other languages get coded as well. After a close reading of the new codings, e.g., in the Codings section, remove instances of codings where your term may mean something other than intended.

The Dictionaries section counts how many times the terms from each category occur in the project or set's documents. From the counts, you can get an idea of how much each category contributes, what terms contribute to it, and if its hits are distributed across documents, or clustered around certain ones. When you choose a dictionary, or alter it or the documents being counted, LemmaLoom will automatically update the counts. In addition to the Hits and Documents columns of the two panes, Category Frequencies displays charts of each category's occurrences, at the bottom of the right pane. Expand or collapse Category Frequencies by clicking it, and resize the chart area by dragging the divider above it. There are two charts here: The first displays bars representing categories in their colors, with the hit count at the end of each bar. The category with the highest hit count is at the top. By Document displays bars representing each document containing hits, segmented into parts colored according to categories. Category Frequencies and By Document for the “Hedges” dictionary in the “Skeptics” set. Clicking Open in a window at the right end of the Category Frequencies row allows you to view the charts larger, and place them alongside whichever document you're reading. The Category Frequencies window displays both of the charts based on the exact same dictionary and project or set they originated from, updating along with the counts. Note that the Category Frequencies window displays one dictionary at a time, so clicking Open in a window from another dictionary replaces the previous content inside. The Category Frequencies window for the “Hedges” dictionary in the “Skeptics” set. The category count is equal to the sum of occurrences of each of the category's terms according to the rules in How terms are matched earlier in this chapter. Which documents get counted depends on the context: In the project's section, all documents of the project. In a set's section, documents included in that set. If it is a smart set (like “Wide Reach”), these are all the documents which currently satisfy its conditions. For a tag, they are the documents that carry it. Counts pertain to the originals alone. When a set has translations, their originals are counted instead. Counts are determined based on the text contents of documents. As a result, documents currently undergoing indexing and documents written in other languages, such as French, also get included in counts.

Each chart contains an Export button in the shape of a square with an arrow. In the case of the first chart, you will find the button on the Category Frequencies row or at the top of the Category Frequencies window, while for By Document, it sits right next to the chart's title. You can export PNG and PDF formats, both of which store a visual representation of your chart, or you can export a CSV file containing the underlying numerical data. Each chart saves its own CSV file; for “Hedges”, the suggested file names are Hedges-categories.csv and Hedges-documents.csv. In the table of the first chart each row is a category, and in the By Document table each row is a document with at least one match. The first table has a Category column alongside a Count column. In the second table, there is a Document column followed by a column for each category. For “Skeptics”, the By Document table contains these counts: Document Approximators Shields Let's Not Panic 8 6 Net Zero Will Cost You 3 3 Science Is Never Settled 8 3 The Models Keep Missing 6 4 Who Pays for the Transition 4 2 These columns add up to give you the figures in the first chart, 29 in “Approximators” and 18 in “Shields”.

When comparing sets, the larger the set is in terms of word count, the more hits you can expect, even if its writers hedge no more than anyone else. To adjust for the size difference between sets, convert the count into a rate. A rate measures the ratio between two quantities. In this case, it measures the hit counts relative to the number of words in the document set, giving the hit count for each 10,000 words of text. Since the Dictionaries section shows counts alone, you must either calculate the rate manually or via a query. To compute a rate, use the formula shown here: $r$ denotes the rate, $h$ represents the hit count of a particular category, and $w$ is the total word count of the documents counted. When dividing $h$ by $w$, you will obtain the ratio for hits per word, a minuscule figure. Multiply that ratio by 10,000, and you get hits per 10,000 words, which is easier to comprehend and compare. Consider this hypothetical example of the hit counts displayed in the Dictionaries section for both the “Activists” and “Skeptics” sets. The word counts are those of the example project, rounded to the nearest thousand; the hit counts of the “Skeptics” match the totals shown previously, while those for the “Activists” are fictional. In the example project, the “Activists” set comprises six texts totaling only three hits altogether.  Activists Skeptics Words 4,000 3,000 Approximators 12 29 Shields 20 18 The activists produce a higher total quantity of “Shields”, 20 versus 18. Their texts, however, hold 4,000 words against the skeptics' 3,000. If for the activists $h = 20$ and $w = 4{,}000$, then: Similarly for the skeptics ($h = 18$, $w = 3{,}000$): Per 10,000 words, the skeptics use shields 60 times while the activists use shields 50 times. For “Approximators” the rates per 10,000 words are $12 / 4{,}000 times 10{,}000 = 30$ for the activists and $29 / 3{,}000 times 10{,}000 approx 96.7$ for the skeptics; hence, the skeptics lead here by far. The total number of words per document is visible from Words in the Text tab of the inspector (see Words and unique words in ). Add up those totals for each of your document sets. The word count in the reader's status bar includes punctuation and is higher. As an alternative, you may wish to construct a query for it all instead: Click Queries under Project in the sidebar, so that both sets are counted. In the Find condition, choose Text · Text Matches. In the text row's second menu, choose Dictionary. “Hedges”, the project's only dictionary, is chosen. Click the control below the dictionary and check only “Shields”. With nothing checked, both categories are counted together. In Show, choose Count. Click Group By, and in the new row's field menu choose Set. In the menu showing Hits, choose Per 10,000 Words. The rows named “Activists” and “Skeptics” provide rates of occurrence for the category “Shields”. Within the example project, “Activists” provides roughly 5, while “Skeptics” gives roughly 55. “Skeptics” comes in below the 60 discussed above as the query divides by the precise number of words found in the documents via the Words statistic in the inspector. The finished query in the “Climate Debate” project, with the rate of the “Shields” category per 10,000 words for each set. The count contains words the authors quote rather than use; take, for instance, I'm not sure in “Science Is Never Settled”. The chart By Document will assist you in determining whether your matches are spread out among numerous documents or are clustered into one specific document. Please note that the bars in the By Document chart represent counts, hence they must be read relative to the size of each document. For comparing multiple groups of documents, use Compare within a query (see Comparing groups in ).

A word sketch provides summary information on the grammatical company of a word, e.g., its most common subjects, objects, and modifiers (see ). A word sketch started from a category allows you to explore the individual terms within it. When starting from “Shields”, the word sketch reveals what writers hedge about. The word sketch of the terms of a category comes from right-clicking the category in the Dictionaries section of the project or a set and selecting Word Sketch. This option is disabled when there are no terms available within the category. For a word sketch of a particular term, you must either double-click the term in the term list or select the term and press Return. Right-clicking a term in the term list and selecting Sketch this word has the same effect. Instead, choose Open in Window in that menu to bring up the sketch in the Word Sketch window, leaving the Dictionaries section visible on screen. With sets, the set's tab displays its Word Sketch section. For word sketches beginning from the project's Dictionaries tab, the project's Word Sketch tab opens. Underneath the bar at the top of the view is a row with the category name and its color, followed by its candidate words, the words the word sketch can start from. A candidate word refers to the lemma corresponding to each term within a category; for “Shields”, I think has the candidate word think, and it seems has seem. Following Word Sketch, the sketch shows the first candidate word, i.e., the most frequently occurring. Click another candidate word to sketch it. A word sketch started from the “Shields” category, with the lemmas of its terms as candidate words above the sketch. A word sketch requires a lemma to be found for the term. The first thing LemmaLoom will need to do is locate the occurrences of your term within the documents you are analyzing and derive its lemma. A single word term (such as seems) would become seem. For a phrase term (I think), however, the sketch would be based on the lemma of its grammatical main word (in this case, think, which has a subject I). It seems becomes seem for the same reason. In Key terms in , more detail is given on the grammatical structure of words. If your term contains contractions, indexing breaks it apart into multiple words; therefore, I'd say ends up under say, while I'm not sure ends up under be, since the grammar analysis marks 'm as the main word. For any Chinese term which indexing breaks apart into several words, the term is treated as a phrase made of those words. If your term cannot be located in documents as written, it would get its lemma from the lemmas of the individual words in it. In other words, your term in dictionary form (seem) can find its lemma even if the documents contain the term only as seems. Any terms which lead back to the same lemma will share the same candidate word. By hovering the mouse pointer over a candidate word, you will see the list of terms linked to it. Candidate words are ordered according to the frequency of appearance of their lemma in your project or set from highest to lowest; a term not occurring anywhere within your corpus in any form will appear last under its own spelling, disabled with the tooltip Not found. Changing the content of the Word field and pressing Return sketches that word and makes the row disappear, unless, of course, the word happens to be a candidate word itself.

When lenses and counts fall short, whether for finding all inflections of a word, computing rates per set, or searching only inside coded passages, use a query. How to construct a query is explained in . For every text row in your query, there are two menus available. The first decides what the terms should match against. The second starts at Terms and decides where your terms originate from.

Open a query. For one document, choose View ▸ Inspector ▸ Multimode and click Query. For a set or the project, open its Queries section. In the Find condition, choose Text · Text Matches. A text row appears in the condition. Open the menu showing Terms in that row and choose Dictionary. The project's first dictionary in alphabetical order is chosen; you can pick another in the menu that appears below. To use only some of the categories, click the control below the dictionary, which reads None, and check them in the panel that opens. With nothing checked, every category is used. Leave the first menu at Text to get the same matches as the lens. A query in the “Climate Debate” project that finds the matches of the “Shields” category of “Hedges”. Results show matches in context, and Show offers the usual counts and charts (see ). The two checkboxes underneath the row, Match Case and Whole Words, influence how the query performs matching. Without Whole Words checked, terms match inside larger words as well (about matches roundabout). When Match Case is enabled, capitals matter, meaning that perhaps matches only perhaps. Lastly, with Text selected in the first menu above, accent and character width differences will be ignored regardless of whether either checkbox underneath is enabled. Text, which is the default choice in the first menu, compares the query terms to what is written in the document text according to the conditions explained under How terms are matched earlier in this chapter. The other three options, Word, Word Form, and Lemma, compare them to individual words in the text as found by indexing: Word compares every word in the query term with each word in the document text, without taking case or accents into account unless Match Case is activated. Lemma compares every word of a query term with lemmas of words in the document text. Write query terms as their lemmas. seem matches seem, seems, and seemed. In order to search for terms written as they occur in the text, as in it seems under “Hedges”, use Word instead of Lemma. Lemma ignores Match Case. Word Form works the same way as Lemma except with regard to accent differentiation; in other words, it distinguishes German schon and schön (refer to What to compare with in ). For all three methods above (word-based comparisons), a phrase is considered to match where the words occur consecutively in a sentence regardless of line breaks or whitespace between the words. Hyphens within terms are treated as spaces, along with any hyphen that indexing splits into a separate word (carbon neutral matches carbon-neutral in English documents). With regard to these three ways of comparing (word-based comparisons), Whole Words will have no impact whatsoever. With a Chinese document, the query term 可能 will only match positions where indexing identified 可能 as a complete word of its own. All three ways of comparison operate as Text if indexing has not been performed on the document.

Additionally, a dictionary can test other query results, whether those queries are looking for sentences containing a shield, or coded passages containing an approximator. In the Find condition, choose what you want to find, for example Text · Sentences. In the Where condition, click Add and choose Add Text. In the new row's second menu, choose Dictionary, then choose the dictionary and categories as above. The row holds whenever there is at least one matching term in the result. Your first menu will start at Word for results that need indexing (such as words and sentences) and at Text for others (codings, paragraphs, etc.). Whenever searching for Words, your results consist of individual words, meaning only one-word terms can match. Should you wish to locate “Uncertainty”-coded passages containing shields, choose Annotations · Codings in the Find condition. Establish a rule that Code is any of “Uncertainty”, then establish a text row for the “Shields” category of “Hedges”.

Library · Dictionary Terms in the Find condition shows the terms themselves. Every row corresponds to a term, whose columns include the term name (Name), its category (Category), dictionary (Dictionary), and hit count (Hits). Hit counts are calculated based on occurrences within documents of the query, according to rules outlined in How terms are matched above. In a document's own query, the current open document becomes the query corpus. A Library · Dictionary Terms query in the “Climate Debate” project, listing the terms of “Hedges” with their categories and hits. When looking at the term list in the Dictionaries section, hits are displayed separately per category. The query shows the entire list of dictionaries of a project at once; rules may be applied in the Where condition to narrow it. A rule on Dictionary limits the list to the terms belonging to one dictionary, while a rule Hits is 0 returns terms that have not occurred.

t: The Dictionary Categories by Document recipe
b: This recipe gives the figures for the By Document chart as a query. Open the Queries section of a set or the project. In the left column, under Recipes, click Dictionary Categories by Document. It is listed under Speakers and Time. The recipe finds Text Matches in the first dictionary of the project, ordered alphabetically. It uses all categories, with the first menu set to Text. The result displays Count grouped first by Document, then by Category. An alternative dictionary may be selected in the Find condition. The recipe will appear in queries that span multiple documents, assuming there is a dictionary in your project.

t: Saving a dictionary query as a lens or an analyzer
b: If a query makes use of the dictionary and builds on it by adding rules regarding the speaker or the usage of particular codes, then you may wish to save it as a lens (see ). Query lenses mark every match with one color under the query name. In order to distinguish matches based on categories from the dictionary, include one query category per dictionary category in the Categories condition (see Categories and Color By in ). Within each category, select Add Text and configure the second menu within the new row as Dictionary. Then, select only that dictionary category. When enabling a query lens, the dictionary's terms get captured as they currently stand in LemmaLoom. If changes are made afterwards to the dictionary, then disable the lens and enable it once again. Analyzers that have been generated from a query execute upon the indexing of every document in all projects. The analyzer also stores its results alongside each respective document (see Turning a query into an analyzer in ). Note that Save as Analyzer… is restricted to queries comparing terms against the words found by indexing. For this purpose, the first menu within the text row must read Word, Word Form, or Lemma. Furthermore, find one of Words, Sentences, or a similar indexed unit. Analyzers store the terms used during their creation until you update them. When a query that generates an analyzer changes, the analyzer gets labeled as Out of Date. To update a query's analyzer, repeat the action through Save as Analyzer… in the query's Save menu. At this point, the dialog reads Update Analyzer, and Update suffices to refresh the stored terms in the analyzer.

Only the LemmaLoom archive (.llz) of a full project contains the project's dictionaries. Importing such an .llz file restores the dictionaries contained in the project archive. Learn more about archives and exchange formats in .

A custom analyzer is a short program in JavaScript. The analyzer reads the grammar analysis of a document and looks for the passages you want. Write the script in Window ▸ Analyzers, and LemmaLoom executes it during indexing of documents in the chosen languages in all your projects. Whatever your analyzer discovers gets stored in association with documents. Afterward, you can view those findings through your analyzer's lens, auto-code them, and perform counts or comparisons in queries. Analyzers are for questions that depend on grammar and that the built-in lenses do not answer in the form you need. Queries provide quicker approaches to answering a single question (see ); generally, an analyzer is worth writing when you repeatedly search for the same pattern in documents (both existing and ones you import later) and require annotations in the reader and counting capabilities. This chapter looks at the example project “Climate Debate”, which gets imported via File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project (see The example project in ). Specifically, it considers whether climate appears as the grammatical subject of clauses, in phrases such as the climate has not waited for us, or as an object, in phrases such as protect the climate. While dictionaries detect all instances of the word climate regardless of context, an analyzer distinguishes between subjects and objects based on their functions recorded in the grammar analysis. In the example analyzer “Climate Roles”, each climate that functions as the subject gets annotated in one color, whereas each climate that is an object gets annotated in another. Writing a first analyzer gives details on how to write this particular analyzer yourself. Analyzers are the only component of LemmaLoom requiring programming skills from you. Although the scripts are relatively short and simple, they involve variables, lists, loops, if statements, and anonymous functions defined by => syntax. If you have never written a program, the free online JavaScript course of the MDN Web Docs introduces you to the basics. If you are not interested in programming, construct a query to retrieve desired data and turn that query into an analyzer to automatically generate the script (see Turning a query into an analyzer in ). Generated scripts also serve as good examples for study.

An analyzer in LemmaLoom is a program executed during indexing which appends findings to the document. (For details about indexing in LemmaLoom, refer to .) Three analyzers come bundled with LemmaLoom, and these include Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric. A custom analyzer may either be built by you or generated automatically by LemmaLoom according to your query. Each custom analyzer belongs to your library, so each one operates on the documents of all projects. The script is written in JavaScript, and must include a function called analyze. LemmaLoom will execute this function on your document analysis, and your analyzer must return the findings to LemmaLoom. The document object is the JavaScript object that will be passed into your function (object here in the programming sense, a bundle of named fields such as text and lemma). This object contains several fields which represent different properties of the document, including the language, sentences with their tokens, phrases, noun chunks, as well as outputs from the built-in analyzers. Tokens are individual word forms and punctuation marks. Associated with each token are its dictionary form, or lemma, the part-of-speech tag, its dependency relation to the word it depends on (its head), and any morphological features such as number and tense. A finding represents one passage reported by the analyzer, consisting of a series of adjacent tokens in one sentence along with its key. Keys represent types of findings, e.g., subject, object, and so forth. The legend is a collection of your keys along with corresponding labels, colors, and styles for visualization. The legend of your analyzer's lens will be created from it. Choose Window ▸ Analyzers to open up the window. The window is split into three columns. The first column on the left is your list of analyzers sorted alphabetically. Within each row lies the list of languages your analyzer operates in; for example, de en. Clicking the Add Analyzer button below initiates creation of a new analyzer. The second column hosts the currently selected analyzer. This area contains the Name, the checkboxes for languages English, German, and Chinese, and the Save button at the top. Following those are the Legend, the script editor, and Try it out, which lets you test your analyzer on a few sentences. Lastly, the third column hosts the Reference panel, which contains the list of helper functions, named constants, and document object members. The Analyzers window with “Climate Roles” selected and its findings in a test sentence under Try it out. When the window opens, the middle column will show a new, unsaved analyzer whose sample script finds every noun. If you want to modify an existing analyzer, click on it in the list on the left. At first, the Try it out pane consumes minimal vertical space at the bottom of the column, but dragging the divider upwards will increase its size during testing. LemmaLoom saves the height setting for you between launches. As you write your scripts, the editor numbers the lines, colors the parts of the script, and suggests names. Following POS., the autocompletion popup will contain suggestions for all parts of speech. Likewise, after LL. the popup contains the list of helper functions. The editor will also underline some mistakes that occur while you type. This includes references to undefined constants for instance. To insert a breakpoint into your script, click in the left margin next to the line number of interest (see Breakpoints and stepping later in this chapter). The editor in the Analyzers window after typing POS. on a new last line, with the parts of speech suggested. Changes are kept only until you save them. Clicking another analyzer in the list, clicking Add Analyzer, and closing the window are actions that would cause unsaved changes to disappear.

In the “Climate Roles” analyzer, there are only two keys, subject and object. The key for each climate depends on whether the word acts as the subject or object within a sentence structure. The full script looks like this: Most of the documents within “Climate Debate” are written in English, whereas “Running Out of Time (German)” is written in German, so “Climate Roles” runs on both languages. Its legend refers to the two keys as “Climate as subject” and “Climate as object”. To create an analyzer: Choose Window ▸ Analyzers. If the middle column shows an analyzer you have saved, click Add Analyzer below the list. Enter a name in Name. Select the languages of the documents the analyzer should run on. English is selected at the start. Click in the editor, press ⌘A to select the sample script, and type or paste your script in its place. Give each key a label in the Legend, where LemmaLoom lists the keys it has found in the script (see Keys and the legend later in this chapter). Test the script under Try it out (see Testing with Try it out later in this chapter). Click Save. A good test for “Climate Roles” is one that involves both uses in a single sentence; for instance, The climate is changing faster than our politics, so we must do more for the climate. If you choose en in the language menu next to it, Run highlights the first instance of climate in blue as subject, while highlighting the second instance in red as object. After saving, the new analyzer gets added to the list, after which LemmaLoom automatically begins to run it on your documents, behind the scenes, in the languages you've selected. The analyzer is made available immediately from the lens menu of each document in its languages, and its annotations appear once it has run there.

If you are familiar with JavaScript, move on to The document an analyzer receives below. Please note that lines are referred to according to the editor line numbering when the code has been inserted. Line 1 (const CLIMATE = …) defines which lemmas count as climate. const assigns a value a name, and square brackets define an array. Climates in English has the lemma climate, whereas German Klimas, like in des Klimas, has the lemma Klima. This array lists these words in English, German, and Chinese. Note that the German word is lowercased, klima, since line 6 lowercases each lemma when trying to match lemmas. On line 2 (function analyze(doc) {), the function called by LemmaLoom is defined with an argument called doc. This argument represents the document object passed by LemmaLoom. Line 3 (const findings = ]`) declares an array variable, `findings`, to hold findings. In line 4 (`for (const sentence of doc.sentences) {`), the script iterates over each sentence of the document; for each iteration, it performs the operations in this block. Similarly in line 5 (`sentence.tokens.forEach(…)`), it iterates over tokens in the current sentence; `(token, index) => { … }` is an anonymous function; `forEach` calls it once per iteration with arguments representing the current token and its position in the sentence, starting from 0. If the condition in line 6 (`if (CLIMATE.includes(…)) {`) is true, meaning `includes` finds the token lemma in the `CLIMATE` list, the statements within the curly braces of this `if` execute. Line 7 (`const role = token.derived.function;`) accesses the grammatical function value of the current token; this is the same value displayed by the **Grammatical function** lens. Lines 8 (`role === FUNCTION.SUBJECT`) and 11 (`role === FUNCTION.OBJECT`) test equality between variables using `===`. Equality operators return true if both operands are equal. Here the script checks whether the grammatical function of the token is `FUNCTION.SUBJECT` or `FUNCTION.OBJECT` (see [Constants later in this chapter). When true, the script pushes objects representing findings onto the findings array on lines 9 and 12 (findings.push(…)); note that an object is surrounded by braces. Each object includes four properties representing the sentence of origin, the starting index of the passage (start, i.e., the current token's index), the position just after the passage's last token (end, here index + 1), and the key. Therefore, each finding corresponds to just one word, whose starting index and ending index will be consecutive. Lastly, on line 17 (return findings;), the script sends the results back to LemmaLoom. Object is one broad category of grammatical functions, and it includes the object of prepositions. Therefore, this script will count instances like do more for the climate, as well as protect the climate. The subjects of passive clauses such as the climate is affected by our emissions would fall under the FUNCTION.SUBJECT grammatical function category; thus, they are counted as subjects. Should you wish to count passive subjects with the objects, modify line 7 to const role = token.dep === DEP.NSUBJPASS ? FUNCTION.OBJECT : token.derived.function;. With ? and :, the line chooses between FUNCTION.OBJECT and the token's own function depending on whether the token is a passive clause subject or otherwise. Keep in mind that this solution applies fully to English alone; the German grammar parser recognizes passive subjects identically to active subjects, and the Chinese parser gives this label to only some subjects of 被 sentences. The script here could trace any word grammatically; for instance, government or industry. Replace the lemmas in line 1 with the respective lowercase versions of your words.

The function analyze takes one argument, referred to hereafter as doc. This argument contains three fields: Field What it holds doc.language The language of the analysis, "en", "de", or "zh" doc.sentences The sentences, in order doc.builtins The results of the built-in analyzers Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric Analyzers can only return results based on the document's analysis. If you want to combine the analyzer's findings with your codings, memos, links, bookmarks, attributes, document properties, or the results of other custom analyzers, you should consider creating a query to do so (see Using the findings later in this chapter). For very large documents, LemmaLoom indexes documents in segments with a maximum text length of half a megabyte (approximately 80,000 English words). For each segment, LemmaLoom will invoke the analyze function once, and the sentence numbering resets to 0. Documents of ordinary length are indexed as a single segment.

Fields contained within entries of doc.sentences include: Field What it holds index The sentence's number, counting from 0. It is also the sentence's position in doc.sentences. text The text of the sentence tokens The tokens of the sentence, in order root The position of the sentence's root token, usually its main verb, or -1 if the sentence has no parse constituents The phrases of the sentence (see Phrases and noun chunks) nounChunks The noun chunks of the sentence

The token numbering starts at 0 within each sentence, and positions in scripts refer to token indices. Tokens consist of either words or punctuation marks. Each token contains these fields: Field What it holds Example text The token as it appears in the text targets whitespace The spacing that follows the token " " lemma The dictionary form; in Chinese the same as text target pos The universal part of speech, with the same codes in every language NOUN tag The fine-grained tag from the language's own tag set NNS dep The dependency relation to the token's head nsubjpass head The position of the token's head; the root points to itself 4 index The token's own position in the sentence 2 morph The morphological features; empty in Chinese { Number: "Plur" } isStop true for very common words such as the and of false derived Three categories LemmaLoom works out from the fields above (see the next section)  Example analyses in the table are based on the sentence The new targets were announced last year. An analysis of this sentence generally follows the form below: index text lemma pos tag dep head derived.function 0 The the DET DT det 2 adjectival 1 new new ADJ JJ amod 2 adjectival 2 targets target NOUN NNS nsubjpass 4 subject 3 were be AUX VBD auxpass 4 connector 4 announced announce VERB VBN ROOT 4 mainClause 5 last last ADJ JJ amod 6 adjectival 6 year year NOUN NN npadvmod 4 adverbial 7 . . PUNCT . punct 4 unknown Read the head column as arrows pointing from each word to the word it depends on. Targets depends on announced, at position 4, as its passive subject, while the and new depend on targets. Announced is the root word, hence it is its own head, and sentence.root is 4. Tags and relations vary per language. In English, the tags follow Penn Treebank, and the relation labels are English dependency relations such as nsubj and dobj. In German, the tags follow STTS, whereas relation labels follow TIGER; for example, sb is for a subject while oa is for an accusative object. In Chinese, the tags follow the Chinese Treebank, while relation labels are the English labels plus Chinese ones such as aux:asp and nmod:assmod. The values of the pos field and all derived fields remain identical across the three languages; thus a script testing only these suffices across all languages. The Reference panel lists tags and labels by name (see The Reference panel later in this chapter).

token.derived consists of three categories calculated by LemmaLoom for each token. Each is the category of one lens and means the same in every language. Field Lens Values derived.function Grammatical function subject, object, predicative, complement, adjectival, adverbial, appositive, agent, conjunct, connector, mainClause, unknown derived.posCategory Word class noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, determiner, preposition, conjunction, number, interjection, other derived.phraseCategory Phrase nounPhrase, verbPhrase, prepPhrase, adjPhrase, advPhrase, conjPhrase, interjection, other, or an empty string LemmaLoom uses the token's dependency relation to infer the function of the token. For several relations, however, the inference takes the token's head into account. If the head is a noun, pronoun, or numeral, a modifier relation such as advmod counts as adjectival; if not, it counts as adverbial. Relations that are classified with a subtype, indicated by a colon, will count according to their prefix, except obl:agent, which counts as agent. The root is assigned the function mainClause, while unknown refers to any remaining relations, including, say, punctuation. The phrase category refers to the category of the smallest enclosing phrase excluding clauses. Tokens belonging solely to a clause-level phrase (like the period punctuation mark) will receive an empty string for their phrase category.

sentence.constituents gives you an array of the sentence's phrases according to the phrase structure tree represented visually in the Phrase lens and the sentence diagrams. Phrases contain the starting and ending indices (start and end) of the phrase's tokens along with an array of the phrase labels, e.g., ['NP'] for a noun phrase. If multiple phrases cover exactly the same tokens, then there will be one object containing the labels in the order they are nested from outside to inside. sentence.nounChunks gives you the noun chunks of the sentence. Noun chunks refer to nouns preceded by words belonging to them, like the new targets. Noun chunks contain starting and ending indices. Here's how the two arrays could look for The new targets were announced last year. S represents a sentence, while VP denotes a verb phrase. Last year is a noun phrase but not a noun chunk. English noun chunks occur exclusively around nouns or pronouns functioning as subjects, objects, or the like in the sentence. Year is actually an adverbial modifier in this instance. Both lists may be empty; e.g., consider a response consisting of a solitary word. Account for such possibilities when implementing your program code.

Your custom analyzer runs on a document last. The three built-in analyzers run first, giving their results in doc.builtins. If you deleted the results from one of the built-in analyzers earlier, those results are still available to your custom analyzer. Field Each entry holds doc.builtins.cohesion One entry per sentence, with sentenceIndex, tie (how the sentence links back to what came before), theme and rheme (the token ranges of the sentence's opening and of its stress position, each as start, end]`; the field is missing when the sentence has none), and `tieWord` (the word that makes the tie) `doc.builtins.metadiscourse` One entry per word the analyzer found, with `sentenceIndex`, `local` (the position of the token), and `category`, such as `hedge` `doc.builtins.rhetoric` One entry per device, with `device`, such as `passiveVoice`, `sentenceIndex`, `range` (the tokens as `[start, end]`), and `note` `tie` has seven different values (`opening`, `pronoun`, `possessive`, `demonstrative`, `repetition`, `zero`, and `broken`). `category` includes five potential values (`hedge`, `booster`, `attitude`, `connective`, and `engagement`); additionally, `category` in German can contain `modalParticle`, while in Chinese it can include `finalParticle`. Lastly, there are thirteen possible values for `device` ranging from `passiveVoice` to `correlative`. All possible values for each field are listed in the Reference panel, along with any lens-defined names. Further information on what each analyzer analyzes can be found in [.

There are several functions available in LL which handle common operations during scripting. Function What it gives LL.isWord(token) true unless the token is punctuation or a symbol such as $ LL.isNominal(pos) true for NOUN, PROPN, and PRON LL.isVerbal(pos) true for VERB and AUX LL.children(sentence, i) The positions of the tokens whose head is token i LL.subtree(sentence, i) { start, end }, the unbroken span around token i made of it and the tokens that depend on it, directly or through others LL.root(sentence) The position of the sentence's root, the same as sentence.root LL.text(sentence, start, end) The text of the tokens from start up to end, with their spacing console.log(...) Writes a line under Try it out; lists and objects are written out in full In the example sentence, LL.children(sentence, 4) gives back an array [2, 3, 6, 7], the tokens depending upon the word announced. Calling LL.subtree(sentence, 2) provides an object which has two fields { start: 0, end: 3 }, spanning the text The new targets, while calling LL.text(sentence, 0, 3) yields the text "The new targets". console.log calls are for debugging only; their output is discarded when the analyzer runs on your documents.

The large majority of fields consist of short codes such as NOUN and nsubjpass. Codes can be specified in quotes as strings, or as named constants; the expression token.pos === POS.NOUN means the same thing as token.pos === 'NOUN'. Named constants should be used whenever possible. Suggestions for named constants will pop up in the editor, and a misspelled constant is underlined. Any quoted string is accepted as-is, regardless of whether the spelling is correct or not. During runtime, an incorrectly spelled constant such as POS.NOUM evaluates to undefined and the script keeps running, so the underline is your only warning. Constant Holds the values of Example POS token.pos POS.NOUN is 'NOUN' TAG token.tag, in all three languages TAG.NNS is 'NNS' DEP token.dep, in all three languages DEP.NSUBJPASS is 'nsubjpass' PHRASE the labels of constituents PHRASE.NP is 'NP' MORPH the names of the features in token.morph MORPH.TENSE is 'Tense' FUNCTION token.derived.function FUNCTION.SUBJECT is 'subject' CATEGORY token.derived.posCategory CATEGORY.NOUN is 'noun' PHRASE_CATEGORY token.derived.phraseCategory PHRASE_CATEGORY.NOUN_PHRASE is 'nounPhrase' COHESION tie in doc.builtins.cohesion COHESION.REPETITION is 'repetition' METADISCOURSE category in doc.builtins.metadiscourse METADISCOURSE.HEDGE is 'hedge' RHETORIC device in doc.builtins.rhetoric RHETORIC.PASSIVE_VOICE is 'passiveVoice' KEY the keys in this analyzer's legend KEY.SUBJECT is 'subject' Constant names in LemmaLoom consist of the codes in uppercase. When there is an occurrence of lowercase characters being followed directly by uppercase characters in a code, put an underscore in between; for instance, nounPhrase is written as NOUN_PHRASE and mainClause as MAIN_CLAUSE. All non-letter symbols that cannot be part of names, like colons, are replaced by underscores. MORPH constants serve as names for the feature codes. Write your feature values as strings; examples include token.morph[MORPH.TENSE] === 'Past' or simply token.morph.Tense === 'Past'. Constant names apply to most codes, but four cases differ: DEP.ROOT holds 'root'; however, the root is labeled as ROOT in analyses. Determine whether a token is the root by comparing indices, like index === sentence.root, or using 'ROOT'. Ten common features are listed under the MORPH constant as Tense, Number, Person, Mood, VerbForm, Case, Degree, Aspect, Gender, and PronType. Use the string representation of any feature not included in the MORPH constant directly, as in token.morph.Definite === 'Def'. Phrase labels that occur exclusively in Chinese, such as IP, DNP, and LCP, need quotation marks around their names. Any tag composed of purely punctuation, such as the English period (.) and comma (,) or the German $,, requires quotation marks too. Avoid assigning names that already belong to constants or to LL or console. When running scripts that define their own const KEY, the processing stops due to errors.

The Reference panel to the right side of the window lists the parts of the document object, the helper functions, and the constants. Under API are listed doc.language, doc.sentences[i].tokens[j], all three lists in doc.builtins, along with the helper functions. Every component's value type will be provided after its declaration, e.g., String, Bool. All fields of the sentence, token, and finding objects may be viewed in tables within this chapter. All sections below API contain constants listed with their names written in plain English: Part of speech (POS), Fine-grained tags (TAG), Dependency relations (DEP), Constituency labels (PHRASE), and Morphological features (MORPH); Grammatical functions (FUNCTION), Word categories (CATEGORY), and Phrase categories (PHRASE_CATEGORY); Rhetoric devices (RHETORIC), Cohesion ties (COHESION), and Metadiscourse categories (METADISCOURSE). All sections above are collapsed by default. Clicking a section header expands/collapses the relevant section accordingly. Find a particular item by typing a substring of it into Search. Constant lookup considers its name, code, or common English name. Lookup for an API entry will search for the literal string of the API declaration. The panel displays a combined listing of all matching items from all sections, or No matches. Click any item to insert it at the location of the caret within the editor panel. The Reference panel after typing subject in Search.

analyze must return a list where each element is a finding consisting of the following fields: Field What it holds sentenceIndex The index of the sentence start The position of the first token of the passage end The position just after the last token key One of the keys in the legend note A short text of your own; optional With respect to the example The new targets were announced, the first token is at position 0 while the last is at position 4, giving the finding start: 0 and end: 5. The number of tokens, therefore, always equals end - start, here 5. A finding must occur in one sentence alone. Overlapping is possible for findings and, consequently, one token may carry several keys; the reader then renders all their styles on it. Note fields are intended for use in queries. You could test them in a query using the field Note (see Using the findings later in this chapter).

There must be a corresponding row in the legend for every key that your findings use. The Legend pane above the editor displays the row for each key, with the following parts: Key contains your key in script form. Label contains the name that will display in the legend of the lens, and is used for the purpose of querying. Labels are initially set as the key name itself. The color well specifies the color used for your key's findings. New keys take their colors in turn from a pool of eight. The style menu defines the rendering method used by the reader. This includes the options Highlight, Underline, Text color, or Bold. Initially, newly added keys have Highlight selected. Legend rows are generated for all keys written out in quotes (key: '...') in your script in order of appearance while you write your script. When you remove a key from your script, the respective row is deleted from your legend. If you modify your keys' names, then that particular row gets deleted, and replaced by a new row containing the modified key as its label and the default color. You should therefore assign colors and labels after deciding on key names. You may update any row, including its label, color, and style, whenever you wish. After you save, changes made to legend rows show in every document where the lens is enabled.

A key may also be generated from the analysis itself. If you replace both if statements of the analyzer “Climate Roles”, along with the push lines inside them, with the line below, the grammatical function becomes the key: A climate that acts as a subject receives the key subject, a climate that is an object receives object, the first part of climate policy becomes adjectival, and so forth for each of the twelve values listed under Derived categories earlier in this chapter. These keys reach the legend via a test run. Upon clicking Save, LemmaLoom executes the script using a sample three-word sentence (Cats sleep soundly in English). Keys produced during this process will be automatically added. These rows keep their labels and colors; a key the script no longer produces is removed at the next save. Keys that the test run does not produce, as in this example, are added by hand: Click Add Key below the legend. Enter the key in the new row's Key field, exactly as the script produces it (such as adjectival). Fill in Label, the color, and the style. Rows that you add will have a minus button at the end of the row that lets you remove the row; the row persists in the legend regardless of what your script contains. At save time, LemmaLoom excludes any row whose Key is blank, and of two rows with the same key, it keeps only the first. The Legend pane of “Climate Roles” with a new row added by Add Key and the style menu open. Should your script generate keys in a document that do not exist in the legend, the analyzer fails, and LemmaLoom discards all its findings in the document. Likewise, Try it out ends with the same failure. All keys that can be produced by the script should therefore be added to the legend. If there exists a key inside your legend, then KEY has a constant for it. When your key subject is listed in your legend, you can write key: KEY.SUBJECT. If you write your key only as a KEY constant, then it needs to be added using Add Key. Any key beginning with a number like 1st or containing letters beyond a to z like über or 主语 should be enclosed in quotation marks.

There are checkboxes next to English, German, and Chinese to select which documents to run the analyzer on. These three languages are the ones LemmaLoom indexes. Only a document in a selected language will show an available option for the analyzer in the lens menu and display it as part of Document Properties. You must choose at least one language. Make sure your script is compatible with the chosen languages. “Climate Roles” is compatible with all three languages, although “Climate Debate” needs only English and German. Its list contains English, German, and Chinese lemmas, and it checks token.derived.function, which has identical values across all languages. Scripts that check token.tag or token.dep work only for the language of their labels. Multiple languages may be handled within one script with doc.language: Even with derived fields taken into account, the analysis of each language will differ in specifics. Therefore, you should test each language you choose. In the case of English, do more for the climate results in a finding because the analysis will regard climate as the object of the preposition for. In German, on the other hand, the noun within the prepositional phrase für das Klima is usually labeled nk (part of a noun phrase) and thus counts as adjectival, resulting in a sentence with no finding. In order to test another language, choose it from the dropdown language menu provided under Try it out, then provide a sentence written in the language. Only those languages chosen by you will be selectable via menu; the menu lists them by their codes, en for English, de for German, and zh for Chinese. Upon saving, LemmaLoom deletes the analyzer's findings from documents in deselected languages, while running the analyzer on newly selected languages' documents.

Try it out executes the script currently in the editor on the text you enter, regardless of whether the script has been saved or not.
