Use Try it out frequently during writing, and include sentences that differ structurally from your initial example, since the analyzer must account for each sentence structure within your documents. Enter one or more sentences in the box under Try it out. Choose the language of the text in the menu beside the box. Click Run. LemmaLoom performs the grammar analysis of your text using the same methods as for documents, then runs the built-in analyzers and then your script. Below the box, your text will appear along with annotations of the findings in the colors and styles specified in the legend. It might initially take a few seconds to prepare the grammar analysis for a particular language before performing your first run on it. Run is disabled while the box is empty (No text entered), and during a run the spinner icon replaces the button. Try it out after a run, with the first climate found as a subject and the second as an object. Below the annotated text, there is a small console which displays everything the script has printed with console.log, one line per call, with every line preceded by ›. If there is nothing found by the script, the console will display 0 findings. If you would like to know the interpretation of the analysis on a particular sentence, you may print the values. This line, placed inside the loop over sentences, prints each token with its relation: For The new targets were announced last year. it generates ["The/det","new/amod","targets/nsubjpass","were/auxpass","announced/ROOT","last/amod","year/npadvmod","./punct"]. The test text is kept inside the box while the window is open, regardless of switching analyzers, allowing you to run multiple analyzers on the same text.

Should the execution fail, LemmaLoom will halt execution of your script, display an error message in red under the editor, and underline the faulty line in the editor when the error belongs to a particular line. For any errors in your findings, the editor underlines line 1. The error after Run when line 6 reads token.lema instead of token.lemma. Message What it means The script must define a function named analyze(doc). There is no function called analyze, perhaps because its name is misspelled. analyze(doc) must return an array of findings. The function returns nothing, or something other than a list. Check the return line. Finding 3 must have sentenceIndex, start, end, and key. A finding lacks one of the four fields, one of their names is misspelled, or a value has the wrong kind (a position that is not a number, or a key that is not text). A misspelled constant such as KEY.SUBJCT has no value, so it causes this message too. Findings are counted from 0, so this is the fourth. Finding 3: sentenceIndex 12 is out of range. No sentence has that number. Finding 3: token range 4..4 is out of range for sentence 0. end is not larger than start, start is below 0, or end lies beyond the end of the sentence. Finding 3: key "objekt" is not in the legend. The key has no row in the legend. Correct the script, or add the key with Add Key. A message beginning with TypeError, ReferenceError, or SyntaxError A mistake in the JavaScript itself. The editor underlines the line. A TypeError often indicates that a field is incorrectly spelled. Suppose your script had token.lema.toLowerCase() instead of token.lemma.toLowerCase() at line 6 of “Climate Roles”. This mistake would halt execution with a TypeError at line 6 because token.lema doesn't exist, and therefore cannot be turned into lowercase. A script stuck in an infinite loop continues executing infinitely. Under Try it out, the spinning circle replaces Run indefinitely. Even the Save button executes the script, thus possibly creating an identical problem. You will need to select the entire script with ⌘A and copy it with ⌘C, since quitting loses your unsaved progress. Then quit LemmaLoom itself (⌘Q), reopen it, and paste your script back in. Typically, scripts that suffer from infinite looping contain a while loop whose condition never evaluates to false. If the script has a loop other than a for … of or forEach over a list, test it on a short text before you save. Press F1 while in the editor to access its command palette. Commands like navigating to a particular line number, searching or replacing text in the script, or commenting out lines (turning them into comments the script skips) can all be found here. Commenting out lines is especially useful in pinpointing problem areas in scripts.

If your annotated text does not meet expectations, you may halt execution in the middle of a test run and examine the current state of the script's variables. Click in the margin to the left of a line number in the editor, or on the number itself. A red dot shows that the line has a breakpoint. Click again to remove it. Click Run under Try it out. The execution of the script pauses just before reaching the line marked by the breakpoint. Highlighting occurs on that line, and a box under the test text shows its line number, such as ● L7, along with the current values of the script's variables. Additionally, hovering the mouse pointer over one of these variables in the script editor displays its value. “Climate Roles” stopped at the breakpoint in line 7, with the values of doc, sentence, token, findings, and index under the test text. There are three buttons taking the place of Run: The play button advances past the breakpoint to the next breakpoint or the end of the run. The bent arrow advances to the next line beginning a statement. This includes advancing into any loop statements as well as functions passed to forEach. Running through steps of “Climate Roles” thus advances past each token sequentially. The square ends the run prematurely. Variables displayed by LemmaLoom are limited to doc, sentence, token, findings, finding, marker, span, clause, i, and index, and they appear only if they currently exist in the script. These names are used in examples throughout this chapter wherever possible. Other variables, such as role in “Climate Roles”, may be logged using console.log. Long values are truncated; lists appear as their lengths (Array(3)), texts are cut after their first 80 characters, and objects after 120 characters. Given “Climate Roles” along with the example test sentence introduced earlier in the chapter, breaking on line 7 (const role = …) pauses execution at the first climate, where index is equal to 1 and findings is equal to Array(0). Clicking the play button pauses execution at the second climate, where index equals 16 and findings equals Array(1), since the finding for the first climate has been added in between. A breakpoint pauses a script only on a line beginning a statement. Thus a breakpoint on lines of closing braces and parentheses like } or }); in “Climate Roles”, on lines beginning with else, or on a continuation of a previous statement is skipped. In a select number of layouts, LemmaLoom can follow the script only from breakpoint to breakpoint, and in a few it executes scripts completely without stopping on any breakpoints. Breakpoints are limited to Try it out.

To save the analyzer, either press Save at the top of the middle column, or hit Return when editing Name or a Label field. Save is disabled while Name is empty (Name is empty) or while no language is selected (No language chosen). Before saving the analyzer, LemmaLoom verifies its script. LemmaLoom extracts the legend keys first before running your script on a sample three-word sentence in each selected language (Cats sleep soundly, Katzen schlafen gern, and 猫 喜欢 睡觉). Because these sample sentences generate blank results for phrases, noun chunks, morphological features, and built-in results, verifying your script also detects any problems arising when processing empty lists. Should there be issues in your script, LemmaLoom informs you below the script editor (see When errors occur earlier in this chapter). Another pair of messages displays only when you save. The script is empty. means that there is no script written in the editor, while No keys found in the script. indicates that the legend table is blank. LemmaLoom applies the verified script across all your documents in the selected languages next. Progress rings show in the navigation sidebar and in Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0). The time this operation takes will depend on how many documents you have and the power of your Mac.

Select an analyzer in the list, update it, and click Save. Depending on the nature of your update, different outcomes may occur: If the update consisted of changing its name, label, color, or style, then the change will be reflected immediately wherever its lens is enabled. In the event of updating the analyzer script itself, updating the language or set of languages it uses, or the keys it uses for analysis, LemmaLoom will rerun the entire analyzer process again for all documents in its designated languages, including any language you have just selected. Until it has processed the document in question, the analyzer's row in that document's Document Properties displays Out of Date. Creating an analyzer, updating it, and deletion are all entries in the undo history of the Analyzers window. While the Analyzers window is active, the operation Edit ▸ Undo Edit Analyzer, for instance, rolls back to the previous version of the analyzer. The middle column keeps showing what you saved until you select the analyzer from the list again. Saving prior to selection re-saves the newer version of the analyzer. More detail regarding undo in particular windows can be found in Which window a step belongs to in .

To delete an analyzer, right-click the analyzer in the list and choose Delete Analyzer. Alternatively, you can select the analyzer first and then choose Edit ▸ Delete Analyzer (⌘⌫). This shortcut function applies while the list has focus, as would happen upon selecting an analyzer. LemmaLoom immediately deletes the analyzer. Analyzers are shared across all projects, meaning deletion causes immediate removal across all projects. Its lens gets disabled for all currently open documents, and LemmaLoom removes its findings from all documents. Edit ▸ Undo Delete Analyzer (⌘Z) restores it and runs it again. Should you merely want an analyzer out of particular documents, disable the analyzer for those documents (described in Analyzers for each document later on in this chapter).

A custom analyzer is executed on your documents at the end of indexing, after the grammar analysis of each document and the three built-in analyzers. Each custom analyzer for the document's language will be executed sequentially as long as it is enabled for the document. Its findings are saved alongside the document itself and accessed through the lens, Auto Code…, and queries. Your analyzers are executed on your document: upon initial indexing, once imported into the project or via Index Now; upon subsequent indexing, for example following changes made to the document's text or language setting; upon saving a new analyzer, or a modification to the analyzer script, selected languages, or keys; via Run in the document's Document Properties. Should modifications be made to an existing analyzer, LemmaLoom generally uses the previously performed grammar analysis on your documents and executes only the analyzers again without redoing everything from scratch. Nonetheless, an analyzer still processes every document within its assigned languages. If the script is inefficiently written, it causes a bottleneck in processing all the documents. Worse yet, should the script become trapped in an infinite loop, it keeps running indefinitely until you quit LemmaLoom. Should that happen, correct or delete the offending analyzer via Window ▸ Analyzers before quitting and reopening LemmaLoom. It is possible that an error occurs while executing the script on a specific document. Perhaps the document contains some particular combination of words or syntax not included in test sentences during development of the script. LemmaLoom discards the analyzer's findings for the document and flags the analyzer in Document Properties as Not Run or Out of Date. From there, you may click Run in order to retry. If the problem persists and causes failure of the analyzer script again, LemmaLoom marks it as Failed in Document Properties, displaying the error message upon hover. To debug the exact problem, place suspicious sentences into Try it out and run the script there. The Analyzers list in the Indexing section of Document Properties for “Running Out of Time”, with “Climate Roles” marked Failed and its error message shown on hover.

Analyzers run on each document within its supported languages unless disabled for a document. You can disable an analyzer that does not suit a document when you import the document or at any time thereafter. How to select analyzers for a document is covered under Choosing analyzers for a document in . When you import a document, in the Import Document dialog (or Import from Web for web pages), you have access to the Analyzers list, which shows the built-in analyzers first and yours after them in alphabetical order. Each entry in the list has a checkbox that you can deselect to prevent that particular analyzer from being executed on the document. When Language is set to Automatic, all analyzers will appear, whereas when a specific language is selected, then only those for that particular language appear. Additionally, the list becomes disabled whenever Index for grammar analysis is deselected. Further details are available under Analyzers and indexing in . On a document currently in your project, the Analyzers list appears in Document Properties: Right-click the document in the sidebar and choose Properties. In the Indexing section, find the Analyzers list. Every analyzer available for the document's language receives its own row indicating whether it is Done, Out of Date, Not Run, Running, or Failed. To remove an analyzer's findings from a document so it stops running on it, you press its trash button, Remove Output. This button appears once the analyzer has run on the document. To execute an analyzer that is Not Run, Out of Date, or removed from a document, you click Run; this action will also enable a removed analyzer on the document again. Run is disabled while either the document has not yet been indexed (Not indexed yet), or indexing has been turned off for the document (Indexing is off). Removal and execution both occur immediately. Both removal of an analyzer and execution of a removed one are actions that appear in the main window's undo history, and Edit ▸ Undo Remove Output restores and runs the analyzer again. The Analyzers list in the Indexing section of Document Properties for “Running Out of Time”. When you remove an analyzer from a document, it no longer appears in the lens menu of the document, and Auto Code… and queries involving it skip the document. If you ever modify an analyzer that has been disabled on a document, it stays disabled there, so the new version runs only on the documents where it is enabled.

Analyzers can be toggled individually through the lens menu to view annotations of their findings directly in the reader. To activate an individual analyzer's annotations, open the lens menu located at the right of the title band; here, your analyzers are grouped together. The lens displays annotations, while its legend displays label names. Clear Analyzers disables all analyzer lenses immediately. Learn more about toggling specific keys and viewing only annotated sentences via Show only the sentences a lens annotates in Analyzer lenses in . “Running Out of Time” with the “Climate Roles” lens enabled.

Enabling the analyzer's lens gives you access to the Document ▸ Auto Code… (⇧⌘A) function, which performs coding on whatever findings were made using the analyzer. This could be done on the currently open document, a document set, or even an entire project. Each key in the findings becomes a row in the Auto Code dialog. Named after its respective label, each of these can either be sent to an already established code (e.g., the row “Climate as object” to “Responsibility” in “Climate Debate”) or turned into new codes (e.g., two new codes from the two rows of “Climate Roles”). In a set or project, LemmaLoom does the same to all documents within it that use the same languages as the analyzer, have been indexed, and have the analyzer enabled. Please note that every mistake of the grammar analysis becomes a coding too. For more information on the dialog, see .

A query that finds Analysis · Findings searches what has been discovered by the analyzers, the ones included with LemmaLoom and any custom ones you may have made. There are three fields that relate specifically to findings. Analyzer checks which analyzer discovered the finding, Finding tests the key under which the finding was recorded (listed under its label), and Note checks the note associated with the finding. Other tests available in queries also apply, including the codes for any finding, and any attributes that belong to its associated document. Queries on Library · Analyzers list the analyzers themselves and can check their Name, Languages, and Legend Keys (see Choosing what to find in ). In “Climate Debate”, each document has an attribute titled “Stance”, taking values of either “Activist”, “Skeptic”, or “Neutral”. As a result, counting the findings from the “Climate Roles” analyzer by both key and “Stance” should reveal any differences between how activists and skeptics represent the topic of climate. When working with your materials, group by whichever attribute divides your documents. To query for the counts of an analyzer's findings by group: Open the Queries section of the project. In Find, choose Analysis · Findings. In the Where condition, click Add and choose Add Rule. In the new rule's field menu, choose Analyzer from the Finding section. Leave the comparison at is any of, and choose the analyzer as the rule's value. In Show, choose Count. Click Group By and choose Finding in the new row's field menu. Click Group By again and choose the attribute in the second row's field menu, such as Attribute ▸ Stance. In the menu showing Hits, choose Per 10,000 Words. For “Climate Roles” in “Climate Debate”, you end up with a table showing the subjects and objects for each value of “Stance”. Each group contains a different amount of text; therefore, what you end up with is actually a table of rates. Rate refers to how many findings occur in each group per 10,000 words of text contained within the documents in the group (see Measures in ). For instance, assuming there were 4,000 words and 3 occurrences of “Climate as object” in the activists' documents (using round numbers purely as examples), the rate will be $3 / 4{,}000 times 10{,}000 = 7.5$. The query in the “Climate Debate” project that counts the findings of “Climate Roles” by finding and by “Stance”, as rates per 10,000 words. As described in Comparing groups in , if you want to test the groups for significant differences, choose Compare in Show, then delete the Finding row from Group By so that only “Stance” remains, and finally add a rule Finding is any of “Climate as object”. The three neutral documents, “Heat Wave Report 2024”, “Carbon Tax Debate”, and “Radio Debate”, participate in the comparison as their own group.

A LemmaLoom archive (.llz) includes the analyzers whose findings are stored alongside the documents contained within the archive, together with the findings. An archive also includes any analyzers that the saved queries of the archive use or were turned into. On importing an archive, an unrelated analyzer having the same name as an existing analyzer in your library is imported next to it. Please refer to  for further guidance.

Choose Save as Analyzer… from a query's Save menu to save it as an analyzer. The query must find words, pattern matches, sentences, phrases, or noun chunks and test only their words and grammar; otherwise it cannot be transformed into an analyzer. Your newly made analyzer will show up in Window ▸ Analyzers among the others available; hence, like other analyzers, you can view its script, test-run it using Try it out, and modify it directly. The keys used in generating the analyzer will either consist of the categories from your query, or just one key, hit, labeled Match, in case there are no categories to speak of. These will appear as legend rows with a Key field, as well as a minus button, similar to what happens when you use Add Key. The analyzer you have just generated is linked back to the saved query it was derived from. If the latter is resaved with updates, a label of Out of Date will appear next to the analyzer name in your list. Updating it is done as follows: Click the analyzer in the list. Click Update Analyzer, to the left of Save. When LemmaLoom writes a new script from the saved query, it preserves the analyzer's name and languages but replaces its script and legend, meaning any changes to the labels, colors, and styles of the analyzer would be overwritten by the newly generated analyzer. The check that the new script finds what the query finds runs only with Save as Analyzer…. Should the newly written script have errors, they are shown underneath the editor. Should the current state of the saved query be unable to transform into an analyzer, then Update Analyzer is disabled with the appropriate explanation why it cannot be done; Edit ▸ Undo Update Analyzer will restore the previous state of the analyzer before updating. The link between the saved query and the analyzer becomes broken upon editing and saving the script. The analyzer then counts as one of your own. Changing only the name, languages, or legend keeps the connection. See Keeping an analyzer in step with its query in  for more ways to handle query-generated analyzers.

As LemmaLoom receives a document into your project, it automatically processes the document by indexing it, provided that your document is in English, German, or Chinese, unless you choose otherwise as you import it. The indexing process parses your text into sentences and words, determines the dictionary form and word class of each word, and computes the syntax structure between all the words of each sentence. Lenses, the Grammar tab in the inspector, word sketches, keyword lists, and most word-based queries rely on indexing results. While LemmaLoom is processing your documents, you are free to read and code them in the reader without waiting. Indexing time depends on how long your documents are and on your Mac's hardware. “Climate Debate”, the example project, comes pre-indexed. For the rest of this chapter, indexing is used for describing the process performed by LemmaLoom, following the naming convention used by its status messages (Indexing, Indexed, Waiting to be indexed). As well, indexing results are referred to as grammar analysis (or simply the analysis).

This analysis breaks a text apart at various levels. Terms such as token and lemma will crop up frequently in this user guide, and Help ▸ Glossary has definitions of the main ones. Tokens refer to individual words or punctuation marks. Each period separating sentences is its own token. Lemmas represent dictionary forms of words. Thus warning is the lemma of warnings, be is the lemma of was, and gehen the lemma of ging. The word class, or part of speech, refers to whether a token is a noun, verb, adjective, etcetera. All three languages share the same universal word classes, such as NOUN, VERB, and ADJ. Tags refer to more detailed parts of speech restricted to a specific language. English warnings is the plural noun NNS. German Klima is the noun NN. Morphology tracks the grammatical properties of word forms. It includes information about tense, number, and case. A dependency pairs a token with another token, known as its head. Dependencies also describe the relationship. In the most urgent steps, both tokens the and urgent have dependencies linking them to steps. Each sentence has one token that depends on no other word. This word is called a root, usually the main verb. Phrase structure (or constituency) organizes tokens into hierarchies, such as noun phrases contained in verb phrases within clause structures. A noun chunk represents a noun, along with preceding tokens that modify the noun. Examples include noun chunks such as the most urgent steps, or pronouns such as we when they act as subjects or objects of verbs. Stopwords represent highly frequent words containing minimal significance themselves, for instance, the, and, or was. Finally, an analyzer executes once grammar analysis has been completed, annotating passages of one kind, such as ties between sentences or rhetorical devices. The passages annotated by an analyzer become its findings.

Document indexing entails the following sequence of actions: LemmaLoom settles the document's language, which decides the models it uses. Text that matches the document's Exclude from indexing patterns is blanked out, so indexing skips it. The text is divided into tokens and sentences. Chinese, which is written without spaces between words, is first divided into words. Each token gets its word class, tag, and lemma, and in English and German its morphology. LemmaLoom works out the dependencies between the words of each sentence. It works out the phrase structure of each sentence. It finds the noun chunks and the stopwords. The built-in analyzers Cohesion, Metadiscourse, and Rhetoric run, and so do any analyzers you have written yourself. Everything is saved with the document. Once the whole document has been indexed, LemmaLoom computes its statistics. A long document is indexed in parts (see After an edit later in this chapter). During indexing, progress stages and percentages are displayed in the reader's status bar, in the Activity window, and via tooltips of the badges in the navigation sidebar. Initially, you see Analyzing until around 5% of the document has been processed, followed by Parsing structure until about 97%, and finally Saving. Percentages indicate how much of the text content has been indexed in the document; parsing of the phrase structure takes most of the time during indexing.

The op-ed entitled “Running Out of Time” in the example project poses a question about what needs to occur now. It answers its own question with the sentence The most urgent steps are not mysterious. Its analysis appears below: Token Lemma Word class Tag Dependency Head The the DET DT det steps most most ADV RBS advmod urgent urgent urgent ADJ JJ amod steps steps step NOUN NNS nsubj are are be AUX VBP ROOT none not not PART RB neg are mysterious mysterious ADJ JJ acomp are . . PUNCT . punct are LemmaLoom employs two distinct encoding systems for the tagging of words in texts. In the word classes scheme, for instance, DET refers to a determiner, ADV to an adverb, ADJ to an adjective, AUX to an auxiliary verb, PART to a particle, and PUNCT to a punctuation mark. In the tags scheme, however, DT corresponds to a determiner, RBS to a superlative adverb, JJ to an adjective, VBP to a present-tense verb, and RB to an adverb. These two schemes categorize words differently; thus, while not falls under particles in the former, it belongs to adverbs in the latter. On the other hand, dependencies encode grammatical relationships between words rather than properties; for example, det signifies a determiner, advmod a modifying adverb, amod an adjective describing a noun, acomp an adjective complementing a verb, and punct a punctuation mark. The Grammar tab provides expanded forms for all these abbreviations, such as Noun, plural for NNS, and Help ▸ Glossary lists all grammatical codes (including morphological features). Consider the following points regarding these annotations: Not is a token of its own, and the Negation lens annotates it. Contractions become two tokens; hence, cannot, which appears later in the same paragraph, becomes can and not, and don't becomes do and n't. Furthermore, the Negation lens annotates n't just as it annotates not. The lemma for steps is step; therefore, queries or word sketches based on the lemma step retrieve both step and steps. Likewise, the lemma for are is be. Word class merely tells you that steps is a noun. On the other hand, the tag NNS informs you that steps is plural. In addition, the morphological annotation reveals the same piece of information in the form of Grammatical number Plural, which you may view in the Grammar tab. Dependencies reveal which words take on what roles in the sentence. Steps is the subject (nsubj) of are, mysterious specifies the characteristics of the subject (acomp), and not negates the action expressed by are (neg). Are is the root of the sentence; therefore, it has no head. Are is the only verb here, although its word class is AUX. The phrase structure categorizes the same words differently. The most urgent steps constitutes a noun phrase (NP); it includes an adjective phrase (ADJP), most urgent. Are not mysterious is a verb phrase (VP), containing an ADJP, mysterious. Finally, NP and VP are the two main parts of the clause (S). Only one noun chunk exists here, the most urgent steps. A noun chunk ends with its noun or pronoun; hence, it can be shorter than the NP enclosing it. In the thermometer outside my kitchen window from the beginning of the op-ed article, the noun chunks are the thermometer and my kitchen window, whereas the phrase structure considers the whole string one NP. Four of eight tokens here are stopwords (The, most, are, and not). If you wish to know how indexing annotated a word, click the word in the reader. Then navigate to the Grammar tab in the inspector; the Grammar facet displays a word's lemma (if it differs from the word itself), Part of speech, and Tag. Moreover, it displays the word's dependency relationship under FUNCTION, its head, and its morphological annotations under MORPHOLOGY. In case you imported “Climate Debate” using File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project (refer to The example project in ), you can examine whether the above information matches the annotation of steps in “Running Out of Time”. For more on this view and on the diagrams of dependencies and phrase structure, see . The Grammar tab describing the word steps, selected in “Running Out of Time”.

The analysis stems from statistical models, i.e., machine learning models built on vast amounts of text data for choosing the most probable analyses of every word or sentence within a document. Separate models exist for each of the three languages, and all come with LemmaLoom. Under LemmaLoom ▸ About LemmaLoom is a list of LemmaLoom’s licenses; the Licenses section shows you the authors and license details of the included models (see Licenses in ). These models will get things wrong sometimes. They were trained mostly on written texts. Thus, analyses become less reliable in transcription-based documents, dialects, or text damaged by PDF extraction. Chinese analysis makes more errors compared to English and German analysis because the models need to locate Chinese words prior to analyzing them.

Three analyzers come with LemmaLoom and process documents in all three languages: Analyzer What it annotates Cohesion How each sentence ties back to what came before, through a pronoun, a possessive, a demonstrative such as this, a repeated word, or, in Chinese, an omitted subject. A sentence with none of these opens a new topic. Metadiscourse Words a speaker or writer uses to guide the listener or reader, namely hedges (perhaps), boosters (clearly), attitude markers (unfortunately), connectives (however), and engagement markers (you, consider). German adds modal particles such as ja and doch, and Chinese adds sentence-final particles such as 吗 and 吧. Rhetoric Rhetorical devices such as passive voice, nominalization (an action turned into a noun, decision for decide), parallelism, fronted openers (a phrase before the subject), periodic sentences (the main verb held back to the end), questions and commands, and sentences that open with the same words. The built-in analyzers provide an easy entry point for posing questions related to how a particular piece of writing is constructed. For instance, they can show how often a writer uses hedge constructions, or where the speaker begins discussing something else entirely. The results generated by these analyzers will then show up in lenses of matching names (see ) as well as the Discourse facet of the Grammar tab (see ). Queries which return Findings (see ) can also reference these analyzers. Custom analyzers that you develop from Window ▸ Analyzers run alongside the built-in ones, on documents in the specified languages (see ).

Once LemmaLoom finishes indexing a document, it counts its sentences and tokens. The Text tab within the document's inspector lists the document's sentence count and performs analyses of word counts, readability, and vocabulary statistics (see ). Until the first piece of the document is indexed, the Text tab shows Statistics become available when indexing completes. There are essentially two counts in LemmaLoom: In a token count, all punctuation marks and symbols are included. When creating a condition in a smart set or a rule in a query, selecting the Tokens field gives results based on token count. Similarly, the reader's status bar displays a token count labeled as words. Word count disregards punctuation and symbols while counting all numbers and numerals in addition to regular words. The Text tab uses word count, as well as the Per 10,000 Words measure used in queries (see Measures in ). The sample sentence from “Running Out of Time” has 8 tokens (7 words plus the period). Contractions, like don't, comprise two words (do and n't), whereas numerals like 2050 form single words. In Chinese texts, LemmaLoom counts individual words according to its indexing process. Prior to indexing, both the Tokens and Sentences counts of a document return 0 in any queries and smart sets. Furthermore, for documents stored in other languages (such as French), the counts always remain 0. Hence, a smart set of documents with fewer than 1,000 Tokens also includes all non-indexed documents. Once edits occur on existing documents, the two counts retain their last known figures until indexing completes. The Characters field comes directly from the document's content and gets calculated immediately. For sorting or comparisons of lengths between documents pending indexing, you should select Characters instead.

Patterns under Exclude from indexing in either the import dialog or Document Properties will prevent matching texts from being analyzed (see Excluding text from indexing in ). These texts include timestamps, speaker labels, headers, footers, etc. LemmaLoom blanks out each matched passage before indexing the text, so these items stay out of word counts, keyword lists, word sketches, and the built-in lenses. You will be able to view excluded text in the reader and apply codes, while the search bar searches it. A query for Text Matches will also search it if the first menu of its text row is set to the default setting of Text. This occurs since the query reads the text itself. In the event you change this menu to Word, Word Form, or Lemma, the query compares tokens instead, so it skips excluded text.

All three languages receive tokenization, sentence splitting, word class detection, tagging, lemmatization, dependency parsing, phrase structure, noun chunking, stopword identification, and all three built-in analyzers. Differences arise in the specifics:  English German Chinese Dividing the text into words At spaces and punctuation; don't becomes do and n't At spaces and punctuation By a model that finds the words, since they are not separated by spaces Tags Penn Treebank STTS (Stuttgart-Tübingen tagset) Penn Chinese Treebank Dependency labels English labels such as nsubj and dobj TIGER labels such as sb (subject) and oa (accusative object, the direct object) The English labels, plus Chinese ones such as aux:asp for aspect markers like 了 Phrase labels Penn Treebank, such as NP and PP TIGER, such as NP and PP Penn Chinese Treebank Morphology lens Tense, Number, Degree (comparative, superlative), Verb form The same, plus Case, Mood, and Gender Not offered Metadiscourse categories Five The five, plus Modal particle The five, plus Final particle Rhetoric devices All thirteen All but Absolute phrase All but Periodic sentence and Absolute phrase Lenses for this language only None Sentence fields (see Sentence fields (German) in ) Constructions and Particles (see Constructions and Particles (Chinese) in ) Penn Treebank, Penn Chinese Treebank, STTS, and TIGER are standard annotation schemes, which the models were trained on. The Grammar tab describing Klima in “Running Out of Time (German)”, with its features under Morphology. Chinese words have a single form, and hence, the lemma of a Chinese word is always the word itself. The stopwords discovered through the process of indexing go into the Stopword share in the Text tab and the Stopword field of words when querying; the Collocates facet of the Grammar tab ignores stopwords. The stopwords lists are internal lists provided by LemmaLoom; LemmaLoom comes pre-packaged with 162 stopwords in English, 211 stopwords in German, and 153 stopwords in Chinese. If a token's form or lemma matches an item on one of the lists, regardless of capitalization, it becomes a stopword. Since the stopword lists are fixed, you may define your own rules when querying to leave out other words. Help ▸ Glossary gives detailed descriptions of every tag, dependency label, and phrase label in use by LemmaLoom. Pick a term category from Help ▸ Glossary's sidebar (such as Part-of-speech tags, Dependency relations, Phrase labels, or Morphology), then search using the Search field above the glossary list. An item labeled EN, DE, or ZH is defined specifically for English, German, and Chinese respectively; otherwise, all three languages use that definition. Any part-of-speech tag, dependency label, or phrase label highlighted with colors in lenses appears in Help ▸ Glossary in matching colors too. Hover the mouse pointer over one of them to know which lens uses that tag, dependency label, or phrase label. The part-of-speech tags in the Glossary after a search for “proper noun”, with the languages each tag belongs to.

Language, set in the import dialog or in Document Properties, determines what models will be used to index the document. In the navigation sidebar, after the document's name, Language appears as a short code such as EN, DE, or ZH; hover the mouse pointer over the code on the navigation sidebar to view its full name. Set Language to Automatic, and LemmaLoom will recognize the language from the first 4,096 characters of the text in the document. With a recording, LemmaLoom will recognize its language based off the transcription language when available; otherwise, it reads the text in the document. LemmaLoom does this both on import and each time you set Language back to Automatic and save. Documents inside a project imported in REFI-QDA format will have their languages recognized the same way. Sometimes, LemmaLoom may mistake one of the three supported languages for another. Therefore, it may use the wrong models to analyze documents after importing them into LemmaLoom. After a large import, check the language codes in the sidebar. Choose the language yourself when the beginning of a document is not representative of the whole document, or when LemmaLoom has misidentified the language. An example scenario may arise where LemmaLoom tells you No grammar analysis for Spanish for an English-language blog post; set Language to English within Document Properties and press Save. Each document will always be indexed using one language across the entirety of the document. Text segments written in another language, e.g., quotations in foreign languages, will still be analyzed according to the models of the main language and yield unreliable results. Translations will have their languages determined by their target languages. Hence, “Running Out of Time (German)” will be analyzed based on the German models. They are indexed with all analyzers for the language, and Exclude from indexing starts blank, whatever the original uses; you may adjust any setting in Document Properties.

LemmaLoom supports importing a document written in any other language (French, Spanish, etc.) as text alone. The badge on the navigation sidebar for the document is a question mark, and hovering the mouse pointer over it produces Language not supported for indexing. In the reader, the status bar at the bottom will tell you No grammar analysis for French, where French stands for whatever the unsupported language is. You may continue reading, searching, editing, and coding documents despite lack of language support, and use them in every view that works without the analysis (see What is available without the analysis later in this chapter).

Indexing occurs on all of your projects regardless of which one you currently have opened. LemmaLoom indexes up to three documents simultaneously or up to three sections of one document at once; everything else is indexed in order. Should you quit LemmaLoom prematurely while indexing, then the remaining indexing process is resumed whenever you start LemmaLoom back up again. The models associated with a language get loaded into RAM upon needing to analyze the first document within that language, and around a minute and a half after the last document is done, they’re unloaded from memory.

A small badge after a document's name and language code in the navigation sidebar shows its index status. Hover your mouse pointer on top of the badge to reveal the status label. These statuses are also available in smart sets and queries via the Index Status field. Badge Index Status Meaning No badge Indexed The document has been indexed. Progress ring; the name is gray Indexing The document is being indexed. The tooltip shows the stage and the percentage, such as Parsing structure 35%. Progress ring or spinner Running Analyzer An analyzer you started with Run in Document Properties is running on the document. The tooltip reads, for example, Running Cohesion. Dotted circle Not Indexed The document waits in the queue (Waiting to be indexed). Pause sign Skipped Indexing is off for this document, because it was imported without indexing (see Importing without indexing below). Question mark Unsupported The document is in another language (Language not supported for indexing). Red warning triangle Failed Indexing failed. The tooltip gives the reason (see When indexing fails below). The sidebar during indexing. The skeptic texts in “Print” are being indexed, those in “Online” wait, and “Heat Wave Report 2024”, imported without indexing, shows the pause sign.

Document counts, including paragraph, sentence, and token counts of a document, are displayed at the far right side of the status bar of the reader. The counts displayed depend on the items displayed in the gutter (see The status bar in ). For instance, the status bar shows 10 ¶ · 65 S · 1,029 words for “Running Out of Time”. Until indexing finishes, and while you run an analyzer with Run, the status bar instead displays one of these: Stage and percentage completed, e.g., Parsing structure 35% accompanied by a progress ring; Indexing with a spinner icon while waiting for its turn (Waiting to be indexed in the sidebar); Running with an analyzer name followed by percentage completed when the document size is large, e.g., Running Rhetoric; Indexing is off with an Index Now link for a document added without indexing; No grammar analysis for followed by the language; Failure reason followed by a Retry Indexing link for the document failing indexing. The status bar of “Heat Wave Report 2024”, imported without indexing. Other components in the reader also await indexing (refer to Before indexing has finished in ).

Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0) displays the activity performed behind the scenes in all projects (refer to The Activity window in ). The following sections of the Activity window describe the indexing activities: Indexing displays the list of documents undergoing indexing activity, along with their stage and progress in percentages, and the documents currently being analyzed with a specific analyzer, e.g., Running Metadiscourse 40%. Failed shows the list of the documents that had their indexing fail, along with the reason for the failure, and a link named Retry Indexing for attempting the operation again. Lastly, Waiting provides the list of documents waiting for their turn in the queue, marked with the status of Waiting to be indexed. All rows indicate the name of their associated projects, so the Activity window is the place to follow indexing in projects other than the active one.

t: Finding documents by their index status
b: The members of a smart set will update automatically as documents finish indexing. A smart set can therefore show which documents are not ready yet following an import containing many documents. Create a smart set as follows: Choose Project ▸ New Smart Set, or click New Smart Set at the end of the Sets section in the sidebar. In the dialog that opens, give the set a name. In the condition row, choose Index Status in the menu showing Attribute or Tags. Choose is none of in the menu showing is any of. Open the value menu, which reads None, and select Indexed. Click Save. As you make changes to your criteria, the number beneath the conditions will inform you how many documents are in your set. Your set can also contain documents that are in other languages, as well as, briefly, documents with an analyzer running via Run on them. Should you wish to see only the documents requiring your attention, select is any of with Failed, Skipped, and Unsupported instead. A smart set of the documents whose indexing has not finished. The Index Status field is part of the Documents unit in queries. Both smart sets and queries also feature the Indexing Skipped field, indicating whether or not a document was imported without indexing and is still waiting for Index Now. To read more about smart sets, refer to .

Should the indexing fail on any document, a warning icon in the form of a red triangle will replace the badge next to the document in the sidebar. The document will also move to the Failed section inside the Activity window. The failure's cause will appear when hovering the mouse pointer over this icon, within the document's shortcut menu inside the sidebar, or in the reader's status bar. When there isn't anything specific enough to say, the reason for the failure reads Indexing this document failed. There is also always an option to retry the indexing process, Retry Indexing, available in these places: from the document's shortcut menu within the sidebar; from the reader's status bar; or, from the document's row in the Failed section inside the Activity window. LemmaLoom then indexes portions of the document which lack analysis and reruns its analyzers. LemmaLoom attempts retrying automatically upon startup, and, once it has waited long enough, again the next time it indexes any document. These waiting times double with each failure, starting at one minute until hitting one hour. After multiple failures occur on the same document, check its Language property under Document Properties. Within the reader itself, locate portions of text which aren't actual text (e.g., random characters caused by a corrupted PDF file), and fix or exclude such portions. Should nothing else work, feel free to report issues via Help ▸ Send Feedback (see ).

You may choose to bring in a document and leave it unindexed and have it indexed later. Some instances that warrant importing documents unindexed could be a large number of documents where you need to keep your Mac free now; a PDF where the extracted text must first be corrected before being indexed; and documents which will only ever be needed for reading and coding purposes. How to import documents without indexing them: Import the document as usual (see ). In the Indexing part of the Import Document or Import from Web dialog, deselect Index for grammar analysis. The Analyzers list below it is disabled. Click Import. A dialog appears once for each file imported, with the checkbox checked at first on each dialog. You can uncheck it on each dialog to import multiple files without indexing. Such a document won't be added to the queue even if its contents change later. Its lens menu remains disabled while the status on the Grammar tab states Grammar becomes available when indexing completes. For indexing this document, click on Index Now in the reader's status bar, or go ahead to Document Properties and hit Index Now. Access Document Properties through selecting the document in the sidebar and choosing Project ▸ Properties, or right-clicking the document itself and hitting Properties. There, Index Now sits at the top of the Indexing part, beside Indexing is off. This button acts immediately. The Indexing part of Document Properties for “Heat Wave Report 2024”, imported without indexing, with Index Now beside Indexing is off. Afterwards, your document will enter the queue for processing. If Index Now is mistakenly clicked on, you may use Edit ▸ Undo Index Now (⌘Z) to revert it back to the previous status Indexing is off. If indexing has already finished by then, the document keeps its analysis. Preventing indexing is only possible at import, or after importing the document, by undoing the Index Now action.

All analyzers working on the language of a particular document will run on it during indexing. There is always an option to exclude an analyzer from processing on individual documents either while importing a document or at any time afterward via deleting the findings generated by the analyzer from Document Properties. It might be appropriate to exclude an analyzer from a document whenever said analyzer does not suit the content. Rhetoric, for instance, identifies devices like nominalization and periodic sentences; however, since these are characteristic of written prose, you might wish to exclude it from analyzing “Radio Debate”, a recording transcript. Whenever it is excluded from analyzing all transcripts, a project-wide query for Findings counts rhetorical devices in the written documents only. Here is what happens when you choose to exclude an analyzer from processing on a document: All findings by the analyzer on this particular document will be removed; The lens for this analyzer will disappear from the document's lens menu; In the Discourse facet of the Grammar tab, you'll find indications like No Rhetorical Devices for the document; When applying an analyzer you created yourself to auto code documents, Auto Code… skips over any documents that the analyzer was excluded from previously.

Analyzers are listed with checkboxes under Analyzers in the Indexing part of the import dialog. The built-in analyzers appear first, followed by yours alphabetically. When the value of Language is Automatic, all analyzers will appear on the list; otherwise, only those capable of processing documents in the chosen language will show. Initially, everything will be checked by default; uncheck those you do not wish to include for this document.

t: The analyzer list in Document Properties
b: For viewing or editing the analyzers associated with an existing document within your project, follow this procedure: Select the document in the sidebar and choose Project ▸ Properties, or right-click it and choose Properties. Scroll down to the Indexing part. Analyzers lists the analyzers that handle the document's language. For a document in another language, it lists them all, with Run disabled. Each row shows the state of the analyzer: State Meaning Done The analyzer has run on the whole document with its current version. An analyzer that ran and found nothing is Done too. Out of Date The analyzer has run on part of the document, or with an earlier version. This is usually brief, because LemmaLoom brings it up to date by itself (see When analyzers are executed again below). Not Run The analyzer has not run on this document, because it was left out, because the document has not been indexed yet, or because the analyzer stopped with an error during indexing. Running The analyzer is running now. In a long document, a progress ring shows how far along it is. Failed The analyzer stopped with an error after you clicked Run. Hover the mouse pointer over Failed to read the error. The analyzers of “Radio Debate” in Document Properties, with Rhetoric left out. Clicking Run links or the trash button in this list will take effect immediately regardless of whether you click Cancel afterward.

If you remove an analyzer's output, LemmaLoom removes the findings and leaves the analyzer out of the document from then on. Open Document Properties for the document and scroll to Indexing. In the analyzer's row, click the trash button. Hovering the mouse pointer over it shows Remove Output. The button appears only for analyzers that are Done or Out of Date. The row now changes to Not Run. When the document gets reindexed (perhaps due to editing), the analyzer remains removed. You may undo the removal with Edit ▸ Undo Remove Output (⌘Z) to restore and rerun the analyzer. Should you wish to run it again in the future, click Run on the same row.

Open Document Properties for the document and scroll to Indexing. In the analyzer's row, click Run. The link appears for analyzers that are not Done. If your document lacked the analyzer, it is added back, and the analyzer runs immediately on the existing analysis. As it analyzes, its row displays as Running, with the sidebar badge and the reader's status bar indicating such, as well as the Activity window, e.g., Running Rhetoric. Should the document originally lack the analyzer, choosing Edit ▸ Undo Run (⌘Z) leaves it out again and removes the results of the run. Run remains disabled until indexing is complete, and for a document imported without indexing. Hovering your mouse pointer over it reveals Not indexed yet or Indexing is off accordingly. Should one of your own analyzers display Not Run in a fully indexed document despite never being left out, chances are that the analyzer failed during indexing due to some error. Clicking Run lets you attempt running it again. An unsuccessful run causes the analyzer to be listed as Failed. Hovering your mouse pointer over Failed provides you with the error message associated with the failure. The error can then be tracked down via Window ▸ Analyzers (see ).

Run isn't usually necessary because LemmaLoom re-runs the analyzers automatically. The two triggers for automatic re-running are when your document is indexed once again (see Indexing a document again) and when you remove/add any of your own analyzers through Window ▸ Analyzers, update its code or its languages, or modify its legend keys. In the second case, LemmaLoom re-runs the analyzer across all projects, on every document in its languages, excluding any document whose previous results you deleted. Only the analyzers re-run, so this is much faster than full indexing. Meanwhile, since all affected documents count as Indexing during this time, their names gray out in the sidebar with a progress ring while the row of the analyzer in Document Properties may display Out of Date until completed. When an analyzer's row displays Out of Date under Window ▸ Analyzers, it signifies something else. This Out of Date label indicates the analyzer comes from a modified query. Save the analyzer again from the altered query (see ) to fix this issue.

t: What is available without the analysis
b: Many features of LemmaLoom rely solely on the text content and your annotations, so these features work in every document, indexed or not: Area Works without the analysis Reader Reading, the search bar, selecting passages, editing the text, and playing recordings Annotations Coding, memos, links, and bookmarks; coded passages and bookmarks are shown in the text Inspector In the Coding tab, Codes, Codings, Links, Code Stats, and the Mosaic of Portrait; in the Text tab, Details (attributes and tags) and Bookmarks Project and sets Codebook, Codings, Memos, Links, Code Stats, Code Matrix, and Relations Dictionaries The counts in the Dictionaries section; Auto Code… with a dictionary lens, which also codes the documents of a set or project that are not yet indexed Queries The units Paragraphs, Text Matches, Codings, Memos, Bookmarks, Links, Speaker Turns, and Alignments, and the library units such as Documents and Codes Other Translating, sets and smart sets, attributes, tags, and exporting and exchanging projects These features require the analysis: Area Needs the analysis Reader Clicking to select a word, sentence numbers in the gutter, counts in the status bar, and clicking a word in a transcript to move the player there Lenses The lens menu, for every lens; until indexing has finished, it is disabled, with the tooltip Lenses become available when indexing completes Inspector The statistics in the Text tab; the whole Grammar tab; Code Sketch and the Codeline of Portrait in the Coding tab; Sketch Space in the Multimode tab Word sketches Word sketches for a document, a set, or the project Queries The units Words, Pattern Matches, Sentences, Phrases, Noun Chunks, and Findings; Collocates and Keywords; the Per 10,000 Words measure, which takes its word counts from the analysis Auto coding Auto Code… with one of your own analyzers' lenses, which skips documents not yet indexed Smart sets The Tokens and Sentences fields Whenever such a view encompasses multiple documents, it omits the documents that haven't been indexed and informs you of how many it included. A query will similarly provide you a document count alongside your hit count in the results bar (see Documents left out in ). 5 of 6 documents were searched, for instance, since one out of the six documents included in the “Activists” set is not indexed yet. A word sketch of a set or project will give you something like 13 of 14 documents indexed. Documents will only be omitted when using a unit that requires the analysis (see the table above). If you use a unit that doesn't require analysis, however, such as Paragraphs, all the documents will be included in your query. For documents not indexed, a text row whose first menu is set to Word, Word Form, or Lemma searches the text as Text does until indexing is done. Query from Selection makes a plain text search there (see ).

The analysis of a document in LemmaLoom remains valid until something it depends on changes. These changes send it back to the queue: Change What LemmaLoom does You edit the text and click Save Indexes the document again; in a long document, usually only the part you changed Edit ▸ Undo Edit Text The same, for the restored text You change Language in Document Properties and save Indexes the whole document in the new language You change Exclude from indexing in Document Properties and save Indexes the whole document again Edit ▸ Undo Delete Document Indexes the restored document, because its analysis was deleted with it You add, change, or delete one of your own analyzers Reruns only the analyzers, on every document in that analyzer's languages Edit ▸ Undo Remove Output Reruns the analyzers of that document A new version of LemmaLoom changes how documents are indexed Indexes every document again, in the background, the first time you open the new version

Saving edits immediately updates the text shown in the reader with your changes, and Saving will appear over it until your new analysis is complete (see What saving does in ). All of your codings, memos, links, and bookmarks travel with the text they are attached to before re-indexing starts. How much needs re-indexing depends on the size of the document. A document that does not exceed around 80,000 words in English is indexed in full as one piece, while a larger document is split up into multiple pieces at paragraph breaks. Any edit triggers the re-indexing of the piece containing the edit, meaning that, for most articles and speeches, edits trigger the indexing of the whole document. However, if editing occurred in long books or reports, then the unedited pieces usually keep their analysis, so the new analysis is ready much sooner. Significant insertions or deletions could push a paragraph forward into the next piece, thus triggering re-indexing of the pieces after it. Generally speaking, it is a better practice to fix mistakes or make larger revisions prior to indexing; for example, you should import a PDF without indexing it yet if you are going to revise a lengthy document extensively (see Importing without indexing earlier in this chapter).

A LemmaLoom archive (.llz) contains the analyses performed on its documents. When importing documents from an archive, you can use these analyses at once. If the archive was made by a version of LemmaLoom that indexes documents differently, its documents are indexed again. Imported documents keep the analyzer findings stored in the archive, too. Under Document Properties in any imported document, any of your analyzers that are not recognized by the archive's own library appear as Not Run; Run starts analyzing these documents accordingly. Any analyzer that was not present in your own library and comes from the archive is added to your library. Documents previously residing in your library can be analyzed by it only when next indexed, or manually via clicking Run. A REFI-QDA project (.qdpx) stores its text documents, and indexing takes place just like it would for new documents. Refer to  for additional information on these two file formats.

Projects are stored in the LemmaLoom library on your macOS device (refer to Where work is stored in ). Work can be taken out of the library or put into the library via exporting or importing respectively. The choice of file type comes from who will access the exported file next. All examples use the project called “Climate Debate”. The project contains eleven made-up opinion pieces written by climate activists and climate skeptics, such as “Running Out of Time” and “The Models Keep Missing”, along with the PDF document “Heat Wave Report 2024”, the web page “Carbon Tax Debate”, and the recording “Radio Debate”. “Running Out of Time (German)” is the translation of “Running Out of Time”, for a total of 15 documents. Following along with these examples requires selecting File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. Upon importation, LemmaLoom will automatically create a new project entitled “Climate Debate” inside your library, already indexed and in the language of the interface.

You want to File Command Back up a project, or move it to another Mac LemmaLoom archive (.llz) File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project Give a colleague a set or some documents with your coding LemmaLoom archive (.llz) File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Set or LemmaLoom Document Import an archive LemmaLoom archive (.llz) File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive Pass a project to software that supports the REFI-QDA standard REFI-QDA project (.qdpx) File ▸ Export ▸ REFI-QDA Project Open a project made in such software REFI-QDA project (.qdpx) File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Project Share a code system without any documents REFI-QDA codebook (.qdc) File ▸ Export ▸ REFI-QDA Codebook and File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Codebook Work on numbers in a spreadsheet or statistics program CSV The export button of the table Put a chart or diagram in a paper or on a slide PNG or PDF The export button of the chart Keep a query result with a record of how it was made Markdown The export button of the query result You would typically opt for LemmaLoom archive export whenever the materials continue to remain inside LemmaLoom, whether that means keeping backups yourself, moving your work to another Mac, or passing along LemmaLoom documents to a colleague who uses LemmaLoom. An archive keeps the indexing, the saved queries, and the tie between a translation and its original, so the material is ready to use right after import. When your work moves in or out of LemmaLoom (either originating somewhere else or destined somewhere else), then you'll want to use a REFI-QDA project instead. This will retain none of the LemmaLoom indexing structure or any of the functionality derived from it. File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Codebook and everything listed under File ▸ Export work on the active project (bolded in the navigation sidebar). These options will all appear disabled until you select a project. The Export submenu of the File menu. Alternatively, you could import .llz, .qdpx, or .qdc files by double-clicking them in the Finder. Doing so will launch LemmaLoom if it hasn’t been started already. A project archive and a REFI-QDA project each become a new project. If you are importing a codebook, set archive, or document archive, it will be imported into the active project, so make sure the right project is active. If you have conflicting programs opening .qdpx or .qdc files on a Mac, you may alternatively right-click a file and choose Open With ▸ LemmaLoom.

A LemmaLoom archive is an export file containing either a complete project, a set, or a selection of documents together with all their LemmaLoom data, such as indexing and recordings. REFI-QDA is an open data exchange format for transferring projects from one qualitative analysis program to another. The format handles documents, codes, codings, memos, links, variables (LemmaLoom attributes), and sets within projects. Scope is the source of an archive (a whole project, one set, or documents you selected) and determines what will be archived and how archives are imported. Archives of sets or selected documents match the groups, codes, and attributes present in the receiving project based on their names. The matching is performed during importing.

Import and export of REFI-QDA files and LemmaLoom archives occur through a dialog, which is attached to the top of the main window. Once you choose a file, or double-click one in the Finder, the dialog appears instantly. The exchange dialog while “Climate Debate” is exported as an archive. The dialog will display a title such as Exporting LemmaLoom Archive, the filename being exported/imported, and a ring that gradually gets filled according to the progress made during import/export operations. For exports of REFI-QDA projects and codebooks, and for imports of codebooks, a spinner replaces the ring icon. Import/export time mostly depends on project size and recording size. An exchange operation cannot happen simultaneously with another exchange operation. Before completion of such operations, all commands related to importing and exporting REFI-QDA files/archives get disabled, both in the File menu and in the sidebar. The Activity window lists the currently running exchange under the Importing or Exporting category. For a detailed description see The Activity window in . Upon completion of the export operation, the dialog displays a new title, for example LemmaLoom Archive Exported. Until the exchange finishes, Done remains disabled and hovering the mouse pointer over it reveals Running. Click Done to close the dialog. Upon completion of the import operation, the dialog automatically closes. A project contained in an archive/REFI-QDA file will become the active project; newly imported documents and codes appear in the receiving project. Should anything go wrong during import/export operations, the dialog will stay open. It would display a failure message in the title (Import Failed or Export Failed), followed by the file's name and a reason. Such reasons include the following: Message What it means The file isn't a REFI-QDA project. The .qdpx file contains no project description. It may be damaged, or have been renamed from another kind of file. The file isn't a REFI-QDA codebook. The .qdc file is not a codebook. The file isn't a LemmaLoom archive. The .llz file was not written by LemmaLoom, or it is damaged. This archive was made by a newer version of LemmaLoom. Update LemmaLoom, then import the archive again. Open a project to import into. The file holds a codebook, a set, or documents, which go into an existing project, and no project was active. Click a project in the sidebar and try again. The file isn't a valid archive. or The archive is damaged. Every .qdpx and .llz file is a ZIP file, and this one is incomplete or damaged. Copy it again from its source. The archive uses a format LemmaLoom can't read. The ZIP file is protected by a password, or compressed with a method other than the usual Deflate. Export it again from the other program without a password. The library isn't available. LemmaLoom could not reach its library or the project. Wait until the sidebar lists your projects, then try again. The exchange dialog titled Import Failed for the file “Letters to the Editor.llz”, with the reason The file isn't a valid archive. Click Done to close the dialog. If LemmaLoom is unable to export your files successfully, the incomplete file will be deleted. If you chose to replace an existing file, the file you were replacing is at risk as well.

Archives are useful when backing up your projects prior to deleting them, transferring your project to another machine, or sharing parts of it with colleagues that use LemmaLoom too. Only archives retain LemmaLoom's indexing and your saved queries.

Regardless of the scope involved, an archive contains the following for each document: the document's text as edited, and for audio and video documents the transcript with its speakers and times, and a copy of the recording; the document's metadata including its properties, color, tags, and attribute values for the project; its indexing including sentences, words, lemmas, parts of speech, sentence trees, along with results produced by built-in and custom analyzers (see ); its codings, bookmarks, and memos; its translations, which themselves include text, indexing, and codings. The rest depends on the scope. A code may be limited to a single document or set (see Where a code can be used in ); such codes are referred to below as limited. Content Project Set Selected documents Documents All documents of the project The set's documents, and their translations The selected documents, and their translations Codes All codes, with their memos The codes that the archive's codings, memos, and queries use, codes limited to one of its documents or to the set, and the parents of all these, with their memos The codes that the archive's codings, memos, and queries use, codes limited to one of its documents, and the parents of all these, with their memos Code sets All None None Links All Links whose two ends both lie in the archive's documents As for a set Groups All The groups of the archive's documents, and groups named in the set's conditions The groups of the archive's documents Sets All sets and smart sets The exported set, with its conditions if it is a smart set None Attributes All All except those defined on a code the archive leaves out, with the values of the archive's documents, codings, and memos As for a set Dictionaries All None None Saved queries Those saved for the project, its sets, its tags, or its documents Those saved for the project, for the set, or for one of its documents Those saved for the project or for one of the documents Custom analyzers Those whose findings are stored with the documents, those an included query uses, and those generated from an included query As for a project As for a project The project's name, color, tags, and project memos Yes No No Queries with Available In set to All Projects will be part of your library and travel only along with a copy of your complete library (refer to Saving queries in ). How queries and analyzers travel is explained in greater detail in Queries in LemmaLoom archives in .

In the sidebar, click the project, for example “Climate Debate”. Choose File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project. The save dialog suggests the project's name, Climate Debate. Change it if you like, choose a folder, and click Save. When the dialog reads LemmaLoom Archive Exported, click Done. The archive file is named Climate Debate.llz. For importing and restoring the project, follow the steps explained in the section on Importing an archive later in this chapter.

A set archive exports a portion of a project with the codes it uses. For instance, the set “Activists” within the “Climate Debate” project contains the six activist documents. In the Sets section of the sidebar, click the set, for example “Activists”. Choose File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Set, or right-click the set and choose Export. The save dialog suggests the set's name. Choose a folder, and click Save. When the dialog reads LemmaLoom Archive Exported, click Done. The shortcut menu of the set “Activists”, with Export. File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Set exports the current set highlighted in the navigation sidebar, or the set open in the active tab. An archive is packaged up with all the set’s documents, including their translations. This means that for “Activists”, you get seven documents, the six activist texts and “Running Out of Time (German)”, which is a translation of one of the documents in that set. The set archive excludes code sets, dictionaries, and any codes except those listed above. If your colleague needs your complete coding scheme, send a codebook export in REFI-QDA format as well (see REFI-QDA codebooks further ahead in this chapter). A smart set exports with the documents meeting its conditions at the point of export, along with these conditions. Upon receipt in another project, the smart set will reapply its conditions to all documents in the project, making it possible that more documents match than when first exported. Exported from “Climate Debate”, the smart set “Wide Reach”, which collects documents where “Readership” is greater than or equal to 100,000, arrives with its six documents, plus “Running Out of Time (German)”, whose original is among the six documents. With a colleague’s project featuring a “Readership” attribute, this smart set collects her documents with a value greater than or equal to 100,000 too. When passing on all the documents with a tag, you first click the tag in the Tags section to view which documents carry it, then select them in the Documents section before exporting as described next.

Export individual documents if you wish to share just a few texts with a coworker for a one-off purpose, like a second reading of three skeptic texts. If your documents should arrive as a named collection, then export a set, because your archive then carries the set along. In the Documents section of the sidebar, click a document. To export several, ⌘-click each of the others, or ⇧-click to select a run of them. Choose File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Documents (or LemmaLoom Document for one), or right-click one of the selected documents and choose Export. The save dialog suggests the document's title, or for several documents the project's name. Choose a folder, and click Save. When the dialog reads LemmaLoom Archive Exported, click Done. The shortcut menu for three selected skeptic texts, with Export. If no document is selected in the sidebar, then File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Document will export the document in the active tab. Exporting an original document includes all of its translations too. As such, exporting “Running Out of Time” will also export “Running Out of Time (German)”. When you export a translation alone, it arrives as a regular document along with its content and codings.

Archive import actions differ based on the archive's scope: Project archive imports will become a new project using the imported project's properties, including name, color, and tags, regardless of what the active project may be. Set or documents archive imports will import the archives into the currently active project. No active project results in failure with the message Open a project to import into. If you don't have any projects yet, create a blank one first (see Creating a project in ). To begin importing an archive: For an archive of a set or of documents, click the project that should receive it in the sidebar. For a project archive, skip this step. Choose File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive. Choose the .llz file and click Open. Alternatively, double-clicking the .llz file inside the Finder will import the archive the same way as the previous method. Reimporting the exact same project archive results in two projects having the exact same name, which means you should rename one of those projects (refer to The project's shortcut menu in ). The imported documents come indexed right away and are ready for lenses, the grammar inspector, and queries. LemmaLoom then checks the library in the background and indexes only the missing items (refer to ). Recordings are copied into the library as well. When wanting to get rid of everything imported via an archive import operation, delete the newly created project. With set/documents archives, delete the imported documents and set (see Deleting documents in ), then any codes, groups, and/or attributes the import added, such as “Adaptation” in the example below.

t: Moving a project to another Mac
b: On the first Mac, click the project in the sidebar and choose File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project. Copy the .llz file to the other Mac, for example with AirDrop or on an external drive. On the other Mac, double-click the file in the Finder, or choose File ▸ Import ▸ LemmaLoom Archive, choose the file, and click Open. Open a few documents and check that codings, memos, and recordings are there. If you no longer need the project on the first Mac, delete it there. Queries with Available In set to All Projects are stored within the library. Copying an entire library copies all of your projects and queries therein at once; please consult Where work is stored in  for further instructions.

t: How an archive joins an existing project
b: When a set or documents archive is brought into an existing project, its documents are added and linked to what exists in the project where there are matching names. Documents are added regardless of duplication of titles within the importing project; thus, re-importing an archive leads to duplicates of the documents. Group matching occurs based upon names while ignoring differences of upper/lower cases and whitespace around names. The documents inside a matched group are moved into the destination group. The matching occurs between codes of the same name residing in the same parent code without regard to upper/lower cases and surrounding whitespaces. Any codings, memos, or queries referring to the code are automatically changed to refer to the code of the importing project. The descriptions and colors of the codes remain as they are in the destination project, whereas the imported memos associated with the code are merged into it. Attribute match-ups take place between attributes with matching names within the code. A limited code is always added; if its document or set is not in the archive, it arrives as a code of the whole project. Attributes are matched by name. The attribute type of the destination project dominates when there are differences. Conversion of values according to the types happens, and unconvertible values are discarded. Sets are always added, regardless of whether a set of the same name already exists within the project, resulting in duplication.
