The conditions of the imported smart set are transformed in accordance with value conversions. Saved queries are added; the queries are tied to the document/set/tag they were saved for. Custom analyzers are universal among projects, and new ones are added and reside inside Window ▸ Analyzers. Consider the situation where your colleague, who has been researching the same debate you have, sends you Letters to the Editor.llz, which contains a set of four letters from her own project. Click “Climate Debate” in the sidebar and import the .llz file. The table below summarizes the impact on the archive’s group, codes, attribute, and set. In the archive In “Climate Debate” Result Group “Print” Group “Print” The letters from “Print” join the existing group. Code “deadlines”, under “Urgency” Code “Deadlines”, under “Urgency” Matched, since matching ignores case. Her codings now use your “Deadlines”. Code “Fear”, at the top level Code “Fear”, under “Emotions” Kept apart, because the parents differ. A new top-level code “Fear” is added. Code “Adaptation” No such code Added. Attribute “Readership”, type Text, with the values 120000, 45000, 310000, and about 80000 “Readership”, type Integer The values 120000, 45000, and 310000 arrive as numbers. about 80000 is text, so it is left out, and that letter's “Readership” stays empty. Set “Letters to the Editor” No such set Added, with the four letters. Now, “Climate Debate” contains 19 documents, while your codebook includes two codes entitled “Fear” appearing at separate points. The letters with 120,000 and 310,000 readers also join “Wide Reach”, giving it eight total. If both codes mean the same thing, merge them according to Merging codes in . Fill out the missing “Readership” figure in Document Properties.

A .llz file is a ZIP file. Unzipping it allows you to view its contents manually. An archive will import into the version of LemmaLoom that generated it or newer versions thereof (refer to The exchange dialog earlier in this chapter). If you plan on exchanging archives with your colleagues, it's helpful for everyone to stay updated to the latest version of LemmaLoom.

REFI-QDA project files (.qdpx) are ZIP files containing a project descriptor called project.qde (XML), along with documents kept in a directory named sources. Project files allow you to share your projects with anyone whose software supports the REFI-QDA format, and to load such a colleague’s project into LemmaLoom. LemmaLoom-specific data such as indexing, saved queries, dictionaries, and analyzers travel only in a LemmaLoom archive. Some common elements use distinct terminology under the REFI-QDA standard: REFI-QDA LemmaLoom Source Document Selection A passage, usually one that is coded Note Memo Variable Attribute Case LemmaLoom writes one unnamed case per document, holding its attribute values; a named case from another program becomes a set. Set A set of documents, or a set of codes

In the sidebar, click the project, for example “Climate Debate”. Choose File ▸ Export ▸ REFI-QDA Project. The save dialog suggests the project's name. Choose a folder, and click Save. When the dialog reads REFI-QDA Project Exported, click Done. Your file name is Climate Debate.qdpx. When looking for your import command, check for either REFI-QDA or QDPX in the other program. LemmaLoom saves your project like so: In LemmaLoom In the .qdpx file Text, PDF, and web page documents Text sources holding the documents' current text Audio and video documents Audio or video sources with the recording and the transcript. The transcript's timing is written as sync points, so codings stay tied to their place in the recording. Translations Sources of their own: text sources for translated text, and audio or video sources with their own copy of the recording for translated recordings. Authors, date, publication, publisher, URL, and DOI The source's description, one line per field, with the field names in the language of the interface, such as Date: 2024-08-21 Codes, with their hierarchy, colors, and descriptions The codebook Codings Coded selections, with the date each coding was made Memos on a passage Notes on the selection Coded memos (see Coded memos in ) Notes on the coding of the same code on that passage, or on the selection if the passage has no such coding Memos on a whole document, on a code, or on the project Notes on the source, the code, or the project Links Links between selections, with their colors. The relation becomes the link's name, and the comment a note. Attributes Variables. A Picker becomes a plain text variable. Attribute values One case per document, holding that document's values Sets and smart sets Sets of sources. A smart set is written with the documents it holds at the time of export. Groups Sets of sources, named after the group Code sets Sets of codes The file omits: Indexing and everything built on it, such as text statistics and word sketches (LemmaLoom will index the imported documents again); Saved queries, lenses based off the queries, dictionaries, custom analyzers, and bookmarks; Tags assigned to documents, codes, memos, and links; Document colors and languages, names of speakers in transcripts, and attribute values assigned to codings and memos; The connection between a translation and its original; The scope limitation of a code to a particular document or set, meaning that all such codes will become project codes upon import; The Format of a code, meaning that all codes will use Highlight upon import; Recordings exceeding 2 GB in size; such a document will be saved as a text source including only its transcript. The exported file records you as its author, under the full name of your macOS user account. The application LemmaLoom and its exact version are saved as well, as the creator of the project.

Choose File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Project. Choose the .qdpx file and click Open. When the import has finished, open two or three documents and check that the codings sit on the words they were made on. Double-clicking a .qdpx file within the Finder imports it in the exact same fashion. Importation creates a new project every time. It uses either the name within the file, if there is any, or just the file name. This newly created project will be the active project, and its documents get indexed in the background. You may monitor indexing progress via the Activity window. If need be, you may repeat the process by deleting the project and re-importing the .qdpx file. LemmaLoom reads the file as follows: In the .qdpx file In LemmaLoom Text sources Documents with the source's text. Formatting in rich text sources is dropped. PDF sources Documents with the PDF's text, from the text version the other program stored, or else read from the PDF itself Audio and video sources with a transcript Audio or video documents. The transcript becomes the text and its sync points become timed passages. The recording is copied into the library if the file contains it. Audio and video sources without a transcript, picture sources, and sources without any text, such as a scanned PDF without a text layer or a source the file refers to but does not contain Left out A source's description The document's authors, date, and other properties, if the description is in the form LemmaLoom exports, with the field names in English or in the language of your interface; otherwise a memo on the document Codes Codes for the whole project, with their hierarchy, colors, and descriptions Codings of selections Codings of the same passages, with their dates A coding of a whole source A coding of the document's entire text A selection's description A memo on the passage Notes A note on a selection becomes a memo on the passage, and a note on a coding a coded memo. Notes on a source or a code become memos on the document or the code. A note that belongs to nothing becomes a project memo, and a note on a link the link's comment. Links between selections Links. The link's name becomes the relation. Variables Attributes. Integer becomes Integer, Float Decimal, Boolean Boolean, Date and DateTime Date, and anything else Text. Cases Their values go to the documents that belong to them. A named case also becomes a set of those documents. Sets Sets of documents and code sets If there is an unnamed source, the title will become Imported document. When documents are missing after an import from another application, re-export the project from there and ensure the sources have been included in the exported file. The language of each document is determined based on its content. Incorrect determination can be fixed manually via Document Properties; LemmaLoom will then re-index the document according to the selected language (see Indexing in ). Since LemmaLoom can only code text, any codings for areas within a PDF file page or image are discarded. Selections are stored with references to where they begin and end, both measured in number of characters, usually along with an excerpt from the text within the selection. Different programs compute the character count differently; in some cases, a line break is counted as two characters. LemmaLoom attempts each common method and keeps the one in which the largest percentage of excerpts correspond correctly.
A REFI-QDA codebook file (.qdc) contains nothing more than a collection of codes, with their hierarchy, colors, and descriptions, and the code sets.

In the sidebar, click the project. Choose File ▸ Export ▸ REFI-QDA Codebook. The save dialog suggests the project's name. Choose a folder, and click Save. When the dialog reads REFI-QDA Codebook Exported, click Done. The codebook contains every single one of your codes organized hierarchically. Any code set containing codes will appear alongside its codes. A code restricted to one document or set is written like any other, without its restriction, and comes back as a code of the whole project.

Imported codes go into the active project. In the sidebar, click the project that should receive the codes. Choose File ▸ Import ▸ REFI-QDA Codebook. Choose the .qdc file and click Open. Double-clicking the .qdc file in the Finder will import the file similarly. For every code in the imported file, LemmaLoom searches among the siblings under the same parent for a matching code name regardless of capitalization. Should there be a match, the matching code is used, and the search proceeds with its children. Should there be no matches, a new code is created with its properties taken from the imported file. Matching code sets is performed in the same manner, adding to the matching code set the codes from the file that are new to it. Importing the file is performed in one undo step. By selecting Edit ▸ Undo REFI-QDA Codebook or pressing ⌘Z, all added codes and code sets are undone, and the added codes are taken out of existing code sets. For example, suppose a research group sends Climate Rhetoric.qdc, which has a code “Science” with the children “Uncertainty” and “Consensus”, a top-level code “Irony”, and a code set “Arguments” holding “Uncertainty” and “Consensus”. If it is imported into “Climate Debate”, LemmaLoom would make changes to the codebook as follows: The top-level code “Science” along with its child “Uncertainty” already exists within “Climate Debate”. The child “Consensus” of “Science” would be imported alongside “Uncertainty”. The top-level code “Irony” would be imported alongside the existing top-level codes. The code set “Arguments”, which contains the codes “Science”, “Uncertainty”, “Costs”, and “Responsibility”, would gain the new code “Consensus”.
Most tables may be exported as CSV files, while most charts and diagrams may be exported as PNG or PDF images.

The export button resembles a square with an arrow pointing upwards. This button appears in the heading of the table/chart, in the header of views on the project shelf, or in the bar of word sketches. The export button functions in either one of two ways: When beside a table not attached to any chart, clicking the button immediately opens the save dialog for a CSV format file. Hovering the mouse pointer over the button reveals Export as CSV. When beside a chart/diagram, clicking the button opens a menu showing PNG, PDF, and then CSV in cases where the chart has a table behind it. When hovered over, the button displays Export. Structure diagrams and the Mosaic are able to export PNG and PDF only. This button becomes visible upon the presence of anything that can be exported. In the Codings, Memos, and Links views of the project shelf, as well as in Relations and the word sketches’ bars, the button remains visible all the time. In these places, when there isn’t anything available for exporting, the button is disabled, showing Nothing to export. Inside the Attributes window and the Diagram window (see The Diagram window in ), the button carries the word Export. The export menu of the Code Matrix for “Climate Debate”. Exporting involves: Set up the view as you want it, with the codes, filter, search, and display you need. Click the export button, and choose a format if a menu opens. Change the suggested name if you like, choose a folder, and click Save. Suggested file names join the document, set, or project to what is exported, such as Running Out of Time-codings or Climate Debate-code-matrix. In some cases where grammar views are concerned, however, the file name reflects whatever word you searched on; e.g., collocates-climate or word-sketch-climate regarding the word climate. Your export will consist of everything visible in the view. Any search or filter conditions will transfer over, including the tag filter in your codebook and the Filter field of a query result. Disabled sectors in Sketch Space and your selected display are preserved as well.

A CSV file is a plain text file with comma-separated values. Each row has one value per column, separated by commas. The very first row contains the names of the columns in the language of the interface. The CSV file can be consumed by spreadsheet and statistical analysis applications. LemmaLoom exports its CSV files using the following formatting rules: All text in the file is UTF-8 encoded, beginning with a byte order mark so that spreadsheet applications will recognize the encoding. All numbers have plain digits and a decimal point, regardless of the locale you have chosen on your Mac computer, e.g., 1234.5. Columns whose name ends with (%) contain percentages represented numerically as portions of 100, e.g., 12.35 for 12.35%. Any cell containing commas, double quotes, or line breaks, or leading or trailing spaces is enclosed by double quotes to meet the standard for CSV formatting. Any cells starting with =, +, -, or @ which cannot be parsed as numbers are prefixed with an apostrophe so that spreadsheet applications will not interpret the value incorrectly, such as taking a memo like + check the figures against the report for a formula. An exception applies for the statistics of the Overview facet found in the Text tab of the inspector, whose CSV file stores all values as shown in the inspector, including the unit label if applicable. For example, a value will read 13.9 words. Should a spreadsheet application set to a language having commas for decimal separators, such as German, expect semicolons to separate columns, and put entire rows in a single cell, open the CSV file using the application's command for importing text/csv files and select the comma as the delimiter.

An image will be rendered anew for the file. You get margins, background color matching the current theme, and width determined by your graph. No hover highlight or selections here. The PNG format is rendered at Retina quality regardless of your monitor. PNG is suited for presentations, websites, and documents made by word processing software. PDF is just one page with dimensions equivalent to your graph size. Everything in a PDF is crisply rendered regardless of zoom level. It suits printing and academic journals requiring vector graphics. Images created with a dark theme are also dark in appearance. If you wish to use your image in a paper, change the theme setting to something lighter, like Light, prior to exporting (see Themes in ).

The export button of query results appears on the far right side of the query results bar, above the actual query results. Within the Query facet of a document, the export button will appear inside the bar on the very top of the facet. The available formats are CSV, Markdown, PNG, and PDF. Following them is Copy. The suggested file name is the name of your query itself. A Markdown file keeps the result together with the query, the scope of the query, how many documents were read, the Corpus setting used for the query, the date of the export, and the LemmaLoom version. The export menu of the Keywords results for “Activists” compared with “Skeptics”, listing CSV, Markdown, PNG, PDF, and Copy. Copy places the table onto the clipboard with tab characters delimiting the column values. The files produced from exporting your query results are discussed more thoroughly in Exporting results in .

In the views of the project shelf, for a project, set, or tag: View Place Formats Columns of the CSV file Codebook The bar below the code list CSV Code, Path, Level, Count, Description, Color Codebook USE IN THIS SCOPE, in the details of a selected code PNG, PDF, CSV Document, Segments Codings Header CSV Document, Code, Text, Start, End, then one column per attribute on the codings Memos Header CSV Document, Code, Memo, Tags, Start, End, then one column per attribute on the memos Links Header CSV Source document, Source text, Relation, Target document, Target text, Comment, Tags Code Stats Header PNG, PDF, CSV Code, Segments, Documents, Characters, Coverage (%) Code Stats Each chart under Attribute Breakdowns PNG, PDF, CSV Attribute, Value, Count Code Matrix Header PNG, PDF, CSV Code, then one column per document or group, and Total Relations Header, with Grid chosen PNG, PDF, CSV Code, Segments, then one column per code Relations Header, with Pairs chosen CSV Code, Code, Overlaps, Characters, φ, p Word Sketch As in the inspector PNG, PDF, CSV As in the inspector Dictionaries Category Frequencies and By Document PNG, PDF, CSV See Exporting the counts in  Queries The results bar CSV, Markdown, PNG, PDF, Copy See Exporting results in  The same export functionality exists in the Codebook window, the Word Sketch window, Window ▸ Queries, and query results opened in a window of their own. From the Attributes window, Export outputs the attribute table (see Attribute values below). Both Start and End within exported files indicate the location of a passage as character counts from the beginning of the document's text. Location specifies which paragraph and sentence number that passage occurs within according to its display on the inspector; therefore, ¶12·3 represents the third sentence of paragraph 12. Exporting a Code Matrix grouped by an attribute, a group, a language, or a format creates one column for each group, followed by Total and columns for the test used. Its first row indicates the base for each group. Exporting tables and charts in  explains what kind of file gets generated by this feature, while Testing the differences between groups explains the meaning of its numbers.

Every code shown in the list appears in the codebook's CSV file, each on a separate row, followed by its children. These are sorted alphabetically at each level. An excerpt of the beginning of the file for “Climate Debate” follows: Code Path Level Count Description Color Costs Costs 1 19 Prices, bills, subsidies and budgets: what climate policy or climate damage costs and where the bill lands. #4F46E5 Emotions Emotions 1 6 Feelings writers express or attribute to others, such as grief, despair, anger or tiredness. #DB2777 Fear Emotions / Fear 2 12 Fear and anxiety about climate change, and arguments about whether fear helps or harms. #E11D48 Hope Emotions / Hope 2 11 Hope and confidence that change is possible, and how writers frame them. #9333EA Responsibility Responsibility 1 19 Who caused the problem, who should act or pay, and what is owed to others, including future generations. #65A30D Science Science 1 15 Appeals to research, measurements, models and experts, and arguments about how science works. #0D9488 Path concatenates the names of codes from the top level down, separated by slashes, allowing you to distinguish codes with identical names but existing under distinct parent codes. Level indicates at which hierarchy level a particular code exists; 1 means a top-level code, 2 means children of those codes, etc. Count represents the numeric value shown next to each code in the tree view, which refers to how many times the code has been used within the original documents of the project, set, or tag whose codebook you export. For “Emotions”, it only includes the 6 occurrences of “Emotions” itself, not “Fear” or “Hope”, which each have their own count values (12 and 11 respectively). The export beside Code System in the Codes facet of the inspector has identical columns. Count here, however, counts the usage within the currently opened document along with coded memos.

Linking is performed between two passages, usually from different documents (see Links in ). An exported CSV file contains one row for every link: Source document Source text Relation Target document Target text Comment Tags The Models Keep Missing Clouds alone probably hide more uncertainty than any press release will admit. contradicts Heat Wave Report 2024 This estimate carries a wide margin of uncertainty and should not be cited without it. The agency states its margin of uncertainty plainly; the column assumes official sources hide it.  Relation refers to the wording that was entered while creating the link. Tags refers to a list of all tags associated with the link, separated by semicolons; in this case, Tags is blank. Exporting from the Links view of the project shelf will yield all links listed in the project, set, or tag selected. The Links facet of the inspector will export the links of the opened document.

The project shelf view of Codings exports a row for every coding made. Where the values of attributes on codings were recorded, those attributes will become additional columns, blank when a coding does not contain a value. In comparison, the project shelf view of Memos operates similarly, except here the memo's text and tags replace coded text. The name of the code of a coded memo becomes part of the Code column in a row, and the column remains blank whenever a non-coded memo contributes to the spreadsheet. The code's tags get inherited by a coded memo, meaning they fill out the Tags cell in a memo row, while a memo's own tags can be captured using the Codings facet of the inspector, with Memos chosen. In a project's Memos view, memos which exist independently of documents receive a row, with the Document column empty.

To open the Attributes window, go to Project ▸ Attributes or, alternatively, right-click on the project and select Attributes. Export will save the table content as displayed, including a Document column and each attribute as its own separate column. Each row represents each document that remains visible through your search, in order of display. Translations share the same row as the original, along with its attribute values. The Attributes window of “Climate Debate” with six documents selected, showing Import and Export in the toolbar. The file takes the format required by the Import function in the window. If you need to update many values at once, export the table contents, edit the contents in a spreadsheet program, then re-import them (see Importing attribute values from a spreadsheet in ).

Changes made via LemmaLoom are immediately saved upon making the modification, and the history of said modifications is tracked accordingly. Undoing these changes can be done via Edit ▸ Undo, one at a time, working backwards through the history in reverse chronological order until the desired point has been reached. Pretty much everything within a project may be undone, including the deletion of documents and auto-coding a whole set of documents. In cases involving the deletion of a project, document, or code, or the merging of two codes, LemmaLoom asks for confirmation. Most other things (such as groups, sets, tags, attributes, dictionaries, and analyzers) are deleted instantly without prompting. Accidental deletions can be reverted using Edit ▸ Undo. Projects are deleted permanently, while importing and/or translating documents erases portions of the history. What cannot be undone outlines these instances further down in this chapter. This guide's examples use “Climate Debate”, which is explained fully in The example project in . For practice purposes, the project may be imported with File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project.

A step is one instance of an action captured by LemmaLoom. Its name, which the Edit menu shows, identifies which command caused the change; examples include Apply Code and Delete Document. A single coding constitutes one step, while running Auto Code (see Coding passages automatically in ) to create two hundred codings and four new codes also counts as one step. Undo history refers to all steps available for undoing changes. Every individual window maintains its own separate undo history (see Which window a step belongs to later on in this chapter).

Click the window where you made the change, so that it is the active window. For most changes, this is the main window. If the cursor is in a text field, click outside it. Open the Edit menu. The first item names the step that will be undone, for example Undo Apply Code. Choose the item, or press ⌘Z. The Edit menu after a passage in “Hope Takes Work” has been coded with “Fear”. If you wish to take multiple steps back in history, select Undo from the menu again. Every successive selection will reveal what the name of the next step is in history. Pressing ⌘Z quickly several times will reverse those actions sequentially. Once nothing remains to undo, the command changes its name to Undo, and the interface disables it. An Undo reverts all elements affected by the particular action. This means that, when performing Undo Delete Document, the document returns, including all the text, codings, memos, links, bookmarks, attribute values, and place in every set. When undoing results in the restoration of text content, LemmaLoom will index the text content again in the background (see Indexing a document again in ). See Window ▸ Activity (⌥⌘0) to track the indexing progress.

When you undo something, there will always be an option in the Edit menu to redo what was done, like Redo Apply Code. Click this menu option, or hit ⇧⌘Z on your keyboard. You can redo as many actions as you undid, starting from the last undone action. Your redo options persist only until you make another change in the same window. If, for instance, you code another passage, you lose the steps you undid for good, and Redo is disabled. The Edit menu after the deletion of “Carbon Tax Debate” has been undone. Undo names the step before it, and Redo names the deletion.

Say you're working on “Hope Takes Work” in the main window. You've coded a passage with “Fear”. In the Details facet of the inspector's Text tab, you've changed the “Outlet” attribute of the essay from “The Weekly Ledger” to The Northern Herald. Finally, you deleted “Carbon Tax Debate”. This table outlines what options appear in the Edit menu after each action, and after the undos and redos that follow. The Details facet of “Hope Takes Work” while the “Outlet” attribute is being changed to The Northern Herald. No. What you do Undo item Redo item 1 Code a passage with “Fear” Undo Apply Code Redo (disabled) 2 Select “The Weekly Ledger” in the “Outlet” field, type The Northern Herald, then click in the reader Undo Set Value Redo (disabled) 3 Delete “Carbon Tax Debate” Undo Delete Document Redo (disabled) 4 Press ⌘Z Undo Set Value Redo Delete Document 5 Press ⌘Z Undo Apply Code Redo Set Value 6 Press ⇧⌘Z Undo Set Value Redo Delete Document 7 Code another passage with “Hope” Undo Apply Code Redo (disabled) “Carbon Tax Debate” makes a return to the project following row 4. Following row 5, “Outlet” becomes “The Weekly Ledger”, while The Northern Herald returns via row 6. Since row 7's coding is new, Redo is disabled, and “Carbon Tax Debate” remains within the project. Row 2 consists of just one step despite your entering 19 characters. The reason is covered below in Values typed into attribute fields.

Each command counts as one step, however much it changes. For example: Delete Documents with six documents selected counts as one step. Likewise, deleting “Running Out of Time” will delete “Running Out of Time (German)” in the same step, since the latter is a translation of the former. Similarly, Save within Document Properties counts as one step, regardless of how many of the document's properties (such as name, tags, attribute values, or language) you changed. An Auto Code run counts as one step; Undo will reverse any codings added during the execution of that command and also delete any codes created by the command. If you click Stop before the command completes execution, Undo will reverse everything performed until that point. Similarly, Bookmark Hits… and Add to Dictionary found in a query's Actions menu, and Import in the Attributes window, each count as one step each time they are invoked, applying to all items they generate. Undoing a command also reverses changes it made elsewhere. When coding a passage in “Running Out of Time”, LemmaLoom performs the equivalent coding on “Running Out of Time (German)”. Undoing Apply Code reverses the changes in both documents.

Text attribute field contents in the Details facet of the inspector's Text tab and in the Attributes window are autosaved as you type into them, while non-text contents are autosaved as soon as they are entered. LemmaLoom organizes all changes made to the same field within a given document as part of a single Set Value step, provided no other step comes between them. Typing The Northern Herald into “Outlet” creates a single step that Edit ▸ Undo Set Value will reverse to restore its initial state prior to entering your text. Changing “Stance” creates another step. Finishing where you started (for example, typing something and deleting it) removes the entire step from the history. This applies also to attribute field values of codings and memos, found within the Codings facet of the inspector's Coding tab. To undo the whole value at once, click elsewhere first, then choose Edit ▸ Undo Set Value.

Deleting multiple documents, auto-coding a set, and importing a codebook take some time. Your current step is only displayed in the Edit menu after it has completed. Until it finishes, ⌘Z will undo the previous step. Before performing an undo action, make sure that the last deleted document has left the navigation sidebar, that the Auto Code dialog displays Done, or that the Importing REFI-QDA Codebook dialog is closed.

t: Which window a step belongs to
b: Each window in LemmaLoom maintains a history. This applies to your main window, your Codebook window, your Document window (from Open in New Window), and any Queries, Query Results, Analyzers, Tags, and Attributes window you might be working on. When creating a new instance of the main window via File ▸ New Window, you'll end up with yet another separate history to track changes. Commands such as Edit ▸ Undo and Edit ▸ Redo are confined to the currently active window. A step belongs to the window that was active when the change began. After renaming the tag “viral” in the Tags window, click the Tags window before choosing Edit ▸ Undo Rename Tag. Changes that occur in response to actions initiated from a dialog belong to the window the dialog opened from. Your Document Properties dialog keeps its changes in history within the main window; reverse those changes with Edit ▸ Undo inside the main window once the dialog has closed. The code palette, similarly, keeps its changes in history in whatever window you opened it from. Any dialogs opened from the Attributes window keep their changes in history in that window. Background operations belong to the window they originated from regardless of which window is active upon completion. Initiating an Auto Code run in the main window means that it would be placed in the history of the main window. The history in your main window covers all of your projects. Once you've coded a passage within “Climate Debate”, then switched projects, and pressed ⌘Z, the coding is undone in your initial project while the second project stays active. If you wish to observe your undone changes, switch back first. The Codebook window of “Climate Debate” as the active window. Its Edit menu offers to undo the change just made to the code “Costs”. In a situation where you edit a particular element twice in two windows, such as editing the code “Costs” first in the Codebook window and then in the Codes facet in the main window, you would need to undo the second edit before the first, in the window where you made it. Otherwise, an edit undone in one window could reappear upon undoing in the other window.
For every table, the rightmost column will contain the name after Undo or Redo in the Edit menu.

For recordings, timing of transcripts gets restored, as well as alignments for documents containing translations. For more detail on this topic, refer to Undoing an edit in . Undone changes made in Document Properties affecting the language and/or Exclude from indexing patterns cause indexing to take place. For additional information about analyzers, refer to .

Deleting a project is a final action, and it also removes the steps regarding the project, its documents, or attributes from every window's history. If you need a backup copy you could restore, export the project first with File ▸ Export ▸ LemmaLoom Project (see ).

Importing a text file, PDF document, web page, or recording clears most earlier steps for that project from every window once the new document arrives. Steps in other projects stay, and so do changes to custom analyzers. Suppose you have previously deleted “Carbon Tax Debate” and merged “Deadlines” into “Urgency”, but now you are importing another PDF file into the same project. The deletion of “Carbon Tax Debate” and the merging of “Deadlines” into “Urgency” are irreversible after this import. Reverse whatever steps you wish before importing. Should you decide to remove the imported document from your project, delete it, and that deletion itself can be undone. For additional details on importing documents, refer to Importing documents in . To remove what a REFI-QDA project, a LemmaLoom archive, or the example project brought in, delete either the whole project or the documents it added. Two imports are steps you can undo, REFI-QDA Codebook and Import Attributes (see the tables above).

As soon as your translation (see ) finishes and appears below its source document, LemmaLoom will prune all earlier steps related to your source document from every window's history. This includes the steps for any codings, links, bookmarks, and attribute values in your original document, as well as any edits and changes made to it. If you decide that you don't need a particular translation anymore, delete the translation document like you would any other, and the deletion can be undone.

The history stores all modifications done to the content of your projects. The changes listed below take effect immediately upon being made, and you revert these modifications by changing them back: the modifications done via LemmaLoom ▸ Settings…, including the theme choice, appearance settings for the reader, and color customization of lenses; adding or removing projects in Favorites; which tabs are open, which lenses are enabled, which codes are hidden in the reader, the inspector tab, and panes' dimensions.

⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z undo and redo your typing just like in any other macOS program when your cursor is inside a text field, such as the code editor's Name field, memo text, a name you're typing in the sidebar, or search bars. Inside the text field, the Edit menu reads Undo Typing. After leaving the field, ⌘Z operates again in LemmaLoom's history. Steps occur only upon confirming whatever text you enter. Confirming means clicking Save in a dialog (or hitting Return or clicking elsewhere while naming). Escape while naming, or Cancel within the dialog, cancels out the typing. Commands such as Index Now, Run, and Remove Output in Document Properties take place immediately. Within the Edit Attribute dialog which appears from the code editor, the Save button does too, making everything that went into editing this attribute into a single Edit Attribute step. All these steps stay even if you click Cancel afterwards. This pattern holds for the document text editor. When making edits, ⌘Z undoes your typing. Hitting Save results in the total edit being an Edit Text step, and Cancel discards it. This is discussed in greater detail in Editing and saving in . The exception to this rule is attribute values, since their fields automatically save whatever value you enter (see Values typed into attribute fields earlier in this chapter).

Your history continues until you exit LemmaLoom. If you close your last open window, LemmaLoom will exit. However, closing any window means the end of that window's history. Upon opening LemmaLoom again, Edit ▸ Undo will remain disabled until something has changed within your current session. If a document containing a media recording gets deleted, LemmaLoom stores the audio/video recording for future undo purposes. This recording will be permanently deleted on the subsequent startup of LemmaLoom (refer to Where work is stored in ).

Command Shortcut Where it works Edit ▸ Undo ⌘Z In any window with a step to undo Edit ▸ Redo ⇧⌘Z After an undo, until you make a new change All the available keyboard shortcuts in LemmaLoom are listed in .

The Settings refer to options that are applicable throughout the entire LemmaLoom application. This includes the theme, language of the interface, transcription model, personal exclusion patterns, reader presentation, and color and style of four lenses. However, the language of individual documents, lenses of a document, and excluded text in documents all fall outside of the scope of this definition.

To access Settings, choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… or hit ⌘,. On the left sidebar of Settings are listed three panes, namely General (gear icon), Reader (book icon), and Lenses (icon of a circle on a square). The first time you access Settings after LemmaLoom launches, the General pane will appear. Pane Sections What they set General Appearance, Language, Transcription, Exclusion Presets The theme, the interface language, the speech recognition model, and your own patterns for leaving text out of analysis Reader Typography, Page, Selection, Preview The reader's font, text size, and layout, the paragraph and sentence numbers beside the text, and how selections and audio playback are shown Lenses Word class, Grammatical function, Phrase, Morphology The color and style of each aspect of these four lenses The changes you make to the settings take effect immediately in the Settings window and in every open document, except in the case of the interface language setting, which takes effect on your next launch of LemmaLoom. Resizing the window by dragging its edges helps you make space when you have a large pane, for example the Lenses pane. If the pane height exceeds that of the window, the extra part is scrollable. Settings changes take effect immediately (see ). Reverting a change entails selecting its previous state or clicking a reset button, such as Reset All to Defaults at the top of the Reader and Lenses panes. For all other settings, this chapter gives the default values. The General pane of Settings.

Theme refers to the set of colors used for the entire app interface. Theme controls whether your windows are light or dark, the colors of your window bars and side panels, the paper color and ink color of the reader, and many other things. Your accent color, which determines the color of active selections like the selected Settings sidebar pane or the Scroll with audio button while it is on, is determined by your theme as well. There are eleven themes available in LemmaLoom: Theme Light or dark Colors System follows macOS the standard macOS colors, light or dark as macOS is set Light light the standard light macOS colors, even when macOS is dark Dark dark the standard dark macOS colors, even when macOS is light Cream light dark brown text on warm off-white, with a brown accent Solarized Light light gray-blue text on pale cream, beige bars, a blue accent Solarized Dark dark pale gray text on deep blue-green, a blue accent High Contrast light black text on white, black dividing lines, a deep blue accent High Contrast Dark dark white text on black, white dividing lines, a yellow accent Protanopia follows macOS the standard macOS colors, lens and code colors adjusted for red-blind vision, a blue accent Deuteranopia follows macOS the standard macOS colors, lens and code colors adjusted for green-blind vision, a blue accent Tritanopia follows macOS the standard macOS colors, lens and code colors adjusted for blue-blind vision, an orange-red accent The theme you start with is System, which automatically toggles between light and dark modes depending on the mode of macOS, including when the macOS appearance is set to Auto. System, Light, and Dark use the accent color provided by macOS for LemmaLoom, which defaults to violet-blue but could be different depending on your settings at System Settings ▸ Appearance. All other themes always use their own accent. To change the theme: Choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,) and click General. Under Appearance, open the Theme menu. Choose a theme. All windows change simultaneously, including the Settings window. Projectors fade light colors easily. With High Contrast selected on a projector display, the panels, lists, and dividers remain visible while the reader displays the same as in Light. The Theme menu open in the General pane.

A theme modifies the appearance of the following elements on every LemmaLoom window, including the Glossary and Analyzers windows: Elements rendered by macOS, such as scroll bars and text fields, are light or dark with the theme regardless of macOS settings. The window's background and the band along its top assume the bar color according to the current theme. When using Cream, Solarized Light, and Solarized Dark, these colors will gradually transition between shades from top to bottom. Paper and text colors in the reader follow the theme, as listed under Reader colors in . In the reader, High Contrast looks the same as Light, and High Contrast Dark the same as Dark. Text selection highlight and the insertion point in text fields adopt either the accent color of the theme or, in System, Light, and Dark, the selection color of macOS. Headers of tables in the five themes with their own colors appear with the bar color, header lines assume the divider color of the theme, and rows alternate between two background shades. Dialogs, including Document Properties and Import Document, inherit paper and text colors from the current theme. The code editor within Window ▸ Analyzers changes its colors to correspond with the selected light/dark scheme according to the active theme. In full screen, the toolbar at the top of the screen displays with bar colors according to the active theme choice. The main window in the Solarized Dark theme, with “Running Out of Time” open and the Word class lens enabled.

Your codes and dictionary categories keep their colors in every theme except Protanopia, Deuteranopia, and Tritanopia, which adjust them for display. So do the aspects of a lens whose color you changed in the Lenses pane. The default color palette of the lens aspects comes from macOS itself, using standard macOS colors that become a little bit brighter in dark themes. After selecting a color (whether it be changing an aspect's color or choosing the color it already had), the choice remains constant. Resetting an aspect's color from the Lenses pane makes it adjust again. When switching between light and dark themes, check that your own colors read well on both. For instance, a light yellow color readable against the background of Solarized Dark fades away into obscurity against the stark white background of High Contrast.

Menus, windows, and messages in LemmaLoom can be displayed in English, German, or Mainland Simplified Chinese. With System Default, the setting you start with, the system decides which one based on the priority listed under System Settings ▸ General ▸ Language & Region. When none of these languages are found in that list, then LemmaLoom reverts to English. For selecting a language for the interface of LemmaLoom specifically, see below: Choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,) and click General. Under Language, open the Interface language menu and choose English, Deutsch, or 简体中文. System Default follows macOS again. Click Quit LemmaLoom, below the note Quit and reopen LemmaLoom for a language change to take effect. Open LemmaLoom again. The Language section of the General pane with Deutsch chosen, the note about quitting and reopening, and Quit LemmaLoom. Each language is listed under its own name. The interface language refers to the language that the menus, label texts, messages, names of lenses and their aspects, Glossary, and sample texts shown in the preview of the Reader pane use. As each document is indexed based on the language it is written in, even if you have the German interface language set, the English documents of “Climate Debate” are still indexed as being English. How LemmaLoom determines the language of each document is covered in How LemmaLoom decides the language in . If you choose an interface language in this menu, the Translate dialog also proposes translating a document into that language first. For example, with Deutsch chosen, it would suggest translating an English article entitled “Net Zero Will Cost You” into German (see The Translate dialog in ). It decides the example project language. With File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project, LemmaLoom gives you “Climate Debate” with the English interface language, “Klimadebatte” with German, and “气候辩论” with Chinese (see The example project in ). Any copy previously imported into LemmaLoom retains its language.

Once you import an audio or video file, LemmaLoom automatically transcribes it for you using a speech recognition model (see How transcription works in ). Choosing which model to use is done via the Model menu under Transcription: Model Notes Apple Speech The setting you start with, and the fastest Whisper Large v3 Turbo The faster of the two Whisper models Whisper Large v3 Slower, and sometimes a little more accurate on difficult recordings Whisper is used for Chinese recordings even if you choose Apple Speech, since Whisper quality is better. Switching which model is being used impacts the next recording imported. To test whether or not switching models would improve your results, try importing a short, difficult excerpt of audio using both models and comparing the transcripts side-by-side.

When importing a document or modifying its Document Properties, you may choose to ignore certain text patterns so as to prevent any kind of grammar analysis from occurring within them. Such patterns may involve timestamps, speaker labels, and many more forms of text (see Excluding text from indexing in ). These patterns are expressed through regular expressions, which are concise representations of a form of text, such as any word surrounded by square brackets. There are five default presets in the Presets menu beside the field for entering your pattern. An exclusion preset consists of a personally defined pattern, which is assigned its own name and stored inside the previously mentioned Presets menu. Suppose that you had several transcripts typed out of radio conversations where pauses, laughter, and inaudible statements were transcribed with [pause], [laughs], and [inaudible], respectively (the notes should stay in the text, but are not actual speech). You could use these steps to create an exclusion preset for these three notes. Choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,) and click General. Under Exclusion Presets, click Add Preset. A new row appears with two empty fields. In the Name field, type Transcriber notes. This is the name the Presets menu shows. In the Pattern field, type [(inaudible|laughs|pause)]. On the line below the field is a description of what the entered regular expression matches, e.g., Matches text like [inaudible]. If the regular expression provided does not allow LemmaLoom to generate a sample text string that would match it, the line will say Valid pattern. An invalid pattern will feature faulty syntax, for example an unmatched bracket. An invalid pattern returns a response saying Not a valid pattern in red font. Backslashes are used to match square brackets literally while the bars serve to provide alternatives within the parenthetical group. By inserting |crosstalk within the parentheses, you would match [crosstalk] as well. This particular pattern is case-sensitive and hence will only match [laughs] in lowercase. The preset saves itself as you type. It shows up in the Presets menu on the import dialogs (Import Document, or Import from Web for a web page) and in Document Properties, right after the five default presets with a line between the two sets. The Exclusion Presets section of the General pane, with the Transcriber notes preset. The Presets menu of the Import Document dialog, with the five default presets. If the name and pattern of the preset are entered, an entry is added to the Presets menu. If the name or pattern does not exist yet, the entry stays in Settings until it is completed or deleted. When selecting a preset from the Presets menu, the pattern for that preset is copied to the document. Any preset whose pattern has been copied to the document is disabled in the Presets menu; changing those patterns would require editing each document's properties separately (Document Properties). Choosing a preset with an invalid pattern will result in indexing the whole document. Check the line under your pattern before choosing a preset. To delete a preset entry, click the little minus sign next to the entry (Remove preset). The entry disappears at once.

The Reader pane controls how the reader presents text. The first two sections of the pane are the Typography and Page sections, which contain the same options as the Font, gutter, and text size menu found in the title band of the reader (see The title band in ). The View ▸ Larger Text (⌘+), Smaller Text (⌘-), and Reset Text Size (⌘0) commands affect the exact same text size, and a change in one place shows in the others. Section Row Choices Starts as Typography Font System Serif, System Sans, System Rounded, System Mono, Georgia, Palatino, Baskerville, Times New Roman, Helvetica Neue, Avenir Next, Menlo System Serif Typography Text Size a slider from 70 to 200 percent, in steps of 10 100 percent Page Layout Single Column, Two-Page Spread Single Column Page Gutter Numbering Off, Paragraphs, Sentences, Both Both The gutter is the column that appears on the left side of your text, where the reader numbers the paragraphs and sentences of the document (see The gutter in ). The curved arrow icon next to the text size percentage, Reset, resets the text to its default size of 100%. At 100%, the curved arrow is disabled, and hovering the mouse pointer over it shows Already default. To learn about fonts, sizes, layouts, and gutter numbers, see Changing how text is presented in . Click Reset All to Defaults, which is located at the top of the pane, to reset every row of the pane at once to its initial value.

The Selection section determines how the reader displays your selections, as well as how it handles the rest of the text surrounding your selections. Row Choice What you see Selected Text Solid block A rounded block in the text color, with the selected words in the paper color  Highlight A light tint behind the selected words Head and Dependents Arcs A curved line from the selected word to its head and to each dependent, with a small arrowhead at the dependent's end  Lines The same connections drawn as square brackets above the text  Labels The name of each relation above the related word  Highlight The head tinted yellow and the dependents pale violet  Off The selection alone Surrounding Text Fade The rest of the document dimmed around the sentences that hold the selection  Light fade The same, dimmed less  Highlight sentence The sentence with the selected word tinted  Off The whole document as usual Audio Playback Spotlight Everything except the passage being played dimmed  Solid block The passage being played on a block of the accent color  Highlight The passage being played tinted lightly with the accent color The first option in every row is the default. The Reader pane with Arcs chosen under Head and Dependents and the Surrounding Text menu open. Head and Dependents applies when a single word has been selected. Head refers to the word that the current word belongs to within the grammatical structure of the sentence; for example, it can be the verb whose subject the selected word is. The dependents of the word are all the words attached to it. More about relations between words and their classifications can be found in . All arcs, lines, and labels are colored according to the Grammatical function lens defaults. In Preview, which can be seen at the bottom of the pane, the passage is displayed as The old fox watched the quiet river. and fox is selected. The word watched is the head of fox since fox is its subject. The dependents of fox are The and old. When Labels is chosen, the preview will show labels above watched (▲ nsubj, nominal subject), above The (det, determiner), and above old (amod, adjectival modifier). Labels represent the relationship between each word and fox in terms of grammatical functions, and the ▲ shows the head. German documents use other labels. For example, nsubj becomes sb. With Surrounding Text, you also control how a passage is shown when navigating to it, for example, via a query hit. If you pick Light fade or Fade, the surrounding text fades out; with Highlight sentence or Off, the passage gets highlighted in light yellow instead. Audio Playback applies only when the reader follows a recording (Scroll with audio toggle on in the player bar; see Following the transcript in ). Depending on the selected setting for Surrounding Text, Spotlight fades the rest of the text more or less. Light fade reduces the fading effect, and the other options fade as much as Fade.

At the bottom of the pane is where you will see Preview, which shows you two brief snippets of text that have been styled according to your preferences (font, text size, and theme). The first snippet contains a selected word with its head and all its dependents. The second snippet contains the text as it looks when you play it. Both change as you change the rows above, and their text is in the interface language. The Reader pane with Labels chosen under Head and Dependents, and the preview below.

A lens annotates your documents’ words, categorizing based on something like word class (refer back to ). Aspects are categories of a particular lens, like Noun under Word class. In the Lenses pane, the colors and styles for each aspect for four built-in lenses are configured. This pane becomes helpful in cases where two aspects appear similar visually, or when working simultaneously with multiple lenses. There is a distinct section for each of the four lenses in the Lenses pane: Section Rows Style at the start Word class Noun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, Pronoun, Determiner, Preposition, Conjunction, Number, Interjection Underline Grammatical function Subject, Object, Predicative, Complement, Adjectival, Adverbial, Appositive, Agent, Conjunct, Connector Underline Phrase Noun phrase, Verb phrase, Prepositional phrase, Adjective phrase, Adverb phrase, Conjunction phrase, Interjection, Noun chunk Highlight Morphology 20 rows, each named after a feature and one of its values, from Tense: Past to Gender: Neuter Highlight The Morphology rows include Tense, Number, Degree, Verb form, Case, Mood, and Gender. Case, Mood, and Gender appear only in German documents, whereas the Morphology lens operates on both English and German documents. Words display only one morphological feature, which means that a German noun in the dative case displays just Case: Dative. See Morphology in  for more on this topic. In contrast, other built-in lenses, such as Modality and Cohesion, come with predetermined colors. However, dictionary, query, and analyzer lenses obtain their colors from their dictionaries, queries, and analyzers, respectively. The aspect name, style menu, and color well are provided in each row along with a reset button once the aspect has been modified. Four different styles, accompanied by their respective icons, can be selected using the style menu. Style How an annotated word looks Highlight A pale band of the color behind the word Underline A line in the color under the word Text color The letters in the color Bold The letters in bold and in the color It’s the style itself that dictates whether the color will appear prominently enough. In Highlight, you’ll get a subtle wash of the color over the background, while a lighter color won’t necessarily stand out much at all. In Text color and Bold, the actual text characters will adopt the full force of the color, requiring it to contrast sharply against your theme’s paper. See also Lens colors and styles in .

The example project includes “Running Out of Time (German)”, which is the translation of “Running Out of Time” into German. It is useful for studying the dative case, which marks the indirect objects in German as well as the nouns following words like mit. Assuming you haven't imported “Climate Debate” already, import it via File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. Each of the cases begins as a pale highlight in the Morphology lens. To differentiate the datives, follow along: Choose LemmaLoom ▸ Settings… (⌘,) and click Lenses. Scroll down to the Morphology section and find the row Case: Dative. Open its style menu, which shows Highlight, and choose Bold. Click the color well (the color swatch) beside it. In the macOS color picker that opens, choose a dark red. Open “Running Out of Time (German)” and enable Morphology in the lens menu (see The lens menu in ). Datives are displayed in bold dark red now, whereas the rest of the cases retain their pale highlighting. Changes to Word class, Grammatical function, and Phrase aspects also apply to the Glossary (Help ▸ Glossary), as it displays each tag or term representing one of those aspects in that aspect's coloration and style. The default coloration of the lenslets in the legend above your text remains unchanged, and therefore the Case: Dative lenslet retains its orange appearance. These exact same procedures apply to any aspect of the four lenses. The style menu for Case: Dative open in the Morphology section of the Lenses pane.

Your modified aspects will receive a reset button, a curving arrow at the end of their rows. Clicking on the button resets them back to default colors and styles. Reset All to Defaults, which appears at the very top of the pane, resets all aspects in all four lenses. The reset is permanent.

Any changes you make within the Settings window affect only the Mac that you are working on. The library, containing your projects (see Where work is stored in ), will also retain your place within each project. Setting Kept Everything you choose in the Settings window on the Mac Scroll with audio, the size and position of the video, and whether it is collapsed on the Mac The divider between two documents in split view, the dividers inside analysis panels (such as the one between a query's builder and its results), and how word sketches are displayed on the Mac Favorite projects, the project you had open, the tabs each project had open, and each document's reading position, lenses, and inspector (whether it is shown, its width, and the active tab) in the library Your projects, along with favorites, opened tabs, and reading positions, are all portable to another Mac with the library or restorable from an older backup copy. Settings, on the other hand, are per-Mac, and so you should personalize your choices on each Mac, including themes, fonts, and lens styles, if you want them to match. When your coworker views the contents of your LemmaLoom archive or REFI-QDA project, everything is seen using their own Mac’s settings, namely the document appearance based on themes, fonts, and lens styles (see ).

The tables below list every keyboard shortcut in LemmaLoom, separated by menu. Where exactly each of these shortcuts applies is also noted. See Conventions in  for descriptions of modifier key symbols used throughout these menus. ⌘ refers to Command, ⇧ to Shift, ⌥ to Option, and ⌃ to Control. Keyboard shortcuts displayed here are for a US keyboard layout. If you are using a different keyboard layout, macOS may remap keyboard shortcuts such as ⇧⌘[ to keys available to you; the menu will reflect that change.

Every shortcut in LemmaLoom corresponds to a command displayed in the menu bar next to the keys needed for the action. Exceptions to this rule include Esc, Return, the arrow keys, and the Delete key (⌫), which act on whichever part of the window is currently being used (see Esc, Return, and the arrow keys later in this chapter). Some actions require you to click or scroll on something in addition to pressing a key (see Clicks with a modifier key later in this chapter). Lastly, the script editor found in the Analyzers window also has its own set of editing keyboard shortcuts (see ). Shortcuts always act on the active window. If the main window is active, commands for a document act on the document in the active tab. In split view, actions will affect the pane you clicked in last; this is known as the active pane (see The active pane in ). A shortcut works only while its command is available in the menu. Document ▸ Code (⇧⌘C), for example, stays disabled until you select a word or a passage in the reader. The last column of each table below says what a command needs. A few commands change their name with certain situations but retain the same keys. Additionally, some key combinations serve different functions depending on which window is being used: ⇧⌘B is either Bookmark, or Remove Bookmark when the selection overlaps a bookmark. ⇧⌘L is either Link, or Finish Link once a link has been started. ⇧⌘A is Auto Code… unless more than one of the enabled lenses has an option to auto code passages. When multiple such lenses are enabled, the key corresponds to the first of the commands named after them, e.g., Auto Code with Hedges…. ⇧⌘P switches between Play and Pause when playing recordings. ⌘W closes tabs (Close Tab) in the main window while a tab is open. Everywhere else, ⌘W corresponds to Close instead. ⌘⌫ deletes projects, sets, groups, or documents when selected in the navigation sidebar (Delete Project, Delete Set, Delete Group, Delete Document, or Delete Documents). It deletes all selected documents simultaneously when more than one is selected. Inside the Analyzers window, ⌘⌫ deletes analyzers from the list (Delete Analyzer) while the list is active. ⌘+, ⌘-, and ⌘0 increase/decrease/reset the text size (Larger Text, Smaller Text, Reset Text Size), but in the Diagram window they respectively zoom in/out and restore actual size (Zoom In, Zoom Out, Actual Size). ⌃⌘F is Enter Full Screen, or Exit Full Screen in full screen. When editing a document's text, Save (⌘Return) and Cancel (⌘.) take the place of Edit (⇧⌘E). While linking passages, Cancel Link (⌥⇧⌘L) becomes visible below Finish Link.

t: Esc, Return, and the arrow keys
b: Esc, Return, and the arrow keys work outside the menus, and what they do depends on where you are. The Esc key closes or clears what you are working in: In the reader, Esc will clear selections, leaving pending links alone. Should you change your mind about making a link, you could use Document ▸ Cancel Link (⌥⇧⌘L). In the search bar, Esc closes the bar and clears any active search. With Esc pressed in the code palette, you close that palette, retaining your current selection. For the Search Documents field and sidebar both, Esc clears the search results and displays all documents. In dialogs with a Cancel button, Esc triggers it. Lastly, should you happen to press Esc while renaming any of your projects, documents, sets, groups, or tags, you keep the old names. In split view, Esc in the reader affects only the active pane. Return accepts an input wherever needed, applies choices, or opens what you selected: With Return inside the search bar, you proceed to the next match of the search string (like ⌘G), whereas Return in the Search Documents field opens the first document found. From the sidebar, you may also click or press Return on a document to open it. In other lists, such as the Codebook, Codings, Memos, and Links views or the Tags window, a click selects an item, and a double-click or Return opens it. Inside the code palette, Return applies the highlighted entry (after typing in Search codes, the highlight goes to the very first remaining entry). If the selection already has the highlighted code, Return removes it. When operating a dialog with the cursor being outside all fields, or in a one-line field that does not handle Return itself, pressing Return clicks the highlighted button, such as Save or Auto Code; the fields in the items below handle Return themselves, even in a dialog. Renaming operations, including renaming a dictionary in the Dictionaries view, always accept Return or clicking elsewhere as confirmation of entered changes. Add a tag fields always accept Return or commas as tag separators. Add term fields in query text rules and dictionary categories accept Return to add the term. In a query, they will accept several terms separated by commas. After entering a new attribute name into its field, pressing Return adds the attribute. Return will add the entered pattern under Exclude from indexing in Import Document or Document Properties dialogs. Within Word fields of Word Sketch, Code Sketch, and Sketch Space, you get sketches of entered terms by pressing Return. Finally, inside the Analyzers window, Return clicks Save while you type in Name or a Label field. ↑ and ↓ move through the sidebar and the code palette: In the sidebar, ↑ and ↓ move through the available rows; pressing Return afterwards opens the newly selected document. With ↓ pressed inside the Search Documents field, you choose the first document from the results and move into the list. Within the code palette, ↑ and ↓ highlight successive entries in the palette, including Add Code “…” and In Vivo “…” at its end. In a category's table in the Dictionaries view, the Delete key (⌫) removes the selected terms. While Auto Code runs, the dialog's highlighted button is Stop, so hitting Return stops the run. Codings applied prior to that remain, and can be undone with Edit ▸ Undo Auto Code (⌘Z).

You select a passage via mouse or trackpad interaction, but nearly everything around it can be done from the keyboard. Suppose you are reading “Climate Debate” for passages about deadlines, with “Running Out of Time” and “Letter from the Climate Strike” open in tabs and “Running Out of Time” active. Feel free to import the example project with File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project to follow along. Press ⌥⌘3. The inspector shows its Coding tab. Press ⌘F and type retired. The reader goes to the only match, in the paragraph about the dates that leaders have promised. Press Esc to close the search bar. Select the sentence A deadline that falls after everyone in office has retired is not a deadline at all. Press ⇧⌘C. The code palette opens with the cursor in Search codes. Type dead. “Deadlines” is the only code left in the list. Press Return. “Deadlines” gets a checkmark, and the palette stays open. Press Esc to close the palette. The passage is still selected. Press ⇧⌘M. The New Memo dialog opens. Click in the Memo field and type a note such as Targets fall after their authors retire; compare Letter from the Climate Strike. Click Save. Press ⇧⌘] to go on to “Letter from the Climate Strike”. When applying a code to an incorrect passage, close the palette and hit ⌘Z. Edit ▸ Undo Apply Code takes the coding back. When the palette is active, hitting Return once more removes “Deadlines”. The code palette opened with ⇧⌘C in “Running Out of Time”, with dead typed in the search field and “Deadlines” as the only code left.

It is possible to define a keyboard shortcut for any menu command within any app in macOS. This allows you to quickly run commands you regularly execute, like Edit ▸ Query from Selection and Project ▸ Add Code. Additionally, you may redefine existing shortcuts to your liking. Open System Settings and click Keyboard. Click Keyboard Shortcuts…. Click App Shortcuts in the list on the left. Click the add button (+). Choose LemmaLoom as the application. As the menu title, type the command's name exactly as the menu shows it, such as Query from Selection. Click in the shortcut field and press keys that are still free (see All shortcuts by key earlier in this chapter), such as ⌃⌥⌘Q. Click Done. When assigning keys to an item whose name has an ellipsis, e.g., Auto Code…, type the ellipsis as a single character. On the US keyboard, this means pressing Option along with the semicolon key, rather than entering three periods. Some items occur twice in the application’s menus (for example, REFI-QDA Project is under both Import and Export). For this sort of case, you would need to input the whole path to the command with the separator -> in between menus, e.g., File->Export->REFI-QDA Project. Once saved, the shortcut appears next to the command in LemmaLoom's menu. If it does not, quit LemmaLoom and relaunch the app. macOS identifies commands based on the names of their respective menu items. This means that the name you type should match the menu entry's name in the currently selected application language. Changing languages thus necessitates setting the shortcuts all over again according to the new command names, such as Abfrage aus Auswahl in German. For the same reason, any command changing names will answer to your shortcut only under the name you typed. Keys assigned to the Auto Code… command no longer function when multiple lenses capable of auto coding are enabled simultaneously, because the menu then offers Auto Code with Hedges… and similar commands instead.

There are three windows for looking up a term in LemmaLoom, contacting the developer, and citing LemmaLoom. Two of them can be found in the Help menu and one in the LemmaLoom menu: Command What it opens Help ▸ Glossary Short definitions of the terms and labels in LemmaLoom, with a search field Help ▸ Send Feedback A window for a bug report, feature request, or question, which becomes an email in your mail program LemmaLoom ▸ About LemmaLoom The version and build numbers, citations in MLA and APA style, and the licenses of the components LemmaLoom contains All three commands open an individual window next to the main window. When the window is already opened, selecting the command again activates the existing window. All examples assume the use of the “Climate Debate” project discussed in The example project of ; to practice the commands yourself, import it via File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project.

macOS adds a search field at the very top of the Help menu that searches the names of LemmaLoom’s commands in the menus. If you were to search something like activity, then Activity would appear among the suggestions in the search result. Hovering the mouse pointer over it opens the Window menu, pointing to where that command exists. ⌘? (⇧⌘/ on US keyboards) brings up this search field in the Help menu. The Help menu, with the macOS search field above the Glossary and Send Feedback commands.

The Glossary defines the vocabulary used in qualitative analysis, such as code, segment, and memo, as well as labels employed in grammar analysis. NNS is an example of a label that marks plural nouns, while nsubj marks the noun that acts as the subject of a clause. It also covers explanations for the statistics shown in the inspector and abbreviations in the status bar and diagrams. The Glossary can always be kept open alongside your project. Every entry in the Glossary provides just a brief explanation of what the label denotes. The Glossary is the same for all projects and is always in the interface language. With a German interface, it contains names and definitions in German, and its alphabetically ordered categories will be sorted according to German rules (refer to The interface language in ). Short forms such as NNS and nsubj remain constant regardless of the interface language since they correspond to actual grammar labels used in grammar analysis.

Within the sidebar of the Glossary window, you'll find an item labeled All, followed by twelve other items, which denote the different categories within the Glossary. Each category lists how many terms it contains. On the right, above the entries, is a Search field.

Choose Help ▸ Glossary. In the sidebar, click All to look through every category, or click one category to look only there. Type a word or a label, such as nsubj, in the Search field. The list narrows as you type. Searching will match any entry name, short form, or definition containing your query. Capital letters are ignored in the search but accents are not, so to find Cramér's V without typing the é, search for cram. Selecting All organizes entries by their categories, displaying the current category name at the top of the list while scrolling. Categories without matching results are omitted. Having no matches at all displays No matches. Counts shown in the sidebar do not reflect the search. As the definitions of entries are included in the search, shorter queries can match unexpected results. Selecting All and performing a search with the query subject returns many results. These results come from most categories. Among them are the function Subject, dependency relations of subjects, the phrase label for a clause (defined as a subject plus its predicate), the grammatical feature Case, and the letter S used in sentence patterns. Choosing another category via clicking narrows the list but keeps the previous query active. Selecting Dependency relations and searching for the same query reduces search results to six. Four of these results are marked with EN ZH (csubj, csubjpass, nsubj, and nsubjpass) while two results are marked with DE (sb and sbp). The Glossary with All chosen and subject typed in the Search field.

An entry is structured into up to four parts: The short form of the entry, in fixed-width font, e.g., nsubj, MDD, or ¶. The name of the entry, in boldface, e.g., Nominal subject. To the right of both the short form and the name is a list of abbreviations indicating in which languages the current entry applies. The abbreviations are EN for English, DE for German, and ZH for Chinese; if there isn’t a particular language indicated, that means it is applicable to all three languages. Lastly, the definition follows the name in plain text. Definitions tend to be examples for tags and relations. The definition for nsubj, for instance, reads she in she runs, meaning that the nominal subject she appears in the clause she runs. Under Morphology, each grammatical feature’s value provides the exact string returned as part of grammar analysis, e.g., Number=Plur, and then the grammatical term describing it, Plural. The grammatical feature itself, Number, has its own entry, with a definition, above the values. There are special entries that denote something that the lenses provided in LemmaLoom automatically annotate. Such an entry shows its short form, or its name when it has no short form, in that lens’s color and style so that you can link that color directly with a concept you might see highlighted within text in the reader. Hover the mouse pointer over the colored word to reveal the name of that particular lens. If you customize the color or style of a lens aspect within the Lenses pane of Settings, then the coloring changes to reflect that customization (see The Lenses pane in ). The Glossary with Dependency relations chosen and the mouse pointer on the short form acl, with its tooltip Grammatical function. Short forms, names, and definitions are selectable individually and copiable via ⌘C. The Glossary with Dependency relations chosen and subject typed in the Search field, showing six entries and the languages they apply to.

Help ▸ Send Feedback launches the window where you compose either a bug report, feature request, or question for the developer. Compose Email takes the content you composed and turns it into an email addressed to info@lemmaloom.app in your mail program.

Choose Help ▸ Send Feedback. At the top of the window, click the kind of message (Bug report, Feature request, Question, or Other). The window opens with Bug report chosen. Type your message in the box under Message. Reporting a problem usefully suggests what to include. Leave Include system information selected to add the details shown on the line below it, or deselect it to leave them out. Click Compose Email. In your mail program, attach any screenshots and send the email. The window closes when either the Compose Email or Cancel button is clicked; upon opening again, it is blank. When unsure whether your mail program's setup works properly, copy a lengthy message (⌘A, then ⌘C) prior to pressing the Compose Email button. When the message is empty or contains only blanks, the Compose Email button gets disabled and displays the tooltip Message is empty. The Send Feedback window with Bug report chosen, a message about “Heat Wave Report 2024” typed, and Include system information selected.

The subject line indicates what sort of email this is.
