If you deselect the checkbox, the line fades. LemmaLoom adds only the separator and these lines, and each can be deleted from the draft prior to sending it.

t: If the mail program does not open
b: Compose Email opens a new message in the default email application on your computer. The default email application is selected in Mail, under Mail ▸ Settings…, General, in the Default email reader menu. If Mail is your default email application and has no account yet, it asks you to add one. If you are using a webmail service to compose emails, then copy the body of your feedback from the Send Feedback window (⌘A, then ⌘C), open a new blank email through your webmail provider, and paste your feedback into the new email. Then send your message to info@lemmaloom.app, which you may also copy from the bottom left corner of the window. Type the line of system information into the email as the window shows it.
A very helpful bug report contains the detailed steps that led to the problem.

Often, a quick test will solve your issue or point you in the right direction: Hover the mouse pointer over a disabled button. If the button is part of LemmaLoom's windows or dialogs, its tooltip explains why the button is currently disabled (see Conventions in ). This is typically because the command needs to wait for something to complete first, like indexing the document, before proceeding. If a document fails indexing, a red warning triangle will appear next to the document name in the navigation sidebar. Hovering the mouse pointer over the warning triangle reveals the problem, after which you may right-click on the document and select Retry Indexing (see When indexing fails in ). Quit LemmaLoom completely, reopen it, and try performing the action once more. Perform the exact actions on a different document or a fresh project with only one small document. Should the problem be isolated to this particular document alone, say so in your report. Check Updates in the App Store to ensure you are using the most recent release of LemmaLoom.

t: What to put in a report
b: Firstly, describe in one sentence what you had hoped to achieve. Then outline, one per line, the actions you took step-by-step that resulted in the issue occurring. Name the menus, buttons, and fields according to what LemmaLoom calls them. Outline your expectations versus what happened. Please provide any error messages verbatim, copied if possible; else retype them. Indicate whether the issue happens all the time, occasionally, or happened only once. In addition, specify the kind of document (text file, PDF, web page, or recording), its language and approximate length, along with the number of documents contained in your project. Please also include the system information, which Include system information adds automatically. To capture a screenshot of an entire window, you can use ⇧⌘4 and press Space, then click the window, after which the image is automatically saved to the Desktop folder. Alternatively, ⇧⌘5 brings up other screenshot options. You can attach the screenshot in your email client once the email is open.

Suppose that the PDF “Heat Wave Report 2024” from the project “Climate Debate” has failed to complete its indexing process. Here is how a useful bug report would read: “Heat Wave Report 2024”, a PDF document in my project, doesn't complete indexing. The badge on it in the sidebar shows a red warning triangle, while its tooltip displays “Indexing this document failed.” I brought it in with File ▸ Import ▸ Documents. The language is English, and there are six pages. In the reader, everything seems fine except that the table displaying regional temperature readings shows up as individual numbers separated by new lines. Retry Indexing in the Activity window failed once more, after roughly a minute. The result did not change upon quitting and restarting LemmaLoom. All of the remaining 14 documents have successfully completed their indexing process. I expected the report to be indexed like the rest of the documents within my project. An image depicting this table inside the reader is attached. Below the message, four lines show your machine's system information. While reports stating merely Indexing doesn't work may warrant multiple inquiries prior to any actual work being done, this example includes details on what was already tested and that the rest of the documents have finished indexing successfully. This allows the developer to determine that the issue occurs solely during indexing of this specific PDF document.

macOS provides a crash reporter window whenever the software crashes unexpectedly. The window provides a Report… button next to a description of the problem encountered. Any report generated using this button goes to Apple and is forwarded to the developer only if you enabled the option Share with app developers in System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security ▸ Analytics & Improvements. Alternatively, you may send the report yourself: Click Report… in the message. Select the text of the report and copy it (⌘C). Open LemmaLoom again and choose Help ▸ Send Feedback. Paste the report into the message box. Above the report, add a few lines on what you were doing just before LemmaLoom quit. A crash report shows where in the program the crash happened; your lines add which document or command you were using. If LemmaLoom crashes as soon as it launches again, copy the report and submit it via email to info@lemmaloom.app. If you wish to attach previous crash reports from LemmaLoom, open the Console application (inside Utilities in the Applications folder) and locate Crash Reports.

When making a feature request, talk about your research need rather than the control you have in mind. Provide information on what materials you work with, what needs to be found, counted, or compared in the material, and what will be done with the result obtained. Should your request rely on a certain technique mentioned in the literature, provide a citation for it. In the world of software engineering, we call this a User Story, a narrative from the perspective of the user detailing what they want to do. A developer can then digest the User Story into technical requirements and a development plan, meaning you need not worry about any technical specifics.

The window starts with the name LemmaLoom followed by its version (e.g., Version 1.2 (1)). The version number is displayed first, and this matches what is displayed on the App Store. After that, the build number comes in parentheses. Next come the developer information, copyrights, and a line of special thanks. Examples throughout this primer will refer to the project entitled “Climate Debate”, included as the example project. In particular, the Code Matrix example refers to actual codings from the example project; these can be seen by importing the example project via File ▸ Import ▸ Example Project. The rest of the numbers are invented but consistent, chosen to keep the arithmetic simple.

A count is a measurement representing the occurrences of something. For instance, you could measure 20 occurrences of hedges in “Radio Debate”, or 6 codings of “Urgency” within the “Activists” set. All measurements in LemmaLoom stem directly or indirectly from a count. Share, on the other hand, is the proportion between parts and the whole they are contained within. Shares run between 0 and 1 and are most commonly expressed as percentages. Share measures in LemmaLoom include coverage, Lexical density, the Share measure for queries, and the percentages used in a Code Matrix. Suppose “Costs” codings span 250 characters out of the 5,000 characters of “Running Out of Time”. Thus, the coverage share for “Costs” equals $250 / 5{,}000 = 0.05$, which means 5.0%. Rates are similar to shares in that they are ratios, yet their divisor is text length. Rates require scaling for readability: Here, $h$ represents the count while $w$ stands for the number of words. Dividing yields hits per word, a very small number. Multiplied by 10,000, rates become hits per 10,000 words, the exact scale used by the Per 10,000 Words measure in queries. Take for example “Radio Debate” with 800 words and 20 hedges, and “Let's Not Panic” with 600 words and 18 hedges. This gives: Whereas the first uses more hedges, the second uses fewer hedges but at a higher rate. Particle density calculates rates per 100 words, just like several of the equations used in readability scores. On a scale of 100 words, both rates become 2.5 and 3.0, respectively. It follows, then, that the ranking does not change. If you need to calculate the rate of occurrence for a whole group of documents, you can calculate either the pooled or document-specific rates. Pooled rates take the total number of occurrences divided by the total word counts. Long documents therefore carry greater weight than shorter ones. The rows of a query show these rates. The alternative method calculates individual rates and ranks them against each other. The rank test in Compare uses this method (see Tests later in this chapter).

The logarithm is an expression of the power to which a number called the base must be raised to get another number. LemmaLoom uses three bases: Log base 10 of 1,000 is 3 ($log_{10} 1{,}000 = 3$) because $10 times 10 times 10 = 1{,}000$. Log base 2 (also abbreviated $log_2$) represents the number of doublings involved; hence, $log_2 8 = 3$ as $2 times 2 times 2 = 8$. Natural log, abbreviated $ln$, has $e$, the number that starts with 2.718, as its base, and is the ln button on your calculator. Regardless of the choice of base, the logarithm of 1 always evaluates to 0. A value above 1 gives you a positive logarithm, while one smaller than 1 yields a negative logarithm, provided it is larger than 0. Zeros cannot give you a logarithm, nor can negative numbers. For this reason, some formulas add 0.5 to the count or omit all zeros. In comparing ratios with each other, logarithms can prove useful. “Four times as often” and “a quarter as often” lie equally distant from “as often”, but on a linear scale, the distance between 4 and 1 amounts to 3 points, while that between 1 and 0.25 lies short of a point. Logarithms of base-2 will yield 2 and −2 respectively, lying equidistant from 0: Ratio 1/8 1/4 1/2 1 2 4 8 $log_2$ −3 −2 −1 0 1 2 3 Base 2 logs ($log_2$) are used for the log ratio scale, MI, and logDice scales because one unit corresponds to either twice as much or half as much. For the Log-Likelihood scale, $ln$ is used. Interpretation of the log-likelihood statistic in relation to a cutoff level can be done via chi-square values associated with p-value thresholds (see p-values below). For those calculators without $log_2$ capabilities, divide the value by $ln 2$ after pressing the ln button ($ln x div ln 2$). So, for instance, since $ln 2.5 approx 0.9163$ while $ln 2 approx 0.6931$, then $log_2 2.5 approx 1.32$, indicating just above one doubling.

Many statistics involve comparing what you have discovered with what you would discover had nothing separated the groups. This latter value is known as the expected count. If the activist texts total 4,000 words while the skeptic texts contain 3,000 words, and the word hope occurs 12 times in the former but 2 times in the latter, the values take on the form shown below in tabular format:  hope Other words Words Activists 12 3,988 4,000 Skeptics 2 2,998 3,000 Total 14 6,986 7,000 When both groups use the word hope at the same rate, its 14 instances should be distributed in proportion to word counts. Since the activists' documents contain four-sevenths of all the words, they are expected to have 14 × 4/7 = 8 instances of hope; the skeptics, 6 instances. The expected count of a cell can generally be found by multiplying its row and column totals together, then dividing by the grand total: In the case of the activists' hope, $E = 4{,}000 times 14 / 7{,}000 = 8$. Thus, while the activists have 12 uses, which is 4 more than expected, the skeptics only have 2 uses, which is 4 less than expected. The expected count is simply an average, hence it may not always yield integers. The chi-square statistic χ² sums the squared differences between each cell's count $O$ and its expected count $E$, each divided by $E$: Here, $O$ is a cell's observed count, $E$ is the cell's expected count, and the symbol $sum$ means “add up over all the cells”. Squaring makes differences in either direction contribute positively to the result. Dividing by the expected count allows differences to contribute more to the final score in small cells than in large ones. The expected counts for the other words amount to 3,992 and 2,994, which both differ from actual counts by 4. As such, Keywords, collocates, chi-square tests, the  in Sketch Space, and φ of overlapping codes begin from calculating the expected counts. However, they vary according to what constitutes a row or column. Keyword lists have rows representing two document groups. Collocates' rows correspond to words inside and outside the windows. Overlapping codes' rows pertain to characters inside and outside each code.

In general, there will almost always be some discrepancy between two groups' usage rates of a particular word, regardless of whether there is anything to distinguish one group from another. This discrepancy can be assessed statistically in order to test its significance, and p-values range from 0 to 1 to express the probability of a difference at least this large if the groups did not really differ. If your p-value is low, then the discrepancy is hard to put down to randomness alone. Log-likelihood for a keyword list in LemmaLoom's queries (see How the two scores are calculated in ) is twice the sum of the products of each observed frequency and the natural logarithm of its ratio to the expected frequency. In notation form, this is written $G^2$, as shown below for hope. Note that $G^2$ measures roughly the same departure from expectations that the chi-square statistic does, with differences in methodology and values being fairly minimal; compare 5.34 to the earlier 4.68. At the observed $G^2$ of 5.34, there is roughly a 0.021 probability that a difference of this size or larger occurs simply by chance, when both groups use hope at the same rate. Out of every 100 instances where the difference between both groups' usage rate was zero, you might expect about two instances like this one, so hope passes the threshold LL ≥ 3.84 but not LL ≥ 6.63. The menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 in the keyword list “Keywords: Activists”, with the three cutoffs of log-likelihood. P-values of 0.05, 0.01, and 0.001 are typically chosen for significance; any p-value below 0.05 is often considered statistically significant. The threshold p-value of 0.05 is used by LemmaLoom wherever it shows significance (see How significance is shown later in this chapter). A p-value of 0.021 is not equivalent to a 98% probability that there is indeed a difference. A p-value does not indicate the magnitude of the effect; rather, the effect size is used for this purpose (see Effect sizes below). Neither does a p-value greater than 0.05 show equivalence between the two groups; with a limited number of documents, a sizable difference could slip past without reaching statistical significance. A p-value also makes an assumption that there was only one test conducted. A keyword list runs one for every word. For example, if 1,000 words that show no real difference undergo a hypothesis test, about 50 (5 in 100) will appear to be statistically significant at LL ≥ 3.84 purely by coincidence. More conservative criteria like LL ≥ 6.63 only admit roughly 10 words in the same circumstances, whereas LL ≥ 10.83 admits about 1. Most hypothesis tests require comparing the calculated value against a distribution. The distribution provides the likelihood, for every value of the test statistic, of obtaining that particular outcome when the groups do not differ; the p-value corresponds to the portion of the distribution beyond that point. Normal distributions are used for the rank test for two groups. Chi-square distributions are used for the rank test for more groups, chi-square tests, and keyword thresholds. Unlike other tests, Fisher's exact test calculates the actual p-value of the test statistic rather than estimating it approximately. All arrangements of cells that retain the marginal sums are accounted for, adding their probabilities together for outcomes no more likely than the observation. As such, it remains a valid approach for cases where chi-square distributions are known to fit poorly, specifically those where the expected counts are relatively low (under five or so, by a common rule of thumb). A two-sided test considers deviations from expectations in both directions, whereas a one-sided test accounts for one direction alone. Compare in queries and the Code Matrix employ two-sided Fisher's exact tests. Conversely, the Sketch Space feature uses one-sided tests, which look only for more relations than expected, as does the Multimode mode of the Word Sketch. The specific shape of a chi-square distribution depends upon its degrees of freedom (df). Tables containing $r$ rows and $c$ columns have degrees of freedom equal to $(r - 1)(c - 1)$; fixing the row and column sums leaves only that many cells free to change. Rank tests with $k$ groups require $k - 1$. Here are some of the minimum values for meeting each cutoff: df p = 0.05 p = 0.01 p = 0.001 1 3.84 6.63 10.83 2 5.99 9.21 13.82 3 7.81 11.34 16.27 4 9.49 13.28 18.47 The first row stores the three values in the menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 in keyword lists. These three values are also the usual threshold values for interpreting the log-likelihood of a collocate.

A p-value is a combination of both the magnitude of your difference and the amount of evidence you have for it. Effect sizes measure only the magnitude of your difference, independent of the number of documents. Take the Code Matrix of “Climate Debate” with its columns grouped by Group, which gives two groups, “Print” and “Online”. The first switch, which chooses what each cell counts, is set to Documents (see Grouping the columns in ). Six documents are in “Print” and six in “Online”. “Heat Wave Report 2024” and “Carbon Tax Debate” form the column Ungrouped, which the test leaves out. Two of the print documents (“Running Out of Time” and “Net Zero Will Cost You”) and all six online documents have a “Deadlines” coding:  With “Deadlines” Without Documents Print 2 4 6 Online 6 0 6 Total 8 4 12 The table will yield expected counts of $6 times 8 / 12 = 4$ in the first cell and 2, 4, and 2 in the other cells, respectively. Every observed count differs by 2 from its expected count, and $2^2 = 4$, yielding a χ² of This χ² statistic exceeds the critical value for the 0.05 significance level of 3.84. However, since there are only two groups, the Code Matrix will employ Fisher's exact test instead, which handles very small expected cell counts. The resulting probability value will be $p approx 0.061$. The effect size is $varphi = sqrt{chi^2 / N} = sqrt{6.00 / 12} approx 0.71$, wherein $N$ is your sample of 12 documents. φ is listed in the Cramér's V column. Consider now that your study is repeated on ten times as many cases as before while preserving the same proportion of your counts. Thus you observe 20 out of 60 print documents and 60 out of 60 online documents. As a consequence, your chi-square statistic becomes ten times greater than before at 60.0, with p below 0.001. However, φ remains equal to 0.71 since proportions were unchanged. Effect size Reported with Formula Values Rough reading r The rank test for two groups $lvert z rvert / sqrt{N}$ 0 to below 1 (see Small groups below) 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large ε² The rank test for three or more groups $H / (N - 1)$ 0 to 1 On a squared scale, 0.01 small, 0.09 medium, 0.25 large φ Fisher's exact test in Compare; overlapping codes in the Code Stats facet and in Relations $sqrt{chi^2 / N}$ 0 to 1 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large Cramér's V Chi-square tests in Compare, where the test line shows it as V; the Code Matrix $sqrt{chi^2 / bigl(N(m - 1)bigr)}$ 0 to 1 As φ for tables with two columns; in larger tables, smaller values already count as large Log ratio Keywords See Keyword and profile scores below No limit; 0 means no difference 1 is twice as often, −1 half as often $N$ represents the total number of observations counted by each test. Documents are observed in the rank tests, the presence test, and the Code Matrix. Words are observed in Chi-Square on Counts, and for a table under Compare, the hits in its cells. Characters are observed in overlapping codes when testing for significance of overlaps between codes. $H$ and χ² stand for the statistic values of the tests. $m$ stands for the minimum of either the number of rows or the number of columns. $z$ measures how far U lies from the value chance would give, $n_1 n_2 / 2$, in standard deviations, the typical distance of U from that value: $n_1$ and $n_2$ represent the document counts of the two groups respectively, while $lvert z rvert$ equals $z$ without the sign.

Some tests are ranking-based. That means each value receives a rank based upon its ordering. Four documents whose rates are 22, 30, 30, and 41 would have ranks of 1, 2.5, 2.5, and 4. Ranks of 2 and 3 would be taken up by both 30s; thus, they share the average of $(2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5$. Note how ranks disregard spacing between values. If the maximum rate changes from 41 to 410, its rank remains unchanged at 4. That is why one document with an extreme rate cannot determine the outcome of the rank test on its own.

The Overview facet of the inspector's Text tab (⌥⌘1) provides access to the statistics of the active document once it has been indexed. All statistics are listed according to five sections titled Overview, Readability, Lexical, Syntax, and Structure. Bar graphs of Parts of speech, Functions, and Phrases come afterward. The statistics of Type-token ratio, MATTR, and Mean dependency distance are all displayed with two decimal places, while LIX is displayed as a whole number. Hapax ratio and the shares are whole percentages, while the remaining statistics are shown with one decimal place. Queries provide access to these statistics through the document field Statistic, and thus allow filtering or grouping based on statistical properties (see Finding documents by a statistic in ). Here, words means word tokens; this measure does not account for punctuation symbols or other non-word characters like #, but includes numbers. Sentences refer to sentences identified during indexing by LemmaLoom.

Statistic What it measures Values Sentences The sentences in the document Whole number Words The word tokens Whole number Unique words The different words, counted by lemma (dictionary form), so cost and costs count once Whole number, at most Words Paragraphs The paragraphs, divided at blank lines when the text has any, and otherwise at every line break Whole number Characters The characters of the text, spaces and line breaks included Whole number Avg. sentence length Words divided by sentences Words, with one decimal Dialogue share The share of words inside quotation marks, estimated by pairing them 0% to 100% Questions and exclamations The share of sentences that end in a question mark or an exclamation mark 0% to 100% Sentences per paragraph Sentences divided by paragraphs 1 or more in practice Parts of speech, Functions, Phrases Words by word class and by grammatical function; phrases by kind Whole numbers The first five stats fall under Overview. Avg. sentence length introduces the Readability section, followed by the next three stats under Structure. Counts and Structure in  explain how each statistic works in detail. When analyzing transcripts, sentence boundaries are defined according to transcription, which means that any statistic based on sentences is influenced by the transcriber's choice of punctuation.

A readability formula estimates the difficulty level of the text based on average sentence lengths and word lengths. Which readability formulas appear varies according to which language is used for the document. All the readability formulas follow notation used in . $W$ represents the number of words while $S$ is the number of sentences. Syllable counts are $Y$, letter counts $L$, and letters/digits counts $C$. Three-or-more syllable words are counted for $P$ and three-or-more syllable words without proper nouns for $H$. Longer-than-six-letter words are counted for $G$ while one-syllable words are counted for $M$. Statistic Language Formula Reading Flesch Reading Ease English $206.835 - 1.015,W/S - 84.6,Y/W$ Higher is easier. Flesch's own scale runs from very difficult (0–30) to very easy (90–100); the app's note puts plain English at 60–70. Values can fall outside 0–100 Flesch-Kincaid Grade English $0.39,W/S + 11.8,Y/W - 15.59$ A US school grade (grade 8 is about age 13 to 14) Gunning Fog English $0.4,(W/S + 100,H/W)$ Years of schooling SMOG English $1.0430sqrt{30,P/S} + 3.1291$ A US school grade Coleman-Liau English $0.0588 times 100,L/W - 0.296 times 100,S/W - 15.8$ A US school grade, without syllable counts ARI English $4.71,C/W + 0.5,W/S - 21.43$ A US school grade, without syllable counts Flesch-Amstad German $180 - W/S - 58.5,Y/W$ Read like Flesch Reading Ease; higher is easier Wiener Sachtextformel German $0.1935 times 100,P/W + 0.1672,W/S + 0.1297 times 100,G/W - 0.0327 times 100,M/W - 0.875$ A German school grade, from about 4 for very easy texts to 15 for very hard ones LIX English, German $W/S + 100,G/W$ The app's note puts average difficulty at 40. Below 30 is usually read as easy, above 60 as very hard Characters per sentence Chinese Characters in words divided by sentences, leaving out punctuation and digits Higher means longer sentences Avg. word length Chinese The same characters divided by words In characters, with one decimal Particle density Chinese Aspect particles such as 了, the particles 的, 地, and 得, and classifiers such as 个, for every 100 words One decimal In Readability in , the various formulas calculate readability scores for a passage of three sentences. In this passage, the grade level predictions range from 2.4 in ARI to 8.8 in SMOG. The weight given to word length and sentence length differs per formula. While SMOG and Gunning Fog count only polysyllabic words (three or more syllables), the ARI and Coleman-Liau count letters, whereas the Flesch formulas measure the total number of syllables. Comparing multiple documents requires applying the formula consistently across all of them. The calculation of syllables occurs by grouping vowels; thus, warned counts as two syllables despite being pronounced with one syllable (see Letters, characters, and syllables in ). This averages out when measuring large amounts of text, but smaller texts may experience bias because of it. Additionally, the formulas assume written text; transcripts like “Radio Debate” show biases due to shorter sentences by individual participants.

The Lexical section analyzes the variety of vocabulary, the proportion of content words, and average word length (see Vocabulary in ). Statistic What it measures Values and reading Type-token ratio Unique words divided by Words 0 to 1; higher means more varied vocabulary. It falls as a text grows, so compare only texts of similar length MATTR The type-token ratio of every run of 100 consecutive words, averaged 0 to 1; comparable between texts of different length. For a text of 100 words or fewer it equals the type-token ratio Lexical density The share of words that are not on the language's list of stopwords, short function words such as the, of, and is 0% to 100%; higher means more content words and fewer function words Hapax ratio The share of unique words that occur exactly once 0% to 100% Avg. word length Letters per word; Chinese documents show characters per word under Readability instead Letters, with one decimal Stopword share The share of words on the list of stopwords 0% to 100%; it and Lexical density always add up to 100% Type-token ratio (TTR), MATTR, and hapax ratio are calculated on lemmas. A report with 4,000 words consisting of 800 unique words would give a TTR of $800 / 4{,}000 = 0.20$. Should 400 of these words appear only once within the report, the report would give a hapax ratio of $400 / 800 = 50%$. The first 200 words of the above report might use 110 lemmas, yielding a TTR of 0.55 since this short stretch hasn’t repeated many instances of its words yet. MATTR circumvents such biases by always measuring the TTR in the same-sized stretches.

The Syntax section appears once LemmaLoom has analyzed the grammatical structure of the sentences (see Syntax in ). Dependency analysis establishes which word, its head, each word depends upon within each individual sentence; for example, adjectives depend on nouns, subjects depend on verbs, et cetera. Everything connects to a head except the root, which is most often the main verb of the sentence. Statistic What it measures Values and reading Mean dependency distance The average distance, in positions, between a word and its head 1 or more; higher values usually mean sentences that are harder to follow Avg. tree depth The average, over all sentences, of the longest chain of dependencies from the root of the sentence 0 or more; higher means more deeply nested sentences Clauses per sentence The clauses the phrase analysis found, divided by sentences 0 or more; higher means more complex sentences Embedded clause share The share of clauses that lie inside another clause 0% to 100% Passive sentences The share of sentences with a passive construction 0% to 100% In We block the roads, we depends upon block one position away, the upon roads one position away, and roads upon block two positions away. This gives a mean dependency distance of $(1 + 1 + 2) / 3 approx 1.33$. Block is the root of this tree and occurs at depth 0, while we and roads branch out of it at depth 1. Meanwhile, the branches off at depth 2, which sets the sentence's depth at 2. For Embedded clause share, LemmaLoom assumes a number of main clauses equal to 1 in every sentence that contains a clause. All other clauses are considered embedded; thus, a sentence with three clauses gives two embedded clauses.

Collocate lists and word sketches measure attraction between a word and its partners using various metrics. In both collocate lists and word sketches, the node refers to the word being looked up; a collocate is any word that occurs near the node. Collocates come from a small window of a handful of words before and after the node, whereas word sketches use the grammatical relation (e.g., the object of a verb) of the partner. All scores in collocate lists and word sketches depend on the following four values: $o$ is the f or Count of a row. This value reflects how often the collocate appeared near the node in its respective windows (for collocates), or in its respective relation (for word sketches). $R$ denotes the number of words accounted for within all windows. For a word sketch, it is the total number of instances in which the sketched word entered into the relevant grammatical relation. $C$ denotes the frequency of the collocate in the text as a whole. In the collocate list of a query, this is the Frequency column. $N$ represents the number of words in the text. The expected count is then $E = R times C / N$. The example column uses the invented figures from The association measures in , in which the word crisis occurs 8 times near climate in a feature of 5,000 words. They are $o = 8$, $R = 100$, $C = 20$, and $N = 5{,}000$, so $E = 0.4$. Score Formula crisis Values and reading Frequency $o$ 8 A whole number. Corpus linguists often look for 3 or more MI3 $log_2 (o^3 / E)$ 10.32 No fixed scale. Gives frequent pairs more weight than MI does t-score $(o - E) / sqrt{o}$ 2.69 0 means as often as chance; 2 or more is the usual rule of thumb for a real pairing. The resulting statistic then looks as follows: The scores are presented in the following contexts: The Collocates facet of the Grammar tab shows Log-likelihood, MI, t-score, and logDice scores for one document. It rounds log-likelihood and t-score to one decimal (36.8 and 2.7 for crisis). Its CSV export adds Expected, MI3, z-score, and Dice. Its window extends from ± 1 to ± 10, initially set to ± 4. Punctuation marks and stopwords occupy positions, and any other word in the window is a collocate. In the Collocates result of a query, you can choose any of the seven available scores in the menu showing logDice, namely logDice, Log-Likelihood, MI, MI3, T-Score, Z-Score, and Dice, shown with two decimals. By default, the score is logDice; the window ranges from 1 to 10 and starts at 5; punctuation is ignored, and stopwords count as collocates. Minimum ranges from 1 to 50, initially set to 3, and the list shows up to 200 collocates. The scores used in word sketches, Code Sketch, and the list of Sketch Space are frequency and logDice only. In a word sketch, $R$ refers to the total number of relations of this kind. In a Sketch Space cell, $R$ stands for the total number of relations of this kind under that code. Under Code Sketch, $R$ refers to the count of relations of all kinds found inside passages coded by this code. $C$ refers to the frequency of the partner in its word class (see logDice in ). The menu showing logDice in a collocate list in the “Activists” set, with the seven association scores. Windows always end at the end of a sentence in both the facet and queries. Windows are otherwise counted in different manners between the facet and queries, which means that the same pair may receive slightly different scores in each according to the same measure. logDice is the safest score when comparing lists from two texts with different lengths ($N$ does not factor into logDice).

Keyword lists compare your target with a reference. Passages Like a Code employs the same scoring technique to compare the words found inside versus outside the codings of one code. In the score calculation formulas, $a$ and $b$ represent occurrences of a word within each side, while $N_1$ and $N_2$ are the word counts of each side. $E_1$ and $E_2$ refer to the expected counts. In Passages Like a Code, stopwords are ignored during scoring calculations. Score Where Formula Values and reading Log-likelihood The Log-Likelihood column of keywords; the weights of a profile $2,(a ln (a / E_1) + b ln (b / E_2))$ 0 or more. Keyword lists keep words at LL ≥ 3.84, LL ≥ 6.63, or LL ≥ 10.83. Common words reach high values easily Log ratio The Log Ratio column of keywords; the rules of a profile $log_2 dfrac{(a + 0.5) / N_1}{(b + 0.5) / N_2}$ No limit; 0 means the same rate, 1 twice as often, −1 half as often. A size of at least 1 either way is a common minimum for a difference worth noticing Score Lists sorted by Score $(w_1 + dots + w_k) / sqrt{n}$ No limit. Compare scores only within one list The log-likelihood of hope (see Expected counts earlier in this chapter) is 5.34. The log ratio is Therefore, the activists use hope almost 4 times as frequently as the skeptics. Raw rates of 30.0 and 6.7 occurrences per 10,000 words respectively yield a ratio of 4.5. Adding 0.5 to each count pulls the log ratio toward 0, particularly with lower counts. Keyword lists consist of two lists. The Positive Keywords list consists of the words the target uses more often, while the Negative Keywords list consists of those it uses less often, with a negative log ratio. Only the words that reach the threshold and occur 3 times minimum on their own side, within the target for positive keywords and within the reference for negative keywords, enter the lists. Up to 200 words are shown for each, ranked based on log-likelihood. For further explanation on how the scores of the keyword list items work, see How the two scores are calculated in . The Passages Like a Code profile is chosen from the words appearing at least 3 times within the codings with a log ratio of at least 1. The top-scoring 50 words by log-likelihood enter the profile along with their log-likelihood values as weights. For more information about how a code profile is formed, see How the profile is learned in . In the score, $w_1$ to $w_k$ are the weights assigned to the different profile words that occur within a passage, each counted once, and $n$ is the total number of words within that particular passage. At least two different profile words should appear within a passage for it to be listed, except when a single word comprises the entire profile, in which case one profile word suffices. The total score of a nine-word sentence containing two profile words of weights 20 and 16 becomes $(20 + 16) / sqrt{9} = 36 / 3 = 12$. Freeze Values converts the first 200 rows of a collocate or keyword list result into a frozen list; for keyword lists, only the Positive Keywords list is retained. All words maintain their scores from the result as weights. A query built on the list can then sort the matching passages by Score in the same way, requiring 2 distinct words of the list at minimum in a passage. See Freeze Values in .

Count, Compare, and Over Time display a selected measure out of five. Select the desired measure from the menu showing Hits (see Measures in ). Measure What it shows Values Hits The number of hits Whole number Documents The number of documents with at least one hit 0 to the number of documents read Per 10,000 Words $h / w times 10{,}000$, pooled over the documents of the row 0 or more Coverage The characters covered by at least one hit, divided by the characters of the documents of the row 0% to 100% Share The row's hits divided by all hits 0% to 100%; the rows can add up to more than 100% when a hit has several values With a document-level key such as “Stance”, the words and characters of a row are those contained within the documents with that value. With any other key, such as Code, they are the words and characters contained within all documents that were read by the current query. With a key set to Position in Document, which is set by Over Time whenever the key is left blank, a strip will be drawn depicting the hits in each document, along with two figures above the strips pertaining to how these hits are distributed across documents (see Where hits fall in each document in ). If the key refers to a date field or Media Time, Over Time draws the chosen measure as a line chart. Figure What it shows Values Range Documents with at least one hit, out of all documents read, as in 5 / 6 0 to all documents DP $frac{1}{2} sum_i leftlvert h_i / T - w_i / W rightrvert$ 0 to just under 1 The DP measure is determined by the number of hits ($h_i$) and the size ($w_i$) of each document $i$, with totals $T$ and $W$. This size is measured either in words or in characters if the query does not count words. A DP value of 0 indicates that the hits were distributed in exact proportion to the sizes of the documents. The highest value of DP that can ever occur is 1 minus the smallest document's proportion of the whole text. Two equally sized documents, where all hits occur in only one of them, would achieve $DP = frac{1}{2}(lvert 1 - 0.5 rvert + lvert 0 - 0.5 rvert) = 0.5$, the highest value two such documents allow.

You may see the base value of a column group by hovering the mouse pointer over the group's heading. Codings will become percentages of the group's total codings; Documents, percentages of the group's documents that have the code; Coverage, the percentage of the group's characters the code covers (see Grouping the columns in ).

The Co-occurrences section of the Code Stats facet lists every pair of codes having overlapping segments in the document, ranked with the highest φ value first. Each row shows φ itself and the number of overlapping pairs of segments, and any pair having a p-value less than 0.05 receives a  after its names. Co-occurrences in a document in  works through the calculation. When computing φ in the Relations view of the shelf, the formula works the same way and uses the characters of all documents in the scope. The table underlying φ assumes that every single character in the document represents one observation. “Running Out of Time” consists of roughly 5,000 characters. For simplicity's sake, this example assumes “Costs” takes up 250 characters, “Responsibility” 200, while both share 100 characters:  In “Responsibility” Not in “Responsibility” Total In “Costs” 100 150 250 Not in “Costs” 100 4,650 4,750 Total 200 4,800 5,000 The expected overlap is $250 times 200 / 5{,}000 = 10$ characters. The codes have ten times as much overlap as that. The other three cells expect 240, 190, and 4,560, so every cell lies 90 from its expected count: To calculate φ, divide χ² by $N$ and take the square root. Here, $N$ represents how many characters were in the document. The p-value was derived from the chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom, giving you a p far below 0.001. With thousands of characters being your observations, the p-value will tend to be tiny for almost any overlap, and neighboring characters are hardly independent. Within a long document, nearly every pair has a . You thus need to evaluate pairs based on their φ, not their . This becomes true to an even greater extent in Relations, since the characters of all the documents in the scope get pooled together. φ has no sign. Should one pair overlap less often than chance predicts, you'd still end up getting a φ above 0, and often a . If “Costs” and “Responsibility” had shared only 2 characters, just one-fifth of the 10 expected, their φ would come out at roughly 0.04, with a . To distinguish between attraction and avoidance, check the observed overlap versus the expected overlap. The CSV export provides you with the former under the Characters column. Expected overlap is simply the characters of one code multiplied by the characters of the other code, divided by the characters of the document.

LemmaLoom reports the smaller of the two possible values, so a smaller U means a clearer separation; 0 means every document of one group is ahead of every document of the other H The same question for three or more groups 0 or more; larger means the groups' average ranks lie farther apart χ² Do the counts of the table lie farther from their expected counts than chance would allow? 0 or more; larger means a bigger departure. In Fisher's exact test, read p and treat χ² as a comparison only G² Does a word's count differ between target and reference by more than chance would allow? 0 or more; compared with the value in the menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 Choosing a test in  sets out which test should be used for each individual question. The menu showing Automatic in a comparison in the “Skeptics” set. Compare, the Code Matrix, and Sketch Space are three different tools within LemmaLoom that conduct tests. The following describes what is tested by each tool: Compare tests documents. When using one Group By key, Compare tests only when the key is document-level, such as attributes like “Stance” or the document's Group itself. Tests available in the menu showing Automatic include Automatic, Rank Test on Rates, Presence Test, Chi-Square on Counts, and No Test. If the measure equals Documents, Automatic chooses the presence test; otherwise, the rank test is chosen instead. The rank test measures each document's rate per 10,000 words or per 10,000 characters if the query did not count words, whatever the rows show. This is shown in more detail in Running a comparison in . All the documents get counted regardless of hits; documents without hits have a rate of 0. The presence test counts how many documents have hits vs no hits, which means you must have at least one of each type for the test to run. Should you specify two Group By keys, Compare will analyze the table formed by Group By rather than individual documents. In that scenario, Automatic will perform chi-square testing only when Find is Documents or any other unit that belongs to the Library group, while Chi-Square on Counts and Presence Test will run the test against table cells. Rank Test on Rates works with one key only. The Code Matrix applies the hypothesis tests to each code separately, whatever the two switches show; specifically, the null hypothesis says that there is no difference between the shares of documents containing each particular code within each group. Groups with No value (or Ungrouped for document groups) are skipped over as part of testing, whereas Compare treats them as a group of their own. If a code is in all or none of the analyzed documents, its test cells display a dash. Sketch Space marks a cell with  only if it contains at least 3 relations, more than what would be expected. Moreover, this difference in frequency must be statistically significant enough that the p-value of the one-sided test is less than 0.05. The Code Matrix of “Climate Debate” grouped by “Stance”, with the columns of the chi-square test after the total.

Wherever LemmaLoom highlights significance, it uses the cutoff p < 0.05, with these differences in formatting for display: Compare prints the test line darker when p is below 0.05, and gray otherwise. It displays the statistic rounded to two decimal places, while displaying the p-value and effect size rounded to three decimal places. Any value of p smaller than 0.001 is displayed as p < 0.001. The Code Matrix darkens the test values associated with a particular code if they are significant (p < 0.05); additionally, a  is appended after the p-value. The statistic and Cramér's V will both display their values to two decimal places, whereas p-values will display to three decimal places, except values smaller than 0.001, which display as < 0.001. Relations marks any cells which are significant within Grid (displayed via a  in the corner of the cell) and Pairs (displayed via a  after the p-value); p-values smaller than 0.05 are also printed darker in Pairs. The Code Stats facet adds a  after the names of a pair of codes. Sketch Space and the Multimode mode of the Word Sketch add a  next to the count within the grid cells. Beneath the grid is a line indicating what this mark means. In keyword lists, any words not reaching the log-likelihood chosen in the menu showing LL ≥ 3.84 are hidden.

When there are only a few documents involved, the rank test won't return a low p-value regardless of how large the difference may appear. Its lowest p-value will occur when every document in one group ranks higher than every document in the other group: Documents in the two groups Smallest p Largest r 2 and 2 0.121 0.775 3 and 2 0.083 0.775 4 and 2 0.064 0.756 4 and 3 0.034 0.802 6 and 4 0.011 0.809 7 and 4 0.008 0.798 10 and 10 < 0.001 0.845 The “Skeptics” set contains three printed documents (“The Models Keep Missing”, “Net Zero Will Cost You”, and “Science Is Never Settled”) and two online documents (“Let's Not Panic” and “Who Pays for the Transition”). Without a shared rate among these documents, a rank test by Group within this set cannot give a p-value lower than 0.083. A gray test line there is to be expected merely from the number of documents contained within the set, even if skeptics in print and online media vary considerably in terms of the frequency of hedges. The numbers presented in the table assume no tied rates between any documents; ties can lower p and raise r considerably. With four documents without hits against two documents with different rates, for example, p is 0.028 and r is 0.894. The maximum r value also depends on the sizes of the two groups. Without tied rates, the value of r never reaches 0.87, and it stays far lower when the two groups differ greatly in size.
These are the definitions shown in Help ▸ Glossary, grouped as in the app.

Analyzer: A module that runs during indexing and adds findings, such as cohesion or rhetoric, to a document. Anatomy: A bar showing how a sentence's words divide among its clause slots, such as subject, verb, and objects. Attribute: Attributes describe your documents; for example author, wave, or rating. Bookmark: A marked passage to return to, with an optional comment. Code: A label for a theme or idea that you apply to passages of text. Code format: How coded text is drawn in the reader: highlighted, underlined, or boxed. Code Matrix: A table of how often each code is applied in each document. Code scope: Whether a code belongs to the whole project, to one document set, or to one document. Code set: A named collection of codes for filtering and comparing. Code Stats: Frequencies and coverage of codes across a scope. Code System: The hierarchy of all codes in a project. Codebook: The codes of a project with their descriptions and how they are used across a scope. Coded memo: A memo attached to a passage and assigned to a code, whose attributes and tags it inherits. Codeline: Codes present in each sentence, top to bottom. Coding: One application of a code to a passage of text. Constituency: Phrase structure: how words group into nested phrases. Custom analyzer: An analyzer written in JavaScript. Dependency: A grammatical relation between a word and the word it depends on, its head. Dictionary: Categories of terms counted across the documents of a project. Document: A text, web page, PDF, or transcribed recording in a project. Document set: A named collection of documents that can serve as the scope of an analysis; a document can be in many sets. Exclude from indexing: Matching text is skipped by indexing, but stays visible in the reader and can still be coded. Form × Function: A matrix of which forms, such as noun phrases or clauses, do which grammatical jobs. Group: A folder in the navigator for organizing documents; a document belongs to at most one group. Indexing: The grammar analysis of a document: sentences, tokens, parts of speech, dependencies, and phrase structure. Lemma: The dictionary form of a word, such as run for ran and running. Lens: A layer that colors or annotates the text in the reader by a grammatical or analytic category. Link: A connection between two passages, with an optional relation and comment. Memo: A note attached to a passage, a document, a code, or the project. Mosaic: Code colors in reading order, sized by segment length. Portrait: A visual overview of where codes appear in a document. Project: A collection of documents with its own codes, sets, attributes, and dictionaries. REFI-QDA Codebook .qdc: A standard file format for exchanging code systems between qualitative analysis programs. REFI-QDA Project .qdpx: A standard file format for exchanging whole projects between qualitative analysis programs. Relations: A table of how often codes overlap in the same passages. Segment: The passage of text that a coding covers. Subcode: A code nested under another code. Tag: A free-form label for organizing projects, documents, codes, memos, and links. Token: A single word or punctuation mark as the parser segments the text. Transcript: The text of a recording, with each passage linked to its time in the media.

Bookmarks: Shows bookmarked passages. Codes: Shows coded segments in their code colors and formats. Cohesion: Shows how each sentence ties back to what came before. Connectives: Annotates words that link ideas, grouped by the relation they express. Constructions: Annotates characteristic Chinese constructions such as 把 and 被. (Chinese) Grammatical function: Colors words by the job they do in the sentence, such as subject or object. Metadiscourse: Annotates words with which writers guide readers, such as hedges and boosters. Modality: Annotates expressions of ability, possibility, necessity, obligation, and volition. Morphology: Annotates grammatical features such as tense, number, and case. (English, German) Negation: Annotates negators and the part of the sentence they negate. Particles: Annotates Chinese aspect particles, structural particles, and classifiers. (Chinese) Phrase: Annotates phrases such as noun phrases and prepositional phrases. Rhetoric: Annotates rhetorical devices found by the Rhetoric analyzer. Sentence fields: Annotates the topological fields of German sentences. (German) Word class: Colors each word by its part of speech.

Ability: Modal meaning of being able to do something. Additive: A connective that adds information to what came before. Adjectival Adj'l: A word or phrase that modifies a noun, doing an adjective's job. Adverbial Adv'l: A word, phrase, or clause that modifies a verb, adjective, or clause, telling how, when, where, or why. Adversative: A connective that signals contrast or opposition. Agent: In a passive clause, the doer of the action, usually introduced by by. Appositive Appos: A noun phrase next to another that renames it, as in my friend, a teacher. Be + adverbial S · be · ADV: “Be” linking the subject to a place or time. (English) Be + complement S · be · SC: “Be” linking the subject to a noun or adjective that renames or describes it. (English) Causal: A connective that signals cause, reason, or result. Classifier: A measure word required between a number or demonstrative and a noun. (Chinese) Complement Comp: A phrase or clause that a word needs to complete its meaning, such as the clause after decide. Complex transitive S · V · DO · OC: A direct object plus a complement that describes it. (English) Concessive: A connective that concedes a point without giving up the main claim. Conditional: A connective that introduces a condition. Conjunct Conj: An element joined by coordination to another of the same kind, such as dogs in cats and dogs. Connector: A word that links clauses or phrases, such as a conjunction or a relative pronoun. Ditransitive S · V · IO · DO: A verb with both an indirect and a direct object (give, send, tell...). (English) Existential 有: 有 used to state that something exists or is present somewhere. (Chinese) Fragment —: Not a complete independent clause. (English) Imperative (You) · V: A command, with the subject “you” understood. (English) Intransitive S · V: A verb with no object; the action stays with the subject. (English) Linke Klammer: The left bracket of the German sentence frame: the finite verb in main clauses, the subordinating conjunction in subordinate clauses. (German) Linking S · LV · SC: A linking verb (seem, become, taste...) joining the subject to a complement that describes it. (English) Main clause: The independent clause a sentence is built around; its verb is the root of the dependency tree. Mittelfeld: The field between the two brackets, holding objects, adverbials, and often the subject. (German) Nachfeld: The position after the right bracket, often holding extraposed clauses. (German) Necessity: Modal meaning of something being necessary or certain. Negation scope: The stretch of the sentence that a negation applies to. Negator: A word that negates, such as not, never, or no. Object Obj: A noun phrase that completes a verb or preposition, typically the one affected by the action. Obligation: Modal meaning of a duty or requirement placed on someone. Possibility: Modal meaning of something being possible or likely. Predicative Pred: A phrase after a linking verb that describes or identifies the subject, as in she is a doctor. Question ?: A direct question. (English) Rechte Klammer: The right bracket: non-finite verbs, separated verb particles, or the finite verb in subordinate clauses. (German) Subject Subj: The constituent a clause is about; usually it agrees with the verb and performs the action. Subjunctive: The German verb mood (Konjunktiv) for reported speech, hypotheses, and polite requests. (German) Temporal: A connective that orders events in time. Transitive S · V · DO: A verb acting on a direct object. (English) Volition: Modal meaning of wanting or intending. Vorfeld: The position before the finite verb in a German main clause; it holds one constituent, often the topic. (German) 了 perfective: Aspect particle marking a completed action. (Chinese) 地 adverbial: Particle linking an adverbial modifier to its verb. (Chinese) 得 complement: Particle introducing a complement of degree or result after a verb. (Chinese) 把 disposal: The 把 construction moves the object before the verb to show what is done to it. (Chinese) 是…的 focus: The 是…的 frame highlights the time, place, or manner of a past event. (Chinese) 的 attributive: Particle linking a modifier to the noun it describes. (Chinese) 着 durative: Aspect particle marking an ongoing action or a resulting state. (Chinese) 被 passive: The 被 construction marks a passive, with the affected participant as subject. (Chinese) 过 experiential: Aspect particle marking that something has been experienced at least once. (Chinese)

Tense: when the action happens; past or present (English, German) Grammatical number Number: singular or plural (English, German) Person: 1st (I), 2nd (you), or 3rd (she) person (English, German) Mood: statement (indicative), command (imperative), or subjunctive (English, German) Verb form VerbForm: finite, infinitive, participle, or gerund (English, German) Case: subject form (nominative), object forms (accusative, dative), or possessive form (genitive) (English, German) Degree of comparison Degree: positive, comparative, or superlative (English, German) Aspect: ongoing (progressive) or completed (perfect) (English, German) Gender: masculine, feminine, or neuter (English, German) Pronoun type PronType: personal, demonstrative, interrogative, relative (English, German) Definiteness Definite: definite (the) or indefinite (a) (English, German) Polarity: negation; not, never (English, German) Possessive Poss: possessive words; my, their (English, German) Reflexive Reflex: reflexive pronouns; herself, themselves (English, German) Number type NumType: cardinal (three), ordinal (third), or multiplicative (once) (English, German) Punctuation type PunctType: period, comma, quotation mark, bracket, or dash (English, German) Conjunction type ConjType: coordinating conjunctions; Automated Readability Index ARI: Grade estimate from characters per word and words per sentence. (English) Avg. sentence length: The average number of words per sentence. Avg. tree depth: Average depth of the deepest dependency chain per sentence. Avg. word length: The average number of letters per word, or characters per word in Chinese. Characters: The number of characters in the text. Characters per sentence: The average number of characters per sentence; a length measure suited to Chinese. (Chinese) Clauses per sentence: Average number of clause constituents per sentence. Co-occurrence: Two codes applied to overlapping passages of the same document. Coleman-Liau: Grade estimate from letters and sentences per 100 words; no syllable counting. (English) Coverage: The share of a text's characters covered by a code, counting overlapping segments once. Dialogue share: The share of words inside quotation marks; estimated from quote pairing. Embedded clause share: The share of clauses nested inside another clause. Flesch Reading Ease: 0–100 scale; higher is easier. 60–70 reads as plain English. Syllables are estimated. (English) Flesch-Amstad: The German adaptation of Flesch Reading Ease; higher is easier. Syllables are estimated. (German) Flesch-Kincaid Grade: US school grade needed to read the text comfortably. Syllables are estimated. (English) Gunning Fog: Years of schooling needed; counts long sentences and words of three or more syllables. Syllables are estimated. (English) Hapax ratio: The share of unique words that occur exactly once. Läsbarhetsindex LIX: Sentence length plus the share of words over six letters; 40 is average difficulty. (English, German) Lexical density: The share of content words (not the, of, is); higher reads as denser. Mean dependency distance MDD: Average distance between a word and its syntactic head; larger distances are harder to process. Moving-average type-token ratio MATTR: Type-token ratio averaged over a moving 100-word window, so it compares across texts of different lengths. Paragraphs: The number of paragraphs, divided at blank lines when the text has any, and otherwise at every line break. Particle density: Particles such as 的, 了, and 着 per 100 words. (Chinese) Passive sentences: The share of sentences containing a passive construction. Questions and exclamations: The share of sentences that end in a question mark or exclamation mark. Sentences: The number of sentences the parser found. Sentences per paragraph: The average number of sentences in each paragraph. Simple Measure of Gobbledygook SMOG: Grade estimate from the number of words with three or more syllables per sentence, normalized to 30 sentences. Syllables are estimated. (English) Stopword share: The share of function words like the, of, and is. Type-token ratio TTR: Unique words divided by total words; higher means more varied vocabulary. Unique words: The number of distinct lemmas (types). Wiener Sachtextformel: German school-grade estimate from syllables, sentence length, and word length. Syllables are estimated. (German) Words: The number of word tokens, not counting punctuation and spaces.

Chi-square test χ²: Tests whether the share of documents with a code differs between three or more groups more than chance would explain; documents without a value are left out. Cramér's V V: The strength of the difference the chi-square test measures, from 0 (no difference) to 1. Cubed mutual information MI3: A variant of mutual information that cubes the observed count, reducing its bias toward rare pairs. Dice coefficient Dice: Twice the co-occurrence count divided by the sum of the partner's frequency and the node's total (the words in its windows for collocates, or its pairings in that relation for word sketches); ranges from 0 to 1. Expected: The number of co-occurrences to expect if the two words were independent. Fisher exact test: A significance test for small counts, used to find characteristic relations in Sketch Space and to compare two groups in the Code Matrix. Frequency f: How often two words occur together: within the window in Collocates, or linked in the relation in a word sketch. Log-likelihood LL: A significance statistic (G²) comparing observed with expected co-occurrence; higher means stronger evidence of association. logDice: 14 plus the base-2 logarithm of the Dice coefficient; its maximum is 14 and it compares well across corpora of different sizes. Mutual information MI: The base-2 logarithm of observed over expected co-occurrence: how much more often two words meet than by chance. p-value p: The probability of an association at least this strong arising by chance; smaller values are stronger evidence. Phi coefficient φ: The strength of association between two codes, from 0 to 1, computed from how their passages overlap. t-score: Observed minus expected co-occurrence, divided by the square root of the observed count; favors frequent, dependable pairs. z-score: Observed minus expected co-occurrence, divided by the square root of the expected count.

Adjective modifiers: Adjectives that modify the sketched noun. Adverb modifiers: Adverbs that modify the sketched word. Characteristic relation : A relation that a code or group of documents uses significantly more often than the rest of the scope (one-sided Fisher exact test, p < .05). Code Sketch: A word sketch whose partners are grouped by the codes that cover them. Collocate: A word that occurs near another word more often than chance would predict. Complement of: Words that the sketched word completes. Complements: Words or clauses that complete the sketched word. Coordinated with: Words joined to the sketched word by and, or, and similar conjunctions. In compounds with: Words that form compounds with the sketched word. Modifiers: In Sketch Space, all modifying relations combined: Adjective modifiers, Adverb modifiers, and Modifies. Modifies: Words that the sketched word modifies. Object of: Verbs that take the sketched noun as their object. Objects: Nouns that act as the object of the sketched verb. Prepositional phrases: Prepositional phrases attached to the sketched word, grouped by preposition. Sketch Space: A comparison of a word's grammatical partners across codes or groups of documents, marking the relations that are characteristic of each. Subject of: Verbs that take the sketched noun as their subject. Subjects: Nouns that act as the subject of the sketched verb. Word Sketch: A one-page summary of a word's grammatical partners, grouped by relation and ranked by logDice.

Absolute phrase: A noun + participle standing apart from the main clause, zooming in on one detail. (English) Anaphora: Consecutive sentences opening with the same words, building rhythm and insistence through repetition. Appositive: A noun phrase set beside another to rename it, adding information without spending a whole clause. Attitude marker: Signals the writer's stance toward the content (unfortunately, remarkably). Booster: Closes down doubt; commits the writer fully (clearly, certainly). Cohesion check: The known to new contract; each sentence should open on familiar ground. Connective: Steers the reader between ideas (however, therefore, meanwhile). Correlative pair: Paired conjunctions that throw extra weight onto the joined elements. Demonstrative tie: The theme points back with a demonstrative, such as this or these. Engagement: Pulls the reader in directly (you, we, consider, imagine). Final particle: Sentence-final stance marker (吗, 呢, 吧, 啊). (Chinese) Focus construction: there-transformations, what-clefts, and it-clefts that reshape the sentence to drop new information into the stress position. Fronted opener: Opens with an adverbial or participial phrase instead of the subject, setting the scene before the actor arrives. Hedge: Softens a claim; opens space for doubt (perhaps, may, suggests). Modal particle: Tones the utterance toward the listener (ja, doch, eben, halt). (German) New topic: The theme does not tie back to the two sentences before, or the sentence has no theme at all; a possible break in cohesion. Nominalization: An action packaged as a noun (decide -> decision). Hides who is doing what and stacks abstractions; unpack to recover a live verb. Opening: The first sentence of the document, which has nothing earlier to tie back to. Parallelism: Coordinated elements built to the same grammatical shape (a tricolon, a balanced pair) so the form carries the meaning. Passive voice: The doer slips out of subject position, foregrounding the receiver. Periodic sentence: The main verb arrives late, after stacked modifiers, holding the reader in suspension until the clause resolves. (English, German) Possessive tie: The theme refers back with a possessive, such as its or their. Power word: A superlative or intensified word that seizes the stress and turns a fact into an arguable claim. Pronoun tie: The sentence's theme refers back with a pronoun to something already mentioned. Question / command: A shift out of plain statement; a question that pulls the reader in, an imperative that addresses them directly. Repeated word: The theme repeats a content word from the previous sentences. Zero anaphora: The subject is left out and understood from the previous sentence; common in Chinese. (Chinese)

Adverbial ADV: In sentence patterns, a required adverbial such as a place or time after be. (English) American Psychological Association APA: A citation style. Chinese Treebank CTB: The Chinese scheme used for fine-grained tags and phrase labels. (Chinese) Collocation window ± n: How many token positions on each side of a word, within its sentence, count as nearby when finding collocates. Comma-separated values CSV: A plain-text table format that spreadsheets open. Digital Object Identifier DOI: A permanent identifier for a publication. Direct object DO: In sentence patterns, the noun phrase directly affected by the verb. (English) Form of be be: In sentence patterns, any form of the verb be. (English) Implied subject (You): In sentence patterns, the unstated subject of a command. (English) Indirect object IO: In sentence patterns, the recipient or beneficiary of the action. (English) Linking verb LV: In sentence patterns, a verb such as seem or become that links the subject to a description. (English) Modern Language Association MLA: A citation style. Object complement OC: In sentence patterns, a phrase that describes the object, as in they elected her president. (English) Paragraph ¶: Paragraph number, as shown in the reader's status bar and locators. Penn Treebank PTB: The fine-grained English tagset and phrase labels. (English) Portable Document Format PDF: A document format; exported graphics are vector PDFs, and PDFs can be imported as documents. Portable Network Graphics PNG: A bitmap image format used for exported graphics. Qualitative data analysis QDA: Analysis of non-numerical material such as texts and recordings, usually by coding passages. Regular expression regex: A text pattern; used to exclude matching text from indexing and to match text in queries. Root ROOT: The head of the whole sentence in a dependency tree. Sentence S: Sentence number, as shown in the reader's status bar. Stuttgart-Tübingen Tagset STTS: The fine-grained German tagset. (German) Subject S: In sentence patterns, the subject. (English) Subject complement SC: In sentence patterns, a phrase after be or a linking verb that describes the subject. (English) TIGER: The German treebank scheme used for dependency and phrase labels. (German) Token T: Token number within the sentence, as shown in the reader's status bar. Universal part-of-speech tags UPOS: The part-of-speech tags of Universal Dependencies, the same for every language. Verb V: In sentence patterns, the main verb. (English) Web address URL: The address of a web page.
